How many planes through a given line can cut the face in a way that adds a line through a specified singular point. An effective form of Bertini's old-style genericity theorem.

Behind the bound sits a factorization method for two-variable math rules due to Kaltofen, presented under relaxed hypotheses. Applied to Artin's conjecture, the tool set confirms it for degree seven and degree eleven forms whenever the residue field is large enough. Improving on bounds due to Wooley.
arxiv-2509-00292:
Zhongwei Shen, working alone, studies boundary value problems for the magnetic Laplacian in semiclassical analysis in 2025. The magnetic Laplacian adds a magnetic potential to the classic Laplacian operator. A small parameter, h, marks the semiclassical regime, where quantum effects are present but close to classical behavior.

Shen treats both Neumann and Dirichlet boundary problems for the zero equation in a bounded Lipschitz domain, whose boundary may have corners. When the magnetic field has finite type on the domain, he proves maximal function estimates for the solution's gradient-like term, uniform for small h. The result extends a classic Jerison and Kenig theorem for the plain Laplacian. It is new even for smooth domains.
arxiv-2509-00392:
Oliver Goertsches and Grigory Solomadin prove in 2025 that certain GKM graphs extend to torus graphs. GKM theory studies spaces with torus actions, which are symmetries by a donut-shaped group, through a labeled graph that encodes fixed points and their links. Realizable Hamiltonian and complexity one graphs arise from manifolds with extra structure.

The extension problem is recast through a representation of the graph's fundamental group, using a coordinate-free form of Kuroki's axial function group. Covers of GKM graphs and acyclicity results for orbit spaces complete the argument. Both the Hamiltonian and the complexity one cases extend as claimed. The result ties graph data more tightly to the geometry of the underlying spaces.
arxiv-2509-00492:
Liesbet Van der Perre leads a team of eight authors on sub-terahertz wireless. These are radio links at very high frequency. They offer wide bandwidth for fast access. They also promise sharp location sensing. But loss and blocking make them hard to deploy well.

The team sends radio signals over polymer microwave fibers. These plastic guides link small radio units in a chain. Each unit sits near its users. That cuts path loss and blocking. A second system at lower frequency gives control signals. It also acts as a backup if the fast link fails. The paired design aims at cheap, low-energy links that work in real time.
arxiv-2509-00692:
Yusen Peng and one co-author, Alper Yilmaz, propose CascadeFormer for skeleton-based human action recognition, identifying actions in video from sequences of joint coordinates. Graph convolutional networks have dominated this field because skeleton data has a natural space-time structure, but transformers with masked pretraining open new options.

CascadeFormer is a family of two-stage cascading transformers. A masked pretraining stage first learns general skeleton representations by hiding and reconstructing parts of the input, then a cascading fine-tuning stage adapts the model for action classification. Peng and Yilmaz evaluate the family on three benchmarks, Penn Action, N-UCLA, and NTU RGB+D 60, achieving competitive performance throughout, and they release code and model checkpoints.
arxiv-2509-00792:
Yorick Herrmann leads six authors in total, with Connor Hill, Merlin Phillips, Daniel Flores, Steven J Miller, and Steven Senger, on sets where sums outnumber differences. A More Sums Than Differences set has a larger sumset than difference set, which is surprising because subtraction is not commutative and was expected to give more outcomes.

Martin and O'Bryant proved a small positive percentage of sets have this property. Herrmann and his co-authors ask what extra structure a chain of such sets can have, and construct sequences alternating between sum-dominated and difference-dominated sets, each properly containing the previous one. Their first constructions fill in all missing elements between minimum and maximum, while the last is more involved and prohibits adding any such elements.
arxiv-2509-00892:
Huanbiao Zhu leads four authors in total, with Andrea Carlo Marini, Mikael Kuusela, and Larry Wasserman, on response matrix estimation in unfolding differential cross sections. Unfolding infers a true particle spectrum from detector-smeared observations, an ill-posed inverse problem where small changes in smeared data can cause large fluctuations in the answer.

The response matrix models detector response and is usually estimated by binning simulated events and counting movement between bins, which can be noisy with small samples. Surprisingly, that noise can inadvertently regularize the problem. Zhu and his co-authors propose estimating the response through conditional density estimation of the response kernel in the unbinned setting, then binning the estimator, and compare both approaches in simulations.
arxiv-2509-01092:
Retrieval-augmented generation feeds a language model with passages pulled from outside sources, but long inputs slow replies and fill memory. Xiaoqiang Lin, with four co-authors, argues that most of that retrieved text is not needed for a given question. Their system, REFRAG, rethinks how decoding handles such context.

Retrieved passages often differ widely from each other, so attention patterns form blocks rather than one rich web. Lin and the team use that fact to cut needless computation during decoding, keeping the useful parts. The goal is faster replies and lower memory use with little loss in quality. The work targets a core cost problem for systems that answer from large document collections.
arxiv-2509-01292:
Composites, sums or weighted mixes of variables, appear across behavioral research as indices, inventories, and formative constructs. Jorg Henseler, with four co-authors, reviews how structural equation modeling handles such composites and finds limits in current practice. Those limits include failing to model how a composite is formed, and being unable to estimate its weights or place it freely in a model.

The team proposes two new specifications. One joins a refined composite setup with phantom variables and treats inverse weights as free parameters. The other blends that setup with a pseudo-indicator approach and frees all but one indicator weight. Together they aim to let researchers model composite creation directly, estimate weights, and test whether a composite fully carries the effects of its parts.
arxiv-2509-01692:
Frederic Galliano leads twenty-seven co-authors in laying out science cases for the PRIMA far infrared probe. Dust grains shape how galaxies grow, yet their traits and life cycle stay poorly known. PRIMA would bring sharp sensitivity across the full far infrared range and smooth spectra across a wide band. The authors center their cases on nearby galaxies, where detail is easier to see.

Planned views would catch the faint glow of spread out gas and dust, even in galaxies poor in heavy elements. Solid state marks in the spectra could reveal what the grains are made of. Pairing dust light with gas lines in the same views adds more power. The cases could fit into a few large observing programs.
arxiv-2509-01992:
Priyanshu Raj, Sourav Mal, Rana Saha, and Prasenjit Sen stack two thin sheets to join a magnet with an electric charge effect. One sheet is a magnet that works at room heat. The other sheet can hold an electric charge pattern. Weak forces hold the stack of thin sheets in place. Such stacks may one day serve in low power spin based chips.

The team slips iron atoms into the gap in the stack of sheets. That step makes the magnet grip its out of plane aim near ten times more strongly. Charge can shift at the join and tune the electric pattern in step. First-principles calculations back the claims the team makes. The join thus gives a way to steer both orders at once.
arxiv-2509-02192:
Khalid Daud Khattak and Muhammad A Choudhry select optimal phasor measurement unit placements for neural fault diagnosis in power grids. Phasor units record synchronized voltage and current waves across the network. Too many units cost too much, too few blind the diagnosis system. Their forward selection algorithm ranks candidate spots with a cross validated classifier, then refines picks by neighborhood search.

The chosen minimal set feeds a one dimensional convolutional network that locates faulted lines and classifies fault types. Tests on two standard feeder systems show top overall network performance from the minimal configuration. Fault location and type accuracies both land in the high nineties on the smaller system. Slightly lower location accuracy holds on the larger, harder system.
arxiv-2509-02292:
Katharine Kowalyshyn and Matthias Scheutz present a 2025 study of whether large language models, the AI systems behind chatbots, can track what team members jointly understand during dialogue. Their test material comes from the Cooperative Remote Search Task corpus, where people work together on a shared search job.

The method runs in two stages. First, a model labels parts of each conversation that show shared mental models, the overlap in what teammates think. Next, a second model compares those labels with human labels and a gold standard to flag gaps. Across six dialogues, the models looked steady on plain wording tasks. They failed more often when answers needed spatial reasoning or tone cues, which limits trust in them as team monitors.
arxiv-2509-02592:
Hunter Gittlin wrote a 2025 solo machine learning paper. It argues that class imbalance is better handled by threshold choices than by fake data. Class imbalance means one outcome dwarfs the other in training data. Synthetic oversampling can create new problems of its own.

The proposed fix sets a distinct threshold for each demographic group. Across experiments, group-aware thresholds beat models trained with SMOTE or CT-GAN synthetic data. Balanced accuracy rose. Worst-group scores improved too. A single global threshold cannot trade these goals as finely. Adding group thresholds on top of synthetic data gained almost nothing. So the two fixes overlap. Results held across seven model families. They span linear models through boosting.
arxiv-2509-02692:
Elena Tomasetti and eight co-authors wrote a 2025 astronomy paper using the oldest Milky Way stars as cosmic clocks. Robust ages for individual stars, measured without assuming a cosmology, can set a floor on the age of the universe and a ceiling on its expansion rate.

Starting from a Gaia-based catalogue, the team selects thousands of old, precisely dated stars near the main sequence turn-off, then applies strict quality cuts. A final sample of about one hundred sixty trustworthy stars remains, the largest of its kind. Their ages peak near thirteen and a half billion years. Allowing a short formation delay gives a lower bound on the universe's age close to the standard value. No star's age forces an older universe beyond the stated limits, and ages below thirteen billion years clash with the data.
arxiv-2509-03192:
D. Canillas Martínez and 5 co-authors studied collisions between Q-balls in a 2025 field theory paper. A Q-ball is a stable lump of a charged field that holds itself together. In the thin-wall regime, where the lump's edge is sharp compared with its size, smashing a Q-ball into its antimatter twin shows chaotic behavior.

The authors explain that chaos through resonant energy transfer, energy sloshing into internal vibration modes of the lumps. Short-lived intermediate states steer what happens next. One is a bubble of a false broken vacuum, a patch of the wrong ground state, which governs annihilation. Another is the charged oscillon, a long-pulsing localized wave. Excited massless modes can press on the bubble's walls and keep it alive far longer than expected.
arxiv-2509-03392:
Xinyue Chen and 4 co-authors examined how much AI help note-takers actually benefit from in a 2025 experiment. AI tools now sit inside cognitively demanding tasks, but help that does the thinking may quietly reduce engagement. The authors call this tension the AI Assistance Dilemma.

Thirty participants took notes on lecture videos under three support levels. Automated AI produced structured notes for them, intermediate AI gave live summaries, and minimal AI offered only a transcript. Post-test scores were highest with intermediate help and lowest with full automation. Participants still preferred the automated setup, praising its ease and low effort. That mismatch between preference and learning is the paper's central warning. Moderate support, the authors suggest, preserves the engagement that makes notes useful.
arxiv-2509-03492:
Matthew Lastovka and five co-authors forecast what the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could find among exomoons in a 2025 research paper. Roman will survey the galaxy for exoplanets through gravitational microlensing, where gravity briefly bends and brightens light. Its sensitivity reaches down toward the mass of Ganymede, Jupiter's giant moon.

Simulations test how a large moon around a wide-orbit giant planet would warp the brightening pattern of its host. Planet masses, orbits, moon masses, and moon separations are all varied across wide ranges. Roman proves sensitive to such moons, yet expected detections number only about one during the survey under their assumptions. Pointing at fewer fields more often could raise that count. The work also stresses better modelling of events with three lensing bodies.
arxiv-2509-03692:
In a 2025 research paper, Andreas Leibetseder and one co-author examine lifeXplore, their entry system for the Lifelog Search Challenge. Lifelogs are large personal archives of photos and sensor records from wearable cameras and devices. The annual challenge asks teams to find one announced memory inside such an archive, live and against the clock.

LifeXplore combines browsing by day summaries, laid out in time order, with interactive concept filters that can be combined freely. Compared with the team's earlier versions, the tool adds temporal queries, richer day summary features, and usability improvements. The authors are long-standing participants in the competition, held alongside a major multimedia retrieval conference since 2018. Their paper documents how the system evolved and what each round of changes was meant to fix. The emphasis stays on helping a human searcher narrow a huge personal archive quickly.
arxiv-2509-04292:
Qinyan Zhang and twenty co-authors test whether language models can break their own trained habits when instructions demand it in a 2025 research paper. Fine-tuned models often cling to standard patterns, a stubbornness the authors call cognitive inertia. Their benchmark, Inverse IFEval, flips the usual test: instructions deliberately clash with training conventions. Eight challenge types include correcting a flawed question, writing code without comments, and answering counterfactually, against the facts.

Human-checked questions number over a thousand, in Chinese and English across twenty-three domains. Leading models were graded by an optimized model-as-judge setup. Results show even top systems struggle to obey odd but clear orders. Future training should value adaptability beside fluency, the authors argue.
arxiv-2509-04592:
Daniel Corrales and one co-author, David Rios Insua, design incentive schemes that persuade citizens to join colorectal cancer screening in a 2025 research paper. Screening saves lives, but participation lags when people's objectives differ from policymakers'. The authors use adversarial risk analysis, a framework for deciding under an opponent's or counterpart's own goals, to compute optimal incentives under uncertainty. Earlier work on cancer risk modeling and optimal screening strategies supplies the foundation.

A simple financial scheme anchors the use cases. Optimal incentives are derived both for individuals and for groups, whose risk and responsiveness differ. Health agencies gain a principled way to spend incentive budgets where they move behavior most, rather than paying everyone equally.
arxiv-2509-04792:
Home networks may have lost a quiet layer of protection as they move from IPv4 to IPv6. Erik Rye, lead author with two co-authors, examine that shift in a 2025 internet measurement paper. Network address translation under IPv4 blocked unsolicited incoming connections by default, limiting the spread of internet-of-things botnets.

The authors introduce a large-scale IPv6 scanning method light enough for low-resource devices. Their scan reached tens of millions of residential addresses across many networks and countries. They compare which devices are publicly reachable under IPv6 and IPv4, including services often exploited by botnets, to judge the security consequences.
arxiv-2509-04892:
Pions could make up dark matter in a hidden strongly coupled sector. Anja Alfano, lead author with three co-authors, survey that theory space in a 2025 particle physics paper. They use a holographic model of a gauge theory with a QCD-like pattern of chiral symmetry breaking, varying the numbers of colours and flavours and a common quark mass.

The authors identify the light particles, called rho, sigma, and pi mesons, that would form the dark sector. Seven distinct effective theories emerge as worth exploring. Pure-pion theories struggle to produce enough relic density alone, while regions with light sigma or rho states help and remain largely unexplored.
arxiv-2509-04992:
Visualising density changes in fast flows often forces a trade between sharpness and sensitivity. Xiang Li, lead author with six co-authors, propose a directional-ray variant of background-oriented Schlieren imaging in a 2025 paper. The standard technique watches a background pattern shift through density gradients, but the camera focus on that pattern limits resolution.

Their setup replaces the usual background with a concave mirror etched with random dots that reflect light directionally, plus coaxial LED illumination. Synthetic images and jet experiments, at low and high speed, show better spatial resolution without losing sensitivity in their tests. The design also relaxes aperture and lighting demands.
arxiv-2509-05092:
A model trained in one setting often fails when the data shift, and privacy rules may block access to the original training data. Mainak Biswas, lead author with two co-authors, develop a source-free transfer method for regression in a 2025 paper. Their setting also assumes only a few labelled target examples, with continuous outputs to predict.

Building on a contradistinguisher framework, their method CRAFT learns a shared model without aligning intermediate representations. They demonstrate it in two neuroscience settings, including gaze prediction from brain recordings. The approach adapts pretrained models flexibly where source data cannot be shared and labels are scarce.
arxiv-2509-05292:
Automatic tuning of ad ranking replaces hand-set dials at Pinterest, in a 2025 industry paper by Xiao Yang and ten co-authors. A ranking utility mixes predictions for several business goals, and its weights balance value for the platform, advertisers, and users.

Hand tuning is simple to read but slow, unprincipled, and blind to seasons or personal differences. The proposed framework treats each ad request as a state and learns settings that maximise a set reward, learning the policy directly from serving logs. In an online A/B test, click rates rose clearly over the manual baseline. Studies of reward choices and personalisation explain where the gains come from.
arxiv-2509-05792:
A shared dataset for training AI foundation models on particle collisions is introduced in a 2025 paper led by Shuhang Li with twelve co-authors. The set holds ten million simulated proton-proton collisions, recorded as if by the sPHENIX detector's Time Projection Chamber at Brookhaven. Particle physics lacks open data at this scale, which slows joint work with machine learning researchers.

Events were generated with the Pythia simulator and passed through Geant4 to mimic real detector signals and noise. Alongside the unlabeled events sit seventy thousand labeled examples for three tasks: finding tracks, identifying particles, and tagging noise. Files come in a common NumPy format so outsiders can start without specialist software. The release gives both fields a common testbed for studying scaling and transfer.
arxiv-2509-06192:
Splitting data into yes-no patterns with a few building blocks is the job of Boolean matrix factorisation. Ellen Visscher and two co-authors release a sharper tool for it in a 2025 paper. Their Python package, bfact, uses a hybrid combinatorial search: candidate factors come from clustering first, then the best disjoint factors are chosen before a second stage recovers the full factorisation.

In simulations bfact estimates the true rank of a matrix especially well. On real single-cell RNA data gathered from the Human Lung Cell Atlas, it recovers strong signal at much lower rank than rivals. The authors present the package for analysts whose data are naturally binary.
arxiv-2509-06492:
Repairing lost data in storage systems while downloading as little as possible is the topic of a 2025 coding theory paper by Wilton Kim and two co-authors. The work concerns Reed-Solomon codes, a widely used error-correcting scheme. A trace-repair method from 2017 promised low repair bandwidth, meaning the amount of data helpers must send.

Two later improvements are unified here. One skips a chosen set of helper nodes entirely; the other exploits repeated patterns among downloaded traces. The authors compute the exact size of a key subspace, map the trade-off between skipping nodes and those repeats, and give an algorithm that picks the cheapest mix. They also name the helper nodes explicitly. A proof shows the tuned scheme never does worse than classic repair, with a firm bandwidth cap whenever trace repair applies.
arxiv-2509-06592:
MRI scans that look different on every scanner are brought into line by Daniel Scholz and six co-authors in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Scanner and setting differences change image contrast, which hurts comparisons across hospitals and studies. Older harmonization methods may need the same person scanned everywhere, or fail on new scanners.

Their method uses a conditioned diffusion autoencoder trained with a contrastive loss and heavy contrast augmentation that ignores scanner identity. Anatomy stays fixed while contrast is restyled, so a brain scan can be synthesized in a target scanner's look from one reference image. On traveling-subject data it beat baselines on image quality, and on age prediction for unseen scanners it improved results markedly. No fine-tuning is needed for new sites, which suits multi-center and long-term studies.
arxiv-2509-06992:
Kun Zhai and 3 co-authors introduce FedAPT in a 2025 paper on tuning vision-language models across separate clients without gathering their data in one place. Tuning prompts in this federated way is cheap and private, but the tuned models can be fooled by adversarial inputs. Attacked images may then be classified wrongly in the tasks that follow.

The team points to a gap in what clients and the shared model know about classes when client data differ from one another. Each client can build attack examples only from its own few labels, yet the shared model faces attacks tied to labels everywhere. Their fix is a class-aware generator that turns text prompts into visual ones. A global label embedding guides it, carrying class information across clients like a beacon. The result is prompts better aligned across the whole system and stronger defence against attacks.
arxiv-2509-07592:
Simon R. Goode heads a 15-author search in 2025 for optical flashes that last under a minute. The Deeper, Wider, Faster programme watches the sky at rapid cadence, producing huge datasets where machine learning must sift quality transient candidates from noise. Single-detection events, seen just once, are the target, since the fast cadence means they rose and faded in under a minute.

The machine-learning pipeline scanned 671,761 light curves in a pilot study and found two high-quality sub-minute transient candidates, reaching a depth never systematically explored on these timescales before. Multiwavelength data help investigate what the flashes might be. The team carefully rejects false positives: electronic artifacts and asteroids are ruled out, satellite glints below 800 kilometers are excluded, and higher ones are strongly disfavored. The work opens a nearly untouched window on fast sky events.
arxiv-2509-07692:
Chen-guang Zhang and 3 co-authors discuss an anomaly in the nucleus osmium-166 in a 2025 paper. The quantity in question, B(E2), measures how readily the nucleus jumps between its first excited state and its ground state. In osmium-166 that value was found to be very small, far below the values in neighboring osmium-168 and osmium-170, which breaks the expected smooth trend.

Using a new technique called SU(3) analysis and a new explanatory framework for the anomaly, the authors argue the anomaly can genuinely exist. Four results are used to fit the experimental data across the three osmium isotopes successfully. On that basis, they judge a level-crossing or level-anticrossing explanation, where two energy levels swap or repel, more reasonable than alternatives. Nuclear structure models must account for such abrupt departures from smooth systematics.
arxiv-2509-07792:
Christopher Hughes returns with 1 co-author in 2025, conjecturing full asymptotic expansions for integer moments of derivatives of the Riemann zeta function at its zeros. Moments average powers of a quantity over the zeta zeros, and mixed derivatives track several derivative orders at once. Exact asymptotics for such moments are a long-standing test of the deep link between zeta and random matrix theory.

The route starts from a conjectured expansion for a product of shifted zeta functions at the zeros; differentiating with respect to the shifts then yields the moment conjecture. Two approaches support it: random matrix theory and the Ratios Conjecture of Conrey, Farmer, and Zirnbauer. The work generalizes the pair's earlier result on complex moments of the first derivative. As with its companion study, everything is offered as conjecture backed by two independent heuristics.
arxiv-2509-08392:
Traffic cameras have to read license plates through rain, darkness, and motion blur, and the plate is often a tiny patch of the image. Cuong Nguyen and 4 co-authors present VRAE, an image restoration network, in a 2025 research paper. VRAE is a vertical residual autoencoder built to denoise and deblur vehicle images fast. Restoration runs before plate recognition, so its quality caps the whole system's accuracy.

An auxiliary block injects input-aware features at every encoding stage. That guidance preserves general information better than a conventional autoencoder. On a vehicle image dataset, VRAE beat autoencoder, adversarial, and flow-based rivals. Image quality scores improved markedly over a plain autoencoder at the same depth, with only slightly more parameters. Cleaner plates mean fewer misread vehicles in real surveillance and tolling systems.
arxiv-2509-08992:
The 5G core network is now a set of cloud services talking over standard web interfaces, and every interface is an attack surface. Anqi Chen and 4 co-authors hunt for flaws in that design in a 2025 research paper. Access between network functions is governed by an OAuth-based framework. A compromised function should not be able to roam freely, but insiders and cloud intruders test exactly that.

Their tool, FivGeeFuzz, derives test grammars automatically from the official interface specifications. It feeds malformed and inconsistent inputs to an open-source 5G core. The hunt found eight previously unknown vulnerabilities, including unauthorized access paths. One attack, which they name the Cross-Service Token Attack, was rated very severe. The vendor team confirmed all eight findings, and most are already patched. The work shows specification-driven fuzzing can secure telecom infrastructure before deployment does.
arxiv-2509-09192:
Doha Nam and 3 co-authors present ReDef, a benchmark for just-in-time software defect prediction, in a 2025 paper. The task is to flag risky code changes during review. Older datasets often carry noisy labels and often miss the true bug inducing commits.

ReDef is built from twenty-two large C and C++ projects, with defective cases anchored by revert commits. Clean cases are validated through later history checks, and ambiguous cases are filtered with model assisted triage. The set holds thousands of defective and clean function level changes. Tests of code models show diff style inputs beat whole functions, yet counterfactual probes reveal reliance on surface cues.
arxiv-2509-09392:
Simon Leistikow and 8 co-authors describe an open source software system in 2025 for building and studying personalised blood flow simulations. Work of this kind matters for conditions such as aneurysms and narrowed vessels, where doctors and researchers need measures tied to one person's anatomy rather than an average body. Their tool brings scan data and fluid simulation together in one place.

Users can create whole ensembles that vary simulation settings, then compare runs visually and through similarity maps. The system draws on structural and four-dimensional magnetic resonance imaging together with computational fluid dynamics. A demonstration case shows how the workflow helps medical and numerical researchers examine results side by side.
arxiv-2509-09492:
Some binary stars feed each other stably for ages before the transfer suddenly runs away and the pair erupts. Karel D. Temmink and 3 co-authors model that long fuse in a 2025 research paper. Their donors are Hertzsprung-gap stars, caught in a brief phase between stable burning stages. Such systems can transfer mass for a long time before delayed dynamical instability strikes.

Using the MESA stellar evolution code, the team modeled donors across a range of masses and mass ratios. Every unstable case shared one story: a long, slow dimming, then a rapid brightening. The brightening is powered by hydrogen recombination and comes with a sharp temperature rise found only in the unstable systems. Many such brighteners should be visible to the Gaia survey across the Galaxy. The framework also reinterprets two known red nova progenitors. Observers now have a checklist for spotting a binary in its last calm years.
arxiv-2509-09892:
Pankaj Mehta and 1 co-author revive a famous line of work in 2025 and aim it at living things. In the nineteen seventies Victor Weisskopf showed a neat trick. Basic constants of physics could explain rough traits of plain matter. Life, though, never entered his ledger. Mehta and Kondev ask what those same constants say about self-copying chemistry.

They blend physics reasoning with a close look at units and scale. From constants alone they gauge key traits of a self-replicator. One trait is how much growth a batch of chemistry yields. One is the fastest doubling time it could reach. One is the least power a dormant form can sip. The answers fence earthly life in from both sides. The same fences would bind life in any other place.
arxiv-2509-10092:
Julian Geis and 4 co-authors trace how electricity prices will be set as Germany's energy system sheds fossil fuels in a 2025 energy economics paper. Today the marginal fossil plant names the price in most hours. In a climate-neutral, sector-coupled system, the authors expect the deciding voice to become the opportunity cost of storage and flexible demand instead, and they build a method to watch that handover happen.

Shadow prices from a detailed system model, PyPSA-DE, are translated into bids and offers, rebuilding the full supply and demand curve for every hour from 2020 to 2045. Price steps tied to fuels melt into a smoother curve ruled by renewables, batteries, and electrolysis. Volatility rises, yet the fully decarbonised market still clears at nonzero prices in three quarters of all hours.
arxiv-2509-10192:
Raveena Gupta and 2 co-authors compute how electrons and lattice vibrations interact inside silicon and germanium in a 2025 first-principles paper. These twin pillars of microelectronics are covalent and nonpolar, a regime the authors call nonpolaronic, and its spectral fingerprints had not been fully mapped. Many-body calculations with a cumulant expansion go beyond the standard approximation to give particle energies, lifetimes, and the phonon echoes trailing each excitation.

The two crystals sing differently at low temperature: silicon shows crisp satellite peaks at both band edges, while germanium's echoes crowd mainly at the valence top. Heat smears every satellite into the main peak, and doping stretches and squeezes features at the edge its carriers occupy. Mobility calculations close the loop, explaining germanium's lasting speed advantage through lighter masses and gentler coupling.
arxiv-2509-10292:
Is cosmic dust porous, full of tiny holes like a sponge? Alexey Potapov and six co-authors review that long-running question in this 2025 paper. Standard models picture dust grains as solid cores. In cold regions, those cores grow thick ice coats. Porous grains would expose far more surface area. They would wear thinner ice. They would also change how molecules stick, move, and react on them.

The authors sort out what porosity means for single grains and for clumps. They gather lab and simulation evidence that grains grow porous in many settings. They also weigh what telescopes can actually tell us. Their verdict favors taking porosity seriously. Models of star-forming clouds, disks, and even exoplanet skies should include it. That matters most when surface chemistry drives the story.
arxiv-2509-10392:
Carole Ibrahim and 5 co-authors study how to diversify cultural recommendations in this 2025 paper. Recommender systems usually chase engagement, and lists end up narrow. Their service wants to widen what audiences actually do culturally, without hurting core business measures. The team turned to determinantal point processes, a sampling method that favors sets of items that are both good and different from each other.

They built a personalized version that weights the quality-diversity balance toward each user's own tastes. Offline and online tests map the trade-off between relevance and diversity. The paper shares practical lessons for running such sampling in production, and the full code for their platform and experiments is released for others to reproduce.
arxiv-2509-10592:
Es-said En-naoui introduces a new arithmetic function in this solo-authored 2025 paper. The modular energy of a number is a sum. It adds the remainders left when the number is divided by each of the first m positive integers. The definition is basic. A child could compute small cases. Yet the function encodes rich arithmetic structure.

This paper is the first installment. En-naoui develops exact identities for the function. Some recast it with floor sums and divisor sums. Others decompose quotients and residues. Sharp bounds, extremal cases, and symmetry relations appear as well. A diagonal identity is the centerpiece. It ties the function at equal arguments to the classical sum-of-divisors function. An exact test for primality follows, phrased in modular energy differences. Congruences, recursions, and special regimes round out the groundwork. A second part, on analytic behavior, is promised.
arxiv-2509-10692:
A drone handing a tool to a power line worker must be safe, on time, and considerate. Giuseppe Silano and three co-authors build the planning and risk framework for that job in this 2025 robotics paper, centered on a multi-rotor aerial vehicle working beside a human.

Mission goals are written in Signal Temporal Logic, a language that can encode safety rules, deadlines, and human comfort preferences such as ergonomics. An optimization-based planner then computes trajectories that respect the vehicle's nonlinear dynamics and actuator limits, using smooth approximations to tame the rough mathematics. Because human poses are uncertain, a risk analysis estimates the chance of breaking a specification, and an event-triggered replanner recovers online when disturbances strike. Simulations in MATLAB and Gazebo carry the framework through its handover scenario.
arxiv-2509-10992:
Zheng Zhang and three co-authors build a Bayesian pipeline for turning raw radio telescope data into sky maps in this 2025 paper. Line-intensity mapping charts the universe by the combined glow of unresolved galaxies in a spectral line. Single-dish telescopes fighting for that faint signal suffer wandering gains, thermal drift, and correlated low-frequency noise. Calibration and map-making contaminate each other if done separately.

Their method does both jointly with Gibbs sampling, exposing the full posterior over calibration and sky together. The data model follows the radiometer equation, tying noise to system temperature instead of assuming it fixed. A new noise model for the low frequencies avoids fake periodic patterns, common in older treatments. Efficient numerics, including a Levinson solver and a polynomial emulator, keep it affordable. Simulations modeled on the MeerKLASS survey demonstrate the method, which transfers to other single-dish programs.
arxiv-2509-11492:
Anirban Saha Anik and three co-authors describe a fact-checking system in this 2025 natural language processing paper, reporting their entry to the CheckThat! 2025 shared task on verifying numerical and temporal claims against retrieved evidence.

The team, calling their system ClaimIQ, compared two strategies: asking instruction-tuned large language models directly, with no task training, and fine-tuning models efficiently with LoRA adapters. They also varied how evidence was fed in, from whole documents to top-ranked sentences selected by BM25 or a small embedding model. A LoRA-tuned LLaMA performed best on the English validation data, but scores dropped noticeably on the test set, exposing a generalization gap. The authors draw lessons about evidence granularity and model adaptation for dependable numerical fact-checking.
arxiv-2509-11792:
Samir Moustafa and four co-authors learn to look at the terrain a graph neural network trains on. This 2025 machine learning paper treats loss landscapes. A landscape's shape affects optimization, expressiveness, and generalization. High-dimensional terrain must be squashed down to be seen.

The authors give a learnable dimensionality reduction method. It rebuilds network parameters more faithfully than the standard principal-component approach. Memory use is lower too. With it, they study several effects on the landscape. Over-smoothing is one. Jumping knowledge, quantization, and sparsification follow. The optimizer's preconditioner is the last. Architecture choices mattered a lot. Sparsification and preconditioning mattered too. Designers get concrete guidance for building and training graph networks.
arxiv-2509-11992:
Amitayu Banerjee, writing alone in a 2025 mathematics paper, studies how to color a graph so that its structure can be told apart. The focus is the list-distinguishing chromatic number, a measure that combines coloring rules with lists of allowed colors for each point. Earlier work in 2006 gave a general sharp upper bound for a related number.

Banerjee improves those bounds for connected graphs that contain only small complete bipartite graphs, networks split into two fully joined groups, as induced parts. The proof draws on combinatorial ideas from the 1970s and on Menger's theorem about connections in graphs. Applications follow for Paley graphs, Cayley graphs on dihedral groups, and circulant Cayley graphs. The work tightens what mathematicians can guarantee about such colorings.
arxiv-2509-12092:
Cool a liquid far enough and it stiffens toward glass. Its relaxation time then grows by huge factors. Anh D. Phan and two co-authors build a way to predict that change in 2025. They test it on small organic molecules. Propanol, glucose, fructose, and trehalose are the cases. These matter from drug making to food storage.

First, stepwise cooling runs in molecular dynamics simulations. Volume changes mark each material's glass transition temperature. Those temperatures then feed a theory with a long name, the Elastically Collective Nonlinear Langevin Equation theory. It returns relaxation times and diffusion rates across temperature. The numbers match published lab results well. Yet no lab data went into the pipeline. The authors offer the paired method as a stand-alone tool. It can chart glassy behavior before a lab cools a single sample.
arxiv-2509-12192:
Dark matter can drift into a neutron star or a brown dwarf. There it can pile up. It can meet its twin and vanish into neutrinos. Basabendu Barman and two co-authors use that chain in 2025. They bound a hypothetical new particle with it, a Z prime boson from an added symmetry of nature.

Capture inside these dense objects sets the limits. Annihilation follows, ending in two neutrinos or four. Those steps bound the boson's mass and its coupling strength. The authors then weigh the new limits against older ones. Rivals come from the cosmic stock of dark matter and from the chemistry of the early universe. Others come from cosmic string signals in gravitational waves, and from direct searches at particle labs.
arxiv-2509-12492:
Purushoth and colleagues evaluate how vision-language models hold up under noisy settings in a 2025 paper. These models handle tasks such as image captioning and visual question answering, but their robustness when inputs are degraded remains little known. The authors present a full scoring system for that question.

They tested several leading models under controlled perturbations, including lighting variation, motion blur, and compression artifacts. Scoring used both word-based metrics and neural similarity measures based on sentence embeddings, which judge semantic alignment. Across diverse data sets, three findings stood out. The descriptiveness of reference captions strongly influenced scores, larger models did not always win despite stronger semantic understanding, and certain noise types, especially compression and blur, sharply degraded results across models.
arxiv-2509-12692:
Riccardo Zuliani, Efe Balta and John Lygeros tackle a control problem in 2025: how to keep a fast math solver smooth when its best answer can jump. Their focus is model predictive control, where a system solves a hard task again at each step to pick its next move.

They reshape the task with care so the new form is smooth by design, yet its answer matches the old task. A stand-in slope can then guide learning methods that need smooth steps. Tests on a free-time control task and on a rolling-horizon control case show the fix works in practice.
arxiv-2509-12792:
Moritz Heinlein and 3 co-authors improve robust model predictive control in a 2025 paper. Model predictive control plans actions over a horizon while respecting limits, and tube-based methods track how uncertainty in the reachable set propagates. Those methods typically use linear feedback policies, while scenario-based approaches offer more flexible feedback through a tree of possible futures but struggle to give rigorous guarantees.

The authors join both strengths by adding a scenario tree formulation to ellipsoidal tube-based control. Uncertainty ellipsoids are partitioned by halfspaces so each partitioned set can be controlled independently. The new ellipsoidal multi-stage approach is showed in a human-robot system. It aims to handle uncertainty while maintaining computational tractability, keeping the method usable in real time.
arxiv-2509-13492:
Aryan Manafi Neyazi, writing alone in a 2025 econometrics paper, examines the Generalized Covariance estimator, a tool for learning about time series models from their long-run patterns. He asks what happens when the model a researcher assumes does not match the process that actually produced the data, a problem called misspecification.

Neyazi shows the estimator stays consistent and follows a normal distribution in large samples even under misspecification. He then builds Wald-type and score-type tests for choosing between two specifications, and checks them on causal-noncausal models, where effects can run both forward and backward in time. An application to a final energy demand index closes the study.
arxiv-2509-13592:
Youval Klioui, in a solo 2025 signal processing paper, speeds up harmonic recovery, the task of extracting pure tones from measurements taken by a sparse two-dimensional sensor array using a single snapshot. Sparse recovery methods for this task spend most of their time on repeated matrix calculations, which grow painfully large.

Klioui shows that two mild conditions, a uniform grid for the candidate tones and array elements placed on a half-wavelength grid, give the key matrices a block-circulant structure. That structure lets two-dimensional fast Fourier transforms do the heavy lifting, cutting the cost of each iteration by orders of magnitude. Experiments with three standard recovery algorithms, including ISTA, FISTA, and ADMM, confirm the speedups in practice.
arxiv-2509-13692:
Yadan Zeng, Jiadong Zhou, Xiaohan Li, and I-Ming Chen build HGACNet in a 2025 robotics vision paper. Robots see objects as partial point clouds because surfaces hide themselves and sensors miss regions, and those holes hurt grasp planning and obstacle avoidance. Completing the missing geometry is the task.

HGACNet encodes the partial cloud hierarchically: a graph attention encoder picks out the most informative local points and refines features level by level to preserve structure. A multi-scale fusion module then aligns those features with guidance from a single ordinary photograph, while a contrastive loss pulls the two data types into agreement. On the ShapeNet-ViPC benchmark and a real-object dataset, the system set the best reported completion results.
arxiv-2509-13792:
Inder Pal Singh and four co-authors close the synthetic-real gap for spacecraft pose estimation in a 2025 space vision paper. Autonomous rendezvous, docking, and servicing all need a spacecraft's position and orientation from camera images. Pipelines trained on synthetic renders score well in the lab but drop sharply on real imagery.

The team propose the first supervised domain adaptation framework built for this task's keypoint regression stage. It learns representations that ignore the domain while keeping task risk low, using labeled synthetic data plus a small amount of labeled real data. On the SPEED+ benchmark it beat source-only, fine-tuning, and even oracle baselines, matching oracle performance with only about five percent labeled target data, in a lightweight design that fits any backbone.
arxiv-2509-13892:
Gustavo Kruger, Nikhil Sachdeva, and Michael Sobolev test synthetic smartphone data in a 2025 human-computer interaction paper. Real screen time and app usage logs could teach researchers a lot about behavior. Collecting them at scale is costly and privacy-sensitive. The samples also skew by who agrees to take part and who drops out.

As a case study, the team asked large language models to generate usage datasets. ChatGPT was among the models used. Four prompt strategies were compared, crossing two factors. One factor was how detailed the prompt was about the persona and the expected output. The other was whether a real usage example was included as a seed. Detailed prompts produced structured, plausible data fit for some uses. Capturing the full diversity of human habits in one synthetic dataset remained an open problem. Judging fidelity against diversity did too.
arxiv-2509-14092:
Michele Boreale and Luisa Collodi make Monte Carlo inference provably correct for universal probabilistic programs in a 2025 paper. Such programs describe statistical models as code. Ones classed universal may sample from any distributions and loop an unbounded number of times. They also condition on observations, which breaks naive inference schemes.

The authors describe programs as automata-like program graphs. They equip them with a semantics based on averages over infinite execution traces, weights included. A finite bounding theorem then bounds that semantics using only fixed-length finite traces. That result frames that semantics as a Feynman-Kac model. It certifies the particle filtering algorithm against it. Their parallel particle filter, built for parallel hardware, outperformed existing inference tools in proof-of-concept tests.
arxiv-2509-14292:
Ben Holmes and four co-authors challenge a common belief about serverless computing in 2025, where code runs only when called and must start fast after idle time. That restart delay is called a cold start. The usual view says sub millisecond starts need state kept in memory.

Holmes and colleagues argue the real block is the operating system, not storage speed. Current snapshot and restore tools either rebuild state piece by piece at high cost or capture too much state. Memory tools from the operating system also make it hard to load data reliably ahead of use. Their co design with the operating system aims to restore from disk far faster and more predictably. If it holds, cheap disk based starts could replace costly always warm memory.
arxiv-2509-14392:
Vikki Anand Varma and Alberto Scacchi set out theory in 2025 for how stuff splits among coexisting polymer phases, phases being regions with unlike traits. In cells, large molecules sit inside unlike biomolecular phases. In plants and labs, water based polymer phases help pull out and clean such stuff.

What sets the split was still not clear, though the effect is used a lot. The pair use a density based theory that can take any count of polymers plus loose stuff in them. One case mixes two polymers that split into phases, with a third stuff spread through them. Size plays a key role in where the third stuff ends up. The work helps cell work and gentle extraction design alike.
arxiv-2509-14492:
Jiali Zhang and three co-authors propose a platform in 2025 to create and probe dipole condensates, quantum fluids made of particle hole pairs. Such neutral fluids barely respond to ordinary electric fields. Their electrodynamics hide in natural materials.

Strongly interacting ultracold atoms in two components form the test bed. Spin serves as a synthetic extra dimension, and spin dependent forces build a synthetic rank two electric field. The authors predict an atomic analogue of perfect Coulomb drag. Stronger interaction pushes the two spin clouds by equal and opposite amounts. A rank two field also gives distinctive responses to measure. Synthetic fields let tabletop atoms answer questions that solids keep obscure.
arxiv-2509-14792:
Carlo Alberto Cremonini and Ivo Sachs connect Yang-Mills theory with a supersymmetric spinning particle model in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Yang-Mills theory describes fundamental forces through gauge fields. The authors embed the perturbative states of the Yang-Mills multiplet into the vertex operator algebra of a path integral for a world line with two supersymmetries.

Pulling that structure back gives an integral form on supermoduli space, the space of shapes of the world line. With a suitable choice of dual object, that integral form amounts to an extended form of Yang-Mills theory. Projecting back recovers the ordinary Yang-Mills action. The construction also explains, from first principles, why the Yang-Mills equations of motion arise as deformations of the BRST differential, a key consistency tool in gauge theory.
arxiv-2509-14892:
Narender Kumar leads a team of seven authors developing a beam monitor for hadron therapy in a 2025 medical physics paper. Hadron therapy treats tumors with ion beams, so the beam's position, shape, current, and energy must be watched in real time for safe dose delivery. Fast FLASH therapy, which delivers doses very quickly, makes that monitoring even more demanding.

Their device uses a supersonic gas curtain: a thin sheet of gas that the beam ionizes, revealing its profile without disturbing it. Built at the Cockcroft Institute, the monitor was installed on a beamline at the Dalton Cumbrian Facility in the United Kingdom. Two-dimensional profiles of carbon beams were measured successfully. The tests support the curtain design as a non-invasive monitor for therapy beams.
arxiv-2509-15292:
Abhiyan Dhakal, Kausik Paudel, and Sanjog Sigdel automate the first pass of a literature review with semantic similarity in a 2025 information science paper. Systematic reviews are slow, and researchers need fast ways to gather the papers that matter around a new idea. Their pipeline starts from just a paper's title and abstract.

Keywords are generated automatically, candidate papers are fetched from an open-access repository, and transformer embeddings rank them by semantic closeness to the input. Three embedding models were compared for the ranking job. A statistical threshold then filters the list to the plausibly relevant, with no heuristic feedback or hand-labeled relevance data involved. The authors present the system as a lightweight, scalable tool for preliminary research and exploration rather than a replacement for expert review.
arxiv-2509-15692:
Pei Zhang leads a large team that makes speech translation run live. Live translation writes the target text while the speech is still coming in. Most past work changed the model's build to handle the read and write dance. With big audio language models, the team wanted to wake the skill with no build change.

Their trick builds live style training data from the model itself. They cut speech at random points and pair the parts with partial translations. That data, mixed into normal training at about one part in a hundred, bridges the gap between full clip training and live use. Tests show the skill wakes up well. No change to the model or its decoding is needed.
arxiv-2509-15792:
Yi-xuan Shao leads a large team that listened for radio waves from a puzzling nebula, Pa 30. The nebula holds a star blowing an ultrafast wind. It may be what is left after two white dwarfs merged in the year 1181. No radio glow had been reported from it before. The team made the first deep radio views of the site.

They found nothing: no diffuse glow and no signal from the central source, down to tight limits at two frequencies. Its radio brightness sits far below that of typical supernova remnants of like size. If it is a remnant, its blast energy was the lowest yet measured for one in our galaxy. Many more faint remnants may await discovery.
arxiv-2509-15992:
A tiny particle held in a beam of light can act as a heat engine smaller than a grain of dust. Amrutayani Panda and four co-authors study such an engine in computer runs, using a Stirling cycle in both calm and active baths. They drive it with a fast, curved control plan based on a swift balance method.

The curved plan lifts engine output a lot compared with the standard cycle, most of all at short run times. Under strong activity it can even turn a heat pump mode into true engine work. The plan is built so labs could test it with real tools.
arxiv-2509-16392:
Smoothness of solutions is a basic need in the study of diffusion-like equations with uneven growth rules. Hlel Missaoui, Anouar Bahrouni, and Hichem Ounaies define a new class of functions in the style of De Giorgi, tuned to spaces where growth varies with place and size. Under added conditions on the growth rule, every function in the class is shown to vary in a controlled, Hölder way.

As a payoff, solutions of a broad family of quasilinear equations gain the same controlled variation, in both standard and critical growth cases. The results unite and extend older theorems for variable-power and Orlicz settings.
arxiv-2509-16692:
Xavier Lamy and Elio Marconi study weak solutions of a key equation in a 2025 math paper. The equation forces a field to have unit length and no net outflow. Such fields arise as sharp limits in models of layered materials. A long-standing guess says that a by-product of these fields must sit on the lines where the field jumps.

The pair prove that guess for a wide class of cases. Their proof allows rougher fields than past work could handle. Only one borderline case stays open. The result firms up the math behind models like the Aviles-Giga energy. It also shows how rough a field can be while its by-products stay tame.
arxiv-2509-16892:
Jiahe Qian and co-authors link tissue images to gene activity by place in a 2025 biology paper. Spatial transcriptomics maps which genes are active in each spot of a tissue slice. Pairing those maps with microscope images is the goal. Large pre-training can teach a model to bridge the two across tissues and labs.

Their method masks parts of gene names, values, and images during training. It aligns image and text forms in a shared space. Tests beat prior methods on varied downstream tasks. It also predicted gene activity with no task training, a first in this line. Such models could speed tissue studies in cancer and development.
arxiv-2509-17092:
Michelangelo Conserva, Remo Sasso, and Paulo Rauber test whether classic hardness measures predict deep learning difficulty in a 2025 paper. In simple table-based learning, measures like path diameter and value gaps are well understood. Deep reinforcement learning lacks such principled benchmarks, so tasks are often picked by fame and gut feel.

Their case study uses a benchmark called Pharos. Tabular measures gave some insight but predicted deep agent performance poorly on their own. The authors call for new measures that account for representation, not just task structure. Pharos is offered as a tool for building those measures, so future benchmarks can be chosen on evidence.
arxiv-2509-17792:
S M A Sharif and 4 co-authors tackle photos spoiled in more than one way at once. Their 2025 paper deals with haze, rain, snow, and low light, which can all harm an image. Past all-in-one fix tools lean on text prompts or hand-built rules, which can break on new mixes.

Their view is to let the tool infer a hidden code for the harm from the image itself. That code then guides which traits to use, where to fix, and what harm to undo. On many test sets, the method beat top tools on image score. It also ran about three times as fast.
arxiv-2509-17892:
Shoupan Liu and 3 co-authors find black holes that grow scalar hair by a non-linear route. Their 2025 paper works in a changed gravity frame with Gauss-Bonnet terms. In that frame, a plain Kerr black hole is a valid state, and small shakes leave it calm.

Big shakes, though, can push it to grow a scalar field and turn unstable. The team maps the set of such hairy holes and how spin shifts them. A squared term in the frame also shapes which holes exist. On heat terms, the hairy holes win over plain Kerr holes of like mass and spin across wide ranges.
arxiv-2509-18092:
Guocheng Gordon Qian and 6 co-authors let users mix photo traits to build a portrait of a person. Their 2025 method, ComposeMe, takes sets of photos for hair, clothes, and face ID as split prompts. Past tools guard the face well but give weak split control over each trait.

Each trait set is coded into its own tokens for a pre-trained image model. A training set pairs one subject in many poses and looks, to teach clean splits. A joint training plan keeps outputs true to all prompts, even when traits clash in pose. Tests show top scores at matching both image and text prompts.
arxiv-2509-18192:
Lavinia Heisenberg gives a step-by-step way to count how many free modes a field theory truly has. Her 2025 paper works straight on the field equations, not on an action or a Hamiltonian form. The line of work traces back to Einstein, Hilbert, and Cartan, with later input from Kuranishi and Seiler.

She gives the method a clear physical reading and proves fresh results with it. A wide set of cases shows its reach across field types. One hard case is a changed gravity form where the classic Dirac method fails. There the count comes out at seven free modes.
arxiv-2509-18292:
Shuaiting Huang and 4 co-authors let each agent in a network rebuild the full state on its own. Their 2025 paper deals with multi-agent systems watched by the agents themselves. Each agent must track both its own state and the states of its peers, from local data alone.

Their observer has each agent build its own state guess by a Luenberger-style rule. Peer guesses are then tracked by leader-follower accord rules. The team proves the error settles if and only if the talk graph is strongly linked. A fully spread design works when agents join or leave. Two joint location methods grow from the same base.
arxiv-2509-18392:
Neutrino detectors need argon kept ultra-pure and at a steady deep cold. The ICARUS Collaboration describes the cryogenic and purification systems of its T600 detector at Fermilab in this 2025 paper. The byline is led by F. Abd Alrahman. The detector holds four large time projection chambers in two vessels of about 275 cubic meters each. Liquid argon serves as both the target and the sensing medium.

Even tiny traces of the wrong impurities can ruin the signal, so contamination must stay at fractions of a part per billion. The detector once ran deep underground in Italy on a beam from CERN. It was then moved, rebuilt, and upgraded for shallow running on Fermilab's intense beams. All cold equipment was redesigned and rebuilt. The paper covers design, installation, testing, and the start of operation. It was a joint effort of CERN, Fermilab, and Italian groups.
arxiv-2509-18592:
Robots that navigate by language must adapt fast in places they have never seen. Neel P. Bhatt and six co-authors present VLN-Zero, a planning framework for zero-shot robot navigation, in this 2025 paper. Older systems either explore exhaustively or follow rigid policies that fail in new settings. VLN-Zero works in two phases, explore first, then deploy.

In exploration, structured prompts steer a vision-language model toward varied, informative paths. Those paths condense into a compact scene graph of places and links. In deployment, a neurosymbolic planner reasons over that graph to build executable plans. A cache reuses past task-to-place routes to speed adaptation. Across varied settings, the system doubled the success rate of top zero-shot rivals. It also reached goals in half the time with far fewer model calls. Code, data, and videos are public.
arxiv-2509-18692:
Sorting food photos automatically helps factories check quality and watch safety on production lines. Xinle Gao, Linghui Ye, and Zhiyong Xiao present a lightweight vision transformer for that task in this 2025 paper. Full transformer models are accurate but heavy, with many parameters and high compute cost. That weight blocks use on modest hardware.

Their design adds two attention tricks. A window mechanism splits the image into patches and reads local and global context at lower cost. A spatial mechanism then highlights the image regions that matter most for the call. On the Food-101 data set the model scored about 95 percent accuracy. On a second food set it scored about 94 percent. Both came with far fewer parameters and operations than baselines. The authors aim the model at resource-limited settings.
arxiv-2509-19092:
Millimeter-wave links steer narrow beams, and laser ranging data can point those beams without costly radio probing. Abolfazl Zakeri and three co-authors tackle a privacy-flavored problem in that setup: how to train a beam-tracking model when the raw ranging data cannot be shared. Their answer is data-free knowledge distillation, where a small student model learns from a large teacher without ever seeing real sensor data.

A generator invents fake ranging sequences from random noise, tuned so their inner features match the teacher's statistics on real data. The student then trains only on that fake data, matching the teacher's raw outputs. On the DeepSense dataset, a teacher that mixes convolutional and recurrent layers gave the best students. A simple squared-error loss matched the standard distillation loss while needing fewer tuning knobs.
arxiv-2509-19492:
TOI-5349b is a warm planet much like Saturn, circling a small red star every three days or so. Angeli Sandoval leads a large survey team that confirmed the planet for a hunt aimed at giant planets around small stars. Space telescope data from TESS first flagged the dip in starlight. Ground telescopes and two precise spectrographs then confirmed the signal and weighed the planet.

The planet holds about four tenths of the mass of Jupiter in a near-Jupiter width. Its low density sits close to that of Saturn. The host star is rich in heavy elements and a bit over half the width of the Sun. The team notes a pattern: such giant planets around small stars often look Saturn-like. That pattern may hint at how these odd systems form.
arxiv-2509-19992:
Topological insulators protect their edge currents by symmetry, and that protection was thought unbreakable. Ming-Jian Gao and Jun-Hong An break it on purpose with periodic driving, the Floquet route. Their system starts in a symmetry class where first-order topological phases are forbidden. Under driving, rich first-order boundary modes appear anyway.

Stranger still, hybrid insulators emerge: helical edge modes and corner modes coexist, sometimes within a single energy gap. Two gaps can host different orders at once. Controllability is the prize, since symmetry-locked phases cannot be tuned. Floquet engineering turns a static material into a driven device with switchable topology. The result widens the design space for lossless transmission and quantum storage ideas.
arxiv-2509-20092:
Gan Zheng and Ioannis Krikidis wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on wireless network design. Engineers must often assign limited resources under strict limits, a task that becomes a hard binary optimization problem. Problems with higher-order terms and inequality constraints resist the standard tools built for simpler quadratic cases. The paper adapts Ising machines, special hardware for such problems, to this harder setting.

Their method builds on the augmented Lagrangian approach for handling constraints. A Taylor expansion turns higher-order terms into quadratic ones inside that framework. Each round then solves a single quadratic problem, with no extra helper variables needed. They test the method on phase tuning for a surface that aids both data and energy transfer. In simulations, the method beat standard heuristic benchmarks and reached sound performance.
arxiv-2509-20292:
Tuning a particle accelerator's beam line is the practical subject of a 2025 arXiv paper by O. Shelbaya and six co-authors. Their machine is TRIUMF's rare isotope postaccelerator in Canada. Realistic tuning needs fringe fields, the messy field edges at each magnet, included in the optics model. The team computed those effects from simulated and measured quadrupole field gradients.

They quantified the fringe field optics with a method due to Matsuda and Wollnik. That step made parallel tune optimizations possible inside the model. Operators can now re-tune the variable-energy drift tube linac efficiently for each rare isotope beam delivery. The work turns a slow, experience-heavy chore into a repeatable computational routine. It sits at the applied end of accelerator physics, aimed at daily operations.
arxiv-2509-20492:
Certifying that light is genuinely quantum usually demands photon-counting detectors that fail at bright intensities. Eva Racz, Laszlo Ruppert, and Radim Filip design a witness that works with ordinary photodiodes in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their API-listed title frames the task as witnessing quantum non-Gaussianity from intensity moments. Bright beams give continuous intensity signals instead of photon counts.

The witness uses only the mean and variance of the photon number, quantities estimable from intensity moments. A second-order correlation measure can substitute for the variance. Because the inputs are so simple, losses and additive noise are easy to correct. The authors give amplification-based measurement schemes where the witness applies directly. The approach opens proof-of-principle tests and applications for states far too bright for photon-resolving hardware.
arxiv-2509-20692:
Satellites joined the 5G standard in 3GPP Release 17, but real test gear for space links is scarce. Lu Hou and three co-authors describe a test platform for 5G non-terrestrial networks in a 2025 engineering paper. Their bench uses software-defined radio with general-purpose processors.

The platform runs a commercial 5G NTN protocol stack from Amarisoft, adapted by the authors for real satellite operation. It supports two-way communication between a radio-based base station and a user equipment emulator through a geostationary satellite link. The setup follows the 3GPP NTN specifications. Such a bench lets engineers prototype services and check performance before commercial NTN equipment is widely available.
arxiv-2509-20792:
Ved Umrajkar tackles a safety weakness in cheap fine-tuning methods for vision-language models in a 2025 workshop paper. The paper was accepted at an ICCV 2025 workshop on safe and trustworthy multimodal AI systems. The proposed method is called DAC-LoRA, short for dynamic adversarial curriculum LoRA.

Methods like LoRA adapt big models efficiently by training only a small set of extra weights. Those adapted models still break under adversarial attacks, which matters for uses like driving and medical diagnosis. DAC-LoRA folds adversarial training into the fine-tuning process. Attacks grow harder in a planned sequence, like a curriculum. The author argues the curriculum idea is general and could strengthen few-shot adaptation wherever parameter-efficient tuning is used.
arxiv-2509-20992:
When oscillators influence each other unevenly, the whole network can descend into chaos. Jung-Wan Ryu, writing solo, maps two routes into that chaos in a 2025 nonlinear dynamics paper. The system is a ring of Stuart-Landau oscillators with nonreciprocal coupling, where influence flows stronger one way than the other.

Ryu combines numerical simulation with linear stability analysis. With reactive coupling and Kerr-type nonlinearity, chaos grows through shifting growth rates. With dissipative coupling, chaos instead grows as eigenfrequencies spread and coherence collapses, then saturates. A dissipative nonlinearity follows yet another pattern. The paper claims both main routes are universal, appearing across parameter choices. The results speak to networks from lasers to power grids where reciprocity fails.
arxiv-2509-21092:
Online threads about everyday dilemmas reveal how crowds bend individual choices, sometimes in a surprising direction. Diletta Goglia, Davide Vega, and Alessio Gandelli study that influence in a 2025 paper accepted by EPJ Data Science. Their setting is anonymous, spontaneous social media conversation.

The authors measure disagreement within each conversation from digital traces of judgments. Bayesian regression then tracks how judgments form before and after exposure to the group's stance. A linguistic analysis follows changes in how people express and justify their views. The results show anti-conformity: individuals keep the majority's positive or negative orientation, yet diverge from its exact stance. The finding refines classic conformity theory for the age of anonymous online discussion.
arxiv-2509-21292:
Citizen proposals on Brazil participation platform arrive in huge volume and mostly go unused. Credit goes to Ronivaldo Ferreira and 3 co-authors. The platform Brasil Participativo lets citizens submit ideas for public policy. The volume is huge, so much input goes unused. Manual sorting cannot scale, and topics must match official taxonomies. The paper seeks a low effort method that still aligns with state categories.

The authors combine BERTopic, a topic modelling tool, with seed words. Large language models then validate the topics on their own. Early results show coherent topics that align with institutional needs. Little human effort was required. The method could help governments turn large volumes of citizen input into usable data for policy work.
arxiv-2509-21692:
A Seyfert galaxy light curve hides a year long rhythm inside its flicker. The paper is the work of Litao Zhu and 4 co-authors. The galaxy hosts a black hole of about a hundred million solar masses, accreting well below its maximum rate. Long term multi band light curves show flicker like variation. A well sampled g band curve reveals a quasi periodic oscillation of about 329 days at solid significance.

Six optical spectra show variation mainly from flux changes blueward of a set wavelength. X-ray and ultraviolet data from the Swift observatory vary in correlation with the optical. Time lags between X-ray, ultraviolet, and optical bands fit a continuum reprocessing picture. The disk origin interpretation gives the oscillation its name in the title.
arxiv-2509-21792:
Yizhou Zhang, Ning Lv, Teng Wang, and Jisheng Dang speed up a popular training method for language models in this 2025 paper. The method, called GRPO, improves reasoning by scoring groups of answers against each other. Training is slow because the model must write many answers for each question. The authors target that writing phase, which is the main bottleneck.

Their system, FastGRPO, guesses ahead with a small draft model, a trick called speculative decoding. It adjusts the guessing plan to match how busy the training run is at each moment. A second trick lets the draft model keep learning from the main model's feedback, so the two do not drift apart. On math reasoning tests across several models, training ran well over twice as fast from end to end, beating simpler approaches.
arxiv-2509-22192:
Elliott Sutton and four co-authors predict how thick industrial fluids split among the branches of a pipe manifold. The fluids are yield-stress materials: they sit like a solid until pushed hard enough, then flow like a paste. Manifolds that distribute them, in food, chemical, and construction plants, often deliver uneven shares to each outlet. Wall slip, where the fluid slides along the pipe wall instead of gripping it, complicates the pattern.

The team built a one-dimensional network model that accounts for friction losses between junctions. Slip enters through a power-law relation measured separately with a capillary instrument. The model's predictions matched both bench experiments and full three-dimensional flow simulations across many conditions. Slip proved to strongly shape how uniform the distribution is, by changing the relative resistance of the branches.
arxiv-2509-22292:
Wonjun Lee and four co-authors probe the safety of text-to-video generators by attacking them. Jailbreak research tests whether a model's guardrails can be bypassed, and video models had barely been examined this way, leaving a safety gap. Their 2025 method, SceneSplit, accepted at ICLR 2026, is a black-box attack: it never sees the model's insides. The trick is narrative structure. A harmful story is fragmented into several scenes, each harmless on its own.

Combined in sequence, though, the scenes constrain the output space step by step, funneling it toward the harmful region. Extra steps polish the attack: scenes are adjusted repeatedly to slip past the safety filter, and a library of successful attack patterns is reused across attempts. On a standard video safety benchmark spanning eleven categories, the method succeeded at high rates against five leading commercial video models, far above prior baselines.
arxiv-2509-22592:
Elaheh Akbari and 7 co-authors make 3D point cloud generation a one-step task without losing quality. Flow-matching models build point clouds well but need many sampling steps. MeanFlow cuts that to one step by learning an average velocity field, yet its quality hinges on how training pairs are matched. Their method adds optimal transport to choose those matches wisely.

A latent-conditioned scheme splits the work: shape-level transport runs in a compact latent space, while exact point-level matching runs inside each shape. That split avoids costly nested transport in raw point space. On standard benchmarks, generation and completion beat fast baselines. Training and inference also cost far less than diffusion and flow rivals.
arxiv-2509-22792:
Eliza Neights leads a large team reporting the longest gamma-ray burst ever recorded. GRB 250702B shone in gamma rays for roughly twenty-five thousand seconds. Normal bursts last from a fraction of a second to a few minutes. Data came from four instruments in the InterPlanetary Network plus an all-sky X-ray monitor. The burst shows a hard spectrum, subsecond variability, and very high total energy.

Those traits point to an ultrarelativistic jet from a rapidly spinning stellar-mass engine. Together with the extreme duration, they rule out all confirmed progenitors and nearly all models in print. The team favors a helium merger: a black hole falls into a stripped star and devours it from inside.
arxiv-2509-22992:
Serving large models means trading accuracy against speed and cost at every step. Yuanyuan Yang and 3 co-authors present T-Tamer, a general framework for those trade-offs. In cascaded setups, each early-exit call weighs saved time against lost accuracy. Current practice is mostly rules of thumb with no firm guarantees. T-Tamer casts the choice as a multi-stage decision process.

Its main result centers on recall, the power to revisit earlier models. Without recall, no strategy can promise a constant-factor match to the best trade-off. With recall, the best trade-off is reachable in polynomial time. Tests on vision and language early-exit tasks backed the theory.
arxiv-2509-23192:
Fluid equations with rough solutions need error bounds that respect that roughness. Xinyu Cheng, Zhaonan Luo, and Sheng Wang analyze a Navier-Stokes scheme in Besov spaces. Besov spaces grade functions by finer smoothness scales than classic Sobolev spaces. The team study a semi-implicit time-stepping scheme for incompressible flow. They derive precise error estimates in two Besov settings.

One case needs a careful integration-by-parts trick. That trick shifts derivatives onto test functions to tame the nonlinear advection term. The bounds tie convergence to the critical regularity of the true solution. The authors argue Besov tools give sharper, more local error control.
arxiv-2509-23292:
Knowing when to call a tool is not the same as knowing how to use it well. Ningning Xu and 3 co-authors teach pattern-aware tool use to reasoning models. Two patterns dominate: direct code computation, and encoding the problem as a program. A wrong pattern choice can sink sound reasoning. Their two-stage framework first builds skill in both patterns.
