Rewriting the method with a Lagrange multiplier, the authors prove it always dissipates energy and converges globally to stationary states. They characterize its sharp local convergence speed. They also uncover a built-in link between this classical numerical scheme and modern Riemannian optimization, connecting two literatures that rarely meet.
arxiv-2510-19592:
Su Ho Han and five co-authors present DecAF, a training-free way to make multimodal language models outline objects in video. The task, video reasoning segmentation, asks for a mask of the object a text query describes. Their trick is to pose the task as video question answering and harvest the model's attention maps.

Raw attention maps are noisy, so DecAF refines them in two ways: contrasting object against background, and combining information across frames. The cleaned maps become rough masks, which then guide the SAM2 segmentation model toward fine-grained results. Without any retraining, the method beat other training-free approaches and rivaled systems that train the language model and segmenter together.
arxiv-2510-19792:
Tomás Dodds and three co-authors examine how Dutch journalists take up AI tools in their work without giving up their professional standing. Chatbots arriving since 2022 promised faster production and new business models. They also threatened reporters' standing as trusted gatekeepers. The study draws on thirteen interviews with editors, journalists, and innovation managers across Dutch outlets.

The authors name the pattern controlled change. Newsrooms adopt AI on their own terms, ahead of pressure rather than under it. Three habits recur. Outlets write adaptive guidelines that tie AI use to ethical codes. They test the tools to judge where the tools are truly needed. And they assess, with a critical eye, what the systems can and cannot do. Reporters, the paper argues, are managing the technology rather than being displaced by it.
arxiv-2510-19892:
Nishant Balepur, Dang Nguyen, and Dayeon Ki propose judging multimodal language models by making them play Dixit, the picture-card game of inventive captions. In Dixit a player writes a clue meant to fool some opponents but not all, demanding creativity, social reading, and visual understanding at once, under fixed objective rules. Static benchmarks test skills separately, and pairwise judging is subjective and gameable.

Five multimodal models played the game, and their win-rate rankings matched their rankings on popular benchmarks exactly, validating the method. Games against humans then exposed differences in strategy and concrete weaknesses in model reasoning. The authors argue game-based evaluation gives a holistic, harder-to-exploit picture of what these models can do.
arxiv-2510-20092:
Hao Yu and six co-authors compare two core tools for image models: self-attention and convolution. Self-attention is flexible, but its cost grows very fast with image size. Convolution is cheaper and carries useful built in assumptions about images. Their 2025 paper asks what still gives self-attention its edge in modern vision systems.

The team names two sources of that edge. One is adaptive routing, where links between positions shift with image content. Fixed convolution filters lack that flexibility. The other is lateral inhibition, where scores compete and weak links fade. They build Attentive Convolution around both ideas using small three by three kernels. They then form a model family called AttNet. AttNet scores well on ImageNet with few parameters. The new operator also helps diffusion based image generation, with faster sampling.
arxiv-2510-20192:
Zhuang Ma and six co-authors demonstrate a phase-based way to tune coupling between superconducting qubits for quantum simulation and gates. Parametric modulation is widely used in these circuits, but normally the coupling strength is set by the amplitude of the flux pulse, which also disturbs qubit parameters strongly. Their scheme instead adjusts the relative phase between pulses applied to two coupled qubits.

The team characterizes the phase modulation for sideband couplings at both sweet spots and off-sweet spots, reaching a broad range of coupling strengths. Population dynamics and spectroscopy measurements agree with each other in confirming the control. The authors present phase-controlled coupling as a promising tool for parametrically driven simulations and gate operations.
arxiv-2510-20392:
Z. B. Cui and sixteen co-authors demonstrate multiplexed heralded entanglement between two trapped-ion quantum network nodes joined by long optical fiber. Linking remote nodes with high-fidelity entanglement is a critical step toward quantum networks for distributed computing, long-distance communication, and sensing. Multiplexing promises to speed up that slow linking process over long fibers.

By multiplexing ten temporal photonic modes, the team achieves a speedup of about four point six times in ion-ion entanglement generation over one point two kilometers of fiber. The entanglement fidelity reaches about ninety-six percent, with a small stated uncertainty range. Their dual-type architecture is designed to scale to multiple nodes, which the authors present as a key building block for large quantum networks.
arxiv-2510-21092:
Nicolas Lanchier, working alone, studies the extinction phase of the contact process with an asymptomatic state, a variant of the classic infection spread model. Infected people spread the disease at one rate while symptom free and another once symptomatic, newly infected start symptom free, and recovery proceeds at a fixed rate.

Earlier work settled the mean field picture, and the spatial extinction regime is the focus here. Whether the infection dies out depends on the balance of the two spread rates and the symptom onset rate. Such models sharpen intuition for diseases where silent carriers drive transmission, a recurring public health concern.
arxiv-2510-21192:
Luca Demetrio leads six co-authors on Gen-Review, a large scale data set of AI generated and human written peer reviews for studying how language models are changing scientific review. Evidence suggests models were already used quietly at major venues, and some boards now integrate them openly.

A shared corpus lets researchers measure quality, bias, and detection questions on real review text rather than anecdotes. Understanding model reviewing matters for the integrity of the scientific process itself, since review gates what gets published. The data set supports both critics and adopters of automated review with common evidence.
arxiv-2510-21292:
Shahaf Bassan, Michal Moshkovitz, and Guy Katz question a common belief about generalized additive models. Such models are often called interpretable. Each input affects the output through its own simple curve. If the models are so clear, explaining their answers should be cheap to compute. The authors test that belief.

Their complexity analysis finds a mixed picture instead. Under standard assumptions, fast explanations depend on the shape of the input space. They also depend on the kinds of pieces the model is built from. The task matters too, with regression and classification behaving differently. Writing a tangled model in additive form can make it easier to explain. That benefit holds only for some explanation types and some input settings.
arxiv-2510-21392:
Alexander Pluska and Sagar Malhotra study what huge sparse networks look like from the viewpoint of a single node, a lens called local convergence. That lens guides the study of random graph models and of message-passing neural networks that learn on graphs, yet its standard form misses some distinctions those networks can feel.

They define a sharper lens, color convergence, based on an iterative coloring procedure for nodes. It sorts exactly which random graph families settle into well-behaved limits for message-passing learning. Building on it, they propose a refined configuration model that generalizes the classic way of wiring graphs from degree lists. The new model can mimic any well-behaved locally tree-like family, including several famous ones, and the framework fully describes the random trees that appear as local limits.
arxiv-2510-22092:
Shaunak Mishra, Reza Samadi, and Diane Bérard protect the precision of the PLATO space mission. PLATO will find Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars. It sizes them by watching them cross their stars. The size target is better than two percent. Radiation damage in the cameras leaves a defect called charge transfer inefficiency. The defect smears recorded light and can shrink the measured dip.

The team worked with simulated star fields from the mission's own simulator. They modeled the defect's lingering signal as a sum of fading exponentials. That identified the trap types involved. Smearing was stripped out column by column. Trap density was mapped across the camera plane. Their correction pulls biased transit depths back inside the accuracy budget. Real planet sizes can then be trusted.
arxiv-2510-22192:
Haoyang Liu, Jie Wang, Yuyang Cai, Xiongwei Han, Yufei Kuang, and Jianye Hao automate a hard translation in operations research. A wordy real problem must become variables, constraints, and an objective a solver can chew. Language models can draft such models. Fixed step-by-step prompting buckles on tangled mathematical structure, though.

OptiTree organizes the territory itself as a tree. Problem categories sit at the nodes, arranged by type and complexity. Each node is stocked with high-level modeling thoughts. Faced with a new problem, the system searches the tree repeatedly. The target breaks into a chain of simpler subproblems with known modeling patterns. The pieces are then composed. The point is adaptive decomposition, not a rigid recipe. Complex models get built the way a good analyst sketches them.
arxiv-2510-22492:
How much speech is needed before a multilingual recognition model stops finding new sound pieces? Siyu Liang, Nicolas Ballier, Gina-Anne Levow, and Richard Wright ask that question in a 2025 paper, tracking the Whisper model as it decodes speech in forty nine languages.

Liang and co-authors log the small token pieces Whisper considers and watch their discovery slow over time. Total discovery barely depends on how much training speech a language had, and each language reaches an acoustic saturation point. Token patterns follow a known skewed rank law, while average token length rises with resource level and differs by writing script.
arxiv-2510-22592:
Axions, hypothetical light particles, could turn into photons inside a magnetic field when their masses line up. Ashu Kushwaha and Rajeev Kumar Jain propose in 2025 a way to hunt that conversion using circular polarization patterns in the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light in the universe.

A twisted magnetic field before that era would leave extra photons carrying net circular polarization. Current measurements of that V-mode signal can therefore limit axion mass and coupling strength. Under an optimistic field strength near one nanogauss, the authors find CLASS telescope observations could probe axion masses in a range that earlier searches had left unconstrained.
arxiv-2510-22792:
A goodness of fit test asks if data match a model family. Florian Bruck, Veronika Reimoser, and Fabian Baier study such a test in 2025. Their test uses the Kernel Stein Discrepancy. It can also fit the best parameter at once. That joint task changes the test distribution.

They derive that distribution in formal terms. It is a weighted sum of chi square variables. An extra disturbance term comes from parameter fitting. They also build a bootstrap frame. It covers degenerate U-statistics with estimated parameters. Bootstrap means resampling data to mimic variation. The new test follows from that general frame.
arxiv-2510-22892:
Robot arms can become rigid and brittle in uncertain settings. Jingzehua Xu leads a team with four co-authors. In 2025 they make virtual model control more adaptive. Virtual model control maps virtual forces to joint torques. Fixed parameters limit its adaptability, though.

Their method adds two learning aids. A language model gives structured priors and high level reasoning. A Lyapunov based reinforcement learner enforces stability. Lyapunov methods prove a system stays stable. Online adaptation thus stays theoretically safe. Tests used a seven degree of freedom Panda arm. Dynamic tasks required balancing competing objectives. The method beat baselines while keeping physical interpretability.
arxiv-2510-22992:
Hitoshi Konno and Andrey Smirnov construct new vertex operators for an elliptic quantum toroidal algebra tied to the general linear group. Their method combines representations of the algebra with formulas for elliptic stable envelopes on a cyclic quiver variety. Compositions of the operators match the shuffle product form of those envelopes.

Expectation values of the operators yield K-theoretic vertex functions for the variety. The authors also derive exchange relations and build an L-operator that satisfies a key RLL identity. The work links algebra, geometry, and counting functions in a way specialists in quantum groups can build on.
arxiv-2510-23192:
Mohammed Charkaoui, Rajae Sammani, El Hassan Saidi, and Rachid Ahl Laamara test a basic claim of the minimal Weak Gravity Conjecture. That claim predicts towers of states beyond the charge limit when a gauge force grows very weak or very strong. In their 2025 work, the team uses M-theory on a special family of Calabi-Yau threefolds, shapes used to hide extra dimensions.

They sort fiber shapes of these threefolds with finite volume, and match curves in the fiber with curves in the base. That match links strong and weak gauge couplings, so hard cases can be studied through their easier partners. Using known traits of stable BPS states, they then show that such towers do appear at both extremes. The result supports the conjecture within the five dimensional effective theory built from this setup.
arxiv-2510-23392:
Yuri Latushkin, Vyacheslav Pivovarchik, and Alesia Supranovych study a spectral problem on graphs, where edges meet at vertices like roads at junctions. On each edge sits a Sturm-Liouville equation, a classic type that links a function to its rates of change. In the 2025 work, Robin-Kirchhoff conditions apply where edges meet, mixing the value of a function with its slope.

The team studies characteristic functions of the problem, whose zeros mark the eigenvalues, the allowed tones of the system. They describe how the eigenvalues behave for large values. They also solve an inverse problem. If the graph shape is known and some Robin eigenvalues are given, the hidden coefficients in the Robin conditions can be recovered. Results of that kind matter for quantum graphs, where a network models a thin physical system. Knowing the boundary rules from measured tones helps check such models.
arxiv-2510-23492:
Jingjie Zhang leads a team of eleven researchers with COMPASS-PTM, a framework for learning the code of post-translational modifications on proteins. These chemical edits form a combinatorial code that regulates protein function, yet linking modified sites to the enzymes that make them remains unsolved, despite its role in signaling and disease.

Their mechanism-aware, coarse-to-fine framework unifies residue-level modification profiling with enzyme-substrate assignment. It integrates evolutionary representations from protein language models, physicochemical priors, and a crosstalk-aware prompting scheme. Decoding the modification code could reveal drug targets hidden in protein regulation. Readers can follow the full argument and data in the paper itself.
arxiv-2510-23892:
Kebin Contreras and ten co-authors grade cocoa beans with light instead of laboratory chemistry. Bean quality — fermentation level, moisture, polyphenols, and toxic cadmium — is normally judged by eye, taste, and lab assays that destroy the sample. Those methods are hard to scale across a production chain that depends on quality for safety and price.

Their system runs beans along a conveyor belt under a visible and near-infrared spectrometer, capturing molecular signatures tied to each property. Learning-based regression models predict the properties from those spectra. The training data came from batches in Santander, Colombia, with lab-measured ground truth, and the models were also tested on beans from other Colombian regions and Cusco, Peru. Scores passed 0.98 in explained variance for every property in-domain and stayed near 0.96 accuracy on the far-away samples. The authors present the setup as a non-destructive replacement for lab grading.
arxiv-2510-24392:
Matteo Giordano writes alone on a deep question in particle theory. Gauge theories describe forces through fields that act on matter particles. The Dirac spectrum lists values that set how those particles gain mass. Chiral symmetry is a left-right mirror symmetry of light particles. At high heat that symmetry returns, and Giordano asks what the spectrum must do.

He works with two light flavors, the two lightest kinds of quarks. He asks if a second mirror symmetry, long thought broken, can stay broken. His answer ties that breaking to sharp traits in the spectrum. Near-zero values must pile up in a thin spike with odd traits. Charge lumps in the field, called instantons, may supply the mechanism. The paper maps what future lattice studies should look for.
arxiv-2510-24592:
Guoxin Chen leads a team of nine authors on autoformalization. Autoformalization turns plain-language math into machine-checked form. Formal form lets a computer verify each step of a proof. Language models write such form with correct syntax quite often. Yet the formal text often drifts from the problem's true meaning.

Their method, ReForm, checks meaning inside the writing loop itself. The model drafts a statement, judges its fidelity, and fixes errors. A training method, PBSO, rewards good drafts and good checks apart. That split stops shallow critiques that fake reflection. Across four benchmarks, ReForm gained about twenty-three points over rivals. A new check set holds 859 expert-annotated items for judging. Even human experts made meaning errors in nearly two of five cases.
arxiv-2510-24792:
Patrick Haller, Fabio Barth, Jonas Golde, Georg Rehm, and Alan Akbik built a new bench to test vision and language models in many tongues at once. Past benches lean on made up content or stick to English, since hand checks of translations are slow and dear. Their bench draws on PISA tests, a school skill test used in more than eighty lands.

Each item keeps the text, image, and answer picks from the source tests, with a tag for the kind of ask. Items were turned into five more tongues, for six in all, laid side by side. Tests of top models showed small models in the non English tongues lag by a lot.
arxiv-2510-25292:
Yannis Voet and Leonardo De Novellis study Kronecker product factorizations. Their 2025 mathematics paper deals with large matrices and networks. The Kronecker product builds large arrays from smaller ones. It helps store large data in sparse form. Sometimes a large matrix hides such a product. Its sparsity pattern may already reveal the structure.

The pair determine all possible factorizations of binary matrices. Binary matrices contain only zeros and ones. They visualize the options through a decomposition graph. A network adjacency matrix may factor similarly. That would mean smaller networks combine into one large network. Such findings can help approximate real matrices later. They may also reveal latent structure in networks. The authors suggest a natural visualization for Kronecker graphs.
arxiv-2510-25492:
Siddharth Iyer establishes a lower bound for cubic polynomials. His 2025 mathematics paper counts sums of two squares. An irreducible monic cubic with negative discriminant is studied. How often can it take sum-of-two-squares values? Grechuk posed a question about infinitude in 2021. Iyer provides a quantitative answer to that question.

His proof uses a two-dimensional unit argument. Arithmetic of degree six number fields also helps. For specific shift values, a concrete bound follows. Count of good inputs grows like a fractional power. The exponent approaches one third minus small error. Arguments may generalize to other quadratic forms. Forms like x squared plus n times y squared qualify. Representing polynomial values by quadratic forms is classical. Quantitative lower bounds are harder than infinitude alone. Number theorists may extend his unit argument further. The result quantifies frequency, not just existence, of representations.
arxiv-2510-25892:
Harris Hardiman-Mostow, Jack Mauro, Adrien Weihs, and Andrea L. Bertozzi improve how to choose which nodes in a graph to label first when labels are scarce. Active learning picks the most useful examples to label next, balancing exploration of new areas with exploitation of known ones. Their guide is Balanced Forman Curvature, a measure of how a graph bends at each edge, which reflects cluster structure.

Hardiman-Mostow and the team build a starting set that mirrors the graph clusters and give a data driven rule for when exploration is enough. Curvature also triggers the switch to exploitation, replacing hand tuned rules. A local rewiring step spreads label information at several scales while keeping the graph sparse, and tests beat prior methods at low label rates.
arxiv-2510-26592:
Marit R Fiechter, Gabriel Laude, and Jeremy O Richardson fix a gap in a practical theory of quantum tunnelling. Instanton theory estimates how particles cross barriers in molecules, and it gives tunnelling splittings, the small energy gaps that tunnelling creates. The classic form fails for asymmetric double wells, where the two sides sit at different energies, because no matching orbit links them.

Fiechter and her two co-authors build a new form based on a projected flux correlation function, which works for such lopsided systems. Against exact quantum results in one- and two-dimensional models, its accuracy matched the symmetric case. They then study tunnelling in alpha-fenchol, a biomolecule with uneven wells, and find good agreement with experiment. The paper also clears up how tunnelling splittings relate to reaction rates.
arxiv-2510-26792:
Tao Tao and Maissam Barkeshli ask in 2025 if a Transformer can learn fake random numbers. A Transformer is a neural network, a program that learns patterns from data. Their source is a permuted congruential generator, a math rule that scrambles a hidden count.

Such rules shift bits, flip bits, turn bits, and cut bits to hide the count. The model still predicts new items in a sequence, even when one bit is shown. It can learn more than one rule at once and tell them apart. Small cases must come first, or large cases stall in training. The need for small cases first is a key lesson. Its inner layers group numbers by how their bits turn.
arxiv-2510-26892:
Mahsa Valizadeh, Rui Tuo, and James Caverlee make generative adversarial networks more diverse by making them Bayesian. A GAN pits a generator against a discriminator, but generators often suffer mode collapse, producing a narrow range of outputs that misses much of the data. Their BI-DCGAN extends a standard convolutional GAN with model uncertainty.

Valizadeh and her two co-authors learn a distribution over network weights with Bayes by Backprop, using mean-field variational inference to keep training efficient. They give what they call the first theoretical proof, from covariance matrix analysis, that Bayesian modelling enhances sample diversity in GANs. Experiments on standard benchmarks show more diverse and robust outputs than conventional DCGANs at similar training cost. The authors pitch the method for applications where diversity and uncertainty both matter.
arxiv-2510-26992:
C. O. Ascencio, D. J. P. de Sousa, and Tony Low study how certain crystals bend light in response to electric fields. The crystals are topological and chiral, meaning their atomic pattern has a handed twist linked to unusual electron states. Attention centers on Berry curvature and orbital magnetic moment, two traits of electrons that shape optical response near special band crossings.

Using model and first-principles calculations across many materials in one symmetry group, the team finds a nonzero effect once thought to vanish there. Uneven energies of opposite-handed crossing points create the signal. A beryllium-gold compound stands out as reachable under realistic electric biases. The work widens the search for new electro-optic materials.
arxiv-2510-27092:
Ziyu Huang, Masatoshi Hirabayashi, and Thomas Orlando explain how tiny space impacts can both darken and rust lunar soil at once. Nanophase metallic iron in Moon samples signals space weathering from solar wind and micrometeoroid hits. Yet oxidized hematite found near the poles seemed to contradict the Moon strongly reducing chemistry, raising a puzzle about iron states.

Using reactive molecular dynamics simulations of impacts on the mineral fayalite, the team finds split outcomes by location. The hot, compressed crater surface favors reduced metallic iron, while the expanding plume stays briefly oxygen-rich and can form oxidized iron. This dual pathway reconciles sample and remote-sensing evidence and matches the uneven hematite pattern across the Moon. It also suggests distinct generations of metallic iron worth separating in future soil studies.
arxiv-2510-27592:
D. Agguiaro and 290 co-authors describe how the ALICE Inner Tracking System is tuned and watched during LHC Run 3 in 2025. ALICE studies collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Its inner tracker uses silicon pixel chips to trace charged paths close to the collision point, with finer aim and faster readout than the prior device.

Stable runs need each sensor's charge threshold set and noisy pixels masked. The full device holds more than twenty-four thousand sensors and billions of pixels across about ten square meters. That scale makes tuning a major task in its own right. The paper sets out the steps used to keep data clean through the run.
arxiv-2510-27692:
Soumitra Kundu, Gargi Panda, Saumik Bhattacharya, Aurobinda Routray, and Rajlakshmi Guha present LifWavNet in 2025, a network that rebuilds heart traces from radar without touch. An electrocardiogram, or ECG, records the heart's electric signal and is key to care. Radar can sense chest motion from a distance, which suits watch without wires or pads.

LifWavNet uses learnable lifting wavelets, which split a signal into layers at distinct scales and can adapt their shape. A joint time-and-frequency loss keeps the rebuilt trace true in both views. Tests on two public sets beat prior methods on trace quality and on heart rate and its variation. Views of inner features aid trust in what the net has learned.
arxiv-2511-00192:
Ali Satvaty, Suzan Verberne, and Fatih Turkmen propose EL-MIA, a framework for measuring membership inference risk at the level of sensitive entities in language models. Membership attacks ask whether a particular item was in training data, but existing methods detect whole prompts or documents. Private risk often lives smaller: a name, a card number, or another sensitive entity inside otherwise ordinary text.

A benchmark dataset for entity-level evaluation is constructed, and existing methods are compared systematically on it. Privacy readers get a finer audit for language models. Entity-level leakage is what harms people, so measuring at that granularity aligns the audit with the actual risk.
arxiv-2511-00292:
Michal Habera and Andreas Zilian fix a quiet flaw in a classic computation: finding the eigenvalues of small three-by-three matrices, numbers that set how a system stretches and rotates. Old trigonometric formulas, rooted in Cardano's and Viète's work on cubic equations, turn unstable when two eigenvalues nearly repeat, exactly the case many applications care about.

Their stable method works through four invariants, including the trace and the discriminant, and comes with tight error bounds. One invariant gets a new algorithm with a proven accuracy guarantee. Benchmarks relate real errors to the bounds and show speed: on a hard test case the method ran about ten times faster than the highly tuned LAPACK library, at comparable accuracy.
arxiv-2511-00492:
Simon Giel, James Hurrell, Shreya Santra, Ashutosh Mishra, Kentaro Uno, and Kazuya Yoshida built a digging tool for the Moon. Using lunar soil where it lies, called in-situ resource utilization, is a key step toward lasting lunar bases, and excavation comes first. Their bucket drum attaches to MoonBot, a modular robot from the Japanese Moonshot program, so missions can swap tools as plans change.

A 3D-printed plastic prototype proved the concept in sandbox tests. The light drum digs continuously at a strong rate with low energy per kilogram, and it also works in slower batch mode. Continuous digging proved far more energy-efficient per kilogram than batch operation. The authors suggest adding sensors and autonomous control next, turning a proven scoop into a smarter excavation system.
arxiv-2511-00592:
Massinissa Merouani, Islem Kara Bernou, and Riyadh Baghdadi let language models drive compiler optimization in a closed loop. Tuning loop nests for modern hardware is notoriously hard, and their framework, ComPilot, hands the search to an off-the-shelf model with no task-specific fine-tuning. The model proposes transformations for a loop nest, and the compiler reports back which are legal and whether the code sped up or slowed down.

That concrete feedback guides the model's next proposal, round after round. Across the PolyBench suite, the zero-shot agent achieved geometric mean speedups of well over twofold in a single run, and higher still when taking the best of five runs. It also proved competitive with Pluto, a leading polyhedral optimizer, beating it in many cases. Grounded feedback, the study shows, turns general models into effective optimizers.
arxiv-2511-00792:
Akshay Sai Banderwaar and Abhishek Gupta look for a faster way to solve eigenvalue problems with physics informed neural networks. Such problems reveal a system's heat response, stability, and natural modes of vibration. Neural solvers need no mesh, but they often train far more slowly than classic numerical methods.

The authors recast the search for eigenpairs, the paired values and shapes that solve these problems, as a biconvex task, meaning each half is well behaved when the other is held fixed. That form allows an alternating search with updates that can be computed directly and are proven to converge. In experiments, their method matched high accuracy while running up to five hundred times faster than gradient based training.
arxiv-2511-00992:
Manfred Droste and Zoltan Fulop work in weighted automata theory on strong bimonoids, algebraic systems that extend semirings and supply the weights for automata. Their subject is polynomials over a set of indeterminates, with an addition and a product suited to this weaker setting.

They show the polynomials form a right distributive strong bimonoid, and that it is the free one over its indeterminates, as well as both left and right cancellative. Pure reasoning shows two terms are equal under the bimonoid laws exactly when their polynomials match under associativity and commutativity rules alone. That yields concrete constructions of the polynomials, an exponential time test for whether terms match, and unique normal forms through term rewriting, with matching results for the idempotent case.
arxiv-2511-01592:
Natália Ribeiro Marinho and five colleagues address a safety problem in aircraft parts made of composite materials. A low-speed impact can crack the inside of a panel while the surface looks untouched. Estimating the impact's energy from sensor signals is the first step to locating damage, but the inverse problem is noisy, data-poor, and full of tangled candidate features.

Their answer is a structured workflow for choosing input features, guided by engineering knowledge. Signals are mined in the time, frequency, and time-frequency domains, then filtered for statistical significance, correlation, reduced dimension, and robustness to noise. The surviving energy indicators feed a neural network. It is trained and validated on experimental impact data. The result is a principled input design, instead of the field's usual ad hoc feature picking.
arxiv-2511-01792:
J. I. Diaz Schneider and five colleagues tune the behavior of silver nanowire networks, tangled mats of microscopic metal wires explored as hardware for brain-like computing. Each wire and each wire-to-wire junction acts as a circuit element, metallic or memristive, so the network's overall response depends on the mix of junction types.

Fresh samples behaved as plain resistors, their impedance flat across frequencies, a sign of an over-percolated metallic network. Combining gentle low-temperature annealing with alternating-current stimulation changed the picture drastically: resistance rose, as if metallic junctions were being depopulated, and a capacitive response emerged. The authors explain the new dynamics with an earlier two-junction model. They argue the thermal step works indirectly. It changes the humidity trapped at junctions. That opens multiple switching schemes suited to neuromorphic processing.
arxiv-2511-01992:
Shreyas Singh, Zhuo Zhang, and A. J. Hildebrand work on a classical topic in number theory: how often each string of digits shows up in continued fraction expansions. A result of Gauss and Kuzmin assigns these frequencies through a specific probability measure on the unit interval. That measure is known to give the same weight to a digit string and its reverse.

The authors prove the reverse symmetry is not a side detail but a fingerprint: any probability measure with a continuous density that shares it must be the Gauss-Kuzmin measure itself. They also show that digit strings of length three admit no other such symmetries, while longer strings sometimes do, supported by numerical evidence.
arxiv-2511-02292:
Hui Li, Ziyu Li, and Chen-run Yu benchmark the approximate methods physicists use for strongly interacting electrons against a model that can be solved exactly. The usual benchmark, quantum Monte Carlo on the Hubbard model, suffers from the fermionic sign problem and from shaky analytic continuation. The Hatsugai-Kohmoto model avoids those problems because its exact answers are known, making it a clean testing ground.

Three many-body approximations, known as GW, HGW, and SGW, were compared with the exact Green's functions, spectra, and response functions. The GW method, often dismissed as too weak for strong correlation, turned out to have an unreported solution branch that reproduces Mott insulating physics accurately in this model. HGW described charge response well, while SGW handled spin correlations best. The study refines what each approximation can be trusted to do.
arxiv-2511-02692:
Keith Briggs and Ibrahim Nur built CRRM, an open-source simulator for 5G mobile networks, and describe it in a 2025 paper. System-level simulators help test new network algorithms, but many are slow or awkward for machine learning work. CRRM is written in pure Python so it can plug straight into modern AI tools.

Most simulators step through events one by one. CRRM instead models the network as linked blocks in a directed graph, each block computed only when its inputs change. The authors call that trick smart update. It lets parts of the system sit idle until needed, which speeds up runs. The design targets researchers who want quick tests of learning-based network control.
arxiv-2511-02792:
Daniel Ting and Kenneth Hung study a tension in online experiments: trimming noise makes estimates sharper but can add bias. Methods like winsorization and surrogate metrics do exactly that. Their 2025 paper asks whether such bias is safe when experiments run for years and small errors can pile up over time.

Their model shows the tradeoff survives in the long run. Sharper signal still helps, even when it costs some bias. That shifts the goal from finding one correct unbiased metric to making the best estimates for each decision. The paper also refines launch rules: loose criteria help when a system is far from its best, while strict criteria win as the system matures.
arxiv-2511-02892:
Graph theorists gathered in Novy Smokovec, Slovakia, in late summer 2025 for the 33rd Workshop on Cycles and Colourings. Each edition of the workshop holds open problem sessions, where participants pose questions they cannot yet solve. Janos Barat, Zdenek Dvorak, Penny Haxell, and six colleagues collected the problems from this edition into a 2025 document.

Each problem comes with notes on the current state of the art and a short bibliography, so readers can see how far known methods reach. Such collections serve the field as shared to-do lists: they record what a community finds hard and interesting at a moment in time. Newcomers can use them to find live questions, and experts can track which problems fall over the years.
arxiv-2511-02992:
Mikhael Djajapermana, Moritz Reiber, Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder, and Ulf Schlichtmann design a search space for tiny vision models that mix two network styles. Hybrids of convolutional networks and vision transformers beat either alone, but they are too big for tiny machine learning hardware. Their 2025 paper builds a space that a neural architecture search can explore for small, fast hybrids suited to tight size limits.

The space mixes blocks that learn local detail with blocks that learn global structure, and adds a new pooling block whose layers are also searchable, shrinking feature maps cheaply. On the CIFAR-10 image set, the search found hybrids that beat ResNet-based tiny models in both accuracy and inference speed under the same size caps.
arxiv-2511-03392:
Viktoria Frohlich and Zsolt Regaly ask whether moons of planets cast loose into the dark could stay warm enough for life to start. Free-floating planets may be common, and some may keep their moons after a violent ejection. A star's explosive death is the ejection scene tested here, with full three-body-style simulations of the blast's mass loss.

Moons that stay bound often end on stretched orbits. Stretching drives tides, and tides can heat an interior for ages without any starlight. Under the right mix of orbit and moon traits, that heat can hold liquid oceans under ice. Such dark oceans would count as places where life could plausibly begin, far from any sun.
arxiv-2511-03492:
Elvis Dohmatob, Mohammad Pezeshki, and Reyhane Askari-Hemmat build a theory for when training on less data beats training on more. Recent results shook the old more-is-better rule, with tiny curated sets beating bulk data on hard reasoning tasks. Their framework imagines an imperfect judge who keeps examples by difficulty and correctness.

Exact scaling curves for test error follow under both label-blind and label-aware judging. Under set conditions, dropping data provably improves generalization, and the curves say by how much. The catch lies in judge quality: poor curation can just as easily harm. A principled account of curation helps builders spend labeling effort where it counts instead of hoarding raw volume.
arxiv-2511-03592:
Annachiara Korchmaros, Guillaume E Scholz, and Peter F Stadler characterize a class of graphs that model gene matches between two species. Best match graphs arise in evolutionary biology when each gene picks its closest counterpart across species. A looser quasi variant, stripped of direction, is the subject here.

That class turns out to be exactly the bipartite graphs avoiding three named patterns. An equivalent test says every connected piece must hold a heart vertex linked to all vertices of the opposite color. A cubic-time algorithm recognizes such graphs and, when they pass, builds a labeled tree that explains them. Clean characterizations help biologists tell whether gene match data can truly arise from a shared family tree.
arxiv-2511-03792:
Alexander Nikolaenko, Pietro M Bonetti, and Subir Sachdev offer a theory for the hourglass-shaped spin excitation spectrum seen in hole-doped cuprate superconductors. Their starting point is a ground state with period-four unidirectional charge density wave order, often called stripe order.

Building on evidence for a fractionalized Fermi liquid in the pseudogap metal, the authors use fermionic spinons that become confined when stripe order sets in at low temperature. The theory reproduces the hourglass pattern near the stripe-ordering wavevector seen in neutron scattering. It also predicts added scattering from spinon continua and bound states at higher energies and elsewhere in momentum space, which neutron or X-ray experiments could look for.
arxiv-2511-03892:
Chiraag Kaushik, Justin Romberg, and Vidya Muthukumar give a general technique for approximating high-dimensional empirical kernel matrices, a core object in kernel methods. Their bounds target the expected operator norm of a random kernel matrix under broad conditions on the kernel function.

Decoupling results for U-statistics and a non-commutative Khintchine inequality yield upper and lower bounds from scalar kernel statistics and a correlation kernel matrix. Applied to inner-product kernels, the method simplifies older moment-based proofs and gives tighter results, including for anisotropic Gaussian data. A sharper lower bound on the bias of kernel regression with such data follows from the same techniques.
arxiv-2511-04392:
Alireza Beygi and two colleagues calculate the binding of kaonium, a short-lived exotic atom. Kaonium would pair a positive and a negative kaon, two heavy mesons, in one bound state. No one has directly detected it, since it lasts only about a billionth of a billionth of a second.

Using chiral perturbation theory, the team finds kaonium should appear as a sharp peak near 992 MeV. It would show up when two photons turn into pairs of neutral mesons. One channel stands out, with a cross-section about nine times the other. That sharp peak gives experimenters a clear target to hunt for.
arxiv-2511-04592:
Gregory J. Herczeg and his co-author recover what the young star HBC 722 looked like before its outburst. FU Ori outbursts are thought to shape how stars assemble and how their disks evolve. The stars that erupt, though, are rarely measured beforehand.

A low-resolution optical spectrum, taken during a survey of the North America Nebula, gives the answer. It shows a spectral type near M3, a cool red young star. Archival brightness data then yields its mass gain rate before the eruption. That rate was high for its class, yet about fifteen thousand times weaker than during the outburst.
arxiv-2511-04692:
Jingqing Wang leads six authors with SARC, a fake news detector that uses sentiment and user roles. Comments and story text both carry feelings that can help spot falsehoods. Earlier work treated sentiment as a side signal and ignored who was speaking.

The same sentiment can mean different things from different kinds of users. SARC first builds user features from comment text with a bidirectional recurrent network. Sentiment-enhanced deep clustering then sorts users into roles for the final judgment. Grouping voices by role gives the detector a finer picture of how a story spreads and who amplifies it.
arxiv-2511-04792:
Gabriel Missael Barco leads five authors solving strong lensing inversion without knowing the lens first. Score-based models act as learned priors for the hidden source galaxy. Earlier work assumed the lens mass, and thus the distortion, was already known.

Their sampler infers the source and a parametric lens profile jointly. It adapts a Gibbs-style diffusion sampler to continuous time for the task. Reconstructions leave residuals consistent with the observed noise levels. Lens parameter posteriors recover the true values without systematic bias. The authors present it as the first joint source-and-lens success with score-based priors.
arxiv-2511-05192:
Yu Mao and Mohamed Saïdi develop the m-step solvable side of mono-anabelian geometry for number fields. The goal is a group-only algorithm that rebuilds a field and its largest m-step solvable extension from a quotient of its absolute Galois group.

Their main result works from the maximal quotient nine steps beyond m, for any m of at least three. For the rationals and for imaginary quadratic fields, they sharpen the input to a six-step quotient. Such results push how far pure group data can pin down a field, a core theme in anabelian work.
arxiv-2511-05392:
Minh-Khanh Luong and Chanh Kieu retrieve tropical cyclone strength and size from climate reanalysis data with a deep learning model. Past fixes for weak storms in climate output leaned on physical downscaling or statistics, each with its own limits.

Their convolutional network reads a set of key environmental fields tied to cyclones. It recovers both peak strength and storm size well from coarse reanalysis. The work tests whether learned maps can stand in for costly physics runs when many past storms must be re-scored for careful risk studies today overall.
arxiv-2511-05492:
Ziqing Guo and co-authors propose a quantum data encoding plan that cuts a circuit into parts and knits the results back, while it respects the chip's wiring map. Encoding data into quantum states can speed some tasks, but today's chips are noisy and not all qubits link to all others.

Cutting splits a big circuit into small ones that fit the hardware, with classical post-work to recombine them. Past encoding frames ignored chip topology, which forced costly swaps. Their model works at the algorithm level and plans around the true links, a step toward usable quantum data loads.
arxiv-2511-05792:
Chi-Zhuo Wang and co-authors extend a long look at how light echoes across the disks of eight active galactic nuclei. Using the Swift satellite's archive, they picked nearby galaxies with rapid, multi-color monitoring. Reverberation mapping of the continuum times how delays grow with wavelength, which sizes up the glowing disk.

Delays grew with wavelength close to the expected rate, but ran larger than the standard thin disk model predicts. Most targets showed an excess delay in the ultraviolet band, blamed on diffuse light from the broad-line region around the disk. A filtering method isolated that component, and its size tracked both the broad-line region size and the galaxy's luminosity. The authors read this as more proof the region adds to the lags.
arxiv-2511-06092:
Kirill Trunov and co-authors grow vanadium dioxide films in a way that fits normal chip production, aiming at brain-like hardware. Vanadium dioxide flips between metal and insulator near seventy degrees, which makes it ideal for artificial neurons built as threshold switches. Standard growth recipes demand strict heat and gas conditions that clash with CMOS fabrication.

Their method deposits the film from a metal target at room temperature using pulsed laser deposition in oxygen, then anneals it in vacuum. Tuning the oxygen pressure during deposition selects the right crystal phase. The process relaxes the need for hot oxygen equipment. Because it works under back-end-of-line CMOS conditions, the authors see a path to large-scale neuromorphic chips.
arxiv-2511-06592:
Zhi Rui Tam and Yun-Nung Chen test whether a patient's voice can sway a medical language model's judgment. Voice interfaces are entering clinics, and tone, age, or emotion in speech might tilt decisions away from the medical facts. One hundred seventy clinical cases were spoken aloud in thirty-six voice profiles varying age, gender, and emotion.

Surgical recommendations for spoken cases shifted by up to thirty-five percent versus identical written cases, and one model recommended surgery eighty percent less often by voice. Young and elderly voices drew recommendations differing by up to twelve percent, a gap that step-by-step prompting did not erase, though explicit reasoning removed the gender gap. The authors urge bias-aware designs before clinical use.
arxiv-2511-06692:
Tao Li and co-authors peel context away from cause inside neural networks that predict molecular properties. Deep models can ace benchmarks by leaning on spurious context that collapses when data shifts, and their reasoning stays opaque. Their framework, CLaP, separates causal signal from context repeatedly, layer by layer, as a molecule's graph representation is refined.

At each layer a causal block softly splits features into causal and non-causal streams, merges causal evidence across representations, and strips batch-linked context away. Across four molecular benchmarks the method improved error and fit measures over strong baselines. Atom-level saliency maps point at the substructures driving each prediction, matching chemical intuition in case studies and suggesting targeted edits.
arxiv-2511-06892:
Kailin Tong and four co-authors build a multi-agent AI system that watches road cameras and drafts traffic alerts automatically. Standard detectors perform well in predefined cases but fail on unseen cases and cannot explain them in words. Their system pairs multimodal large language models with vision-based perception, assigning separate agents to detection, distance estimation, decision-making, and message creation for cooperative transport systems.

Evaluated on 103 images drawn from twenty traffic videos, the system achieved perfect recall in situation detection and perfectly formed messages. Weaknesses remained: false-positive detections, and errors in lane counts, lane status, and cause codes. Surprisingly, the newer Gemini 2.5 Flash model performed worse and slower than Gemini 2.0 Flash, motivating specialized fine-tuning for transport applications.
arxiv-2511-07092:
Wei-You Liao and seven co-authors cut the measurement cost of quantum error mitigation, the set of tricks that clean up results from noisy quantum processors. Mitigation avoids the huge overhead of full error correction, but tools like zero-noise extrapolation must remeasure every circuit variant. The cost grows linearly when a whole family of circuits is parameterized by classic inputs. Their surrogate-enabled version moves the extrapolation onto classic computers.

A classic learning surrogate is trained to imitate the noisy device, after which the extrapolation runs entirely on the surrogate. The measurement overhead becomes constant for an entire circuit family rather than growing with its size. Theory indicates accuracy comparable to standard extrapolation in many useful cases, and numerical tests on systems up to one hundred qubits, covering ground-state energies and quantum metrology, confirm the method works.
arxiv-2511-07392:
Hyeryun Park and six co-authors give surgeons a voice-controlled agent for patient data in the operating room. During robotic surgery a surgeon's hands and eyes are fully committed, so pulling up clinical information or manipulating CT scans normally means breaking workflow. Their system, VISA, is a hierarchy of language-model agents: an orchestration agent coordinates three task experts that plan, refine, validate. Reason over voice commands to retrieve records, adjust scans, or navigate 3D anatomical models in the surgical video.

The team built a dataset of two hundred forty commands in hierarchical categories and a two-level evaluation metric scoring both single commands and categories. VISA achieved high stage-level accuracy and workflow success, and proved robust by correcting transcription errors, resolving ambiguity, and handling free-form phrasing from different speakers.
arxiv-2511-07592:
Wei Hou Tan and colleagues design a brighter electron source for hard X-ray lasers. Photoinjectors fire lasers at a cathode to release electron bunches, then radio waves accelerate them fast to preserve brightness. Breakdown inside the gun caps the field strength that materials can survive.

Shortening the radio pulse to nanoseconds may raise fields before breakdown starts. The proposed CUPID demonstrator couples a klystron with pulse compression to reach three hundred megawatts in twenty nanoseconds. Simulations explore whether such pulses can drive a photogun to brighter beams. Brighter beams mean sharper X-ray probes of atoms and materials.
arxiv-2511-07692:
Michael Tobar builds a mirror theory for electric dipoles beside the familiar magnetic one. Electric dipole moments probe broken symmetries and possible new physics, but their theory lacks the tidy operator tools magnetism enjoys. Tobar places both dipoles on parallel footing under electromagnetic duality.

A pseudo angular momentum in parity space, with its own electric Landé factor, organizes induced orbital dipoles. Following Ohanian current picture of the Zeeman effect, the electric dual recasts polarization as an effective magnetic current. The symmetric framework could sharpen how experiments design and read electric dipole searches that test the Standard Model limits.
arxiv-2511-07992:
M Pugachev and five co-authors report very high surface carrier mobility in a three dimensional topological insulator with no bulk states at the Fermi level. Their material is a tin bismuth antimony telluride sulfide compound, studied as bulk crystals and thin flakes. Cooling below about one hundred kelvin shifts conduction toward the surface in crystals.

Applying a two liquid model to magnetoresistance data gives surface mobility near twenty thousand in the stated units. A steep low field response and nonlinear Hall effect point to at least two surface carrier types. Mobility falls at stronger fields, and Zeeman splitting plus anomalous Hall terms improve the full description.
arxiv-2511-08092:
Julian Irigoyen, Arthur Sohler, and Andreas Kirkedal argue that pruning a speech recognition model can act as regularization, not just compression. Removing weights usually aims to shrink a network, yet chosen well it may also improve generalization. Using Whisper small, they combine gradient and Fisher sensitivity checks with targeted pruning of single components.

Some parts prove fragile, especially decoder feed forward layers, while decoder attention and late encoder layers hold spare capacity. Pruning half of those safer parts, with no fine tuning, cut word error rates on LibriSpeech and gains held on other sets. At forty percent sparsity their approach preserves accuracy where global pruning fails badly.
arxiv-2511-08192:
Lydia Kakampakou and Jennifer Wadsworth adapt the geometric approach to extreme value statistics for spatial data. Multivariate extremes can be described through a limit set and its gauge function, which becomes the target for inference. The authors tailor spatial gauge functions and build on a framework where extreme radii follow a truncated gamma distribution.

Two candidate models handle the angular distribution of extremes. Combining radial and angular draws gives estimates of very rare event probabilities. Against two established spatial methods, the geometric approach gives mostly unbiased answers, though with wider uncertainty. A space weather example uses daily geomagnetic field fluctuations to show the method in action.
arxiv-2511-08292:
Pritipriya Dasbehera, Akshunna Dogra, and William Redman propose that the brain can encode distance simply by watching grid cell activity decorrelate. Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex fire in repeating spatial patterns and are thought to support navigation. Real grid populations are slightly uneven in their properties, and that small heterogeneity may be a feature rather than a flaw.

Their one dimensional theory predicts that decorrelation of population activity tracks distance, matching simulations of noisy grid cells. Oddly, some farther distances are encoded better than some nearer ones, a sweet spot also hinted in rodent behavior. Two dimensional simulations reveal a trade off between encodable range and sharpness.
arxiv-2511-08592:
Azza Bouleimen and seven co-authors test whether language models can fake a group conversation well enough to fool readers. They gathered real Reddit threads and generated artificial ones on the same topics with two models, Llama 3 and GPT-4o, then showed both kinds to study participants side by side.

Readers mistook the model-made threads for human writing thirty-nine percent of the time. For the Llama 3 threads, people spotted the machine authorship only fifty-six percent of the time, barely better than a coin flip. The authors read the result two ways: simulated communities could help test platform policies and recommendation designs, but the same realism could flood social media with fake discussion.
arxiv-2511-08792:
Shravan Saoji investigates higher Nash blow-ups, a refinement of a classic algebraic geometry construction that resolves singularities by tracking tangent directions. Yasuda introduced the higher versions, and the natural question is whether Nobile's classical theorem about them survives the upgrade.

The higher Nobile theorem links smoothness of a variety to the behavior of its Nash blow-ups. Saoji proves it in the graded case with an argument that avoids any assumption on the characteristic of the ground field. A separate proof covers second-order Nash blow-ups in characteristic zero. Characteristic-free arguments matter in algebraic geometry because many techniques collapse in positive characteristic, so a proof that travels across all characteristics widens where the theorem can be used.
arxiv-2511-09092:
Zezhen Ding and three co-authors automate the operations research pipeline. There, an expert must translate a word problem about schedules, fleets, or supply chains into a formal optimization model and then into solver code. Language models can attempt both steps, but earlier systems needed mountains of annotated or synthetic data to learn how.

OR-R1 trains in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning on limited labeled data teaches the basic formulation and coding patterns. Then a test-time reinforcement method, TGRPO, squeezes learning out of abundant unlabeled problems. The system reaches state-of-the-art solving accuracy near sixty-eight percent while using a tenth of the synthetic data its predecessor needed, and it still wins with only one hundred synthetic samples. Test-time training also narrows the gap between first-try and best-of-eight performance.
arxiv-2511-09192:
Shenghua Feng, Jie An, and Fanjiang Xu tackle runtime safety prediction for systems whose behavior is partly random. Operators need the probability that a running stochastic system will stay safe or reach a target while avoiding danger. Offline models alone cannot use what the system observes as it runs.

The authors introduce observation-aware barrier functions, which update probability bounds as new observations arrive. Offline computation pairs with an online backward iteration, keeping the estimates rigorous yet responsive. The framework handles discrete-time stochastic systems with a given safety or reach-avoid specification. Experiments on benchmark systems show the method works in practice, not just in theory.
arxiv-2511-09592:
Himashi Peiris and five co-authors build a promptable foundation model for tumor segmentation. It works anywhere in the body and knows when it is unsure. General segmentation models struggle in medical scans, where tissue is heterogeneous, artifacts abound, and tumor boundaries fade. Their model, SAT3D, works volumetrically and is deliberately lightweight.

A shifted-window transformer builds hierarchical 3D features, while uncertainty estimates feed back in as prompts to guide boundary decisions in low-contrast areas. Adversarial training sharpens performance in ambiguous regions. Training used over seventeen thousand volume-mask pairs spanning modalities and cancer types, with thousands of cases for evaluation. A 3D Slicer plugin supports interactive medical use, and the model generalizes strongly to out-of-distribution scans.
arxiv-2511-09792:
Tianmeng Hu, Yongzheng Cui, Rui Tang, Biao Luo, and Ke Li revisit how teams of learning agents split a shared value function into local parts. For decentralized action to match the joint best action, methods usually force a monotonicity constraint that limits what the value function can express. The authors instead analyze unconstrained, non-monotonic factorization through the lens of dynamical systems.

Modeling learning as continuous gradient flow, they prove that bad equilibria violating the consistency condition are unstable saddle points, while only consistent solutions attract the dynamics. Experiments on synthetic matrix games and hard multi-agent benchmarks confirm that plain non-monotonic factorization finds the right solutions and beats monotonic baselines. They also study how temporal-difference targets and exploration choices shape the outcome.
arxiv-2511-09892:
Zhiyuan Yao, Anita Schöbel, Lei Nie, and Sven Jäger tackle train timetabling that mixes a regular periodic pattern with one-off adjustments. Periodic timetables are easy for passengers and coordinate connections well, but demand swings across the day call for extra or altered services. Their problem adds schedule tweaks and inserted trains to a base periodic timetable while respecting rolling stock circulation.

Because changes can reroute passengers, passenger routing is built into the model, which is cast on a time-space network as a service network design problem. The solution method combines Benders decomposition with column generation plus several speed-ups. Numerical tests showed the method working effectively and hybrid timetables cutting passenger travel costs compared with staying purely periodic.
arxiv-2511-10092:
Simon Alinder, Thomas Bensby, and Paul McMillan ask how much the measured structure of the Milky Way's two discs depends on how stars are sorted into them. The thin and thick discs differ in chemistry, motion, and shape, but their distributions overlap, especially at high metallicity. The authors apply five selection methods to red giant stars from the APOGEE survey, mixing chemical cuts, dynamics, ages, and a kinematic likelihood.

For each sorting they fit density profiles with height and radius. Chemical and age-based selections separated the discs most cleanly, while kinematic methods suffered more contamination. Every method found the thin disc flaring outward and the thick disc holding a scale height near one kiloparsec, with the thin disc's scale length longer, most strongly under chemical selection.
arxiv-2511-10192:
Qifeng Cai, Hao Liang, Chang Xu, Tao Xie, Wentao Zhang, and Bin Cui build Text2SQL-Flow. The approach grows small seed data into a large, diverse training set for translating questions into SQL queries. Text-to-SQL models are limited by data sets that are scarce, narrow, and structurally simple. Their augmentation works along six dimensions and checks quality at every stage, from database selection to verifying that generated SQL actually runs.

The pipeline produced SQLFlow, a data set of more than seventy-five thousand annotated examples with reasoning traces. Fine-tuning open models on it improved benchmark results under equal data budgets. For closed models, a masked alignment retrieval method that matches examples by fine-grained question-SQL alignment beat existing retrieval plans.
arxiv-2511-10292:
Zhengtao Zou, Ya Gao, Jiarui Guan, Bin Li, and Pekka Marttinen counter a failure mode of large vision-language models. As generated text grows, the initial visual evidence dilutes and language habits take over, so the model hallucinates objects. Earlier fixes contrast output scores or refine answers repeatedly, both costly in latency. Their approach, RUDDER, builds a persistent visual anchor from the model's own prefill computation.

An evidence direction extracted from residual updates is injected during decoding, gated by an adaptive trust mechanism that applies the reminder only when needed. Across five model families, hallucination scores fell by roughly a quarter on standard measures while throughput stayed above ninety-six percent of normal. The method works with plain greedy decoding and needs no retraining.
arxiv-2511-10492:
Yunkai Zhang leads a team of ten tackling a waste problem in modern recommender systems. The practical knowledge companies have gathered for years, such as item categories and time patterns, is usually applied only as post-hoc adjustments after a model ranks items. Generative recommenders, which now learn end to end, mostly ignore that knowledge.

Their framework feeds these structured human priors directly into training through lightweight adapter heads attached to the backbone model. The heads teach the model to separate user intent along human-understandable axes, like interaction types or short-term versus long-term interests, and a hierarchical strategy combines several prior types. Experiments on three large-scale datasets show gains in accuracy as well as diversity, novelty, and personalization, with better use of long contexts and larger models.
arxiv-2511-10892:
Feng Li, Ke Wu, and Yongwei Li present MCN-CL, a system for recognizing emotions from combined face, voice, and text signals. The task is plagued by three problems at once. Emotion categories are unevenly distributed, facial action units evolve over time in complicated ways, and features from different modalities are hard to fuse because they do not naturally align.

The network attacks all three with a cross-attention design, a triple query mechanism, and hard negative mining to prune redundant features while keeping emotional cues. Contrastive learning disciplines the fused representation. On the IEMOCAP and MELD benchmark datasets, the method outperformed state-of-the-art approaches, improving weighted F1 scores by roughly three and a half percent and nearly six percent respectively. The authors pitch the framework for social media scale data.
arxiv-2511-11092:
Jeffrey Seely recasts linear predictive coding networks as cellular sheaves, a math frame that attaches data to the cells of a network and tracks how local values must agree. Predictive coding replaces one global training pass with local updates on weights and activity, which makes it attractive for brain-like computing. In the sheaf view, the sheaf map turns activity into edge-wise prediction errors.

Inference then acts like diffusion under the sheaf Laplacian, a spread operator on that frame. Sheaf cohomology, which counts patterns that cannot be smoothed away, marks the error patterns inference can never remove. Feedback loops can create such clashes on their own, and the frame gives tools to spot risky layouts.
arxiv-2511-11292:
Santiago Arranz-Olmos, Gilles Barthe, and their colleagues study the Jasmin compiler. They prove it keeps the security of ML-KEM. ML-KEM is a key encapsulation method. The proven implementation is the one used in the Signal messenger.

Jasmin code is hand-tuned for speed. Compilation must not break correct behavior. It also must not break the strong security notion called KEM-IND-CCA. Both traits were proven earlier for the source code. The new proof is fully mechanized in the Rocq prover. Three general tools support it. One is a framework for game-based security under compilation. One is a new semantics for Jasmin and assembly based on interaction trees. It handles random choices and rejection sampling. The third is a relational Hoare logic for those trees.
arxiv-2511-11792:
Faizuddin Ahmed, İzzet Sakallı, and Ahmad Al-Badawi build a rotating black hole solution. The hole sits inside a cloud of strings. A uniform magnetic field runs along its spin axis. The starting point is the Kerr-Bertotti-Robinson family. That family places Kerr black holes inside an external magnetic universe.

The string cloud adds a new layer to the geometry. It mimics a network of one-dimensional defects. Turning off rotation gives the static Schwarzschild-Bertotti-Robinson hole with strings. Removing the field leaves a Kerr-like hole with strings alone. Exact solutions with layered parts let theorists test key questions. How do environment and exotic matter reshape a black hole?
arxiv-2511-11992:
Hung Du and four co-authors give decentralized vehicle teams a goal-oriented way to learn together when communication is scarce and no central controller exists. Land, water, and air vehicles in their setting see only part of the world, pursue their own objectives, and still must avoid chaos as a team.

Their multi-agent reinforcement learning framework lets each vehicle communicate selectively, sharing only information relevant to local goals and observations. Selective messaging respects visibility and bandwidth limits while preserving collaboration. Tests use complex navigation tasks with obstacles and changing team populations. Swarms that talk less but say the right things are the design ideal for real fleets.
arxiv-2511-13092:
Hayato Shimabukuro reads the early universe through the shapes of absorption lines. The 21 centimeter forest is a set of absorption troughs in radio signals from the cosmic dawn, when the first stars heated the gas between galaxies. Traditional statistics use amplitudes and correlations. Shimabukuro instead applies topological data analysis to simulated forest spectra, tracking how troughs are born and merge as a threshold sweeps. It condenses that history into three numbers tied to trough density, persistence, and Betti-curve asymmetry.

Forecasts show the descriptors pull differently on the two unknowns, X-ray heating strength and warm dark matter mass, breaking a degeneracy that plagues simpler statistics. Under realistic telescope noise, the long-lived troughs carrying the signal survive a persistence cut while noise washes out. The study presents topology as a sturdy probe of heating and dark matter.
arxiv-2511-13192:
Yantong Liu, Junjie Wu, and Lingling Lao decode quantum color codes by letting the decoder notice correlations it used to ignore. Color codes are attractive for fault-tolerant quantum computing because they encode efficiently and allow transversal Clifford gates, but their standard matching-based decoders underperform. The restricted decoder splits the problem into separate lattices and decodes each alone. The authors map the correlated matching decoder known from surface codes onto the color code lattice, producing a correlated decoder for the 4.8.8 color code that exploits correlations between those lattices.

Analytical and numerical results give it higher error thresholds than both the restricted and unified decoders, matching the unified decoder at very low error rates. Estimated thresholds against bit-flip noise are about ten point four percent under code-capacity noise and about three point one percent under phenomenological noise. The same mapping yields surface-code thresholds against depolarizing noise.
arxiv-2511-13592:
Chen Xu improves a zeroth-order optimization method for non-convex problems where gradients cannot be taken directly. The base method maximizes a Gaussian-smoothed surrogate that mixes function values under a power transform. Xu shows the smoothing radius drives a trade-off: wide smoothing explores well but can shift the answer, while narrow smoothing preserves detail but weakens the signal far from good regions.

The new GS-PowerHP method shrinks the radius step by step along a homotopy schedule, exploring broadly first and refining later. Theory shows the schedule improves that trade-off over any fixed radius. Tests, including adversarial attacks on ImageNet at very high dimension, beat the fixed-radius baseline and other smoothing methods by wide margins.
arxiv-2511-13692:
Rhys Seeburger and 6 co-authors measure six binary star systems once flagged as possible star and black hole pairs. Radial velocity data from Gaia's third release raised the black hole idea, but the systems were soon suspected to be post-mass-transfer pairs with stripped companions instead. High-resolution spectra over many epochs settle the question.

Spectral disentangling gives temperatures, radii, spin rates, and mass ratios for both stars in each system. Every system holds two glowing stars and no black hole: a fast-spinning A-type accretor plus a cool, very low-mass donor that shines too brightly for its mass. No current transfer appears, and the accretors spin fast yet well below breakup, which challenges standard spin-up models.
arxiv-2511-13792:
Herbert Baaser gives a uniform analytic check for the stability of isotropic, incompressible hyperelastic material models. Stability here means the Hill condition: the material modulus in the stress and log-strain relation must stay positive definite. For incompressible response, every possible deformation sits between uniaxial and biaxial states, with shear in between, a fact made plain in the invariant plane.

Baaser uses that same plane to draw stable and unstable regions for any chosen strain energy function and parameter set. Some fits that look stable in simple tension turn unstable in shear, which would poison a finite element run before it starts. The check gives modelers a standard early warning before simulation.
arxiv-2511-13892:
Badhan Chandra Das, Md Tasnim Jawad, Md Jueal Mia, and two co-authors probe the safety of large vision-language models used in transport systems. Such models can answer questions about traffic images, but attackers can jailbreak them into giving banned answers. The team built a test set of harmful transport-related queries drawn from standard prohibited categories.

Their attack hides instructions in image typography and spreads the push over several conversation turns. Against leading open and closed models it exposes serious weaknesses. The authors also propose a layered filter that screens responses before they reach users, and they rate results with both automated judging and manual checks, comparing their attack with earlier jailbreak methods.
arxiv-2511-14192:
Göktuğ Karpat examines how exotic quantum processes can loosen the limits on measurement predictability. Entropic uncertainty relations cap how well two measurements can both be predicted, and a quantum memory correlated with the system softens the cap. Karpat asks what happens when the memory itself passes through noisy channels arranged in indefinite causal order or with flipped input-output direction.

Using the quantum switch and the quantum time-flip with Pauli noise channels, he shows total entropic uncertainty can drop significantly compared with applying the same noise directly. The memory qubit here is also the measured system, an unusual setup. The results present indefinite causal order as a practical resource against noise.
arxiv-2511-15292:
Jianming Chen, Yawen Wang, and five co-authors present AdapAM, a framework for attacking multi-agent AI systems from the outside to test their defenses. Teams of cooperating agents are spreading into real applications, and their security is largely unprobed. Older attack methods need inside access to the system, or they clumsily strike every agent or one fixed agent, which is easy to spot.

AdapAM works black-box: an adaptive policy picks which agent to victimize and which harmful action to aim for, weighing damage against stealth. A proxy model then crafts the perturbation that nudges the victim toward that action. Smarter, quieter attacks give defenders a realistic sparring partner for hardening agent teams.
arxiv-2511-15492:
Andrea Barbero and seven co-authors show an optomechanical disk resonator prepared in the quantum ground state of motion. Disk resonators have advanced optomechanics, yet had not reached the quantum regime. The semiconductor disk vibrates in a breathing mode near a gigahertz. Cooled in a dilution refrigerator, its excitation falls below a single phonon.

Brillouin sideband spectroscopy with a fiber coupled optical mode measures the phonon occupancy. Stokes and anti Stokes photons from phonon creation and annihilation are counted singly. Suppression of the absorption side signals an occupancy below one. Laser heating ways are investigated experimentally as limits. Ground state preparation opens disk devices to quantum sensing and phonon based quantum experiments.
arxiv-2511-15692:
Mohammed Alkhatib introduces SS-MixNet, a lightweight deep model for classifying hyperspectral images with very few labels. Hyperspectral images carry rich spectra per pixel for land and material mapping. The model blends three dimensional convolutions for local spectral spatial features with two mixer blocks. Those blocks capture long range links along spectral and spatial axes separately.

A depthwise convolution attention step sharpens discriminative features at low cost. Only one percent of labeled data train and validate the model in tests. It achieves the highest accuracy among compared methods on two coastal data sets. Classification maps support the numeric gains. Label efficient, light models matter for remote sensing where ground truth is expensive to collect.
arxiv-2511-15792:
Jasleen Matharu and seventeen co-authors present a first complete view of spatially resolved star formation in distant galaxies using space telescope slitless spectroscopy. A key hydrogen line that traces dust obscured star formation can now be mapped at cosmic noon. Data from two survey programs are combined for thirty-one galaxies. Dust obscured and unobscured tracers are compared directly for the first time.

Stacked emission maps in three stellar mass bins yield brightness and equivalent width profiles. Both tracers rise with radius across all masses, giving direct evidence for inside out galaxy growth. Obscured and unobscured growth share that pattern on the main sequence. Resolved maps move beyond global rates to where stars actually form inside young galaxies.
arxiv-2511-15992:
Shahin Zanbaghi and three co-authors present a real time system to detect sleeper agents in large language models through semantic drift analysis. Sleeper models behave safely in training but turn malicious under deployment triggers. Prior work showed such backdoors survive safety training, yet practical detectors were missing. Their dual method compares response meaning against safe baselines continuously.

Sentence embeddings measure semantic deviation from baseline behavior. Injected canary questions monitor response consistency as a second signal. On an official sleeper agent model, the combined system reports high accuracy with no false positives in tests. Detection runs in under a second per query without modifying the model. The approach offers deployers a first practical screening layer against hidden backdoors.
arxiv-2511-16092:
Xing Hu, Raula Gaikovina Kula, and Christoph Treude report a meeting of thirty-three experts on the future of development environments with AI foundation models. Generative models now generate code, tests, reviews, and repairs with strong results. Higher abstraction away from hand written code could transform how programmers interact with their tools. Experts from software engineering, AI, and human computer link met to map challenges and opportunities.

Discussions at the Shonan meeting examined what integrated development environments become when AI is a collaborator. Link design, trust, and workflow change are central themes alongside raw capability. The report records consensus and open questions from the gathering.
