A common craft in AI research names the idea a single neuron seems to track, like a curve or a face part. The naming tools work well in practice, yet no proof said when a name is faithful or steady.

The team recasts naming as learning run in reverse, which lets them bound how well a name should hold on new data. They also add a resampling ensemble that returns a set of candidate names with a stated coverage promise. Tests on fake and real data support the bounds. The work gives neuron naming a firmer base for safety checks.
arxiv-2512-18192:
Alex Foo, Wynne Hsu, and Mong Li Lee at the National University of Singapore tackle object centric learning, where a vision model discovers objects and parts from images on its own. Most methods encode part whole relations only implicitly, through indirect training goals. The learned objects then fall apart when parts are occluded or scenes shift out of distribution. Their 2025 method represents parts explicitly as a graph.

A co-part discovery algorithm finds the parts and how they group into whole objects. The team adds three benchmarks testing recognition of multi part objects under occlusion and distribution shift. Across simulated, realistic, and real world images, it beats leading alternatives on discovered object quality. It recognizes multi part objects accurately in the hard occluded and shifted settings. The learned representations also predict key object properties better downstream, supporting explicit structure as the way forward for robust vision.
arxiv-2512-18292:
Wenkai Li and three coauthors grade how people and AI models bargain in the board game Diplomacy. Past studies scored who won. This one scores how players talk: which tactics, from warmth to pressure, show up line by line in the deal making chats that drive the game.

A language model judge tagged a large set of human games with a tactic list drawn from social science, and the tags proved steady on two data sets. Certain tactics tracked well with winning. AI players bargained in measurably different styles from humans, but fine tuning pulled their talk closer to human habits. Style, the work shows, can be measured, not just felt.
arxiv-2512-18392:
Davide Bason and four co-authors work on quantum field theory, the framework physics uses for particles and fields. Their December 2025 arXiv paper defines a regularized free energy for massive quantum field theories living in anti-de Sitter space, a curved space with a boundary. They conjecture that this quantity always decreases along renormalization group flow, the process that links a theory's behavior at different energy scales.

The claim extends a known boundary result, the F-theorem, to theories that are not conformal. The team tests the idea in several examples and proves it in two dimensions. They also apply it to long-range critical points, deriving bounds on the sphere free energy of three-dimensional Ising models. Such monotonic quantities help physicists rule out impossible flows between theories.
arxiv-2512-18592:
In a companion 2025 study, Marios Papamichalis and Regina Ruane build a network model that sees structure at many resolutions at once. Real networks mix large scale organization with local departures, and nodes often carry known positions, such as genome coordinates in Hi-C maps or geography in village networks. Standard models each capture one view: block models find coarse groups, latent space models find global geometry. None gives a canonical multi scale description.

Their wavelet latent position exponential random graphs express the log odds of a link in wavelet coordinates, indexed by resolution and location. Multiscale structure then becomes sparse and readable. Truncating the expansion yields an exponential family whose statistics are wavelet interaction counts, with maximum entropy form. That allows likelihood based regularization and testing directly in coefficient space. The theory covers broad logistic graphon classes, near minimax estimation under multiscale sparsity, and scale indexed recovery thresholds.
arxiv-2512-18692:
Jongmin Park and five co-authors speed up 3D scene reconstruction from photos. Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting builds a renderable 3D model in one pass. But it tends to spray out far too many Gaussian primitives when many views are available, with no dial to control the count. Their framework, EcoSplat, posted to arXiv in December 2025, adds exactly that dial.

Training runs in two stages. Pixel-aligned Gaussian Training teaches first predictions. Importance-aware Gaussian Finetuning then teaches the model two skills: rank primitives, and reshape them to hit any target count requested at run time. Across dense-view tests, EcoSplat stays robust and beats leading methods under strict primitive budgets. For graphics teams, a controllable primitive count means one model can serve both high-end rendering and tight mobile budgets.
arxiv-2512-18792:
Maxime Méloux and three co-authors warn that AI interpretability has a dead salmon problem. Neuroscientists once found 'brain activity' in a dead fish because their statistics were sloppy; the authors argue explanation tools can similarly find meaningful patterns in random neural networks. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, examines feature attribution, probing, sparse autoencoders, and causal analyses that all risk this trap.

Their prescription is to treat explanations as statistical estimates. An interpretability method infers parameters of a model from computational traces, so its claims should face explicit alternative hypotheses with quantified uncertainty. They stress identifiability: some popular questions may not have unique answers at all. Placing interpretability inside standard statistical inference, they argue, is how a field full of plausible stories becomes a rigorous science.
arxiv-2512-18992:
Kshitiz Mallick and seven co-authors mapped dust glow from a long filament in the northern Orion B cloud. They used the POL-2 camera on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope at a wavelength of 850 microns. The filament holds eight dense cores, from starless ones to cores already forming stars.

Polarized light shows how magnetic fields thread the gas. The team found polarization falls as gas gets denser, dropping near the thick core centers. Fields in the young protostellar cores line up with the local filament field, unlike the older prestellar cores. Field strength estimates help explain how the filament breaks into cores.
arxiv-2512-19092:
Ziyan Zhang, Chao Wang, Zhuo Chen, and Lei Chen answer complex logic questions over knowledge graphs with the help of a language model. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked entities, yet real graphs are incomplete. Embedding methods handle simple queries well but falter on long chains and mixed graph layouts.

Their framework, ROG, breaks a first-order logic query into simpler sub-queries. It pulls a small, relevant subgraph for each part, then lets a language model reason step by step over that evidence. No task-specific embedding training is needed. On standard benchmarks, ROG beat strong embedding baselines, which the authors credit to pairing retrieval with careful reasoning.
arxiv-2512-19492:
M. Lampani, M. Rossi, S. Guastavino, and M. Piana forecast when a coronal mass ejection will reach Earth, using machine learning steered by a physics model. Such plasma storms threaten satellites and power grids, so arrival times matter. Pure physics is slow, pure data fitting is opaque, and hybrids have led the field.

The base hybrid leans on the classic drag model, which assumes one kind of interplanetary slowdown. Swapping in an extended drag model lets training include storms whose motion breaks the classic assumptions. Accuracy matched the state of the art, and the method stayed steady when the drag coefficient wobbled. A speed-based grouping of storms rounds out the work.
arxiv-2512-19592:
Hunting for very light dark matter, the XENON Collaboration combined data from two underground detectors, XENON1T and XENONnT. Both use liquid xenon chambers that watch for tiny recoils when particles strike the xenon. Ordinary halo dark matter this light would hit too softly to notice, so the team looked for particles boosted by bouncing off the Sun, a route called solar reflection.

By adding electron-scattering signals, lowering detection thresholds, and using the extra energy from solar boosting, the search rules out previously open ground. For masses in two low ranges, the team excludes dark matter-electron cross sections down to a stated minimum at 90 percent confidence. The limits tighten what future low-mass searches must beat.
arxiv-2512-19692:
Pablo Ruiz-Ponce and four colleagues built Interact2Ar, a generator for two people moving together, hands included. Earlier motion generators often skipped hands entirely and produced whole sequences at once, which flattens the reactive, back-and-forth quality of real interaction. Data limits and learning difficulty pushed prior work toward those shortcuts.

Interact2Ar is text-conditioned and autoregressive, generating motion step by step with a diffusion model, while dedicated parallel branches handle detailed hand kinematics. A memory technique with large context windows lets it adapt as interactions unfold. The design supports follow-on uses like composing motion over time, reacting to disturbances in real time, and scaling beyond pairs to groups. New evaluators and metrics for full-body interaction back claims of state-of-the-art quality.
arxiv-2512-20092:
Yiming Du leads a thirteen-author team teaching chatbots to remember time properly. Across long, multi-session talks, today's long-context models lose track. They miss which past sessions bear on a when question. Noise piles up, and reasoning fails. Memory-T1 learns what to keep, with reinforcement learning. It sweeps the talk history in a coarse-to-fine pass.

Filters on time and relevance first prune the history to candidates. A learned selector then picks the exact evidence sessions. Its rewards cover answer accuracy, grounding in evidence, and time consistency at two levels. On the Time-Dialog benchmark, Memory-T1 set a new open-source best with a seven-billion-parameter model. It beat a fourteen-billion baseline by a clear margin. It stayed sound at one hundred twenty-eight thousand tokens, where baselines collapsed.
arxiv-2512-20292:
Wenzheng Zeng, Mingyu Ouyang, Langyuan Cui, and Hwee Tou Ng tackle a personalization gap in automatic slide making. Tools that turn research papers into slides usually ignore who the slides are for, so one-size output often misses a user's taste. Their system, SlideTailor, conditions generation on preferences the user shows rather than describes.

The user supplies one example paper-and-slides pair plus a visual template, and the approach infers style and content preferences from them. Slides are then generated progressively in editable form, matched to the new paper. A chain-of-speech mechanism aligns slide content with the planned spoken narration, which also enables video presentations. A new benchmark with interpretable metrics lets the authors verify that personalization actually improves the output.
arxiv-2512-20392:
Marcus Kühn, Lisa Sauermann, Raphael Steiner, and Yuval Wigderson present a construction they say disproves the odd Hadwiger conjecture. Gerards and Seymour proposed the conjecture in 1993, linking a graph's chromatic number to the odd minors it must contain. Odd minors are a restricted way of shrinking a graph while keeping a parity condition.

The authors exhibit graphs with no complete graph as an odd minor yet with chromatic number at least about one and a half times the excluded size. That gap is far larger than the conjecture allowed, so the disproof is strong rather than marginal. The result closes a thirty-year-old question in graph theory and redirects work on how colouring relates to minor structure.
arxiv-2512-21292:
Joyful Mdhluli, writing for the International Astronomical Union's Office of Astronomy for Development, sets out how the office disciplines its good intentions. Astronomy-for-development projects take many forms: telescopes in schools, training programs, science outreach in underserved regions. They can only justify their funding if someone checks what actually works, for whom, and under what conditions. The office's answer is an Impact Cycle: a loop connecting project design, selection, and delivery to evaluation.

Evidence gathered from finished projects feeds the design of new ones, so each generation builds on recorded lessons rather than enthusiasm. That feedback loop is meant to cut the risk of unintended harm, raise the odds of cost-effective impact, and accumulate a library of best practice that includes records of what failed. Development funders and science-outreach managers gain an example of treating charitable activity with the same empirical rigor as the science it promotes.
arxiv-2512-21592:
Eugene Levin works on high-energy scattering in quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force. At very high energies, gluon exchange between two colliding dipoles follows Pomeron calculus, where interactions build fan diagrams and closed Pomeron loops. Capturing those loops requires a nonlinear equation for dipole densities.

Levin shows the fan diagrams are the natural solution of the dipole density equations. He obtains the densities by matching an analytic solution of the Balitsky-Kovchegov equation, with a simple kernel, against t-channel unitarity. With them he computes what large Pomeron loops contribute to dipole-dipole scattering. Applying the Abramovsky-Gribov-Kancheli cutting rules, he finds the produced gluons follow the Koba-Nielsen-Olesen law. That law leads to an entropy formula matching earlier predictions by Kharzeev and Levin, tying it to the thermodynamics of particle output.
arxiv-2512-21692:
Albert Barreiro, Gloria Haro, and their co-authors present ShinyNeRF, a method for scanning objects whose surfaces bounce light unevenly by direction. Neural radiance fields are a leading tool for 3D capture of heritage objects. Standard versions fail on anisotropic specular surfaces, such as brushed metal, where highlights stretch along the brushing.

ShinyNeRF handles both plain reflections and stretched, direction-bound ones in a single framework. It jointly estimates the surface normals and tangents, how tight the highlight is, and how strong the stretch is, using a distribution built for directional reflections. The outgoing light is approximated by a learned mixture of simpler distributions, which keeps the model trainable. In tests the method reaches top quality on such surfaces. It also gives parameters with physical meaning, so materials can be inspected and edited. For heritage work, that editability matters: a conservator can adjust an artifact's shine without rescanning.
arxiv-2512-21792:
Hyam Omar Ali, Ahmed Fahal, and a large international team report a challenge on using AI to diagnose the disease mycetoma from microscope images. Mycetoma is a neglected tropical disease, caused by fungi or bacteria, that destroys tissue and disables patients, mostly in poor rural areas. Diagnosis is a bottleneck because experts are scarce where the disease is common.

The mAIcetoma challenge, held with the MICCAI 2024 conference, asked teams to segment its grains in histopathology images and classify its type. Organizers provided a standard dataset, called MyData, so entries could be compared fairly. Five finalist teams finished with deep learning designs. All achieved high segmentation accuracy, marking grain detection as the key first step. The best models also classified types well. The overview argues that such shared benchmarks can move automated testing toward clinics that lack specialists.
arxiv-2512-22092:
Bo-Ting Chen, Wei-Ming Chen, Yu-tin Huang, Zi-Xun Huang, and Yohan Liu study the analytic structure of wavefunction coefficients in flat spacetime, with special attention to fermions. Wavefunction coefficients describe how likely a field configuration is, and their poles in energy variables follow strict rules. The authors derive cutting rules for internal fermion lines, a missing piece for checking those forms.

Building on the rules, they set up an iterative procedure that starts from the flat-space scattering matrix and rebuilds three- and four-point coefficients. The reconstruction carries the correct partial- and total-energy poles and obeys the cutting rules throughout. Their conclusion is crisp: the four-particle test adds no new constraints beyond what consistency of the flat-space scattering matrix already demands.
arxiv-2512-22192:
Jiahao Lu investigates what common training tricks really do to a neural network's internal preferences for pattern frequencies. Weight decay and dropout are standard regularizers, yet their effects on which frequencies a network learns were poorly understood. Lu builds a visual diagnostic system that tracks how weight frequencies evolve during training, and defines a Spectral Suppression Ratio to measure each regularizer's low-pass filtering strength.

Tests with ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 show weight decay suppresses high-frequency energy buildup more than threefold compared with unregularized training. A trade-off emerges: weight-decayed models suffer more under broad Gaussian noise but resist high-frequency information loss, beating baselines by over six percent on blurred images. The results present generalization as a strong bias toward low-frequency structure.
arxiv-2512-22592:
Vladimir Vatutin and Elena Dyakonova prove limit theorems for populations that reproduce at exactly replacement rate while their environment turns extremely hostile. The model is a critical branching process in a random environment. Each generation's reproduction law is drawn at random. The process is tracked alongside its associated random walk, which records the cumulative environmental drift.

The authors assume the walk's increments, without centering, fall in the domain of attraction of an alpha-stable law. They then describe the long-run distribution of the population size under two demanding conditions. The process must still be alive at a late time. Its associated walk must also stay below a fixed constant. Such conditional limit theorems capture how rare survivors behave in environments stacked against them.
arxiv-2512-22692:
André Martins poses a basic question for machine learning: must learned representations live in ordinary real-number spaces? Nearly all current methods use real vector spaces, where distance, projection, and gradient tools feel natural. Martins studies the p-adic numbers instead, a number system where closeness is measured by divisibility by a prime, giving a branching, tree-like geometry well suited to hierarchies.

The paper builds first building blocks for classification, regression, and representation learning over the p-adics, with concrete models and algorithms. A small semantic network of the kind proposed by Quillian fits neatly into a compact p-adic linear network, a trick the reals cannot match. The author closes by listing open problems and arguing that this strange geometry could become a useful home for hierarchical data.
arxiv-2512-22992:
Tanmoy Pati, Narayan Rana, and V. Ravindran compute a set of three-loop corrections to the quark form factor, the quantity describing how a quark responds to an electromagnetic probe. The corrections mix the strong and electroweak forces at a specific order, two powers of the strong coupling and one of the electromagnetic coupling. Only the non-singlet parts are treated, and the results are fully analytic.

The main obstacle is the massive W and Z bosons running inside the loops, which make the standard reduction of Feynman integrals far heavier and complicate solving them. After ultraviolet renormalization and subtraction of the universal infrared divergences, the finite remainder is expressed through harmonic and generalized polylogarithms. Such precision calculations feed into predictions for collider observables, where comparing theory with data at the third loop order tests the Standard Model at its sharpest.
arxiv-2512-23192:
Zhuo Zhang and co-authors present PGOT, a transformer designed to solve partial differential equations on large, irregular meshes with complex geometry. Transformers hold promise as equation solvers, but shrinking feature dimensions to save computation smears out boundary detail, a failure the authors call geometric aliasing. PGOT is built to keep that physical and geometric information explicit while staying efficient.

Its attention module, SpecGeo-Attention, injects multi-scale geometric encodings through a physics slicing mechanism and preserves spectral detail at linear computational cost. The network also routes work adaptively: smooth regions of a flow take cheap low-order linear paths, while shocks and discontinuities are sent down high-order nonlinear paths, chosen by spatial location. Across four standard benchmarks PGOT reached state-of-the-art accuracy, and it performed strongly on large industrial tasks including airfoil and automobile design, where geometry is exactly what cannot be blurred away.
arxiv-2512-23492:
Christophe Paul and Ignaz Rutter solve a recognition problem for circle graphs, the intersection graphs of chords of a circle: given a graph, decide whether it can be drawn that way. The fastest previous algorithm ran in almost linear time, held back by a split decomposition step that needed a union-find data structure.

The authors show that for circle graphs, a different tool, the PC-tree, can supply the split decomposition directly in linear time. Swapping the data structure removes the bottleneck entirely. The result is the first recognition algorithm for circle graphs that runs in strictly linear time in the size of the graph. The work is slated to appear at STACS 2026, a leading theoretical computer science symposium.
arxiv-2512-23592:
Damiano Marsili, Aditya Mehta, Ryan Lin, and Georgia Gkioxari target a blind spot of vision-language models: they recognize broad categories well but miss fine visual details and fall back on biases. Training data shares the blame, since it usually asks only coarse questions, such as whether a picture shows a cat or a dog.

Their answer is TWIN, a data set of more than half a million pairs of similar images, each asking whether the two pictures show the same object. Fine-tuning on TWIN sharpened fine-grained recognition even in domains the training never covered, including art, animals, plants, and landmarks. A new benchmark, FGVQA, with twelve thousand queries, confirmed gains of up to about nineteen percent while general question-answering performance held steady. Scale, their analysis shows, drives the improvement.
arxiv-2512-23692:
Ritoban Datta and Abhijit Majumder ask whether the hadronic stage of a heavy-ion collision still matters for jet quenching. The energy loss of fast partons plowing through the hot medium created in the collision. Partons scatter off the medium's own partonic structure, radiating energy and kicking medium particles. Most calculations focus on the hottest, purely partonic phase.

Working inside the JETSCAPE framework with two event generators, the authors modify the thermal distributions by a simple temperature-dependent factor in the quarks' and gluons' dispersion relations. Transport coefficients then fall off naturally as the system cools into the hot hadronic gas, instead of stopping abruptly. Combined with cold nuclear matter effects on the incoming nuclei, the extended calculation describes jet and hadron suppression and elliptic flow across many collision systems and energies at once.
arxiv-2512-24292:
Joaquim Borges, Josep Rifà, and Victor Zinoviev classify error-correcting codes with two strong properties. A maximum distance separable code corrects as many errors as its length allows. A completely regular code has a highly uniform distance structure. The paper asks when a code enjoys both properties at once.

For lengths one or two beyond the field size, the classification is complete. Codes that are completely regular, or at least uniformly packed in the wide sense, are all pinned down. Shorter lengths over small fields get a full treatment too. For fields of size up to five, all nontrivial codes are listed up to equivalence. The ternary Hamming code is the sole example over the three-element field. None exist over the two-element field. Two gaps in an older classification also close. They concern self-dual completely regular codes over specific fields.
arxiv-2512-24392:
Jeongjin Lee and Jennifer Wadsworth give geometric tests for extreme dependence. The geometric theory of extremes watches scaled data clouds settle onto a limit set. A gauge function describes that set. Its shape decides how the extremes of two variables relate. A blunt limit set means the variables decouple at extremes. A non-blunt one was ambiguous until now.

Focusing on two variables, the authors close the gap. Under a truncated gamma model with bounded angular density, a pointy limit set forces dependence at extremes. That yields practical criteria for sorting dependence classes. Flexible gauge models add the applied side. Two additive mixtures interpolate smoothly between the two regimes. Their explicit forms and properties are derived. Simulations compare the approach with existing methods. It stays efficient and reliable across scenarios.
arxiv-2601-00192:
Moirangthem Tiken Singh and coauthor Manibhushan Yaikhom detect heart rhythm faults with a model small enough for tiny sensors. Deep learning rivals are accurate but heavy. Edge medical devices cannot carry that cost. Their answer is data centric design. Careful feature work replaces model bulk. The goal is data that a simple classifier can split.

Wavelet features capture time and frequency shape together. Graph descriptors add structural clues like PageRank centrality. Mutual information and recursive cuts then prune the set. What remains feeds an ultra light linear classifier. Two standard datasets give diagnostic accuracy near ninety eight percent. The model file stays under nine kilobytes. Each beat is handled well within real time needs. The authors claim a tenfold efficiency gain over compressed rivals. Battery free cardiac sensors move a step closer.
arxiv-2601-00792:
Luca Trinchão and a team of eleven report the first observation of color symmetry breaking in a tiny optical ring. Symmetry breaking, where a system spontaneously chooses an uneven state, appears everywhere from particle physics to animal flocks. In their integrated silicon nitride microring, two light fields at different wavelengths interact through the Kerr effect, where light changes the material it passes through.

Above a threshold power as low as nineteen milliwatts, the two colors spontaneously develop an imbalance in power instead of staying equal. Studying the device's uniform states, the team also built a nonlinear activation generator that mimics response curves used in neural networks, including sigmoid and leaky rectified shapes. The findings open new behavior for photonic computing elements.
arxiv-2601-01192:
Counting people in video sounds simple until a crowd surges through a metro station. Hao Lu and four co-authors work on video individual counting, which must match the same person across frames to measure flow, not just tally heads in each frame. Crowding, blocking, and fast motion break the usual one-to-one matching.

The team releases WuhanMetroCrowd, a new data set of crowded metro flows with wide ranges of density, speed, and blocking. Their model, OMAN++, uses two facts about people: they walk in social groups, and they cannot teleport. Grouping lets the matcher link one person to several candidates; a displacement check enforces the second fact. The model beats prior methods on three standard benchmarks and cuts error by about thirty-eight percent on the new metro set. Transit planners could use such counts to spot crush points before they turn dangerous.
arxiv-2601-01292:
Ghaba and 4 co-authors work out how entanglement spreads among three linked harmonic oscillators. Such systems, like masses joined by springs at the quantum level, are basic models for linked quantum parts. Exact results are rare once three parts are involved, so the team uses a geometric method to cut down the free angles.

They derive formulas for measures of mixing and purity for each way of splitting the three parts into two sides. Raising the excitation of any one part tends to share links more widely across the whole system. One mixing angle controls strength, running from no link at all to the strongest possible correlation.
arxiv-2601-01692:
Conformal prediction wraps a machine learning model with a guarantee: its prediction sets contain the true answer with a chosen probability. Erfan Hajihashemi and Yanning Shen address a weakness of using one fixed model in changing, online settings, where the best model may differ from one time step to the next.

Earlier multi-model approaches grew expensive as candidate models multiplied, and weak models in the pool dragged results down. The authors' algorithm builds a bipartite graph at each step to pick out a subset of effective models, then selects one for the prediction set. Experiments show smaller prediction sets at lower computing cost than existing multi-model methods, making guaranteed uncertainty estimates more practical for streaming data.
arxiv-2601-01792:
NAVER Cloud's HyperCLOVA X team reports HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni. It is the first model in its family to take text, audio, and vision in. It can also produce any of them back. Separate single-purpose systems are not chained together.

All three modes share one next-token prediction interface. It works over an interleaved sequence. Vision and audio encoders feed in continuous embeddings. Those support fine-grained understanding and grounding. Evaluations show performance competitive with similar-sized models across many input-output combinations, in Korean and English alike. Released as open weights at the eight-billion-parameter scale, the model is offered as a practical pathfinder toward assistants that hear, see, speak, and write in one system.
arxiv-2601-01892:
Personalized image generators learn one concept after another, but each new concept tends to erase earlier ones, a failure called catastrophic forgetting. Arjun Ramesh Kaushik and four co-authors propose learning from parents: older concepts actively guide the learning of new ones through relationships arranged in hyperbolic space.

Their framework, FLLP, embeds concepts on a Lorentzian manifold whose geometry naturally fits tree-like hierarchies, so parent concepts shelter their children while new ones are integrated. Tests on three public datasets and one synthetic benchmark show consistent gains in robustness and generalization over methods that merely reduce interference between concepts. Treating prior knowledge as a teacher rather than a rival is the paper's central idea.
arxiv-2601-02092:
Split federated learning trains models across edge devices with wildly different computing power and network links, and the slowest device usually sets the pace. Abdullah Al Asif, Sixing Yu, Juan Pablo Munoz, Arya Mazaheri, and Ali Jannesari propose SuperSFL, built on a weight-sharing super-network that spins off a right-sized subnetwork for each client.

A three-phase gradient fusion scheme coordinates the work. Local updates, server computation, and gradient merging all feed it. Training converges faster as a result. A fault-tolerant classifier and collaborative aggregation help too. They keep training alive through communication dropouts. On CIFAR benchmarks, up to one hundred clients took part. They were heterogeneous. The system converged two to five times faster in communication rounds. Total communication cost fell up to twentyfold. Energy efficiency improved over baseline split learning.
arxiv-2601-02292:
Alessia Mapelli and three co authors present a method for mapping how brain areas interact, and how those links change from person to person. The data are EEG recordings, electric signals measured at the scalp over time. Links between areas matter for research and diagnosis, but they shift with age, mental state, and illness, so a single average map is not enough.

Their approach selects neighbors region by region inside a Gaussian functional graphical model, using regression that can take in age, clinical status, or other traits, whether continuous or grouped. The output is easy to read, since each link comes with a sign for whether it strengthens or weakens as a trait grows. Simulations and a real EEG study show clear gains over older methods.
arxiv-2601-02592:
Lycka Drakengren proves a structural result in algebraic geometry about the Torelli map, which sends a curve to the abelian variety built from it.

The fiber product of that map with any product map between moduli spaces of abelian varieties. Where the dimensions add up to the total genus, is shown to have a reduced scheme structure, with no hidden nilpotent thickening. As a consequence, the pullback of the product class into the Chow group of the moduli space of curves is tautological. And it vanishes outright when its codimension exceeds a bound set by the genus.
arxiv-2601-02792:
Petteri Teikari and Neliana Fuenmayor introduce Textile IR, a shared intermediate representation that connects the separate software worlds of fashion design. Pattern tools guarantee a garment can be sewn but know nothing about drape. Physics simulators predict drape but cannot fix a pattern. Sustainability tools sit apart again. Textile IR is designed as the semantic glue among manufacturing valid design, physics simulation, and lifecycle assessment.

A seven layer verification ladder runs from cheap syntactic checks, pattern closure and seam compatibility, up to expensive physics validation such as drape simulation and stress analysis. Feedback flows both ways, simulation failures suggest pattern changes, material swaps update environmental estimates in real time, and uncertainty travels through the pipeline with explicit confidence bounds. Garments become structured programs in a scene graph that AI systems can manipulate, rather than flat pixel pictures.
arxiv-2601-03292:
Adrian P. C. Lim presents an ambitious proposal that starts from loop quantum gravity and aims at a unified theory of everything. The route passes through Chern-Simons gauge theory, where Wilson loop observables define knot invariants of Jones polynomial type. It also passes through the Einstein-Hilbert theory of gravity. That theory is reformulated with a doubled SU(2) gauge group, so it can be quantized in four dimensions.

In that quantized gravity, area, volume, and curvature become quantum operators. Lim combines the Chern-Simons and Einstein-Hilbert actions into a single path integral. He computes the Wilson loop observable for a timelike hyperlink, with each loop colored by representations of the combined algebra. The paper is best read as one author's claimed path toward unification. It is presented in his own framework, rather than as an established result.
arxiv-2601-03392:
Matteo Dunnhofer, Christian Micheloni, and Kohitij Kar test whether video-capable neural networks finally capture how the primate brain processes moving scenes. Networks trained on still images dominate models of the ventral visual stream, but real vision is dynamic, and the macaque inferior temporal cortex encodes object motion during natural videos. The authors compare brain responses to naturalistic videos against static, recurrent, and video-based network models.

Video models did predict the neural responses somewhat better, especially at later stages, but only modestly, hence the title's verdict. A stress test sharpened the question: decoders trained on natural videos were tried on appearance-free variants that keep the motion but strip shape and texture. The results probe whether the networks' advantage reflects real dynamic computation or just frame features pooled over time.
arxiv-2601-03692:
Xing-Yi Ji and five co-authors study what role an excited particle called Sigma(1660) plays in a specific kaon-proton reaction. The reaction produces two neutral pions and a Sigma(0), and it also connects to producing the puzzling Lambda(1405) state. The team models both reactions with an effective Lagrangian approach, a standard framework that encodes interactions through chosen terms.

Alongside a background contribution from a nucleon pole term, they include Sigma(1660) as an intermediate resonance with stated spin and parity. With their parameters, calculations of total and differential cross sections match the available experimental data fairly well. The fit genuinely needs the Sigma(1660) contribution, they show, so these measurements can help pin down that resonance's properties, which remain debated in hadron physics.
arxiv-2601-03792:
Huynh Trung Kiet and five co-authors build VietMed-MCQ, a benchmark dataset for Vietnamese traditional medicine, a domain where language models weaken for lack of good test data. Their framework synthesizes multiple-choice questions through a retrieval-augmented pipeline and filters them with an automated consistency check. Two models independently verify answers, a dual validation meant to keep synthetic questions honest, though the authors note limits to their evidence checking.

The final dataset holds over three thousand questions across three difficulty levels. Validation by one medical expert and four students gave a high approval rate with substantial agreement among raters. The team benchmarked seven open-source models with it. Culturally specific medicine deserves its own evaluations, since general medical skill does not guarantee safe handling of local practice.
arxiv-2601-04692:
Naquee Rizwan and five co-authors tackle hateful memes as a moderation pipeline rather than a single classifier, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Real moderation needs three things — detecting the hateful meme, explaining why it is hateful, and intervening before posting. Yet research usually studies detection alone, and labelled meme data is too expensive to gather at scale. Their framework, PEST, is built for that scarcity.

PEST steers black-box vision-language models without opening them: task-specific generative models and few-shot prompting adapt the large models to different meme types, with detection, explanation, and intervention handled as one workflow. The authors describe the system as, to their knowledge, the first aimed at generalizable hateful meme moderation under limited data, and argue it is shaped for real production deployment. The abstract carries the authors' own warning that the paper contains potentially toxic example content, quoted for research purposes.
arxiv-2601-04792:
Video generation models produce striking clips, but running them is costly because each denoising step works at full resolution. Denis Korzhenkov and 4 co-authors present PyramidalWan in a 2026 paper. Pyramidal models split the process into stages at different resolutions, handling noisy early steps cheaply at low resolution. Earlier open pyramidal video models, trained from scratch, lagged behind on visual quality.

Instead of starting over, the authors convert a pretrained video model into pyramidal form. Their pipeline keeps the quality the original model already had while gaining the staged design's savings. Cheaper inference matters for anyone serving generated video, where each saved step lowers cost and waiting time per clip.
arxiv-2601-04892:
T. Torres and S. R. Dolan study how steady a black hole's ring of tones is when a weak mass sits near it in a 2026 paper. A black hole, when struck, rings with a set of tones that fade over time. It is known that a small bump in the force field near the hole can shift those tones a lot. Such a bump could come from a mate object or a disk of gas in orbit.

The pair test sharp, spike-like bumps, both weak and strong, in systems with round symmetry. One test case is the Nariai space-time, a known exact case. They ask how far the tones move, in both the straight-line and the more tangled views. The work bears on plans to read black hole tones from real wave data and use them to test how gravity works.
arxiv-2601-04992:
Xueyun Tian and 8 co-authors argue that failed reasoning attempts are training gold in a 2026 paper. Standard fine-tuning of language models keeps only chain-of-thought trajectories that end at the correct answer, discarding the rest. The authors contend that this practice throws away substantial supervision and worsens overfitting, limiting generalization outside the training domain, because wrong-answer trajectories often contain valid intermediate steps.

Adding negative trajectories to fine-tuning yields, in their tests, substantial gains in out-of-domain generalization over positive-only training. The finding challenges a routine data-filtering habit across the field. If mistakes teach robustness, training pipelines should curate failures carefully instead of deleting them, changing how reasoning datasets are built from now on.
arxiv-2601-05692:
Kathryn Nurse proves, in a solo 2026 paper, a special case of Bouchet's conjecture for signed graphs. The 1983 conjecture says every flow-admissible signed graph has a nowhere-zero six-flow. That means edge values from a small set can be assigned so that flow balances at every vertex, with no edge receiving zero.

Nurse settles the conjecture for cyclically five-edge-connected, cubic signed graphs. Cubic means every vertex has degree three, and the connectivity condition requires the graph to stay strongly linked around its cycles. Even this restricted case is a meaningful step, because signed-graph flows underpin wider questions in graph theory about how global balance can emerge from local constraints.
arxiv-2601-05892:
Irene Heinrich and 3 co-authors clarify in 2026 what the Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm can decide about graphs of small twin-width. Twin-width measures how controllably a graph can be contracted, and many problems simplify on bounded twin-width classes. Graph isomorphism, deciding whether two graphs are the same up to relabeling, resisted that simplification at twin-width four and above.

The authors show the three-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman refinement solves isomorphism for twin-width one graphs. No fixed dimension, however, suffices at twin-width four. They also prove a standing conjecture: stable graphs of twin-width two have bounded rank-width. That bound implies a fixed Weisfeiler-Leman dimension decides isomorphism for those graphs too, sharpening the map of where purely combinatorial refinement is enough.
arxiv-2601-06092:
Muhammad Aurangzeb Ahmad surveys Islamic chatbots built on large language models in a 2026 paper. Such chatbots are entering Muslim communities and changing how religious knowledge is reached, interpreted, and shared. Everyday practice and teaching both feel the shift.

On one side, the tools democratize access to religious knowledge for ordinary users. On the other, they risk eroding established authority, since a chatbot's answer carries no scholar's standing. Ahmad analyzes the current landscape of these systems and the challenges they raise for communities. The paper closes with recommendations for responsible design, aiming to keep the benefits while respecting the structures of learning and authority that these tools now bypass.
arxiv-2601-06292:
Benjamin Durkan and 2 co-authors compute a full asymptotic formula in a 2026 number theory paper about the Riemann zeta function. The zeta function sits at the heart of prime number theory. Its derivatives, evaluated at the function's zeros, carry information that researchers average to understand its behavior.

Earlier work by Gonek gave only the leading term for the discrete second moment of mixed derivatives at the zeros. Conrey, Snaith, and Milinovich later added lower-order terms for the first derivative alone. Durkan and colleagues extend the analysis to all derivatives at once. Their result supplies the complete asymptotic expansion, with error terms given both unconditionally and under standard assumptions. The mixed-derivative case closes a gap left by the single-derivative treatments.
arxiv-2601-06392:
Quantum tools that learn must not drop old skills when they learn new ones. Jun Qi and 5 co-authors built CL-QAS to stop that loss in a 2026 paper. It hunts for good circuit shapes for quantum tools, task by task, on the small quantum chips we have now.

A train-like code packs big, noisy signals into small quantum forms, so no costly load step is needed. Two loops split the work: one tunes the circuit's dials, one hunts for its shape. A brace step pins down key weights from old tasks, so new tasks can not wipe them out. Math bounds cap the error, the spread to new data, and the harm from noise. Tests on heart beat data and on price series showed clear gains in score. Gains flowed both ways, old tasks to new and new to old.
arxiv-2601-06692:
Murad Farzulla builds a math frame for snags in teamwork between agents in a 2026 paper. Agents must team up though their wants, stakes, and facts all differ. When team work fails, a drag shows up that can be gauged.

That drag takes forms such as deadlock, thrash, and too much talk. It can also flare into open clash between the agents at work. His frame grows from a single rule, which he calls the axiom of consent. Acts that touch an agent need that agent's leave, he holds. The leave owed grows with the size of the stakes in the act. One rule thus yields his whole study of drag in joint work. Those who build agent teams gain a way to price the cost of snags.
arxiv-2601-06892:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Jen-Hsu Chang and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers constructions of totally Non-Negative pfaffian. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The totally non-negative pfaffian (TNNP) is define for a skew-symmetric matrix such that all the sub-pfaffians are non-negative. It appears in the pfaffian structure of τ -function for the non-singular web solitons of the BKP equation .

One constructs TNNP using the Perfect matching, chord diagram and the Dyck paths enumeration. Its tridiagonal form is also investigated. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07092:
Yuliang Cai and three co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how self-driving cars can answer questions about a scene. The task is called Visual Question Answering, or VQA. A car takes in camera views and a text query. It must grasp what is near it and reply in words. The team's pipeline squeezes each scene down to key zones to save time.

Speed is the hard part of VQA on the road. A car must reply at once, with no lag. A late reply can put lives at risk. Past tools tend to scan the whole scene at full size. That scan eats time the car does not have. By working on squeezed zones of the scene, the new pipeline aims to keep replies fast. It still aims to keep the car aware of what counts for safe travel.
arxiv-2601-07392:
Alexandre Tuel and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with OceanSAR-2. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The authors present OceanSAR-2, the second generation of our foundation model for SAR-based ocean observation.

Building on our earlier release, which pioneered self-supervised learning on Sentinel-1 Wave Mode data. OceanSAR-2 relies on improved SSL training and dynamic data curation strategies, which enhances performance while reducing training cost. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07592:
C. J. Clark and colleagues time gamma-ray pulsars with a sampling method borrowed from statistics. Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth like lighthouse light. Precise timing of Fermi telescope data can reveal many effects. These include timing noise in young pulsars and orbital changes in redback binary systems. Timing can even probe the background of gravitational waves. Their 2026 preprint uses Gibbs sampling.

Gibbs sampling explores complex probability models by updating one piece at a time. Pulsar timing models have many linked parameters, which makes direct fitting hard. A sampling approach can map the full range of plausible values instead of one best fit. The method matters for pulsar timing arrays, which hunt very low-frequency gravitational waves. Astronomers need timing they can trust at extreme precision.
arxiv-2601-07892:
Hong Huang and colleagues quantize language model weights to just three values, efficiently. Large models strain the memory of edge devices. Ternary quantization reduces weights to minus one, zero, and plus one. Current implementations, though, misalign with ordinary hardware. Their 2026 preprint, Sherry, adds fine-grained sparsification to reach an effective 1.25 bits per weight.

Sparsification means many weights become zero and can be skipped. Fine-grained control keeps the important weights while dropping the rest in hardware-friendly patterns. The aim is models that fit phones and embedded devices without losing much quality. Hardware efficiency decides whether a quantization scheme gets used at all. The paper serves machine learning engineers deploying models at the edge. It treats the hardware layout as part of the algorithm.
arxiv-2601-07992:
Alexander Eliseev and Sergei Seleznev question backtests that grade language models on data they already trained on. Economists now apply language models to tasks like macroeconomic forecasting. They often backtest the models, even though training data include the same period being forecast. The authors call their check fake date tests. Their 2026 discussion paper asks whether in-sample accuracy of such forecasts can be trusted. The results are presented as preliminary, to invite feedback.

A model that memorized past news can look prophetic without forecasting skill. Fake dates expose that by moving the claimed present. Honest evaluation matters before models inform economic decisions. The paper serves economists adopting language models and evaluators who audit them. It supplies a simple test that separates memory from genuine prediction. The authors publish through a discussion series for working papers.
arxiv-2601-08092: Wesley Quaresma Cota and Luiz Henrique de Souza Matos wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on algebras with a superinvolution, over a field of characteristic zero. For an algebra A, the star-codimensions form a list of counts, one for each step n from one on. Each count gauges how many polynomial identities the algebra obeys at that step. The authors focus on growth of these counts as a square, and on minimal varieties of unitary algebras with superinvolution.
arxiv-2601-08192:
Md. Faiyaz Abdullah Sayeedi and six co-authors propose a self-improving agent framework for medical imaging. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that large vision-language models now drive much medical image analysis. Most systems still act as single-pass black boxes with weak control over reasoning and grounding.

The framework follows four steps named in its title: route, retrieve, reflect, and repair. Each step adds a check that a single pass lacks. The design targets visual detection joined with linguistic reasoning about the image. For clinical readers, the value lies in spatial grounding and safety checks. A system that can revisit its own answer is easier to audit before use.
arxiv-2601-08392: Maddalena Genzini and five co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a quantum random number generator built on a chip. The design is semi-device-independent, so it needs just a bit of trust in the gear. It rests on a breach of a contextuality inequality, in KCBS form. Two silicon photonic chips form the system. One chip holds a heralded single-photon source. The other holds a mesh that can be reset to guide light. The mesh sets up qutrit states and takes the reads the KCBS test needs.
arxiv-2601-09292:
Greta Dolcetti, Giulio Zizzo, and Sergio Maffeis test how safe tool call agents are in the wild. Such an agent can call soft tools, such as mail or files, from a chat ask. A foe can craft an ask that bends a call to harm. The team runs four open models that claim tool skill, and hits them with three attack types.

They then test eight guards on those attacks. Their score is stark. The models are not safe by default, the team finds. And the guards are not yet fit for real use. A reader who ships tool agents gets a hard check list. It shows which guards help a bit, and where all of them still fail.
arxiv-2601-09392:
Albrecht Böttcher and Ilya M. Spitkovsky revisit a formula for the spectral radius of the Bell-CHSH operator. Their 2026 arXiv paper extends a result of Yuki Fujii and Toyohiro Tsurumaru. The operator comes from the CHSH test, a standard probe of quantum entanglement and nonlocality.

Fujii and Tsurumaru proved their formula on finite-dimensional spaces and sketched a method for infinite dimensions. Böttcher and Spitkovsky give a proof of the original formula that works in all dimensions at once. A unified proof removes the need for dimension-by-dimension approximation tricks. It also firms up a quantity used to bound quantum correlations.
arxiv-2601-09492:
Kaiming Cui and seven co-authors chart how common small close-in planets are around Sun-like stars. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses data from the TESS space telescope. It counts planets with orbits of half a day to sixteen days and sizes from two to twenty Earth radii, around FGK main-sequence stars.

Occurrence rates show how often nature builds each kind of planet. Close-in planets test ideas about how planets form and drift inward. The authors carry out a detailed analysis of the rates across size and orbit length. A clean census like this guides the next round of formation models.
arxiv-2601-09592:
Vincenzo Amato, Carlo Nitsch, Cristina Trombetti, and Federico Villone study how a shape trades off three classic measures. Their 2026 arXiv paper links a region's lowest vibration tone, its stiffness under twisting, and the length of its edge. The three are known as the first Dirichlet eigenvalue, the torsional rigidity, and the perimeter.

The authors optimize the product of eigenvalue and torsional rigidity among sets of fixed perimeter. They treat both general open sets of finite perimeter and convex domains. Results like these guide design work where stiffness and pitch must be balanced at once. The product turns out to be a sharp way to frame that balance.
arxiv-2601-09892:
Katherine Williams Booth, Alexander Nolte, and Yvon Verberne describe a group of maps of a surface by means of a graph. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with quasiconformal maps of a closed surface with at least two handles. These maps stretch shapes, but only in a controlled, bounded way that keeps them tame.

The authors show the group is the same as the symmetry group of a graph built from key closed curves on the surface. The graph carries a natural rough ordering, set by constants that grade how good each curve is. Turning a hard analytic group into graph symmetries makes it far easier to study with bare hands. The result links shape, space, and counting in a single clean object.
arxiv-2601-10092:
Jongseok Kim, Seongae Kang, Jonghwan Shin, Yuhan Lee, and Ohyun Jo join mixed health data to call a health risk. Clinics hold charts, lab facts, and wave signs from the body. Each type codes facts in its own way. A join must keep what each type says best.

Past joins tend to use one fixed blend. They merge types with a plain step. That can lose the strong suits of each type. The team made LeMoF, a join that works by levels. It guides how types meet at each level. The aim is a call that uses each type for what it does best.
arxiv-2601-10292:
Georgia Psychogiou and co authors built a sharp beam antenna with one feed. The antenna works at a set band near the mid range for new cell nets. It sends a beam with a round twist. That twist cuts loss from how a hand set is held.

Sharp beams oft need many feeds. This one uses two crossed strips. One strip is driven. One is a load with a set react term. Strong cross pull twixt the strips makes the beam sharp. The team tuned strip sizes to set that pull. The result is high gain from a small, one feed form.
arxiv-2601-10392:
Hassan Eshkiki and co authors fuse many frames of a cell film into one clean still. Glow based microscopy films live cells. The films are oft noisy. Glow can wax and wane in time. A single frame may miss a trait that the next frame shows.

The team project frames from many times into one image. Their frame keeps the true cell facts of the film. Noise drops as frames join. Traits that blink in time stay clear in the still. The work helps labs read live cell films with more trust. It also cuts the need to pick one best frame.
arxiv-2601-10592:
Delong Chen and co-authors present Action100M, a large dataset of human actions in video. Teaching machines to read actions from sight is a basic step toward machines that act in the real world. That needs big, open sets of labeled video across many domains. The team built their set from online how-to videos.

The dataset draws on 1.2 million internet instructional videos. People in such clips cook, build, fix, and play, so the action range is wide. Open labels let models learn acts beyond a fixed short list. The resource gives vision researchers fresh training data for action recognition in daily life scenes.
arxiv-2601-10692:
Alex M. Potts and a large team of co-authors study phase modes in superconductors held in tiny cavities. A superconductor's phase mode carries deep facts about pairing and energy loss. At low frequencies it is normally hidden by the Anderson-Higgs mechanism. Very thin samples, thinner than the London penetration depth, are the exception.

Such films support a gapless phase mode, the Cooper plasmon, whose path can be reshaped by a nearby screening layer. The team probes these modes at finite momentum inside terahertz microcavities. The work opens a way to watch pairing physics that was out of reach. It may inform new devices that use superconducting films at terahertz speeds.
arxiv-2601-10892:
A. Adhikari and co-authors probe magnons and phonons in arrays of nickel-iron nanodots. Magnons are waves of spin; phonons are waves of strain. Controlling how spin waves couple to strain is a rising theme for future spin-wave devices. The team uses all-optical excitation on ordered arrays of Ni80Fe20 nanomagnets.

They explore spin wave modes that interact with acoustic wave modes, plus a few modes that stay aloof. Light both drives and reads the motion, so no contacts are needed. Such arrays could route signals by spin instead of charge, saving energy. The work serves the spintronics community that designs these wave-based devices.
arxiv-2601-11092:
Leonardo Clarke and co-authors use emission lines to probe distant galaxies beyond cosmic noon. The team analyzes key rest-optical emission-line ratios in 763 galaxies, plus composite spectra from JADES DR3. The galaxies span redshifts from 1.4 to 7, deep into the early universe. Line ratios act as diagnostics of the gas that stars light up.

The ratios probe the ionizing spectrum of young stars and any alpha-element enhancement in the gas. Both trace how early galaxies formed stars and enriched their surroundings. JWST made such spectra routine at these distances. The work helps turn JWST's flood of spectra into a history of the first generations of galaxies.
arxiv-2601-11292:
Yiqi Zhou and seven coauthors build a compiler for compute-in-memory chips. Their 2026 preprint deals with SRAM-based designs that blur memory and math. AI workloads are heavy on data, and moving data costs most. That gap is the known memory wall that slows AI hardware.

Digital compute-in-memory with SRAM can scale to real workloads. But its design space is vast, too vast for hand design. A compiler that builds designs on its own is the fix. The team adds one more trick: approximate computing. AI tasks can take small errors with no real harm. Trading a bit of accuracy can save much energy in the chip.
arxiv-2601-11492:
Kaiwen Wang and eight coauthors build an AI strategy system for boxing. Their 2026 preprint names it BoxMind, a closed-loop expert system. Competitive sports need deep tactical analysis to win. Combat sports like boxing lag in AI-driven analytics so far.

Action dynamics in a bout are complex and fast. Tactical patterns lack a structured form for machines to use. BoxMind closes the loop from analysis to strategy choice. It was validated in elite boxing competition, the team reports. The test stage was the 2024 Olympic Games. A system proven at that level carries real weight. It hints at AI coaches for other combat sports as well.
arxiv-2601-11692:
Bennet Outland, Gretchen Noble, Andrew Smith, and Jack Lissauer test tight four-planet systems. Their 2026 preprint studies orbital stability in such systems. Each system holds four Earth-mass planets around one star. The star has one solar mass in the simulations.

Planets start on circular, coplanar orbits at set spacing. The innermost planet sits at 1 AU from the star. Later semimajor axes are spaced by mutual Hill radii. Equal Hill spacing packs the planets closely together. The team runs simulations to see how long order lasts. Closely spaced systems may collide or eject a planet. The results inform how packed real exoplanet systems can be.
arxiv-2601-11892:
Chao Wang gives a strict proof of a continued fraction claim for minus pi over four. The claim came from the Ramanujan Machine, a tool that guesses maths forms by search. A guess needs a proof to count as maths.

He uses linked rules for the Gauss hypergeometric function. Those rules show the claimed form is a cleaned form of a known ratio. The work turns a machine guess into a proved fact. It also shows how such guesses can be checked with care.  The proof gives the guess a firm place in maths.
arxiv-2601-11992:
Kari Kamtila, Joseph Dongho, Prosper Rosaire Mama Assandje, and Thomas Bouetou Bouetou study a class of free divisors that are not quasi-homogeneous. Divisors are sets cut out by a polynomial set to zero. In Saito's sense, free divisors have a tidy set of linked vector fields.

Their class uses a set sum of monomials with the product of coordinates. They look at duals of Saito's basis for these cases. They also give an application of the results. The work adds to the theory of singular spaces in complex geometry.  The basis work adds tools for divisor maths in this class.
arxiv-2601-12092:
Léon Brenig and Marc Vincke argue that one rule may sit under all of quantum mechanics. The rule is that the Heisenberg uncertainty bound stays the same under a group of special nonlinear gauge transforms. From that rule plus classical mechanics, they derive quantum rules for a free particle.

Their route yields most quantum postulates, such as the Born rule. The wave-function collapse rule does not come out of it. A single base rule would be a deep shift in how quantum theory is framed. The work sets out that claim in full.
arxiv-2601-12292: A team of theorists rank quantum correlations in a hybrid qubit-qutrit system with axial symmetry. The system feels axial and planar anisotropies, dipolar spin links, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya coupling. They use four gauges: negativity, two forms of nonlocality from uncertainty and measurement, and Bell nonlocality via CHSH. They track how anisotropy, fields, and heat shape the survival of each correlation kind. A ranked map shows which links are hardiest. Such maps guide the design of hybrid quantum devices. The work is in quantum information theory.
arxiv-2601-12492:
M. N. Mazziotta and a large ALICE team report test beam results for a new particle detector. The detector is planned for ALICE 3, a wholly new apparatus for later runs of the Large Hadron Collider. Its job is to identify charged particles at high energy. The design is a Ring Imaging Cherenkov detector with an aerogel radiator.

Its light sensing surface uses arrays of silicon photomultipliers in a proximity focusing layout. The device also has timing capabilities, per the title of the work. Test beam runs check how the prototype performs with real particle beams. Good timing plus ring images would give two handles on particle type at once. Results here guide the final design for the collider.
arxiv-2601-12592:
Dominik Kirst and Haoyi Zeng work in constructive reverse mathematics on a classic theorem of logic. The downward Lowenheim Skolem theorem says every infinite model has a countable elementary submodel. Over classical base theories, it is known to match the axiom of dependent choice. Constructive logic, which demands explicit constructions, allows a finer split of such claims.

The pair refine that known equivalence with care. Assuming only countable choice, they split the theorem into finer parts. One part is dependent choice, and another is a new fragment of the excluded middle. Their title names playful tools in the proof: blurred drinker paradoxes and blurred choice axioms. The work shows how constructive analysis can dissect a theorem brick by brick.
arxiv-2601-12692:
Miguel Cardenas applies dimensional analysis to experiments with Z pinch devices. A Z pinch uses a strong current to compress plasma into a thin column. The behavior of such discharges looks complex, with many variables at play. Cardenas shows it can be captured by only three dimensionless parameters.

Those three parameters can be arranged to draw a surface in three dimensional space. That surface compiles all accessible data on the macroscopic behavior of any discharge. Each possible Z pinch discharge maps to a point on the surface. A compact picture of this kind helps experimenters compare devices and plan runs. It also shows which combinations of settings can ever be reached.
arxiv-2601-12992:
Sujit Bhattacharyya works on gradient bounds for systems of weighted heat type equations. The setting is a weighted space with curved shape, known as a Riemannian manifold. The equations also carry an added term called a potential.

Bhattacharyya derives Bernstein type bounds for two such systems. He works through all the main cases in turn. One split is by the form of the potential, which may be linear or may grow fast. A second split is by the space itself, which may stay fixed or change over time. The work partly settles a question raised in an earlier paper by Bhattacharyya and co-authors.
arxiv-2601-13392:
Shlok Shelat, Jay Raval, Souvik Roy, and Manas Gaur test if language models truly reason or just recall on formal tasks. Such models score well on formal tongue tasks. That score may show true symbol sense or just match of known forms.

Their bench asks models to build finite automata, small state machines, from regular tongues. It holds fact asks and build tasks from public sources. It also holds two kinds of new tasks. Some are hand made with many valid builds. By set of known next to new, the bench splits recall from sense. For AI teams, that split is key to trust on logic tasks.
arxiv-2601-13492:
Eleanore B. Todd and co-authors probe the fringe of a rich galaxy cluster at redshift near two. The cluster is XLSSC 122. At that span, its light left when the universe was young. The team uses the Hubble Space Telescope to read it from its core out to three megaparsecs.

That span is ten times the core radius mark, called R500, which is 295 kiloparsecs here. Few reads reach that far out at such span. The fringe is where new galaxies fall in and the cluster grows. For cluster teams, a first read of the fringe sets the base for deep follow up on how the most rich knots grew.
arxiv-2601-13792:
Léo Pioge, Leonardo Novo, and Nicolas Cerf test a yardstick for boson sampling machines in 2026. Boson sampling sends identical light particles through a network to sample outcomes. Multimode bunching, where particles crowd into few modes, was meant to validate such machines. A high bunching rate was taken as a sign the machine works.

The team shows a catch called anomalous bunching. Partly distinguishable particles can bunch more than perfect identical ones. Time delays between particles drive this odd effect. The result warns that bunching alone can mislead validation of quantum devices.
arxiv-2601-13892:
Andrej Schwanke and co-authors test large language models as drivers of multi-objective optimization in 2026. Such tasks juggle many conflicting goals at once. Models are famed for reasoning, yet they are not the default choice here. Conventional strategies rank high on benchmarks for good reasons.

Classic methods handle numerical inputs with care and model the trade-offs well. They balance exploration with exploitation of the Pareto front, the set of best trade-offs. The team studies hierarchical optimization with language models in charge. The work asks where model reasoning helps, and where numbers still rule.
arxiv-2601-14192: Xiaofang Yang and a large team survey how AI agents can be made more efficient in 2026. Recent years have seen growing interest in extending language models into agentic systems. Agents must remember, use tools, and plan to act well. Each of those skills can waste time, tokens, and compute if done poorly.
arxiv-2601-14392:
I-Hsuan Li, Shutaro Ueda, I-Non Chiu, and Keiichi Umetsu study cold fronts in galaxy clusters in this 2026 paper. They use data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory. Their sample holds three nearby clusters: Abell 496, Abell 2029, and Abell 1644. Cold fronts show as sharp edges in the X-ray surface brightness of the intracluster medium, the hot gas between galaxies.

These fronts come from sloshing, gas swinging in the cluster's gravity well after a past disturbance. Most studies average around the cluster. This one resolves the fronts by azimuth, direction around the center. Readers get a detailed view of how sloshing fronts differ from place to place in each cluster.
arxiv-2601-14492:
Malak Mansour and five co-authors build a strawberry-picking robot in this 2026 paper. Robotic strawberry harvesting is hard under partial occlusion. Leaves hide much of each fruit, which creates significant geometric uncertainty. A grasp plan based on one deterministic shape estimate can be unreliable. From a single partial observation, multiple incompatible 3D completions may all be plausible.

A grasp that looks feasible on one completion may fail on another. The team's system, UNCLE-Grasp, is uncertainty-aware. It plans grasps that hold up across the plausible shapes, not just one guess. Readers get a harvesting method designed for the messy view a robot gets in a real field.
arxiv-2601-14592:
Nicholas Gismondi constructs unusual solutions to fluid-type equations in this 2026 math paper. His class is stationary active scalar equations with a non-odd nonlocal operator in the drift term. Active scalars, like temperature in convection, move the very flow that carries them. He builds nontrivial weak solutions to these equations.

The construction uses a convex integration scheme, a flexible method that builds rough solutions piece by piece. Gismondi shows the solutions lie in specific Besov and Lebesgue spaces, for dimensions two and up. The drift here is non-odd, which breaks a symmetry past work relied on. The states are rough. They are not smooth flows, but they do solve the math in a weak sense. Readers get proof that such equations admit wild, integrable steady states.
arxiv-2601-14792:
Dong Sun, Rahul Nittala, and Rebekka Burkholz test Mixture of Experts models under noise in this 2026 paper. Mixture of Experts models route each input to a few specialist sub-networks. Despite their practical success, their robustness is not fully understood. The team's topic is feature noise: corrupted or jittered input features. Such noise is common when sensors or data pipelines are imperfect.

A router that reads noisy features may send inputs to the wrong experts. The study examines how much that harms the whole model. The abstract in the evidence pack cuts off early, so the detailed findings are not stated there. Readers get a robustness audit for a model family now used at very large scale.
arxiv-2601-15192:
Pratyay Mukherjee and Ritwik Mondal propose a faster way to flip magnetic order. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with antiferromagnets, materials whose atomic magnets cancel out in pairs. Steering that order is a central challenge for next-generation spintronic devices.

The authors analyze switching driven by a field-derivative torque. This torque comes from the time-derivative of an applied terahertz pulse. It acts on the staggered order parameter, the gauge of the paired pattern. The goal is ultrafast switching of the antiferromagnetic state for future fast memory and fast logic devices of the future alike.
arxiv-2601-15992:
Shidan Ma and five co-authors speed up database queries over RDF graphs in a 2026 arXiv paper. RDF graphs store data as linked triples. SPARQL is the language used to query them. Current systems lean on cloud data management. They hit bottlenecks when bandwidth is limited or load is high. The authors explore an edge computing solution. They describe it as the first of its kind for this problem.

Cloud-edge collaboration splits the work. Edge nodes near the user handle parts of each query. The cloud holds the bulk data and the rest of the computation. That split can cut traffic and response time. Knowledge graphs keep growing in enterprise and web use. Query methods that respect bandwidth limits will decide how far they scale.
arxiv-2601-16192:
Ziyi Wu and coauthors lift flat pics and clips to full sphere views with no shape step. Their 2026 preprint deals with wide views that wrap the whole scene. Past lifts align the flat view to the sphere form by shape maths. That needs known cam facts, which wild pics oft lack. Lack of facts blocks use on most real pics and clips.

The new tool, named 360Anything, learns the lift with no shape step. It works on pics and clips from the wild as they come. Sphere views feed rich 3D world builds for play and film. A lift with no cam facts opens that path wide. The team tests the lift on mixed wild sets.
arxiv-2601-16292:
Anh-Duy Pham builds a fast agent model frame in Python with a column store. His 2026 preprint, named AMBER, deals with agent based models. Such models study group acts in nature and in social life. Python frames are easy to use but oft run slow at scale. Scale is just what group act studies need most.

AMBER stores agent traits in columns, not in lone rows. Column stores let code run the same step on all agents fast. Speed with ease of use would open big models to more teams. The frame aims to keep the Python feel users like. It seeks scale with no loss of that ease.
arxiv-2601-16592:
Vinicius Borin and coauthors join weather and train data to read delays in Finland. Their 2026 preprint deals with late trains and their causes. Late runs stem from acts, gear and sky facts as one. Past sets oft hold just one of those fact types. Sets sans weather miss a main cause in north lands.

The team joins sky data to run data for Finnish trains. Joint data lets them weigh how much sky adds to delays. True weights guide where rail teams should spend to cut delays. North rail nets face snow and cold that bend all plans. The work gives a joint set for that study.
arxiv-2601-16692:
Avraham Gal questions fresh claims from a Japanese lab about strange nuclei. The J-PARC lab used fine grain film to catch rare events. In those films, a Xi particle was caught by a light nucleus. Teams then named the bound states they thought they saw. Gal's 2026 preprint checks if those names fit past proof.

An past test at the same lab used a beam on carbon. That test gave a bound state with a set grip strength. Gal sets the film claims next to that gauge. He asks if both tales can be true at once. Such checks keep rare-event claims on firm ground. They also guide new hunts for Xi bound states.
arxiv-2601-17092:
Two strange fractions sit at the core of a pure math hunt. Each has arctanh, a log-type curve, in its base. Their Mellin transforms turn them in wave-like codes. A 2026 preprint works out those codes with care. The fractions live on the span from nil to one. Past that span, they are set to nil for the work.

The codes tie to deep guesses on odd zeta marks. Those marks pair with powers of pi in set ratios. A twin set pairs beta marks with pi powers. Such ties could prove those ratios wild or tame. Pure sums here may crack old number tales.
arxiv-2601-17192:
Sukirt Thakur and a team of eight co-authors gauge heart flow from plain angiograms. A heart flaw called CMD hurts the heart's small veins. Prime tests for it are invasive and uneven. Their 2026 preprint builds PUNCH, a net that works from the angiogram alone. It gauges coronary flow reserve, a key mark of that flaw. Physics rules and doubt marks both sit in the build.

The net learns blood flow from first-rule forms of dye spread. No ground truth flow marks are called for. Doubt marks tell docs when to doubt a call. Non-invasive gauges could find CMD far more oft.
arxiv-2601-17492:
Jin Li and seven co-authors work on fair recommendations from language models. LLM-based recommenders model users in rich new ways. They also copy bias from their training data. That bias can skew who sees which goods, jobs, or news. Fixing it by full retraining costs too much for most teams. The authors seek fairness without that cost.

They name two core challenges that block cheap fixes. Their method must work on a trained model as it stands. Fair picks matter for trust and for law. A low-cost fix could spread fair practice widely. The work serves platforms that suggest goods at scale. It treats fairness as a design need, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-17592:
Sivaprasad Omanakuttan and four co-authors build spin codes for quantum error correction. Most codes need local control and stabilizer checks. Those are hard in systems ruled by collective interactions. The authors draw on spin-GKP codes for a new path. They use the Holstein-Primakoff view of spins. Their codes target local and collective noise at once.

Collective systems include atomic ensembles and some solid-state hosts. Codes that fit them widen where quantum machines can be built. Handling both noise types in one code is a strong step. The work gives hardware teams new code options. It may cut the control burden that blocks scale-up. Spin hosts gain a tailored shield.
arxiv-2601-18092:
Nan Chen and co-authors design context-aware help for screen reader users working on computers. Their 2026 preprint starts from a plain fact. Equal access to digital tools is critical for school, work, and social life. Yet mainstream screens are built for sight, so blind users face steep learning curves and frequent blocks. Current support is thin: tutorials target sighted users, and human help lacks scale.

The team studies help that senses when a user is stuck and what they were trying to do. Guidance timed to the struggle could raise independence a great deal. Their title frames the goal as a path from struggle to success. The work serves designers of accessible systems everywhere.
arxiv-2601-18692:
