Wei Wu and many colleagues build a base model that lets robots see, read, and act in one frame. Such a model takes a shot and a line of text, then sets the moves of a robot arm. A prized base model must work on new tasks and new arms with small cost in data and chip time. Most past models fall short on one of those counts.

Their model, LingBot-VLA, learns from a huge set of real runs: tens of thousands of hours on nine kinds of twin-arm robots. Real runs teach what mock worlds miss, such as slip and wear. A base trained at that scale could be bent to new jobs with far less fresh data. That would bring arm robots close to the ease of use of text tools.
arxiv-2601-18792:
Brian Liu and Oiwi Parker Jones link brain waves to the feel of speech, to open a new path in the study of how we feel. To read feel from brain acts could change how we grasp joy, fear, and grief. Past sets pair brain data with speech and with its writ form. None pair it with the feel of the speech: glad, sad, cross, or calm. That gap blocks work on feel from the brain.

The pair fill the gap with a tool that grades the feel of text. They run that tool on the writ form of tales read to folk while their brain waves are caught by a fine cap. The brain set thus gains feel tags with no new lab work. A tagged set could teach tools to read feel from the brain. It could also test how feel is built in the mind.
arxiv-2601-18892:
Gleb Aminov and three colleagues show that a deep mark of curved space maths drops out of a classic chain of steps. The mark is a flaw in how a set kind of wave world acts when its shape is stretched in a set way. Such worlds should not care about shape in that way, but a faint flaw stays. The flaw comes in two kinds; the team take on the first kind. It lives in worlds with an even count of dims.

They start from a shape that sums up the curl of space in its full form. A chain of steps, long used for twin flaws of the force kind, then gives the shape flaw in a plain way. That puts the two flaw kinds on the same base for the first time. A shared base firms the maths of such worlds.
arxiv-2601-19392:
Martynas Skrabulis and five co-authors measure shoves smaller than a sensor's own quantum jitter. A mechanical sensor's sensitivity ends at its inherent quantum fluctuations, or so the standard story goes. The team uses an optically levitated nanoparticle, a bead of glass held by light, as their sensor.

By squeezing the bead's motion in a reversible way, they resolve impulsive forces below its zero point uncertainty. The trick does not break quantum rules; it reshapes where the noise sits. Such sensors could weigh the faintest kicks in physics, from tiny particles to faint fields.
arxiv-2601-19592:
Salvatore Tringali and Weihao Yan work in algebra on a question about torsion groups. Their setting is a monoid, a set with an operation for combining elements. From any monoid they build a new one whose elements are finite sets containing the identity. The combining rule multiplies sets element by element.

This construction is called the reduced finitary power monoid. The paper connects its torsion behaviour to a conjecture of Bienvenu and Geroldinger. Torsion concerns elements that return to the identity after repeated combination. Such questions sound abstract, but they test how structure passes from a monoid to sets built from it. The results sharpen our grip on power monoids, a tool in factorization theory.
arxiv-2601-19692:
Jukka John and five colleagues improve a correction used in electronic structure theory. Standard density functional methods contain a known flaw: an electron partly interacts with itself. Self-interaction correction removes that error, but doing it in a fully variational way is hard. Locally scaled versions apply the correction unevenly, where it is needed most.

The team presents a fully variational, locally scaled functional that uses complex-valued optimal orbitals. Complex orbitals give the method more freedom than real ones. Reaching a fully variational form is described as an important milestone for this family of methods. Better functionals mean better predictions of atoms, molecules, and solids, in both ground and excited states. The work strengthens a tool used across chemistry and materials science.
arxiv-2601-19792:
Peter Zeng and a large team of colleagues compare how humans and vision-language models build common ground. In referential communication, a speaker describes an object so a partner can pick it out. Partners succeed by modeling what the other knows. AI agents that partner with people need the same skill.

The authors study how large vision-language models ground references, side by side with humans. They find the two ground language differently. That gap limits collaboration, since the model may misread what its partner intends. Pinpointing the difference shows where training and design must improve. The work matters for any assistant that talks about the visible world with a person.
arxiv-2601-19992:
Soham Sarkar, Tanmay Sen, and Sayantan Banerjee hunt defects in factory images with very few examples. Industrial anomaly detection is hard because defective samples are rare and classes are badly imbalanced. Few-shot settings make it harder still: only a handful of labelled defects exist. Their method, BayPrAnoMeta, generalises an existing meta-learning approach in a Bayesian direction.

Proto-MAML, the base method, adapts using fixed class prototypes and distances. BayPrAnoMeta replaces those deterministic prototypes with probabilistic ones. Modelling uncertainty in the prototypes should help when examples are scarce. Factories need inspection systems that learn new defect types quickly. A method that works from a few shots could cut the cost of quality control. Few shots must do the work of many.
arxiv-2601-20192:
Xiaokai Luo and three colleagues study online change point detection for streams of events that arrive in bursts over time and across many channels. The data are modeled as inhomogeneous Poisson processes, where the event rate itself varies. The task is to spot, as data arrives, the moment the pattern shifts.

Such shifts matter in earthquake monitoring, climate watching, and epidemic surveillance. The authors note this setting is still underexplored in statistics and machine learning. Methods that catch changes quickly, with few false alarms, would give agencies earlier warning when a monitored system starts to behave in a new way.
arxiv-2601-20592:
Ali Basirat, Danial Namazifard, and Navid Baradaran Hemmati probe language contact inside the internal layers of a monolingual language model. They ask whether structural traces of contact with other languages survive in the representations a model learns. Their case study is Persian, a language with a rich contact history.

They expose a Persian-trained model to languages with varying degrees and types of contact with Persian, then inspect its intermediate representations. If contact leaves a measurable trace, model internals could become a new source of evidence for historical linguistics, complementing texts and speaker data.
arxiv-2601-20792:
Thomas Brackin argues that where a privacy policy puts facts can hide them in plain sight. His 2026 paper studies how major companies organize their policies. Policies are meant to give users notice of data practices. Brackin finds a pattern he calls jurisdiction-siloed disclosure. Key facts appear in firm, specific form only inside regional sections.

Those sections carry labels like California Residents or EU and UK Users. The general sections, by contrast, use vague or qualified words for the same practices. Most readers never reach the regional parts, so the clear facts stay unseen. His audit covered more than a hundred major companies and flagged hundreds of possible instances. The paper shows how structure alone can blunt the notice a policy claims to give.
arxiv-2601-21092:
Marvin Sextro, Weronika Kłos, and Gabriel Dernbach teach models to predict how cells respond to perturbations in new settings. Their 2026 paper presents MapPFN, which learns causal perturbation maps in context. Planning interventions in biology needs models that adapt to unseen contexts. A model must spot the mechanism at work in each new system. Single-cell datasets, though, span few contexts. Old methods cannot use new evidence at test time.

MapPFN is built to adapt on the spot. It uses fresh evidence as it predicts. That style mirrors how a scientist updates beliefs after one experiment. Better adaptation could guide drug and gene studies with less data. The paper targets treatment-effect modeling in biology.
arxiv-2601-21192:
Wun Yu Chan and seven co-authors ask if smarter reasoning makes for better text embeddings. Their 2026 paper compares embedding models built from unlike backbones. Top embedding models now derive from decoder-only language models. Contrastive learning adapts them for search and matching. Reasoning models raise a natural question. Does enhanced reasoning yield superior semantic pictures? The team tests reasoning-trained models as embedding starts.

An embedding turns text into numbers that capture meaning. If reasoning training deepens grasp, embeddings should improve. If it narrows the model, they might not. The paper measures that transfer at once. Search, retrieval, and recommendation all ride on embedding quality. The answer guides which base models builders should pick next.
arxiv-2601-21392:
Chunpeng Du, Zongyang Li, Yali Zhang, Yikang Lu, and Attila Szolnoki study how cooperation grows when agents learn from a shared score signal. Q-learning is a standard frame for such studies, since it says how agents update the value of each act. Reputation is known to help cooperation grow.

Past models baked reputation into payoffs, states, or partner choice. Those routes blur the effect of the learning signal itself. The authors instead shape the learning signal directly inside a combined Q-learning rule. That clean design shows how much of the cooperation gain comes from the signal alone.
arxiv-2601-21892:
Jian-Feng Cai, Haixia Liu, Zhengyi Su, and Chao Wang revisit a standard trick for steering image generation. Classifier-free guidance lets users push a diffusion or flow model toward a prompt by extrapolating between two predictions. It works well in practice, but it rests on a heuristic linear step that is sensitive to the guidance scale.

The authors give the method a principled reading through optimization. On that basis, their 2026 preprint improves guidance for flow matching. It projects the guided path onto a manifold. That keeps the path on the surface where valid data live. Better guidance means stronger prompt control with fewer artifacts, a daily concern for everyone generating images and video with these models.
arxiv-2601-21992:
Simon Ekhammar, Nikolay Gromov, Bogdan Stefański, and Charles Thull test a conjectured tool for string theory across its full range. The Quantum Spectral Curve should give the spectrum of strings in a particular curved space. That space is a stack of spheres and flat directions. It carries Ramond-Ramond charge.

The team solves the curve numerically from weak coupling to strong coupling. At strong coupling, the spectrum organizes into flat-space string mass levels. The masses follow a universal square-root scaling in the string tension. Finer splittings appear beyond that leading order. Their 2026 preprint confirms that picture. Checks like this build confidence that the spectral curve truly captures string physics where no other method can compute.
arxiv-2601-22292:
Manuela Chacon-Chamorro, Luis Felipe Giraldo, and Nicanor Quijano study how groups of agents can stay strong when things go wrong. Their 2026 preprint centers on shared resilience: the power to foresee, resist, bounce back from, and adapt to shocks. Mixed groups, where each agent has its own aims, face the strain most.

The team focus on how to learn reward rules that build that shared strength. Their setting is learning by trial and error, with many agents at once. Strong rules could help fleets of robots or grids ride out faults. The work names a goal the field has largely skipped.
arxiv-2601-22392:
Scott Hagen, Chris Done, Gabriele Matzeu, and Hirofumi Noda use sharp new X-ray spectra to map the gas around black holes. The XRISM satellite gives the clearest view yet of X-ray lines from active galaxies. Their 2026 preprint notes that the iron line near the core has a complex shape.

At least three zones add to that line: the inner disc, a mid ring of fast gas, and an outer torus of dust and gas. Sorting their shares shows how matter flows near the hole. It also tests how gas is lit and blown out. The work opens a new window on black hole feeding.
arxiv-2601-22692:
Yiheng Liu and a large team fingerprint large language models so owners can prove a copy is theirs. Building such models costs a fortune, and open releases invite theft. Their 2026 preprint, FNF, builds a functional network fingerprint: a mark drawn from how the model acts as a network.

A sound fingerprint lets a developer prove misuse in court or in talks. It should also survive the tweaks a thief would try. The work guards the rights behind open models. It may help keep sharing safe for builders. Theft fears chill release; proof tools thaw them.
arxiv-2601-22792:
Muhammad Shakeel and four co-authors present CALM, a system for speech recognition when several people talk at once. The name stands for joint contextual acoustic-linguistic modeling. It is built for personal AI tools that must pick out one target speaker from a crowded, overlapping conversation.

CALM joins two kinds of clues: the sound of a voice and the words around it. Sound alone can confuse speakers, and words alone can miss who said what. Joining both should help machines follow group talk, take notes, and serve the right user.
arxiv-2601-23092:
Haitham S. Al-Sinani and Chris J. Mitchell automate parts of wireless security testing with governed AI. Ethical hackers read recon results by hand and run long, time-sensitive command chains. That craft is slow, hard to scale, and open to human error and subjective calls.

Their WiFiPenTester uses generative AI under governance rules to guide the work. Targets can be found, handshakes captured, and password strength assessed more consistently. Governed automation aims to keep the speed of AI with the judgment of a careful practitioner. Governance is built in from the start, keeping automated hacking steps bounded, logged, and answerable to human judgment.
arxiv-2602-00092: Neha Kalibhat and coauthors learn a verifiable constitution for model behavior: a plain language summary of how prompt changes shift a specific behavior such as alignment, correctness, or rule following. Their black box method applies atomic concept edits, which add, remove, or replace one interpretable concept in a prompt. Each edit is then mapped to its observed effect across tasks. The learned constitution both explains and steers behavior, and tests span math reasoning and text to image alignment, with distinct model habits emerging.
arxiv-2602-00192: Elif Nebioglu and colleagues show that AI image detectors lean too hard on global artifacts from inpainting. Modern inpainting edits local regions with realism, yet detectors often key on side effects spread across the whole image. The authors trace this to VAE reconstruction, which shifts spectra subtly even in untouched regions. Their Inpainting Exchange operation restores pixels outside the edited region to their originals while keeping all made up content. Under that test, top detectors, including commercial ones, fall sharply, at times near chance, from high accuracy.
arxiv-2602-00292: Rory Driscoll and team introduce LogicGaze, a benchmark for causal consistency in visual narratives. Sequential reasoning helps vision language models on complex tasks, yet grounding reasoning chains in visual evidence remains weakly tested. It asks whether models can validate causal chains against visual inputs, targeting hallucination. Built from 40000 video segments and Flickr30k images, it pairs causal sequences with visual contradictions that still read plausibly. Its three part test, causal validation, grounded narrative synthesis, and perturbation rejection, reveals major flaws in leading models.
arxiv-2602-00392: Arjun Rao and team propose local, high resolution geographic maps with Slepian functions. Geographic data is local at heart: outbreaks cluster in population centers, patterns emerge along coastlines, and activity gathers within country borders. Models that encode location, however, spread capacity evenly across the globe, struggling at fine resolutions. Their encoder, built from spherical Slepian functions, puts capacity inside a region of interest and scales to high resolutions. For global context, a hybrid encoder bridges local and global performance while keeping pole safety and distance preservation.
arxiv-2602-00492: Jeffrey P. Bigham offers HIDAgent, an open-source hardware and software toolkit that lets interface agents run computers as people do. Current control still relies on system-specific interfaces or VNC links, limiting the platforms and uses open to study. HIDAgent mimics a physical keyboard and mouse for any HID-compatible system, built from three off-the-shelf parts costing less than $30 plus a Python library. Bigham validates the kit with five prototypes across mobile and desktop platforms, supporting study of agents kept separate from the devices they steer.
arxiv-2602-00692: Dario A. Leon and colleagues review excitations in solids, including plasmons, excitons, and intra- and interband transitions. These shape changing screening, optical response, and energy transport. Methods that resolve momentum and frequency include energy-loss spectroscopy and X-ray scattering. Many-body perturbation theory now maps excited states across the Brillouin zone with high precision. The review surveys how dielectric-response spectra from experiment and theory are shown and read, with emphasis on band structures for direct and inverse dielectric functions via multipole-Padé approximants.
arxiv-2602-00892: Jebacyril Arockiaraj and colleagues sustain up to 1.5 TOPS with a compact single-wavelength photonic SRAM array of 1 by 256 bits, built with the standard silicon photonics process. They model system-level speed of photonic in-memory computing, a fast, low-energy alternative to chip-based digital computing. Their model captures delays from outside memory access and opto-electronic conversion, mapped across workloads like the Sod shock tube, MTTKRP, and Vlasov-Maxwell. System overheads still leave photonic in-memory computing fast for high-performance workloads, with strong efficiency.
arxiv-2602-01592: Gisela Charo and colleagues bridge homology and template views of chaotic attractors with the templex. Homology builds a cell complex from points in space and reads its topology, but ignores how flow moves across that complex. Templates capture flow direction yet stay tied to three dimensions through knot theory. The templex adds a directed graph to the cell complex, prescribing flow between its largest cells, supporting a classification of attractors. The authors test it on spiral and funnel Rossler, Lorenz, and Burke Shaw attractors, linking them to template descriptions.
arxiv-2602-01692: Hao Huang and Rui Rao study degrees in intersecting families, ordering degrees. Huang and Zhao showed that when the ground set exceeds twice the set size, the smallest degree obeys a bound. The authors strengthen that result, proving the bound holds for the degree ranked two k plus one. This needs the ground set to reach twice the set size plus one, and confirms the Frankl Wang conjecture. For large cases and ground sets beyond twelve times the set size, the degree ranked k plus two obeys the bound.
arxiv-2602-01992: Gouki Minegishi and colleagues frame analogical reasoning as inferring links across categories, via class functors. They build synthetic tasks testing emergence, finding it keyed to data traits, optimization choices and model scale. Mechanistic study shows reasoning splits into geometric alignment of relational links in vector space and functor use within the Transformer. These mechanisms move relational patterns from one category to another, making analogy, with the same trends in trained models. The work moves analogy from abstract notion to concrete fact in neural networks.
arxiv-2602-02192: Jingwei Song and others present ECHO-2, a distributed reinforcement learning method making post-training cheaper by running rollouts on remote inference workers. Distributing rollouts taps cheaper compute. Wide-area coordination and policy dissemination latency complicate training. The design centralizes learning, distributes rollouts, and lets output, dissemination, and training overlap under a tunable staleness bound. An overlap-based capacity model turns training time, dissemination latency, and rollout throughput into a real provisioning rule. Pipelined broadcast and cost-aware worker activation cut dissemination cost with rewards comparable to strong rivals.
arxiv-2602-02692:
Federico Escudero and 5 co-authors map what strain does to twisted bilayer graphene's moiré bands, treating strain as a design variable equal to twist angle, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Twisting two graphene sheets produces flat bands hosting correlated and topological phases, most famously at one magic angle. Real devices are always strained, yet that second knob was far less charted.

A new global method first constructs the commensurate supercells for any twist-and-strain pairing. Tight-binding calculations on atoms and continuum models extended for strain then survey the landscape. Some pairings flatten the bands even further than the magic-angle benchmark. Shear strain distorts the bands more than uniaxial strain does, and lattice relaxation matters throughout. Adding electron interactions broadens the bare bands while weakening electrostatic renormalization. Strain can also flip the bands' topology where narrow and remote bands merge.
arxiv-2602-03092:
Generative artificial intelligence designs burgers in a 2026 paper by Vahidullah Tac and 2 co-authors. Food choices shape human and planetary health, yet making food that is delicious, nutritious, and sustainable at once is hard. The system learns the structure of human taste directly from large-scale human recipe data, within a structured design space for new foods.

Without explicit supervision, the system rediscovered the classic Big Mac. It also generated burgers optimized for taste, sustainability, or nutrition separately. In a blinded restaurant tasting with over a hundred participants, its delicious burgers matched or beat the Big Mac. A mushroom burger cut environmental impact sharply. A bean burger nearly doubled the nutritional score.
arxiv-2602-03292:
Adapting image segmentation to a new domain without source data is made stabler by Jianghao Wu, leading a group of 5 collaborators, in a system called A3-TTA. Test-time adaptation updates a model on target data alone, but pseudo-label methods rely on perturbation ensembles with little distributional grounding. Their unstable signals can accumulate errors and cause catastrophic forgetting of the original task during adaptation on medical or natural images.

Anchors solve that problem here. Well-predicted target images, identified by a class compactness density metric, serve as stable references for pseudo-label output. Meaning consistency and boundary-aware entropy terms regularize the process, while a self-changing averaging strategy mitigates label noise. Evaluations on heart, prostate, and natural image segmentation showed large average gains over the source model and strong continual adaptation across sequential domains.
arxiv-2602-03592:
Deciding whether a messy formula is secretly a derivative is a core question in symbolic integration. Shaoshi Chen and 5 co-authors solve it for transcendental Liouvillian fields in a 2026 paper. Such fields model polylogarithms, trigonometric functions, logarithmic integrals, and their nested combinations.

The authors construct a complement to the subspace of derivatives inside the field. Their method splits any element into a derivative plus a remainder drawn from it. The element is a derivative exactly when the remainder is zero. The same tools decide elementary integrability by working out the logarithmic parts. It also yields a route to building telescopers, given an order bound in advance.
arxiv-2602-03692:
Generative recommenders write the next item token by token, but Xinyu Lin and 7 co-authors show that habit quietly narrows what users get recommended. Their 2026 paper diagnoses bias amplification: small token-level biases grow as generation proceeds, shrinking diversity. Older multi-stage pipelines avoid this through cascaded ranking, and the authors borrow that lens.

Two flaws drive the amplification: every token leans on the same encoded history, and each step gets a fixed compute budget. Their CARE method answers with progressive history encoding, feeding finer-grained history as generation proceeds. It adds query-anchored reasoning that spends parallel steps on a deeper grasp of preferences. On three backbones and four datasets, CARE improves accuracy, diversity, and efficiency.
arxiv-2602-03992:
Searching inside scanned documents takes more than text search. Gabriel de Souza P. Moreira and colleagues present Nemotron ColEmbed V2, a family of embedding models for visual document retrieval, in a 2026 paper. The models embed page images directly, skipping error-prone text extraction.

Three sizes, built on different pretrained vision-language backbones, were released. A late-interaction design compares query and page at fine granularity rather than through one summary vector. The largest variant ranked first on the ViDoRe benchmark suite at release. For companies feeding document catalogs into retrieval-augmented generation, such models promise retrieval that sees layout, tables, and figures, not just words.
arxiv-2602-04492:
Jan-Matthis Lueckmann, Viren Jain, and Michał Januszewski use a simulated zebrafish to test how well scientists can discover models of brain activity in a 2026 paper. Real neural recordings lack a known ground truth, so model quality is hard to judge.

Their testbed simulates a larval zebrafish, including its body mechanics, so the true system is fully known. A language-model-guided search found predictive models that beat standard forecasting baselines. Yet sensory input alone was not enough for faithful discovery. Models could exploit statistical shortcuts instead. Structural priors, meaning built-in knowledge about the system, proved essential. With them, the search recovered interpretable models that generalized to new conditions.
arxiv-2602-04692:
Sijia Chen and 9 co-authors add depth sensing to language-guided object tracking in a 2026 paper. Referring multi-object tracking follows targets named in a description, which matters for robots and self-driving cars. Earlier methods used only ordinary color images, where different three-dimensional arrangements can look identical.

The team built DRSet, a dataset pairing color images, depth maps, and referring expressions, including descriptions that depend explicitly on depth. Their framework, DRTrack, uses a fine-tuned multimodal model to detect targets with geometric awareness. Explicit depth cues also help link detections into stable trajectories. Experiments on the new dataset showed the framework works well. The authors plan to release both dataset and code.
arxiv-2602-05092:
Inverse kinematics, working out the joint angles that place a robot's hand where it should be, has two standard solution families. Thomas Cohn and 3 co-authors combine them in this 2026 robotics paper. Analytic solvers are fast and exact where they apply; optimization solvers handle extra limits like collision avoidance but often fail on hard cases.

The new setup uses an analytic answer as a change of variables inside the tuning task. That swap makes the landscape the optimizer sees much friendlier, even when nonconvex limits pile on. The team tested the idea on three solvers standing for three varied styles of constrained nonlinear tuning. Across tough tasks, including collision avoidance, grasp choice, and keeping a humanoid balanced, the new setup reached higher success rates than the standard form and baseline methods.
arxiv-2602-05492:
Turning a 3D scene into clean, editable vector art with smooth shading has no standard method. Ryusuke Sugimoto, Christopher Batty, and 5 co-authors present a way to build diffusion curves, vector lines that spread color across a page, straight from noisy Monte Carlo rendering samples. Their approach treats the task as a stochastic optimization over the shapes and colors of the curve handles.

A new differential boundary element method sits at the core. It rebuilds colors from the curves and gives gradients for tuning them, while a costly matrix step runs only once at the start. Unlike mesh-based methods, theirs tolerates crossing curves and noisy target colors, so rough samples can be used as they are. Tests across several cases show the method is robust and broadly usable. The authors also flag open questions for graphics researchers.
arxiv-2602-05592:
Statistical tests should give the same answer when the parameters are merely relabeled, a property called invariance, and the bilinear form test was shown to lack it. Angelo Garate, Felipe Osorio, and Federico Crudu revisit that finding, which came from a simulation study on likelihood-based tests used in extremum estimation. Their paper asks what conditions restore invariance for this test under one-to-one reparametrizations.

The authors state suitable conditions under which the bilinear form test keeps its invariance for linear and nonlinear hypotheses. Those conditions lead to a simple modification of the test statistic. A Monte Carlo simulation study then checks the modified test and suggests it performs well. The short paper speaks to econometricians and statisticians who use such tests in method-of-moments and related settings. It turns a known flaw into a small, principled fix rather than a reason to drop the test.
arxiv-2602-05692:
Errors in clinical text, such as a wrong diagnosis or treatment, can seriously harm patients, and language models now write much of that text. Congbo Ma and 8 co-authors introduce MedErrBench, a benchmark for detecting, locating, and correcting medical errors, built with experienced clinicians. It rests on a taxonomy of ten common error types and covers English, Arabic, and Chinese.

Cases are natural clinical texts, annotated and reviewed by domain experts. The team tested general purpose, language specific, and medical language models on all three tasks. Results show notable gaps, worst in the non English settings, which the authors link to weak clinical grounding and language awareness. The benchmark and its evaluation protocols are public. The authors aim to push multilingual clinical language technology toward safer, fairer AI in health care worldwide. The data set is released through supplementary material and a public repository.
arxiv-2602-05892:
Coding agents are graded on whether they fix an issue, yet almost nothing is known about how they gather code context along the way. Han Li and 9 co-authors introduce ContextBench, a process oriented benchmark for context retrieval in coding agents. It holds over a thousand issue resolution tasks from dozens of repositories across eight programming languages, each with human annotated gold context.

An automated framework tracks agent trajectories and measures context recall, precision, and efficiency during resolution. Four frontier models and five coding agents were evaluated. Sophisticated agent scaffolding bought only marginal gains in retrieval quality, a result the authors call a bitter lesson. Models consistently favored recall over precision, and a wide gap separated the context agents explored from the context they actually used. The benchmark adds intermediate signals to end to end scores.
arxiv-2602-06092:
Measurements of how fast the universe expands do not fully agree, and Brett Bochner and Aiden Jin ask whether the expansion rate itself changed over time. They use cosmography, a method that maps expansion history without assuming a specific model of the universe. The standard model fits early-universe data well, but strains show up at later times.

The pair fit straight-line cosmography forms to groups of exploding stars, called Type Ia supernovae, sorted by distance. Their data mixes a five-year survey release with an older standard set. The rebuilt expansion history hints at wiggles during the era when expansion began speeding up. They stress the hints are weak and shift with grouping choices.
arxiv-2602-06392:
Carbon nanotubes twisted into a chiral shape may slowly spin when heated, according to Raimu Akimoto and 2 co-authors. They study heat-carrying vibrations, called phonons, in semiconducting chiral nanotubes using lattice dynamics and Boltzmann transport theory. Chirality splits vibration modes that stay paired in straight zigzag and armchair tubes.

The split modes carry angular momentum, because individual atoms move in tiny circles. That momentum peaks in thin tubes at middle chiral angles. Adding it up across the heat flow predicts a rigid rotation of the whole tube: a thermal form of the Einstein-de Haas effect, where magnetization changes spin a body. The predicted spin should be large enough to observe in experiment.
arxiv-2602-06492:
Estimating a galaxy's stellar mass normally requires fitting its full light spectrum, a costly process. E Elson shows a far simpler model can do the job from just brightness and color. The model is a single-hidden-layer feed-forward neural network, trained only on synthetic galaxies from a semi-analytic simulation.

Transferred to real galaxies from the GAMA survey, its mass predictions tracked the costly spectrum-based values closely across thousands of times in mass range, with modest scatter. The result argues that deep architectures are not required for robust mass estimates: broad-band photometry carries the dominant physical signal. The method was then applied to thousands of GAMA galaxies lacking spectrum-based masses, with uncertainties propagated through the network.
arxiv-2602-06592:
ProtoQuant, a neural network design from Mikołaj Janusz and three co-authors, classifies images by matching parts of a picture to learned example parts. Models of this kind are valued because their choices can be explained in plain terms: a part is classed by what it looks like. Earlier versions struggled on very large image sets and needed costly retraining.

ProtoQuant keeps its example parts fixed inside a learned codebook, which stops them from drifting away from real training images over time. It also works without retraining the main body of the network, so it acts as a light, clear add-on head. Tests on ImageNet and on fine-grained sets of birds and cars show accuracy close to rival methods, with explanations that stay grounded in real data.
arxiv-2602-06892:
M. Dadashzadeh and K. Azizi examine a rare decay of the B meson into a scalar kaon resonance and a lepton pair, as a probe for physics beyond the Standard Model. Rare decays of this kind are sensitive to new particles because the Standard Model rate is small and precisely constrained. The authors first compute the decay in the Standard Model, then add contributions from scalar leptoquarks, hypothetical particles that couple quarks to leptons.

Their predictions cover the differential decay rate, branching ratios, ratios between channels, forward-backward asymmetry, and lepton polarizations, and they test how sensitive each observable is to the leptoquark scenario. They also flag momentum regions where long-distance charmonium effects are weakest. The results are aimed at future measurements by the Belle II and LHCb experiments.
arxiv-2602-07492:
Adding fractional stochastic forcing to Burgers-type equations can regularize them, but singular noise defeats classic methods. Shuolin Zhang and two co-authors build a generalized method for singular fractional Burgers systems with stochastic forcing, applied to Degasperis-Procesi.

They prove the system is locally well posed in a negative Sobolev space for noise of this type, using an enhanced structure to derive effective rules for generalized solutions. They also prove convergence of the linked non-Gaussian rough structures. PDE teams get a general method for systems where roughness is not a nuisance but the hard part.
arxiv-2602-07892:
Safety training can make language models safer while dulling their general abilities, a cost known as the alignment tax. Guanglong Sun and five co-authors view the problem through continual learning: successive alignment stages shift data and objectives, and their gradients can interfere with directions supporting earlier capabilities.

Their method, orthogonal gradient projection for safety alignment, estimates a low-rank subspace from gradients on general-capability data and strips that component from each safety gradient. The update is then the steepest safety-improving step that preserves general skills to first order. The lightweight rule offers alignment teams a principled way to pay less capability tax for the same safety gain.
arxiv-2602-07992:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has unlocked striking compositional reasoning in language models, but theory has lagged behind: which compositional problems can outcome-only feedback actually teach? Daniel Barzilai and two co-authors identify the task-advantage ratio, a joint property of the problem and the base model, as the key quantity.

When correct intermediate steps give a clear advantage, compositional problems are efficiently learnable from outcome feedback, and the authors analyze how such advantage arises in different problems. Without it, training may converge to suboptimal compositions, and base-model quality can become the limiting factor. The paper gives a principled map of when reward-only training suffices for compositional reasoning and when it cannot.
arxiv-2602-08092:
AI alignment usually trusts human feedback as noisy but fundamentally honest, an guess that breaks when evaluators are sycophantic, lazy, or adversarial. Majid Ghasemi and Mark Crowley prove that under that guess, standard reinforcement learning suffers objective decoupling: the learned objective separates permanently from ground truth, guaranteeing misalignment.

Their remedy, epistemic source alignment, judges the source of feedback using sparse safety axioms instead of trusting majority consensus. They prove it converges to the true objective even when most evaluators are biased. Tests support the theory. Alignment teams gain both a diagnosis of a shape failure in social feedback settings and a sound mechanism for judging the judges.
arxiv-2602-08192:
Scrum rules software project running, and language models now touch its knowledge-heavy habits, but evidence has focused on coding rather than running. Mirko Perkusich and six co-authors survey 70 Brazil pros about language-model use in Scrum running tasks.

Of those surveyed, 49 now use Scrum and 33 report using language-model helpers in Scrum work. Skill runs high, with 85 percent at mid-level or top levels and 52 percent using the tools daily. Use centers on trying Scrum habits, with items and events getting aimed but uneven support, while broader running tasks are adopted more slowly. Reported benefits center on productivity. Agile coaches and managers gain a grounded snapshot of adoption, not just vendor promises.
arxiv-2602-08792:
Arcing at the pantograph-catenary interface threatens rail power delivery, wearing contacts and disrupting service, yet arcs are brief, noisy, and hard to tell from other transients. Hao Dong and two co-authors propose a multimodal framework combining high-resolution images with force measurements for robust arcing detection. Their arXiv paper builds two synchronized visual-force datasets.

One dataset comes from Swiss Federal Railways data, the other from public arcing videos plus synthetic force data mimicking real characteristics. MultiDeepSAD extends a deep anomaly-detection method across modalities with a new loss, aided by tailored pseudo-anomaly generation per data type. Tests show clear wins over baselines, even under domain shift and scarce real arcs. Readers get a practical detector for a elusive rail hazard.
arxiv-2602-08992:
Sunspots in the north tend to twist one way, and in the south the other, a pattern called the hemispherical helicity rule. Jacob B. Noone Wade and one co-author test the leading explanation, the Sigma-effect model, which credits the twist to helical turbulence that rising magnetic tubes pass through. They run fully nonlinear, three-dimensional simulations of twisted flux structures rising through rotating, turbulent convection.

The result is skeptical: they find little evidence linking the turbulence's kinetic helicity to the tubes' evolving magnetic helicity, and no clear hemispheric dependence at all. The authors stress their simulations are far from a perfect copy of the original simplified model, but the mismatch raises serious questions about a widely cited explanation.
arxiv-2602-09092:
A faint nanohertz gravitational-wave hum, seen by pulsar timing arrays, might come from a violent phase transition in a hidden dark sector. Torsten Bringmann and four co-authors test that idea across three model families: a dark Higgs, a two-step transition with two scalar singlets, and a conformal scalar with loop-induced breaking. For each, they map the tuning needed to fit the signal while respecting all constraints.

All three scenarios can in principle explain the data, but conformal models rank as the broadest and least adjusted. The authors stress that future pulsar-timing and collider observations will be decisive: if the hum truly comes from a strong first-order transition, its parameters will narrow fast.
arxiv-2602-09192:
Dust in distant galaxies shapes cooling and molecule formation, yet its makeup remains poorly known. Viacheslav V. Klimenko and two co-authors describe a JWST program targeting dust in gas-rich galaxies below redshift 1.2, seen through strong 2175-angstrom absorption bumps toward background quasars. This methodology paper presents mid-infrared spectra for five quasars, the first part of a larger sample.

The team identifies artifacts in the MIRI data that distort integral-field backgrounds and proposes corrections, and models quasar continua that vary with active-nucleus shape, redshift, and black-hole mass. All five spectra show significant 10-micron silicate absorption, differing from Milky Way diffuse dust in peak position, width, and asymmetry. A detailed silicate study follows in a companion paper.
arxiv-2602-09292:
Ana B. M. Bett and five co-authors work toward a Pre-filed Report form for set trials in software building, hosted on the Open Science Framework. Pre-filed Reports pre-file guesses, ways, and reviews for peer review before data gathering, curbing p-hacking, print slant, and unfit after-the-fact review. Yet trial write-ups in the field still lack bite, hurting rerun-ability and openness.

The team read chosen OSF Pre-filed Report types against write-up rules for set trials. One type matched many rule hints, but none covered them fully, and OSF form tweaking proved tight. The paper ends that taking up OSF-based Pre-filed Reports pays off, but setting report-specific rules for software-building trials remains needed work.
arxiv-2602-09592:
Saharon Shelah's single-author 2026 paper revisits Super Black Boxes, a combinatorial prediction principle for cardinals. In a simplified case, a triple of cardinals has the property when, for a suitable stationary set and family of clubs, every coloring admits a guessed sequence. That sequence matches the coloring's restriction along stationarily many clubs. Earlier work established the property for many cardinal pairs in a broad class.

The most interesting cases for Abelian groups, involving the countable and first uncountable cardinals, remained uncovered. Shelah restricts here to continuous colorings, a class including colorings computed stepwise along each club. Within that class, the paper proves results without further caveats, including existence of a suitable larger cardinal for every regular pair. Multiple club families and quite free subsets of function spaces are also treated.
arxiv-2602-09892:
High-quality training data is the bottleneck for coding agents that aim at real-world software mastery, since environment setup, test generation, and problem curation are all hard to scale. Jiale Zhao and thirteen co-authors propose ScaleSWE, an automated, sandboxed multi-agent workflow for building such data at scale, in their 2026 paper. Three specialized agents handle environment setup, test creation, and problem description synthesis.

Running over six million pull requests across fifty-two hundred repositories, the system produced ScaleSWE Data. It holds one hundred thousand verified instances, the largest such dataset to date, with broad repository diversity and realistic task complexity. The team distilled seventy-one thousand four hundred ninety-eight high-quality trajectories and fine-tuned a model to produce ScaleSWE Agent. It achieves a sixty-four percent resolve rate on SWE-Bench Verified, nearly triple the base model. ScaleSWE will be publicly available.
arxiv-2602-09992:
Linguists have long debated whether children could learn grammar from the limited speech they hear without built-in syntactic knowledge. A 2026 paper led by Xiulin Yang, with three co-authors, tests that poverty-of-the-stimulus question for neural language models. The team builds a unified benchmark spanning four canonical phenomena and trains Transformer, LSTM, and n-gram models under shared protocols.

The models generalize above chance from as little as ten million words, yet they learn less efficiently than children as input grows. Cognitively motivated biases improve broad syntactic skill but do not reliably help on the stimulus-poor phenomena. The findings push back on the idea that built-in syntax is the sole route to generalization, while suggesting human-like efficiency still needs biases beyond those tested.
arxiv-2602-10192:
Brightest group galaxies anchor their groups, yet different galaxy building models paint their stars in other ways. A 2026 paper led by Ruxin Barré, with nine co-authors, compares brightest group galaxies across four cosmic runs. The runs are ROMULUS, SIMBA, SIMBA-C, and OBSIDIAN, tested against COSMOS field systems from X-ray-picked groups. Stellar masses, star birth rates, and stellar ages are studied jointly.

Model groups hinge on active galactic nucleus feedback strength and workings. OBSIDIAN's three-regime feedback matches data best, including quenched fractions and star birth change, with gradual decline as mass grows. SIMBA models quench rapidly when strong jets switch on, while ROMULUS under-quenches through weak thermal feedback. Physics-led recipes, the authors conclude, shape true-to-life group systems.
arxiv-2602-10292:
Erdős and Sós asked for the largest family of k-element subsets of an n-element set with no two sets intersecting in exactly t elements. A 2026 paper by Andrey Kupavskii and Yakov Shubin addresses the supersaturation version. For a family of fixed size, what is the smallest number of intersecting pairs it may induce? For fixed k as n grows large, the authors find the exact threshold where the minimum pair count matches the expected count in a random family up to a constant factor.

An exact answer is also found for family sizes slightly above the extremal function. The work sharpens understanding of how forced intersections accumulate once a family passes extremal size, giving extremal set theory a precise supersaturation picture for the Erdős-Sós problem.
arxiv-2602-10392:
Designing a new material means searching an exponentially growing design space. Testing every combination is impossible, and even finite-element simulation grows too costly. A 2026 paper led by Shaan Pakala, with three co-authors, proposes tensor completion as an all-in-one approach to material design, both predictive and interpretable. Classical tensor methods match traditional machine learning on predictions, with interpretable tensor factors thrown in for free. In experiments, those factors rediscover known physical phenomena, suggesting predictions aligned with the physics.

The paper also compares surrogate models under non-uniform sampling of the design space. Some specialized tensor methods generalize better there, thanks to the low-rank constraint, and the best improves on baseline machine learning by up to five percent on aggregate fit. It halves errors in some out-of-distribution sections. Experimentalists could thus use the factors to spot novel patterns, having already seen them recover existing ones.
arxiv-2602-10892:
Marwa Mouallem and three co-authors design alarm rules that resist bribery in blockchains in a 2026 paper. Smart contracts secure huge deal value each year, and high-risk contracts rely on fast alerts about outside events. Prior work had not studied toughness when an attacker bribes people to kill alerts.

The alarm problem is set as a game. A bribing foe faces self-seeking people who pay fines if caught cheating. The problem allows a squared upper bound on bribery cost. A plain protocol achieves only straight-line cost. An at-once game achieves the squared bound in the end, giving the best bribery defense possible. Two rules build that game, offering contract builders alerts that foes cannot cheaply silence.
arxiv-2602-11092:
Quantum machine learning needs shared tests, not lone demos. Cassandre Notton and nine co-authors present MerLin, an open-source discovery engine for photonic and hybrid quantum learning. It plugs fast simulation of straight optical circuits into PyTorch and scikit-learn workflows.

That design lets quantum layers train end to end with gradients, like ordinary model parts. The team also reproduces eighteen published photonic and hybrid works as reusable, modular tests, covering kernels, reservoirs, convolutional and recurrent nets, and generative models. Hardware-aware traits allow runs on real quantum gear. MerLin aims to link recipes, benchmarks, and hardware in one co-design tool.
arxiv-2602-11192:
Expert models waste memory because every expert must sit in GPU memory. Arian Raje and two co-authors present MELINOE, a fine-tuning method that pushes a mixture-of-experts model to prefer fewer experts per sequence. Caching those preferred experts cuts churn and transfer overhead.

Throughput rises sharply over fast rivals and far more over transfer-heavy ones, while downstream results holds or even improves. The method attacks a practical bottleneck: offloading experts to CPU memory incurs latency that swamps compute gains. By shaping expert preference during tuning, MELINOE makes expert models viable in resource-constrained settings.
arxiv-2602-11592:
Quantum blockchains need a way for many parties to agree even when some act maliciously, yet existing quantum agreement protocols explode in communication cost or demand complex multi-particle entanglement. Chen-Xun Weng and six co-authors propose a circular protocol with a semi-decentralized layout, gathering messages around a ring and sealing them with quantum digital signatures. The design reaches quadratic rather than exponential communication cost and tolerates faults better.

Crucially, it needs only weak coherent states, the kind of light already used in quantum networks, and it fits star-shaped network layouts. Simulations over a global satellite-to-ground network show high consensus rates across users and key-generation methods under realistic conditions. The authors offer it as a practical foundation for large, secure, fault-tolerant decentralized services.
arxiv-2602-11692:
Recommendation tools for open-source projects usually rank technical fit and ignore the human side: how a team talks, replies, and welcomes newcomers. Shashiwadana Nirmani and three co-authors survey 198 open-source workers to learn how team habits shape which projects people join and stay with. Communication traits such as quick replies, kind tone, and clear answers rank high across respondents.

Their relative weight, however, shifts with motive. People seeking reputation or networking favor open groups that encourage broad participation, while other motives weight habits differently. The study argues future human-aware suggestion tools should weigh social quality and motive fit alongside code, since the team a contributor joins often matters as much as the project itself.
arxiv-2602-11792:
Reinforcement learning with checkable rewards now trains many reasoning models, but hidden training data raises leakage worries for benchmarks. Standard likelihood-based spotting falters because this training tunes models from reward feedback on own thought paths, not token odds. Hongbo Zhang and five co-authors show the training leaves a behavioral mark. Prompts seen during training yield more rigid, similar outputs, while unseen prompts keep more variety.

They introduce Min-kNN Distance, a simple black-box test that samples several completions per prompt and averages the smallest nearest-neighbor edit distances. It needs no reference model and no token odds. Across several trained models the test cleanly separates seen from unseen examples, beating existing membership inference and leakage spotting baselines. Rigidity, in short, betrays prior sight.
arxiv-2602-12092:
Safety work for large models is often split across separate tools. One checks behavior, another finds causes, a third aligns the model, and the three rarely talk to each other. Bo Zhang and 19 co-authors present DeepSight, an open-source toolkit that joins evaluation and diagnosis into one workflow.

DeepSight pairs DeepSafe, a checking toolkit, with DeepScan, a cause-finding toolkit, under shared task and data protocols. That turns black-box behavioral checks into white-box insight about internal mechanisms. The authors describe it as low-cost, reproducible, efficient, and highly scalable, and as the first open toolkit supporting frontier risk checks together with joint checking and cause-finding.
arxiv-2602-12192:
Long documents and long chats strain retrieval, because a reranker must judge which passages truly fit a question. Yuqing Li led this work with seven co-authors, training a reranker on the attention scores of chosen heads in a large language model. That design looks at the whole shortlist at once, rather than scoring each passage in isolation.

It also yields smooth relevance scores, so training can use any retrieval set without Likert-style labels. A model of only about three billion parameters already beats strong pointwise and listwise rivals across several domains, and it sets a new mark on the LoCoMo dialogue memory test. Adding passage context helps further, while middle-layer heads keep speed up without losing accuracy.
arxiv-2602-12292:
Arctic shipping depends on speed, and speed depends on ice, wind, depth, and traffic rules in tangled ways. Mauli Pant led this work with two co-authors, analysing Automatic Identification System data from 2010 to 2019 for vessel speed over ground. Over half the records show zero speed, so treating stopped and moving ships as one process would blur key patterns.

A two-stage model first predicts whether speed exceeds zero, then predicts speed when moving. Gradient boosted trees with random effects capture non-linear responses while handling repeat sightings. Distance to coast and water depth dominate both stages, with course changes, vessel group, and status adding smaller effects. Wind and ice matter modestly. The results map Arctic operating regimes for speed management and corridor planning.
arxiv-2602-12592:
Power grids need anomaly flagging plus reasons: what type of fault, and where did it start? Yue Sun led this work with three co-authors, giving PICODE Networks, a unified, cause-guided design that jointly flags faults and explains them. It covers root cause finding, fault type sorting, and fault shape description.

Old time series models often act as black boxes, giving only binary outputs without reason. PICODE, standing for Power Interpretable Causality Ordinary Differential Equation Networks, offers better clarity and reduced reliance on tagged data or outside causal graphs, while keeping strong flagging scores in power systems. Theory results align fault function shapes with changes in weights of found causal graphs. Readers get a model that not only flags grid faults, but also tells operators why and where, a crucial step for safety and toughness in real systems.
arxiv-2602-12792:
Stars are born inside shrinking gas cores, but tying collapse models to sky data needs a tool that tracks motion, chemical change, and spectra at once. Olga Kochina and three co-authors present PrestaLine: Gorynych, a code with three parts. Kamelung handles 1-D collapse gas flow, Presta handles chemistry that changes with time, and Uran(IA) gives mock line spectra. It tracks cores from the pre-star phase through first core birth to outer-shell infall.

Applied to 5-solar-mass and 50-solar-mass cores, the code finds much alike past paths, apart mainly in spatial scale. Chemical mix shifts sharply at first-core birth, most of all for CO, water, and HCO+, while starting chemistry matters little for most species. Mock spectra show clear infall and loss signs, with massive cores glowing over wider areas, giving sky watchers a test kit.
arxiv-2602-13392:
Galaxy growth hinges on star formation and feedback at scales too small for cosmological simulations to resolve, so subgrid recipes fill the gap. Yet recipes tuned to match stellar masses can still diverge elsewhere. This first ARCHITECTS paper tests that degeneracy with three zoom-in simulations of one galaxy in a five hundred billion solar mass halo at redshift near one. Each run uses a different recipe: mechanical feedback, mechanical plus thermal feedback, or delayed cooling. All are calibrated to the same stellar mass.

Despite matching masses, the runs produced distinct feedback modes and circumgalactic gas properties. Delayed cooling ejected gas and metals most violently, halving baryon mass, while mechanical feedback kept most baryons and the hybrid sat between. Maxime Rey leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13492:
Macdonald polynomials are central objects in algebra. Earlier work gave them a chance-based reading at q equals one through a particle system called the multispecies t-Push TASEP, where particles hop around a ring. In that picture, stationary probabilities match ASEP polynomials. The normalizing constant is the Macdonald polynomial itself. This paper extends the story to interpolation Macdonald polynomials, an inhomogeneous variant due to Knop and Sahi.

A new Markov chain, the interpolation t-Push TASEP, is introduced. Its steady-state odds are shown to equal interpolation ASEP polynomials, and its total weight equals the interpolation Macdonald polynomial at q equals one. The result generalizes the earlier Ayyer, Martin, and Williams reading to the inhomogeneous setting. Houcine Ben Dali leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13692:
Agentic workflows chain many language-model and tool requests, yet current systems assemble inference engines and tool orchestrators separately, scheduling each request without end-to-end knowledge of the workflow. That separation wastes KV cache and tool execution environments. ThunderAgent instead abstracts workflows as LLM Programs, giving a unified view of heterogeneous resources including KV caches, system states, and tool assets such as disk memory and network ports.

A program-aware scheduler and a tool resource manager built on that abstraction maximize cache hit rates, mitigate memory imbalances, and enable asynchronous environment preparation. Across coding, routing, and scientific discovery agents, throughput improved 1.5 to 3.6 times in serving and 1.8 to 3.9 times in RL rollout, with up to 4.2 times disk memory savings. Hao Kang leads the work with nine co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14192:
Dennis Zaritsky and 19 co-authors report a 2026 arXiv find: a thin stellar stream around galaxy NGC 3938. Spotted in LIGHTS survey images, the stream is very faint, lies nearly in the plane of the sky, and wraps over halfway around its host. The host itself looks otherwise isolated.

The stream's parent likely held about 37 million solar masses in stars. Its orbit center seems offset from the galaxy center, yet simple models reproduce that offset with a thin disk in a standard spherical dark halo. Finer details, such as shifts in curvature and density, will need richer models to explain.
arxiv-2602-14492:
Jiahao Yuan and eleven co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv setup for industrial user representation that tune to each query. Old paradigms yield static, task-blind codes that strain to square varied downstream scenes in one vector space, while mixed multi-source data add noise and mode clashes.

Query-as-Anchor shifts user modeling from static coding to live, query-aware building. A pre-training set called UserU lines up multi-mode act runs with user-knowing meanings, and a Q-Anchor code design joins ranked coarse-to-fine coders into dual-tower language models via joint contrastive-autoregressive tuning. Cluster-based soft prompt tuning then bridges broad pre-training and special business logic, forcing scene-aware tuning for downstream tasks.
arxiv-2602-14592:
Michelle Döring and three co-authors build a 2026 arXiv logic setup for time graphs. Algo meta-theorems show doability for graph problems under shape limits, but such setups for time graphs stay narrow. The paper revisits past uses of logic meta-theorems on time graphs and builds a wider joined logic setup.

Logic codes are offered for vertex-span-membership width and tree-span-membership width, knobs that grasp vertex and part activity over time. Old monadic second-order meta-theorems for bounded life span and time degree are widened to those widths, and new first-order meta-theorems are set for all four knobs. A modular word list of reusable first- and second-order formulas for a wide range of time graph problems lets new problems be stated piece by piece, with a case showing the approach.
arxiv-2602-14892:
Shengtao Jiang and others use an improved dynamical density-matrix renormalisation group method on the spin-half triangular-lattice J1-J2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet. There, an intermediate non-magnetic phase is agreed but its nature is disputed: gapped Z2 spin liquid, gapless Dirac spin liquid, or weakly symmetry-broken phase.

On cylinders of circumference six to nine, two distinct variational states appear depending on initial state and boundary conditions. The higher-energy state matches a Dirac spin liquid, while the lower-energy state's static and dynamical properties point elsewhere, as detailed in the paper. A contested quantum magnet gains sharper, state-resolved evidence. Frustration keeps its secrets close.
arxiv-2602-14992:
Schuler and colleagues investigate rotational quantum friction, a predicted drag on a moving body from the quantum vacuum field. Their test case is a diatomic polar molecule spinning about its own center of mass in free space. The team quantizes the rotational motion and traces the energy loss that follows from spontaneous decay. Vacuum forces and fluctuations form the wider field to which the work belongs.

In the Markovian regime, they find a friction torque that persists even at zero temperature. That result matches the classical outcome in the limit of large rotational quantum number. The paper also examines the short-time non-Markovian regime, rounding out a quantum account of how rotation alone can bleed energy into the vacuum.
arxiv-2602-15192:
Parusiński and Păunescu study Zariski equisingularity of surface singularities in complex three-space through a local invariant. They attach to every analytic surface singularity, not always isolated, a marker called the multiplicity sequence. The marker accounts for multiplicities of later discriminants under generic corank-one projections.

The main result states when a family holds its type in terms of that marker. A family of such cases is generically Zariski equisingular if and only if the marker stays constant across the family. That sequence thus offers a concrete local test for when a family holds its singular type steady.
arxiv-2602-15292:
Burgin and colleagues study arithmetic combinatorial traits of whole-number Cantor sets. They consider the standard Cantor sets, with a base and a fixed set of allowed digits. Classical here means sets built from a fixed base with only certain digits allowed in digit expansions.

For such sets, they give examples satisfying the intersective trait with power gains, describe even spread, prove poly mean ergodic rules, and study distance pairing of integer Cantor sets. Together, the four results map how these digit-limited sets behave under number, means, and gaps tests.
arxiv-2602-15392: Crooks shows the relative entropy of a non-equilibrium set to the matching balance set is the extra free energy. He shows the reverse relative entropy also has a thermodynamic meaning: it is the extra free energy of a dual set in which the roles of energy and entropy are swapped. The dual swaps which thing takes the role of energy and which takes the role of entropy.
arxiv-2602-15892:
Wang and colleagues built FlipSet, a test of Level-2 visual perspective taking in vision-language models. Perspective taking means grasping how a scene looks from the viewpoint of someone else. It sits at the base of social thought. The test asks models to spin 2D letter strings by 180 degrees as seen by another agent.

That task splits spatial skill from 3D scene detail. Across 103 models, most scored below chance, and about three quarters of the errors just repeated the camera view. Control tests showed a split skill. Models scored high on theory of mind and fair on mental rotation alone, yet failed badly when the two had to join. The gap points to a missing link between social grasp and spatial skill.
arxiv-2602-16192:
Hiroaki Yamanaka and coauthors rethink what memory should mean for artificial superintelligence. The dominant paradigm, extract then store, pulls out information judged useful from events and saves only that extract. That risks losing valuable knowledge, since material discarded as useless for one task may matter for another. The authors favor the reverse: store then on-demand extract, keeping raw events and applying them flexibly to varied tasks as needed.

Two further paths get attention: discovering deeper insights from large collections of probabilistic events, and improving collection efficiency by sharing stored events. Simple experiments support the intuitive appeal of these directions. The paper also discusses major challenges that have limited investigation into these promising paths and proposes research topics to address them. It is a design exploration, not a claim of novel methods, aimed at lifting the world with memory.
arxiv-2602-16292:
Dong-Hui Yu and coauthors study gravitational waves from primordial black holes formed when the null energy condition is violated during inflation. A transient break during inflation provides a novel mechanism for producing primordial black holes and random wave backgrounds. Extending previous studies, the authors compute wave parts from both the ringdown phase of black hole formation and later binary mergers.

The scenario produces a rich, multi-component spectrum. It includes early waves, scalar-induced waves, and signs from black hole ringdown and binary mergers. Those correlated signatures across different frequency bands provide a novel avenue to probe or constrain null energy violation through future multi-band surveys.
arxiv-2602-16592:
Marko Erceg, Petar Kunštek, and Marko Vrdoljak address design problems ruled by multi-state steady diffusion laws. The aim is to tune shape and the layout of two plain materials at once, in set shares. That generalized solutions exist is shown by a hybrid route. It joins a relaxed averaging method inside the domain with limits on allowed shapes.

On that base, the authors build a code method that joins averaging with shape tuning. The edge moves by a level set method driven by the shape derivative. The inside layout updates by a simple criteria rule. A sample case shows the method at work, giving engineers a joint tool for shape-plus-material design.
arxiv-2602-16692:
Wouter Cames van Batenburg, Daniel Cranston, and František Kardoš extend a classic coloring result to disjoint correspondence colorings. Thomassen proved every planar graph is 5-choosable. Correspondence coloring generalizes list coloring: each vertex gets a set of color copies, and each edge pairs copies that must not match. Two colorings are disjoint when they never give the same copy at any vertex.

For every K5-minor-free graph and every correspondence 6-cover, the authors build three pairwise disjoint colorings. In contrast, they give K5-minor-free graphs with correspondence 5-covers that admit no three disjoint colorings. Graph theorists get a sharp boundary: six copies suffice for triple disjoint colorings, while five do not always.
arxiv-2602-17192:
Alejandro Flores led a seven-author team securing task offloading for remote internet-of-things deployments beyond terrestrial reach. Non-terrestrial networks with onboard edge computing can serve such sites, but malicious actors could drain their resources unless users are authenticated. The paper proposes a four-layer edge-enabled network: drones as access nodes, a high-altitude platform as coordinator and authenticator, and low-Earth-orbit satellites as remote servers.

A tag-based physical-layer authentication scheme admits legitimate users, and joint offloading plus resource allocation for admitted tasks is solved by block coordinate descent. Numerical results show the authentication scheme works efficiently and beats benchmarks, staying robust against attacks even under relaxed false-alarm constraints. The design offers a secure path to computing for far-flung sensors and devices.
arxiv-2602-17492:
Sarah Dinkelacker-Steinhoff led a two-author team formulating a variational multi-phase model for elastoplastic materials with microstructure evolution. The model covers elasto-plastic matter under linear kinematic hardening, where phase change drives shifts in microstructure. Built on infinitesimal strain theory, it rests on variational rules for inelastic matter. A dissipation distance stands for a phase switch that happens at once in time, steered by an underlying probability matrix.

Shares of fresh phases are tracked with Young measures, giving a microstructure story that runs smoothly through time. The team checks the model on a two-dimensional benchmark run with the Finite Element Method. The result is a broad variational frame that ties phase change, dissipation, and microstructure growth into one account for hardening elastoplastic matter.
arxiv-2602-17892:
Ryan Bentley and team develop hybrid ABBA-GMRES methods for unmatched backprojectors in large-scale X-ray computerized tomography. Matrix-free repeat methods matter in tomography given the cost of forming the system matrix. Forward and back projectors use varied grids or speedups, yielding unmatched pairs. Those pairs violate adjoint rules behind old least-squares solvers, so runs no longer match a least-squares problem.

Prior work explored Krylov solvers such as AB-GMRES and BA-GMRES, showing semi-convergence. Under matched conditions, they reduce to LSQR and LSMR. This paper builds hybrid AB- and BA-GMRES methods folding Tikhonov regularization into iterations. It examines links to hybrid LSQR and LSMR variants. L-curve and broad cross validation rules for auto parameters are assessed for settling and images. Tests on 2D CT problems show the methods curb semi-convergence, yield better images, and stop steadier than rivals.
arxiv-2602-17992:
Xinyi Zhang proves that the half-space exponential last passage percolation model, viewed away from the boundary, converges to the directed landscape. The same convergence was already known for the full-space model, so the open point was whether the half-space version follows suit away from its edge. The note settles that question for the interior region, leaving boundary behavior aside.

Zhang couples the half-space and full-space models and builds two barrier events from the monotonicity of last passage paths. Combined with moderate deviation estimates for both models and the known full-space convergence, the coupling yields the desired convergence. The result extends a central limit theorem from the full-space setting to the half-space setting, confirming that the interior behaves like the unrestricted model at large scales.
arxiv-2602-18192:
Maryam Hadipour and one co-author study how spacing controls a tiny quantum battery. Their 2026 paper models two matching two-level systems tied to a structured waveguide, one acting as charger and the other as battery. The gap between them sets a geometry-driven phase that steers how the pair interferes.

That phase tunes the decay routes and the flow of energy between charger and battery. By choosing the spacing, the team can favor bright or dark joint pathways, and together with the environment's memory this lifts charging power, peak stored energy, and revivals of usable energy. The work shows spacing itself can serve as a control knob for quantum energy storage.
arxiv-2602-18392:
Carlo Broggini and four co-authors report first results from RadioAxion, an underground hunt for axion dark matter. Their 2026 paper watches the alpha decay of americium-241 through its fifty-nine point five kilo-electron-volt gamma line, using a sodium iodide detector at the Gran Sasso Laboratory. Deep underground, cosmic-ray systematics are strongly suppressed.

The team presents measured spectra and a time-series analysis hunting periodic modulations that axions might induce in decay rates. No periodic modulation appears. From the null result the team derives constraints on the axion decay constant across masses from ten to the minus twenty-one to ten to the minus nine electron-volts. The work opens a new underground window on ultra-light axion dark matter.
arxiv-2602-18792:
To explain why a model changed its mind, it helps to show the smallest change to an image that would flip its prediction. Generating such counterfactuals with diffusion models is usually slow and sloppy about location. Changlu Guo, with three co-authors, presents MaskDiME in 2026, a diffusion framework that unifies semantic consistency with spatial precision through localised sampling.

The method adaptively focuses on the regions that actually drive the decision, so edits stay local and meaningful while image fidelity stays high. It needs no training, runs far faster than the baseline at inference, and matches or beats leading methods across five benchmark datasets in diverse visual domains. For practitioners, that combination makes counterfactual explanation practical rather than merely illustrative.
arxiv-2602-19092:
Pricing options under random volatility and jumps demands accurate numerics. Neda Bagheri Renani, with one co-author, proposes a high-order scheme in 2026 for the transformed Bates equation. The method pairs a mixed Crank-Nicolson frame for local terms with Simpson sums for the jump integral.

Benchmarks confirm near-fourth-order spatial exactness. That beats second-order finite differences and quadratic finite elements. Temporal convergence is second-order for all integrators tested. Efficiency tests show similar scores at far lower runtime than finite-element methods. Runtime falls by up to two orders of magnitude. The scheme thus offers a practical baseline for jump-diffusion option pricing.
arxiv-2602-19292:
In signaling games, a sender encodes information and a receiver acts on it, but the two sides may not want the same thing tracked. Hassan Munif and two colleagues study a case where the mismatch is linear: the sender wants the receiver to follow a transformed version of the true state, not merely a shifted one. That twist changes which messages are worth sending, in both noiseless and noisy channels.

With a clean channel, the equilibrium has a spectral shape: the sender reveals information only along certain directions picked out by the mismatch, leaving other directions silent. With noise, the paper derives thresholds that decide when informative signaling survives at all. The analysis extends classic cheap-talk results to a richer kind of disagreement, relevant wherever a sender's preferred reading of a signal differs systematically from the receiver's.
arxiv-2602-19492:
Cody Trevillian and two co-authors propose a temporal magnon-qubit Mach-Zehnder interferometer. It rests on controllable entanglement between a microwave qubit and a magnonic state. A pulsed magnetic field creates that entanglement, acting as a temporal beam splitter for magnons and qubits. Like a standard Mach-Zehnder device, the interference pattern in the final qubit population reveals the magnon dynamics.

One key application is studying single magnon decoherence, the loss of quantum coherence in one magnon. The scheme separately determines the rates of two possible decoherence channels, a distinction other approaches blur. That ability may enable single magnon state applications and help answer fundamental questions about quasi-particle decoherence at single quantum levels.
arxiv-2602-19792:
Quantum sensors reach their best precision only if the flood of detector clicks can be interpreted fast enough for real-time use. A 2026 arXiv paper by Mateusz Molenda and three co-authors compares two inference tools for photodetection: Bayesian likelihood-free methods and deep learning.

Likelihood-free methods are the more intuitive of the two. Once trained, though, deep networks give estimates far faster at comparable precision, with similar error predictions. That challenges a common belief that deep learning cannot supply errors. Both approaches are first checked on an analytically tractable two-level emitter. The main test is a driven nonlinear optomechanical device emitting non-classical light, where only deep learning meets real-time speed while learning complex multi-photon click patterns. The work points toward live sensing and control of quantum devices.
arxiv-2602-19892:
Governments borrow by issuing bonds across a ladder of maturities, and whether that debt path stays sustainable depends on the whole maturity mix. A 2026 arXiv paper by Christopher Cameron, working alone, builds a discrete-time model of sovereign debt dynamics under deficit-driven nominal growth.

New issuance follows fixed shares across a finite maturity ladder, while the budget constraint sets total borrowing. In a no-shock baseline the author finds when debt settles to a steady state, with explicit formulas for steady portfolio shares and cost and risk metrics.
