With random interest rates and deficits added, he finds a matching condition for settling to a single long-run distribution, so long simulations recover long-run means regardless of starting point. Correlated rate and deficit shocks add intuitive correction terms.
arxiv-2602-19992:
The anomalous mole fraction effect is a hallmark of calcium-versus-monovalent selectivity in negatively charged pores. Why it arises in wide synthetic nanopores, where anions also carry current, is less clear. A 2026 arXiv paper by Eszter Lakics and three co-authors studies ionic transport in a negatively charged plastic nanopore using a reduced simulation framework.

The team compares fixed point-charge models of surface groups with explicit-particle representations of surface oxygens. Two parameters control the outcome: closest-approach distance for ionic versus pore charges, plus grid spacing that modulates localization at fixed average surface charge. Fitting pore diffusion coefficients to a few experimental conductance points reproduces the full effect curve and anion leakage. Strikingly, very different surface models give indistinguishable conductance curves when that distance matches, despite differing local calcium profiles. In wide pores, selectivity emerges from an interplay of charge inversion, anion leakage, and ionic mobility.
arxiv-2602-20092:
Language models are usually trained on billions of words. Children learn language from far less. The BabyLM project asks what models can learn from child-scale data. A 2026 arXiv call for papers by Leshem Choshen and nine co-authors invites contributions to the BabyLM Workshop and its fourth BabyLM Challenge.

The challenge offers two standard tracks, Strict and Strict-Small. Participants must train language models on under one hundred million or ten million words respectively. This year the challenge moves beyond its previous English-only datasets. A new Multilingual track covers English, Dutch, and Chinese. Workshop papers are invited on the broader BabyLM theme: training efficiency, small-scale training datasets, cognitive modelling, model evaluation, and architecture innovation. The goal is stimulating new connections between cognitive modelling and language model pretraining.
arxiv-2602-20192:
Polynomial families often have zeros that settle into a predictable pattern as degree grows. Describing that pattern precisely is a classical problem. A 2026 arXiv paper by Luc Ramsès Talla Waffo, working alone, studies the long-run zero pattern of a rescaled family of polynomials. The family is expressed through Eulerian polynomials of type B.

Zeros in the unit interval are listed in increasing order. Their observed measures are formed. The paper proves those measures converge weakly to one fixed probability measure on the unit interval. An exact formula is given for the limit density and the limit curve. The proof rests on the type-B Eulerian form, a ratio limit from a classical series result, and Stieltjes transform techniques. Computed tests show the settling.
arxiv-2602-20792:
Muhammad Saif Ullah Khan and one co-author tackle a gap in computer vision: the spine moves through many joints, yet large 3D spine annotations are scarce. Their biomechanics-aware simulation adds anatomically consistent 3D spinal keypoints to existing pose data, drawn from musculoskeletal modeling.

The result is SIMSPINE, the first open set of sparse vertebra-level 3D spine labels for natural full-body motion, with 2.14 million frames from indoor multi-camera capture. Released baselines lift 2D spine detection from 0.63 to 0.80 AUC in controlled tests and improve in-the-wild tracking, giving vision research a shared benchmark for spine motion.
arxiv-2602-20992:
Homotopy groups gain power when given a shape structure, but several rival shape structures exist. Naghme Shahami and Behrooz Mashayekhy weigh them in this 2026 arXiv paper. They start by recalling known shape structures on homotopy groups, then review famed subgroups of those groups and apply the idea of subgroup shape structure.

Weighing shape structures through their subgroups yields results on shape-carrying homotopy groups, showing how the other structures relate. The paper serves readers who need to pick or join shape structures for algebraic topology problems. Its value lies as much in ordering as in technique: a clear map of which shape structure does what, grounded in subgroup structure rather than lone meanings.
arxiv-2602-21092:
Graph curvature is supposed to explain where message passing breaks down, yet the link to learned behavior is murky. Floriano Tori, Lorenzo Bini, Marco Sorbi, Stephane Marchand-Maillet, and Vincent Ginis probe that link in this 2026 arXiv paper through massive activations, extreme edge values in graph transformers. Tests on synthetic graphs and molecular benchmarks yield a surprise.

Massive activations do not concentrate on curvature extremes, despite the theoretical tie between curvature and information flow. On a long-range benchmark, global attention worsens topological bottlenecks, sharply raising the share of negative curvature. The authors reframe curvature as a diagnostic probe: it reveals when and why graph learning fails, even when it does not predict activation hotspots.
arxiv-2602-21392:
Gérard Daligou and six co-authors report the first experimental demonstration of a germanium-tin thermophotovoltaic cell for mid-infrared heat harvesting. Thermophotovoltaic cells turn heat radiation into power for waste-heat recovery and aerospace uses, but mid-wave devices have relied on costly III-V materials like InAs and GaSb.

Their germanium-tin diodes, 1 millimetre wide and grown on silicon, reached peak responsivity near 0.2 amps per watt at 1.7 micrometres and output near 0.41 milliwatts per square centimetre at room temperature. Trends matched a commercial InAs diode under the same light, though at lower absolute levels. Device modeling predicts power above 1 watt per square centimetre is possible, with defects and transport losses now the main limits.
arxiv-2602-21492:
Ningyuan Yang and four co-authors propose GradAlign, a gradient-aligned data selection method for reinforcement learning of large language models. Reinforcement learning is now central to post-training, but its results depend heavily on training-problem quality. Rollouts come from an evolving policy, so learning shifts with exploration and reward feedback, unlike supervised fine-tuning with fixed trajectories.

Earlier work leans on manual curation or simple heuristic filters like accuracy, which can admit incorrect or low-utility problems. GradAlign instead uses a small, trusted validation set to prioritize problems whose policy gradients align with validation gradients, forming an adaptive curriculum. Tests across three hard regimes, unreliable rewards, distribution imbalance, and low-utility corpora, show GradAlign consistently beating baselines, with more stable training and better final performance.
arxiv-2602-21692:
K. Pomorski and seven co-authors calculate barium and xenon yields in actinide fission and heavy-light fragment systematics. Isotope-resolved post-neutron fission yields in barium and xenon chains are calculated and benchmarked against listed reference data. Emphasis falls on isotope chains at fixed fragment charge and heavy-light fragment correlation consistency.

Runs use a Langevin design with Fourier-over-Spheroid shape model. The benchmark covers spontaneous fission of curium and californium, including Cm-244, Cm-246, and Cf-250. Neutron-induced fission at thermal and 14-MeV energies is covered for thorium-plutonium actinides, including Th-229, U-235, Pu-239, and Cf-249. Dominant neutron-number maxima are reproduced for most isotope chains, indicating mean charge partition and average neutron content of main channels are consistent. A residual gap appears in isotope widths: calculated yields fall off too rapidly on spread tails, producing spreads narrower than listed data, notably for heavy-fragment chains.
arxiv-2602-21892:
Greybox protocol fuzzing is a random testing approach for stateful protocol implementations. Input is protocol messages generated from mutations of seeds, and search in the input space is driven by feedback on coverage of both code and state. State and message models are core parts of communication protocols and shape protocol fuzzing strongly. Yu Wang and three co-authors propose APFuzz, an automatic greybox protocol fuzzer with novel designs to increase smartness of greybox protocol fuzzers from both state model and message model perspectives.

APFuzz pairs static checks with live runs to pick out state variables, then builds a faithful state model while fuzzing. APFuzz also introduces field-level mutation operations for binary protocols, using message structure awareness from large language models. Extensive experiments on a public protocol fuzzing benchmark compare APFuzz with the baseline fuzzer AFLNET and several state-of-the-art greybox protocol fuzzers.
arxiv-2602-22092:
Chest X-ray reading is hard because most diseases are rare and new findings keep appearing, yet most benchmarks test only common classes from one hospital. Hexin Dong and nine co-authors run the CXR-LT 2026 challenge, the third round of a benchmark built for this open world. Its multi-center dataset spans two large public collections, with tasks for known diseases and for unseen rare ones.

Teams tackled robust multi-label classification across thirty known classes plus generalization to six unseen rare diseases. The winning entries scored well on both tasks, and the results point to large vision-language pretraining as a strong remedy for rare-disease weakness. The challenge gives clinics a fairer yardstick for models that must face whatever walks in.
arxiv-2602-22292:
Peer review upholds science, yet it often neglects the well-being of everyone involved: authors, co-reviewers, organizers, and editors. Oliver Karras draws on ten years in academia to propose an ethos for reviewers built on two values: scientific care for quality, and collegial welfare for joint progress and well-being. The paper is an experience report, shaped by exchanges with colleagues, literature, and reviews both written and received.

From that reflection comes a guideline of sixteen practical recommendations for reviewer conduct. The ethos asks reviewers to hold rigor and empathy together, treating review as care for the work and for the people behind it. For a system strained by volume and speed, it offers a humane standard to review by.
arxiv-2602-22592:
Wenzheng Zhang and five co-authors push language models toward extremely low-bit weights for edge devices. Training with quantization awareness from scratch promises tiny, fast models, but accuracy and scale have lagged. The team blames a parameter democratization effect: every parameter's sensitivity flattens out, throttling what the model can express.

Their method, pQuant, splits each linear layer into two branches. A dominant one-bit branch handles cheap computation, while a compact high-precision branch shelters the most sensitive parameters, steered there by tailored feature scaling. That branch then fans out into sparsely activated experts for extra capacity. In tests, pQuant reached leading accuracy among extremely low-bit quantization methods.
arxiv-2602-22792:
Kunika Agarwal and six co-authors dissolve the idea of a fixed hierarchy of quantum complementarity. Bohr's principle bars simultaneous access to certain properties in one experimental setup. Sets of observables are often ranked by how incompatible they are, measured by the sharpness that still allows joint measurement.

The team proves a No-Comparison Theorem: no global ranking survives across all finite-copy setups. Two observable sets can reverse their complementarity order depending only on whether resources arrive as identical copies or as parallel-antiparallel pairs. Incompatibility thus depends on the global arrangement of prepared probes, not on observables alone, with entanglement quietly shaping measurement limits and urging a rethink of finite-resource protocols.
arxiv-2602-23192:
Thomas Woergaard and one co-author introduce FairQuant, a framework for shrinking image-classification networks without quietly worsening fairness. Quantization lowers the precision of model weights to save compute. It is usually judged on overall accuracy alone, leaving its effects on different patient groups unexamined. FairQuant instead plans mixed-precision quantization under explicit bit budgets with fairness in view.

The framework combines group-aware importance analysis, budgeted allocation of bits across units, and a learnable bit-aware quantization mode. That mode tunes weights and per-unit bit shares jointly under bitrate and fairness penalties. Tested on the Fitzpatrick17k and ISIC2019 skin-image sets across several small networks, near 4-to-6-bit setups recover much of uniform 8-bit accuracy. They also improve worst-group performance over uniform 4-bit and 8-bit baselines at comparable fairness.
arxiv-2602-23392:
Christian Aebi and one co-author study triangles whose vertices lie on the integer lattice, asking when their three classical centers also land on lattice points. The circumcenter, centroid, and orthocenter are the triangle's natural center points, each defined by a different construction. For most lattice triangles, the paper shows, these three centers never all sit on the integer lattice at once.

The exception is trivial examples, which the authors set aside before proving the main result. Several further observations about the circumcenter, centroid, and orthocenter round out the paper. The charm of the work lies in its elementary statement: a question anyone can pose about whole-number coordinates leads to a proof that the three centers almost never cooperate.
arxiv-2602-23592:
Zebin Yang and five co-authors present KEEP, a KV-cache-centric memory system for lean embodied planning. Memory-augmented language models handle complex, long-horizon embodied planning well. They track past events and environmental states to maintain a global view and avoid repeat exploration.

Current methods often store memory as raw text, causing overly long prompts and high prefill latency. Storing and reusing KV caches helps, but frequent cache updates cut the speed gains. KEEP offers three innovations. Static-dynamic memory building cuts cache recomputation via mixed-granularity memory groups. Multi-hop memory re-computation finds key cross-attention among memory groups and rebuilds memory links step by step. Layer-balanced memory loading ends uneven cache loading and cross-attention work across layers. Tests show KEEP achieves two point six eight times speedup with tiny accuracy loss versus text-based memory methods on the ALFRED data set.
arxiv-2602-23792:
Xiangzhong Luo and four co-authors present DiCo, a faster decoding method for diffusion-based language models. The 2026 paper notes that such models can in theory emit many tokens at once, yet in practice they still emit one at a time. Decoding many masked tokens together harms quality and stability.

DiCo splits the work into three phases. First it picks seed tokens among the masked positions and grows local clusters around them. Then it decodes clusters in parallel, repeating the split-and-decode loop until convergence. Finally it decodes the few tokens left with a fine-grained compound scheme. Tests show large speed gains while keeping generation quality competitive with slower baselines, closing much of the gap between theory and practice.
arxiv-2602-23892:
Vyacheslav Kungurtsev and Giovanni Russo generalize fully probabilistic design, a unified frame for stochastic control, learning, and decision-making, by swapping in Tsallis divergence. The 2026 paper replaces the usual Kullback-Leibler cost term with Tsallis divergence, a generalization rooted in non-extensive statistical mechanics. It flexibly handles processes with heavy, non-Gaussian tails.

The authors formulate Tsallis fully probabilistic design and present a double iteration scheme that runs a sequence of backward inductions, rather than the single backward pass used for classical design. The extra structure gives designers more freedom in how strongly deviations from a reference policy are penalized, which matters when rare events carry outsized weight. The paper offers a broader design language for control problems where Gaussian assumptions fail and tail behavior shapes the best policy.
arxiv-2602-23992:
Yoshiho Akagawa and Kazunori Matsui present a projection method for a dynamical elasto-plasticity model with Kelvin-Voigt viscosity and linear kinematic hardening. The 2026 paper formulates the system variationally, with a stress constraint set that evolves in time and shifts with an internal backstress variable, coupling the flow rule to the equation of motion.

To build solutions the authors use Rothe's method with a projection-based time discretization. Each step solves a linear viscous-elastic subproblem for a trial stress, then projects it onto the shifted constraint set. Stability of the discrete solutions is established, and passage to the limit as the time step shrinks proves existence of a weak solution, with uniqueness from an energy argument. The results allow time-dependent yield bounds without spatial continuity or a strictly positive lower bound, and the scheme gives a constructive base for numerical approximation.
arxiv-2602-24092:
Erwan C. Escudie and two co-authors present an epsilon-optimal sequential approach for solving zero-sum partially observable stochastic games. The 2026 paper tackles a known barrier: reductions to transition-independent games admit dynamic programming in theory, but the simultaneous minimax backup is nonlinear and exponentially complex.

The authors recast the simultaneous interaction as a sequential decision process through a separation principle. Distinct sufficient statistics for valuation and execution, the sequential occupancy state and the private occupancy family, reveal latent geometry in the optimal value function. That structure linearizes the backup operator, cutting update complexity from exponential to polynomial. In short, a hard update turns into a simple one. The simple update still finds safe policies. That swap is what makes the hard games solvable. The team proves it on tests. That swap is the whole trick. Tests show that algorithms built on the sequential framework beat leading methods.
arxiv-2603-00192: Miller and Blume study prediction wobble in healthcare models, where fixed data and design still yield different risk scores for the same patient through training chance. Standard overall metrics hide this person-level wobble, so models that look equal can still show real arbitrariness and shake clinical trust. The authors propose two checks: prediction interval width for risk, and decision flip rate for threshold calls. Applied to simulated data and the GUSTO-I dataset, neural networks prove less steady than logistic regression, and wobble near thresholds can change treatment calls.
arxiv-2603-00392: Ge and Elfring simulate sheared suspensions of squirmers, tiny swimmers modelled as spheres with surface slip, to track energy loss and structure. Shear lifts total dissipation yet lowers relative viscosity for both puller and pusher types. At low shear, activity rules and fluid links raise active loss, more for pullers at dense loadings, while pushers stay more viscous. At high shear both types act like passive spheres, and shear driven collisions yield negative normal stress gaps, paired with stronger alignment order.
arxiv-2603-00792: Tao and five colleagues model two way fluid solid interaction with Fisale, a data driven system inspired by Arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian methods and partitioned coupling. Most deep learning methods handle only one way interaction with rigid static solids, missing dynamic mixed two way coupling. Fisale treats the coupling interface as its own part and uses multiscale latent ALE grids for unified geometry aware codes across domains. A partitioned coupling step splits the problem into structured substeps, steadily modelling nonlinear links among solid, fluid, and their coupling.
arxiv-2603-00992: Cheng and four colleagues remove concepts from text-to-image diffusion models without the usual compensation step of re-teaching kept data or constraining drift from the original model. They argue such fixes still leave generations outside their scope degraded, so their MiM-MU method instead minimizes mutual information to pinpoint and erase only the unwanted knowledge. Tests show effective removal with high-quality generations elsewhere, achieved with no post-remedial compensation at all.
arxiv-2603-01092: Artiles and eight colleagues hunt the alien space of science: research directions that fit the literature yet no existing group is placed to propose. They split papers into idea atoms, score pairings for coherence and for how few groups could make them, and rank for high coherence with low reach. On over sixteen thousand machine-learning papers, the sampler beats frontier baselines on diversity at equal quality. Picking under one percent of candidates finds next-year pairings at about 36 times chance.
arxiv-2603-01292: Zhang and five colleagues propose PPO-LTL, a framework adding safety constraints written in linear temporal logic to PPO for safe RL. Büchi automata watch for breaks of the logic constraints, and a logic-to-cost step turns them into penalty signals that guide policy learning through the Lagrangian scheme. Tests on the Zones and CARLA worlds show PPO-LTL always cuts safety breaks while keeping strong scores against state-of-the-art methods.
arxiv-2603-01392: Tricouros and three colleagues test a box orifice man-made jet for destroying wall-bounded whirls. Vortex flows near an edge push nearby walls through low pressure within the vortex. Man-made jets disrupt oncoming calm with wobbly flow at the orifice, a vortex taming plan. Testing orifice shapes, vortex side spots, and vortex sizes in a flat plate edge layer, each jet cut vortex calm by up to 70 percent. That brought back pressure in the vortex wake, though speed wakes stayed, most jets making wakes of their own.
arxiv-2603-01492:
Chun Pang Chow, Hiroyuki Kasahara, and Yoichi Sugita prove a result that overturns a common belief in economics. Their 2026 work asks what firm revenue data alone can reveal when firms compete with distinct goods. Many held that output amounts are a must to learn markups and cost traits from revenue.

The team shows that production traits, firm prices and amounts, and demand can all be pinned down from revenue alone. No fixed shape for demand is assumed in the core result. With one added demand structure, even the buyer utility function can be recovered from revenue data. That opens fair welfare checks with no set shape for tastes. A trial estimator works well in simulations, and real factory data from Chile favors the new demand shape over the standard one.
arxiv-2603-01992:
Haiyue Yuan, Shujun Li, Fatima Gillani, and colleagues ask whether trip stage changes how travelers share personal data. Their 2026 study surveys leisure travelers before, during, and after a trip in one design. Privacy attitudes have been studied a lot, but their shift across trip stages was little known.

An online survey with hundreds of participants shows attitudes vary by data type, purpose, and stage. People prove more relaxed about classic sensitive items like name and birth date than expected. Booking sites have made sharing such items feel normal and required, the authors suggest. Social media sharing of travel content stays minimal on most platforms across all stages. Facebook and Instagram buck that pattern, while gender, travel history, and home country also shape attitudes at each stage.
arxiv-2603-02092:
Yushun Zhang, Bingran Li, Congliang Chen, and colleagues defend a famous training method in this 2026 paper. Adam is the default trainer for neural networks, including large language models. A known counterexample showed Adam can fail to settle, raising safety doubts. The authors spot a mismatch: the counterexample picks the problem after the settings.

In real work, the problem comes first and settings are tuned to fit. With settings matched to the problem, Adam always settles, they prove. One regime needs a large second setting with the first below its square root. A small second setting leaves a zone where Adam can blow up. The border between zones shifts with batch size, which guides practical tuning.
arxiv-2603-02192:
Oshani Seneviratne, Manan Shukla, and Jianjing Lin tackle messy personal health data in this 2026 paper. Watches and home devices collect daily health facts in many formats. Clinics need those daily facts to treat long-term illness well. Yet device data rarely fits clinic record systems or shared standards.

Their system pairs a shared health format with smart contracts on a blockchain. The format gives each fact a clear, shared meaning across devices. Contracts guard how data is shared, without tying users to one vendor. Together, they give doctors a fuller view of daily life than clinic visits alone. The design aims to be secure, trusted, and able to grow with use.
arxiv-2603-02292:
Alexander Petrov, Anna Linnik, Jacek Kłos, and colleagues model collisions between a carbon cage and rare gas atoms in this 2026 paper. The cage is C60, a sphere of sixty carbon atoms with high symmetry. Such cages have been proposed as shells to hold single atoms as quantum bits. New cooling and laser tools now resolve the cage's rotation in fine detail.

The team builds a quantum account of C60 meeting argon gas near one hundred fifty kelvin. They map the electronic structure and how the pull between partners varies with angle. Collisions can knock the cage out of its spin, a process called rotational quenching. Its symmetry makes that quenching depend on spin state in complex ways. They also compute how the cage bends light fields, which sets long-range forces.
arxiv-2603-02492:
Georgii Potapov and Yuri Kalnishkan build hypothesis tests from e-variables in this 2026 paper. E-variables are a newer tool for testing claims with strong error control. They grew from algorithmic randomness tests, a concept from information theory. Building good e-variables for whole families of distributions is the practical challenge.

Their approximability method constructs e-variables for popular distribution classes. The idea approximates a complex class by simpler pieces where e-variables are known. That yields explicit tests usable in applications. The same construction gives an explicit randomness test for a distribution class. Such tests judge whether data look truly random under the class. The work links modern safe testing back to its algorithmic roots.
arxiv-2603-02792:
Qi Huang, Furong Ye, Ananta Shahane, and colleagues show that good examples matter more than clever prompts when language models design algorithms. Their 2026 paper studies token-level credit inside the prompts used for automated algorithm design. Prior work mostly tuned prompt wording and search tricks.

Tracing which prompt tokens shaped the generated code, they found that high-quality example algorithms drive much of the improvement. Feeding strong benchmark algorithms in as priors then lifted results on two black-box optimization suites, covering Boolean and continuous problems. The lesson is practical: benchmark studies are not just scoreboards. Their best solutions are fuel that makes model-driven search faster and more robust.
arxiv-2603-02992:
Sheikh Moonsun Pervez maps the phases of a honeycomb magnet in an applied field. His 2026 paper studies the Kitaev model, a prized system whose spins can form a quantum spin liquid. A broad mean-field study tracks how hidden fields behave as the outside field grows and tilts.

With the field along one axis, the hidden fields stay stable up to a set strength. The way they fail depends on the field's direction. A tilted field splits the middle range into two phases. One is disordered, with random field values. In the other, the hidden fields nearly vanish, while spin directions swing wildly in length-fixed ways. Exact checks on small systems back parts of this picture. In one limit, the system's topology fades, then returns as the field grows.
arxiv-2603-03092:
Gabriele Domaine, Mihir Date, Sydney Dufresne, and a large team photograph the electronic life of a superconductor's rarely seen side face. Cuprate superconductors are expected to host suppressed pairing and flat zero-energy bands on their side surfaces, inviting exotic orders. But these crystals almost never split along that face, so momentum-resolved probes had never looked.

The team milled a controlled breaking point with an ion beam and exposed a clean side surface of an overdoped crystal. The superconducting gap was indeed suppressed, yet the expected flat band peak was missing too, despite a smooth surface. Calculations show roughness alone cannot erase the band, but the bulk disorder typical of these materials can smear it beyond detection. Disorder, not geometry, is the current blocker.
arxiv-2603-03392:
Patrick Sorrel Mvoto Kongo and three others hunt by computer for organic semiconductors that serve two masters at once. Such substances suit solar cells and biosensors, offering flexible structure and cheap processing, but high results means little if a molecule cannot actually be made. Their 2026 screen balances both demands from the start, rather than checking feasibility afterward.

More than seventeen thousand candidate molecules from a quantum chemistry data set were scored by one combined measure: predicted solar yield minus a synthetic ease-of-making penalty. Machine learning, density functional calculations, and molecular docking worked jointly across the screen. Seven dual-use candidates emerged with strong predicted yield and strong protein binding for sensing. One stood out as the best overall. The authors present the pipeline as a systematic route from theory toward molecules labs can in practice build.
arxiv-2603-03592:
Hadi Mohaghegh Dolatabadi and seven others guard spread-out model training stage by stage. Training across untrusted, scattered machines invites sabotage, and the classic defenses assume data parallelism, where gradients get averaged and bad actors can be outvoted. Pipeline parallelism breaks that assumption: layers live on distinct workers and activations flow between stages, with nothing to average. Their 2026 mechanism, Sentinel, verifies that flow without repeating any computing work.

Lightweight monitoring tracks exponential moving averages of the signals passing between stages and flags corrupted transmissions, a momentum-based tripwire rather than a second full pass of computing. Theory guarantees settling that recovers the standard rates when the setting relaxes to standard training. In tests, models of up to four billion settings trained successfully across as many as one hundred seventy-six untrusted workers, holding that settling and the results.
arxiv-2603-03792:
Haowei Zhu and nine colleagues speed up diffusion image generation by letting every token pick its own shortcut. Diffusion models are slow because each sampling step re-runs the whole network. Predictors can forecast a token's trajectory and skip work, but one fixed predictor fits all tokens badly. Their 2026 framework, TAP, chooses per token and per step, with no retraining at all.

A single full pass through the model's first layer acts as a cheap probe. From it, proxy errors are computed for a small family of candidate predictors, mostly Taylor expansions of varying order and horizon. Each token then gets whichever predictor the probe rated best for it. The overhead is negligible, the speedups large, and perceptual quality barely moves. Across architectures and tasks, TAP beats fixed global predictors and caching-only baselines on the accuracy-efficiency frontier.
arxiv-2603-03892:
Frederik Hagelskjaer presents a neural network for sorting the metadata of cuneiform tablets. The surviving corpus of tablets, produced from the fourth to the first millennium BCE, far exceeds the number of experts on hand to analyze it, so automated labeling has real use. The task is hard because annotated data sets are limited and each tablet is captured as a detailed point cloud.

The design takes its cue from convolution: it gradually down-scales the point cloud while folding in local neighbor information. It then computes neighbors in feature space so the final representation also carries global structure. Compared with the transformer-based Point-BERT, the state-of-the-art baseline, the method consistently performs best. Source code and data sets are to be released at publication, supporting wider computer work on the tablet corpus.
arxiv-2603-03992: Chan and colleagues propose metrics for tracking AI research and development automation and its effects. Automation of AI research could matter greatly, yet its extent and effects stay uncertain, and benchmarks alone may miss real-world automation. The metrics span capital share of research spending, researcher time allocation, and subversion incidents, addressing whether automation outpaces safety work and oversight. The authors urge companies and third parties to track these metrics, with government support, aiding decisions on consequences, safety measures, and development pace.
arxiv-2603-04092: De Alwis and others characterize machine learning force fields as emerging molecular motion workloads on graphics processors. Classical force fields use fixed fitted forms, offering speed and broad use but limited score in diverse or reactive settings. Machine learning force fields learn contacts from electronic structure data, reaching near quantum score at molecular-mechanics cost, yet adding descriptor and inference overhead. Using poly alanine chains as a controllable benchmark, the analysis finds bottlenecks in descriptor and force computation plus memory handling, pointing to drug-finding gains.
arxiv-2603-04592: Tong and colleagues survey streaming large language models from static use to live exchange. Standard models assume static, pre-defined inputs, limiting real time live use. Streaming models emerged, yet meanings fragment across streaming output, streaming inputs, and live setups without a full map. This paper unifies streaming models by data flow and live exchange, clearing mix-ups. A full map sorts current streaming models with in-depth methods talk. Uses in real world cases and likely paths round out the survey, backed by an always fresh paper list.
arxiv-2603-04792: Cheung and colleagues search for continuous gravitational waves from neutron stars in five globular clusters. Using LIGO data from eight months of the fourth run, they apply WEAVE semicoherent analysis. No signal appears in the 20 to 475 Hz band. Simulated signal injections show the most sensitive results to date across the parameter space. Median upper limits reach 4.2 times ten to the minus 26 near 282 Hz for NGC 6397. Ellipticity limits fall below 10 to the minus 5, with r-mode amplitudes below 10 to the minus 3.
arxiv-2603-04892: Sina Hajimiri and team add a locality bias to vision transformers so the models keep fine spatial detail for splitting without losing image-level spotting skill. Their add-on steers self-attention toward nearby patches with a learnable Gaussian kernel and refines patch embeddings so each position carries a meaningful form. On three benchmarks the changes deliver large splitting gains. Gains on ADE20K run over 6% and 4% for Tiny and Base variants, with no change to training and no sorting loss.
arxiv-2603-04992: Trapoom Ukarapol and colleagues introduce ThaiSafetyBench, an open-source benchmark of 1,954 malicious prompts in Thai covering general harms and attacks rooted in Thai cultural, social, and contextual nuances. Evaluating 24 language models, they find closed-source models generally safer than open-source ones. Thai-specific culturally contextualized attacks succeed more often than general Thai attacks, exposing a vulnerability in current safety alignment. The team also fine-tunes a DeBERTa-based harmful-response classifier reaching a weighted F1 score of 84.4%, matching leading-model judgments.
arxiv-2603-05092: Jiafeng Lin and team offer Aura, a wide method organizing mixed external information for aviation time series by interaction mode. Aviation maintenance involves three distinct exogenous factor types influencing time dynamics through distinct interaction modes. Aura's tripartite encoding embeds mixed features into set up time series models for smooth joining of non-step by step context. Tests on a large-scale three-year China Southern Airlines data set covering Boeing 777 and Airbus A320 fleets show steady state-of-the-art scores across older models with superior adaptability.
arxiv-2603-05192: Tim Wittenborg and team present Aerospace.Wikibase, a platform that lets aerospace engineers share and curate knowledge as one. That knowledge infrastructure is still split up, which leads to redundant work as aviation data volumes grow fast. The platform starts from a recent systematic literature review and already holds over 700 terms covering processes, software, and data, openly ready for growth. Linking project concepts to a persistent independent base lets them work as one on shared knowledge with no risk to project information.
arxiv-2603-05492: Ivashkov and team present a protocol that learns sparse Lindbladians from samples with ease, with no set interaction structure assumed in advance. Earlier protocols needed a set structure in advance, which fails when noise channels or control flaws are unknown ahead of time. Their protocol needs no ancilla and uses product-state preparations with Pauli-basis measurements, gives stable coefficient reconstruction that is proved, and reaches near-optimal time resolution. It offers a clear path to describing open-system quantum dynamics at scale, above all where error mechanisms are unknown.
arxiv-2603-05792: Krentsel and team present CrossCheck, checking inputs to software-defined net controls in wide area networks. Faulty inputs from control-base bugs cause major outages, and CrossCheck warns staff before bad inputs trigger failures. Staff study showed it would have stopped events. Deployed as a shadow checker for four weeks in live use, it caught the invalid-input event with no false alarms. Models show it flags bad inputs, spotting demand shifts as small as 5 percent with full score. False alarms stay near zero even with heavily mangled data feeds.
arxiv-2603-06092: Benić, Hagiwara, Šarić, and Vivoda compute the leading-twist gluon and sea-quark broad sideways push spreads at small x and fading tilt. All gluon spreads reduce to the basic gluon dipole, which also holds proton spin-twist flips, yielding all links between other spreads in the small-x limit. The results project onto sideways push tied and broad parton spread cases, getting back results where found. Sea-quark spreads follow from folding the gluon dipole with a hard kernel, broad to nonzero push moves with proton spin-twist flips.
arxiv-2603-06192: Babicz and colleagues benchmark transformer models operating directly on digitised waveforms for pulse shape discrimination in high purity germanium detectors, used in rare event searches like neutrinoless double beta decay. Models learn accept and reject labels for four standard cuts and regress calibrated energy. The comparison covers supervised training from scratch, masked autoencoder pre-training, and a gradient boosted tree baseline. Transformers beat the baseline across all targets, with the largest gains on the hardest labels. Masked autoencoder pre-training cuts labelled data needs by factors of 2 to 4.
arxiv-2603-06492: Smith brings NOBLE, an augmentation adding low-rank nonlinear branches to transformer linear layers, built for pretraining from scratch rather than fine-tuning. Unlike LoRA and other plug-ins, the branch is a fixed architecture part, doing a learnable nonlinearity between down and up steps. NOBLE reaches baseline test loss with up to 1.47x step speedup and fewer training steps, at parameter and step-time cost, for a wallclock speedup. Tests on LLMs, BERT, VQGAN, and ViT show better efficiency, though Mixup-style add-on clashes in ImageNet classification.
arxiv-2603-06592: Rohweder and team unify the Hydra effect, induction heads, and function vectors as consequences of latent structures in data generation. They couple spread gradients across additive model parts with curve in geometry. Studies have tied phenomena to data spread properties, architecture, or information handling. Yet a grasp of data, design, and tuning remains lacking for why they appear all over across model families and scales despite gap. The authors validate their theory in a toy model regime and synthetic data, testing with language models trained on language data.
arxiv-2603-06692: Gergely Bérczi studies three hard combinatorics problems through small local fix steps that build to a whole answer. The cases cover rebuilding graphs from parts, a parity problem for Latin squares, and Rota's Basis Conjecture. Using AlphaEvolve as a search tool, he reports setups, scores, and results, and states plain conjectures. He claims no proofs, only clear routines and patterns for later proof work.
arxiv-2603-06992: Ma and colleagues image the HD 34282 disk with ALMA across four millimeter bands, hunting signs of a dust-trapping vortex. Arcs in millimeter light from young disks are often blamed on dust-trapping vortices, but firm proof of vortices is still lacking. Sharp views resolve a bright arc on a compact double-gap, triple-ring shape, clearest at short waves. The arc has a lower spectral index than nearby rings, fitting more grain growth or denser dust, and its width shrinks with wavelength, fitting tighter hold on larger grains.
arxiv-2603-07192: Yune and colleagues speed space-time auto video generation with FastSTAR, a training-free speedup system. Scaling detail and frame counts causes a token flood that jams the final polish stages. Their space-time token pruning keeps only key tokens. Spatial match skips polish where structure has already settled, and time match tracks active motion against the prior clip. Mixed with a partial update tool, FastSTAR preserves video quality while cutting compute.
arxiv-2603-07292: Bahadori, Shariatpanahi and Bahrak reframe coded caching when file popularity starts out unknown. Rather than estimating each popularity precisely, their method ranks files against each other from request counts and splits them into groups. Earlier methods also ended up grouping files, but only after an estimation step this approach skips. The ranking view wins out especially with few users, tight cache space, or polluted request logs, where regret grows more slowly than the horizon.
arxiv-2603-07392: Kim and colleagues benchmark whether language models can adapt online as facts change over time. Their OAKS suite streams fine-grained context chunks in which individual facts evolve repeatedly, with dense labels tracking whether models follow each change. Across fourteen models and varied inference styles, even top models and agentic memory systems adapt poorly. State tracking lags and streaming distractions trip the models up, showing online adaptation remains an open problem.
arxiv-2603-07692: Gunther, Kercheval and Sowunmi investigate the long-only global minimum variance portfolio under factor models of returns. For a one-factor model they give a strict, exact account of the solution in terms of covariance inputs. For multiple factors they describe it in geometric terms. Real daily returns of United States stocks show the results, linking factors to the limited optimum.
arxiv-2603-07792: Pandey and Chhetri analyze biases in seven leading language models in the Nepali context, using over 2400 sentence pairs on gender roles. Their Dual-Metric Bias test joins agreement and completion habits. Models show open bias and higher hidden bias, peaking at moderate stochasticity. Open bias aligns with stock bias but weakly predicts hidden bias, so metrics poorly capture made-up bias. For race and social tropes, hidden bias runs strongest, while open bias is similar across them.
arxiv-2603-08192: Reali and colleagues propose a Hodge-based framework for analyzing services on serverless platforms. Such services consist of linked functions that can show tangled, non-conservative information flows when separately deployed functions interact under coarse control. The authors build a topological model of serverless services and use the Hodge decomposition to split observed flows into locally fixable parts and globally lasting harmonic modes. Harmonic flows arise from function interactions and count as structural traits of the system, not setup errors.
arxiv-2603-08392: Ng and colleagues align user, expert, and developer on LLM counselling with QUORUM and COACH. Apps logging sleep, mood, and activities can counsel people living with chronic disease. Building them extracts patterns from data, grounding them in medical knowledge, and shaping advice. QUORUM unifies the perspectives, and a case study tracks where stakeholders converge and diverge. COACH, an LLM pipeline, generates counselling for Healthy Chronos, a diary app used by cancer patients and survivors. All groups judge the counselling relevant, reliable, while differing on tone, error sensitivity, and hallucinations.
arxiv-2603-08792: Tetyana Pitik and colleagues predict gamma-ray lines from r-process nuclei in a collapsing magnetized white dwarf. Ejecta from a relativistic magnetic-fluid simulation with neutrinos, aged with a radiation code and live nuclear network, give angle-dependent spectra. Early light is ruled by iodine-132 fed by tellurium-132, later by cobalt-56, and the brightest lines stay visible to about ten megaparsecs.
arxiv-2603-08892: Clovis Lambert and colleagues document phase-shifting dealiasing for pseudo-spectral turbulence simulations. The standard two-thirds truncation rule eats up to 80 percent of the cost in three dimensions. Phase shifting cancels aliasing from nonlinear terms on shifted grids, matching the same resolution on coarser grids. Their open Fluidsim code runs up to three times faster than the standard rule with small accuracy loss.
arxiv-2603-08992: Santiago Badia and colleagues solve incompressible nonlinear elasticity with a stable finite element scheme. Their four-field scheme uses displacement, displacement gradient, Piola-Kirchhoff stress, and pressure, with a broken displacement field that needs no stabilization in 2D or 3D. A Newton-Raphson linear step, inf-sup element pairs, and a postprocessing step yield soundness, error bounds, and optimal or super convergence in tests.
arxiv-2603-09192: Renwei Meng proposes an engine that upgrades retrieval-augmented generation by treating methods, not text chunks, as the stored units. Two trees hold the store: one traces where each method came from, the other groups methods so search can start broad and narrow down. At query time an agent picks a named way to combine ideas, builds new method nodes, and logs each step. A checker then drops weak nodes and writes the sound ones back for later use.
arxiv-2603-09592: Joanna Matulewicz and colleagues analyze Yb-implanted beta gallium oxide crystals in three orientations, in both structure and optical response. The material is an ultrawide bandgap semiconductor eyed for power and optoelectronic devices in harsh radiation settings. Crystals got three fluences of 150 keV Yb ions, then X-ray diffraction, Rutherford backscattering, and Raman and photoluminescence probes. That orientation held the fewest defects and showed compressive stress, while the others showed tensile stress.
arxiv-2603-09992: Izzat Alsmadi and Anas Alsobeh present TAMUSA-Chat, a framework for building a domain adapted chat system for a single institution. General foundation models need careful tuning, retrieval support and evaluation before they fit local needs safely. The paper walks through data gathering, cleaning, embedding, training and deployment as linked modular parts. Tests across model sizes and training rounds reveal how quality trades against cost in domain adaptation.
arxiv-2603-10092: Borjigin and coauthors argue that acts, not wrong answers, are the new danger zone for agent driven crypto trading. Local tools turn model intent into real trades, while skill shops add a chain of add on skills that can be bought and set up in one click. Their guard layer sits between plan and exchange, enforcing spend caps, cooldowns, slip bounds and allowlists that cannot be bypassed. A logged plan spec makes such handed off acts testable.
arxiv-2603-10292: Yeongjun Jang and co-authors build a controller that steers nonlinear systems using only noise-free input and output data, aiming at practical regulation of the output. An inverse model, found by kernel interpolation, maps a wanted output and current state to the input that should produce it. A second part picks a suitable target output from the same data used for identification. They state a checkable condition on the data under which regulation is guaranteed, and simulations, including noisy tests, support the design.
arxiv-2603-10592: Jiarui Cao, Zixuan Wei, and Yuxin Liu give a precise frame for a new family of generative models they call Gradient Flow Drifting. They prove the recent Drifting Model equals, up to a bandwidth scaling, the Wasserstein gradient flow of forward KL divergence under kernel density approximation. The family also covers MMD-based generators, as flows of other divergences. A mixed strategy combining reverse KL and chi-squared flows aims to dodge mode collapse and mode blurring, and extends to Riemannian manifolds. Early synthetic tests support the framework.
arxiv-2603-10692: Xian Qin, Xue Yang, and Xiaohu Tang repurpose backdoors for good, using them as built-in proofs that aggregation in cross-silo federated learning was done right. Secure aggregation hides client updates, but a malicious server can silently drop or tamper with them. Their design embeds verification signals into model parameters by backdoor injection. The signals fade naturally through catastrophic forgetting, so final model utility survives, while a random audit checks them at once. Tests showed high detection of malicious servers and huge speedups over proof-based baselines.
arxiv-2603-10892: Noah Schnitzer and coauthors show two methods can be done at very low heat. Atomic-resolution electron microscopy and ptychography work at liquid-helium temperatures, down to 20 K. They use a commercial helium-cooled holder. Such cold imaging matters for quantum materials. Their ground states can differ from what room-temperature measurements probe. Fast scans tame drift and vibration for imaging. A multi-stage registration workflow helps too. Ptychography needs scan-position correction. That correction also handles coupling with probe aberrations.
arxiv-2603-11092: Haokun Sui and Feida Jiang study the far field refraction problem in materials with negative refractive index, where part of the energy is lost. Earlier work left this case open. They split the analysis by the relative refractive index, covering the range below minus one and the range between minus one and zero. For each case the Minkowski method yields weak solutions, whether the target measure is discrete or a finite Radon measure. They derive a Monge-Ampère type inequality the solution satisfies.
arxiv-2603-11192: Eric Heller and David Limmer show that the stability of patterns in driven reaction-diffusion systems hinges on the paths between them. It does not hinge on thermodynamics. Such systems can hold several long-lived spatial patterns. At finite particle numbers, random fluctuations trigger rare switches. Mean-field descriptions miss those switches. Exact simulation stays prohibitively expensive. Their instanton rate calculations match master-equation benchmarks. They include fluctuation and symmetry prefactors. An effective path entropy can tilt stability. It can favor one switching direction over the other.
arxiv-2603-11492: Du and co-authors present SPEGC, a method that helps medical image segmentation models adapt as test domains keep shifting. Models trained on one site's scans often falter on another's, and weak self-training signals can snowball into collapse. SPEGC first boosts local features with semantic prompts drawn from shared and distinct prompt pools. A differentiable graph clustering solver then sharpens the feature map into a clean structural picture. That structure guides adaptation, keeping cluster-level predictions consistent. On two benchmarks, SPEGC beats other test-time adaptation methods.
arxiv-2603-11692: Zhao and co-authors demonstrate high-fidelity single-qubit gates on a C-shunt flux qubit with rare traits combined. The qubit pairs a large anharmonicity, 848 MHz, with a long relaxation time of 23 microseconds. Big anharmonicity holds leakage to higher levels down, which allows fast, precise microwave control. With DRAG pulses and randomized benchmarking, gate fidelities pass 99.9 percent. The team frames C-shunt flux qubits as a promising base for scalable quantum information processing.
arxiv-2603-11792: Berdysheva and co-authors study Delsarte-type problems for positive definite functions on compact Gelfand pairs. They frame the problems as infinite-dimensional linear programming problems. This setup covers compact Abelian groups as one case. Two sign choices give two classic problems, the Turán problem and the Delsarte problem. Such problems link to number theory, sphere packing, and statistics. The authors describe the dual problems and prove a strong duality result.
arxiv-2603-11992: Guo and co-authors reshape personalized federated learning as a few-for-many problem. Instead of one model per client, a few shared server models serve all clients at once. The team proves this setup can stay near optimal for each client. Error shrinks as the shared model count grows and as client data grows. Their FedFew method, with just three shared models, beat leading rivals on vision, language, and medical imaging tests.
arxiv-2603-12192: Carlson, Roggero, and Neill follow neutrino flavor change where fluxes run very high. Core-collapse supernovae and neutron star mergers flood space with neutrinos that interact with each other. Their semi-classical treatment adds non-forward scattering between neutrinos and antineutrinos. Random phases and conserved momentum let the many-body system settle in a rapid way. Energy and angle spreads even out across flavors, as do density products for each flavor. The scheme reduces to standard MSW oscillations in the right limits and can shift energy deposition and nucleosynthesis.
arxiv-2603-12292: Haut and co-authors run genetic programming on GPUs with a new framework named Beagle. Symbolic regression searches formulas that fit data, a task CPUs grind through slowly. Beagle processes the population and fitness cases in a layout tuned for GPU throughput. Benchmarks use the Feynman Symbolic Regression dataset under a fixed wall clock budget. Rivals include a fast CPU system, StackGP, and the widely used PySR. With both point error and correlation fitness, Beagle's GPU-aided search beat the leading CPU frameworks by a clear margin.
arxiv-2603-13092: Wei Xing and co-authors break the tuning barrier in yield multi-corner circuit analysis with learned priors. Checking 25 or more process-voltage-temperature corners makes simulation cost grow fast. Simple models automate well but fail on nonlinear circuits, while AI models need hours of tuning. Their method swaps hand-built priors for a foundation model trained on millions of regression tasks. In-context learning adapts it to each circuit with no tuning at all. Total validation cost fell by over 10x at top accuracy.
arxiv-2603-13292: Ming Wen and co-authors introduce Pragma-VL, an alignment method for multimodal large language models. Such models face jailbreak attacks and can also produce harmful content for benign users. Standard tuning often refuses harmless queries or misses cross-modal risks instead. Pragma-VL first sharpens visual risk perception through a risk-aware cold-start fine-tuning stage. A reward model with synergistic learning then weighs safety against helpfulness by context. Tests show gains of 5 to 20 percent on most safety benchmarks, with general skills preserved.
arxiv-2603-13492: J. Miles and co-authors demonstrate qubit syndrome measurements with a high fidelity Rb-Cs Rydberg gate. They report an inter-species entangling gate between rubidium and cesium atoms with fidelity near 0.975. A two-species atom array enables in-place quantum non-demolition measurements, a key capability for quantum error correction. Multi-atom error syndrome measurements reached high QND fidelities for two-qubit plaquettes. Three-qubit plaquettes scored lower in the same setup. The work supports Rydberg arrays as a path to practical error correction.
arxiv-2603-13592: The CMS Collaboration measures the t-channel single top quark cross section in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV. Data came from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC in 2017, with an integrated luminosity of 302 pb inverse. It is the first CMS measurement of this process at that energy. Events with one electron or muon and two or more jets, at least one from a b quark, are analyzed. The combined cross section for single top quark and antiquark production agrees with standard model predictions.
arxiv-2603-13692: Yakun Zhang investigates a general Mayer-Vietoris sequence in algebraic K-theory for the Milnor square. Such sequences often involve elusive intermediate terms that resist direct description. Zhang gives an explicit characterization of the key group in a new, more general variant of the sequence. He identifies that group as a categorical pullback and gives a full, constructive proof. The group also fits into a structural exact sequence involving relative K-groups. A homotopy-theoretic description presents it as the homotopy group of a suitable fiber.
arxiv-2603-13792: Cui and co-authors tackle a flaw in LoRA, a cheap way to fine-tune large language models. LoRA gives every layer the same rank, though layers differ in how much they matter. Their method, IGU-LoRA, scores each layer with integrated gradients, which track effects along a path, not just at one point. A smoothing scheme based on moving averages cuts noise in the scores. The authors report better accuracy than rival methods at the same parameter budget.
arxiv-2603-13892: Nakayama proves global well-posedness for a fourth-order nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a potential. The setting is the energy-critical case, in dimensions five and up, with radial initial data. Under stated conditions on the radial potential, solutions exist for all time in the H2 space. Each solution also scatters, settling toward a free biharmonic wave. The proof leans on Strichartz estimates, wave operator bounds, and a Morawetz-type estimate adapted to the potential.
arxiv-2603-14492: Abadi and Desmedt present Oblivis, a framework for delegated oblivious transfer. Thin clients on cloud and edge setups must fetch records without exposing their queries. Older transfer tools assume direct client contact with the database. Oblivis adds four parts: delegated query transfer, multi-receiver transfer, a constant-size response compiler and a fast proxy-based protocol. The designs carry formal security proofs under a non-collusion assumption. In tests, the fast protocol runs at least 92 times quicker than a strong baseline, they report.
arxiv-2603-14892: Lee and co-authors prune visual tokens in vision-language models with sample-adaptive budgets in PromPrune. High-resolution inputs flood models with visual tokens and compute cost. Static pruning mixes saliency and diversity in one fixed ratio. Semantic prominence shifts a lot from sample to sample, though. PromPrune sizes local and global budgets per sample first. A two-stage selection then spends those budgets. On LLaVA-NeXT-7B, FLOPs fall 88% and prefill latency 22%, they report. Output quality holds at 97.5% of the full model.
arxiv-2603-14992: Tian and co-authors catch fake short videos by exposing cross-modal consistency gaps with MAGIC3. Each channel of a fake can look plausible while the mix clashes. Real videos show high text-visual match but middling text-audio match. Fakes flip that pattern on Chinese and English bench sets. One global consistency score orders fake risk in a smooth way. MAGIC3 models pairwise and global consistency at several grain levels. Scores top non-VLM baselines on both benches, they report.
arxiv-2603-15092: Binosi gives a self-contained account of gauge symmetry in Yang-Mills theory beyond perturbation theory. Starting from path integral quantization, he reviews gauge fixing and Faddeev-Popov ghosts. He then builds the BRST and anti-BRST formalisms together. Their joint use yields strong functional identities that constrain the ghost and gluon sectors. Background field gauges turn these into simple Ward identities. From them he defines an effective charge that is unique, gauge invariant, and process independent, from ultraviolet to infrared scales.
arxiv-2603-15192: Fry and co-authors benchmark Formula 1 results with normal models that split car and driver effects. Four elite teams have won every major race for four years, which clouds driver comparisons. The authors fit univariate and bivariate normal models at driver and team level. Elite and non-elite teams get separate treatment. The models set fair performance expectations for each side. They illustrate the approach on the full 2025 season, the last one completed.
arxiv-2603-15292: Gloeckler and co-authors present PRISM, a simulation-based method that picks among huge families of scientific models. PRISM is an encoder-decoder that infers a joint posterior over model structures and their parameters. Users can tune the model prior at test time to control complexity, rather than fixing it before training. It scaled to billions of model variants on a symbolic regression test. A diffusion MRI study showed real model selection on synthetic and live brain data.
arxiv-2603-15392: Alhilal and co-authors report the first doctoral thesis defense run as a hybrid extended reality event. Their framework lets people join in person, through immersive virtual reality, or from a plain browser. Full-body motion tracking drives avatars, so gestures and body language carry to remote guests. WebXR keeps access cross-platform with easy setup. Feedback from the event was positive for the virtual reality side. The study shows one setup can host talks, questions, and social parts of an academic rite without splitting the crowd.
arxiv-2603-15492: Acharya and Dhakal recast grokking, the late jump from memorization to generalization, as a variance-limited phase change. They study AdamW on modular arithmetic tasks. A spectral gating picture emerges: the generalizing solution sits in a sharp basin that low-variance training cannot enter. Delay is the time needed for gradient variance to build and lift the stability ceiling. Three regimes appear as task size grows, from capacity collapse to stability override. Flat minima ideas fail here, since plain noise injection does not trigger grokking.
arxiv-2603-15592: Maffei and co-authors compare turbulent jet flames fed by hydrogen and by methane. The two fuels differ sharply in Lewis number, so older scaling rules may not fit hydrogen. The team ran flames across wide ranges of Reynolds and Karlovitz numbers. They read flame shape with OH chemiluminescence imaging. A shared framework with a flame speed factor and a shape factor fits both fuels well. The data give a benchmark for testing combustion models.
arxiv-2603-15692: Zhang and co-authors defend language models against hidden backdoor triggers. Attackers plant triggers that flip model outputs on cue. Finding the trigger by inversion is key to defense. Text is discrete, so noise-based generators built for images fail here. Their BadLLM-TG uses a language model to write candidate triggers. Prompt-driven reinforcement learning tunes it with the victim model's loss. Found triggers then support adversarial training. Attack success fell by 76.2 percent on average in tests.
arxiv-2603-15892: Dey and co-authors replay two clashing studies on time-stale facts in language models. DYNAMICQA found outside context barely moves time-based facts. MULAN found such facts the easiest to update. The team reran both studies, then crossed each method onto the other's data. Shared settings and fresh synthetic contexts enable a fair match. MULAN's findings hold under both frameworks, they report. DYNAMICQA under MULAN scoring gives mixed outcomes instead. Model size also shapes how stale facts stick or yield.
arxiv-2603-16192: Sun and co-authors propose Structured Semantic Cloaking, a new jailbreak attack on language models. Modern safety systems read deep meaning, so surface tricks often fail. Their method splits and reshapes the harmful request across a prompt. Full intent then takes multi-step inference to rebuild. Three parts do the work: reframing, fragmentation, and clue-guided camouflage. On HarmBench and JBB-Behaviors, attack success rose 12.4% and 9.7% over the best prior method.
arxiv-2603-16292: Yang and co-authors answer spoken questions without first transcribing the speech. Cascaded systems that use speech recognition add delay and spread errors. Their AEG framework reads the speech model's own cross-modal attention. That attention locates the key evidence inside the model's latent space. A fine-tuning method, Learning to Focus on Evidence, sharpens the attention. Tests on SQuAD, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue cut hallucinations. Latency fell by about 62% versus strong cascaded baselines.
arxiv-2603-16392: Galanakis, Koliousis, and Zafeiriou generate fake skin lesion images to aid diagnosis. Real clinical datasets are small and skewed toward benign cases. Their DermaFlux system turns text descriptions into lesion images. It fine-tunes a Flux model with low-rank adaptation on curated photo sets. Captions came from a language model, using standard dermatology traits. Adding synthetic images lifted classification by up to 6%. A fine-tuned ViT reached about 78% accuracy, beating rival models.
arxiv-2603-17092: Daneshmand and co-authors present SLowRL, a method for safely fine tuning robot locomotion policies on real hardware. Policies trained in simulation degrade in the real world, yet naive fine tuning risks breaking the robot. SLowRL combines low rank adaptation with a recovery policy that enforces safety during training. It was tested in simulation and on a real Unitree Go2 quadruped, on jump and trot tasks. The authors report a 46.5 percent cut in fine tuning time and near zero safety violations versus PPO baselines.
arxiv-2603-17592: Koutsiaris builds a browser extension that explains tech acronyms on hover for low-skill web users. A curated dictionary plus a language model supplies short tooltip definitions. A two-step AI pipeline checks that a page is tech-related before the tooltips switch on. In a study with 25 users, 92 percent said the tool improved their grasp of terms. Dictionary answers landed in about 2.1 seconds, far faster than manual search.
arxiv-2603-17692: Jeon and Lee test whether language-model traders use real signal or memorized tickers. Their BlindTrade setup hides all ticker symbols and company names from four agents. Each agent scores stocks and writes its reasoning in the blind setting. A graph network built from those texts feeds a PPO trading policy. On 2025 data the Sharpe ratio hit 1.40 across 20 seeds, they report. Gains faded in trending bull markets, though.
arxiv-2603-18292: Zhou and co-authors contrast evolutionary paths of fast- and slow-rotating galaxies in the green valley. MaNGA data splits the sample by stellar spin for metal comparisons. Fast rotators hold higher metal levels in both gas and stars. Chemical models point to stronger outflows in slow rotators at low mass. At high mass, mergers and AGN feedback likely cut gas inflow and speed gas loss for slow rotators.
arxiv-2603-18592: Lin, Zheng, and Chen map where fidelity zeros fall in two-band topological models. They push the tuning parameter into the complex plane. Within a biorthogonal setup, zeros link to momentum modes where the real energy gap closes. They test the Kitaev chain, the Haldane model, and the Qi-Wu-Zhang model. Finite systems show discrete lines, while large systems fill extended regions. Transition points bound the reachable real range, or show as zeros crossing the real axis.
arxiv-2603-18692: Seoane, Benali, and Oriols show how Bohmian trajectories can teach basic quantum electrodynamics. Critics often say trajectory views cannot handle photon creation or annihilation. The authors revive older proposals that pair electron trajectories with well-defined fields in time. A photon partition noise test anchors the account, along with the origin of the Born rule. The frame treats photons as non-ontic, yet field traits still get measured through matter pointers. The aim is a clear tool for computing and picturing quantum optics effects.
arxiv-2603-18892: Lee and co-authors release MultihopSpatial, a benchmark for step-by-step spatial reasoning in vision-language models. Most tests ask about single spatial relations. Real tasks chain relations across one to three hops and varied viewpoints. Their metric, Acc@50IoU, demands both the right answer and a tight bounding box. A large training corpus, MultihopSpatial-Train, ships with the benchmark. Tests of 37 top models yield eight findings and show compositional spatial reasoning stays hard. Fine-tuning on the corpus also lifts robot manipulation scores downstream.
arxiv-2603-18992: Tang lays out the math base of Schroedinger bridges for generative modeling. Such bridges frame the task of turning a simple spread of data into a complex one. The path between the two should stray as little as possible from a fixed reference process. The guide draws on transport theory, stochastic control, and path-space methods. It builds the bridge tools from first principles. It then shows how these tools yield broad and task-specific methods. Diffusion and flow models appear as kin under this one view.
arxiv-2603-19292: Yu and co-authors review how talk between people can be mined to judge teamwork. Conversation is the main channel for sharing facts and lining up joint work. The review covers theories, coding schemes, tasks, and model types for this field. It asks how task-based human dialogue data can best serve teamwork analysis. Gaps in current data and methods are flagged for future work. The authors aim to give researchers a practical map of the area. Verbal cues are the focus throughout.
arxiv-2603-19992: DeWitt and co-authors measure water and methanol gas around the young star SVS 13-A. They used the EXES instrument on the SOFIA airborne observatory at 26 micrometres. The spectra resolve lines of both species at high detail. The gas is warm, at about 140 to 170 kelvin. Methanol turns out about four times more abundant than water. That ratio is far above what interstellar ices usually show. The authors suggest selective sublimation or layered ices in the inner envelope. These zones are where planets form and gain their chemistry.
arxiv-2603-20592: Haward and Shen test how fluid type and pore layout shape flow resistance in porous media. They push two polymer fluids through microfluidic post arrays. One fluid keeps constant viscosity, the other thins under shear. Posts sit in ordered rows, aligned or staggered, with random shifts added. Both fluids show higher resistance past a Weissenberg number of one. Disorder raised resistance in aligned arrays but not staggered ones. Flow films show the two fluids resist for distinct reasons.
arxiv-2603-20792: Dutta and Tushar study a phase space measure of magic in qubit systems. Magic is the resource that lifts quantum circuits past stabilizer limits. For one qubit they derive an exact closed form for the measure. It depends on the l1 norm of the Bloch vector. They extend bounds to products of many qubit states. Frame choice matters for qubits, so they check which findings stay frame free. Some key bounds hold in every frame they test. The measure is not a magic monotone, though.
arxiv-2603-21292: Dao and co-authors study the parabolic variant of the Erdős-Falconer distance problem in finite fields. For odd q, they seek size thresholds past which any subset of the plane determines many distinct parabolic distances. The parabolic distance shares traits with the standard distance but behaves differently in key ways. They start with Fourier analytic arguments. Additive combinatorics then handles the central obstructions. They give a suite of positive results, plus sharpness examples that show the bounds cannot be improved in general.
arxiv-2603-21492: Zhang and co-authors study how to pick a representative subset under a partition constraint, scored by a near-submodular objective. Older local-search methods need many function queries and hard-to-get structural parameters. Their Multinoulli-SCG algorithm needs no such parameters and far fewer evaluations, while matching the old approximation guarantees. The core tool is the Multinoulli Extension, a continuous relaxation with a lossless rounding scheme for any set function. They also give two online variants built on the same extension.
arxiv-2603-21592: Park and co-authors test whether electric vehicle battery health reports can be trusted. State-of-health figures from on-board management systems are what owners and regulators see, but nobody had checked them across brands. Studying 1,114 vehicles from five manufacturers over 375 days, they found real capacity gaps of 12 to 25 percent within single models. The reported health scores barely tracked those gaps, and 384 vehicles exposed no score at all. A marker based on partial charging windows classified degradation far better in lab checks.
arxiv-2603-21692: Vispute and Kadam argue that autonomous AI agents need records of their reasoning, not just their state. Checkpoints give fault tolerance and traces help debugging, but neither shows why an agent acted. Their Agent Execution Record stores intent, observation, and inference as queryable fields at each step. It also holds versioned plans with revision reasons, evidence chains, and scored verdicts. Such records support group-level analytics: pattern mining, calibration checks, and replay tests. They add a domain-free model, a reference build, and lessons from a live root-cause agent.
arxiv-2603-22392: Girichidis and co-authors model the X-ray glow of a Local Bubble twin inside a simulation. The Local Bubble is the hot, thin cavity that holds the Solar System. The team tracks the emission in a magnetohydrodynamic run. Soon after a supernova, most X-ray light comes from under one percent of the volume. In quiet phases, the glow spreads out and fills more space. Thick gas columns absorb soft X-rays and hide much of the sky. The flux also swings hard on million-year scales.
arxiv-2603-22592: Das and Pramanik study an inverse scattering problem in three dimensions. The setting is the nonlinear fractional Helmholtz equation with cubic nonlinearity. An inverse problem works backward from observed effects to a hidden cause. Here the goal is to recover a compactly supported potential from the scattering amplitude. That is, they ask what the wave pattern far away reveals about the hidden term. The work sets up this nonlocal problem and examines the recovery task at its core. It adds to the theory of inverse problems for fractional equations.
arxiv-2603-23192: Fang, Ge, and Xiao present GTLR-GS, a LiDAR-regularized 3D Gaussian splatting framework. Standard splatting starts from sparse structure-from-motion points, which lack scale and geometry priors. Their method builds LiDAR metric priors into the whole optimization. A geometry-texture allocation step spends primitives where structure or appearance is complex. A curvature-based step splits Gaussians toward complex geometry during training. Depth regularization anchors the scene to true scale. Tests on ScanNet++ and a custom dataset reach top scores for metric reconstruction.
arxiv-2603-23292: Cruz and Aji argue that language model scores need a sealed-exam style of testing. Leaderboard numbers can reflect test chasing, hidden scoring choices, or leaked test items. Closed benchmarks help but hide how results were produced. The pair propose an Olympiad-style event with problems sealed until test day. Entries freeze in advance and all run through one standard harness. After scoring, the full task set and code are released for audit. They say the design makes strong scores harder to fake and easier to trust.
arxiv-2603-23392: Limame and nine co-authors grow quantum dots that emit at telecom O-band wavelengths on demand. Such sources matter for fiber quantum links and shared quantum computing. Their trick is a buried aluminum-based stressor layer under the dots. The layer strains the surface in a set pattern, pulling emission toward 1.3 micrometers. Dots also nucleate at mesa centers, giving site control without coherence-harming layers. The dots emit pure single photons at 4 K and hold up at 77 K. Models of the exciton states match the measured spectra well.
arxiv-2603-23592: de Vries and three co-authors compute radiative corrections to two-neutrino double-beta decay. They work inside heavy-nucleus effective field theory. Their result is a universal correction factor for double-weak decays. Like the Sirlin function for single decays, it needs no nuclear matrix elements. It does hinge on the two electron energies and their angle. It departs from doubling the single-decay fix. The part of the corrections stays small for now. The spectra shifts, though, rival structure effects, so past fits need a second look.
arxiv-2603-23892: Connolly and co-authors give faster ways to prepare graph states for quantum computing. Graph states support measurement-based computing and quantum networking, but they cost many entangling steps. States linked by local complement moves are equivalent, so a cheaper representative may exist. Their quotient-augmented split tree describes these orbits for distance-hereditary graphs. It finds states with fewer controlled-Z gates or shallower circuits. A split-fuse construction scales linearly for those graphs. They also sketch greedy methods for general graphs.
arxiv-2603-23992: Suleymanli and co-authors study how added Lambda hyperons change collective modes in atomic nuclei. They model closed-shell hypernuclei of calcium, nickel, tin, and lead with Hartree-Fock plus random phase approximation. As hyperon number grows, the energies of monopole, dipole, and quadrupole modes shift upward in a systematic way. The incompressibility modulus also rises steadily. In the lead hypernucleus it reaches 322 MeV, the largest value found. Matter calculations confirm the stiffening is a bulk effect of the interactions involved.
arxiv-2603-24192: Brusca and co-authors prove compactness results for non-local energies used in free discontinuity problems. These energies are modeled on a class introduced by Gobbino.
