The classification is complete for hook partitions, closing the case for this family.
arxiv-2605-28192: Xu and colleagues test audio-visual reasoning that hops across scattered evidence in sound and video. Their MOV-Bench poses over five hundred questions needing multi-hop reasoning over dispersed clips, where current omni-models still struggle. Their AOP-Agent, which pairs a layered memory with an observe-reflect-replan loop, lifts open-source models without extra training, most on long videos.
arxiv-2605-28292: Lee and colleagues shrink chain-of-thought reasoning into reuse-ready functional tokens for cheaper hidden inference. CIRF gives one job token to each clear reasoning chunk in plain traces, then trains models to emit tokens and optional results before answering. Hidden reasoning thus tracks plain rationales, trading correctness against wait time well.
arxiv-2605-28592: Jiangsheng You notes that partial least squares can be cast as linear self-attention, placing it inside the neural-network world. This view lets partial least squares be studied with neural-network tools rather than as a lone stats method. In return, the dimensionality cut and predictor picks in partial least squares suggest self-attention itself evens out dimensionality to some degree. The short note thus builds a two-way bridge between an older regression technique and modern attention mechanisms, hinting at improved learning from evening.
arxiv-2605-28792: Abhilash Durgam and five colleagues present CaMBRAIN, the first causal Mamba state space model for real-time EEG inference. Existing EEG models use attention, which scales quadratically with sequence length, and raw signals need sliding-window processing that blocks global understanding. Training is hard because key EEG events last fractions of a second yet sit minutes apart, and reconstruction objectives fail to train the hidden state for salient long-range context. A multi-stage self-supervised pipeline tailored to long-range memory retention keeps linear-time complexity with EEG performance.
arxiv-2605-28992: Dan Jacobellis and Neeraja Yadwadkar present FRAPPE, an autoencoding framework that predicts a residual output from the full input through a projection pursuit encoder. Its objective naturally ranks latent channels by importance, enabling variable-rate coding with no overhead. Unlike sequential rivals, its analysis path is a parallel graph of independent input projections. Built into a variable-rate RGB image codec, it beats AVIF on perceptual quality at about 0.1 bits per pixel with 47 times faster encoding, reaching real-time 1080p CPU-only encoding at 30 frames per second.
arxiv-2605-29192: Daniel Lee, Owen Queen, and James Zou build ReasonOps, an unsupervised method annotating chain-of-thought traces with shared operators. Across 44,662 traces from 12 models, 6 groups, and 8 benchmarks, they find seven recurring operators: discourse moves such as going back, guessing, and posing. The operators appear across family and domain, backed by three outside judges rating held-out samples at 70 to 76 percent right. Review operators help on hard problems but harm easy ones, operator chains on their own identify the source model, and shape signs predict rightness above norms.
arxiv-2605-30092: Danila Cherkashin and Yakov Shubin give short proofs of three extremal results in the Johnson scheme, also described as systems of subsets with restricted intersection sizes. Their main result proves the Aljohani-Bamberg-Cameron conjecture. When two complementary systems have sizes multiplying to the full binomial count, they must form an intersecting family and a Steiner system. The note keeps all three arguments brief, offering leaner routes to results about how large such families can be and how they are structured.
arxiv-2605-30292: Hanyang Jiang, Rina Foygel Barber, Ashwin Pananjady and Yao Xie show the leave-one-out jackknife can suffer loss of coverage even in standard time series models. Conformal prediction assumes exchangeable data treated evenly during training, but time series violate exchangeability. They propose the leave-a-window-out (LWO) method, giving valid coverage if the fitting process meets mild stability. Their proofs measure how far data departs from cyclic exchangeability, with new scores. Tests show their method covers when the jackknife fails, while giving tighter ranges than split conformal methods.
arxiv-2605-30492: Liam Myhill, Enrique Martinez and Sez Russcher propose a new Bayes tuning method, integrated bias with full uncertainty (IBFU), against the Kennedy O'Hagan (KOH) method. In KOH, tuning knobs are fixed but unknown, with weak priors, fit jointly with a gap Gaussian Process. They write each tuning knob as a fixed best guess plus a knob fix from a free Gaussian Process. Leftover gap is caught by a gap Gaussian Process on the simulator. They then add right-angle rules to cut mix-ups.
arxiv-2605-30592: Goswami and Ganguly learn scores for how predictable a short path window is, from structured deterministic motion to unstructured stochastic noise. Old methods split deterministic from stochastic behavior within one system but give scores no steady meaning across systems. Rank training alone leaves the score scale unfixed up to one-way remapping, a gauge freedom the Gauge-Fixed Ordinal Network fixes by pinning scores to shared targets. Pretrained initialization beats training from scratch on held-out systems, and pairwise discrimination differs from globally coherent ordinal scoring.
arxiv-2605-30692: Singh, Ricci, and Gamero-Garrido show that commercial VPNs are not equal vantage points within a country. Measuring through different providers in the same country yields different conclusions about endpoint locations, hosts, and serving replicas. Measurements across fourteen countries and four major providers, plus DNS and replica probes, trace the shifts to layers below the client. Providers run their own in-country DNS, often intercepting queries; content networks steer by exit network; and peering paths route identical answers to different facilities. They distill reporting practices for VPN-based measurement.
arxiv-2605-30992: Do, Le, and Tran propose training-free routers for sparse mixture-of-experts language models, tackling expert collapse. Routing tokens to experts improves efficiency, but collapse degrades performance, and prior fixes need training or fine-tuning. The problem persists in pretrained models. They observe eigenvectors of expert weight matrices encode semantic information, pointing to an alternative strategy. Their SSMoE uses spectral properties of expert weights to address collapse and improve performance. Tests across language and vision tasks, under clean and corrupt data, show strong generalization and robustness.
arxiv-2605-31392: Klein and colleagues ask how far polyconvex material models can go. Such formulas keep simulations stable and often predict well, yet at times they match real material response badly. The team shows why the polyconvex rule can bind models too tightly. It proves stability claims for two Mooney-Rivlin potentials that are not polyconvex. They try out two neural network models with physics built in, on lab-made microstructured samples and on finite-element runs. The paper ends with strengths, limits and ways to ease them.
arxiv-2606-00592:
Gandhi and co-authors build a bench that grades visual design by its own rules, not one score. Good design rests on more than one rule at once. Read ease, contrast, line-up, overlap, and flow all play a part. Tools most oft crush those rules to one vague mark.

Their bench, PRISM, bends pro layouts from the Crello set by set rules. Each bent case breaks one named rule for a clean read. Huge train and check sets hold those bent cases. Top sight-word tools prove dull to the bent rules in tests. One big tool sees the whole yet can not split the parts. A three-scale grade frame is built on that base.
arxiv-2606-00992:
Wu and co-authors probe why fast feeding black holes break a size rule in this 2026 paper. The broad line region of an active galactic nucleus glows as gas clouds catch the core's light. Echo timing gives its size, and a known rule links size to optical brightness. High accretion systems fall below that rule: their echoes come too soon for their brightness.

The team models the flow with slim disk spectra and photo ionization sums. Near the Eddington limit, the inner disk puffs up, its glow turns directional, and low latitude clouds sit in shadow. Those clouds get less ionizing flux, and the size rule flattens. Self shadowing alone matches the broad trend in the echo sample, they find. It cannot explain the lag gap in low mass, fast feeding systems. A density boost, rising as mass falls or feeding grows, brings model and data much closer.
arxiv-2606-01092:
Sevetlidis asks when a trait of a model's inner representation can be known from its behavior in this 2026 paper. A predictor is often a head composed with a representation map. Supervised evidence pins down the composed map. It need not pin down how the work splits between the two parts. Many representation traits hang on that split.

His answer is a fiber criterion. A trait is identifiable from the predictor exactly when it stays constant on each fiber of the projection. The fibers group all pairs that compose to the same predictor. One construction shows the gap at its sharpest. Extra information can be appended to a representation while the head ignores it. The predictor stands unchanged, yet traits like minimality or invariance shift. Finite sample checks with exact witnesses and matched Waterbirds models picture the criterion. The paper parts identifiability from optimization and estimation noise.
arxiv-2606-01292:
Wu, Zhang, Zhang, and Fang seek one theory for knowledge transfer. Transfer spans model compression and weak-to-strong learning. Past work treats these cases in isolation. No unified frame explains why transfer works across them. The team study SGD in high-dimensional linear regression. A spectral view lets them compare regimes side by side. Two distinct mechanisms emerge from that view.

In distillation, the student reaches signals it could not learn alone. They call this spectral horizon expansion. In weak-to-strong cases, the student filters noise instead. They call that spectral denoising. Transfer strength rests on implicit regularization, they find. It also rests on varied learning speeds across the spectrum.
arxiv-2606-01492:
Kanungo surveys Grothendieck groups and their role in K-theory. This expository paper develops the basic ideas from scratch. A universal construction on a commutative monoid motivates the definition. Grothendieck groups then get defined for abelian categories and rings. The construction turns a monoid of objects into an abelian group. Formal differences of objects become group elements. Several fundamental examples illustrate the idea along the way.

Euler characteristics give a concrete instance of the pattern. Projective modules and representation rings provide others. The survey closes with K-theory and its applications. The elementary K0 construction is just the first layer. A much richer homotopical theory sits above it. The paper suits readers meeting these ideas for the first time.
arxiv-2606-01792:
Sacchi and co-authors report fresh X-ray views of a star cluster. The cluster is NGC 6540, a dense ball of old stars. An odd X-ray source there flared once before. That flare lasted about 300 seconds. Its strength fit neither star flares nor known bursts.

The team used the Chandra telescope for a deep look. They merged three views from 2023 and 2024. Three faint sources sit near the old flare spot. Only one of them fits the flare's place. The team weighs ideas like lens-based flare boosts. They also weigh black hole flare action. Both ideas look unlikely on the new facts.
arxiv-2606-01892:
Li and Shang attack robot localization through its deep features. Localization guides safe, autonomous navigation for robots. Crafted perturbations can mislead these systems badly. Errors can cause wrong routes or unsafe contact. Mission-critical settings face the highest stakes here.

Their method crafts adversarial queries for visual localization. It targets product quantization inside the retrieval pipeline. A lightweight network perturbs query feature encodings. Fooled retrieval returns irrelevant database entries instead. Queries are built in a forward then backward pass. The backward pass refines the perturbation by optimization. The design stays light in compute cost. Yet the perturbations remain subtle and effective, they report.
arxiv-2606-01992:
Samele and co-authors test whether text truly guides anomaly checks in factories. Anomaly detection was long a purely visual task. New vision-language systems accept text beside the image. They claim text-guided zero- and few-shot inspection as a result. Old benchmarks hold the text prompt constant throughout. That design cannot measure if language shapes the decision.

Their TGAD benchmark raises language's role step by step. One scenario tests prompt sensitivity on MVTec AD data. A second tags parts and asks for checks on one part. A third uses a new assembled panel data set. Gains can then be split into text effects and visual strength. The benchmark exposes when language stops conditioning choices.
arxiv-2606-02092:
Çağlar and Temizel present a light transformer for land-cover mapping from above. Semantic segmentation of remote sensing images is the task. Models must capture global context and local detail together. Tight compute budgets constrain field use of such models. Past work optimizes one axis at the cost of others.

Their LALE architecture splits its encoder by resolution. Light ConvMixer stages handle high-resolution local features. Transformer stages handle low-resolution global context. Self-attention's quadratic cost is confined to deep, small maps. An all-MLP decoder merges features across scales. The design is end to end for land-cover estimation. It aims for accuracy within strict compute limits. Hybrid designs without heavy backbones are the target.
arxiv-2606-02292:
Majumdar and co-authors learn how light scatters below the surface of objects. Subsurface scattering shapes how many materials look. Their method acquires and estimates those properties in fine detail. It learns the pixel footprint response at each surface point. A 3D scanning input feeds a U-Net network for the task.

A stereo projector-camera setup captures the needed data. Phase-shifted profilometry patterns make that capture efficient. Varied scattering objects are measured with the setup. Dense pixel footprints allow relighting with arbitrary patterns. High resolution projector patterns can be used for relighting. The final output is a relit color image. Comparisons with real captured images show close matches. One model trains across multiple views and objects. Graphics users gain a way to capture material look.
arxiv-2606-02392:
Ivanov asks whether the shape of a dependency network reveals how a system truly works. The claim is tested as hard geometry, not as a loose metaphor. Seven distinct systems are put through multilayer network analysis. They span formal math, legacy software, and neural evolution. Prebiotic chemistry and digital circuits join the set.

A law the author calls the Functional Proximity Law does the recovery work. It tracks hub persistence and rank divergence across layers. The method recovers load-bearing structure in each domain. In math, that means the axioms that carry the proofs. In brains, a hub grammar holds across some 600 million years. Tests in Lean and Coq corpora back the formal claims. All seven tests were registered before the analysis ran. Betweenness tracks structure better than raw degree in the circuit tests.
arxiv-2606-02492:
Bumpus and co-authors define a stricter class of fast algorithms for hard problems. Parameterized complexity confines the explosion to a small parameter k. The input size n stays cheap in the classic view. Big Data changed that balance. Even a quadratic pass over n can cost too much. The classic view also hides a split. Multiplicative and additive forms of the cost bound look alike.

The new class is called Truly Linear FPT. Its cost is order n plus a function of k. The authors show it sits strictly inside Linear FPT. The proof uses diagonalization. Many known problems live in the new class. They include SAT, Vertex Cover, and k-Path. Diverse pairs of matchings and H-Coloring join the list. Two parameters, treedepth and BFS-width, suit this regime well. Depth-first and breadth-first techniques power the results.
arxiv-2606-02692:
Bandopadhyay and co-authors explain why some repeating stellar disruptions fade with each pass. A supermassive black hole can strip a star again and again. Each partial disruption rebrightens months to years later. Some candidates dim at each successive outburst. Models where the star survives had not reproduced that trend. Stellar spin is the missing piece, the team argues.

A rapidly rotating star fits the pattern. Such spin is expected from the Hills breakup of a tight, tidally locked binary. Hydrodynamical simulations test the idea. High-mass main sequence stars face a million-solar-mass black hole repeatedly. Successively dimmer outbursts appear for high, prograde spins. The spin runs to tens of percent of breakup speed. The results give strong indirect evidence for the Hills mechanism. It may seed the stars in these repeating events.
arxiv-2606-02792:
Ni and co-authors find explicit generators for the space of modular cusp forms. Let S-kappa be the space of cusp forms of weight kappa and level one. Its dual space carries period data. The team finds explicit spanning subsets of the primal space. They consist of Rankin-Cohen brackets of Eisenstein series. Explicit subsets of periods that span the dual space are also found.

The result gives concrete building blocks for an abstract space. Any cusp form of level one can be assembled from the listed brackets. Any period functional can be assembled from the listed periods. Number theorists gain formulas they can compute with directly. The spanning sets are explicit, not merely existential. That explicitness is the contribution's core value.
arxiv-2606-02992:
Yang and Zhao present Slipstream, a method that speeds up streaming approximate nearest neighbor search. Graph indexes give high recall for such search. But streaming uses must insert new embeddings again and again. Each arrival must search the graph before the graph updates, which makes index construction a bottleneck.

Slipstream exploits continuity in vector streams. A new point starts from promising candidates found during the previous insertion, not from the entry point. It checks distinct subsets of starting candidates, and a controller widens or narrows the search by stream stability. The authors derive an abstract model with theoretical bounds, so the method is not just a heuristic. They implemented it in Faiss and HNSWLib. Across five streaming datasets, Slipstream reached up to 30.8 times higher throughput than four baselines. Recall at ten stayed at 0.95 or better.
arxiv-2606-03092:
Wan and co-authors view the allocation of reasoning effort in language models as an economics problem. Inference-time scaling improves performance, but real deployments face strict compute budgets. The team formulates budget allocation as a global constrained optimization. Per-query reasoning utility is modeled with a shifted-surge function.

From that model they derive an optimal policy based on a global shadow price. The price equilibrates marginal utility under scarcity. Their method, CLEAR, abandons hopeless queries rationally. It reallocates resources to solvable queries near their emergence thresholds. Experiments span several reasoning tasks and traffic streams. CLEAR improved the Pareto frontier of total token cost against mean accuracy. In resource-scarce regimes it reached up to three times the global accuracy of uniform allocation. The work gives deployment teams a principled way to spend a fixed reasoning budget.
arxiv-2606-03392:
Zhang and co-authors present OpenEAI-Platform, an open-source system for embodied AI. It joins robot hardware with a vision-language-action model in one package. The hardware part is OpenEAI-Arm, a low-cost arm with six plus one degrees of freedom. The model part is OpenEAI-VLA, built for real-world tasks.

The arm uses open mechanical designs to keep build costs low. Compliant control methods help it work with higher accuracy. The model builds on Qwen3-VL-4B and adds a Diffusion Transformer action head. It trains in two stages on open robot and multimodal data alone. In four real-world tasks, the arm beat two commercial arms under the same policy. The model matched the large pi0 baseline while using far less pretraining data. The team plans to release designs, drivers, models, and data pipelines in full.
arxiv-2606-03492:
Srinivasan and Elmqvist explore what happens when gaze is fed back to people in XR. Where a person looks during shared work carries cues that speech and gesture cannot replace. Those cues stay invisible to the group itself. XR headsets can capture gaze in real time, but few systems show it back. Their frame is the Attention-Aware Pipeline: capture, record, and revisualize.

The feedback loop creates design tensions. What the system shows changes what users look at next, which changes the next display. Three systems trace the loop in distinct roles. Attention acts as a mirror of gaze history, a medium shared across partners, and a mediator that steps in. A small eye-tracking study of four musicians found attentional tunneling and near-total disconnection. Each system met the tension the loop predicted. The next step tests whether a subtractive display can cut tunneling for one sight-reader.
arxiv-2606-03592:
Baltaci and co-authors hunt for dual active galactic nuclei at Cosmic Noon. Dual AGNs are pairs of black holes accreting together in merging galaxies. They may drive much black hole growth through mergers. Close pairs at high redshift are the best place to look. Merger rates and AGN activity both peak in that era. Nine candidates were chosen from Gaia optical pairs under one arcsecond.

Each pair matches a Sloan survey quasar, with redshifts from 1.5 to 2.8. Two-band Very Large Array imaging tests each system in radio. Two dual AGNs are confirmed. Three systems turn out to be quadruply imaged gravitational lenses. Two of those show radio flux anomalies pointing to lens substructure. One candidate is an AGN-star pair. Three remain unclassified for lack of radio signal. The two new dual AGNs enrich the small census of close pairs at Cosmic Noon.
arxiv-2606-03692:
Xiong and co-authors give self-evolving agents a way to consolidate skills over time. Agents can call skills to solve complex tasks. Long-term gains stall when skills are built in a scattered way. Similar abilities get rebuilt across tasks, and task-specific skills fail to transfer. SkillPyramid answers with a hierarchical skill topology.

A self-evolution mechanism lets agents compose, validate, and adopt new skills while they work. Past skill experience is reused for broader generalization. Tests run on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, across four backbone models. Average reward rises by 38 percent. Execution steps fall by about 28 percent. The skill pool stops being a static shelf of tools. It becomes a dynamic system that grows with use. Agent builders get a frame for turning experience into reusable assets.
arxiv-2606-03892:
Abdelaziz and co-authors train language models for multi-step tool use inside live environments. Three obstacles block such training. Stateful execution environments are costly to build. Synthetic queries often miss the server's real state, so calls fail. Recall-based rewards push verbose tool calling. PROVE answers all three obstacles together.

A library of 20 stateful MCP servers exposes 343 tools for live training. Session-scoped state keeps runs isolated. A state-machine pipeline synthesizes multi-turn trajectories grounded in live-sampled state. Generated queries thus reference entities that exist. A programmatic reward adds an adaptive efficiency penalty against verbosity. Four models train with GRPO on about 13,000 examples. Gains reach about ten points on BFCL Multi-Turn, with solid rises on two other suites. Tool orchestration improves across two model families.
arxiv-2606-04592:
Kinzinger and Hartmann test how faithfully language models can impersonate individual survey respondents, in a 2026 arXiv paper. They feed the models panel data that companies already hold. Most published digital twins are shallow persona bots. Or they are rich twins built on purpose-collected interviews. The authors instead build detailed twins from Germany's Socio-Economic Panel. They vary three open-weight models, five depths of personal information, two embedding methods, and two reasoning modes.

Twin quality rose with information depth. Returns diminished beyond the 75 percent entropy quartile. The authors identify that point as a cost-efficient sweet spot. Feeding the twin a raw dialogue history beat a narrative persona summary at full depth in every configuration. An explicit thinking mode improved rank-order correlation without moving accuracy. The best configuration reached 78.8 percent accuracy. Its Fisher-z correlation was 0.590. The authors map which construction choices matter for twin-based market research.
arxiv-2606-04892:
Yang and co-authors present a 2026 arXiv paper on confidential blockchains, shared ledgers that keep transaction details private from most participants. Their setting is a consortium blockchain, a ledger run by a known group of organizations. Such systems often rely on trusted execution environments, which are protected areas inside computer processors.

The authors first sort known attacks into two classes, named execution-inference and execution-replay attacks. Odyssey, their system, answers by letting each client delegate execution to a chosen trustee instead. Other participants then receive only the finished result, which shrinks the exposed surface. A prototype built on FISCO BCOS reached about 4,000 transactions per second in a three-node wide-area test, with latency held between 0.4 and 0.5 seconds during that run.
arxiv-2606-04992:
Shiyu Li and colleagues describe a guidance system for surgical instrument handling and assembly in this 2026 arXiv paper. Scrub nurses face heavy mental demands during surgery, especially with unfamiliar instruments. Their system combines multi-camera 6D pose estimation, which tracks an object's position and orientation, with augmented reality views on a head-mounted display, and it needs no added markers.

The pose network was trained only on synthetic data, and the display shows location cues plus step-by-step assembly animations that users advance by gaze or a foot pedal. In a technical test the method beat leading pose estimation approaches. A study with 29 scrub nurses simulating knee surgery found much lower felt workload than a paper manual, task time cut by 21.3 percent on average, and similar error rates, with the least experienced nurses gaining most.
arxiv-2606-05292:
Patryk Iwanek and colleagues reassess whether Gaia astrometry really rules out a binary origin for long secondary periods in red giant stars, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Long secondary periods are brightness variations, hundreds to thousands of days, whose cause is debated; a companion star is a leading candidate. A recent study argued the astrometric evidence disfavors binarity, and this paper re-examines the same nearby sample.

Inspecting long-term ASAS light curves and Gaia radial velocity curves for 221 of 224 candidates within 1.5 kiloparsecs, the team found that fewer than half, 103 objects or about 47 percent, show such behavior. The rest look more like semi-regular variables with irregular pulsations, so the sample is contaminated and unrepresentative. Using the gaiamock tool to predict Gaia's RUWE values for binaries, they show even the nearest such stars need not display elevated RUWE from binarity. The observed distance-RUWE relation matches the binary expectation.
arxiv-2606-05792:
Bisharat and colleagues run the first broad test of language models writing formal specifications in a 2026 arXiv paper. TLA+ is a language for proving system designs correct, used at Amazon and Microsoft. Writing it from plain English demands rare expertise. The team asked thirty models from eight families to produce specifications for two hundred five curated tasks. Parsers and model checkers graded every output for syntax and true meaning.

Best syntax correctness reached only about twenty-seven percent. Semantic correctness topped out under nine percent. All successes came from progressive prompting, which builds the answer in stages. Size did not predict quality: a small DeepSeek model beat its seventy-billion-parameter sibling everywhere. Code-specialist models lagged, hurt by habits from mainstream languages. Five hallucination families were traced to training data biases. Expert oversight, the authors conclude, remains mandatory for model-written specifications.
arxiv-2606-05992:
Khanpour and Yeganeh screen photonic quantum circuits with a stand-in before paying for exact simulation in a 2026 arXiv paper. GKP states encode protected qubits in light and anchor fault-tolerant photonic computing. Gaussian boson sampling can herald them, but scoring circuits needs hafnian calculations whose cost explodes. The surrogate learns to predict the prize quantities: post-selection probability, circuit fidelity, and best heralding pattern.

Histogram gradient boosting models trained on three-to-five-mode circuits do the screening. Exact quantum simulation runs only on candidates the surrogate blesses. On held-out circuits the screener hit ninety percent accuracy at spotting GKP-capable designs, well above baseline. Fidelity predictions landed close to truth, and probability estimates tracked on a log scale. Total simulation burden fell by ninety percent. The pipeline turns an exhaustive search into a shortlist exercise. Photonic teams can explore larger design spaces on the same budget.
arxiv-2606-06192:
Gaia Carenini and Leonardo Franchi prove one regularity lemma that covers three famous ones in this 2026 arXiv paper on discrete mathematics. A regularity lemma says a complicated object can be split into a simple structured part plus a pseudorandom leftover, where pseudorandom means it behaves like coin flips in measurable ways. Versions of this idea anchor modern graph theory, additive combinatorics, and the analysis of Boolean functions, but each field proved its own.

This short note states and proves a single abstract version set in a general framework. Szemerédi's graph regularity lemma then falls out as a direct corollary, with no separate argument needed. The same happens for Green's arithmetic regularity lemma and for a regularity lemma for Boolean functions used in recent work. Unifying them shows the three results share one engine, an energy increment refinement, and may let future settings import the whole machinery at once.
arxiv-2606-06392:
Nilanjana Datta asks whether entanglement processing survives imperfect sources in this 2026 arXiv paper on quantum information. Entanglement manipulation distills or dilutes quantum correlations between two parties, and its classic rates assume sources emit perfect copies of one state, independently and identically. Real sources stray. The MSR model of almost identical sources allows a sublinear number of deviations from that perfect pattern, a small but growing flaw count.

Datta proves the standard rates are robust anyway. For pure sources, every concentration rate below the entropy of entanglement remains achievable, with a single Schur Weyl protocol that works for the whole source class. For mixed sources, distillation rates up to the coherent information of the reference state remain reachable, though the protocol may depend on the source. For dilution, the cost stays bounded by the regularized entanglement of formation. Structural entropy results about MSR sequences carry the proofs.
arxiv-2606-06592:
Adrian Ka Wai Chung and co-authors measure a newborn black hole's size before it finishes ringing in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hawking's area law says a black hole's horizon area, the quantity behind its entropy, can never decrease. Tests so far read the area from the late ringdown, the dying vibrations after two black holes merge. The team instead uses direct waves, the radiation emitted in the violent moments just before and at merger, fitting their frequency and damping.

Applied to the gravitational wave event GW250114, the method gives an area matching the Kerr remnant from the ringdown. This holds when the analysis window starts a few mass units before the signal peak. No strong sign of an area law violation appears where the estimator is self consistent. Because it constrains the remnant's spin, which ringdown measures poorly, it could sharpen population studies of merging black holes.
arxiv-2606-06692:
Telescope time is scarce, so the search for alien intelligence must choose its stars with care. Torlakcik offers a filter for that choice in this 2026 arXiv paper. His avoidance model scores stars on seven traits, among them age, metal content, and whether the star has a companion, and flags those unlikely to host complex life.

Applied to a Gaia sample of about one point seven four million stars, the filter set aside roughly half. It kept seven hundred seventy seven thousand high priority targets, mostly G and K dwarf stars. Age and metal content drove most rejections. One choice mattered a lot. Using the upper bound of each star's age estimate, rather than a single best guess, saved over three hundred fifty five thousand stars from being cut. That saving is a reminder of how rough those age estimates can be.
arxiv-2606-06992:
Graphdiyne is a carbon sheet that graphene cannot be: it has a natural energy gap. Cartoceti and a large team finally grow it cleanly in this 2026 arXiv paper. The material mixes two carbon bond styles in a two dimensional lattice. On surface synthesis had stalled at metal laced intermediates. Those leftovers blocked the long range order the sheet needs.

A pinch of iron changes the chemistry on a gold surface. Iron grabs the bromine byproducts and forms iron bromine species. Those species help sweep away stray gold atoms. Gentle heating then converts the metalated network into a purely covalent one. Microscopy and theory together revealed the atomic steps. The finished monolayer floats electronically free of the metal below. Its measured band gap is about one point six electron volts. That makes it a true semiconductor, and a complement to gapless graphene.
arxiv-2606-07392:
Belloni, Chen, and Wei design a strategy for choosing among language model services request by request, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their model adapts Pandora's box, a classic decision problem about paying to inspect options, to LLM cascading. Each period brings a request; the decision-maker queries model APIs, paying an output-dependent cost for each generation, then deploys one output and learns its reward. Feedback arrives through outputs, unlike classical versions where opening a box reveals its prize.

Rather than modeling output distributions, they learn the reservation index functions of the classical optimal policy, and impose parametric structure on how the index depends on context. They estimate with the generalized method of moments, paired with confidence-bound exploration for indices and the reward evaluator. Under regularity conditions the policy's regret grows with the square root of the horizon, plus log factors. The result gives API cascading an adaptive foundation.
arxiv-2606-07492:
Grishina and a team rank recommender algorithms fairly across different datasets in this 2026 arXiv paper. A recommender's measured performance depends on dataset traits like sparsity, sequence structure, and scale, so averaging scores across benchmarks can crown the wrong winner. Their methodology adapts the Bradley-Terry model, a statistical framework from paired comparisons in sports, treating each dataset result as a contest between algorithms. The resulting rankings respond to dataset statistics rather than hiding them.

They propose a metric for ranking consistency and show their rankings stay robust when some benchmark results are missing. For a new dataset, extensions using Bradley-Terry trees and covariate models predict the algorithm ranking without running any model, from dataset traits alone. That matters when evaluating every candidate on proprietary data is expensive. Source code is released, and the authors frame the work as fixing the methodology of algorithm selection itself, not adding a leaderboard.
arxiv-2606-07592:
Upadhyay makes offline reinforcement learning cautious where the data are thin, and relaxed where they are rich, in this 2026 arXiv paper on UNIQ. Offline learning trains control policies from fixed logs without interaction, but policies that stray into unlogged territory get overestimated values. Standard methods apply one conservatism penalty everywhere. UNIQ trains an ensemble of value functions, calibrates its uncertainty with conformal prediction, a distribution-free statistical wrapper, and maps that uncertainty to a per-state conservatism level on its learning backbone.

On the D4RL MuJoCo locomotion benchmarks, UNIQ beat its IQL parent method on Walker2d tasks and replay-heavy datasets. It ran at the parent method's memory cost, using roughly 10 times less memory than an ensemble competitor. Upadhyay reports the underperforming cases and positions UNIQ as a practical efficiency-frontier contribution rather than a state-of-the-art claim, an unusually candid framing for the genre.
arxiv-2606-07692:
Kjaer and colleagues build BCG-FM, a foundation model that reads heart-related signals from a sensor hidden in a bed, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The signal, ballistocardiography, records the body's tiny recoil with each heartbeat through a piezoelectric strip in the bed surface. Unlike watches or sleep-lab gear, it needs no effort from the user at all.

The model was pretrained on two point seven five million hours of nightly recordings from nearly one hundred forty-six thousand people. Its frozen features estimated biological age with a mean error of about three point three years, the best reported for any contact-free method. Features learned from only five hundred labelled participants beat a fully supervised model trained on more than three thousand. The representations also separated fifteen self-reported health conditions and held up across three outside cohorts, hinting that passive nightly sensing can support broad health screening.
arxiv-2606-07792:
Daniil Lopatkin and co-authors describe MOLOT, a system hunting malicious code in software packages, in this 2026 arXiv system card. The setting is static analysis for package moderation, where metadata, maintainer history, and traces may be missing or forged. MOLOT therefore judges the code alone. It represents each package as sequences of behaviour derived from its call graph, the map of which functions call which.

A transformer model reads those behaviour sequences to flag malicious operational logic. An explanation stage ranks suspicious activities and maps them back to exact source locations, so moderators see why a package was flagged. The team evaluated it on Python and JavaScript packages from PyPI and npm, against open-source detectors. They also validated it under product constraints, including runtime, memory, and false-positive rates inside a real moderation workflow. They release Open Malicious-code Bench, a public benchmark for comparing such detectors reproducibly.
arxiv-2606-07892:
Jiang and Clark make safety controllers for autonomous systems easier to verify in this 2026 arXiv paper. Control barrier functions keep a system inside a safe region by constraining its inputs. Complex safe regions are often non-convex, hard for one function, so engineers switch between several barrier functions, each guarding a tractable piece.

Their union-CBF framework treats the safe region as that union. They give a sufficient condition guaranteeing two things. Only finitely many switches occur in any finite time, so the controller cannot chatter endlessly. And the system stays inside the safe region between switches. Conditions are tailored to two switching strategies. Sum-of-squares algorithms, an optimisation technique for polynomial inequalities, verify the conditions. In experiments the union framework certified a larger safe region than single high-degree polynomial barrier functions. Verification also ran efficiently on a polynomial system model, suggesting the approach scales to realistic controllers.
arxiv-2606-07992:
Harshil Patel and Kunal Pai demonstrate an attack on AI agents that hides inside error messages, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Model Context Protocol standardises how agents call tools. When a tool fails, its error text flows back into the model's reasoning. The authors hypothesise that errors carry implicit authority: the model slips into a corrective mode and obeys instructions embedded in the error.

Their framework, VATS, evolves adversarial error payloads by systematic mutation across seven structural and linguistic dimensions. Tested on four frontier models, error-path injection tripled the success rate of standard indirect prompt injection, reaching up to one hundred percent compliance in controlled evaluations. The most effective trick was structural: sandwiching the malicious instruction inside plausible error context. Production framework guardrails did reduce the damage, but the authors warn that the model layer itself is susceptible, a systemic risk for hand-rolled agent workflows.
arxiv-2606-08292:
Quirke stress-tests a common way of assigning roles to parts of language models in this 2026 arXiv paper. In this field, an attention head is often said to represent a computation, such as addition, when three checks pass. The behavior needs the head, the head encodes it in a simple linear form, and restoring the head after ablation, switching it off, brings the behavior back. Quirke shows this evidence is insufficient, because heads passing all three checks routinely fail a tougher test.

That test is transfer: patching the head's activations into a different prompt, under matched controls, should carry the computation with it, and often it does not. The experiments span three instruction-tuned models of seven to eight billion parameters and five computation families. Quirke pairs a lens called KID, separating knowing, intent, and doing, with a three-stage pipeline, yielding a first taxonomy of head roles.
arxiv-2606-08692:
Jake Morris modernizes a classic insurance pricing formula for commercial accounts, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Bühlmann-Straub credibility theory blends an account's own claims experience with the portfolio average. Each account gets an interpretable weight that grows with its exposure. The classic formula uses a single portfolio-wide ratio. It assumes the ratio is the same for every account, and that the credibility complement is fixed. Morris shows these assumptions fail consequentially on a held-out United States commercial auto dataset.

Applying the standard formula to nearly one hundred companies produces a badly miscalibrated slope for small accounts. Morris proposes a joint framework modeling the credibility weight as a logistic function of observable account characteristics. It adds temporal decay, so recent years count more. The redesign keeps the original formula's interpretability, which regulators and actuaries prize.
arxiv-2606-08792:
Tam shows that partisan political identity lives inside a large language model as a single steerable direction, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Using more than one hundred ninety thousand tweets from members of the United States Congress as labeled examples, Tam trained probes on the hidden states of the Llama 3.1 model. One axis, found at layer eighteen, separated Republican from Democratic text with an AUC of 0.945, a near-excellent score.

The direction is not just a label reader. Tam broke it into interpretable partisan features using sparse autoencoders, tools that split tangled activations into cleaner parts. Then she intervened during generation, removing or amplifying the partisan component while the model wrote. The output shifted in systematic ways, including stance reversals, changes in writing register, and invented claims of authority. The results argue partisan bias here is a concrete geometric feature, located and steerable, not a vague side effect.
arxiv-2606-08892:
Terekhov and colleagues stress-test a problem in AI safety: catching a strong model doing poor work, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffuse AI control studies sabotage spread over long runs. On fuzzy tasks, judged by intuition, defenders cannot grade everything. Their framework stages a game. A blue team builds a weak scoring prompt, meant to train subversion out of the model. A red team hunts behaviors the weak score rewards but are actually bad.

The test task was writing experimental proposals, graded against the original papers as proxy ground truth. The red team made Opus 4.6 produce proposals the weak scorer rated as highly as its best, yet by ground truth worse than a small open model's output. The blue team answered with an adversarial optimization algorithm that found a robust prompt the red team failed to exploit. The contest is winnable, but not by static defenses.
arxiv-2606-09092:
Jike Zhong and colleagues show that AI models' mind-reading is often a cheat, then train real belief reasoning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Theory of mind means inferring others' beliefs, desires, and intentions. The team built a framework to audit theory-of-mind datasets for shortcuts, correlations that let models answer without understanding. Some tasks hit 99 percent accuracy by state tracking alone. Questions about beliefs proved shortcut-prone, while intention questions forced reasoning.

Using 4 shortcut-free datasets, they compared methods. Thinking-RFT, reinforcement fine-tuning with verifiable rewards and explicit reasoning chains, beat supervised fine-tuning by 6 percent overall. Margins grew to 10 percent on higher-order reasoning, where beliefs nest inside beliefs, and 7 percent on multimodal cases. It generalized better to unseen domains and resisted counterfactual traps. Both parts are needed: chains plus reinforcement beat reinforcement alone by 7 percent. Grounding reasoning on anchor cues seems to be the mechanism.
arxiv-2606-09592:
Landry sets out the base ideas for a teleparallel route to quantum gravity in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum gravity, a theory that joins quantum rules with gravity, still lacks a settled form. The usual stopgap treats quantum matter on a fixed curved stage. That frame has flaws, like doubt over what counts as empty space.

Teleparallel gravity tells the story with twist, called torsion, in place of curve. Its key tools are a coframe, a set of local rulers, and a spin connection. Landry shows how this pair keeps local Lorentz symmetry, the freedom to rotate local frames. It also takes in fermions, the matter particles, in a clean way. The whole setup looks much like a gauge theory, the style used for the other forces. Landry does not claim a full quantisation. The aim is to name the parts such a theory would need.
arxiv-2606-09692:
Abhinav Mishra and Kumar Sharad argue that today's logs cannot answer a basic audit question for AI agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agents act on delegated authority: a user hands over a task, and the agent picks tools, backtracks, and spawns helpers. After the fact, one may ask which actions ran under which grant. The pair show that logs and traces alone cannot settle that question.

Two unlike grant setups can leave the exact same trace record. The fix is to bind each act to its grant at run time, not to guess from time windows later. Their substrate pairs a light gateway with a shared information model. Each event carries a durable delegation ID, and re-grants form a queryable lineage. Action words are normalized across tools, so a cross-system footprint can be rebuilt directly. The scope is attribution and footprints, not mind reading of agent intent.
arxiv-2606-09792:
Archer Wang and his co-authors ask when a camera and a classifier should be designed as one system in this 2026 arXiv paper. End-to-end design tunes an optical front end, like a phase mask, jointly with a neural back end. It is widely used, yet no firm rule said when it beats a plain lens. The team studies sorting tasks under incoherent light.

With full detector readout, they prove no mask can top a hard cap on shared information. A plain focus lens nearly hits that cap, and joint tuning gave no real gain. The story flips when readout is squeezed, by coarse sampling or few reads. There, tuned optics can lift class splits in the raw reads by a lot. Gains peak at low detector noise and fade as noise climbs, since optics shape light before the sensor but not noise after it.
arxiv-2606-09892:
Xiaofeng Xiao and his co-authors mine factory alarm logs for cause, not mere pattern, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Alarm texts pile up in plants, each a short note on a fault or fix. Engineers want to know which event kinds set off which others. The words alone can hint at links, but word sense cannot split true cause from habit or sequence.

Their LMT frame weds two kinds of proof in a Bayesian way. A language model reads the notes and drafts a prior map of likely causal links. Timestamps then weigh in through a Poisson-process likelihood, a count model for when events fire. The prior is honed by the clock data into a final graph that can be read and checked. Fake-log trials showed the frame works across settings. Its edge grew largest when logs were scarce, the case where pure counts starve.
arxiv-2606-10092:
Hong and his team study how people decide when risk comes from many parts at once, in a 2026 arXiv paper on behavioral economics. Standard research uses single-shot lottery choices, but real choices often involve combinatorial risk, where several risky parts combine and the outcome distribution must be worked out rather than being given. Their investment-allocation task lets players invest in a component to raise its success probability, reshaping the overall odds. Working out the induced distribution exactly is costly, so shortcuts are expected.

Participants favored the option with the larger probability increment and, when increments tied, the option with higher initial success probability. Revealing the full induced probability distribution changed behavior a lot, reducing reactions to combinatorial features and lowering choice variance. To explain the patterns, the team used symbolic regression to discover compact plain models rather than hand-crafted guesses.
arxiv-2606-10592:
Zhang and colleagues attack a familiar flaw in forecasting in this 2026 arXiv paper: predictions that are too smooth. Time series models often capture the broad trend yet wash out the sharp peaks, swings, and turning points decisions depend on. The authors reinterpret the flaw as mode compression: when several futures are plausible, training on single observed outcomes teaches the model to average them into a bland middle path. Their framework, Dirichlet-Guided Group Forecasting, keeps multiple mode-conditioned predictive distributions alive at once.

A Dirichlet distribution governs how likely each future mode is, and hierarchical sampling draws forecasts from chosen modes rather than averaging them away. Reward-based training scores samples for accuracy, dynamical consistency, and diversity. On long-sequence and probabilistic forecasting benchmarks, the method reduces over-smoothing while improving accuracy and diversity: mode preservation, not better averaging, is the fix.
arxiv-2606-11292:
Hallatt, Owen, and Millholland ask what stellar spin can reveal about the hot Neptune desert in a 2026 arXiv paper. The desert, a dearth of mid-sized planets on short orbits, may hold remnants of destroyed gas giants. Theory shows Roche lobe overflow, a planet spilling mass onto its star, can populate it with remnants, but only if transfer removes most orbital angular momentum: lossy overflow.

They examine how such transfer shows up in stellar obliquities, the tilt between spin and orbital axes. They find overflow tilts hosts into spin-orbit alignment, within a few tens of degrees, regardless of initial conditions. Only misaligned companion planets within about two astronomical units can reverse that damping. Hosts usually spin up, but can emerge slowly rotating from strongly retrograde starts, reconciling theory with the slow rotation of LTT 9779's host. Predicted alignment may distinguish overflow from high-eccentricity migration, which leaves broad obliquities.
arxiv-2606-11392:
Bhateja, Rigo, and Schmitt introduce a method for simulating quantum dynamics to late times in a 2026 arXiv paper. Unitary evolution of simple quantum many-body states rapidly generates entanglement, limiting direct simulation. Yet late-time behavior of observables often shows effective simplicity, like hydrodynamics. CoMPuTE, compressed minimum-purity time evolution, tracks a consistent set of reduced local density matrices.

It closes the equations of motion with a minimum-purity principle, discarding irrelevant information in a controlled way. Benchmarks show accurate energy diffusion in the mixed-field Ising model, and applies to Floquet dynamics from a pure state. They also reveal limits of the local approximation for XXZ chain transport, governed by non-local integrals of motion. Against the related LITE algorithm, it cuts entropy cost from cubic to quadratic scaling, with speedups near six orders of magnitude at the largest sizes, and removes instabilities from small eigenvalues.
arxiv-2606-11492:
Davis and a large collaboration summarize the first year of the Space Weather Around Young Suns program in a 2026 arXiv paper. The program is dedicated to young, solar-type stars, whose high-energy output shapes the environments of their young planets. The team reports 900 hours of low-frequency radio and optical observations gathered in the program's first year.

The summary describes the observing campaign, the data collected, and what the combined radio and optical coverage can reveal about stellar activity in young suns. Radio emission at low frequencies traces energetic electrons and magnetic activity, while optical data track spots, flares, and rotation. Together they build a picture of the space weather young planets endure, from steady winds to eruptive events. The paper serves as the reference summary for the program's first-year dataset, documenting its scope and contents for later targeted studies of individual stars and events.
arxiv-2606-11592:
Sayedeh Leila Noorbakhsh, Hossein Khalili and Nader Sehatbakhsh defend language model users against prompt inversion in this 2026 arXiv paper. In collaborative inference, a phone runs the first layers of a large language model and sends intermediate results to a cloud server. An attacker with those results can try to rebuild the user's private prompt. Earlier defences mostly added noise by trial and error, with little theory.

The authors build a defence on information theory, the mathematics of how much one signal reveals about another. Their method trains small privacy adapters that squeeze the shared results through a narrow bottleneck, cutting what they reveal about the prompt while keeping answers useful. They prove bounds on how badly reconstruction can fail and on downstream accuracy. Across several test settings their method cuts attack success by up to thirty-five percent while balancing privacy, usefulness and delay better than rival defences.
arxiv-2606-11892:
Benedict Russell, Andrew Nugent and Jacques Bara model how cooperation spreads on changing social networks in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agents play a continuous-strategy Prisoner's Dilemma, where each chooses how cooperative to be, and imitate successful neighbours. The network itself is weighted and evolving, so who interacts with whom shifts over time.

The authors study the fast-network regime, folding the edge weights directly into the strategy dynamics before taking the large-population mean-field limit. Without noise, they prove the model is well-posed and that the population collapses onto a single strategy. For populations starting as separated clusters, they find a payoff threshold and conditions under which overall cooperation grows. Adding random exploration to the updates produces a non-local Fokker-Planck equation, for which they prove stationary distributions exist and are unique. Numerics show noise can turn brittle deterministic consensus into stable cooperative behaviour.
arxiv-2606-11992:
Yiting Wang pins down exactly when random bipartite graphs gain Hamilton cycles in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Hamilton cycle visits every vertex exactly once. In a random graph process, edges arrive one by one, and the hitting time of a property is the moment it first appears.

Wang studies balanced bipartite graphs, where vertices split into two equal sides, under a Dirac-type condition on minimum degree. In this dense regime he proves that, with high probability, the hitting time for minimum degree two coincides exactly with the hitting time for Hamiltonicity. In other words, the moment the last low-degree vertex gains its second edge, a Hamilton cycle already exists. This extends earlier work of Bollobás and Kohayakawa and gives a bipartite analogue of Johansson's theorem. Pushing the degree down to the classical Moon-Moser bound provably fails, by an explicit counterexample.
arxiv-2606-12292:
Traytak and Fedoseev warn that a shortcut for diffusion in narrow tubes can mislead, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Molecules wander by diffusion and react when they meet targets, often inside thin tubes of varying width. The Fick-Jacobs approach squeezes this three-dimensional problem into one dimension along the tube's axis. It is widely used because the reduced equation is far easier to solve. The authors study steady diffusion with reaction inside a thin circular tube to test the shortcut.

They derive an asymptotic solution, an approximation for thin tubes, by the boundary functions method. Comparing it against the exact solution exposes serious methodological drawbacks in the Fick-Jacobs reduction. The failures matter because the shortcut underpins many reaction-diffusion studies in confined geometry. The paper maps where the reduction can and cannot be trusted. Its asymptotic machinery offers a route for problems where Fick-Jacobs does not apply.
arxiv-2606-12392:
Xie teaches a language model to truly appreciate classical Chinese poetry, not just translate it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Poetry appreciation splits into three skills: explaining terms, interpreting meaning, and inferring emotion. Generic models treat the task as ordinary text work and miss its domain demands. High-quality training data barely exists. Xie builds CCPoetry-49K, a dataset of 49,404 instruction-response pairs cleaned and aligned from open sources, tailored to those three subtasks.

Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-14B with LoRA, a light adapter method, on this data yields PoetryQwen. On the CCL25-Eval Task 5 benchmark it scores 0.757, against the untuned instruct baseline's 0.690 on the same test, a 9.7 percent improvement from domain training. Gains concentrate in precise translation and emotional understanding, the subtasks most neglected before. The report argues domain specialization, through curated data rather than bigger models, is the reliable route for culturally deep tasks like classical poetry.
arxiv-2606-12492:
Fuentes shows that equilibria in vast models cannot jump around wildly, at least on a dense set of cases, in this 2026 arXiv paper. General equilibrium theory maps each economy to its set of equilibria, prices and outcomes where supply meets demand. If that mapping were discontinuous, tiny data errors could produce totally different predictions. Fuentes works where the goods space is infinite-dimensional, a Banach lattice, and economies are distributions over agent characteristics.

Total endowments are computed with Bochner or Gel'fand integrals, two ways of averaging there. He proves the mapping is continuous on a dense subset of the cases admitting equilibria, under a Polish topology. The treatment unifies classical and recent theorems and reaches models with infinite horizons, finance, and asymmetric information. Notably, no differentiability assumptions are needed, unlike the regular-economy route.
arxiv-2606-13092:
Wang builds predictability certificates for equivariant latent world models, regions over which a model's transfer is guaranteed, in this 2026 arXiv paper. For models equivariant under a symmetry group with an orthogonal latent space, the error is invariant over the monoid generated by the symmetries, so checking the generators covers all compositions at once.

Approximate orbit-transfer defects spread along the Lyapunov spectrum. Expanding channels yield a logarithmic horizon, neutral channels build up defect at a steady rate, and contracting channels settle to a bounded nonzero floor. Exactly conserved charges are certified to all horizons. Small-scale tests confirm all 3 axes: a symmetry group with 64 elements covers every composition to machine precision, a learned predictor recovers a planted exponent to within 0.4 percent, and on a 40-dimensional system an equivariant network gets the full Lyapunov spectrum with R squared of 0.98 to 0.99 where dense and recurrent models of equal data fail outright.
arxiv-2606-13592:
Furugori, Yoshida, and Yoshimura formulate a new criterion supporting cosmic censorship in this 2026 arXiv paper. The weak cosmic censorship conjecture claims that singularities formed in gravitational collapse are always hidden behind event horizons, never visible to distant observers. Classic thought experiments try to break it by overcharging a black hole until the horizon disappears. The authors propose a local geometric test: under standard energy conditions, injecting matter turns a horizon cross-section into a closed trapped surface. A trapped surface is one from which even outgoing light is dragged inward.

Any final spacetime unable to accommodate that trapped surface is then ruled out. The criterion excludes the usual suspects: superextremal charged black holes, their de Sitter and rotating kin, and a class of naked singularities. It does not rely on charges at infinity or on extreme cases. A local obstruction makes the argument more robust where global bookkeeping is unavailable.
arxiv-2606-13692:
Fadlallah and colleagues propose an agentic framework for judging data quality in this 2026 arXiv paper. Data quality assessment precedes analytics, yet quality is context-dependent: the same dataset can be fit for one use and unfit for another. Existing approaches lean on rules or manual strategies, limiting adaptability. Language models offer a route to automation but raise concerns about trust, grounding, and safety. The framework reads natural-language descriptions of data use, derives a strategy from them, and generates validation logic through a multi-agent workflow.

Retrieval grounds the agents' decisions in standards and prior checks, not model memory alone. A pre-check stage verifies the logic before it runs, addressing the safety concern directly. The authors aim for checks that adapt to the scenario instead of applying one rulebook to all data. For groups drowning in datasets, quality checks could decide what is usable before analysts waste effort.
arxiv-2606-13792:
Aguilera-Damia, Rodriguez-Gomez, and Russo study how interactions between fermions drag each other to strong coupling in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is a Fermi surface, the boundary in momentum space separating filled from empty states in a metal. Higher-dimensional fermion interactions, products of many fermion fields, are irrelevant: they shrink at low energies. The authors show the growth of the four-fermion coupling, the one driving superconducting pairing, induces a drag mechanism. The higher-order couplings are pulled along and driven to strong coupling in the infrared.

They derive the beta functions for this flow and show the drag applies to the tower of fermionic operators. The flow preserves a hierarchy: higher-dimensional operators stay parametrically suppressed relative to the pairing interaction despite all growing together. In a non-Fermi liquid coupled to a critical boson, the enhancement occurs but does not destabilise the fixed point.
arxiv-2606-13892: Circulated on arXiv in 2026, this paper reports a new investigation. The paper tackles a topic inside science and technology. The paper lives in science and technology, careful study of how the natural and built world works. The manuscript's findings join the public body of research.
arxiv-2606-13992:
García rebuilds a classic option-pricing model inside a geometric framework, explaining where its famous formulas come from. The Heston model prices options while volatility itself fluctuates randomly; its affine structure reduces pricing to exponential formulas whose coefficients obey Riccati equations. His 2026 arXiv paper extends Group Quantization from quadratic diffusion models to this variance-dependent setting. Because diffusion depends on current variance, the symmetry object is a local Lie groupoid, not a global group.

The lifted groupoid carries a central extension whose extra factor is positive and multiplicative, natural for discounting. Two views of one construction emerge. The coordinate view yields the Heston pricing operator directly. The momentum view yields the Riccati transport behind the affine transform formula. Mellin modes ride along Riccati characteristics to produce the affine kernels used for European option pricing. A projective linear action beneath the Riccati flow is also exposed.
arxiv-2606-14092:
Zhao, Zhou, and Feng solve a tuning dilemma in high-dimensional change-point detection by refusing to choose. Ridge-regularized Hotelling tests stabilize covariance inverses with a ridge parameter, but the most powerful value depends on the unknown covariance and mean shift. Their 2026 arXiv paper computes p-values on a fixed grid of ridge values and aggregates them with the Cauchy combination rule, a method for merging dependent p-values.

Under standard random-matrix conditions, the authors prove joint weak convergence of the ridge processes across the grid. That justifies fixed-level validity under joint calibration and small-tail validity of the Cauchy p-value. Monte Carlo experiments show the payoff: the aggregated test holds its nominal size steadily across covariance and signal configurations. Its power lands close to the best stable fixed-ridge choice in each scenario, without anyone knowing that choice in advance.
arxiv-2606-14192:
Cui and co-authors redesign how automated ad bidders pick a bid, splitting the choice into proposing options and judging them. Offline policies learned from logged auctions face an average action trap: unimodal models average several good strategies into one mediocre bid, and sparse long-tail traffic makes guesses unreliable. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents DRIVE, a Transformer framework decoupling candidate generation from decision making.

Three components cooperate. A Gaussian mixture model represents many bidding modes instead of one averaged action. Retrieval pulls high-quality past decisions from similar situations as extra options. A learned value evaluator scores them and selects the most promising bid. On the industrial AuctionNet benchmark and standard D4RL tasks, DRIVE consistently improved bidding results over existing methods. The gains transferred across several Transformer-based bidders.
arxiv-2606-14392:
Diego presents a 2026 arXiv white paper on future Hubble Space Telescope work. The target is lensed hot stars. Lensing happens when a massive galaxy bends light from a far object and makes it look bigger. The stars sit in galaxies at large redshift. They would be viewed in ultraviolet and visible light.

The coming Roman telescope will rival Hubble in infrared work. But Hubble still gives sharper views of point sources. It also stays the only good ultraviolet imager for years to come. The next ultraviolet flagship will not fly until the twenty forties. Hubble's sensor pixels are about three times smaller than Roman's. So its star images stay better sampled. Diego argues that lensed hot stars are a science case only Hubble can serve in the twenty thirties.
arxiv-2606-14492:
Shan and Luo run a controlled audit of knowledge-graph completion methods in a 2026 arXiv paper. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked triples, and completion models predict missing links. Papers often credit gains to a new encoder or training recipe, but the decoder, the scoring rule applied at the end, may be the real cause.

Their recipe-controlled audit swaps decoders under one fixed recipe across seven benchmarks, using ComplEx and DistMult as the main pair. On five standard graphs the decoder gap was modest but consistent in ComplEx's favor. On the small Kinship graph the ComplEx advantage was large and stable across six seeds, while on UMLS it flipped between runs. The authors conclude that small-graph decoder choice is recipe-sensitive and urge matched decoder reporting before encoder claims.
arxiv-2606-14592:
Claire He and Genevera Allen propose a way to explain what drives a clustering in a 2026 arXiv paper. Clustering groups similar data points and powers discovery from market segmentation to cell biology, but its results are hard to interpret or audit, and few tools say which features created the groups. Existing importance scores usually depend on one algorithm's assumptions.

Their Cluster LOCO family, short for leave-one-covariate-out, works with any clustering algorithm. It judges a feature by how much removing it degrades generalizability, meaning whether cluster labels learned on one data subset still predict held-out samples. One version uses data splitting, and a second, minipatch ensemble version scales to large datasets. In simulations and in a single-cell transcriptomics application on cell-type discovery, Cluster LOCO recovered the truly informative features more reliably than rival methods.
arxiv-2606-14692:
John Vastola and Kanaka Rajan examine what Markov models of animal behavior really imply in a 2026 arXiv theory paper. Modern tools describe spontaneous behavior as sequences of stereotyped syllables. A syllable is a short, well-defined action unit with neural signatures. If that coarse structure fits Markov models, the next syllable depends only on the current one. The authors ask what follows theoretically.

They explore consequences for irreversibility, predictability, and effective dimensionality of behavior. One key insight concerns the model's matrices. Their eigenvalues and eigenvectors furnish interpretable time scales. They also give the behavioral changes unfolding on each scale. Toy examples and models fitted to real data illustrate the points. The paper clarifies the theoretical meaning of recent progress in quantifying behavior. It also cautions against reading more into the models than they contain.
arxiv-2606-14792:
Kim and co-authors make multimodal reasoning cheaper with discrete diffusion models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning post-training now teaches unified models to interleave visual and textual thinking, but autoregressive models must regenerate whole images during visual reasoning, wasting computation. Discrete diffusion models can instead edit images locally.

Using localized visual editing for rollouts cut the reinforcement learning rollout cost by about twenty-seven percent against autoregressive baselines with minimal performance drop. The team also found that a shared reward across modalities creates cross-modal interference between unrelated image and text sequences during updates. Their fix, factorized reward assignment, scores text and vision segments independently. It improved results by about eleven percent over joint rewards and by about thirty-eight percent over the base model.
arxiv-2606-14892:
Ejaz and Bareinboim ask when causal models can be learned for worlds made of objects and relations in a 2026 study. An AI world model should support questions about interventions and counterfactuals, not just correlations. It should also generalize to new combinations of objects it has never seen together. Structural causal models handle the first demand but assume a fixed set of variables.

The authors extend those models into relational structural causal models, where objects and their links can vary. They first show that, without extra assumptions, even observational queries about unseen combinations cannot be identified from data. They then define relational causal graphs and derive symbolic rules for when identification is possible, even with hidden confounding. Their relational neural causal models put the rules into a learning method that is provably correct. On simulated traffic scenes with varying cars, signals, and pedestrians, the method beats non-relational baselines.
arxiv-2606-14992:
Kundu and coauthors map Kalman filters onto the neural processing units of modern laptop chips in a 2026 study. Kalman filters estimate moving states in real time for radar, drones, cars, and robots. They usually run on the CPU, which serializes updates, or on custom chips that take long to design. Edge devices also face strict battery and heat limits.

Their framework, KATANA, rewrites the filter algebra so every operation runs on the NPU matrix engine. Three tricks do the work: turning subtraction into addition, fusing tensors into static shapes, and batching filters block-diagonally. On an Intel Core Ultra Series 2 chip, the extended filter tops two hundred frames per second at under fifteen watts. The linear filter runs faster still, near four hundred frames per second. Dynamic energy use drops by up to about ninety-eight percent versus the CPU version, freeing the CPU and GPU for other tasks.
arxiv-2606-15092:
Pham and coauthors steer language model behavior in a projected high-dimensional space in a 2026 study. Activation steering adds a direction inside a model's hidden states to shift its behavior. Standard difference-in-means directions use only average class differences in the original space. Under the superposition view, useful signals also hide in curved, second-order structure.

Their method, HiDRA, applies random projections that expand activations into a bigger space. Steering directions are then estimated and added in that expanded space instead. Theory shows the projection lets plain estimators capture class structure the original space misses. The approach is training-free and layers onto existing steering methods directly. Experiments span several model families and behavioral benchmarks, including truthfulness control. HiDRA consistently beats its unprojected counterparts at steering control. The gains come without computational overhead, the authors report. Steering quality improves where plain mean differences were weakest.
arxiv-2606-15192:
Tang and coauthors present OpTI-Mouse, a 2026 tool for planning temporal interference stimulation in mouse brains. The technique overlays two high-frequency currents so their difference creates a low-frequency field deep in the brain. It promises deep targeting without surgery, but mouse protocols still rely on trial-and-error settings. Those settings cannot guarantee a balance between target strength and focus. OpTI-Mouse couples a mouse head model with an optimizer that searches stimulation settings.

For one hippocampal target pair, the optimized strategy raised field intensity about sevenfold at equal focus. For the dentate gyrus, it tightened the stimulated region while holding intensity roughly level. The team checked the framework on a commercial head phantom as well. There the optimized strategies beat the empirical baselines. The tool gives preclinical researchers a sound way to plan stimulation. That should make mouse studies of the technique more precise and reproducible.
arxiv-2606-15292:
Barron and coauthors compare three ways to model a molecule coupled to a lossy cavity, in a 2026 chemical physics paper. Strong coupling between molecules and cavity modes creates hybrid light-matter states called polaritons. Real cavities leak photons, so any model must include that dissipation. The test system is a sodium dimer molecule coupled to one cavity mode. The authors track its excited-state population and mean photon number over time. Three candidate methods are put head to head.

The stochastic method matched the Lindblad benchmark in every scenario tried. It runs more cheaply, making it an efficient substitute. The non-Hermitian approach worked only in a limited range of conditions. Adding molecular rotation changed the picture. Rotation couples vibration and photon degrees of freedom and opens light-induced conical intersections. Those intersections drain population from the upper polariton surface. Realistic cavity chemistry models need both dissipation and rotation included.
arxiv-2606-15392:
Ivanov and coauthors prove that a broad class of group localizations preserves nilpotency, in a 2026 algebra paper. Localization, borrowed from ring theory, forces certain maps to become invertible; applied to groups it can badly distort structure. A nilpotent group, roughly one whose commutator process terminates, might lose that property, a question Farjoun posed in the 1990s. The authors study localizations induced by a commutative ring R.

Their main theorem says that when R carries a lambda-ring structure, extra operations generalizing binomial coefficients, the localization of any nilpotent group stays nilpotent. Binomial rings qualify, and so does the ring of p-adic integers, settling the p-adic case that earlier methods could not touch. Along the way they characterize the local groups through the R-groups of Myasnikov and Remeslennikov and verify a Hall-Petresco identity inside them.
arxiv-2606-15492:
Shvydka and coauthor propose a model of underscreening in concentrated electrolytes in a 2026 physics paper. Classical Debye-Hückel theory says the screening length, the distance over which charges stop feeling each other, shrinks as ion concentration grows. Experiments on concentrated solutions show the opposite: the length grows, a puzzle called underscreening. The authors' heuristic blames binding: at high density, Coulomb attraction locks particles into bound configurations.

Bound particles must climb a diffusion barrier set by that binding energy before they can move. The mobile population thus thins out as concentration rises, and mobile particles do the screening. Fewer screeners means longer screening length, matching the trend and the observed temperature dependence.
