The model also speaks to FLASH radiotherapy, where ultra-high dose rates spare tissue: bound electron-hole pairs slow the chemistry that makes damaging radicals. One mechanism thus links battery electrolytes to a cancer treatment effect.
arxiv-2606-15592:
Wang and colleagues introduce DenseControl in 2026, a pipeline for generating dense crowd images with control over every individual. Crowd synthesis is hard because each person must land at a set position and scale while the crowd still hangs together as a scene. Two obstacles dominate: embedding the control signals into the generator, and keeping scale guidance from breaking the image structure.

DenseControl answers with an Isolated Object Embedding map, which encodes where each person goes, and an Implicit Scale Embedding that adds precise size information on top. A Position Shortcut mechanism strengthens cross-attention to ease the projection problem. The system also lets users steer background, style, and person attributes. Across control conditions it reaches state-of-the-art synthesis quality for dense crowds. The authors further show the synthetic images help in practice, augmenting crowd analysis when real data are scarce, supporting transfer learning, and generalizing across weather conditions.
arxiv-2606-15692:
Huang and colleagues present a surface-based framework for analysing Alzheimer's disease in 2026, built for several data types and tasks at once. Cortical measurements live on curved brain surfaces, which clashes with standard image models, and clinical cohorts are small. Multimodal learning also struggles to align scans with clinical records.

A spherical diffusion model first generates paired cortical thickness and tau PET maps on the brain surface, augmenting data while keeping anatomy matched. A contrastive model then learns aligned, fused features across the two imaging modes. Those features join cognitive scores and demographics in an in-context learning model doing classification and regression without task-specific fine-tuning. On the ADNI cohort of eight hundred two people, the framework improves across five diagnostic and longitudinal tasks, beating six baseline models. Making matched pairs of surface data is what lets the small clinical sample stretch further.
arxiv-2606-15892:
Bi, Elena, and Pinilla argue in 2026 that the scalar channels of equivariant interatomic potentials are an underexamined design dimension. These potentials represent local geometry, but the energy surface emerges only through invariant scalar channels, whose aggregation and resolution get little attention. The authors probe that pathway with two modifications acting only on a MACE backbone's scalar channels, leaving its equivariant tensors untouched.

One probe, physics-aware neighbourhood pooling, adds coordination-sensitive amplitude modulation; the other adds radial and tapered spectral bases to edge and readout features. Together they cut MACE force errors by twenty-two to twenty-seven percent, and energy errors by about twenty percent. The gains span metals, silicon, an ionic system, and molecular benchmarks, at roughly five percent extra compute. A capacity-matched backbone gains only four to seven percent, so the improvement is not bought capacity. Gains on Allegro and NequIP suggest the correction travels.
arxiv-2606-15992:
Hazarika presents a multi-task pipeline for tennis stroke biomechanics from ordinary monocular video in 2026, with no manual segmentation. Stroke boundaries come from a weighted joint-velocity score; pose features from MediaPipe's 33 landmarks in metric world coordinates. Each stroke becomes a short sequence for a compact transformer of about half a million parameters. Three heads predict stroke type, shot direction, and posture quality; a rule-based layer adds shot-selection feedback.

Trained on 1,281 strokes from seven professionals and one amateur, it reaches about eighty-four percent stroke-type accuracy, sixty-two on direction, sixty-three on posture. Cross-player, professionals to amateur, stroke type holds at about eighty-three percent. Direction, however, collapses to the majority class: directional transfer is not achieved. An ablation shows the metric coordinates are critical: image-plane landmarks roughly halve cross-player accuracy. It runs on free-tier hardware, making instrument-grade feedback cheap.
arxiv-2606-16292:
Han and co-authors present a 3D visual analytics system in 2026 for auditing license compliance and provenance across the AI model ecosystem. Models on public hubs reuse each other through fine-tuning and adapters, forming a supply chain with multi-hop dependencies and tangled provenance. Static reports and older compliance tools struggle to trace risk through such networks. Their system, AI Supply Chain Galaxy, plots models in a 3D layout and pairs the map with a rule-based compliance engine.

The team then runs an ecosystem-scale empirical analysis over 908,449 models from Hugging Face. The audit finds that 55.46 percent of models carry compliance risks or metadata conflicts and omissions, per the report. Adapter derivations omit licenses at a rate of 56.67 percent, and fine-tuned models show license drift in 8.05 percent of cases. The scale of quiet non-compliance is the headline warning.
arxiv-2606-16492:
Ferrante settles in 2026 a question about the Lyapunov equation, a matrix equation at the heart of stability analysis, when the system matrix has companion form. Standard theory ensures the solution is positive semidefinite. Ferrante asks the sharper question motivated by positive systems: is every entry nonnegative? The answer is yes when the Hurwitz companion matrix has only real eigenvalues.

The proof reduces matters to rank-one forcing terms and expands entries of the solution as quadratic forms. Those forms belong to a class of Cauchy-like matrices whose entries are built from elementary symmetric polynomials. Their positive semidefiniteness then delivers the entrywise claim. A stronger total-positivity property does not hold in general, but returns under an extra sign condition on the forcing vector in the eigenbasis. Such entrywise results matter where components carry physical meaning, as in positive systems theory.
arxiv-2606-16592:
Xu studies how to compress execution logs in a 2026 paper on reversible computing, where program steps can be undone. A log records facts from a run, and rollback reasoning depends on the closure of those facts under Horn rules, which are simple if-then rules without functions. Keeping every fact is costly, yet dropping the wrong fact changes what rollback can conclude.

A deletion scan splits any log into an irredundant core that preserves the closure, plus a redundant remainder. Xu shows the remainder is invisible under a fidelity measure based on closure difference, so the compression problem reduces to the core alone. At zero distortion the best rate becomes a hypergraph entropy built from overlapping reconstruction sets. Tests using the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm and Monte Carlo reconstruction check end-to-end loss. The theory points to smaller, faithful logs for debugging and fault recovery.
arxiv-2606-16992:
Bhartiya leads a large team disentangling multi-spin correlations in a quantum magnet in a 2026 condensed matter paper. How several spins move together, beyond pairs, is central to exotic quantum phases, yet standard neutron scattering sees only two-particle correlations. A probe for higher-order motion was missing.

The probe is resonant inelastic X-ray scattering on a copper oxide chain compound, a model spin-one-half Heisenberg chain. By detuning the incoming X-ray energy, the team selectively enhances two-spin or multi-spin responses. The two channels resonate at energies separated by a clear fraction of the exchange coupling. Their shapes differ too: the two-spin response is Lorentzian, from one dominant setup, while the multi-spin response is Gaussian-like, fed by many spin-flipped states. Exact calculations reproduce both fingerprints.
arxiv-2606-17192:
Hadou, Uslu, and Ribeiro present a 2026 arXiv paper on diffusion models that must respect constraints while they sample. Many optimisation problems, from wireless resource sharing to portfolio choice, have best answers that are probability distributions with average constraints. Standard diffusion models have no reliable way to enforce such limits during generation, which is the gap this work addresses with a primal-dual method.

Instead of fixing the constraint's dual multiplier before sampling, their method infers it jointly with the samples themselves. Each reverse diffusion step denoises with the score field for the current multiplier, then nudges the multiplier by dual ascent using the estimated violation. A single score network is trained across the family of distributions the multipliers induce. The authors prove the averaged multipliers settle near the optimum and test the method on three tasks.
arxiv-2606-17492:
Tate presents a 2026 arXiv paper on the horizontal Laplacian of a Riemannian submersion, a geometric setup where a space fibres over a base with geodesic fibres. The horizontal part of the Laplacian has long been used to probe how eigenvalues behave when the metric is varied in a standard way. Tate assumes the horizontal distribution is also integrable, a tidy extra condition that unlocks a clean new form for the operator in terms of objects on the base alone.

The horizontal Laplacian turns out to match, up to a unitary map, a twisted Laplacian on sections of a flat, infinite-rank bundle over the base. That picture lets Tate compare it with the ordinary Laplacian on a covering space of the base. When the holonomy group is infinite and amenable, their essential spectra coincide exactly. The result sharpens an earlier theorem from foliated geometry in this special setting.
arxiv-2606-17792:
Early and Volkov study a 2026 probability question posed by Robert Connelly: what happens to a stretched infinite membrane when random holes are punched through it? Earlier work treated holes spread at a steady average rate. Here the holes follow a non-homogeneous Poisson process whose density fades toward zero far from the center, while hole shapes stay random and independent.

The authors prove that if the density fades slowly enough, tension is still lost across the whole plane, just as in the steady case. They also give conditions under which complete loss of tension does not occur. So both outcomes remain possible even as holes grow sparse, which signals a phase transition in the model. The paper ends with an open problem about whether that transition has a sharp threshold curve.
arxiv-2606-17892:
Gooijer and colleagues compare two activated carbons for catching carbon dioxide from power plant exhaust, in a 2026 materials study. Activated carbons resist moisture and flue gas impurities, but most past work measured them at rest rather than in flowing beds like real capture units. The team paired experiments with simulations on a coal-based commercial carbon and a renewable one made from miscanthus straw biochar.

The coal carbon showed higher overall porosity. Yet the study digs into the finest pores, the ultramicropores, and the surface chemistry. Those traits govern how fast carbon dioxide is caught and how cleanly it separates from nitrogen under flow. The biomass carbon, activated with carbon dioxide at high heat, held up as a serious rival. The findings guide how renewable carbons can be tuned for post-combustion capture duties.
arxiv-2606-18492:
Brady and Nero show how a pair of volume holograms can physically perform the retrieval step of a modern Hopfield network in a 2026 optics paper. That network is the dense associative memory used as a model of content-addressable recall. Associative recall, mapping a partial or noisy pattern to the stored one it most resembles, is what a volume hologram naturally does.

Their cascade places a one-dimensional coded layer between two holograms, and that routing supplies the separating nonlinearity the original Hopfield model lacked while removing a Bragg degeneracy that troubles direct plane-to-plane designs. Faithful storage, they argue, needs a recording medium that captures connections between neurons without the self-energy losses of ordinary photorefractive materials. They propose a nonlocal, gradient-responsive medium that restores better efficiency scaling, demonstrate its reception, combination, and storage functions in a small diode cell, and outline routes to larger realizations.
arxiv-2606-18592:
Chen and colleagues prove that a strong enough shear flow prevents blow-up in a class of chemotaxis models in the whole plane, in a 2026 partial differential equations paper. The Hillen-Painter systems considered are volume-filling models of organisms moving toward chemical signals they secrete. Without any flow, their solutions can form finite-time singularities for any initial cell mass, the notorious aggregation blow-up of chemotaxis.

The authors show that imposing a Couette flow of sufficiently large amplitude guarantees solutions exist globally and stay bounded for all initial masses, with no smallness assumption. A novel frequency decomposition technique does the heavy lifting, removing the mass threshold that constrained earlier results proved on a strip domain. The result strengthens the picture of shear-enhanced dissipation: fast laminar flow mixes away the density peaks before chemotactic attraction can collapse them.
arxiv-2606-18692:
Nguyen and the team ask what qualitative education research can teach designers of learning analytics views, in a 2026 visualization study. It flips the usual flow of borrowing. Their testbeds are two platforms built on WordStream, a topic-evolution visualization. One is a dashboard for reading formative student assessments. The other is a maker tool for making custom views of how cohort language changes over time.

Ten STEM teacher-scholars used the platforms on journal responses from a data visualization course. They rated the in-context dashboard easier and more useful, especially for digging into response detail. The thematic analysis surfaced a valuing of control and context. The central result is an unresolved disagreement. Some saw frequency-based visualization as a productive entry point into qualitative analysis. Others warned it buries rare but critical responses. The authors distill five design implications, including treating frequency as an entry point, not an endpoint.
arxiv-2606-18792:
Sahu and the team present optical spectroscopic evidence that gas is still funneling onto the star AB Aurigae, despite the cavity carved in its disk, in a 2026 astronomy paper. Transition disks have depleted inner regions, yet their stars keep accreting vigorously. Exactly how gas crosses the gap to feed the star has resisted observation.

Using the PARAS-2 spectrograph on the Mount Abu telescope, at resolving power around one hundred seven thousand, the team resolved the kinematics of hydrogen, helium, oxygen, and sodium lines. The oxygen emission sits near the stellar rest velocity, with symmetric broadening. It traces a stagnant reservoir of gas at about one astronomical unit, which collects the infall and feeds the cavity. From there, gas crashes inward at a high accretion rate. Its ram pressure crushes the stellar magnetosphere to just above the stellar surface. That explains the restricted helium velocities and the variable inner wind.
arxiv-2606-18992:
Tran and colleagues tackle composed image retrieval in 2026, where a search starts from a photo plus a short text change. Such a query rarely points to one exact image. It points to a broad set, and which member the user wants is often unclear. Past fixes ask follow-up text questions, but text is a poor channel for fine look and viewpoint details that vision shows at a glance.

Their system, CLARA, shows the user a small panel of rendered candidate images and lets them pick the closest one. That pick gives a rich, direct signal with no model guessing its own answer. The method also reweights its calibration step so its coverage promise still holds after each turn, not just the first. That turn-valid guarantee is the first of its kind here.
arxiv-2606-19092:
Lotfibagha and colleagues use a contextual Markov decision process to set follow-up intervals for type 2 diabetes care in 2026. Guidelines now fix the same visit gap for all patients, ignoring wide differences in health paths. The team models visit timing as a sequential decision that depends on patient context. Data come from electronic health records for a large patient group across ten primary care clinics.

Contexts are found by reducing trajectory variables with principal component analysis, then clustering patients by those components and other traits. Two contexts emerge, a lower-risk and a higher-risk group. Optimal policies advise a visit within a month when a key lab value is missing. Elevated values or recent hospital stays call for a visit within three months. Sustained control allows six to twelve months, with shorter gaps for the high-risk group. The policies achieve lower expected cost than benchmark rules.
arxiv-2606-19192:
Ashkenazy and colleagues report in 2026 the first large-area look at subsurface plastic activity in conditioned copper electrodes. High-field conditioning lets radio-frequency structures in accelerators reach their operating fields, but its physical mechanism is still open. Models point to subsurface dislocation dynamics, yet large-area structural evidence has been missing. The team measures a copper cathode conditioned at high pulsed direct-current fields in a sloped-anode setup with a known exposure gradient.

Diffraction scans span large regions across nine zones of field exposure. The mean misfit in exposed regions exceeds unexposed references by a large margin, across three metrics. This misfit falls into three tiers that match the profile predicted by Monte Carlo simulations. The observations point to evolving defect networks under the surface as the driver that the process builds into the electrode.
arxiv-2606-19292:
Zhang and colleagues study risk prediction for ICU delirium from ambient sensing data in 2026. Delirium is a common, serious intensive care complication tied to worse outcomes, longer stays, and higher costs. Early prediction is hard, and environmental factors like sound and light are often overlooked in risk scores. The team tests whether light intensity and sound pressure alone can predict delirium across several time horizons, using pervasive sensors in real units.

Data come from nine intensive care units and hundreds of patients. Four efficient sequential neural models are compared across ten prediction window sizes. Shapley-based analysis reports which features matter and in which direction they push risk. The convolutional model discriminates best, with strong scores on sound data and on combined sound and light data. Sound features dominate overall, which suggests ward noise is an underused signal. Ambient sensing could feed low-burden delirium risk monitoring.
arxiv-2606-19492:
Sergiy Koshkin proves in 2026 that complex relations on finite sets can be rebuilt from simple two-place ones. A relation links several items at once, like a row in a table with many columns. Primitive positive formulas build new relations using joins and hidden witnesses, and the claim traces back to Peirce.

Koshkin treats each relation as the graph of a partial multi-valued function. Such functions split into ordinary functions because two-input functions are functionally complete in many-valued logic. That step cuts any relation down to three-place ones. A second trick turns key disjunctions into existential statements, cutting three-place relations down to pairs. The uniform proof confirms Peirce's reduction thesis on finite domains. It also shows one Sheffer function, a single all-purpose operation, can compose every relation there.
arxiv-2606-19592:
Anshuman Pandey and five colleagues probe hypersonic shock and boundary layer interplay in wind tunnel tests reported in 2026. A slender cone at Mach 5 and 8 carries a hyperbolic slice that acts as an expansion corner. A finite-span compression ramp follows at thirty degrees.

High-frequency pressure sensors, fast schlieren imaging, temperature-sensitive paint, shear gauges, and oil flow pictures record the field. Freestream Reynolds number varies so the incoming boundary layer is laminar, transitional, or turbulent. At low Reynolds number the separation shock locks onto the expansion corner. The separation zone then covers most of the slice, and its shear layer flaps at a favoured frequency. Higher Reynolds number shrinks the bubble and moves the shock downstream. Flapping speeds up while its swing drops, and slow breathing motions persist throughout. At Mach 8, strong relaminarisation past the corner keeps the flow from turning fully turbulent.
arxiv-2606-19792:
Masato Murata, Koichi Miyazaki, Tomoki Koriyama, and Tomoki Toda study phoneme addition in speech synthesis in 2026. Text-to-speech systems often borrow a pretrained model, then fine-tune it for a new language or voice. When the target speech uses sounds absent from pretraining, the model must add those phonemes mid-training.

Two settings test whether skill with known sounds speeds learning new ones. One uses language-model-made corpora with controlled phonemes, free of confounds. The other transfers real speech from English to Japanese. Fine-tuning beats training from scratch on naturalness in both settings. Yet new-phoneme error rates need as much or more data to match, despite pretraining. Pretraining thus mainly buys naturalness, not faster phoneme addition. Low-resource speech builders should budget data for new sounds accordingly.
arxiv-2606-20092:
Ganlin Yang and twelve colleagues give robot policies a memory built from visual evidence, aiming at manipulation tasks that unfold over long horizons. Their 2026 paper, EventVLA, responds to a common failure: a vision-language-action policy forgets a cue once it leaves the camera view, so tasks hinging on something seen earlier fall apart. Prior memory systems either squeezed history through a narrow bottleneck, ran a slow second system, or stored every frame and drowned in redundancy.

EventVLA keeps foundational anchors for early context and adds a Keyframe Evidence Memory that predicts which current views will matter later, storing only those sparse keyframes. The team also built RoboTwin-MeM, a benchmark of tasks unsolvable from the present view alone. Across seventeen simulated and four real bimanual tasks, success rates rose by about forty percent over strong memory-based rivals. Robots that remember the right moments finish more jobs.
arxiv-2606-20192:
Bastien Oriot, Peter Namdar, Émilie Gillet, R. L. Rincón Celis, and Valentina Parigi replace black-box optimization with a physics-based algorithm for squeezing light across many spectral modes. Their 2026 paper concerns coherent detection, where a signal interferes with a classical local-oscillator beam. Losses at that stage depend on how well the two beams match, pixel by pixel. Generic machine learning can search for the best match, but gives no guarantees and little insight.

Working from a physical model of the process, the authors build a deterministic sequential method. It provably reaches the global maximum of visibility in a pixel basis and scales linearly with pixel count. In their waveguide setup, the optimized mask raised visibility from 76 to 84 percent, a twenty percent gain in mode-matching efficiency. Squeezing measurements confirmed the payoff: the most squeezed mode improved from minus 2.08 to minus 2.64 decibels.
arxiv-2606-20392:
Hyukjung Kim, İlayda Kuzu, Kerem Özsoy, Zeynep Kahraman, Wan-Il Park, and Heeseung Zoe study the violent finish of thermal inflation and the gravitational waves it should produce. Their 2026 paper examines the first-order phase transition that ends this early-universe epoch, a proposed late, brief inflationary stage that dilutes unwanted relics. The authors first describe the transition semi-analytically through the bounce action, checking against numerical results from CosmoTransitions.

They then simulate it in real time on a 3D Langevin lattice, including Hubble expansion and the cooling temperature history. The dynamics match the bounce estimates: localized bubbles nucleate and grow, rather than the transition proceeding by phase mixing. From the resulting parameters, the team computes the gravitational-wave spectra from bubble collisions and acoustic motion in the plasma. The predicted background falls inside the projected reach of future observatories, including BBO and DECIGO.
arxiv-2606-21092:
Kelvin Idanwekhai and three colleagues introduce BASIL in 2026, a desktop application that brings Bayesian optimization to experimental process tuning without code. Bayesian methods build surrogate models of a process. Acquisition functions then choose which experiment to run next. BASIL offers those tools through a graphical interface. Users enter parameters, objectives, and legacy data directly.

Both single and multi-objective problems can be solved. Predefined surrogate model templates support model building. Surrogate and acquisition functions guide the process toward a desired objective. Any experiment with defined inputs and outputs can be optimized in this way. A friendly tool matters because many lab and process engineers could benefit from Bayesian design but lack the programming time to build it. Fewer, better-chosen experiments save materials, instrument time, and months of trial and error.
arxiv-2606-21492:
Basheer Qolomany and seven colleagues build risk models in 2026 that flag patients likely to harbor high-risk colorectal polyps before any colonoscopy takes place. Such triage could prioritize scarce colonoscopy slots and spare low-risk patients needless procedures. Working with records from Howard University Hospital, the team used only demographic, lifestyle, and comorbidity data, in a mostly African American urban cohort where equitable risk tools are especially needed.

Models trained on 4,681 patients from 2015 to 2022 were checked on 1,562 later patients, a true temporal validation. Eight model families were compared, from logistic regression to XGBoost, and a neural network gave the strongest discrimination, though overall performance stayed moderate. SHAP analysis shows which features drive each prediction. Pre-procedure features alone, the study suggests, carry real but limited signal about polyp risk.
arxiv-2606-21592:
De Zhang Lee, Han Fang, and Ee-Chien Chang strengthen stateful detection in 2026, a defense that spots adversarial attacks on classifiers by watching for suspiciously similar query sequences. Attackers probing a black-box model must send many near-duplicate queries, and detectors such as Blacklight flag them by similarity. The authors notice an unused signal: the temporal correlation of the model's soft labels across a query run, which is characteristic of attacks.

They also expose a flaw in deployed detectors. The fast approximate similarity used in practice can be gamed by queries that look dissimilar to the approximation yet stay close in the true metric, as demonstrated against Blacklight. Their two-phase fix randomizes the similarity screen, then validates candidates by soft-label timing. It detects four standard attacks at perfect true-positive rates with false positives at most six percent.
arxiv-2606-21692:
Fabián Ramírez-Pacheco, Andrea Basilio-Zárate, Hans Marin Florez, Pablo Solano, and Carla Hermann-Avigliano build a theory of image-bearing twin light beams in 2026. In four-wave mixing, a pump beam in an atomic vapor converts photon pairs into bright probe and conjugate beams that can carry pictures. Their continuous-variable model handles arbitrary transverse profiles of pump and seed, to all orders in the interaction strength.

Expanding the pump field in a Dirac comb makes photon statistics computable, pixel by pixel, from one set of formulas: mean intensity, variance, and covariance. In the plane-wave limit the classic amplifier results return. Beyond it, the math shows information routing seen in experiments: the seed's angular spectrum lands in the twin-beam intensities, the pump's in their cross-correlation. A fidelity window for image transfer, set by waist ratio and interaction strength, is mapped.
arxiv-2606-21792:
Kamtikar and colleagues present THREAD in 2026, a planner for robots that combine a stiff arm with a soft, bendable segment. Such hybrid manipulators can squeeze through narrow openings, but shapes that work in open space often collide once contact begins. Planning the rigid and soft parts separately also ignores how strongly their motions affect each other.

THREAD learns a diffusion model, a generative method that builds solutions by gradual refinement, over physically realistic backbone shapes shaped by nearby geometry. Extra loss terms reward smooth, low-curvature paths that avoid collisions across both segments at once. Trained in simulation, THREAD reached 92.4 percent task success with five times fewer collisions than the strongest baseline. It also transferred to real hardware, threading openings only 1.3 times wider than the soft segment itself.
arxiv-2606-21892:
Pandey, Tewari, and Laskar present AgroSense 2.0 in 2026, a system that recommends crops by fusing several kinds of farm data at once. Earlier tools treated soil photos and chemical nutrient profiles as separate problems, joining them only at the end. That shallow fusion misses how visual and chemical traits interact when a crop decision is made.

Three changes define the new version. A seven-band soil raster covering all of India adds local context on nitrogen, acidity, carbon, and texture that the first version lacked. A cross-modal transformer then lets tabular nutrient features attend directly to image features, learning links between them. Finally, one shared network learns soil classification and crop recommendation together as joint tasks. A TreeSHAP analysis explains the model's choices: rainfall and soil acidity matter most overall, while potassium and temperature drive its coffee recommendations.
arxiv-2606-21992:
Zheng and Yao present MCAI in 2026, a method for measuring how precise a static program analysis really is. Abstract interpretation analyzes programs by approximating their possible states inside a simplified abstract domain, but comparing the precision of rival domains has long been difficult. Earlier assessments tied precision to one specific analysis query, which skewed the comparison toward that query's needs.

MCAI instead uses model counting, tallying how many concrete states an abstract value actually represents, to score imprecision directly. Both the program's true semantics and each abstract value are encoded as logical formulas, giving a client-independent metric of the semantic loss an abstraction causes. Applied to four abstract domains through their best transformers, the study found the simple Interval domain often matched the richer Octagon domain. Many octagonal constraints proved semantically redundant, and bit-level KnownBit domains consistently beat word-level ones, offering concrete guidance for choosing abstractions.
arxiv-2606-22192:
Schönlein and Wirth develop, in 2026, ensemble feedback methods for one-parameter families of linear systems over compact parameter sets. Ensemble control steers every system in the family with one shared control. Classical ensemble feedback induces compact control operators, which cannot modify the essential spectrum of the free motion, blocking stabilization in many such settings.

The authors introduce multiplication feedback operators to overcome that obstruction. For systems with constant Hermite indices, they prove an analogue of Heymann's lemma, a pole placement theorem, and stabilization results. They also investigate how the pointwise and ensemble notions of control relate. For nonconstant Hermite indices, corresponding results hold under additional assumptions on the parameter set's structure. The work extends finite-dimensional feedback design to whole families at once.
arxiv-2606-22292:
Sarenac and colleagues introduce, in 2026, a method using helical neutron wavefronts to separate two quantities that conventional experiments blur together. One is the transverse coherence length of a neutron beam. The other is the spatial extent of each single neutron's wavepacket. Helical states produce ring-shaped profiles whose peak radius depends on the wavepacket extent, while coherence length only broadens the profile.

In their setup the team measures a beam spread of about 1.1 milliradians, giving a transverse coherence length near 180 nanometres. The same measurement also bounds that extent from below, at two micrometres. That exceeds the coherence length by more than tenfold. The results give direct evidence that the two quantities are physically distinct, resolving a longstanding confusion in the neutron literature.
arxiv-2606-22392:
Yi Zhang analyses algorithms for the monotone inclusion problem in this 2026 paper. That problem asks for a point where a sum of operators, rules that map inputs to outputs, reaches zero. It sits behind many applied tasks, but standard methods usually demand Lipschitz continuity, a strong smoothness condition.

Zhang works instead with Hölder continuity, a weaker condition that still fits some real problems. Under it, the paper proves convergence rates for Tseng's splitting method, a basic algorithm for this problem class. The same treatment covers two faster variants, the composite extra anchored gradient method and the symplectic composite extra gradient method. A convergence rate states how fast the error shrinks as steps proceed. Tests on numerical examples then check all three methods in practice. Their observed speeds matched the proven rates, so the theory holds without the stronger smoothness demand.
arxiv-2606-22592:
Hamed Alimohammadzadeh and Shahram Ghandeharizadeh present a single-drone light drawing system in this workshop paper from 2025. A Flying Light Speck is a small drone carrying a light source. Using its onboard camera and computing, it localizes itself and follows a trajectory that traces out a shape in the air, here the letters of the English alphabet.

The authors evaluate the illuminations both quantitatively and qualitatively. The qualitative side rests on an approved human subject study with twenty participants who watched the letters being drawn and tried to detect them. The measured trajectory error ran from forty-two to fifty-six millimetres, large enough to affect whether viewers could detect the letters. A key finding concerns presentation order: the sequence in which letters are illuminated has a significant effect on how long detection takes. The work complements the pair's swarm-based LightBender research with a single-device design.
arxiv-2606-22692:
Tuomo Kiiskinen presents a health AI system in this 2026 paper. Clinicians preparing for tumor boards must rebuild each patient's story from electronic records fragmented across notes, labs, and reports. Doing that by hand takes fifteen to thirty minutes per case, and language models falter on records spanning years and thousands of events.

His system, VISTA Architect, pre-computes a two-tier graph of the record at ingestion. One tier preserves the documentation structure; a Timeline Object Architecture layer synthesizes deduplicated, time-ordered events and episodes into a knowledge graph. An agentic interface plans its own traversals for case preparation, dashboards, and chat, following provenance links to evidence only when needed. Validated on thoracic oncology tumor boards at Stanford Medicine, the system scored ninety-six point four percent accuracy across 1,180 patients on fifteen tumor-board variables. Automated case preparation took just over two minutes for a held-out cohort.
arxiv-2606-23392:
Alex Grilo, Lucas Hanouz, and Anne Marin explore what single-qubit rotations can do for quantum cryptography in a 2026 paper. Quantum protocols often assume that parties own trusted sources of qubits or trusted detectors. Recent work on a setup called the Qline showed that several protocols still work when parties can only rotate single qubits. This paper pushes that idea much further. The authors give two composably secure constructions. Together they let parties hand qubit preparation and measurement to an untrusted provider. The parties keep only a trusted device that rotates qubits.

Grilo and colleagues show the measurement construction works in any context at all. The second one, for preparation, needs some assumptions about the protocol in use. Those assumptions hold for the vast majority of common protocols, the authors show. The results formally validate the Qline as a versatile base for single-qubit protocols.
arxiv-2606-23492:
Alswaidan, Jin, and Varner revisit a classic verdict against hidden Markov models as generators of stock market returns, in a 2026 quantitative finance paper. Such generators create synthetic return series for stress testing, since one real market history is never enough. Old results held that simple hidden Markov models, which switch between hidden regimes, fail to reproduce how return sizes stay correlated over long spans. That failure shaped two decades of modeling choices.

The authors separate the two jobs: the regime chain governs timing patterns, while each regime's distribution shapes the overall return profile. One fitting framework tests Gaussian and three heavy-tailed families. A spectral result shows slow decay needs only a few regimes, so distribution choice explains most of the remaining gap. With a heavy-tailed family, the model reproduces the standard facts of daily returns, and its regime-based risk forecasts pass out-of-sample checks.
arxiv-2606-23692:
Zheng and colleagues survey how researchers recover data type information from stripped program binaries, in a 2026 survey paper on software security. Stripped binaries are executable files with symbol tables and debugging data removed, leaving raw machine instructions. Recovering the original types, which values are pointers, structures, or arrays, is central to reverse engineering, vulnerability hunting, and decompilation. Without types, a decompiler cannot turn flat assembly into readable code.

The survey traces the field from early rule based heuristics and constraint solving systems to context aware neural models. It then covers the newest transformer and graph neural network architectures, which read code structure as a graph. Core challenges include meaning lost to compiler optimization and the recovery of structural types such as nested records. The authors close with future directions, including neuro symbolic methods that combine learned models with logical reasoning about program behavior.
arxiv-2606-23892:
Zhao, Lou, and Zheng build the first shared arena for fairly comparing attacks on vision language models that operate in the physical world, in a 2026 paper on AI safety. Such models steer robots, vehicles, and wearable assistants, so a perception failure can become an unsafe action. Red teaming methods exist in plenty, but each was evaluated on its own datasets and threat assumptions, making results impossible to compare honestly.

ReaLM unifies twelve red teaming methods, three defenses, and thirteen vision language models under one black box protocol. An agentic pipeline generates physically grounded attack objectives for each scene. Typographic and text based injection attacks cause the most failures. Cheap single pass attacks nearly match costly iterative ones, and larger models are not automatically more robust.
arxiv-2606-23992:
Mukherjee improves an AI pipeline for assembling clinical value sets, the code lists that define medical concepts for quality measurement and research, in a 2026 paper on clinical informatics. Language models cannot generate these codes from memory: the systems are huge, versioned, and imperfectly memorized, and invented codes are dangerous. The earlier RASC approach retrieves similar published value sets, pools their codes, and selects. Mukherjee optimizes each stage for its own job: retrieval for recall, selection for precision.

A Qwen3 based retriever raises candidate pool recall from about fifty five percent to seventy three percent on a test set of three thousand seven hundred forty four value sets. Swapping the original selector for a blinded GPT-5 adjudicator nearly doubles accuracy, the macro F1 score rising from about zero point two nine to about zero point five five. Every returned code still comes from the auditable pool.
arxiv-2606-24092:
Qiu, Shen, and Zuo fuse visible-light and thermal images for object detection without paying the full cost of global attention. Standard cross-attention compares every location with every other. That cost grows quadratically and strains small deployment hardware. Two observations motivate their 2026 design, PNAFusion. Slight misalignment between the two image types usually sits in local neighbourhoods. And the true match between the two views bends non-linearly across the scene.

A pixel-neighbourhood cross-attention module restricts matching to nearby regions. That cuts wasted computation and background noise. An adaptive deformable alignment module learns per-pixel offsets. Features can thus shift by different amounts in different places to line the two views up. An iterative feedback loop then refines the fusion step by step. Qiu's team frames the combination as progressive alignment: local, learned, and repeated. It targets multispectral detection on resource-constrained platforms, not data-centre hardware.
arxiv-2606-24592:
Yusuke Nakamura and Kohsuke Shibata study two open conjectures about singular shapes. Their field, birational geometry, studies shapes defined by polynomial equations. It focuses on singular points, where a shape fails to be smooth. The pair work with hyperquotient cases. One target is the precise inversion of adjunction conjecture. The other is the lower semi continuity conjecture for minimal log discrepancies. Earlier proofs here needed a mildness condition called klt. Without it, one conjecture already has a counterexample.

Nakamura and Shibata define a local notion of virtually free actions. They pin that notion down using arc spaces of quotient varieties. From this they derive an exact test for when precise inversion of adjunction holds. The test works for all hyperquotient cases, with no klt assumption. It also explains how the known counterexample arises. As a direct payoff, the authors prove the lower semi continuity conjecture in this setting without conditions.
arxiv-2606-24692:
Dakshina Tharindu, Sahan Sanjaya, Philip Baptist, and Prabhat Mishra present PowerFuzz, a fuzzer for firmware that cannot be inspected. Fuzzing feeds inputs to a system to expose faults. Grey box fuzzers steer by feedback such as branch coverage, but closed firmware gives no such readout. PowerFuzz instead watches power side channel traces, a substitute signal that needs no view inside the target.

The framework first recovers which branches a run executed. It applies a sliding window and then a growing window correlation method across the full power trace. From those branches it builds a high level control flow graph of the closed firmware. That graph steers the fuzzer toward paths not yet explored. Tests span three embedded hardware platforms and ten firmware benchmarks. PowerFuzz came within 13.5 percent of grey box branch coverage. It beat leading black box fuzzers by up to 22 percent.
arxiv-2606-24892:
Abdur Rasool, Xiaohui Huang, Yanqing Hu, and Linyi Yang present ReviewGuard, a system that teaches language model reviewers to value long term scientific impact. Peer review guards quality, yet it often undervalues papers that later collect many citations. Language models can draft reviews, but they mainly mimic what human reviewers prefer at the time. ReviewGuard instead aligns generated reviews with citation based estimates of future impact.

The testbed holds 20,861 AI and machine learning papers from OpenReview, enriched with Semantic Scholar citation data. On papers that were rejected yet later published, ReviewGuard's scores correlate with future citations at 0.776. Human reviewers reach only 0.492 on the same measure, and a supervised expert model 0.681. At a fixed decision threshold, ReviewGuard flags about ten percent of high impact rejected papers. Humans flag under two percent, a fivefold gap. The authors offer the system as a complementary signal for editors, not a replacement for judgement.
arxiv-2606-25092:
Tony Salomone, Deep Gandhi, and Ali Asaria test whether the experts inside a frontier MoE model are modules. Sparse MoE models send each token to a few of many experts, suggesting specialisations by capability or language; Cohere's Command A+, studied here, has 128. They map routing patterns, pre register six hypotheses linking families to capability axes, and ablate each family at inference time. A family counts as a module if the damage stays selective, against a size matched random ablation baseline.

The verdict is cautionary. Of six families, just one survives a corpus and a bar as a clean selective module: the Arabic language family. Every other family has an effect yet fails selectivity. Modularity flips with the measuring instrument: Spanish is selective on one corpus yet bleeds into Arabic on another, and math changes verdict between metrics. Strong modularity is rare, and whether it shows up depends on the measurement.
arxiv-2606-25492:
Bayesian updating can be viewed as an optimisation: pick the distribution balancing fit to data against closeness to a prior. Hien Duy Nguyen and Jacob Westerhout solve that problem exactly in 2026 for a wide menu of such measures, without restricting the answer to a parametric family first. Ordinary variational inference uses one specific penalty. Generalised versions swap in other divergences, and closed forms for the unrestricted optimum were largely missing.

For f divergence penalties, a scalar formula gives the optimal density directly, with famous cases like Kullback Leibler and squared Hellinger worked in detail. Reverse and mixed versions follow from the same principle. Bregman divergences between densities get their own density space solution, and Rényi penalties yield a threshold equation characterising every global optimum. Simple model weighting cases show the formulas in action.
arxiv-2606-25692:
Interpolation inequalities bound a function's middle behaviour by its extremes, and the Caffarelli Kohn Nirenberg family, weighted by powers of distance, anchors much of modern analysis. Anh Tuan Duong and Van Hoang Nguyen extend that family in 2026 for curl free vector fields and second derivatives, territory where earlier sharp results covered only part of the parameter range. Sharp means the best possible constant in the inequality is identified, not just estimated. Their proofs rest on splitting functions into spherical harmonics and sharpening one dimensional integral bounds.

Two stability results follow: when a field nearly achieves the best constant, it must sit quantifiably close to the extremal shapes that achieve it. One covers the curl free inequality proved by Cazacu, Flynn, and Lam; the other covers the new second order family itself. Stability turns a sharp inequality from a static bound into a measuring tool for near optimal fields.
arxiv-2606-25792:
A spinning body falling through curved spacetime does not follow the path of a non spinning one. Modelling that difference matters for future gravitational wave observatories listening to extreme inspirals. Vojtěch Witzany and Viktor Skoupý build a Hamiltonian formalism in 2026 using frames adapted to the body's own worldline. Their Hamilton Jacobi equation holds to first order in spin. It turns on a clean condition. When background geodesic motion splits by variables, and parallel transport along those paths does too, the spinning problem splits as well.

A companion choice of frame makes the body's centre definition into a simple constraint, generalising textbook variables. Three families illustrate the theorem: rotating black holes, gravitational plane waves, and expanding universes. Such splitting is precious: it makes motion integrable and waveforms computable. The result tells modellers when that luck survives adding spin.
arxiv-2606-26492:
Sigma Jahan studies how tools that diagnose deep learning failures are themselves evaluated. Deep learning programs often fail during training. Finding the cause is slow and costly. Diagnosis tools are usually tested by cross-validation inside one program. Cross-validation rotates which data is held back for testing. Deployment instead means facing programs the tool has never seen. That mismatch can flatter the tools.

Jahan used DynFault, a corpus of over five thousand fault-injected training runs. The runs came from thirty-eight real programs. Existing diagnosis techniques lost a clear margin of balanced accuracy on unseen programs. Balanced accuracy averages success across fault types fairly. The gap traced to program-level structure in the input features. Two feature sets behaved differently. Curvature features, describing the error surface's shape, still helped on new programs. Optimizer and activation features helped only on programs seen in training.
arxiv-2606-26892:
Viktor Mirjanić and Challenger Mishra survey how symmetry helps machine learning compute the hidden geometry of string theory. Calabi-Yau manifolds are the shapes proposed for the universe's extra dimensions. Their Ricci-flat metrics, the exact distance rules, have no closed-form solution. Physicists need them numerically to predict particle masses and couplings. Learning the field is steep for machine learning researchers.

The manuscript first overviews the needed background and literature. It then surveys how a manifold's symmetries affect learned metric approximations. The isometries of Ricci-flat metrics, symmetries that preserve distances, are characterised rigorously. Symmetry breaking in point sampling is addressed, with a new formula for volume ratios on a broad manifold family. A new symmetry-aware graph neural network model closes the work, avoiding failures seen in rivals.
arxiv-2606-27092:
Ismayilov proposes zQR, a framework that lets phones check privacy proofs carried inside QR codes. Zero-knowledge proofs let someone prove a claim without revealing the secret behind it, but the maths is hard for everyday users. Compact zkSNARK proofs are a leading kind, small enough to encode in a code symbol. A blockchain layer adds auditable logging and non-repudiation, meaning signers cannot later deny their records. Large language models help generate the needed proof circuits automatically in the 2026 design.

Security discussion covers several attack surfaces, from forged codes to tampered logs. Timing tests measure proof creation, checking, and code reading and writing delays on mobile hardware. Chain fees are measured as gas consumption, the standard unit of blockchain computing cost. Results show the full loop works as a proof of concept. Proofs fit in a mid-sized code symbol with low error correction.
arxiv-2606-27192:
Wang and colleagues improve how side networks steer image and video generators. In the dominant dual-branch design, a frozen main network makes pictures while a side branch encodes visual conditions like edges or poses. Score-based theory clarifies the split: the main branch supplies an unconditional score, a guide toward realistic images. The side branch quietly supplies a likelihood score, a guide toward matching the condition. Their LISA method makes that hidden role explicit in 2026 experiments.

Features are hooked from a chosen side-branch layer and projected by a small decoder into score space. An approximated likelihood score target is built, and the gap to that target becomes an extra training loss. Joint training with the normal diffusion loss speeds convergence markedly. Final image quality also improves across tasks, architectures, and model types. Side features grow more disentangled, easing conditional control. Extra inference cost is zero.
arxiv-2606-27292:
Raxit and colleagues present BOWConnect, a motion planner for robots whose moves must obey real dynamics, not just geometry. Sampling planners often waste effort in high-dimensional state spaces, trust poor cost guesses, and stall in narrow passages. BOWConnect steers with Bayesian optimisation over windows, learning local cost maps as it goes. Two trees grow at once, one from the start and one from the goal, across parallel threads, in a robotics paper appearing in 2026.

A boundary solver builds bridge paths that respect the dynamics, linking the two trees cleanly. Ten benchmark settings test the planner, including tight passages and non-convex spaces where leading rivals fail. Success reaches one hundred percent across those tests, with the fastest or near-fastest times in hard cases. A ground vehicle and a quadrotor both run it in real time with no collisions. Code and videos are public.
arxiv-2606-27392:
Modanese studies what happens to conserved amounts when a quantum system is opened to its environment. In a closed system, an observable that commutes with the Hamiltonian keeps a constant average forever. Couple the system to a Markovian environment, described by a Lindblad master equation, and that conservation can break. Starting from the adjoint Lindblad equation, simple formulas give the time derivatives of the observable's mean and second moment. In the 2026 quantum physics paper, the collapse operators are pinpointed as the agents breaking the law.

Worked examples keep the formulas concrete: one-qubit amplitude damping, a two-qubit excitation-number model, and momentum diffusion where the mean survives while the variance grows. The Jaynes-Cummings model shows the mirror case, a reservoir coupled via a conserved quantity, where dephasing proceeds without touching that quantity's statistics. Conservation in open systems becomes a case-by-case question.
arxiv-2606-27492:
Tian, Yao, and Cui treat the communication wiring of a language model agent team as a skill the system can learn and reuse. In their QueenBee Planner, worker agents, a task adapter, and the scoring function stay frozen. Only an outer planner learns, generating temporal communication graphs that say who informs whom in each round, who merges messages, and who answers. Execution traces are boiled down into evidence-backed design rules labelled preserve, modify, or avoid.

Held-out acceptance gates, variance-aware credit assignment, and falsification checks stop lucky runs from hardening into policy. On an aggregation benchmark, the best self-evolved graph cuts error from about twelve point five to about seven point nine in the reported results. It also sends fewer messages and spends fewer tokens. Agent systems can accumulate architectural knowledge, not just task habits.
arxiv-2606-27592:
Caesium lead chloride is a model inorganic perovskite. Perovskites are a crystal family prized for solar cells. Heat tests on such materials are only trustworthy when the true sample temperature is known. Ethan Cronk and six colleagues built a careful testing method in 2026. It probes how halide powders change phase and break down during heating.

The team made two compounds by ligand-assisted re-precipitation. That method regrows crystals from solution under controlled chemistry. One compound was the parent perovskite itself. The other was a double perovskite, caesium silver antimony chloride. They checked starting crystal structure and particle shape first. Temperature conversions came from a control substrate. X-ray diffraction then tracked the samples during heating itself. The method reproduced known high-temperature behaviour of the model compound. It also verified the actual sample temperature. Phase change points and the onset of breakdown were pinned down for both materials.
arxiv-2606-27892:
Wearables and Internet-of-Things sensors must process signals on the device itself. Nonlinear functions for inference, calibration, and preprocessing are costly in digital form. Analog computing offers a low-power alternative. Flexible electronics suit wearables well. But they impose tight area and power limits. Paula Carolina Lozano Duarte, Georgios Zervakis, and Mehdi Tahoori introduce analog Kolmogorov–Arnold networks in 2026. Hardware and software are co-optimised together.

Circuit-level error modelling enters the training process. Pruning is applied at both software and hardware levels. Tests validate the approach across several function approximation tasks. Pruning cut area by up to fifty-five percent. It cut power by up to fifty percent too. Average reductions sat near thirty percent across datasets. Surprisingly, pruning sometimes improved accuracy as well. Removing spline parameters regularises the analog design. The framework is presented as robust and general. It targets low-power function approximation on flexible substrates.
arxiv-2606-28092:
Telling which diffusion model made an image matters for provenance. The images themselves are unreliable evidence. Models trained on different data can converge to similar outputs. Pragati Shuddhodhan Meshram and Varun Chandrasekaran propose Spectral Denoising Signatures in 2026. The method fingerprints each candidate model's denoising behaviour instead. A model's score function has a distinct spectral geometry. It shows in how energy moves across frequency bands as noise is removed.

Frequency-controlled probes test that response. Only standard forward passes are needed. No inversion or enrollment at generation time is required. Attribution accuracy reaches about ninety-nine point nine percent across eight diverse models. Under cross-domain prompt shift, it holds at ninety-six point two percent. Baselines are beaten across changes in data, architecture, and procedure. The authors note the signature idea may extend to detecting fine-tuning or distillation. Spectral geometry is offered as a principled basis for the task.
arxiv-2606-28192:
Qicheng Bai, Ziru Wang, Teli Ma, Guang Dai, Jingdong Wang, and Mengmeng Wang study robots that work with two arms at once. Most existing systems either keep the arms from truly cooperating or treat them as equals, even though people naturally let one hand lead while the other supports.

Bai and colleagues propose PA-BiCoop, a single model that assigns a leading primary arm and a helping auxiliary arm, and can swap those roles as a task moves through stages. Two specialized decoders plan each arm's motion while sharing one view of the scene. In tests, the system beat leading rivals by about half on simulated two-arm tasks, and by more than half on real-world tasks.
arxiv-2606-28392:
Jiasheng Wang, Tanun Jitwatcharakomol, Piyawadee Jongpradubgiat, and Simeng Zhu segment lesions in PET/CT scans, where healthy organs and imaging artifacts can glow like tumors and fool image-only models. Their RADIANT-PET system adds a reasoning layer that second-guesses each candidate spot before accepting it as a lesion.

Wang's team first segments generously, catching nearly everything suspicious, then converts each candidate into a structured text summary of intensity, shape, and anatomical context. A language model judges each candidate as true lesion or false positive, optionally reading the radiology report too. Reinforcement learning sharpens that judge, rewarding correct calls and correct anatomical placement. Across two cohorts the system beat strong image-only baselines, with the largest gains when reports were provided.
arxiv-2606-28492:
Mark N. Costantini, writing alone, audits a popular way of quoting uncertainties in particle physics fits. The Monte Carlo replica method refits a model on many copies of the data, each perturbed by noise, and reads the spread of best-fit parameters as the uncertainty. It matches the true Bayesian answer exactly when the model is linear in its parameters, and only then.

Costantini derives the leading-order distribution the replica method actually produces in the nonlinear case. It differs from the standard Laplace approximation of the Bayesian posterior by one computable matrix, the residual-weighted Hessian at the best fit. Its sign and size dictate whether uncertainties are overstated or understated. Two single-parameter examples that can be solved in closed form illustrate the formula. Evaluating it inside full parton-distribution and effective-theory fits is the natural next step he points to.
arxiv-2606-28692:
Shanghua Gao, Ayush Noori, Richard Zhu, and colleagues, together with the ATHENA-R1 Evaluation Consortium, built an artificial intelligence agent. It reasons about treatments the way a careful clinician must: by gathering evidence before concluding. Choosing a therapy means integrating disease context, other conditions, current medications, contraindications, and fast-moving biomedical knowledge, then revising as facts arrive.

Their agent works over a universe of two hundred twelve biomedical tools covering every drug the United States has approved since 1939. A two-level self-learning scheme first has multi-agent systems manufacture tools, tasks, and reasoning traces for supervised training. Then reinforcement learning with scientific feedback rewards good evidence gathering and non-redundant logic. Across thousands of drug reasoning tasks it reached accuracy in the mid-nineties, beating a leading frontier model by wide margins, and physicians rated it favorably on complex hospital cases.
arxiv-2606-28792:
Burkhawala, Barad, Prajapati and Dabhi built a phone app that lets shoppers see a jewellery ring on their own hand before buying. A customer photographs their hand in the app, built with React Native, and picks a ring from the catalogue. The challenge is placing the ring image at the right spot, angle and size so the preview looks believable.

Hand landmarks come from MediaPipe, a vision tool that finds points such as knuckles and finger joints, which define where the ring should sit. A custom YOLOv8 detector, trained to spot rings, finds the ring's own points and strips its background away. Simple vector maths then corrects the angle between finger and ring, and the ring is scaled to match finger thickness while keeping its shape. The finished picture shows the ring in place on the customer's hand.
arxiv-2606-28892:
This reply by Ansari, Jafari, Akbari and Abdi answers a Comment by Sirker on their earlier work about dynamical quantum phase transitions in noisy systems. Such transitions are sharp changes in return behaviour after a sudden quench. Sirker argued that one way of extending the key measure, the Loschmidt echo, to mixed states forbids these transitions under any noise.

The authors accept that conclusion for the measure Sirker studied, which rests on the Uhlmann-Bures fidelity comparing noise-averaged mixed states. Their paper, they stress, studied a different quantity, built by an operational two-stage protocol. It first averaged excitation probabilities from the noisy ramp. Then it evolved a pure state built from those probabilities. The sharp features they reported belong to that protocol, not to zeros of the fidelity Sirker analysed. Both results can stand, because they concern different observables.
arxiv-2606-28992:
Li, Zhang, Liu and Sun propose AgriTune-R, a reproducible framework for adapting general-purpose language models to agriculture. Farm advice is safety-critical, time-sensitive, region-dependent and domain-specific: wrong guidance on crop disease, pesticides or fertiliser can do real harm. The authors state plainly that the paper reports no performance claims, because no training run or expert evaluation has yet been carried out under it.

Instead, it lays out an auditable workflow built around Qwen3-8B, a publicly verifiable model, as the recommended base. It covers farm data governance, instruction building, and fine-tuning methods that adjust only a small part of the model. Retrieval-augmented generation and safety controls for high-risk questions are built in. A testing protocol targets knowledge questions, pest and disease advice, crop management and policy explanation. An expert rubric scores factuality, safety, evidence consistency and how uncertainty is expressed.
arxiv-2606-29292:
Zhao proves size estimates for random tensors built from Gaussian chaos of a fixed finite order. Such tensors arise when several independent Gaussian inputs interact through a fixed kernel, and bounding their size in strong norms is basic to probability and analysis. His setting allows the tensors to take values in Hilbert spaces, which may be infinite-dimensional.

The main estimate bounds a mixed moment of the tensor, measured in Schatten norms, by the largest of a family of flattened versions of the kernel. The proof inducts on the number of stochastic factors, starting from a rectangular form of the non-commutative Khintchine inequality. He then derives consequences for operator norms, tail bounds, and related chaos constructions. The constants depend only on the fixed order, not on dimensions or cutoffs, and the infinite-dimensional case follows by completion in the flattening norm.
arxiv-2606-29592:
Polat, Serpedin, and two colleagues named Kurban present STEMGym, a benchmark for autonomous electron microscopy. In scanning transmission electron microscopy, every measurement deposits damaging electron dose. Smarter navigation is widely assumed to be the main lever for dose-efficient imaging. Their evidence points the other way.

STEMGym offers fifteen physics-simulated microscopy worlds: five materials, three difficulty levels, four test tasks. A single score, the area under the dose-efficiency curve, captures the trade-off between information and dose. Across thirty-three agent setups under realistic dose budgets, the analyst pipeline dominates. Pairing a trained convolutional network (CNN) analyst with naive raster scanning multiplies the score several-fold. Swapping in Bayesian or adaptive navigation brings no clear further gain. Large vision-language models trail task-specific networks badly here.
arxiv-2606-29792:
Kumar argues, in a position paper, that humans are evolved instruction followers. Adults can often carry out a novel task correctly on their first attempt after only verbal or written instructions. Such rapid instructed task learning is a hallmark of human cognitive flexibility.

He proposes an evolved instruction-following bias, an inductive bias that evolution shaped to interpret and execute language instructions. The analogy is with large language models, which gain zero-shot performance through instruction tuning. In humans, Kumar posits, the ability is innate. He synthesizes evidence from three fields and outlines testable predictions.
arxiv-2606-29892:
Chen and three colleagues improve robot control models called vision-language-action models, which take camera input and instructions and output movements. Reinforcement learning, training by reward, usually needs an outside success signal, and the authors replace it with the model's own confidence.

They first show that action sequences the model generates confidently are much more likely to succeed. Their framework, T2VLA, works at test time and uses closeness to high-confidence expert demonstrations as an internal reward. A dual-expert scheme balances a local pseudo-expert that explores boldly with a global pool that keeps training stable. On the LIBERO and RoboTwin benchmarks it beats supervised baselines and nears the performance of reinforcement learning given true rewards.
arxiv-2606-29992:
Yao-Yi Zeng, Zhi-Jie Liu, Jie Zhou, and Jing-Ling Chen study an additive uncertainty relation for three quantum observables. Such relations limit how sharply incompatible quantities can be known at once. The additive form captures a joint limit for a triple that does not commute. The authors ask exactly when that bound is achieved. This is the equality, or saturation, condition.

Zeng and colleagues give a short proof by rotating the triple. They apply the classic Robertson relation to the two sideways parts. This route makes the mechanism clear. It yields a condition both necessary and sufficient for equality. The condition holds for general mixed states. At equality, the covariance ellipsoid flattens into a disk. The disk faces along the mean commutator direction. An inverse construction uses a small Lie algebra. It builds triples whose chosen states reach the bound.
arxiv-2606-30192:
Hyunwoo Park and Sang-Hyun Lee help robot policies trained in simulation survive contact with reality. Vision-based reinforcement learning suffers when real images differ from simulated ones. Domain adaptation can bridge that gap, but it usually needs much target data. Real target data is exactly what practice rarely provides. Their framework, AIDA, works under severe target data scarcity.

AIDA's core idea is adaptive imagination for augmenting the little data available. It generates imagined rollouts, but only trusts the reliable ones. A distribution-shift-aware discriminator cuts rollouts that drift into low-confidence regions. On the trusted transitions, a self-consistency loss adds training signal. That loss cycles state to image and back to state. Representations become semantically meaningful rather than superficially matched. Experiments cover five MuJoCo tasks and two robotics tasks. AIDA outperforms the baselines across that whole suite.
arxiv-2606-30292:
Daniyel Ayupov and Artur Markov-Tsoy present a technical report from DreamForge AI Lab on a low-compute, real-time world model. World models simulate interactive environments frame by frame under user control. Frontier systems demand heavy compute for that simulation. DreamForge-World 0.1 Preview targets consumer graphics hardware instead. It adapts an open autoregressive video stack for the task.

The system supports live keyboard and mouse control during generation. Multimodal starting inputs and mid-stream reprompting are also supported. Dual-view operation and minute-scale interactive rollouts run at native 480p. Speeds reach fourteen to fifteen frames per second on one RTX 4090. Memory footprint stays low throughout those rollouts. A residual action pathway, inspired by game world models, carries control signals. The authors are candid about the preview's limits. It is neither memory-complete nor frontier quality yet. Targeted adaptation of open backbones keeps costs down.
arxiv-2606-30392:
Qianyuan Yin, Changkun Wei, and Bo Zhang prove that a standard trick for cutting off infinite wave problems converges for sound in fluid-filled porous rock. Poroelastic media mix solid frames with fluid in pores. Wave scattering there follows Biot's theory. Computations need the unbounded domain truncated somehow. The perfectly matched layer, or PML, absorbs waves in an artificial border. Its convergence had never been proved for poroelastic scattering.

A change of variables simplifies the system first. The displacement–flow system becomes a displacement–pressure system with fewer unknowns. That form yields the fundamental solution more easily. Positivity of the complex wave numbers also follows. The PML is built in spherical coordinates. Existence and uniqueness hold under stated assumptions. Exponential convergence in layer thickness and parameters is established. The proof uses decay of the stretched fundamental solution. The result is the first of its kind for this medium.
arxiv-2606-30692:
Francisco Delgado-Vences analyses fade duration in wireless channels, the stretches of time a signal spends too weak to use. Knowing that distribution is basic to robust communication design. Classical level-crossing theory lacks precision for rare, extreme fades, and brute-force simulation needs impossibly many samples to see them. His framework attacks the problem with three tools from stochastic analysis.

Wiener chaos expansion gives accurate moments and tail curves while minimising simulation variance. A Markovian projection squeezes the channel models down to at most three dimensions. Importance sampling, weighted using Malliavin sensitivities, then focuses effort on rare events, cutting variance by factors in the hundreds to thousands. An adaptive gradient algorithm with a classic step-size schedule estimates the needed parameters. Numerical tests showed relative errors under half a percent, even for event probabilities near one in a quadrillion.
arxiv-2606-31092:
Zhou and Xie tackle catastrophic forgetting in fine-tuned language models. Full fine-tuning teaches a model a new task, but it can erode skills the model already had. Older remedies guard the weights themselves, through distance penalties or output matching. The authors argue that a skill lives in activation patterns, not in weight geometry. What should be protected is the set of activation directions a skill actually uses.

Their method, Fora, works in function space. From label-free calibration inputs, it finds the main activation directions of the skill to preserve. Updates are then projected so they cannot read those directions, with a narrow spectral channel left open for controlled change. Tests on the Qwen3-1.7B model covered three learning setups. Fora preserved old skills better than weight-space projection and standard regularization, with only a small cost to the new task.
arxiv-2606-31192:
Le and two colleagues settle a gap in the theory of Okamura-Seymour quasimetrics, distance-like functions that fit inside a flat directed graph. Earlier work by Chen and Tan tested in polynomial time whether such a quasimetric exists, but one key step only proved existence. Testing is not the same as building the embedding itself.

Le turns that existence step into an algorithm with linear programming. The result is the first polynomial-time method that actually finds a planar embedding for any given Okamura-Seymour quasimetric. As a payoff, they give a near-optimal distributed algorithm for approximate single-source shortest paths in planar directed graphs. It runs in the CONGEST model in a round count close to the diameter lower bound, resolving a standing open question.
arxiv-2606-31392:
Zhang and Shou introduce ReGRPO, a training method that teaches tool-using vision-language agents to fix their own mistakes. Supervised training mostly shows success, so agents learn little about recovery when a tool fails. Sparse end-of-run rewards also fail to say which step went wrong or how to repair it.

ReGRPO first runs near-miss actions on purpose to gather grounded failure cases. It builds Reflection-of-Thought triplets that name the error type, the evidence, and a fix plan, paired with corrected actions for warm-start training. Group-relative policy optimisation then trains reflection and correction together, with a cost term that discourages needless reflection. On GTA and GAIA it beats strong open-source rivals under the same backbone and tools.
arxiv-2606-31692:
Gasco and ten colleagues overview the second TalentCLEF challenge, a shared evaluation for language technology in human capital management, held as a lab at the CLEF 2026 forum. Fragmented datasets and protocols have made it hard to compare systems that match people, jobs and skills, even though such systems influence real hiring decisions.

Task A covers contextualized job-person matching, ranking candidates described by resumes for a vacancy in English and Spanish. Task B covers job-skill matching, retrieving the most relevant skills for a job title in English while classifying each skill as core or contextual. The edition drew 113 registered teams and more than 400 submissions across both tasks, and the overview describes the datasets, evaluation settings and the main results the teams obtained.
arxiv-2606-31892:
Yu Wei builds a comparative epistemic logic of understanding, arguing that understanding, unlike knowledge, comes in degrees. One agent can understand why something holds better than another, by giving a deeper or more robust explanation. Standard epistemic logic has rich tools for knowledge but almost none for graded or comparative understanding.

Graded modalities indexed by agent and level express understanding at standards from minimal to ideal. A comparative connective states directly that one agent understands why a claim holds better than another does. Models add agent-indexed graded explanation structures and a justification-style term algebra. Soundness and strong completeness are established, and each fixed finite-level fragment of the language is decidable.
arxiv-2608-00092:
Cabada, Cambeses-Franco, and López-Somoza study differential equations with a twist. A functional term adds weighted linear maps of the solution. Two-point boundary conditions close the setup. The form covers piecewise constant arguments. It also covers integral-type dependence.

They work out the Green's function for this class and its adjoint problem. That route links distinct types to each other. Piecewise cases tie to impulsive forms and nonlocal boundary problems. Sign results mark where the Green's function keeps one sign. The adjoint side gets the same treatment. Worked examples show the findings in use.
arxiv-2608-00192:
Saunders and co-authors present an upgraded laser tool for CMB bandpass checks. Bandpass error is a top challenge for CMB work. It can limit foreground removal and spectral fits. Those steps matter for inflation and cluster science. Fourier spectrometers now do this task, but systematics cap them.

Their tool uses a laser whose frequency can be set by the user. A coupled unit dims the laser power as needed. First tests used a prototype of the tool. The team then built an upgraded version with better performance. They describe the upgrades and test the new laser source. Field tests with microwave tools are planned next.
athanasius-against-the-heathen-contra-ge:
Young Athanasius of Alexandria opened his career with a broad case against pagan religion, Against the Heathen. Idols, he argues, are dead wood and stone dressed up by human hands. The treatise appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, often paired with his work on the Incarnation.

He calls the old myths immoral and finds them unable to explain the order of the world. Only the Christian God, he claims, accounts for both creation and human reason. The logic is confident and systematic for so young a writer. Readers meet the future champion of Nicaea already armed with formidable arguments.
athanasius-de-decretis-defence-of-the-ni:
Critics attacked the Council of Nicaea's key word, homoousios, meaning of one substance with the Father. Athanasius defended that choice in De Decretis, his Defence of the Nicene Definition. The treatise appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

The fathers at Nicaea chose the term, he argues, precisely to block Arian evasions about the Son. Every softer phrase had been twisted, so a hard one was needed. Athanasius walks through the council's reasoning like an insider, which he was. No other writer did more to make Nicaea's decision stick across the empire. The treatise still anchors study of what the council meant by its boldest phrase.
athanasius-de-sententia-dionysii-npnf2-1:
