Cells that stop dividing with age, called senescent, leak signals into their surroundings, and Glyn Nelson and six colleagues ask what those signals do to healthy neighbors. Their 2012 study grows normal fibroblasts, a connective tissue cell, beside senescent ones and watches for aging signs next door.

Neighbors develop a DNA damage response, the same internal alarm seen in senescence itself. The effect passes through gap junctions, direct channels between touching cells, and involves reactive oxygen species. Long exposure pushes intact bystanders into senescence. In mouse livers, marked hepatocytes cluster together, hinting the spread may occur in the body too. Aging tissue, the study suggests, can recruit more aging.
europmc-pmc3602092:
Carl May set out a general theory of implementation in Implementation Science in 2013. Getting a new practice to stick inside real health services is a social process, not a delivery problem, and scattered partial theories left it hard to predict or judge. May builds on his own Normalization Process Theory, which explains how new ways of working become routine, and welds it to ideas from sociology and psychology about agency and collective action.

Core pieces include how people make sense of a new practice, commit to it, do the shared work it requires, and judge its worth, set within the social systems where they act. Mental and social mechanisms link those pieces into one frame. The theory aims to serve designers, managers, and evaluators at once: a shared language for forecasting where an implementation will snag and for comparing cases across settings.
europmc-pmc3604592:
Ilhan Satman and colleagues resurveyed diabetes in Turkey in the European Journal of Epidemiology in 2013. Twelve years after a first national survey, TURDEP-II drew a random sample of 26,499 adults aged twenty and over, with a response rate of eighty-seven percent. Blood tests plus a glucose tolerance test on eligible participants caught both known and hidden cases. That let the team price the epidemic and its trends on the same definitions as the earlier round.

Diabetes prevalence reached 16.5 percent, about 6.5 million adults, higher in women than men, and the age-adjusted rate had risen ninety percent since the first survey. Prediabetes covered large shares of adults, obesity stood at thirty-six percent, and hypertension, unusually, had fallen by eleven percent. Risk factors differed somewhat by sex, with age, waist size, and blood pressure central in both. The authors present the surge as a warning for health planning.
europmc-pmc3664492:
Thyroid cancer is being found far more often, and Pellegriti, Frasca, Regalbuto, Squatrito and Vigneri ask why in a 2013 Journal of Cancer Epidemiology review. Counts have risen sharply for decades worldwide. Many experts blame better scans that catch tiny cancers early, and part of the rise is surely that. Yet large tumours have risen too, and death rates have not fallen despite earlier finds and better care.

A real rise, the authors argue, likely runs beside the detection effect. Medical radiation is their prime suspect, since exposure has grown and the thyroid is sensitive to it. Higher iodine intake and more chronic thyroid swelling may add to the trend, while obesity is not specific to this gland. The review closes with a mixed verdict: sharper detection plus a true rise driven by radiation and other unknown agents.
europmc-pmc3665892:
Seven talking therapies for depression land close together, Barth and seven colleagues find in a 2013 network meta-analysis in PLoS Medicine. Head-to-head trials of every pair of therapies do not exist, so the team used a network method that also draws on indirect proof, where two therapies are compared through a shared third. Adults with depression were the patient group, and the methods were tested in randomised trials.

Effects across the therapies were much the same, in the moderate-to-large range overall. In larger trials, three approaches held up most firmly: cognitive-behavioural therapy, interpersonal therapy and problem-solving therapy. Effects looked weaker for psychodynamic therapy, supportive counselling and behavioural activation. Small studies bent results upward, a bias the authors flag. Choice in practice, they say, can rest partly on what local services can actually offer.
europmc-pmc3698792:
Singer and colleagues built a new risk score to predict stroke and other clots in people with atrial fibrillation, where judging risk guides the decision to anticoagulate. Their ATRIA score was derived from a cohort of nearly eleven thousand patients and then tested in a separate community cohort of over twenty-five thousand.

Eight factors made the final model, including age, prior stroke, diabetes, heart failure, hypertension, and poor kidney function, with extra weight where age and prior stroke combined. The score sorted risk better than the standard CHADS2 and CHA2DS2-VASc schemes in both cohorts, especially for severe events. The authors offer it as a firmer basis for treatment decisions.
europmc-pmc3701992:
Tice and colleagues update Tox21, a multi-agency American programme rebuilding chemical safety testing. The programme launched in 2008, joining federal toxicology, environmental, and genomics institutes. The Food and Drug Administration came aboard in 2010. Its aim is to replace slow animal tests with fast, mechanism-based laboratory assays.

The update describes the screening technology and interpretation methods developed so far, the programme's current state, and the problems still blocking progress. The authors frame the work as systems toxicology: progress depends on covering wide chemical and biological ground, and full success will take decades. Even now, though, the data are reshaping how hazards are characterised.
europmc-pmc3708292:
Bell and colleagues review the IGF2BP family of RNA-binding proteins. These three related proteins steer what cells do with their messages. The review covers their growing links to cancer. The proteins are mainly active before birth. There they shape cell movement, growth, and differentiation. They are quiet in most adult tissues.

Two family members switch back on in several aggressive cancers, where they support the traits that make tumours dangerous. The review connects these cancer roles to the proteins' normal developmental jobs. It argues they may drive tumour growth rather than merely mark it. It also weighs them as drug targets and biomarkers worth testing.
europmc-pmc3728292:
Gitanjali Singh and co-authors, writing for a large global collaborating group, published a pooled analysis in PLoS ONE in 2013 on metabolic risk factors. Blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, and body mass index all raise the risk of heart disease and diabetes. What was missing was a consistent set of effect sizes split by age and sex.

The team pooled data from an average of 123 cohorts, covering 1.4 million people and 52,000 cardiovascular events. Each risk factor was firmly tied to disease. For ages 55 to 64, higher blood pressure hit hypertensive heart disease hardest, while higher body mass hit diabetes hardest. For all factors, the proportional effects shrank with age, were much the same in men and women, and varied little by region.
europmc-pmc3783192:
Liang Sun and eight co-authors presented a classification tool in Nucleic Acids Research in 2013 for telling protein-coding transcripts from long non-coding ones. Sequencing now produces floods of transcripts, above all in species with poor annotation, and older tools leaned on known proteins or evolution signals that can mislead.

Their tool, the Coding-Non-Coding Index, profiles patterns of adjoining nucleotide triplets in the sequence itself, with no need for prior annotation. It classified transcripts accurately across species, handled incomplete transcripts and sense-antisense pairs, and revealed evolutionary divergence between vertebrate and invertebrate genes, and between plants. Applied to orangutan data, it produced a catalog of that species' long non-coding RNAs. The authors offer the software freely online.
europmc-pmc3894192:
Shanrong Zhao, Wai-Ping Fung-Leung, Anton Bittner, Karen Ngo, and Xuejun Liu compare two gene profiling tools in PLoS One, with the record dated 2014. RNA sequencing and microarrays both read which genes are active in a sample. The team run both on the same human T cell activation samples and stress the gaps, not the matches.

Overall profiles agreed well between the two. Sequencing won on faint genes, on telling apart near-identical gene versions, and on spotting DNA variants in the reads. Its wider range caught more changed genes with bigger swings. Arrays suffer probe flaws such as cross-talk that sequencing avoids by design. The head-to-head case helps labs weigh cost against depth when planning gene activity studies.
europmc-pmc3910392:
Odessa Addison, Robin L. Marcus, Paul C. LaStayo, and Alice S. Ryan review fat stored between muscles in the International Journal of Endocrinology in 2014. Called intermuscular adipose tissue, this fat grows with age and illness. The review starts from a puzzle: older adults lose strength faster than they lose muscle, so something besides muscle size must be at work.

Higher levels of this fat predict weaker muscles and poorer mobility in older adults and in people after stroke or spinal cord injury, and in diabetes and lung disease. The fat is also linked to insulin resistance, a step toward diabetes. The authors weigh what causes the fat to build up and what treatments might slow or reverse it.
europmc-pmc3928792:
Sofia Costa, André Almeida, António Castro, and Lucília Domingues review fusion tags for making proteins in the bacterium E. coli in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2014. E. coli is still the workhorse host for producing recombinant proteins cheaply and at scale, but foreign proteins often clump into useless insoluble lumps inside the cell. That clumping is the system's main weakness.

Attaching a partner tag to the protein can keep it soluble, ease its purification, or make it provoke a stronger immune response when used as a vaccine ingredient. The review surveys the main strategies and factors that decide success, with special attention to a newer tag called Fh8, recently ranked among the best solubility helpers. The authors aim the survey at users designing their own production setups.
europmc-pmc3930492:
Elad Noor and colleagues build a way to spot the steps that slow down a cell's chemistry in PLoS Computational Biology in 2014. Thermodynamics is normally used in metabolism research just to say which direction a reaction can run. But energy also governs speed: a reaction running near equilibrium wastes enzyme, because much of the enzyme's work runs the reaction backward, and the cost climbs steeply as balance nears.

Their framework scores a whole pathway with a single number, the Max-min Driving Force, which marks the pathway's weakest step in energy terms. Pathways with a low score need far more enzyme to carry the same flow. The method gives metabolic engineers and cell biologists a map of where a pathway's true kinetic obstacles sit, and which steps redesign should target first.
europmc-pmc3989492:
Hiroshi Mori and nine co-authors present a new primer set for reading microbe communities, in DNA Research in 2014. Studies of such communities often copy a gene called 16S rRNA, found in bacteria and their kin. A flaw in common primers is that they also copy matching genes from larger organisms, wasting reads and skewing results.

The team compared gene sequences from genome-sequenced strains and screened fifty candidate primers for reach across microbe groups and for low reach into other groups. One pair, named 342F-806R, covered many microbes but not the other genes. Tests on a soil sample, checked against a common primer pair and against shotgun sequencing, gave a community profile with no strong bias. The set should suit surveys of many kinds of microbial community.
europmc-pmc3991392:
Ivan Bedzhov and Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz study how the early mouse embryo takes shape as it implants, in Cell in 2014. At that stage a ball of stem cells, the epiblast, must turn into a cup-shaped sheet. The step is key to later growth but was poorly understood, and many thought cell death did the shaping.

Watching embryos grow in the womb and in the dish, the pair found a new event instead. The loose ball sorts itself into a rosette, a ring of aligned cells, without death driving the change. Signals from the base membrane below, passed through proteins called integrins, align the cells and pinch their tops. That step then opens a hollow space inside. In the dish, matrix proteins could stand in for the membrane, and stem cells formed the same rosettes. The result gives a fresh model of this early stage.
europmc-pmc4033792:
Sophia Davidson, Stefania Crotta, Teresa M. McCabe, and Andreas Wack show that a front-line antiviral signal can worsen flu, in Nature Communications in 2014. Type I interferons are the body's early alarm against viruses. Flu severity varies a lot, and host genes are one suspected reason.

In one mouse strain, flu brought higher interferon levels yet worse lung damage, more illness, and more deaths than in a hardier strain. Giving interferon to the hardy strain also made flu worse. Mice of the frail strain that lacked the interferon receptor fared better, with less lung damage and fewer inflammatory cells. The signal drove a death receptor on lung lining cells and its trigger on incoming immune cells, killing the lining. Blocking that pair guarded the frail mice. The work warns that boosting this signal in severe flu could backfire.
europmc-pmc4054092:
Paul Geeleher, Nancy J. Cox, and R. Stephanie Huang predict how patients will respond to chemotherapy using models trained on cell lines, in Genome Biology in 2014. Response to cancer drugs varies wildly and side effects can kill, yet few markers predict who benefits.

Their method learns from a large panel of cell lines, fitting whole-genome expression against measured drug sensitivity and letting every gene speak. After cleaning and matching the data, the cell-line models are applied to a patient's tumour expression before treatment. The output is a forecast of drug response in the body. Tested on three independent clinical trial data sets, the forecasts matched or beat signatures built from patient data itself. The approach turns the huge cell-line screening archives into a clinical tool. It also sidesteps the need for a fresh marker hunt for each drug and cancer pairing.
europmc-pmc4056792:
Linda Denehy and nine colleagues run a year-long trial of exercise rehabilitation for survivors of critical illness, in Critical Care in 2013. Long intensive care stays leave patients weak, and recovery of walking and daily function can crawl. Whether structured exercise from the ICU onward speeds that recovery was untested at this length.

A hundred and fifty patients who had spent at least five days in intensive care were split between usual care and an intensive programme spanning the ICU, the ward, and outpatient visits. Walking distance at twelve months, the main outcome, did not differ between the groups. Neither did strength tests or quality-of-life scores. The trial also fell short of its enrolment goal, weakening its power. A side look at change over time hinted the exercise group improved faster early on.
europmc-pmc4075492:
Mandy Stahre, Jim Roeber, Dafna Kanny, Robert D. Brewer, and Xingyou Zhang updated national estimates of deaths and lost years of life caused by excessive alcohol use in the United States. Their study appeared in Preventing Chronic Disease in 2014. It used a federal disease-impact tool covering fifty-four alcohol-linked conditions.

For 2006 through 2010, excessive drinking accounted for an average of nearly eighty-eight thousand deaths a year and about two and a half million years of potential life lost. Among working-age adults, one in ten deaths was alcohol-attributable. State death rates varied widely, highest in New Mexico and lowest in New Jersey. The authors point to proven community strategies that reduce heavy drinking and its harms.
europmc-pmc4144092:
Katia Aquilano, Sara Baldelli, and Maria R. Ciriolo reviewed new signalling roles for glutathione, a three-part molecule long known as a cell antioxidant. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2014. Glutathione also feeds nutrient handling, gene activity, and decisions between cell growth and death.

The molecule exists in reduced and oxidised forms, with the reduced form normally far more abundant. That balance sets the cell's redox state, the chemical climate many switches read. Recent work links glutathione to the tuning of nitroxidative stress, to autophagy, the cell's self-digestion, and even to viral infection. The authors argue the old antioxidant is really a versatile regulator, and that crosstalk between its forms and other signals is the frontier.
europmc-pmc4182392:
Carl Deirmengian, Javad Parvizi, and four co-authors tested joint fluid markers for infection in Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research in 2014. Infection around an artificial hip or knee is a serious problem, yet standard tests often miss it or cry wolf. The team checked whether proteins in the joint fluid itself could give a clear answer.

They sampled fluid from 95 patients facing revision surgery, 29 with infection by the standard society definition and 66 without. Sixteen candidate markers were measured in each sample. Five of them, including alpha-defensin and lactoferrin, sorted every patient correctly, with perfect sensitivity and specificity. Eight more scored nearly as well. The patients included people with inflammatory disease and people already on antibiotics, groups that often confuse other tests.
europmc-pmc4238192:
Noah M. Ivers, Jeremy M. Grimshaw, and six co-authors asked whether audit and feedback research is still learning in the Journal of General Internal Medicine in 2014. Hospitals often audit clinicians' practice and feed the results back to nudge better care. Trials of that simple idea number in the hundreds, yet effects stay modest and uneven.

Reanalysing a Cochrane pool, the team kept 98 comparisons from 62 trials. Piling studies in publication order showed the average effect settled by 2003, after just 30 trials. Later trials added little about what makes feedback work better or worse. Feedback helped most under conditions the early trials had already revealed. The authors conclude the field keeps repeating itself and should test new questions, such as how feedback interacts with other improvement tools, instead of rerunning the same trial.
europmc-pmc4284392:
L W Pisa and a large group of co-authors assess what neonicotinoids and fipronil do to invertebrates that are not their targets. Their review appeared in Environmental Science and Pollution Research in 2015. Bees, butterflies, earthworms, and water invertebrates all meet these chemicals in fields and streams.

Honey bees get the deepest coverage, since they are the most studied non-target species, with effects from death down to impaired learning and navigation at low doses. Sections follow on other bees, moths and butterflies, earthworms, and freshwater and marine species, where far less is known. The assessment shows a wide evidence base on land and a thin one in the water.
europmc-pmc4365692:
Xiao-Ming Meng, Patrick Tang, Jun Li, and Hui Yao Lan reviewed a signaling path that drives kidney scarring, in Frontiers in Physiology in 2015. The signal protein TGF-beta sits at the center of renal fibrosis, the scarring that advances chronic kidney disease. Inside cells, its messages pass mainly through Smad proteins. The review explains how the balance among those Smads tips toward scarring, and where treatment might push back.

One family member, Smad3, becomes highly active in scarring and helps shut down Smad7, a natural brake, while Smad2 works in the opposite, protective direction. With the brake off, scar-forming cells build up and lay down excess matrix. Small RNAs add another layer of control on Smad3. Raising Smad7 or adjusting those small RNAs eased scarring in mouse models, marking this path as a focused target for kidney therapy.
europmc-pmc4381092:
Alessandro Careghini, Andrea Mastorgio, Sabrina Saponaro, and Elena Sezenna reviewed four emerging pollutants in the environment, in Environmental Science and Pollution Research in 2015. Their compounds are bisphenol A, used in plastics, nonylphenols, benzophenones, and benzotriazoles. Such chemicals are rarely monitored, yet they spread widely and may expose people through many routes. Data on the last two, and on soil and groundwater for all four, were especially scarce.

The review gathers what is known about each compound's physical and chemical traits, how it moves and breaks down in soil, groundwater, surface water, and sediments, and what breakdown products it leaves. It also covers findings in food. Pulling the scattered record together matters because these compounds reach wildlife and people quietly. The authors frame the gaps that monitoring should close first.
europmc-pmc4423992:
Zachary Kurtz, Christian Müller, Emily Miraldi, Dan Littman, Martin Blaser, Richard Bonneau, and Christian von Mering presented a method in PLoS Computational Biology in 2015. It maps links among gut and environmental microbes. Gene surveys give counts of many microbe types per sample, but those counts sum to a whole, so simple correlations can invent false links.

Their method, named SPIEC-EASI in the article, seeks a sparse network, one with few links, that stays stable under this kind of data. It is built to handle hundreds of microbe types measured in far fewer samples. Tested on known and real data sets, it recovers truer patterns of which microbes rise or fall together, a step toward learning how microbial communities hold together or break down.
europmc-pmc4457892:
Tatiana Varanita and a team of co-authors studied a mitochondrial pathway that decides how tissues respond to damage, reporting in Cell Metabolism in 2015. Mitochondria, the cell's energy plants, change shape inside during programmed cell death and self-eating. A protein called OPA1 controls the folds of their inner membrane, called cristae, and that remodeling was suspected to matter beyond single cells.

Blocking the remodeling pathway in mice did not disturb normal development. Yet it protected tissues on several fronts. Muscle wasted less after nerve loss. Heart and brain suffered less after blood flow was cut and restored. Liver cells resisted death signals. Steady cristae kept energy production efficient and cut both the release of a death trigger and the production of harmful oxygen radicals. The authors present the pathway as a drug target for limiting tissue damage.
europmc-pmc4468292:
Li Chen, Rui Chen, Hua Wang, and Fengxia Liang reviewed how inflammation dulls the body's response to insulin, in the International Journal of Endocrinology in 2015. Obesity is now worldwide, and its long-lasting, low-grade inflammation is a main reason tissues stop answering insulin well. That resistance drives type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome.

Overfeeding fills fat cells with lipid, and fat tissue then releases inflammatory messengers and switches on signaling pathways that jam insulin's own signals in muscle, liver, and fat. Messengers and pathways influence each other, so both must be weighed together, the authors argue. They gather recent experimental work on each factor, from immune proteins to stress pathways inside cells. They also judge the promise of anti-inflammatory treatments. Such treatments could restore insulin action at its source, rather than only lower blood sugar.
europmc-pmc4494392:
Lucas Lara and Marcos Rostagno reviewed the impact of heat stress on poultry production in Animals in 2013. Hot conditions are among the most important environmental challenges for chicken farming worldwide. Heat stress harms the welfare and productivity of both broilers, birds raised for meat, and laying hens, yet responses to it are still being worked out.

Effects range from slower growth and fewer eggs to poorer meat and egg quality and safety, the review reports, drawing on many published studies of productivity and immune response. Public concern for bird welfare under heat has also grown. Knowledge of the basic mechanisms behind the effects, and of behavior and welfare under heat, remains scarce by comparison. The authors survey what is known and the intervention strategies proposed, from housing and ventilation to feeding changes, and mark where research is most needed.
europmc-pmc4497592:
Robert Dickson, Gary Huffnagle, and William Goldman set out new principles for lung bacteriology in PLoS Pathogens in 2015. Textbooks still call the lungs sterile. The authors find that claim implausible. Few places on Earth lack bacteria. The warm, moist airway sits just below the bacteria-rich mouth, under a constant flow of inhaled microbes and micro-aspirated fluid. Molecular studies have found bacteria in healthy lower airways, and none has found their absence.

Unlike the gut, the lung is a low-nutrient, high-clearance environment. So its microbiome is shaped by a balance of two flows: immigration from the mouth, and elimination by cough, mucus, and immunity, rather than local growth alone. The article builds an ecological model of that balance for health and disease. It explains how changes in immigration or clearance reshape lung bacteria and their effects. That applies in conditions from asthma to critical illness.
europmc-pmc4523692:
Mika Kivimäki and Ichiro Kawachi review work stress and heart disease in Current Cardiology Reports in 2015. Whether strain at work truly causes chronic disease has been argued for years. Skeptics cite weak effects and confounding. The pair set out to weigh the best long-term evidence on heart and vessel outcomes.

The evidence covers 27 cohort studies. Together they followed over 600,000 men and women in Europe, the United States, and Japan. Job strain and long working hours went with a moderately higher risk of heart disease and stroke. The excess ran 10 to 40 percent above stress-free workers. It looked alike across sex, age, and class. Links also appeared for type 2 diabetes, but not for common cancers or chronic lung disease. Trial evidence on cutting stress remains thin.
europmc-pmc4525192:
C. Kratochwil leads a nine-author team reporting a first-in-human cancer treatment in the European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging in 2014. Patients with neuroendocrine tumors had kept growing despite therapy with beta-radiation drugs aimed at a surface receptor. Few options remained for them. The new approach swapped the beta emitter for an alpha emitter, bismuth-213, on the same targeting drug, DOTATOC.

Eight patients were treated, seven through an artery into liver tumors and one through the whole body for marrow spread. Seven had follow-up beyond two years. Scans confirmed the drug bound the tumors, and lasting responses appeared in all treated patients. Side effects on blood, kidneys, and hormone glands were tracked against standard criteria.
europmc-pmc4528092:
Steson Lo and Sally Andrews argue for a better way to analyze timing data in Frontiers in Psychology in 2015. Psychology often measures reaction times, which bunch at fast values with a long slow tail. Common advice says to bend skewed data with a mathematical transform before fitting mixed models, tools that track both people and items.

The authors warn that bending the scale can bend the conclusions: effects that add cleanly on raw times can look crossed after a transform, or the reverse. Generalized linear mixed models solve this by building the skew into the model itself, so no transform is needed. The paper walks through the key choices in setting such a model up, with examples, so results stay in the units researchers actually think in.
europmc-pmc4530492:
Petter Dyverfeldt leads a long author list issuing shared guidance on 4D flow heart imaging, in the Journal of Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance in 2015. Blood flow through the heart and great vessels changes direction beat by beat. Four-dimensional flow magnetic resonance records that flow across a whole volume over time, at scan times of roughly 5 to 25 minutes.

The statement comes from physicists, doctors, and engineers who build and use the method. One capture volume can be set with ease, then flow through any plane inside it can be computed afterward with good accuracy. The paper explains how to acquire and analyze such scans, where they help in the clinic, mainly in the heart and big vessels, and what research still must settle.
europmc-pmc4636492:
Seth M. Noar and colleagues published a 2016 meta-analysis of experiments on pictorial cigarette pack warnings. Many countries were weighing picture warnings against text-only ones. The team searched seven databases for controlled experiments that reported both formats. The work appeared in Tobacco Control.

Thirty-seven studies with 33,613 participants qualified. Picture warnings beat text on twelve of seventeen effectiveness measures. They held attention longer, stirred stronger thoughts and feelings, and soured attitudes toward packs and smoking. Intentions to avoid starting and to quit both rose. Participants also judged picture warnings as more effective on every perceived-effectiveness measure. The authors note that actual smoking behaviour was rarely measured, a gap for future studies.
europmc-pmc4686892:
Tamás Baranyai, Kata Herczeg, Zsófia Onódi, and a large team compared two ways to pull exosomes from blood plasma in PLoS ONE in 2015. Exosomes are tiny sacs shed by cells, prized as research targets and possible disease markers. The catch is purity: blood plasma is full of the protein albumin, which contaminates samples. The team tested hard spinning, called ultracentrifugation, against size-based column separation.

Spinning recovered only a small share of exosomes, and albumin came along under every setting tried. Longer or warmer spins raised yield but not purity. Column methods could deliver a small fraction nearly free of albumin, yet most exosomes still traveled with the albumin. The honest conclusion is that clean plasma exosomes cost yield. Labs choosing a method now have clear numbers on that trade-off.
europmc-pmc4699692:
Ilya Belevich, Merja Joensuu, Darshan Kumar, Helena Vihinen, and Eija Jokitalo described the Microscopy Image Browser in PLoS Biology in 2016. Modern microscopes produce rich three-dimensional images of cells, but turning those stacks into measured objects is slow. Segmentation, the step of outlining structures, is the bottleneck. Their free, open-source program was built for fast segmentation and analysis of multidimensional data from both light and electron microscopes.

Worked examples show the program processing real datasets from each microscope type. Because the code is open and accepts plug-ins, labs can adapt it to odd projects instead of bending projects to the tool. Tutorials help new users get up to speed quickly. The authors aim to close the gap between how fast images can be collected and how fast they can be understood. The browser is free from a dedicated website.
europmc-pmc4704492:
James Fraser, Carmelo Ferrai, Andrea M. Chiariello, and a large team, including the FANTOM Consortium, mapped chromosome folding during cell differentiation in Molecular Systems Biology in 2015. Mammalian chromosomes fold into blocks of about a million bases, called TADs, which cluster into larger compartments. Whether those blocks join into still higher structures was unclear. Using contact mapping as nerve cells formed, the team looked for organization above the block level.

Blocks did join into trees of domains within domains, reaching up to whole-chromosome scale. These metaTAD trees looked similar across cell types, yet their rearrangements during differentiation tracked changes in gene activity. Computer models of folding polymers showed the hierarchy packs DNA tightly without scrambling which parts touch. The work gives chromosome structure a family-tree shape and ties its reshaping to the gene programs that define a cell's identity.
europmc-pmc4728192:
Anne J. Ridley reviewed Rho GTPase signaling in cell migration in Current Opinion in Cell Biology in 2015, writing solo. Cells move in many styles, sliding with broad front sheets, squeezing with balloon-like blebs, or crossing vessel walls. One protein family, the Rho GTPases, sits at the center of every style, though each member's share shifts with context. The review sums recent advances in how these switches steer movement.

The famous trio Rho, Rac, and Cdc42 get their due, but less-studied family members are brought into the picture too. Ridley compares sheet-driven and bleb-driven crawling directly, then follows cells as they cross the endothelium, the vessel lining, a key step in both immune defense and cancer spread. The synthesis helps readers see migration not as one mechanism but as a kit of modes, with Rho proteins as the common control board.
europmc-pmc4765192:
Silvia Juliana Serrano-Gomez, Mazvita Maziveyi, and Suresh K. Alahari review a cell shape change tied to cancer spread, in Molecular Cancer in 2016. In the change, called EMT, settled surface cells loosen their grip, lose their surface markers, and gain the loose, moving style of inner tissue cells. The shift drives normal embryo growth and wound repair, but tumors hijack it to invade.

The review centers on the fine controls that lock the shift in. Gene-silencing marks laid on DNA and chemical tags added to proteins after they are built both help repress the glue protein E-cadherin, the loss that starts the change. Master switch proteins work with these tag-writing enzymes. The authors close with drug ideas that aim to block the shift and so slow spread.
europmc-pmc4779792:
Ian J. Jacobs leads a wide author team in The Lancet in 2016 reporting the UKCTOCS trial of ovarian cancer screening. Ovarian cancer kills often because it is found late; only about four in ten patients live five years. The trial asked whether yearly screening of older women could cut deaths by catching the disease early.

Over 200,000 women aged 50 to 74 were assigned to blood-marker screening, ultrasound screening, or none, and followed for about eleven years. Deaths from ovarian cancer ran lower in both screened groups, by about fifteen and eleven percent, but neither gap cleared the bar for firm proof in the main analysis. The blood-marker group's edge grew in the later years, and the authors call for longer follow-up before firm verdicts.
europmc-pmc4785292:
Gayan Perera leads a team of many co-authors in BMJ Open in 2016 describing a mental health data resource built from clinic records. The register covers patients of a large mental health provider in southeast London, drawn straight from its electronic record system. Names are stripped, and researchers query the records through a search tool launched with the register in 2008.

By the end of 2014 the register held over 250,000 patient records, growing by about 20,000 cases a year. Text-reading software has since mined the free-text notes for thinking scores, schooling, smoking, diagnoses, and drug use that forms alone missed. Links outward add deaths, hospital visits, and cancer records. The profile sets out the security rules and the kinds of study the register can support.
europmc-pmc4805592:
Jyoti P. Tamang, Koichi Watanabe, and Wilhelm H. Holzapfel review the microbes of fermented foods worldwide in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. Nearly every culture ferments something: soy and vegetables in Asia, breads and cheeses in Europe, grain porridges in Africa. The microbes doing the work, some willing to grow in labs and many not, form a vast, little-catalogued heritage.

Culture-free gene methods have lately exposed species no lab had grown, redrawing the cast lists of famous foods. The review tours major food and drink classes region by region, naming their working microbes: acid bacteria, bacilli, yeasts, and molds. It also notes that a microbe's genes alone do not prove its role; its active messages in the food tell more. The authors frame these food webs as a genetic storehouse worth guarding.
europmc-pmc4840492:
Linda S. Zhang and Sean S. Davies reviewed how gut microbes turn food parts into active compounds, in Genome Medicine in 2016. Studies that compare sick and healthy people often find microbe-made compounds among the most changed. The review gathers the most striking cases, where a food-derived product shapes gut health, immunity, blood vessels, energy use, or behavior.

Cases covered include short-chain fatty acids, a compound called trimethylamine N-oxide, products of the amino acids tryptophan and tyrosine, and oxidized fats. Each case suggests a treatment path: change the microbes, or block or boost the compound itself. The authors note that such steps need care, since the same compound can help one system and harm another.
europmc-pmc4880792:
Jonathan Le Roy and co-authors reviewed sugar tagging of plant phenylpropanoids in 2016. Plants build a huge family of compounds from two amino acids along this path, ending in flavonoid pigments and lignin wall material. Tagging a sugar onto these molecules, a step run by enzymes called UGTs, changes how they dissolve, how long they last, and how toxic they are.

Tagging also decides where a compound is stored and whether it acts at all, while untagging frees it again. This on-off switch thus governs supply of pigments, scents, and defense compounds. The review covers the tagging enzymes, their cell locations, and fresh finds. Growers and chemists both care, since the switch steers crop traits.
europmc-pmc4882692:
Colleen R. Martin, Pei-Ra Ling, and George L. Blackburn reviewed infant feeding in 2016, comparing breast milk with formula over the first year of life. A mother's own milk is the best food for nearly all infants, the review holds. Beyond growth, milk shapes gut function after birth, immune growth, and brain development. Yet feeding at the breast is not always possible or enough.

Formula, built on cow's milk or soy, tries to copy milk's makeup as closely as factories can. Variants serve babies with cow's milk allergy and other needs. The review lays out the content of each food side by side, so parents and clinicians can judge when a substitute is required and which kind fits.
europmc-pmc4932192:
Hui Gong leads a large team presenting a fast imaging method that maps a whole mouse brain at single cell detail. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Brain maps need both the labeled neurons under study and landmarks that show where they sit. Mapping to flat atlases drawn from other brains leaves position errors. The team's system collects both kinds of data from the same brain at once, in two colors.

It images a full mouse brain in three days, at voxels finer than a cell body across. One channel shows fluorescent neurons and their long projections. The other stains all cell bodies, giving a built in reference map. With both layers aligned, the team traced long range connections and located cell clusters with care. The authors argue the paired data make connectome maps, charts of brain wiring, far more precise.
europmc-pmc4945892:
Maggie R. Wagner and five co-authors ask how much a wild plant's genes and age shape the bacteria on its leaves and roots. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Plant microbes affect health, disease resistance, and drought tolerance, so breeders care about genetic control. Lab studies, though, may misjudge that control because pots lack field variety. The team ran a large field experiment with Boechera stricta, a perennial wild mustard, across sites and years.

Host genes shaped leaf communities clearly, but root communities barely at all. The leaf effect also changed from site to site. Communities shifted as plants aged. Many leaf bacteria matched root bacteria, which points to soil as a seed source. The authors conclude that gene by environment interplay makes microbiome assembly in nature complex. They warn that breeding for microbe traits must be tested in real fields.
europmc-pmc4977492:
Hitomi Shirahama, Bae Hoon Lee, Lay Poh Tan, and Nam-Joon Cho tune the recipe for GelMA, a light setting gelatin used in bioengineering. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2016. GelMA is among the most used photopolymerizable biomaterials, yet labs made it with untested settings. The team varied buffer strength, starting pH, reagent amounts, gelatin level, temperature, and time, then measured how fully the gelatin was substituted with the reactive groups that let it set.

The best balance kept amino groups reactive while limiting reagent breakdown. Nearly complete substitution followed from a low reagent feed, a set buffer strength and pH, and moderate gelatin levels. The winning recipe needs just one reagent addition in one pot. The authors offer the conditions as a shared standard. Consistent GelMA, they argue, would make results across tissue engineering labs easier to compare.
europmc-pmc5021692:
Adam H. Marblestone, Greg Wayne, and Konrad P. Kording argue for joining deep learning with neuroscience, in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience in 2016. Brain science studies how nerve circuits are built in fine detail. Machine learning instead tunes simple networks by brute-force correction against a cost, a measure of error. Two shifts in machine learning, richer built-in structures and layered training rules, open a bridge between the fields, the authors propose.

They suggest the brain likewise runs on cost functions, but many of them, differing by place and by stage of growth, inside a pre-built structure fitted to the problems of behavior. On this view, the brain's special systems for attention, memory, and recurrence are tools that make learning fast and data-thrifty. The paper maps which known circuit features fit this picture and sets out tests by which neuroscience could check or refine the claims.
europmc-pmc5030092:
Caroline Townsend Stork and eight co-authors report in eLife in 2016 that estrogen can damage DNA through structures called R-loops. Estrogen switches on gene programs in breast tissue and drives cell growth, but high lifetime exposure also raises breast cancer risk. R-loops form when a fresh RNA strand sticks to its DNA template as genes are read, leaving the other DNA strand exposed.

After estrogen treatment, R-loops rose fast across the genome of breast cells, crowding at the very genes estrogen switches on, the same regions where breast cancers show rearrangements. Double-strand breaks in the DNA followed, and many of them vanished when R-loops were removed, marking the loops as their cause. The breaks also needed DNA copying to be under way. The study names a direct route by which a normal hormone signal can unsettle the genome.
europmc-pmc5057092:
Xiaoping Chen, Ping Han, Tao Zhou, Xuejiang Guo, Xiaofeng Song, and Yan Li build a database of human circular RNAs in Scientific Reports in 2016. Circular RNAs are loop-shaped RNAs found across human tissues, with roles in health and disease, but no fully annotated collection existed. Their database, circRNADb, gathers 32,914 human exonic circular RNAs chosen carefully from many sources.

Each entry carries genome position, splicing pattern, sequence, and references. The striking feature is protein-coding annotation. 16,328 circles carry a reading frame longer than one hundred amino acids. 7,170 of them also bear an internal entry site that could start protein building, and mass checks found matching proteins for 46 circles from 37 genes. Circles were long classed as non-coding, so the coding clues open a new question. The site offers search, browsing, download, and a way to submit new finds, and the team plans steady updates.
europmc-pmc509292:
Anke Steppuhn, Klaus Gase, Bernd Krock, Rayko Halitschke, and Ian T. Baldwin tested whether nicotine truly defends tobacco plants in nature, reporting in PLoS Biology in 2004. Many plant chemicals harm insects in the lab, yet few have been shown to protect the plant where it actually grows.

The team silenced two genes in wild tobacco so the plants made almost no nicotine, then checked them in the field. Hornworm caterpillars grew faster on the low-nicotine plants, and other insects chose them over normal plants. Planted in their native habitat, the altered plants were attacked more often and lost three times more leaf area. The results give direct field proof that nicotine works as a defense.
europmc-pmc5120092:
Luria Leslie Founou, Raspail Carrel Founou, and Sabiha Yusuf Essack reviewed antibiotic resistance in the food chain from a developing country view, writing in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. Farm animals are a key reservoir of resistant bacteria, fed by heavy antibiotic use in food production, and resistance crosses borders with ease.

The review traces where resistance arises, how bacteria travel from farm to fork, and why levels differ between rich and poor countries. It argues that weak local control can undo strong policies elsewhere, so national plans must join human medicine, animal care, and the environment under one health approach. The authors follow world guidance in urging farm-to-fork steps that keep antibiotics working for future generations.
europmc-pmc5192492:
Yuhai Zhao, Peter N. Alexandrov, Vivian Jaber, Walter J. Lukiw, and George A. Calin report a broken RNA circuit in Alzheimer's disease brain. The circular RNA ciRS-7 carries about 70 binding sites for microRNA-7 and works as a sponge that soaks it up. In healthy brain this keeps miRNA-7 in check. In Alzheimer's neocortex and hippocampus, ciRS-7 levels fall. Free miRNA-7 then rises and suppresses its targets, including the gene for UBE2A.

UBE2A normally helps the ubiquitin-proteasome system clear amyloid peptides. With less of it, amyloid builds up and senile plaques form. The team confirmed the pattern with DNA and miRNA arrays, blotting methods, and an enzyme test specific to circular RNA. They present the ciRS-7, miRNA-7, and UBE2A circuit as another layer of gene control that the disease disrupts, and a possible point of intervention.
europmc-pmc5216692:
Anna V. Kudryavtseva and eleven colleagues reviewed mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in aging and cancer in Oncotarget in 2016. Cancer grows more common with age, yet the molecular links between the two are still unclear. A shared suspect is oxidative stress: reactive oxygen species, or ROS, build up when mitochondria, the cell's energy producers, work badly.

The review compares how oxidative damage looks in aging tissues and in tumours, treating faulty mitochondria as a common trait of both. Mitochondria make ROS during normal work, and ROS in turn attack mitochondrial membranes and DNA, causing still worse function and more ROS. The same chemistry damages nuclear DNA, proteins, and cell membrane fats. The authors lay out this self-feeding loop as one main driver shared by aging, age-related disease, and cancer growth.
europmc-pmc521692:
James W. Varni, Sandra A. Sherman, Tasha M. Burwinkle, Paige E. Dickinson, and Pamela Dixon introduced the PedsQL Family Impact Module in Health and Quality of Life Outcomes in 2004. A child's long-term illness affects the whole household, yet standard quality-of-life tools focused on the child alone. The new questionnaire measures how a child's chronic condition affects parents and family life.

The 36-item module asks parents about their own physical, emotional, social, and thinking function, plus communication and worry, and about daily family activities and relationships. It was given to 23 families of medically fragile children with complex conditions, some living in a long-term care hospital and some at home. Scores were highly consistent, and the module separated the two family groups as expected. The authors present it as a sound first version, to be tested further in other childhood conditions.
europmc-pmc5223492:
Julie Storr and ten colleagues, with the WHO Guidelines Development Group, set out the World Health Organization's core components for infection prevention and control in Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Control in 2017. Infections picked up during health care are among the most common harms in care delivery, driving illness, death, and cost, yet a large share of them can be prevented.

The guideline rests on systematic literature reviews and expert consensus, weighing evidence quality, patient values, costs, and feasibility. It issues eleven recommendations and three good practice statements covering what national programs and acute care hospitals each need in place. Better control at both levels is also central to containing antimicrobial resistance and stopping outbreaks of highly catching diseases. The core ideas apply, with changes, to community, primary, and long-term care settings as well.
europmc-pmc5266792:
Benoit Witkowski and a large team hunted a genetic marker for piperaquine-resistant malaria in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2017. Western Cambodia is the world center of multidrug-resistant Plasmodium falciparum, and failures of the front-line drug pair dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine were climbing. Artemisinin resistance already had a tracking marker in the K13 gene; piperaquine resistance had none.

Whole-genome reading of 31 lab-grown parasite lines tied resistance in the dish to extra copies of the plasmepsin 2 and 3 gene cluster. Copy number also matched survival in fresh patient isolates tested outside the body. In 725 treated patients followed for 42 days, carrying multiple plasmepsin 2 copies before treatment multiplied the risk of failure roughly twenty-fold and predicted failure with high sensitivity. Country-wide samples from 2002 to 2015 showed the marker spreading in step with treatment failures.
europmc-pmc5295692:
Johanna Birkhäuer, Jens Gaab, Joe Kossowsky, Sebastian Hasler, Peter Krummenacher, Christoph Werner, and Heike Gerger pooled the evidence on patient trust and health outcomes in PLoS ONE in 2017. Trust in one's doctor or therapist is treated as a foundation of care, but whether it actually tracks with better health had not been quantified. The authors searched four databases and screened 400 full texts.

Forty-seven studies fed the meta-analysis. Overall, trust correlated with outcomes at r = 0.24. The link was clearest for outcomes patients rated themselves, at 0.30, covering satisfaction, healthier behavior, quality of life, and milder symptoms. For objective measures the correlation was essentially zero, and observer ratings were non-significant too. The authors warn the pooled figures may be biased upward, and that only prospective studies can untangle whether trust improves health, good results breed trust, or both.
europmc-pmc5346692:
Yue-Lun Zhang and co-authors pooled studies of a gene flaw in lung cancer in Oncotarget in 2016. The gene, EGFR, drives growth signals in cells. Flaws in it mark a set of lung tumors that answer to matched drugs. Knowing how common the flaw is, group by group and land by land, guides testing and care.

The team found more than four hundred studies with well over a hundred thousand patients in all. Across the whole set, about a third of patients with non-small-cell lung cancer carried the flaw. Rates ran high in China and low in Europe. Women carried it far more than men, and non-smokers far more than smokers. Tumors of the gland type bore it three times as often as other types. The pooled map gives clinics a firm base for who to test first.
europmc-pmc539292:
Donna M. Wilcock and six co-authors report a 2004 study in the Journal of Neuroinflammation on antibody treatment for Alzheimer's disease in old mice. The mice were bred to build up amyloid, the protein clumps tied to the disease. Most past work treated younger mice. Here the team gave weekly antibody shots to mice at ages near the end of a mouse life span, for up to five months.

Treatment fully reversed learning and memory loss in the oldest mice, and the gain held through the full course. Brain tissue clumps shrank sharply, showing that even old deposits can be cleared. Yet amyloid in blood vessel walls grew, and some spots showed tiny bleeds tied to longer treatment. The authors say human trials would need guards against that risk.
europmc-pmc5442792:
Tao and co-authors pack healing vesicles into a chitosan dressing for diabetic skin wounds. Their research article appeared in Stem Cells Translational Medicine. Chronic wounds heal badly in diabetes. Poor blood flow stalls repair. Stem cells from joint lining boost skin cell growth. They fail, though, to grow new vessels. The team fixed that gap with a small RNA. They made the stem cells overproduce microRNA-126.

Vesicles from the altered cells carried the benefit. In dishes, the vesicles sped growth of skin and vessel cells. They also drove vessel cells to form tubes. The team loaded the vesicles into chitosan dressings. The dressings released them slowly. On full-thickness wounds in diabetic rats, healing sped up. New skin covered the wounds faster. Vessel growth switched on. Collagen matured more fully. The authors frame modified-cell vesicles as a drug delivery system.
europmc-pmc5445292:
Decho and Gutierrez survey the sticky secretions that microbes release throughout the oceans. Their overview appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. The secretions are called extracellular polymeric substances, or EPS. They include sugars, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids. Microbes use them to stick to surfaces. The glue builds biofilm communities. In open water it binds cells into marine snow. That snow drifts down as food for deep life.

EPS shapes many ocean processes at once. It changes how light moves through water and sediment. It helps minerals form and genes pass between cells. Algal blooms pour out excess EPS late in their run. Some of it breaks down fast. Other forms resist decay for long periods. The matrix can ferry pollutants up food chains. It can also shelter harmful microbes. EPS thrives in sea ice, salty pools, and hot vents. The authors call it a basic microbial adaptation.
europmc-pmc5465292:
Jan reviews the tiny bubbles that Gram-negative bacteria shed into their surroundings. His perspective appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. The bubbles are spheres of cell membrane. Making them seems vital for survival. They carry active proteins and toxins as cargo. Harm factors that drive disease ride inside them. Through them, bacteria interact with each other and with hosts.

The bubbles help bacteria adapt to new niches. They blunt attacks from viruses and microbe-killing peptides. They also serve as signals between cells. In hosts, they tune immune responses. Famous toxins, such as Shiga toxin and cholera toxin, travel this route. Sticky proteins on the bubbles help them bind host cells. How bacteria build the bubbles is still not fully known. The rules for choosing cargo are another open gap. The author sees promise for tests and vaccines. That promise grows as antibiotics lose power.
europmc-pmc5468692:
Cunningham, Daszak, and Wood present a review on One Health and new infectious diseases. Their focus is diseases that pass among people, farm animals, and wildlife. Many such diseases start in wild animals. The authors look back over about two decades of work in this field. They ask how much real progress has been made.

The review notes better knowledge of why diseases emerge. Habitat loss and human spread of germs remain key drivers. Yet policy action has stayed weak, the authors say. They argue that joint action for human, animal, and ecosystem health offers the best chance of success. Readers get a clear map of past gains and gaps.
europmc-pmc5544892:
Peretti and co-authors present a review of telerehabilitation. That field delivers rehab care from a distance, using video, sensors, and other devices. It is a branch of telemedicine, and its use has grown fast in richer countries. The authors map where it is used and how.

Remote rehab can cut costs for patients and providers alike. It also serves people who live far from clinics. The review notes a real drawback, though. Some patients doubt care that lacks face-to-face contact. Training for staff and feedback from patients are stressed as needs. Readers get a broad survey of the field's tools, uses, and open problems.
europmc-pmc5588692:
Khan and co-authors report a pilot trial in Critical Care. The drug GSK2586881 is a lab-made form of ACE2, an enzyme tied to lung injury. Patients had acute respiratory distress syndrome, a severe breathing failure. The trial ran in ten intensive care units in North America.

Part A raised the dose step by step inside each patient. It was well tolerated, with no major blood pressure changes. Part B compared twice-daily doses with placebo. It stopped early after 39 of 60 planned patients, on a futility check. The drug cut angiotensin II fast and raised its breakdown products. Oxygen measures and organ scores showed no clear gain. Readers get safety data and proof the drug hit its target.
europmc-pmc5592592:
An 1840 review in The British and Foreign Medical Review greets the first part of Richard Owen's Odontography. Owen's book compares teeth across vertebrate animals. It covers their structure, development, and fine detail under the microscope. Over 150 plates were planned for the full work.

The reviewer singles out two of Owen's findings. Teeth grow from within, by mineral laid down in living tissue, much like bone forms. They are not dead, bloodless add-ons, as earlier authorities held. Owen first saw this in the teeth of an unborn shark. Second, a tooth's minute structure is so steady within each group that a tiny fossil fragment can reveal its owner's class, order, and family. The review saves detail for the finished book. Readers get a period verdict on a landmark of anatomy.
europmc-pmc5598692:
Edward Jenner tells the story of his own discovery in The Medical and Physical Journal, dated May 1801. His inquiry into cowpox began more than twenty-five years earlier. In the country, he met dairy workers he could not infect with smallpox. They had caught cowpox while milking cows with sores on their teats.

Jenner explains two puzzles that slowed him down. Cows suffer several kinds of teat eruption, and dairies called them all cowpox. Only one kind, the true cowpox, protects against smallpox. The others are spurious and give no shield. He also found that cowpox matter can spoil over time. In its worn state it still raises sores but loses its protecting power. Sorting true from spurious cases cleared his path. Readers get the discovery in the discoverer's own words.
europmc-pmc5601792:
Zheng reviews why cancers resist chemotherapy, in Oncotarget. Resistance, whether present from the start or gained later, drives relapse and spread. It remains a chief cause of treatment failure and death. The review maps the molecular tricks behind it.

Drug-pump transporters throw medicines out of cells. Oncogenes like EGFR and PI3K/Akt push growth and block cell death. A broken p53 tumor suppressor does the same. Other routes include faster DNA repair and altered mitochondria. Cells can also recycle their own parts, shift shape, or turn stem-like. Tiny vesicles called exosomes carry resistance signals between cells. These paths cross-talk often, so single blocks may fail. The author argues for matched, combined therapy. Readers get one map of a tangled problem.
europmc-pmc5662692:
Ikram and co-authors present an update in the European Journal of Epidemiology. It describes the Rotterdam Study, a long-running Dutch cohort. The study began in 1990 in one city district. It follows residents for diseases common in later life. Targets range from heart and liver disease to dementia and eye disease. By 2008 the cohort held 14,926 people aged 45 or over.

A new expansion started in 2016 for people aged 40 and up. About 4,000 more participants were expected. Members get home interviews and deep clinic exams. Imaging and stored samples support genetic work. Exams repeat every three to four years. Findings have filled over 1,500 articles and reports.
europmc-pmc5685192:
Tukiainen and co-authors report a genomics survey in Nature. It maps X chromosome inactivation across human tissues. Females silence one of their two X chromosomes. That balances gene dosage against males with one X. Human silencing is known to be incomplete. Many genes still speak from the silent copy. The team mined over 5,500 transcriptomes from 449 people. Samples spanned 29 tissues from the GTEx project. Nearly a thousand single-cell profiles were added.

Silencing proved largely uniform across tissues overall. Still, clear differences appeared between tissues, people, and cells. At least 23 percent of X genes escape inactivation. Seven new escape genes gained strong support. Escape produced sex biases in gene expression. The catalogue updates how incomplete silencing shapes traits.
europmc-pmc5687192:
Barbour and co-authors present a Vital Signs report in MMWR. It updates US estimates for arthritis and its limits on activity. Arthritis is a common and disabling chronic condition. It can cause severe joint pain and poor function. The CDC team analyzed survey data from 2013 to 2015. The National Health Interview Survey covers US civilian adults yearly. It is nationally representative and done in person.

About 54 million adults had doctor-diagnosed arthritis on average. That is close to a quarter of all adults. About 24 million of them reported activity limits from arthritis. The share reporting limits had risen since 2002. Rates ran highest alongside heart disease, diabetes, and obesity.
europmc-pmc5751192:
Ko and co-authors review resveratrol, a plant compound found in grapes and other foods, as a cancer agent. Resveratrol is a polyphenol with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory traits. Lab and population studies link such compounds to lower disease risk. This review gathers the cancer evidence in one place.

The authors cover tests in cells and in animals across many cancer types. Resveratrol can undo drug resistance in cancer cells, they report. Paired with standard chemo, it can make cells more sensitive to treatment. New analogs aim to raise its strength and uptake. Clinical trials to date are summed up as well.
europmc-pmc5753192:
Tacutu and co-authors present the Human Ageing Genomic Resources, a set of databases on ageing. Ageing is still poorly grasped despite growing data. This collection has served ageing genetics for over ten years. The paper sets out its main parts and recent additions.

Six core databases make up the set. GenAge lists ageing genes in humans and model organisms. AnAge covers ageing and lifespan in over 4,000 animal species. Other parts track dietary restriction genes, longevity studies, ageing drugs, and cell senescence genes. All parts are hand curated by experts and updated often. Cross links join the parts to each other and to outside sources.
europmc-pmc5801292:
Liu and co-authors review gastrodin, the main active part of a Chinese herb. The herb, Tian ma, comes from the orchid Gastrodia elata. Healers used it for centuries for headache, dizziness, and seizures. Gastrodin was first isolated in 1978.

The review gathers lab studies on brain and nerve disorders. They cover epilepsy, Alzheimer's, and Parkinson's disease. They also cover stroke damage, mood disorders, and memory loss. Gastrodin seems to calm nerve signals and cut cell stress. The authors note that firm clinical trials are still lacking. Readers get a broad survey of promise and gaps.
europmc-pmc5820392:
Wang reviews neutrophils as both wreckers and repairers of tissue. Neutrophils are the blood's most common white cells. They rush to infection and attack germs fast. That attack was long cast as blind and self-harming.

New work shows a subtler cell. Neutrophils cast web-like traps that snare germs. They come in varied forms with flexible behavior. Beyond fighting, they help wounds close and tissue regrow. They also help keep healthy tissue in balance day to day. Readers get an updated portrait of a cell once dismissed as a simple killer.
europmc-pmc5842392:
Chan and co-authors report a single case where a virus rescued a patient from a stubborn graft infection. Their case report appeared in Evolution, Medicine, and Public Health. Pseudomonas aeruginosa had built a chronic infection on the patient's aortic graft. Antibiotics alone could not clear the biofilm.

The team chose phage OMKO1 with care. The phage attacks the very pump the bacteria use to expel drugs. Any bacterium that evolves phage resistance loses that pump and turns drug-sensitive again. One application of phage plus ceftazidime ended the infection. No return of symptoms followed.
europmc-pmc5857192:
Durski and co-authors report on the emergence of monkeypox in Africa. Their article appeared in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. It covers human cases in West and Central Africa from 1970 to 2017. Monkeypox is an animal-borne virus akin to smallpox. Most past cases occurred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. More countries have reported cases in the past decade than before.

The report draws on a 2017 meeting of WHO, CDC, and health partners. Since 2016, confirmed cases arose in six African countries. Nigeria faced the largest West African outbreak on record. The authors call for better surveillance, lab testing, and infection control. They also flag gaps in knowledge of the virus's ecology.
europmc-pmc5915392:
Kim and co-authors create a silk fibroin bioink for light-based 3D printing. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. Bioprinting lacks inks that are both cell friendly and printable. Their ink, called Sil-MA, starts from silk protein. A chemical step makes it harden under light. That suits digital light processing printers.

The gel showed strong mechanical and flow traits, they report. Changing ink content tuned those traits with ease. Complex shapes printed well, including heart and ear forms. Vessels, brain, and windpipe models also held their shape. Cells stayed compatible with the printed structures. Tissue engineers get a precise, gentle ink option.
europmc-pmc5915792:
Yao and co-authors test manganese oxide nanozymes against inflammation in living mice. Their article appeared in Chemical Science. Harmful reactive oxygen drives many inflammatory diseases. Natural enzymes clear it but are fragile and costly. Artificial nanozymes are tougher and easier to make. Few manganese versions had been tried inside the body.

Their Mn3O4 particles mimicked key antioxidant enzymes, they report. The particles scavenged several reactive oxygen types well. They protected live mice from ear inflammation caused by such species. That is the first in-body proof for this class, they note. Stability and tunable activity add to the appeal. Readers get a candidate tool for inflammatory care.
europmc-pmc5934392:
Oh and a large team of co-authors map the gene and health traits of one type of stomach cancer. Their study was published in Nature Communications. Stomach cancer varies a lot, so drug response is hard to foresee. The team split tumours into two groups by their gene traits. One group has traits of skin-like cells. The other has traits of soft tissue cells.

The soft tissue group had few gene faults, the authors report. Its patients lived less long and shrugged off standard drug care. The skin-like group did better on those drugs. A growth signal path was very busy in the soft tissue group. Blocking that path hit those cells hard. The two groups may guide care choices.
europmc-pmc5986692:
Colyer and co-authors review the evolution of vision-based motion analysis toward a markerless system. Their narrative review appeared in Sports Medicine - Open. Motion study in sport and rehabilitation has advanced for decades. A system that is accurate, quick, and unobtrusive is still missing. Marker-based optical systems dominate current practice. They need markers stuck on the body and controlled settings. Long processing times also limit routine use.

Markerless methods are emerging from entertainment technology, the authors note. Computer vision and machine learning drive the new tools. Some already measure walking angles within two or three degrees. Accuracy across movements and settings is not yet proven. Joint work between fields is needed.
europmc-pmc6023992:
Ferrante and La Grutta assess the burden of asthma in children. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Pediatrics. Asthma is the most common chronic disease of childhood. Rates of symptoms have risen worldwide in recent years. The rise is sharpest in low- and middle-income countries.

Genes, allergy, smoke, and air pollution all play roles. City children suffer more than rural children. The review breaks costs into direct, indirect, and intangible kinds. Hospital stays drive much of the direct cost. Missed school and lost parent workdays add more. Children in poorer countries bear the heaviest toll. Early detection and proper treatment, the authors argue, can cut that burden.
europmc-pmc6043492:
Cheng and co-authors use protein networks to find new drug uses. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. The team measured distance between disease genes and drug targets. Close pairs in the network suggested possible effects. They screened over 900 approved drugs this way.

Hundreds of new drug-disease links emerged from the screen. Four predictions were tested in patient records. Those records covered over 220 million patients. Two predictions held up under careful matching. Carbamazepine was tied to higher heart disease risk. Hydroxychloroquine was tied to lower risk instead. Lab tests supported a calming effect on vessel cells. Readers get a full pipeline from network guess to validation.
europmc-pmc6048292:
Abdalkader and co-authors examine a brain protection factor against ferroptosis. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Ferroptosis is a newer form of regulated cell death. Iron and lipid damage drive it forward. Its signs match features of several brain diseases.

The factor Nrf2 controls hundreds of protective genes. Many of those genes govern glutathione and iron handling. Others affect lipid metabolism and mitochondria. That reach places Nrf2 at a control point for ferroptosis. Direct proof is still limited but supportive. Boosting Nrf2 protects neurons in many disease models. Whether that works by blocking ferroptosis needs more study. Readers get a focused link between two hot research topics.
europmc-pmc6078992:
Lee and co-authors evolve a sharper CRISPR-Cas9 enzyme in bacteria. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Cas9 cuts DNA at guided targets. It also cuts near-matching sites by mistake. Earlier fixes for that flaw often weakened the enzyme.

The team built a selection system inside E. coli. Cells lived only if Cas9 hit its target. They died if it cut a look-alike site. The survivor, Sniper-Cas9, kept full on-target strength. Off-target cuts fell even lower than rival variants. It worked with varied guide lengths too. Delivered as a ready protein complex, it allows DNA-free editing. Readers get a safer editor for future therapy.
europmc-pmc6096492:
Afonine and co-authors describe real-space refinement in the PHENIX software suite. Their article appeared in Acta Crystallographica Section D. Refinement nudges an atomic model until it fits its map. Real-space methods score fit at map points directly. Cryo-EM maps make that approach natural.

The paper explains the program's targets and optimizer. Each map term depends on only a few atoms. That makes local fixes fast and safe. The same code serves crystal maps as well. Examples re-refine published cryo-EM models. Settings and validation receive close care. Readers get a technical guide to a workhorse step in structure building.
europmc-pmc6156492:
Tanaka and co-authors present a research article in Aging Cell on the protein signature of age in human blood plasma. Chronological age is easy to count, but the body ages in ways a birthday does not show. The team asked which blood proteins track age in healthy people.

They measured 1,301 proteins in 240 healthy men and women aged 22 to 93. None had disease, treatment, or physical or mental impairment. In all, 217 proteins were tied to age, most rising with it. One protein, GDF15, showed the strongest link. The findings offer candidate markers for studying healthy aging and the pathways that drive it.
europmc-pmc6185992:
Rowe and co-authors offer a systematic review in The Lancet Global Health on improving health-care provider practices in poorer countries. Weak provider performance is a major barrier to quality care in low- and middle-income countries. Many strategies claim to fix it. This review, called the HCPPR, set out to test them all.

The team searched 52 electronic databases and 58 document inventories for studies from the 1960s to 2016. Only controlled trials and interrupted time series with comparison groups counted. Results are expressed as percentage improvements in correct practice. Strategies ranged from training alone to packages adding supervision, infrastructure, and community support. The review gives policymakers the broadest evidence map yet for this problem.
europmc-pmc6283892:
Peterson and Kaur review how antibiotic resistance genes move from soil bacteria into disease causing ones. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Resistance is not born in hospitals. Soil bacteria that make antibiotics carry genes to protect themselves. Other environmental bacteria carry built in resistance of their own. Those genes pose no threat while they stay put.

Trouble starts when the genes move. They can hop onto plasmids and other mobile elements in new hosts. Human activity then adds pressure that favours resistant strains. The review details self protection in Streptomyces, the main antibiotic producing genus. It traces likely paths from soil to clinic with concrete examples. The authors frame a model of how resistance spreads. That frame can guide steps to slow the flow.
europmc-pmc6288292:
Ferreira and co-authors review how lab conditions can change what mesenchymal stromal cells release. The review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology in 2018. These cells can renew themselves and turn into several cell types. They also calm or stir immune responses. Much of their healing effect comes from the mix of active molecules they secrete. That mix is called the secretome.

The authors explain that the secretome is not fixed. It shifts with the cues around the cells. Growing the cells under set conditions before use can thus tune what they release. The review weighs how such pre-conditioning shapes immune control and tissue repair. It also covers cell-free options, such as conditioned media and tiny vesicles from the cells. Readers get a clear map of ways to boost the secretome for therapy.
europmc-pmc6303992:
Cleland and co-authors test a standard activity questionnaire in older UK adults. Their study appeared in BMC Medical Research Methodology. The questionnaire is the International Physical Activity Questionnaire, or IPAQ. It had not been validated in this group before. Participants wore an activity monitor for seven days. They then filled in the questionnaire.

About 250 adults took part, with a mean age near 72. The questionnaire matched monitor data fairly well for active time. Weekday sitting time also matched well. Weekend sitting matched far less well. Most people under-reported both activity and sitting. The authors favor group-level use over judging one person. Clearer examples could sharpen recall, they suggest.
europmc-pmc6323892:
Rentzsch and co-authors describe updates to CADD, a tool that scores genetic variants. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. CADD predicts how harmful a variant may be. It blends over sixty genome features into one score. A machine learning model does the scoring. Training contrasts new simulated variants with ancient fixed ones.

The newest version supports the GRCh38 genome build. Variant lookup on the website is now simpler. Documentation grew, and an interface for other tools was added. Scores cover single-letter changes across the genome. Short insertions and deletions are scored too. The tool helps labs rank causal variants. It is widely used in severe inherited disease studies.
europmc-pmc6323992:
The UniProt Consortium describes updates to its worldwide protein knowledge hub. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The knowledgebase holds sequences for over 120 million proteins. Expert curators annotated more than half a million in detail. Rule-based systems add notes to the rest. Reference Proteomes grew greatly in two years.

Viral reference sets got special focus this round. The website gained new data displays. Views now show where proteins sit inside cells. Structure and interaction displays were added too. Resources ship under an open CC-BY license. Sister sets cluster sequences by similarity. An archive keeps every known sequence, even outdated ones. The hub serves all branches of life.
europmc-pmc6327992:
Zolghadri and co-authors review substances that block the enzyme tyrosinase. Their review appeared in the Journal of Enzyme Inhibition and Medicinal Chemistry. Tyrosinase drives pigment making in skin and other tissues. It also browns cut fruit, fungi, and vegetables. Blocking it serves several industries at once. Cosmetics use blockers as skin-lightening agents. Food makers use them to stop browning.

The review gathers blockers found over four decades. They come from nature, labs, and mixed sources. Each entry was tested and described in lab studies. Few blockers have yet qualified for clinical use. Demand from medicine and industry keeps rising, though. Better test methods are part of the story. The catalogue helps chemists pick strong candidates to refine.
europmc-pmc6365492:
Cortes and co-authors present a phase II trial report in Leukemia. The trial tested glasdegib, a Hedgehog pathway inhibitor, added to low-dose cytarabine. Patients had newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia or high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome and could not receive intensive chemotherapy.

A total of 132 patients were randomized, two to one, between the combination and cytarabine alone. Median survival was 8.8 months with the combination versus 4.9 months without it. Complete remission reached 17 percent in the combination group, against 2.3 percent for cytarabine alone. Serious side effects were similar in both groups. The authors call the benefit-risk profile favorable for this hard-to-treat group.
europmc-pmc6370592:
Crawford and co-authors present a review in Prostate Cancer and Prostatic Diseases on androgen-targeted therapy for prostate cancer. Blocking testosterone has long been the base treatment for advanced disease. Recent drug approvals and better hormone assays have changed how doctors aim and monitor that blockade.

Modern assays show surgical castration leaves testosterone near 15 ng/dL, far below the old 50 ng/dL cutoff. Trials link levels under 20 ng/dL with longer survival and slower progression.
