New drugs that block androgen signaling push hormone activity close to zero. The authors advise routine testosterone checks alongside PSA tests. They also discuss tailoring dose timing to each patient's risks and lifestyle.
europmc-pmc6429292:
Zhang and co-authors review recent progress with aptamers, short strands of DNA, RNA, or synthetic XNA that fold to grip a chosen target tightly. Labs create them through SELEX, a selection process that fishes the best binders out of vast random pools. Their uses already span basic research, food safety checks, and environmental monitoring.

Newer selection methods get the most attention, followed by applications in biosensing, biotechnology, and medicine, where aptamers serve as diagnostics and as drugs in their own right. Against antibodies they offer faster production, lower cost, and no batch variation. Remaining limits concern targeted delivery and real-time detection, and the closing sections map where developers are pushing next.
europmc-pmc6461692:
Zhang and co-authors build dual-targeting polyprodrug nanoreactors that amplify reactive oxygen species inside cancer cell mitochondria until the cell dies. Cancer cells already run about ten times the oxidant load of normal cells, and roughly 90 percent of it originates in mitochondria. The particles carry chains of the drug camptothecin and home to both tumor cells and their mitochondria.

Mitochondrial oxidants free the first camptothecin, which jams respiration and raises oxidant output further, releasing more drug in a self-feeding loop. The sustained burst overcomes the short life and tiny range of reactive species, the usual weakness of such therapies, and needs no external light. Treated cells showed wrecked mitochondria and apoptosis.
europmc-pmc6558092:
Wu and co-authors review PD-1 blockade, the checkpoint therapy that reshaped cancer care, writing in Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal. PD-1 is a brake on T cells. Tumors exploit it through its partner PD-L1, switching off attacks and shrugging off chemotherapy. Antibodies that block the pair release the brake.

The review explains the pathway's grip on tumor evasion. It then surveys the approved drugs — nivolumab, pembrolizumab and atezolizumab among them — cancer by cancer, from melanoma to Hodgkin lymphoma. Responses can be deep and lasting, but many patients gain nothing, and unleashed immunity can inflame healthy organs. Closing sections weigh what predicts benefit, including the tumor surroundings and the gut microbiome, and how combinations might widen the responder group.
europmc-pmc6678092:
Annesley and Fisher introduce a special issue on mitochondria in health and disease. Their editorial appears in Cells. Mitochondria make most of the cell's respiratory ATP. They carry their own small genome as well. Most mitochondrial proteins still come from nuclear genes. These organelles sit inside core metabolic and signalling networks. Their defects now feature in ageing and many diseases. Cancer and neurodegeneration are prominent examples.

The issue collects twelve publications in total. Nine are reviews and three report original research. Topics span DNA repair inside mitochondria and ROS production. Biogenesis, fission and fusion, and mitophagy also feature. Model organisms recur as a source of insight. The editors frame the collection as a field snapshot.
europmc-pmc6730892:
Petersen and co-authors report racial and ethnic gaps in pregnancy-related deaths in the United States. About 700 women die each year from pregnancy or its complications. The team analyzed federal surveillance data from 2007 to 2016. Deaths were counted per 100,000 live births.

The overall rate was 16.7 deaths per 100,000 births. Black women faced a rate of 40.8, and American Indian and Alaska Native women 29.7. For women aged 30 and older, those rates ran about four to five times the white rate. The gaps persisted over time and across states. Heart conditions, other medical conditions, and infection were leading causes.
europmc-pmc6751792:
Park and co-authors surveyed master protocol trials, a new family of clinical trial designs. A master protocol runs several sub-studies under one roof. Basket trials test one drug across diseases sharing a marker. Umbrella trials test many drugs in one disease. Platform trials can add or drop treatment arms as they go.

The team searched the literature up to July 8, 2019. They found 83 master protocols: 49 basket, 18 umbrella, and 16 platform trials. Most ran in the United States and nearly all tested cancer drugs. Basket trials were mostly early-phase and not randomized. Use has grown fast in five years, despite the designs' clear efficiency gains.
europmc-pmc6785792:
Loktev and co-authors developed fibroblast activation protein-targeted radiotracers with better tumor retention. Cancer-associated fibroblasts fill the stroma of over 90% of epithelial cancers. They overexpress a protein called FAP, which imaging tracers can target. An earlier tracer, FAPI-04, lit up many tumors in patients. It washed out too fast for therapy, though.

The team synthesized new quinoline-based variants. Eleven of 15 bound FAP better than FAPI-04 in cell tests. Seven showed higher tumor uptake in mice. Tumor-to-normal-organ ratios improved for most compounds. The most promising tracers went into PET scans of 8 cancer patients. Longer retention could let doctors deliver higher, more effective radiation doses.
europmc-pmc6803592:
Khellaf and co-authors review recent advances in traumatic brain injury. TBI is the most common cause of death and disability in people under 40 in the United Kingdom. Worldwide, about 50 million cases occur each year. Seatbelts, helmets, and workplace rules have cut severe cases in rich countries. Specialized neuro-intensive care has improved outcomes there.

The update covers three fronts. First, refined intensive care protocols for moderate and severe injury. Second, the evidence for decompressive craniectomy, surgery that relieves pressure by removing part of the skull. Third, new drug therapies. Blood biomarkers get attention too: short-lived proteins track injury windows better than long-lived ones. Future research directions close each section.
europmc-pmc6940392:
Sanchez and co-authors show how gut-made fatty acids tune antibody production. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. When gut microbes ferment dietary fibre, they release short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate and propionate. These compounds already shape T cells and other immune cells. Their direct effect on B cells was less clear.

In mouse and human B cells, low doses modestly raised antibody class switching. Higher doses lowered key genes for switching, mutation, and plasma cell formation. The fatty acids acted by blocking enzymes that remove chemical tags from DNA-packaging proteins. That change raised small RNAs which silence those genes. Gut and body-wide antibody responses fell as a result. In lupus-prone mice, autoantibody production also dropped.
europmc-pmc6996192:
Yan and co-authors write a practical guide to analysing ATAC-seq data, from raw reads to insight. Their review appeared in Genome Biology. ATAC-seq maps which parts of the genome sit open and active. It is now a standard tool in chromatin biology, but no full review of its analysis tools existed.

The guide walks through each major step. Early stages cover quality checks and aligning reads to the genome. Core analysis finds the open peaks. Advanced steps compare peaks between conditions, annotate them, hunt for binding motifs, and read protein footprints and nucleosome positions. The authors also cover rebuilding gene control networks by joining ATAC-seq with other data types. Single-cell ATAC-seq and its special tool needs close the review.
europmc-pmc7023392:
Arneth reviews the tumour microenvironment in the journal Medicina, writing as sole author. A tumour is not just a mass of cancer cells. It sits in a living setting of blood vessels, immune cells, and support cells. Those neighbours help decide whether the tumour grows, spreads, or is held back.

Arneth searched four databases for studies published from 2008 to 2017. Thirty articles were kept for close review. The synthesis names the main parts of the setting. They include fat cells, fibroblasts, tumour vessels, lymphocytes, and dendritic cells. Cancer stem cells also live in this setting. Arneth argues that treating the setting itself, not only the cancer cells, could improve cancer control.
europmc-pmc7066092:
Hufnagl and co-authors review microbiome imbalance in asthma in Seminars in Immunopathology. About 300 million children and adults worldwide live with asthma. The disease grows out of genes and the environment together, and the lung microbiome, shaped at birth and in early life, sits in the middle of that process. A healthy lung community is dominated by Bacteroidetes, Actinobacteria, and Firmicutes.

Viral infections shift that community toward Proteobacteria such as Haemophilus and Moraxella, a dysbiosis that fires up inflammation and narrows the airways. Farm settings protect the microbiota; allergens and air pollution harm it. Gut microbes matter too: antibiotics and acid-blocking drugs damage both gut and lung communities, upsetting the two-way talk along the gut-lung axis and raising sensitivity to allergens. Work to rebuild balance with probiotics and engineered bacteria is under way, though human studies do not yet confirm they prevent asthma.
europmc-pmc7067892:
Jensen and Teng ask whether laboratories should move from flat to three-dimensional cell culture in Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences. Cell culture underpins drug discovery, cancer research, and stem cell study, and most of it still grows cells on flat plastic. Three-dimensional methods let researchers shape the cell's surroundings to mimic the body, yielding richer data on cell interactions, tumour behaviour, and drug responses.

The review compares the two approaches and details the main 3D techniques. Scaffold-based options include hydrogels, hard polymer supports, glass fibre, and organoids. Scaffold-free options include hanging drop plates, magnetic levitation, and low-attachment spheroid plates. Each carries its own advantages and uses. Organoids in particular promise a way to study whole-organ behaviour in a dish. The authors expect 3D culture to bridge the wide gap between flat cultures and animal models, while noting the transition is still under way.
europmc-pmc7164392:
Gao and co-authors solve the structure of the COVID-19 virus's RNA-copying enzyme, in Science. The polymerase, called nsp12, builds new viral RNA and is central to the virus's replication cycle. Working with its two helper proteins, nsp7 and nsp8, they imaged the complex by cryo-electron microscopy at 2.9 angstrom resolution.

Nsp12 is the target of nucleotide-analog antivirals such as remdesivir, which mimic RNA building blocks. Seeing its exact shape, including a newly resolved front section that stabilises the whole complex, gives drug designers a template. The authors present the structure as a basis for designing improved antivirals against this virus and its relatives.
europmc-pmc7176892:
Davis and co-authors describe the mental health questionnaire built for UK Biobank. Their reanalysis appeared in BJPsych Open. UK Biobank follows over 500,000 participants with genetic, lifestyle, and imaging data. An expert group designed an online questionnaire to add mental health depth. A patient group helped shape the questions.

In all, 157,366 participants completed the questionnaire. The team set clear rules for spotting likely lifetime depression and mania. They also defined generalised anxiety disorder, unusual experiences, and self-harm. Results show what such a large volunteer cohort can reveal about mental illness. The resource lets other researchers link mental health to genes and brain scans. It also shows the limits of self-reported answers in a healthy volunteer group.
europmc-pmc7202792:
Li and Ma ask whether the breathing failure of COVID-19 matches typical acute respiratory distress syndrome. Their article appeared in Critical Care. COVID-19 can end in fatal ARDS, a severe lung failure syndrome. Knowing how the COVID form differs should sharpen early recognition and treatment. The authors set out its features one by one.

In COVID-related ARDS, damage centers on the lung's air sac lining cells. The blood vessel lining suffers less, so fluid leakage is milder. Some patients show fairly gentle symptoms despite meeting full ARDS criteria. Their lung stiffness can also look near normal while oxygen levels run dangerously low. That mismatch breaks the usual ARDS pattern. The authors argue treatment should respect these differences.
europmc-pmc7216192:
Ahmed and co-authors survey dentists about fear and practice changes during the COVID-19 outbreak. Their study appeared in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Dentists work inches from patients' mouths, a high-risk position. The online survey ran from March 10 to 17, 2020. It measured anxiety about infection and knowledge of new safety steps.

Most dentists reported real fear of catching the virus at work. Eighty percent knew which authority to contact over a suspected case. Hand hygiene before and after patients was widely reported. Knowledge of practice modifications varied across respondents. The authors stress training and clear protocols for dental settings. Their snapshot captures a profession adapting under pressure in the pandemic's first weeks.
europmc-pmc7223792:
Salje and co-authors estimate the true burden of SARS-CoV-2 in France during the first wave. Their study appeared in Science. The team fitted transmission models to hospital admission data. France had taken a heavy toll in March and April 2020. Lockdown cut transmission sharply, by 84 percent on their estimate.

They forecast 2.9 million infections by May 11, 2020. That is 4.4 percent of the population, far below herd immunity. Before lockdown, each case generated about 2.9 new cases on average. Daily critical care admissions were set to fall from hundreds to tens. Even so, the authors warn that control stays a delicate balancing act. Any easing of restrictions would need careful monitoring. The study informed France's exit from its first lockdown.
europmc-pmc7262592:
Murray Brunt and co-authors report five-year results from FAST-Forward, a large trial of shorter radiotherapy after breast cancer surgery. Their report appeared in The Lancet. The trial asked whether treatment in 1 week could match the standard 3-week course for early breast cancer. It ran at 97 hospitals in the United Kingdom.

A total of 4096 patients were assigned to 40 Gy in 15 fractions over 3 weeks, or to 27 Gy or 26 Gy in five fractions over 1 week. At a median follow-up of 71.5 months, the five-fraction schedules controlled local cancer as planned, within the preset non-inferiority limit. Clinicians, patients, and photographs were all used to judge late effects on normal tissue. A one-week course, if safe, eases travel and cost burdens for patients.
europmc-pmc7290392:
Laronha and Caldeira review human matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes that cut apart the extracellular matrix. Their review appeared in Cells. Collagen, the matrix's most abundant protein, forms tough triple helices that resist almost all protein-cutting enzymes. Only these metalloproteinases can degrade it, so their activity decides how the matrix is remodeled.

The body keeps the enzymes on a tight leash with its own inhibitors, called TIMPs. When that control slips, diseases follow, from tissue destruction to abnormal growth. The authors explain the structure of the enzyme family, how each member works, and how inhibitors restrain them. Their account shows why these enzymes are both essential maintenance tools and attractive, difficult drug targets.
europmc-pmc7324092:
Whitelaw and co-authors set out a framework for using digital technology across every stage of pandemic response. Their viewpoint appeared in The Lancet Digital Health. With no vaccine or effective therapy available, countries depended on containment and mitigation, with very uneven success. Those keeping deaths low shared early surveillance, testing, contact tracing, and strict quarantine.

Running those strategies at national scale requires coordination and data management that manual methods cannot deliver, and successful countries leaned on digital tools integrated into policy and health care. South Korea, for example, kept deaths near 0.5 per 100,000 people, while the United States sustained ten times as many per capita. The authors map digital applications for planning, surveillance, testing, tracing, quarantine, and care.
europmc-pmc7355792:
Dhuri and co-authors present a review in the Journal of Clinical Medicine on antisense drugs. These short strands bind to a chosen RNA and change how much protein a cell makes. The review covers how they work and how the field has grown. Drug delivery is a major theme.

The authors sort the drugs by chemical design and by mode of action. Chemical tweaks help them last longer and cut side effects. Delivery methods aim to get more of the drug into the right cells. The review lists drugs approved by US and European regulators. It also covers candidates now in clinical trials. MicroRNA targets get a look as a future path. Readers get a full tour of a fast-growing drug class.
europmc-pmc7406792:
De Cicco and co-authors review myeloid-derived suppressor cells as a target in cancer immunotherapy, in Frontiers in Immunology. These immature immune cells are the tumor neighborhood's main suppressors, damping T cell attacks and helping cancers invade, grow blood vessels, and spread. In patients, their blood levels track tumor burden, stage, and poor prognosis.

That makes them the major obstacle to many immunotherapies, and a tempting target. The catch is variety: the cells differ by tumor, in both form and method, so identifying them in human cancer is hard. The review argues that careful characterization per tumor type must come before targeting pays off. Readers get a clear statement of a bottleneck, and of the strategies gathering against it.
europmc-pmc7484992:
Bianchi and Mezzapelle review the chemokine receptor CXCR4 in cell growth and tissue repair. When ligands bind CXCR4, signals guide cell movement and blood cell making. The receptor also keeps stem cells in the bone marrow.

CXCR4 directly controls growth of cells outside the blood system too. New reports give it a central role in tissue regeneration and stem cell activation. The same paths help tumors grow, since repair often replays growth programs from development. Movement and growth seem to flow from shared signals below the receptor. The authors map these paths and their links. Deeper knowledge, they argue, is needed to repair organs safely with this system. The review weighs promise against cancer risk.
europmc-pmc7514392:
Shreffler, Petrey, and Huecker review how COVID-19 affected healthcare worker wellness. Frontline staff faced infection risk, shifting plans, and heavy loads. Their psychological burden drew wide notice in news and research.

The scoping review searched studies from April 6 to May 17, 2020. It included 37 studies with original data on provider wellness. Reports of stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms were consistent across the studies. The review also gathers what is known on distress and burnout in these workers. Hard data on what helps remain thin, the authors note. They urge research on steps that protect staff well-being. Health systems need such proof before the next crisis hits their workforce at full force.
europmc-pmc7589192:
Kaszak and co-authors review the role of cadherins in cancer. Cadherins hold cells together in healthy tissues. They guide embryo growth, tissue shaping and cell sorting.

Cadherins join with catenins to form adhesion complexes. Faults in these complexes can drive tumor progression. Loss of E-cadherin marks a shift in tumor cells. That shift helps cells move and invade tissue. Nuclear beta-catenin and p120 signals also matter here. Other pathways affect cadherin adhesion during tumor growth. They include growth receptor, Rho and Hippo signals. The review covers human and animal cancers. Cadherin-targeting drugs may limit malignant tumor spread, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc7643892:
Zambrano and co-authors update data on women with COVID-19 by pregnancy status in the United States. Their report covers January 22 to October 3 in national case data. Pregnant women may face a higher risk of severe illness from the virus.

Reports covered 1,300,938 women aged fifteen to forty-four with confirmed infection. Pregnancy status was known for 461,825 of them. Among women with symptoms, 23,434 were reported to be pregnant at the time. After changes for age, race and health conditions, pregnant women faced more risk. Intensive care admission was ten point five versus three point nine per thousand cases. Use of a breathing machine and of ECMO support were also higher in pregnancy. Death was one point five versus one point two per thousand cases in the groups. The true risks for each woman stayed low, but the group gap was clear.
europmc-pmc7671692:
Ilik and co-authors identify the core proteins that build nuclear speckles. Speckles are dense spots in the cell nucleus, rich in RNA-processing factors. Their job is unclear, in part since no one knew what holds them together. A common marker antibody for speckles guided the search.

The team found that the antibody in fact targets SRRM2, a splicing-linked protein. Removing SON alone only partly broke speckles apart. Removing both SON and SRRM2 made speckles nearly vanish. The pair thus forms the speckle core. This gives researchers a handle to test what speckles do in health and stress.
europmc-pmc7782692:
Murphy and co-authors study the psychology of COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy in Ireland and the United Kingdom. They used nationally representative surveys of adults in both countries. The Irish sample held 1,041 people and the UK sample 2,025.

Hesitancy or resistance appeared in 35% of the Irish sample. The UK figure was 31%. Hesitant respondents differed from accepting ones on some social and health traits. Across many psychological measures, though, the two groups looked alike. Resistant respondents used traditional news sources less for pandemic news. They also trusted those sources less. The authors note the method can transfer to other countries. They caution that these two similar populations limit wider claims.
europmc-pmc7857392:
Röltgen and co-authors define how antibody responses to SARS-CoV-2 vary and how long they last. Blood tests can reveal past infection. Response shape may track how sick a patient gets. The team studied patients across the severity range.

Severe illness matched a more focused antibody response. The mix of antibody targets differed by outcome. In most patients, antibody levels fell over time. That fall does not by itself prove lost protection. Memory cells may still stand guard. The authors set out which response traits matter most. Their map helps judge test results and vaccine follow-up.
europmc-pmc7935892:
Aguilera and co-authors report an observational study of wildfire smoke and breathing health in Southern California. Wildfires are growing more frequent and destructive as the climate changes. Their smoke carries fine particles, PM2.5, that harm the lungs. Rules on air quality treat such particles as equally toxic from all sources. The team tested whether that assumption holds.

They used statistical methods to separate wildfire particles from particles of other sources. A rise of 10 units in wildfire particles lifted respiratory hospital visits by 1.3 to 10%. The same rise in other particles lifted visits far less. The gap suggests wildfire smoke is the more toxic of the two. The authors urge air policy to weigh the source of particles, not just their amount. Their evidence comes from real hospital records across the region.
europmc-pmc8027892:
Aggarwal and co-authors weigh how accurately deep learning finds disease in medical images. They searched Medline and EMBASE up to January 2020. From 11,921 studies, 503 met the bar for their systematic review. Meta-analysis covered ophthalmology, breast disease, and respiratory disease. The other specialties got a qualitative review.

In eye imaging, accuracy scores ran from 0.933 to a perfect 1. Those covered diabetic retinopathy, macular degeneration, and glaucoma. Lung imaging scores ranged from 0.864 up to 0.937 for nodules and cancer. Breast imaging fell from 0.868 up to 0.909 across mammogram, ultrasound, MRI, and tomosynthesis studies. But methods varied wildly between studies. That spread can inflate the apparent accuracy. The authors call for AI-specific reporting rules, built on the STARD guidelines, without delay.
europmc-pmc8080692:
Lee and co-authors survey single-cell multiomics, the craft of reading several molecule types from one cell. New isolation and barcoding tools made the field possible. Bulk multiomics had already shown the gain from joining data layers. Single-cell versions add cell-by-cell resolution to that gain. Gene control can then be tied to the exact cell type using it.

The review splits the field in two halves. The first covers the bench tools that capture the molecules. Pairings include mRNA with genome, with DNA methylation, with open chromatin, and with protein. Each pairing needs its own capture trick. The second half covers the math that fuses the layers. Integration methods sort cells into types and states. Disease processes come into focus through those molecular signatures.
europmc-pmc8091792:
Tan and co-authors review pyroptosis as a fresh way to fight cancer. Pyroptosis is an inflammatory cell death set off by infection signals. Inflammasomes wake, and the cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 mature. Gasdermin proteins then punch pores in the cell membrane. The cell spills its contents and dies loudly. That noise can rally the immune system.

In tumors, such death does double duty. It kills cancer cells and calls in anti-tumor immunity. Chemotherapy, radiation, and targeted and immune drugs can all trigger it. The review explains the controls on the pathway in detail. It then shows how pyroptosis reshapes the tumor's surroundings. The flip side gets fair weight too. When normal cells die this way, treatment side effects follow. Harnessing the fire without burns is the goal.
europmc-pmc8212592:
Campbell and co-authors estimate how much faster the SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern spread around the world. They used sequence data from the GISAID sharing platform across many countries. The new variants replaced older lineages with striking speed almost everywhere they landed.

Estimated transmissibility rose 29% for the Alpha variant and 25% for the Beta variant. It rose 38% for the Gamma variant and 97% for the Delta variant. Country-level reproduction numbers tracked each takeover as it happened. The analysis was current as at June 2021. It gave health agencies hard numbers for planning and showed why variant watch systems matter.
europmc-pmc8339292:
Győrffy scans the whole transcriptome for breast cancer markers with the strongest survival power. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women. Two markers, ER alpha and HER2, now guide systemic therapy.

They define the main molecular subtypes doctors treat. The study ran survival analysis across every gene's expression. Kaplan-Meier curves tested each candidate marker. Chemotherapy response entered the weighing as well. The aim was rank, not just significance. Markers with the highest prognostic power rose to the top. Clinicians gain a sharper shortlist for testing and care. Molecular subtype frames how each marker should be read.
europmc-pmc8546092:
Xiong and co-authors review new display technology for augmented and virtual reality. Fast communication and computing push AR and VR toward the next display platform. Near-eye modules must match human vision while staying small and light. That demand strains classic optics hard.

Holographic optical elements and lithography-built devices offer fresh ways through. Volume holograms select strongly by wavelength and angle. Liquid crystal versions switch with polarization and can turn active. Micro-LEDs and metasurfaces widen design freedom further. The review explains how each device works. It then shows how they lift headset performance in leading designs. Future paths close the survey.
europmc-pmc8617292:
Friedman and Robbins examine the role of the prefrontal cortex in cognitive control and executive function. These terms cover goal-led thought, as opposed to habit and reflex action. The authors ask how the ideas fit together and what brain systems support them. They draw on tests, brain scans, and lesion studies across species.

Test data point to one shared control trait plus two narrower ones. The narrower ones involve shifting mental sets and updating working memory. Shared control links closely to response inhibition, but not to general intelligence. The review also covers drive, mood, and mental illness. Faults in control may help explain symptoms across many disorders.
europmc-pmc8725892:
Zhang and co-authors test how far the Omicron variant escapes immunity from past SARS-CoV-2 infection. The team built a lab-made pseudotype of the variant. They then tested blood from 28 patients who had recovered from the original strain. Other variants of concern and interest were tested for comparison.

Blood strength against Omicron fell about 8.4-fold versus the reference strain. Other variants fell only 1.2 to 4.5-fold. The mean blocking level for Omicron dropped to 66, from 556 for the reference. The authors warn that Omicron may dodge protection from past infection. It may also reduce the cover given by current vaccines.
europmc-pmc8807692:
Mei and co-authors update what is known about the causes of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a lethal scarring lung disease. The disease strikes mainly middle-aged and older adults. Its burden should grow as life expectancy rises. The exact mechanism is still unknown, but the last decade brought real progress.

The current model starts with repeated injury to lung surface cells. That injury switches on fibroblasts, which turn into scar-forming cells. These cells lay down excess matrix and distort the lung's air sacs. Lung function then falls for good. Two drugs slow this decline but do not cure it. The review highlights new therapy strategies in development.
europmc-pmc8816392:
Korstjens and Moser close a four-part guide to qualitative research in primary care. The guide speaks to new researchers and to seasoned quantitative researchers trying qualitative work for the first time. This last part takes up two themes. One is trustworthiness, meaning how readers can judge a study's quality. The other is publishing, meaning how such work gets written and accepted.

The authors name four quality criteria: credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability. They stress reflexivity as part of honest reporting. They also note that writing a qualitative article is itself part of the analysis. Data work continues while the text takes shape. Practical advice covers journal editors and the cover letter. The piece gives novices a clear standard to aim for.
europmc-pmc9095492:
Brown and co-authors report that a gain-of-function change in the TLR7 gene causes human lupus. TLR7 is a sensor that detects viral RNA inside cells. The team found a new missense variant, TLR7 Y264H, in a child with severe lupus. More variants turned up in other patients with the disease.

Tests showed the variant made TLR7 react more strongly to guanosine. When put into mice, it was enough to cause lupus-like disease. The authors trace the harm to poor survival control of certain B cells. Blocking a partner protein, MyD88, rescued the mice from these effects. The findings point to TLR7 and MyD88 as drug targets for lupus care.
europmc-pmc9132392:
Castanares-Zapatero and co-authors comprehensively review how long COVID may arise and persist. Long COVID means symptoms that last long after the acute infection ends. It can follow mild or severe first illness alike. Its cause remains unclear despite nearly two years of study at the time.

The team searched 11 databases and included 98 articles. Of those, 54 put forward theories, while 44 studied patients directly. Long-term organ damage from the acute phase likely explains some symptoms. Other proposed drivers include immune dysregulation, autoimmunity, vessel lining harm, hidden virus, and clotting activation. Nerve damage may explain symptoms with no clear organ harm. The authors stress that studies differ widely and proof is still thin.
europmc-pmc9299092:
Lv and co-authors review how immunotherapy reshapes the tumor immune microenvironment. That setting holds tumor cells, immune cells, and signals that fight or favor growth. Tumors dodge attack by building a suppressive local climate. Immunotherapy aims to remodel that climate and restore killing by T cells.

The review first sorts immune cells into anti-tumor and pro-tumor camps. It then shows how each main therapy type shifts the balance. Checkpoint blockade frees stalled T cells. Macrophage reprogramming cuts suppressive cell numbers. Dendritic cell vaccines restart antigen display. Tracking these shifts should guide smarter drug combinations. The authors stress that local immune change, not the drug alone, decides success.
europmc-pmc9513992:
Wu and co-authors flag myeloid-derived suppressor cells as a rising target for cancer immunotherapy. Checkpoint drugs help many patients, but many more gain nothing. Resistance and relapse often trace to suppressive cells in the tumor setting. These immature myeloid cells are a chief part of that network.

The cells blunt T cell activity with strong effect. The review sorts them by type and suppressive trick. Arginase and reactive oxygen species are key tools they use. Cross talk with other myeloid cells gets close review. The cells also shift form, which adds to their threat. Therapy plans aim at the cells in four ways. Teams can deplete them or force them to mature. Teams can block their suppressive work or their buildup. The authors argue such plans could lift immunotherapy results.
europmc-pmc9753292:
Alonge and co-authors present RagTag, a toolset that automates genome assembly scaffolding and patching. Crop genetics needs fast genetic systems on good assemblies. Pan-genomes show wide crop variety now on record. Studying trait effects still needs solid genotype references.

RagTag orders and patches draft pieces against a guide genome. The team built chromosome scale genomes for tomato M82. M82 is a widely used lab and field genotype. They also bred a new fast-cycling line for editing work. Sweet-100 cycles fast to speed editing tests in tomato. Its genome joins M82 as a fresh reference pair. The pair supports high-throughput genome editing tests. The authors lay out how to spread such systems fast. Other plant species can copy the same path. Better local references cut bias in crop gene studies.
europmc-pmc9825492:
Richardson and co-authors report MGnify in 2023, the microbiome sequence analysis and archive resource. The platform assembles and annotates microbiome DNA and RNA. It archives the source data for later reuse. Nearly half a million analyses sit in the system now.

They span marker gene, RNA, and genome based studies. Samples come from a wide range of environments. The protein database passed two billion distinct sequences. Those proteins are now held in a relational store. Users can trace each protein back to its assembly. Sample details ride along with that trace path. Deep learning methods added fresh annotation layers. Support for long read sequences was built in. The website and its data interface were upgraded. A notebook server now allows downstream work in place. The authors aim to keep pace with biome sampling growth.
europmc-pmc9825592:
Terlouw and co-authors present the third MIBiG release, a community effort to annotate biosynthetic gene clusters. Gene clusters build nature's drug like compounds in microbes and plants. Genome mining hunts those clusters for new medicines. A shared standard makes cluster records comparable worldwide.

The standard and database both date back to 2015. This release rechecked and re-annotated the older entries. It added 661 new cluster entries to the store. Compound structures got special care in the pass. Biological activities of the products were annotated too. Protein domain choices within clusters were refined. Crowd curation drives much of the entry work. Mass online annotathons powered the validation drive. The data are free for all users to take. The authors pitch the set as training gold. Learning models can learn cluster to compound rules from it.
europmc-pmc9954192:
Fock and Parnova set out how gut-derived short-chain fatty acids protect the blood-brain barrier. Barrier damage links to neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, and aging disorders. Short-chain fatty acids come from bacterial fermentation of dietary fiber in the gut. The main ones are acetate, butyrate, and propionate.

These acids help keep the barrier sealed under disease conditions. They lower leakiness by restoring junction proteins between brain vessel cells. The review covers receptor-mediated effects of the acids. It also covers histone changes from blocked histone deacetylases. Crosstalk with NF-κB and Nrf2 factors gets close attention. Direct and indirect routes to barrier repair are both weighed. The work ties gut signals to brain vessel health.
eusebius-the-church-history-of-eusebius-:
Around the year 325, Eusebius of Caesarea wrote the first full history of the Christian Church. His Church History traces the faith from the apostles, through waves of persecution, to the triumph under Constantine. The 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, second series, carries the work.

Eusebius preserves letters, decrees, and traditions that would otherwise be lost forever. Bishops, martyrs, and heretics move through his pages in careful order. Later ages named him the father of church history, and the title sticks. Any reader who wants Christianity's first three centuries has to start with his indispensable record.
eusebius-the-life-of-constantine-npnf2-1:
Eusebius knew the first Christian emperor and wrote his Life of Constantine as both history and praise. Conversion, a vision of the cross, the Council of Nicaea, and new laws favoring the Church fill its pages. The biography appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Imperial letters and edicts quoted at length give the book lasting value beyond its flattery. Eusebius plainly idealizes his subject, and readers should keep that in mind. Even so, no other source tells us so much about the man who changed the Church's fate. Scholars still argue over where the record ends and the panegyric begins.
eusebius-the-martyrs-of-palestine-npnf2-:
Eusebius lived through the Great Persecution and knew many of its victims by name. The Martyrs of Palestine records the Christians of his own region who died under Diocletian. The account appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Year by year he lists their trials, tortures, courage, and final words. Some were friends; others he watched suffer in prison or the mines. The writing stays plain, which gives its witness extra weight. Historians treat the book as the most reliable record we have of what that persecution actually cost ordinary believers. It stands close to the events in a way later martyr tales rarely manage to do.
eusebius-the-oration-of-eusebius-in-prai:
On the thirtieth anniversary of Constantine's reign, Eusebius delivered a formal speech in the emperor's praise. The Oration of Eusebius in Praise of Constantine is preserved in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Ceremony and theology blend in every paragraph.

Out of the praise grows a whole political idea: one emperor on earth mirrors the one God in heaven. Empire and monotheism, for Eusebius, fit each other by design. Later Christian rulers inherited that way of thinking for a thousand years. The speech also stands as a polished piece of ancient rhetoric in praise of power.
famous-affinities-of-history-the-romance:
Volume four of Lyndon Orr's Famous Affinities of History turns from courts to men and women of letters. Dean Swift and the two Esthers open the book. Orr calls Swift's relations with Stella and Vanessa one of the most puzzling cases in the annals of love. No definite explanation, he admits, has ever been given.

Shelley and Mary Godwin follow, then the Carlyles and the Hugos in their stormy marriages. George Sand receives her own story of famous attachments. The mystery of Charles Dickens hints at a hidden devotion. Balzac and Evelina Hanska, loved across decades of letters, precede Charles Reade and Laura Seymour. Orr ends his four-volume survey with writers, whose romances he treats as keys to their books. Devotion, genius, and damage mingle here.
fitzpatrick-secret-service-under-pitt-18:
Fitzpatrick lays bare the spy system of Pitt's age in Secret Service under Pitt, printed in 1892. William John Fitzpatrick was known for his work on Irish biography and the papers of Daniel O'Connell. His subject here is the web of paid informers and secret agents that the British state ran in the years of the French Revolution, above all in Ireland.

The sampled pages turn to London in riot. A mob attacked a great gaol at a cost the text puts at 150,000 pounds, and its gates fell like frail partitions. Five hundred felons, some freed from Clerkenwell, were loosed on the burning city. The writer calls it a second 1666, and says the fall of the Bastille, nine years later, was its mere echo. Fitzpatrick writes history as exposure: the hidden hand behind the politics of the day.
fontane-jenny-treibel-1892:
Frau Jenny Treibel, Theodor Fontane's novel of 1892, is given here in the German original. No English translation of the book is in the public domain. Jenny Treibel, a grocer's daughter who married a rich manufacturer, rules Berlin dinner parties with sentiment and steel.

She sighs over youthful love poems while steering her family toward money and rank. Her son's wish to marry a professor's daughter tests her fine feelings against her plans. Fontane draws her with amused precision, never with open scorn. The comedy shows how feeling itself can become a social tool. Many judge it the subtlest German society novel of its century.
freeman-jane-field-1892:
Jane Field appeared from Harper with pictures, signed by Mary Wilkins. Chapter one settles readers in Amanda Pratt's cottage, raised on banks above the road. Great pink-lined shells flank the doorstep, and smaller shells line the path.

Amanda rents half her house to Mrs. Jane Field, the widow at the story's heart. Two old neighbors sit at the front windows over needlework as the tale begins. Jane, poor and proud, fights to keep her dignity and her daughter in a judging world. Freeman writes with pity for her heroine and no mercy for smug folk who fail her, in one of her best novels.
frus-1861-d192:
John Appleton, the outgoing American minister to Russia, wrote to Secretary of State Jeremiah Black on 31 December 1860. The letter is document 192 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Appleton wrote on the last day of 1860, as the Union came apart. South Carolina had left eleven days before, and more states would follow. His New Year's Eve page from Russia closes the old year of the file in a somber key. The somber close of 1860 in this letter opens the volume's tale on a true note. A true note at the start sets the key for all the music that follows.
frus-1861-d292:
Dated 30 July 1861, a report from Mr. Harvey went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 292 in the President's message volume for 1861. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d92:
From Washington on 23 October 1861, William H. Seward sent a further letter to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 92 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two letters in two days close the October run to London in this file. Within weeks, the Trent affair would throw the whole tie with Britain into crisis. These calm late October pages stand just before that storm, a baseline of order before the shock. The Trent storm, when it came, would test this calm routine to its limit. The calm routine he kept would be the very thing the crisis broke against.
frus-1862-d192:
Filed after later letters, Document 192 is a report dated 6 November 1862 from Charles Francis Adams in London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister to Britain, reporting on his post.

Adams wrote this report in the very days when the British cabinet debated the French call for a joint truce proposal. What he sent home shaped Washington's sense of how the debate would end. The printers placed his letter among mid-November papers, so date and position part ways; the text belongs to the crisis week itself. The State Department printed the London mail in full for Congress, enclosures and all.
frus-1862-d292:
A Dayton report dated 28 June 1862 stands as Document 292 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Dayton wrote in the middle of the Seven Days, though word of the fighting had not yet crossed the ocean. His letter thus reflects the older picture, of a Union army at Richmond's gates. The gap between the Paris view and the Virginia facts is the story of Civil War diplomacy in miniature. And papers like this one document it exactly. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d392:
Simon Cameron reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 September 1862, in a letter printed as Document 392 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Cameron served as American minister in Russia.

Cameron wrote a week before Antietam, in a capital where the American war was watched with sympathy but from afar. His report is among the last of his term; he left the post that fall. The letter belongs to the Russian file's closing stretch for 1862, written as the war's decisive autumn opened in Maryland. Prince Gorchakov, Russia's foreign minister, made his government's sympathy for the Union plain.
frus-1862-d492:
On 2 April 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Shepherd Pike at The Hague, the same day Pike was writing to him. The instruction is Document 492 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Letters crossing in the mail were the normal condition of Atlantic diplomacy, since a round trip took a month or more. Seward's April order to The Hague carried the government's line on the war's progress. It also stated the neutral duties the Union expected of Dutch ports. Those ports lay at home and in the West Indies. Reading the crossed letters side by side shows the lag at the heart of Civil War foreign policy. Each side answered news that was already old.
frus-1862-d592:
Thomas Corwin reported from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 June 1862. The dispatch is Document 592 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

Corwin wrote in the early summer of the French invasion. The republic's forces were falling back. Its government was appealing for American help it would not get in arms. His reports mixed hard fact with open sympathy, and Washington valued both. They told Seward what Mexico faced and what Mexico hoped from the United States. The June letter is one of the file's steady middle pieces. It keeps the record complete between the spring crisis and the autumn. That autumn, French plans for a Mexican empire began to take visible shape.
frus-1862-d692: A letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to a Mr. McMath is dated 28 April 1862. It is document 692 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, printed among the letters that follow the Egypt file. The record names the writer, the man addressed, and the date, but it does not give McMath's post or the letter's subject.
frus-1862-d92:
Writing from Washington on 7 July 1862, William H. Seward addressed Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 92 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d192:
On 7 May 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 192 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Mail crossed the Atlantic by steamship, taking roughly ten days or more each way. News in a dispatch like this one was already old when Seward read it, yet it guided his next orders. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d292:
Reports like this one carried London news to Washington. This one went from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 17 September 1863, and it is document 292 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Read in sequence, these reports show a diplomat testing how far he could push a stronger power without provoking a second war. That balance was the heart of Adams's whole mission. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d392:
On 17 February 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 392 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

British ships stopped by the Union blockade, and British subjects held as prisoners, supplied much of London's complaint list. Lyons delivered those protests in formal notes like this one. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d492:
Under the date 6 May 1863, the record holds a letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d592:
Secretary of State William H. Seward directed a letter to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington on 22 July 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d692:
On 11 November 1863, Lord Lyons wrote from Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Lyons served as Britain's minister to the United States. His letter is document 692 in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

British notes in this series give the other half of the story. Lyons spoke for a government that traded with both sides yet chose to stay neutral. He had to press British claims while keeping ties with the Union intact. This letter shows that press in his own words. Read against Seward's notes of the same week, it lets a reader weigh how each side framed the same hard issues.
frus-1863p1-d92:
Three days of writing to London closed with this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, dated 26 February 1863. Adams was the American minister there, and Adams letters of the same date follow in the volume. The letter is document 92 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Three letters in three days from Washington matched three from London in the same stretch. The exchange ran at full heat in late February 1863. Seward's closing sheet of the run sums up the rhythm: write, send, and write again, since each steamer might carry news that changed the brief. This letter is that third stroke of the pen.
frus-1892:
Turkey takes the longest run in the 1892 volume. Venezuela and Spain follow close behind. Russia files at unusual length this year. Britain's legation correspondence outweighs its main file. The mid-volume letters turn to Canada and canals. Foster warns that Canadian toll discrimination cannot stand. If it continues this season, he writes, America must impose matching tolls. Talks can then proceed on equal terms.

Chile shrinks back to a normal section. China holds its steady size. Italy's file stays at legation level. Haiti and Hawaii shrink to a few papers. The volume's center sits in the Near East and the Caribbean. Tolls, canals, and claims supply its friction. It is a quieter book than its predecessor.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d192:
Prime Minister Churchill telegraphed President Roosevelt on 6 November 1943, in message number 493, about one phrase in Roosevelt's telegram 407 on Turkey. That message had said no forces needed for Overlord or Italy would go to the eastern Mediterranean, judging by what the commanders responsible thought.

The British Chiefs of Staff objected to that wording. In their view, handing out forces among Overlord, Italy, and the eastern Mediterranean was the job of the Combined Chiefs of Staff, not of local commanders. Churchill asks Roosevelt to strike the words commanders responsible and insert the Combined Chiefs of Staff instead. He adds, mildly, that he imagines they all mean the same thing.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d292:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 406 at Cairo on 23 November 1943, proposing a new body for staff-level talks among the main Allies. It grows out of the Combined Chiefs' 127th meeting, where Chinese military representatives had joined the Anglo-American body.

The paper seeks two things at once: keep the Combined Chiefs of Staff an exclusive American-British body, and still give the other big Allies a proper forum. Its answer is a United Chiefs of Staff, made up of the four Moscow powers, meeting only when need arises and only with the members a given problem concerns. Each nation would send one representative. In theory the new body would rank above the combined one, leaving no ally grounds to complain of exclusion.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d392:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull telegraphed President Roosevelt on 29 November 1943 about postwar civil aviation, warning that the question would not wait for the conferences to end. The message was sent by the White House Map Room, and a copy in Hull's papers is marked secret.

Unless America moves ahead with its study of international air problems, Hull argues, the present fluid situation may harden in Allied minds along lines at odds with Roosevelt's own thinking. He proposes a practical start: a committee of himself with Secretaries Stimson and Knox to weigh the tangled problems. The three would also be authorized to pick an able, disinterested man, such as Owen D. Young, to study the question and draw up a report and recommendations for the President's consideration.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d492:
Andrei Gromyko, the Soviet ambassador in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on December 6, 1943, the day the Second Cairo Conference closed. Gromyko had taken up the Washington post that year and was becoming Moscow's chief voice in America. The State Department printed his message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

While the leaders met abroad, the embassies in Washington kept working, and a Soviet note to Hull formed part of that parallel traffic. Gromyko would handle Soviet-American business for decades, and this message comes from the start of that long career. Readers see the alliance being maintained on the home front as well as at the summits.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d92: On November 3, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, keeping up the near-daily rhythm of the autumn. The message is Document 92 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Less than three weeks remained before the Cairo Conference, and the two governments were settling who would go, and on what terms. The record gives the date and the names and no subject. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d192:
White's secondhand memorandum is again the source for this dinner conversation of September 14, 1944. Churchill and Eden, Morgenthau reported, feared Russia would go into Bulgaria, Yugoslavia, and Greece and never get out. The British were planning to land troops in Greece. When Morgenthau spoke of a million British troops in the Middle East, Eden corrected him: only a couple of brigades.

Other fragments survive in the same memo. Leahy reported that American troops could not be moved across British troops in Germany, and Roosevelt answered, "Nonsense. It could be done." The president also told Morgenthau he now knew why the British wanted into the Pacific war: "All they want is Singapore back."
frus-1944-quebec-d292: Secretary of War Henry Stimson wrote to President Franklin Roosevelt on 15 September 1944, while Roosevelt was meeting Prime Minister Winston Churchill at Quebec. The letter survives as document 292 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on that conference, published by the Department of State. Readers get the full message exactly as the Office of the Historian printed it.
frus-1944-quebec-d92: Standing at Document 92 of the Quebec 1944 volume is an editorial note. The State Department's historians wrote it long after the events described. Such notes supply background, clarify names, and link related papers nearby. The volume gathers papers around the September 1944 Quebec Conference. British and American officials prepared heavily for that meeting. Questions about defeated Germany filled much of their work. The note is a brief pause where the editors guide the reader.
frus-1945-50-intel-d192:
The title "Circular Instruction From the Department of State" heads a text dated 9 April 1947. It is document 192 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

Directives were the rule books of the new system. A short one could fix the duties of a whole office. Directives set who may do what, what must be reported, and which office has the final say. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d292:
A text titled "National Security Council Directive on Office of Special Projects" bears the date 18 June 1948. It survives in print as document 292 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. By then the National Security Council met often, and questions about secret operations abroad were moving to the center of its work.

Directives were the rule books of the new system. A short one could fix the duties of a whole office. They name the office in charge, the work to be done, and the limits that apply, line by line. The directive is the order that set up the Office of Special Projects, the part of the CIA charged with covert operations abroad.
frus-1945-50-intel-d392:
Secretary of State Dean Acheson wrote to Roscoe Hillenkoetter, the Director of Central Intelligence, on 1 August 1949. The letter is document 392 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950. That volume gathers the once secret papers behind the birth of the Central Intelligence Agency.

A direct letter from the Secretary of State to the head of the CIA was a top level channel in 1949. The new agency was only two years old, and its place beside the State Department was still being worked out. Readers get a short, formal exchange between the two men who had to make that new system run. The exchange also marks how new the CIA still was in the summer of 1949.
frus-1945-50-intel-d92:
William Eddy, the secretary of state's special assistant for research and intelligence, wrote to Peurifoy, an acting assistant secretary for administration, on 27 January 1947. Eddy had succeeded McCormack in the intelligence post. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A new chief in the chair signals the office's second phase: no longer a wartime inheritance to defend, but a going concern to run. Eddy's memorandum to the administration side keeps the old pattern of the thread, intelligence needs meeting housekeeping limits. Readers meet the succession plainly here. The volume honors continuity as well as drama; offices outlast their founders, and their papers change tone when the founders go.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d192:
Grew answered the Secretary's hold order on Italy on 1 February 1945. His top secret cable to Stettinius, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, reports where the proposed joint statement stands. It was drafted in Washington on 31 January, the departmental copy notes.

The statement, drawn up by the Combined Civil Affairs Committee, is now before the British Foreign Office. When London replies and an agreed text exists, Washington will telegraph it to the Secretary. The committee plans to send the agreed text to the Combined Chiefs of Staff for approval before any release to the press. Grew ends with a firm promise: in any event, nothing will be released without Stettinius's own approval.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d292:
The combined chiefs opened their Malta sittings on 30 January 1945 by settling how to work. These Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, record the first meeting of the Anglo-American staff conference. Sir Alan Brooke takes the chair, at the American chiefs' suggestion.

Brooke hopes an American will chair when the staffs meet again at Yalta. Marshall agrees to the proposal. The chiefs settle on a daily meeting hour of half past two, circumstances permitting. Brooke then tables the proposed order of business for each day, and the Americans accept it. Two subjects are marked for earlier treatment if time allows: the U-boat threat, and the planning date for the end of the Japanese war. German flying bombs and rocket attacks come next on the record.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d392:
Staff planners drafted the script for the first American-Soviet staff meeting in this paper of February 7, 1945. They set out the subjects and questions to raise with the Red General Staff. Even the wording for presenting each subject was supplied. Most points, they note, repeated earlier papers, gathered here for the chiefs' convenience.

The paper recalls two questions the President had already put to Stalin. Once war broke out between Russia and Japan, Roosevelt had asked, what would follow? An early reply at the conference was wanted. The planners' draft shows how much of a summit is written before the leaders sit down.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d492:
Trade, not territory, fills Stettinius's memorandum to the President of February 10, 1945. Its subject is Article VII of the Lend-Lease agreement, the clause on postwar commercial policy. Before leaving Washington, the Secretary had learned something from Will Clayton. The British said Roosevelt had never mentioned Article VII to Churchill.

Churchill had therefore gained the impression that the President cared little about the subject. That misimpression, Stettinius argued, encouraged Britain's unyielding stand on empire preferences and trade barriers. He urged Roosevelt to send Churchill the attached letter before leaving Yalta. The memo links wartime aid to the trade order the peace would need.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d92:
Six decisions had to be taken at the three-power meeting, Leo Pasvolsky advised on 23 January 1945. His memorandum to the Secretary of State is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It is a checklist for the talks that became the Yalta Conference.

First comes the voting text: adopt the President's formula, with a small change to one section. Trusteeship machinery should go into the Charter, with the sponsors consulting before the conference. France should become the fifth sponsoring power. Invitations should match the forty-four nations asked to earlier wartime conferences. The founding conference itself should sit in the United States, at a time still to be fixed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d192:
Three of Truman's closest advisers summed up the conference stakes in a memorandum dated July 6, 1945. The memo from John Snyder, Samuel Rosenman, and George Allen is document 192 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It records the consensus reached on a July 4 cruise aboard the presidential yacht Potomac.

Their list puts Russia's entry into the Japanese war first. Then comes stabilizing Europe's economy: coal, food, transport, and raw materials now, and long-term rebuilding later. Full British participation in the Pacific war follows, then policy toward Germany, from demilitarization and dismemberment to reeducation. They add holding the peace conference in the United States and gaining some military and naval bases. The memo closes with a joke: as a well-known Missouri horse trader, Truman is expected to bring something home.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d292:
From Sofia on June 23, 1945, Barnes, the American representative in Bulgaria, backed the line President Truman had taken with Stalin on recognizing the Bulgarian government. He told the Acting Secretary of State that no elected government meant no restored ties. Barnes also doubted that American work on the Allied Control Commission could ever count for much.

Seven months of watching the Russians led Barnes to list their top aims in Bulgaria. He named a one-party system under Communist control, a militia shaped like the Soviet secret police, close trade ties, and command of the army. His cable shows why Washington faced Potsdam with few illusions about Soviet plans in the Balkans.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d392:
Admiral King, the Chief of Naval Operations, corrected the record in a telegram to Admiral Leahy dated July 11, 1945. The Joint Chiefs had just approved a memorandum to the President on the disposition and distribution of the German fleet. King writes that it was his intention that one paragraph be deleted from that memorandum.

The paragraph, labeled e, dealt with the treatment of a Soviet request for the American share. King asks Leahy to so advise the President. The editors note the message was sent to rectify a misunderstanding of the conclusions the Joint Chiefs had reached, and that their secretariat knew of it before dispatch.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d492:
Harriman's candid reaction to the Polish agreement fills his cable from Moscow of June 28, 1945. He is somewhat disappointed, he writes, that the outsiders did not win seven posts in the new government instead of five. One more Socialist and one member from the Christian Labor Party, he believes, could have been gained had the outside Socialists bargained harder.

A gentlemen's agreement, he reports, will admit the Christian Labor leader Popiel on his return from London. Mikołajczyk, Harriman feels, is better off not being Prime Minister in so hard a situation. If America takes a sympathetic interest in Polish affairs, and is reasonably generous in economic relations, he concludes, there is a fair chance things will work out satisfactorily.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d592:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson wrote to President Truman on July 2, 1945, about a warning to Japan. His top secret letter, with two enclosures, is document 592 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The Secretaries of the Navy and of State had both approved the memo's line.

Stimson argues that invading Japan could mean a long, costly, last-ditch fight on ground worse than Iwo Jima or Okinawa. He urges a clear warning and a real chance to yield before any landing. Japan, he notes, has no allies, a ruined navy, and cities open to air attack. His draft terms would let Japan trade again and would not bar a limited monarchy under the present dynasty. A draft proclamation by the Allied heads of state is attached.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d692:
Ambassador Wilson reported a dinner-table talk with the Soviet ambassador in Ankara on June 29, 1945. His top secret wire is document 692 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Wilson had asked what was taking place between Moscow and Turkey.

The ambassador said Molotov had told Sarper that a new friendship treaty required prior settlement of certain questions. They included the return of Kars and Ardahan and measures to insure Black Sea security. No bases, he said, had been named as such. The land claim, he argued, was for the Armenian Republic, which lacked room. Few Armenians lived in the eastern provinces, since Turks had massacred most of them there. On the Straits, his point was stark. Turkey could close them to Russia in wartime and open them to Russia's enemies. Moscow could not permit that to go on.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d92:
Ambassador Harriman carried three open requests to Vyshinsky in a letter dated June 23, 1945. The letter, marked top secret and urgent, is document 92 in the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. General Parks had been warmly received in Berlin by General Kruglov, but Kruglov said some matters lay beyond his power to decide.

Harriman asks for room to scout the Zehlendorf district for extra camps and billets, since Babelsberg alone may not hold the overflow. He asks to run supply trucks on the Halle-Berlin highway without case-by-case permission. He also asks to grow Parks's party as needed, since signal experts under Major General Stoner must reach Berlin by June 25 to build communications. He closes by asking for prompt action.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1092:
The United States submitted this tightened Italy proposal to the foreign ministers' meeting of July 21, 1945. It keeps the aims of the delegation's earlier drafts. Italy is to gain early independence and recovery, and her people will in time choose their own government. The three powers would take steps that credit Italy's part in Germany's defeat.

They would announce their intent to conclude a peace treaty soon, promise practical economic aid, and restate the wish for early Italian elections. The Allied Commission would speed the transfer of duties to the Italian government. By September 1, the three ambassadors in Rome, with the Supreme Allied Commander, must report which surrender terms should lapse.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1192:
The Combined Military Transportation Committee of the Combined Chiefs of Staff reported on 21 July 1945. This joint British-American body handled the armed forces' shipping and transport needs across both nations' services. Its report put the transport picture before the summit's military leaders.

Armies move on ships, trains, and trucks, and so does relief for freed peoples. The committee's work joined those needs into one plan the chiefs could judge. Transport rarely makes headlines, yet every choice at Potsdam rested on it. This report is the logistics view, stated plainly for the men at the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1292:
Hornbeck, the American ambassador to the Netherlands, wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on 21 July 1945. The Netherlands had been freed from German rule only weeks before. Its government was rebuilding at home and fighting to regain its empire in Asia.

An envoy's report from a newly freed land carried facts the summit could get nowhere else. The Dutch case touched the talks through trade, colonies, and the shape of the peace. This dispatch fed the Dutch picture into Washington mid-summit. It shows the web of posts keeping the center informed while the great bargaining ran.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1392:
The Polish deputy prime minister's diary entry of 30 July 1945 comes next in his run of papers. Mikołajczyk mixed diary pages with formal memoranda all through the last week of July. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Two days before the conference closed, the diary shows what it felt like to wait on other men's choices. Mikołajczyk had staked his return to Poland on a promise of free elections that the West struggled to secure. Readers who know his later flight from Poland in 1947 will read these pages with care. Even without that knowledge, the entry stands as a plain record of a statesman in a trap.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-92:
Averell Harriman, the United States ambassador to the Soviet Union, wrote this memorandum on July 24, 1945. Harriman was at Potsdam with the American delegation. Few men in the room knew the Soviet leaders as well as he did. His memos drew on years of hard talks in Moscow during the war.

A Harriman paper carried a Moscow view that Washington staff could not supply. He knew how the Kremlin phrased demands and where it might yield. Readers get the judgment of a man who dealt with Stalin face to face. The memo forms part of the staff record in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d792:
Dunn replied to Novikov, the Soviet delegation's secretary, on July 27, 1945. Document 792 answers the Soviet letter of July 25 in this volume. The exchange ran between the two delegations' senior staff. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A prompt reply between secretaries kept the machinery oiled. Dunn's answer shows the American side honoring the forms even in small things. Readers can pair the two letters and watch a piece of conference business close. The document proves that Potsdam ran on courtesy as well as conflict. Without the clerks' civility, the leaders' talks would have stalled.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d892:
William Clayton and Emilio Collado sent this long secret telegram from London to Willard Thorp on August 16, 1945. Both men had served at Potsdam on German economic questions. They write to explain the conference's German economic decisions before returning home. Questions from Washington had convinced them not to wait.

They say every effort must be made to win Soviet agreement on an import program in the Control Council. If that fails, zone commanders will set their own first charges on exports. On finance, Truman's signed directive makes the War Department carry full American responsibility. They also argue that care of displaced persons should not fall on UNRRA, whose funds are limited.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d992: American staff drafted this one-sentence proposal at Babelsberg on July 25, 1945. It amends the declaration on reparations and related matters, at the point dealing with German-owned external assets. The added words call for proper steps to take control and power of disposal over such assets. That call applies only where the power is not already exercised by a United Nation that took a direct part in the war against Germany. Another copy of the paragraph in the Pauley Files carries the date July 27.
gabirol-fons-vitae-baeumker-1892:
Ibn Gabirol, the Jewish poet and thinker of Muslim Spain, wrote the Fons Vitae, the Fountain of Life, in Arabic in the eleventh century. The Arabic is lost, but the Latin version by John of Spain and Dominicus Gundissalinus kept the work alive. Clemens Baeumker edited that Latin text in 1892. Christian readers knew the author only as Avicebron and did not guess he was a Jew.

The dialogue argues that all created things, souls included, are made of universal matter and form. Only God stands outside that pairing. The claim fed debates in the schools for centuries. No English version in the public domain exists. Baeumker's edition is the base for study of this bridge between worlds.
galton-finger-prints-1892:
In Finger Prints, published in 1892, Galton set out to prove that the ridges on a fingertip can name a person for life. He collected prints from thousands of hands and studied their arches, loops, and whorls. Police forces were then still searching for a sure way to name repeat offenders.

Galton showed that prints stay fixed from youth to old age and that no two fingers match. He worked out a first system for sorting prints so a single finger could be traced in a file. His book gave fingerprint proof its firm scientific base.
gao-gaoreports-b-297392:
Language Services Associates protested a Homeland Security deal in GAO decision B-297392, dated January 17, 2006. The winner was Bowne Global Solutions. The work was interpreter help for the asylum program. The deal ran for 5 years. The winner had the low price quote. The firm hit how the winner was scored.

GAO denied the protest. The winner's quote was scored by the call terms in a sound way. Small flaws in the buy, if any, did the firm no harm. Harm must be shown to win. A firm must show it lost a real chance due to a flaw. That show was not made here. The deal thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-299092:
