Encompass Group, LLC protested the rejection of its bid by the Department of Veterans Affairs. The buy covered reusable operating room scrubs. Bids ran through federal supply schedule holders. GAO decided B-299092 on December 22, 2006.

The agency judged the firm's sample garments against the stated terms. It found the samples missed those terms in more than one way. The firm called each miss minor. It pointed to a letter and sales sheets pledging fit goods. GAO backed the agency's read of the samples. Samples that miss core terms can sink a bid. Side pledges do not cure flawed samples. The rejection was fair. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-307892:
Small gifts for sailors who sign on again are allowed, with terms, in this GAO decision, B-307892, dated October 11, 2006. A Navy command in Maryland wished to give gifts with its crest. The gifts ran from pens and mugs to caps and bags. Each gift marks a new enlistment term. A pay officer asked if funds could buy them.

GAO held that 10 U.S.C. section 2261 lets the Navy buy such gifts. Each gift may cost no more than $50. But the Navy must first write rules for the plan. Gifts must then match those rules. The gift power ends on December 31, 2007.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-192:
Social Security Statements, GAO-05-192 of April 1, 2005, tests whether a key mail-out makes sense to the workers who get it. The statement reaches more than 140 million workers. By law, it shows each worker's pay record, sums paid in, and the benefits they may draw later. The agency also uses it to spur saving for old age.

GAO ran a national survey and group talks with those who get the form. It asked how well they grasp it. It asked how the agency itself tests that grasp. It set both next to the best habits of firms and of Canada, Sweden, and the United Kingdom.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-292:
Child Welfare, GAO-05-292 of June 13, 2005, looks for a faster path to homes for foster children with special needs. On September 30, 2002, about 126,000 foster children waited for adoption. Many had a health flaw or a trait that made homes slow to take them. Federal cash backs their care through grants and bonus pay to states that place them.

GAO names the chief blocks to place and keep such children in new homes. It lists what states and the health department have tried. It grades two aid plans built for this aim. More sharp data and tests could lift both the path and the plans.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-392:
A joint program tests whether security products do what vendors claim. In GAO-06-392 (March 24, 2006), GAO reviews the National Information Assurance Partnership. The National Security Agency and the National Institute of Standards and Technology formed it in 1997. Accredited labs test and validate security products for national security systems. Those systems hold classified data or support intelligence work.

GAO weighed the benefits and challenges of the testing process. It also asked what would happen if the requirement spread to other systems. Those include sensitive but unclassified systems. GAO found the partnership offers benefits. It also faces considerable challenges. Readers get a clear view of product testing and its limits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-592:
Weapons must keep working after a chemical or biological attack. Report GAO-06-592, issued April 28, 2006, reviews survivability policy at the Defense Department. A fiscal year 2005 defense law ordered a plan by February 28, 2005. The plan was to include a central database on agent effects on weapon materials. The department did not submit the plan as mandated. That failure frames the study.

GAO judged how far survivability is addressed during the buying process. It checked internal controls over the research and test database. Consistent policies and clear processes are needed, GAO said. Readers see a defense requirement that lacked both a plan and a settled process.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-692:
Destroying Russian chemical weapons is the subject of GAO-06-692, a GAO report dated May 31, 2006. Until destroyed, Russia's stockpile remains a proliferation threat, open to theft and diversion. Since 1992, Congress has authorized more than $1 billion in aid to build a destruction plant at Shchuch'ye. The plant would burn through nerve agent weapons stored nearby. GAO checked the project's cost and schedule data.

GAO found that construction had progressed, but the project was behind schedule and faced substantial challenges. Russia had drawn up a destruction plan and raised its own funding. Even so, GAO said Russia might not meet its destruction deadlines. Weak earned value data left the Defense Department unable to estimate cost and schedule reliably. GAO urged more reliable data.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-792:
Weather Service upgrades are planned in GAO-06-792 of July 14, 2006. The National Weather Service issues the forecasts and storm warnings the nation relies on. It was upgrading its systems and technology to serve the public better. It also planned to change its concept of operations, which could reshape its nationwide set of forecast offices. GAO judged the service's plans and the training behind them.

GAO found that the upgrades positioned the service to provide better forecasts. New training was expected to improve service as well. But the process for picking who gets trained lacked enough oversight. GAO also warned that the impact of the office changes was not yet known. Effects on service, staffing, and budget all remained open questions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-92:
Theft of explosives from state and local stores is probed in GAO report GAO-06-92, dated October 3, 2005. Over 5.5 billion pounds of explosives are used each year in the United States. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives licenses private stores. A July 2004 theft of several hundred pounds raised alarm.

GAO sized up thefts from government stores, which sit outside much of that licensing reach. It mapped what power the bureau holds over such stores, and what data it keeps on them. It checked guard steps at picked sites. Thefts proved few, GAO found, but they may be undercounted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1092:
Farmland passed to the Fish and Wildlife Service needs more flexible care, GAO finds in report GAO-07-1092, dated September 18, 2007. For two decades, farm law has let the Farm Service Agency hand rich farmland to the wildlife agency. Land joins the National Wildlife Refuge System, by full ownership or by easement. The nearest refuge office runs each tract.

GAO sized how much farmland the service has taken in. It asked how far the service now tends those lands. It set out other ways to run them. The work drew on visits to five refuges, and a poll of managers for a sample of 98 farmlands.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-592:
Tracing a sick cow in days, not weeks, is the aim of the National Animal Identification System, reviewed in GAO-07-592, dated July 6, 2007. Livestock added nearly $123 billion to the U.S. economy in 2006. The Department of Agriculture announced the system in December 2003 after disease scares abroad. It would tag animals and sites so outbreaks can be traced fast.

GAO asked how well the build is going and what gripes farmers, markets, and states raise. It traced how grant funds to states were spent and judged. It also priced the system for the agency, states, and industry. Staff met 32 outside experts for the work. The dream is sound, GAO finds, but key choices stay open: how data get shared, who pays, and how small herds join. Until those settle, rapid traceback stays a goal, not a fact.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-892:
Health screening for World Trade Center responders is updated in GAO-07-892, dated July 23, 2007. Responders breathed dust and fumes that may harm health for years. The Health and Human Services Department runs screening for federal responders. Its health institute funds care for others through grants. GAO's 2006 work flagged problems in both efforts. This report checks the status of screening services. It also tracks treatment grants and cost estimates.

Screening exams stopped and started more than once, GAO found. The program halted scheduling from January 2007 to May 2007 during a management change. Specialty care, such as lung and heart exams, lapsed for almost a year. A new provider contract did not cover those services. Services for responders outside New York City also lag. GAO urged the secretary to ensure steady screening and monitoring for all responders. The department called the report generally accurate. It did not comment on the advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-92:
Agency reporting on bad payments is graded in GAO-07-92, dated November 14, 2006. Fiscal year 2005 was the second year under a 2002 reporting law. GAO read the annual reports of 35 agencies. Reports varied wildly in depth and detail. Big risk-prone programs sat outside the government total. Some included estimates lacked valid statistics behind them. Of the 35 agencies, 23 said they had assessed all their programs. Twelve had not finished that first step.

Because of the gaps, the true scale of bad payments stays hidden, GAO said. Recovery auditing results were also part of the review. GAO suggested Congress tighten the law's definitions. Programs should face set criteria for risk checks. Four recommendations went to the budget office. They aim at complete, accurate reporting across agencies. The office broadly agreed and listed steps under way. Progress is real but patchy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-292:
New federal ID cards get a progress check in GAO report GAO-08-292 (February 29, 2008). Many worker badges can be forged or altered with ease. An August 2004 presidential directive ordered one secure standard for federal identification. The result is a smart card meant to open both doors and computer systems. Agencies have rolled the cards out at varied pace.

GAO studied eight agencies with a range of card experience. It asked how far each has turned on the card's security features. It also tested whether cards work across agency lines. Gains are uneven, GAO found. The title calls for stronger leadership from the budget office to make the cards pay off.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-492:
The Information Sharing Environment is assessed in GAO report GAO-08-492, issued June 25, 2008. The Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 ordered this system to help agencies share terrorism-related information. A Program Manager leads the build, helped by a council of 16 agency officials.

An implementation plan lays out 89 action items in two phases, due by June 2009, and some are done, including draft common sharing standards. State and local fusion centers are being linked into a national network under the plan. But officials concede the 89 items do not cover all the work. The scope of what counts as terrorism information is not set, and the results the system must deliver are not defined. GAO recommended clear scope, goals, and measures. The Program Manager generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-692:
Pension funds have begun buying into hedge funds and private equity, deals that sit outside many federal rules. GAO-08-692, dated August 14, 2008, maps how much pension money sits in such deals, what gains funds hope for, and what risks and guards come with them.

Surveys show 21 to 27 percent of mid to large plans hold hedge funds, and over 40 percent hold private equity. The share is still small next to total plan assets. Gains can beat the stock market, but fees, hidden holdings, and hard-to-sell stakes add risk. GAO asked the Labor Department to issue clear guidance for plan managers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-892:
Domestic workers brought to the United States by foreign diplomats sit outside normal labor shields, since their bosses hold immunity. GAO-08-892, dated July 29, 2008, counts abuse claims on special visas and reviews how the government probes them.

GAO found 42 workers who alleged abuse from 2000 through 2008. The true count is likely higher, since fear and scattered records hide cases. No single office holds all claims. Immunity blocks some proof gathering, and slow legal calls stall probes. GAO tells the State Department to keep one case file, flag risky employers at visa time, and spot-check visa practice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-92:
Stopping a flu pandemic before it spreads is the subject of GAO-08-92, issued in December 2007. A repeat of the 1918 pandemic could kill between 30 million and 384 million people worldwide by some estimates. The world strategy leans in part on antiviral drugs and vaccines to forestall an outbreak. GAO examined what limits those tools and what is being done about the limits.

Both tools face hard constraints. Antivirals work only if a new strain is spotted fast and drugs are given within 48 hours of symptoms, and resistant strains could blunt them. A vaccine cannot be made until the strain is known, and making one takes 20 to 23 weeks, too slow to matter early. Production and delivery capacity could also fall short, the World Health Organization has warned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-992:
Checking flyers against the No Fly and Selectee lists was still the airlines' job in 2008, and report GAO-08-992, dated September 9, 2008, grades how that work was watched. The Transportation Security Administration was to take over the task through its Secure Flight program, but delays left it with the carriers. Names must be matched even when spelled in varied forms.

GAO found that, until April 2008, the rules never said which name variants carriers must catch. Staff who spoke with 14 of 95 carriers heard uneven methods, and some did no such checks at all. One flyer could match at one carrier and pass at another. The agency has since set a base method, GAO notes, but its own checks of carriers still need work.
gennadius-of-marseilles-lives-of-illustr:
Gennadius of Marseilles continued Jerome's catalog of Christian writers into the later 400s. His Lives of Illustrious Men adds roughly a hundred more short biographies. The continuation appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, beside the work it extends.

Many authors in these pages survive only because Gennadius remembered them; their books are lost. He notes what each man wrote and where he stood in the disputes of the day. Together, Jerome and Gennadius give the ancient Church's own account of its literary tradition. The pair forms a rough map of early Christian reading.
gilman-yellow-wallpaper-1892:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote The Yellow Wallpaper after her own doctor prescribed a rest cure that nearly destroyed her mind. The story appeared in a magazine in 1892. Gilman later said she wrote it to save people from being driven crazy by the same treatment.

A young mother, ordered to rest and forbidden to write, is shut in a nursery with ugly yellow wallpaper. As her husband dismisses her fears, she studies the paper's pattern until she sees a woman creeping behind it. Her descent into madness unfolds entry by entry in her secret diary. The story indicted the patriarchal medicine of its day. It is now a landmark of feminist literature.
gracian-art-of-worldly-wisdom-jacobs-189:
Baltasar Gracián, a Spanish Jesuit, published his Oráculo manual in 1647 as a pocket guide to worldly wisdom. Joseph Jacobs Englished it in 1892 as The Art of Worldly Wisdom. The book holds three hundred short maxims on prudence, power, and the conduct of life.

Gracián teaches when to speak, when to wait, and how to keep friends and fortune. His counsel is cool, exact, and often surprising in its candor. Schopenhauer admired the book so much that he translated it into German himself. He called it absolutely unique among books of counsel. Jacobs's rendering kept it in English hands for a century. Few breviaries of practical sense have lasted so well.
gregory-of-nazianzus-select-letters-npnf:
The reluctant bishop speaks most freely in his letters, and the Select Letters of Gregory of Nazianzus gather that private voice. They appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Basil the Great, his dearest friend, receives some of the finest of them.

Brilliant and sensitive, Gregory keeps trying to retire to quiet and keeps getting dragged back to duty. The letters range from deep theological counsel to affectionate, funny notes between friends. Weariness and wit share nearly every page. Together they sketch a man who loved words, solitude, and God, in no simple order. Readers finish the set feeling they know the Church's greatest orator personally.
gregory-of-nazianzus-select-orations-npn:
Byzantine Christians gave Gregory of Nazianzus a title they gave no other preacher: the Theologian. The Select Orations gathered here show why, including the five Theological Orations that defined belief about the Trinity. They appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Funeral speeches and festal sermons display the same soaring beauty in a softer key. Gregory could argue doctrine like a lawyer and mourn like a poet, sometimes in one address. His sentences shaped Greek preaching for a thousand years. Readers new to him meet the early Church's most eloquent voice at full strength. Few ancient speakers reward slow, aloud reading so richly.
gregory-of-nyssa-against-eunomius-npnf2-:
Eunomius claimed that human reason could grasp God's very essence and name it correctly. Gregory of Nyssa, the most philosophical of the Cappadocian fathers, spent twelve books proving him wrong in Against Eunomius. The long refutation appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Few ancient debates reach this level of care.

We know God by what he does, Gregory argues, never by what he is in himself. Every name we give God falls short of the reality it points toward. The argument defends divine mystery without surrendering clear thought. Dazzling logic and deep reverence run side by side through the books. Judges have called the work the high-water mark of ancient Christian philosophy, and its questions about language and God still stir debate.
gregory-of-nyssa-answer-to-eunomius-seco:
Eunomius answered Gregory's attack with a second book of his own, and Gregory replied once more. His Answer to Eunomius's Second Book appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Shorter than the first round, the reply strikes sharper and with even greater confidence.

Gregory returns to the core claim: no human concept can capture God's nature itself. Words about God, he insists, name his works and gifts, not his hidden essence. The sequel completes the demolition of a system that promised more knowledge than creatures can hold. Readers who finish both rounds witness ancient theological debate conducted at its highest pitch. Few sequels in the fathers match the first work so well.
gregory-of-nyssa-funeral-oration-on-mele:
Meletius, bishop of Antioch, died in 381 while the Council of Constantinople sat in session. Gregory of Nyssa preached his funeral sermon before the assembled bishops, and the Funeral Oration on Meletius survives. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Gregory honors a peacemaker whose patience had held a divided church together. Between lines of praise runs a plea for unity among the grieving bishops. The sermon belongs to ancient funeral rhetoric at its most eloquent. Its setting adds weight: the men listening were deciding the faith's future that same month. Few occasional pieces carry so much history in so few pages.
gregory-of-nyssa-letters-of-gregory-of-n:
Friends, bishops, and imperial officials all received letters from Gregory of Nyssa, and many survive. The Letters of Gregory of Nyssa appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Theology shares the pages with personal sorrow and the running controversies of his age.

Readers meet the private side of a great thinker: warm, witty, and deeply human. He consoles, recommends, argues, and occasionally complains about his health or his enemies. Travel notes and requests for help fill out a working bishop's life. Anyone who wants the man behind the treatises should start here. The correspondence also fills gaps in the public record of his embattled career.
gregory-of-nyssa-on-infants-early-deaths:
What happens to babies who die before they can believe or choose? Gregory of Nyssa faced that sorrow in On Infants' Early Deaths, a work of comfort for grieving parents. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

His answer is gentle: such children enjoy God's presence without the struggles of earthly life. Their souls, he suggests, mature in heaven rather than perishing unfinished. Nothing in the book scolds or frightens the mourning reader. It stands as the Church's first sustained reflection on infant death. Pastors and parents have returned to its tenderness for centuries, and its compassion has lost none of its force.
gregory-of-nyssa-on-not-three-gods-npnf2:
If Father, Son, and Spirit are each fully God, why is there not a trio of gods? Gregory of Nyssa answers that puzzle in On Not Three Gods, a short and famous treatise. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

The three persons, he argues, share one divine nature, much as three men share one human nature. Counting gods by persons mistakes how the word God works in the creed. The comparison is bold, and readers have debated its edges ever since. Brief and brilliant, the treatise remains the classic statement of how monotheism survives Trinitarian faith. Students of doctrine still start arguments from its pages.
gregory-of-nyssa-on-pilgrimages-npnf2-18:
Pilgrimage to the Holy Land was booming, and Gregory of Nyssa told his readers to think twice. His letter On Pilgrimages, in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, argues against the fashion with surprising bluntness. The short piece still startles readers who expect only encouragement.

God is everywhere, Gregory insists, so Jerusalem offers no spiritual advantage over home. Worse, the road and its inns bring real temptations, especially for monks and nuns. True devotion, he says, shows in a changed life rather than in miles traveled. The letter serves as a bracing corrective to religious tourism in any age. Its honesty about holy places remains quotable and bracing.
gregory-of-nyssa-on-the-baptism-of-chris:
Why did the sinless Jesus submit to John's baptism in the Jordan? Gregory of Nyssa takes up that question in his sermon On the Baptism of Christ. The short piece, preached for the feast of the baptism, appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Christ entered the water, Gregory says, to make the waters holy for our baptism. The sermon unfolds that idea with lyrical beauty rather than dry argument. Heaven opens, the Spirit descends, and the Father's voice completes the scene. Short enough for one sitting, the sermon repays many readings. It shows Gregory the preacher at his most musical and clear.
gregory-of-nyssa-on-the-faith-npnf2-1892:
Confusions about God, Christ, and the Spirit crowded the churches of the later fourth century. Gregory of Nyssa summed up sound belief against them in On the Faith, a compact statement of orthodoxy. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

With a teacher's clarity, he sets out what Christians confess and why each clause matters. Every sentence carries the weight of fights he had already waged in longer books. For readers daunted by his vast philosophical works, this short piece offers Gregory at his most accessible. It works well as a doorway into Cappadocian teaching. The whole faith, he shows, can be held in a few careful pages.
gregory-of-nyssa-on-the-holy-spirit-agai:
A party called the Macedonians denied that the Holy Spirit is fully God. Gregory of Nyssa answered in On the Holy Spirit, Against the Macedonians, printed in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Basil the Great had argued the same cause, and Gregory carried it forward.

He proves the Spirit's divinity from scripture and from the Church's own worship, where the Spirit is honored beside Father and Son. Baptism, prayer, and blessing all treat the Spirit as God, he notes. Together with Basil's treatise, the work secured belief in the full Trinity. The Nicene Creed's final clause about the Spirit rests on arguments like these. Careful and decisive, the book rewards patient readers.
gregory-of-nyssa-on-the-making-of-man-np:
Human nature itself is the subject of On the Making of Man, Gregory of Nyssa's rich treatise on what people are. The soul's origin, the body's design, and the meaning of male and female all come under review. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Gregory asks what it means that people bear the image of God. Body and soul, reason and sense, death and rising again each get careful treatment. Scripture and the natural knowledge of his day meet on friendly terms here. The book shaped Eastern Orthodox thinking about humanity for centuries after. Reverent and curious at once, it treats the human creature as God's finest work on earth.
gregory-of-nyssa-on-the-soul-and-the-res:
Beside his dying sister Macrina, Gregory of Nyssa argued for the soul's survival and the hope of resurrection. Their deathbed conversation became On the Soul and the Resurrection. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, and many call it his most beautiful book.

Macrina takes the teacher's role, answering her brother's doubts with calm, ordered reason. Grief sharpens every question: where is the soul, and how can scattered bodies rise? Philosophy here wears the dress of a family farewell. Readers have nicknamed the work the Christian Phaedo, after Plato's dialogue on the soul. Few ancient books join tenderness and argument so gracefully.
gregory-of-nyssa-on-virginity-npnf2-1892:
Gregory of Nyssa was himself a married man, yet he wrote the early Church's most thoughtful praise of virginity. On Virginity appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. His case never rests on contempt for marriage, which sets the book apart from harsher works of its age.

Virginity, for Gregory, means freedom for undivided devotion to God, not escape from a tainted world. He writes about the body's changes and life's burdens with honesty. Philosophical and tender by turns, the treatise treats celibacy as a chosen path of love. Its humane tone still surprises readers who expect ancient strictness. Few early works on the single life read with this much sympathy.
gregory-of-nyssa-the-great-catechism-npn:
Teachers preparing new converts needed one orderly account of the whole faith, and Gregory of Nyssa supplied it. The Great Catechism explains the Trinity, the incarnation, baptism, and the Eucharist in sequence. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Each doctrine gets defended against the objections a sharp hearer might raise. Jews, pagans, and heretics all receive answers fitted to their doubts. The plan stays clear from first page to last, like a well-built course. Judges rank the book as the most complete doctrinal summary of the fourth-century Eastern Church. Clear, orderly, and profound, it shows ancient teaching at its finest.
gregory-the-great-register-of-the-epistl:
Over eight hundred fifty letters of Pope Gregory the Great survive in his official Register, the working archive of a revolutionary papacy. The Register of the Epistles appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Rome was crumbling around him, and the letters manage a Church across that collapse.

Gregory appoints bishops, ransoms captives, feeds a starving city, disciplines monks, and sends missionaries to distant England. Lombard invaders, imperial officials, and Frankish kings all get their answers. Historians call Gregory the man who invented the medieval papacy, and this correspondence shows the work in progress. Few ancient archives let readers watch government happen letter by letter. The scale alone commands respect.
gregory-the-great-selected-epistles-of-g:
Daunted by the full eight-hundred-letter register? The later books, nine through fourteen, offer the essential Gregory in a smaller compass. Selected Epistles of Gregory the Great, Books Nine to Fourteen, appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. These letters come from the busiest years of his reign.

The English mission takes shape here, as Gregory guides Augustine of Canterbury's young church from far away. Relations with Constantinople, always delicate, fill other pages. A Church under siege still finds its pope arranging food, justice, and worship with care. Readers meet the administrator and the pastor in the same handwriting. The selection suits anyone who wants Gregory's voice without the full mountain of paper.
gregory-the-great-the-book-of-pastoral-r:
Gregory the Great never wanted the papal throne, yet his Book of Pastoral Rule became the handbook for bishops for a thousand years. The guide teaches the art of pastoral care: how to teach, correct, and adapt to every kind of soul. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Different hearers need different handling, Gregory insists: the proud one way, the despairing another. He sets out dozens of paired temperaments and the approach each one requires. Augustine of Canterbury carried the book to England with the mission Gregory sent. Medieval Europe treated it as the manual for ministry. Practical wisdom from a pope who knew the burden himself fills every chapter.
grinnell-blackfoot-lodge-tales-1892:
George Bird Grinnell learned Blackfoot stories during years spent hunting and traveling in the northern Plains, often in Blackfoot camps. His 1892 book gathers myths and histories told to him there, while the old life of the tribe was still in living memory.

Many tales center on Napi, the trickster and creator whose cleverness and folly explain the world. Others cover the beaver medicine, sacred bundles, and legends of the stars. Grinnell wrote the stories down much as they were told to him. The book is still read as a warm, faithful record of Blackfoot tradition from the buffalo days.
harper-iola-leroy-1892:
Frances Ellen Watkins Harper published Iola Leroy in 1892, subtitled Shadows Uplifted, her novel of slavery and freedom. A light-skinned enslaved woman's journey to freedom and activism makes it a pioneering Black feminist novel of Reconstruction. Harper, a famed abolitionist lecturer and poet, wrote it at sixty-seven to urge her people.

Iola, raised in ignorance of her birth, is sold into slavery when her white father dies and his will fails. Rescued by Union troops, she serves as a nurse, refuses to pass for white, and seeks her scattered family. Debates among Black doctors, teachers, and ministers fill chapters with the era's arguments on race, temperance, and the vote in Reconstruction. She weds a doctor who shares her vow to work for their people's future in the South. It was among the first novels published by a Black woman.
haydn-dictionary-dates-1892:
Joseph Haydn first published his Dictionary of Dates in 1841, and Benjamin Vincent's twentieth edition of 1892 is the version here. Haydn aimed to answer every 'when did it happen' question a reader could ask. The book grew with each edition into a vast store of facts.

Entries cover foundations, laws, governments, inventions, wars, and the births and deaths of notable people. British affairs get special depth, and an index of painters is a noted extra. Before search engines, this was the quick way to check a date. Historians still use it to catch the period flavor of fact itself.
heart-and-science-a-story-of-the-present:
Collins's Heart and Science, here in the text prepared from his 1883 novel, opens with two prefaces, one to readers in general and one to readers in particular. You are the children of Old Mother England, on both sides of the Atlantic, he tells his public, and you judge fiction by inbred preferences. The two qualities that hold the highest rank in your estimation, he says, are character and humour. Incident and drama hold only second place in your favour.

The tale itself pits heart against science: a young doctor's love and health against a household where experiment rules and feeling is dissected. Collins aims his plot against vivisection, which he hated. A theatrical thief, he jokes in the preface, could find nothing to steal in a story-less novel; his own has story in plenty. A reader watches a great craftsman argue with his audience before the curtain rises.
hilary-of-poitiers-homilies-on-the-psalm:
Hilary of Poitiers wrote the first Latin commentary on the Psalms, and parts of it survive as the Homilies on the Psalms. The fragments appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. He reads each psalm as prophecy of Christ and as a guide for the soul's life.

Allegory, doctrine, and devotion blend in his handling of the ancient songs. Only pieces of the complete work remain, yet what survives shows real depth. Augustine admired Hilary deeply, and these pages help explain why. Readers get the Psalter as the early Latin Church prayed it. The loss of the rest stands among the sad gaps in early Christian literature.
hilary-of-poitiers-on-the-councils-de-sy:
Exile in the East taught Hilary of Poitiers how confusing the creed fights looked from outside. On the Councils, called De Synodis, explains the bewildering series of fourth-century councils to his fellow Western bishops. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Hilary walks through what each council actually meant and which formulas stayed sound. Eastern bishops, he found, often confessed the same faith in different words than Latins expected. His patience made him a bridge between two halves of a divided Church. Writers named him the Athanasius of the West for stands like this one. Readers lost in the synods' alphabet of creeds will find no better ancient guide.
hilary-of-poitiers-on-the-trinity-npnf2-:
Twelve books defend the Son's full divinity in Hilary of Poitiers's On the Trinity, the West's great answer to Arianism. Written during his exile, the work appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Hilary argued from scripture with relentless patience, verse after verse.

He had learned Greek theology in banishment and brought its riches home to Latin readers. Augustine later drew heavily on Hilary for his own teaching about the Trinity. The treatise taught the Latin Church what the Council of Nicaea really meant. Demanding in places, it rewards the effort with unusual clarity about a hard doctrine. Few Western books of the century carry this much weight.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r:
Edward Gibbon's third volume, separately transcribed by David Reed and Dale R Fredrickson from Milman's edition, opens with chapter twenty-seven and the reign of Theodosius. Gratian's death, the ruin of Arianism, and Saint Ambrose's confrontation with the emperor lead the contents. Chapter twenty-eight covers the final destruction of paganism and the rise of saints' relics.

Chapter twenty-nine divides the empire between Theodosius's sons, and later chapters follow the Goths, Vandals, and Huns into the west. The middle pages show princes educated in riding, archery, grammar, and rhetoric by the East's most skillful masters. This record stands beside the library's other volume three as an alternate transcription of identical chapters.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1590-9:
John Lothrop Motley's chapters twenty-four and twenty-five join Dutch reform to French war in 1590 to 1592. Prince Maurice and the state of the republican army come first. His martial science, learned from classical authors and his cousin's practice, remakes siegecraft. Then the scene shifts to Brittany and Normandy.

The death of La Noue, the Huguenot captain, opens the French narrative. Paris murders its magistrates while the League offers France's sceptre to Philip. Farnese marches to relieve Rouen, and Henry IV is wounded in a skirmish. Motley shows Parma drawn ever deeper into France, away from the Netherlands he was conquering. The diversion saved the republic as surely as any battle. These chapters reward readers who want the war whole, in its French and Dutch theatres at once.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1592:
John Lothrop Motley's chapters twenty-six and twenty-seven cover Prince Maurice's war and England's diplomacy in 1592. Maurice returns to the siege of Steenwyck and takes its capitulation. The young stadtholder's sieges were becoming lessons in a new martial science. Motley then casts a glance at negotiations between Elizabeth and the States.

Dutch complaints of English piracy embitter the alliance that protects both nations. Envoy Caron's interview with Elizabeth ends with the Queen's promise of redress. England and the republic, Motley observes, could not injure each other without corresponding damage to themselves. The chapters pair the rising Maurice with the ageing Elizabeth. One learns siegecraft; the other practises delay. Together they show why the republic increasingly trusted its own arms more than its ally's promises.
hymns-of-orpheus-taylor-1792:
Thomas Taylor published his translation of the Hymns of Orpheus in 1792. The volume holds all eighty-seven Orphic Hymns in English verse. These hymns formed the primary liturgy of Orphism, Greece's mystical religious movement.

Each brief hymn invokes a god with offerings, incense, and secret names. The sequence runs from Prothyraia, a birth goddess, through to Death. Worshippers used the hymns at rites whose details remain partly mysterious. Taylor's rendering first carried this ritual songbook to English readers. He translated as a believer in the old Platonist religion himself. Short and solemn, the hymns keep a strangely musical power in his English.
jacobs-celtic-fairy-tales-1892:
Joseph Jacobs, a scholar of folk tales, made this set of Celtic fairy tales in 1892. He retold the tales in plain, brisk English for both young and old readers. The Celts of his title are the folk of Ireland, Scotland, and Wales.

Among the tales stands 'The Sea-Maiden,' a Scots tale of a fisher lad and a maid of the sea. Kings' sons, wise beasts, and bold girls fill the rest of the bright store. Jacobs gave the Celtic tales their main English form, in a book still read with joy.
james-psychology-briefer-course-1892:
Psychology: Briefer Course, published in 1892, is William James's own shortening of his monumental Principles of Psychology for classroom use. Generations of students knew it simply as the Jimmy, beside the two-volume Jamesy of the Principles.

James covers habit, attention, memory, sensation, and emotion in his vivid, untextbook prose. His famous claim that we feel afraid because we tremble, not the other way round, is stated here with charm. The book made psychology teachable in America and spread James's pragmatic temper. It remained a standard text for decades and still reads with startling freshness today.
jerome-against-jovinianus-npnf2-1892:
Jovinian taught that married Christians stood equal to virgins in merit, and Jerome's answer caused a scandal of its own. Against Jovinianus, in two books, praises virginity so fiercely that even Jerome's friends winced. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Marriage comes off so poorly in places that readers accused Jerome of condemning it outright. The backlash forced him to explain and soften his position in later letters. Genius and excess share these pages in equal measure. The affair remains a fascinating case of polemic overshooting its mark. Historians of marriage and celibacy still have to reckon with this book.
jerome-against-the-pelagians-npnf2-1892:
Old age did not cool Jerome's temper, and Pelagius gave him one last great target. Against the Pelagians, a dialogue in three books, came from his Bethlehem monastery late in life. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

The dialogue defends grace and original sin against the claim that people can live sinlessly by willpower alone. Jerome marshals scripture the way he had against every opponent of his long career. At nearly seventy, his fire burned undiminished. The work joined Augustine's campaign from the other end of the Christian world. It stands as the last major controversy of a famously combative life.
jerome-against-vigilantius-npnf2-1892:
Relics, night vigils, and the celibate life all came under attack from a priest named Vigilantius. Jerome responded with Against Vigilantius, among the most abusive treatises ever penned by a saint. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

He calls his opponent a monster and worse, and charity takes a clear second place. Yet the fury preserves precious evidence: Jerome defends the popular piety of ordinary believers in detail. Candles at tombs, prayers to martyrs, and gifts to the poor all get their hearing. As manners the book is indefensible; as history it is invaluable. Both facts keep it in print.
jerome-jerome-s-apology-against-rufinus-:
Jerome's Apology Against Rufinus fires back at his former friend across three books of argument. The counter-blast defends Jerome's own soundness while attacking Rufinus's handling of Origen. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Sarcasm flies; Jerome could be brilliant and brutal in the same paragraph. He marshals his learning to prove that Rufinus, not he, bent the faith. Scholars mine the treatise for its evidence about Origen's teaching and its reception. Other readers come for the spectacle of a genius unleashing every weapon he owns. Either way, few ancient quarrels read with this much fire on the page.
jerome-lives-of-illustrious-men-jerome-n:
One hundred thirty-five short lives of Christian writers, from the apostles down to his own day, fill Jerome's Lives of Illustrious Men. Each entry names the writer and lists his works. The catalog appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Jerome produced the first history of Christian literature, and he did it in haste. Hasty or not, the book preserves names and titles that would vanish without it. His opinions are brisk and sometimes unfair, which keeps the pages lively. Scholars still start here when tracing what the early Church wrote, read, and valued.
jerome-prefaces-to-the-vulgate-and-other:
Before his great Latin Bible, the Vulgate, Jerome wrote prefaces explaining what he was doing and why. The Prefaces to the Vulgate and Other Works gather those introductions with similar short pieces. They appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Readers watch the translator at work: defending his Hebrew learning, stating his rules, and answering critics in advance. He complains about copyists, rivals, and readers who prefer familiar errors to fresh truth. For anyone curious how the Bible reached the Western world, these pages shine. They also reveal the scholar's daily grind behind a famous name. Few prefaces in history carry this much personality.
jerome-the-dialogue-against-the-luciferi:
The Luciferians refused to forgive bishops who had bent under Arian pressure and later repented. Jerome answered them in dialogue form with The Dialogue Against the Luciferians. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

His speaker argues for mercy: lapsed clergy who repent can be restored, and their baptisms stand. The debate format lets the hard-line case speak before it falls. Jerome turns his famous wit toward reconciliation for once, which makes the piece unusual in his output. The dialogue became a key text on how the Church healed its own divisions after the Arian crisis. It still speaks to fights over purity and pardon.
jerome-the-letters-of-st-jerome-npnf2-18:
Lively is too weak a word for the letters of Saint Jerome, the ancient Church's most entertaining correspondent. The Letters of Saint Jerome appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Widows, virgins, monks, and rivals all passed through his mailbox at Bethlehem.

He counsels the devout, demolishes heretics, describes his desert and his books, and feuds with old friends, all in Latin prose of unmatched vigor. Tenderness and savagery can share a single page without warning. Reading the set feels like eavesdropping on the whole fourth century at once. No other ancient letter writer rewards casual browsing so richly, page after page.
jerome-the-perpetual-virginity-of-blesse:
Helvidius argued that Mary had other children after Jesus, born in the usual way. Jerome fired back with The Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary, a treatise of characteristic force. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Verse by verse, Jerome works through the passages about the brothers of the Lord. He insists the texts allow, and tradition demands, Mary's lifelong virginity. His insults to poor Helvidius are nearly as memorable as his arguments. The treatise fixed Western teaching on its subject for well over a thousand years. It also displays, in miniature, both the learning and the temper that made Jerome famous.
jerome-to-pammachius-against-john-of-jer:
John, bishop of Jerusalem, tolerated the teachings of Origen, and Jerome decided to prosecute him for it. His letter To Pammachius Against John of Jerusalem addresses a Roman senator while aiming at the bishop. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Jerome lays out the charges with all his learning: dangerous doctrines excused, discipline lax, orthodoxy in doubt. The letter documents the Origenist controversy that split Christians across the Holy Land. Allies became enemies over the legacy of one brilliant, troubling thinker. Modern readers can judge the fairness of the case for themselves. The piece shows controversy run like a courtroom campaign.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ibn-sarga:
Aaron ibn Sargado was gaon in Pumbedita and a son of Joseph ha-Kohen. Sherira's chronicle puts his term from 943 to 960, though others say he died in 942. He succeeded the gaon Hananiah. A very wealthy merchant, not from a family of scholars, he rose through his family's influence.

Aaron was likely the Caleb ibn Sargado who spent 60,000 zuzim to bring about the fall of Saadia, gaon of Sura. Four of his legal decisions are kept in the collection "Ḥemdah Genuza," one answering a query from Kairwan. Like Saadia, he wrote on the Bible. Parts of his commentary survive in St. Petersburg, and Abraham ibn Ezra quotes his sayings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdallah-ibn-ub: Abdallah ibn Ubaiy was a chief of the Arab tribe Banu al-Khazraj at Medina, and a strong opponent of Mohammed. Mohammed had cut down his sway in the city, and he led the party his foe named in the entry. As an ally of the Banu Ḳainuḳa'a, he kept them from slaughter after they had surrendered. He also urged the Banu al-Nadhir to resist, but sent no help when the attack came. In 630 his camp stood apart from the Syria force and never joined it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abigdor-ben-sam: Abigdor ben Samuel served as rabbi in four towns of Lithuania and Poland. They were Pruzhany, Rushony, Wilkowyszky, and Selva, and his service ran from 1719 to 1768. Toward the close of his life he moved to Wilna. His son Samuel was rabbi in that city. Abigdor died at Wilna on March 1, 1771. Some of his responsa, his formal rulings on points of law, can be found in the collection of Saul ben Moses of Lomzha, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-sol:
Historian Abraham ben Solomon of Torrutiel lived at the end of the fifteenth century and into the sixteenth. At age nine or ten he was driven from Spain in 1492 with the exiles of Ferdinand and Isabella. He went to Fez in Morocco, where the exiles suffered want and a city fire.

Later he wrote an appendix to Abraham ibn Daud's Sefer ha-Kabbalah. It carries the story from 1180 to 1525, listing learned men and Spanish kings. Its third part tells the expulsion and the exiles' fate at Fez. He saw much of it himself and writes with feeling. He blamed Spain's rich Jews who chose conversion over exile.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acacia-13592:
Acacia is a hard, light wood that lasts well. It starts pale yellow and turns dark with age, like ebony. The Ark, its altars, and the bars of the Tabernacle were made from it. The Hebrew name is shiṭṭah, plural shiṭṭim. The tree is a thorn tree of Africa and Arabia. Its name shows up in place names such as Shittim.

Rabbinic notes count the shiṭṭah among the kinds of cedar. One tale says Jacob cut knot-free acacia trees in Palestine and took them to Egypt. His children kept them for use in the wild, as Ark wood. A later question asked if such trees could serve common needs. The reply was to hold to the old custom and keep them set apart. The entry links the wood to the sin at Shittim and to a spring that would heal that fault.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ageda-alleged-c: Ageda is the alleged site of a great Jewish council in Hungary. An English tract of 1655 tells the tale. Its author, Samuel Brett, sets the meet on October 12, 1650. Three hundred rabbis and three thousand Jews weigh the claims of Christ. Six Catholic friars sent by the pope take part. The entry shows the tale is made up. No place in Hungary bears the name Ageda. No Jewish source of the age backs the tale. Brett's aims were to shame Rome and to raise funds for missions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahishar-992: Ahishar was the overseer of Solomon's household. His post carried real weight and trust. The entry compares it to Joseph's place in the house of Potiphar. It also compares it to Obadiah's place in the palace of Ahab. No deed of Ahishar himself is recorded. He stands in the record by his office alone, as the man in charge of a king's household.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alcan-moyse-109: Moyse Alcan was a French publisher and man of letters, born in 1817. He died at Metz on May 14, 1869. He was the father of publisher Felix Alcan. He sat on the Jewish consistory of Metz and judged cases at its Tribunal of Commerce. He wrote for the "Archives Israelites" and the "Revue d'Austrasie." His works include poems, sonatas, and cantatas. "Noema" came out in 1841, and "Ruth," a Biblical hymn, in 1843. His cantata "Spartacus" was performed at Metz in 1852, and again at Damascus in 1860.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfasi-isaac-be: Isaac ben Joseph Alfasi came from a Spanish family and worked in Adrianople in the sixteenth century. He turned a work by Ghazzali into Hebrew. He gave it a Hebrew title that means the chamber of light and the garden of flowers. The entry notes that the work still survives in manuscript. A copy sits in the Bodleian Library.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almon-diblataim: Almon Diblataim was a stopping place in Moab. Israel camped there on the long march out of Egypt. The book of Numbers names it in chapter thirty-three. Two verses of that chapter are cited. The prophet Jeremiah uses a second name for it. He calls it Beth Diblataim in chapter forty-eight. The hosted entry runs to two short lines. It gives no size, no site, and no events for the place. That spare record is all the entry holds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-american-jewish:
American Jewish Publication Society was a second group of that name. New York Jews founded it in 1873. It first called itself the Jewish Publication Society. In 1874 it added the word American to the name. Five rabbis and editors formed its book board. Its first book came out in 1873.

That book was a part of the great history by Graetz. It came out in English dress that year. Two more books came out in 1875. One held tales of Jewish family life. One held short pieces from old moralists. Hard times forced the group to halt in 1875. The cash panic of 1873 lay at the root.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ancona-alessand:
Alessandro d'Ancona, born at Pisa on February 20, 1835, was a historian of Italian literature and a philologist. He was the youngest of five brothers, each of whom won fame. At a Florence school he focused on Italian rhetoric and verse.

At fifteen he wrote elegies on a dead teacher, in close imitation of classical verse. Three years later his essay on Campanella showed a firm grasp of medieval sources and drew Liberal notice in Tuscany. Party leaders then brought him into newspaper work. The entry follows his long career in letters and public life from that early start.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antiochus-vii-s:
Antiochus VII Sidetes, named for Side in Pamphylia, was king of Syria, son of Demetrius I. Born in 164, he died in 129 B.C. In 138 B.C. he rose against the usurper Tryphon, who had taken his captive brother's place.

He first wrote kindly to Simon the Hasmonean, confirming all past privileges to win his help or his silence. Once Tryphon weakened, the tone changed. Antiochus demanded Jaffa, Gazara, and the Jerusalem citadel, or 1,000 talents instead. Simon refused, and his sons beat the Syrian general sent against him in 137. Years later Antiochus invaded Judea in force, wasted the land, and besieged John Hyrcanus in Jerusalem until terms were made.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arad-1692: Arad is a name the entry treats in two parts. First, it is a son of Beriah in the family list of Benjamin, in First Chronicles, chapter 8, verse 15. Second, it is a Canaanite city in the wilderness of Judah. Judges, chapter 1, ties the place to a Jewish win in fight, told also in Numbers. Later the Kenites lived there. Robinson matched the site with Tell Arad, southeast of Hebron, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aschenburg-simo:
Simon ben Isaac ha-Levi Aschenburg was a Talmudic scholar who lived at Frankfort-on-the-Main and later at Jerusalem. He died at Jerusalem about 1598. His book Debek Tob, A Good Bond, is a supercommentary, a commentary built on a commentary. It explains Rashi's notes on the Pentateuch. Aschenburg printed it himself for the first time at Venice in 1588.

The work proved useful enough to be reprinted often in later years. The entry gives little of the man beyond his two cities and his one book. A Frankfort scholar who ended his days in Jerusalem, he left his mark in the margins of Rashi, where students of the Torah text kept meeting his name long after 1588. His dates rest on the sources listed below his entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-simon:
Simon Ashkenazi of Galicia was rabbi of Dobromil and Jaroslav at the end of the eighteenth century and the start of the nineteenth. He was a disciple of Jacob Isaac of Lublin, who died in 1815. He carried on a learned exchange of letters with Jacob Meshullam Orenstein, chief rabbi of Lemberg, who died in 1839.

His book Nahalat Shimon, Simon's Inheritance, is a series of cabalistic discourses on the Pentateuch. It appeared in 1815, the year of his master's death, and a second edition came out at Lemberg in 1848. The entry rests on Benjacob's catalogue and Walden's Shem ha-Gedolim. It gives his two towns, his teacher, his correspondent, and his one book, and no birth or death dates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-atonement-2092:
Atonement means setting two estranged parties at one again. In the Authorized Version the word renders the Hebrew kapparah and kippurim. The entry first asks what the root meant at the start. One line of scholars links it to a Syriac word for wiping out. Another links it to kofer, a ransom or peace gift.

Kofer was the payment that settled a killing by a goring ox. No kofer could be taken for a murderer. Jacob used a gift to soften Esau's anger, in the same spirit. From there the entry moves to sacrifice. In the priestly laws the offering itself works as a kofer for the people. Later sections follow the idea into rabbinic and medieval teaching, where shame, confession, and a changed life come to stand at the center of atonement.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-az-shesh-meot-2:
Az Shesh Meot is a poem of three stanzas by R. Elias Priscus. It stands in the northern rite at the close of the poems in the Additional Service on the Feast of Weeks. The entry is about its music, not its words. Two tunes go with the poem, and both are borrowed from the music of the Days of Penitence. The more common one is taken whole from the prayer U-netanneh Toḳef.

That borrowing had a point, the entry explains. The poem sings of the giving of the Law. A cantor long ago set it to the tune of man's fate being written and sealed, to stress that fate hangs on obeying the Law. Inside that borrowed tune sits a shorter quote from the Kol Nidre melody. It lands where the older text names the Day of Atonement, the one day Kol Nidre is sung.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bacchides-2292:
Bacchides was a Syrian general and a friend of King Demetrius. Demetrius sent him in 161 B.C. to Judea with a large army. His task was to set the renegade Alcimus in the high priest's office. The Assideans trusted his oath. He broke it and slew sixty of them.

Bacchides came back after Nicanor fell to Judas Maccabeus. This time he led twenty thousand foot and two thousand horse. At Eleasa he met Judas, whose force had shrunk to eight hundred men. Judas routed the wing Bacchides led in person, but the other wing crushed him, and he died. Bacchides then set the Hellenists over Judea and ringed the land with forts. Beaten again and again by Simon, he at last made peace with Jonathan and went home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bakst-nicolai-i:
Nicolai Ignatyevich Bakst was a Russian physiologist born in 1843. He took a degree in natural science at St. Petersburg University in 1862. The Ministry of Public Instruction then sent him abroad for three years to prepare for a professorship. Back home he lectured at the university and, from 1881, to women medical students. In 1886 he joined the science committee of the ministry.

Most of the entry is a list of his writings. His early papers, printed at Berlin in 1867 and 1870, measured how fast a stimulus travels in human motor nerves. Later work treated sight, the heart's nerves, and the heat of the blood. He also wrote a course on the senses in 1886 and turned works by Ritter, Odling, and Schleiden into Russian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baraita-of-jose: Baraita of Joseph b. Uzziel is a cabalistic Baraita named more than once by Recanati. The hosted entry is only two lines long. It says the work lies in manuscript form at Oxford. It also says what the work is: a commentary to the Sefer Yeẓirah, the Book of Creation. A cross-reference sends readers to the entry on Joseph b. Uzziel himself. No date, contents, or extracts from the commentary are given in this short note.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruk-she-amar-:
Baruk She-Amar names the opening words of a benediction said before the Psalms in the daily morning service. The closing benediction is Yishtabbaḥ, and both come before the Shema. The prayer has two parts, a solemn invocation and the main benediction.

The entry traces the prayer's style to ancient Ḥasidean writers and notes its use in the gaonic period. It gives the full text in translation, with added responses shown in parentheses. It also notes that the Sephardic and German rites place and word the prayer in slightly different ways.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beaucroissant-2: Beaucroissant is a community in the canton of Rives, in the district of St. Marcellin, in Isère, France. The whole entry is a single short notice. It states that the locality was inhabited by Jews in the year 1337. No names, numbers, events, or later history are given for that community. The one source cited is a volume of a French journal of Jewish studies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berlin-moses-mo:
Moses Berlin, a scholar and government adviser, was born at Shklov, in Russia, in 1821. He died at St. Petersburg on March 25, 1888. After study at Königsberg and Bonn, he taught in a government Jewish school. From 1853 he advised the state on Jewish affairs, a post he kept at St. Petersburg.

He helped frame laws on the Jews and helped order the Imperial Public Library. His books include a study of the ways of Russian Jews, written for the Imperial Geographical Society. He also sat in two Jewish deputations to Russian emperors, in 1868 and 1881.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bet-talmud-3192: "Bet-Talmud" was a Hebrew monthly review. It was devoted to Talmudical and rabbinical studies. Isaac Hirsch Weiss and Meïr Friedmann founded it in 1881. They published it at Vienna. Weiss kept it going until 1886. Then the review was discontinued. Its contributors were leading Jewish scholars. The entry names Buber, Brüll, and A. Epstein. It also names Güdemann, Reifmann, and Schechter. Some of its articles were also printed separately.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bikhakhanim-329: Bikhakhanim was the reigning princess of the Taman peninsula. That land lies in the Crimea. In 1419 she married Simeone de Guizolfi. He was a Genoese Jew. The marriage made him possessor of that country. An heir, Zacharias, still reigned there in 1482. The historian Brun questioned her name. He suggested it was really Bikhakhatun. If so, she was a Georgian prince's daughter. Her father was Bek II, who died in 1391.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-louis-or-: Louis Bloch, also called Leo, was a Swiss educator. He was born in 1864. Since 1896 he has taught at Zurich's university. His post covers archeology and mythology. He writes widely on classical life and literature. His book on Eleusis treats its cult and mysteries. It appeared in 1896. His "Römische Altertumskunde" followed in 1898. That manual covers Roman institutions and customs fully. Private life, religion, and culture all appear there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonafos-or-en-b: Bonafos, or En Bonafos Alfaquin, gets only two lines here. He was a French physician who lived in the second half of the fourteenth century. His home was Perpignan, where he served as president of the community. The entry gives no works, family, or death date for him. It rests on a responsum of Nissim Gerondi and on Gross's Gallia Judaica for those bare facts alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bosnia-3592:
Bosnia is a province of the Balkan peninsula, on the frontier of Austria and Montenegro. It was formerly under Turkish rule. By the Treaty of Berlin in 1878 it came under Austria's protection.

Some historians date Jewish settlement there to 1575. Tombstones at Sarajevo dated 1551 point to an earlier presence, the entry notes. Merchants from Salonica traded at Sarajevo in 1541 without their families. In 1645 Jews won a special quarter of about 2,000 square meters. A cemetery grant followed from Suleiman the Magnificent. In 1901 about 7,500 Jews lived in the province, 4,000 of them at Sarajevo.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bresselau-meir-:
Meir Israel Bresselau was a German notary and secretary of the Reform congregation of Hamburg. He was born in 1785, the entry marks with a question, and died in Hamburg on Dec. 25, 1839.

Bresselau stood with Hamburg's Reform movement from its start. When Orthodox writers attacked the Hamburg temple in 1819, he answered them. His reply, a sword avenging the covenant, won praise even from Grätz for its Hebrew style. With Isaac Säckel Fränkel he also made the temple's Hebrew-German prayer book that year. Gabriel Riesser followed him as secretary of the congregation after his death in office there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bucuresteanu-bu: Abraham Cohen Bucuresteanu was a Rumanian publicist born at Bucharest in 1840. He loved the theater from youth and had some stage success, but family advice sent him into commerce. His wit produced satirical poems, epigrams, love songs, and stage skits. The public received them warmly from 1860 to 1874, and his songs were still heard in Bucharest in 1902. He himself printed only two books, in 1873 and 1874. He also founded the Zion Society, which grew into a B'nai B'rith lodge. He died at Bucharest on Jan. 24, 1877.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantor-jacob-a-:
Jacob A. Cantor was an American lawyer and politician born in New York city on Dec. 6, 1854. He took his law degree from the University of New York. He sat in the state assembly in 1887 and in the state senate from 1888 to 1898. There he chaired the finance committee and led the Democratic side. He presided over the senate in 1893 and 1894.

In 1901 a nonpartisan ticket made him president of the borough of Manhattan, an office ranked just below mayor. He backed good city government, public schools, and canal measures. In Jewish life he directed aid groups for prisoners and a protectory. His laws won equal worship rights for inmates of prisons and reformatories.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-casablanca-span:
Casablanca is a Moroccan port on the Atlantic Ocean. Its Jewish community, counted at 6,000 in a total of 20,000 people, was of recent date when the entry was written. Most members traded in grain and spices, and a few worked as tinsmiths. A council aided the poor and funded schools from meat tax income and gifts.

Schools included two run by the Alliance Israélite Universelle, with 295 boys and 161 girls, plus eight Talmud-Torahs with 500 pupils. The town held eleven synagogues. One, for the poor, dated to about 1750. Chief rabbis since 1837 are named in a short list ending with Isaac Marasch, still living in 1902. Three charitable societies are also named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-circumstantial-:
Circumstantial evidence means proof built from facts around a case rather than from direct witness words. The entry opens by correcting a common claim. Such evidence is often said to be barred under Jewish law, and the entry calls that assertion wrong. All proof, it argues, is circumstantial to some degree; direct and indirect proof differ only in how many links join fact to finding.

Mosaic law still demands two witnesses for every fact, and Talmudic law bars witnesses from patching each other's accounts. Yet courts may draw findings from facts once proved. The entry sorts criminal cases, where the two-witness rule holds firm, from civil ones, where one witness can shift an oath. Legal presumptions close the survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-levy-bare:
Levy Barent Cohen, an English financier and communal worker, was born at Amsterdam in 1740 and died in England in 1808. Son of a rich Amsterdam merchant, he moved to England with his brother and built a large London business by 1778. He was naturalized in 1798 and ranked among the city's leading merchants.

His charity work ran deep. He helped found the Bread, Meat, and Coal Charity and the Jews' Hospital, leading the first. Yet his lasting fame is family. The entry calls him founder of the Cohen family in England. His daughter Hannah married Nathan Mayer Rothschild. Judith married Sir Moses Montefiore. Other children wed into the Goldsmid, Samuel, and Lucas families.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-conferences-rab:
Conferences, Rabbinical, are assemblies of rabbis set on fixing shared courses of action or shared points of faith. They are a late growth in Jewish history, the entry stresses, starting only in the eighteen-forties. Earlier synods mixed rabbis with laymen, so they do not count here.

Emancipation forced the question. Freed from medieval law, Jews had to square old belief and practice with a new age. Five great conferences anchor the tale: Brunswick in 1844, Frankfort in 1845, Breslau in 1846, Philadelphia in 1869, and Pittsburg in 1885. Their platforms, printed at length, reframe exile as a mission to teach the nations. Later pages reach American unions of congregations and a New York convention of 1900 with 104 congregations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-costa-israele-d: Israele di Emanuele Costa was an Italian rabbi, born in 1819. He died in 1897. In 1864 he succeeded Abraham Baruch Piperno as rabbi of Leghorn. His works center on prayer books. He issued an annotated festival volume in 1869 and a full Sephardic prayer book with Italian rendering in 1892. He also printed the Zohar with vowel signs in 1888. Story books, a children's Hebrew grammar, and a Hebrew-Italian dictionary round out the list. He was a Freemason of the thirty-third degree.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cracow-polish-k:
Cracow, formerly the capital of the kingdom of Poland, was founded about 700 C.E. No records survive for its first Jews. They likely gained a foothold after 1311, when German residents lost favor with King Ladislaus. A massacre came in 1348, in the Black Death riots. By 1400 Jews owned stone houses in the city. Easter week riots in 1407 set the Jewish quarter ablaze.

The long article then runs for centuries. It covers royal charters, taxes, blood charges, and expulsions, town by town and reign by reign. Long lists name the rabbis of Cracow in order. Among them stand Joel Sirkes, Yom-Ṭob Lipman Heller, and Aaron Samuel Kaidanower. Community records and Polish chronicles support the whole account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-danon-yom-tob-4: Yom-Ṭob Danon was an author and a rabbi of Smyrna. He lived in the first half of the nineteenth century. In 1821 he went to Jerusalem. There he succeeded Joseph Ḥazan as chief rabbi. His work is Kebod Yom-Ṭob. It comments on the Yad ha-Ḥazaḳah, the great code of Maimonides. The book was printed at Salonica in 1846. The entry is only a few lines. It names no birth or death date and cites a single source. His son Berakah wrote on the same code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-davidson-andrew:
Andrew B. Davidson was professor of Hebrew and Oriental languages at New College, Edinburgh. Born at Kirkhill, in Aberdeenshire, Scotland, in 1831, he graduated from Aberdeen in 1849 and entered New College in 1852 to study for the ministry. He became Hebrew tutor there in 1858 and professor in 1863, by the unanimous vote of the Free Church Assembly.

Davidson wrote an elementary Hebrew grammar and a Hebrew syntax, plus commentaries on Job, Ezekiel, and other Bible books for the Cambridge Bible series. In 1871 he joined the Old Testament revision committee. He also wrote many major articles for Hastings' Bible Dictionary. He died at Edinburgh on January 26, 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dietary-laws-in:
Dietary laws in Islam are fewer and lighter than those in Judaism, this short study says. They entered the religious code only in the Medinian period of Mohammed's career. He had not wished to force food rules on poor converts at first. For the rules he did give, he followed Biblical models, and the entry quotes the Koran directly.

Carrion, blood, and swine's flesh are forbidden, as is meat hallowed to another god. Necessity excuses a breach. No clean animal is lawful unless God's name was spoken at its slaughter, so meat killed in the Jewish fashion is allowed. Fish and locusts are exempt from that rule, as in Jewish law. Wine was banned by slow stages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dosetai-or-dosi:
Dosetai, or Dositheus, is a Greek name matching the Hebrew Mattaniah or Nethaneel. The entry surveys many bearers of the name in Palestine and Alexandria. They range from a pupil of Shammai to later teachers. Sorting them out is the entry's main work.

Pride of place goes to Dosetai ben Jannai, a tanna of the late second century. He passed on sayings of Meïr and other masters. Ill-treated at Nehardea, he answered with a mocking portrait of its rulers. His wit shows in replies to pupils, including why Jerusalem lacks warm springs. A sermon of his praises almsgiving through a reading of the Psalms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elhanan-ben-isa: Elhanan ben Isaac of Dampierre was a tosafist and prayer poet. He was put to death as a martyr in 1184. On his grandmother's side he was a grand-nephew of Jacob Tam. Judah Sir Leon of Paris sat among his pupils. His father outlived him and added notes to his tosafot. Later rabbis treated Elhanan as a great authority. His other works deal with phylacteries and with the calendar. He also wrote verse for the eighth evening of Passover.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elkin-benjamin-: Benjamin Elkin was a reformer in the London Jewish world. He was born at Portsea on Jan. 9, 1783. He died in London in Jan. 1848. At twenty-one he sailed to Barbados to work as a watchmaker. He soon left that trade to become a general merchant. In a few years he stood among the richest merchants there. He worked to better the affairs of the Barbados flock. In 1830 he came home to England for good. There he backed a new synagogue with a more seemly service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephraem-syrus-5: Ephraem Syrus was a church father of Syria. He was born at Nisibis at the start of the fourth century. His surname Syrus marks that Syrian birth in Latin. His many works gloss the books of the Old Testament. He read them in the Syriac Peshitta text most days. Yet he knew Hebrew and went back to the source. His notes hold a great store of haggadot in them. One says the new grass at creation looked a month old. The trees looked a year old on that first day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-falk-hayyim-sam:
Hayyim Samuel Jacob Falk, called the Ba'al Shem of London, was an English cabalist and mystic born about 1708. He died in London on April 17, 1782. Writers split on his birthplace: Furth or Podolia. His diary survives, mixing dreams, charity records, angel names, and cooking recipes. Jacob Emden attacked him as a follower of the false messiah Shabbethai Zebi.

Falk claimed power to work wonders and to find hidden treasure. In Westphalia he was sentenced to burn as a sorcerer and escaped to England. London tales credited him with a taper that burned for weeks and a cellar filled with coal by a spell. When fire threatened the Great Synagogue, he was said to save it by writing four Hebrew letters on its door pillars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ferrara-moses-b: Moses ben Meir of Ferrara was an Italian tosafist of the thirteenth century, a peer of Eleazar ben Samuel and Isaiah ben Mali. No details of his life are known, the entry states plainly. He is quoted three times as a tosafist in Haggahot Maimuni, on prayer and on festival law. The same work says he copied R. Judah's tosafot to Berakot. That copying note and those three quotes are the whole record the entry can give. Its sources are Mortara, Zunz, Heilprin, Benjacob, and Gudemann.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-flood-the-hebr-:
The Flood, told in Genesis, came when God resolved to destroy mankind for its wickedness. Noah and his family alone were spared. Pairs of every living kind were saved with them. Noah built a huge ark at God's command. When the waters fell, the ark rested on a mountain of Ararat. Noah sent out a raven and then doves. The second dove came back with an olive leaf. The third did not return, a sign the ground was dry.

Noah then offered sacrifice, and God promised not to curse the earth again. The rainbow marked his covenant with Noah's seed. Rabbinic tales add a respite of 120 years for repentance and list the sins of that age. Later sections weigh the two Bible accounts against each other. They also compare the Babylonian flood tale and the telling in the Koran.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankel-hirsch-: Hirsch Fränkel was chief rabbi in the margravate of Ansbach, with his seat at Schwabach, from 1709 to 1713. He died in prison in 1723. He was a brother of Elkan Fränkel. With his brother he was accused of holding blasphemous and superstitious books. After a searching inquiry, and by the judgment of the University of Altorf, he was sentenced to imprisonment for life. The brief entry gives no further facts of his life or work. One short source line closes it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedrichstadt-:
Friedrichstadt was a town in Courland, Russia, where 3,800 of its 5,223 people in 1897 were Jews. A Jewish community formed there near the end of the seventeenth century. Settlers came from towns in Lithuania and from White Russia. Rapids in the River Duna above the town made it a handy stopping place on trips downriver toward Riga.

Trade shapes most of the account. Jews carried lumber, grain, hides, furs, and bristles toward Riga and to buyers abroad. Floods in 1771 and 1837 swept away much of the town. Factories later made cigars, soap, needles, and chocolate. After the Riga-Dunaburg Railroad opened in 1862, the town lost trade ground, though its people kept growing in number.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gamala-6492:
Gamala, a city in Palestine across Lake Tiberias from Taricheae, took its name from a camel-like spur of rock. Its site was strong by nature. A road reached it only from the south, where a ditch had been cut across. A high hill on that side added defense. A well lay inside the wall.

Alexander Jannaeus took the fort, and Gamala stayed a Jewish holding. In the great war it first held to Rome, then revolted and was walled by Josephus. Agrippa men failed to take it. Vespasian force broke in at last on the 23rd of Tishri in 68. The Romans killed all the people inside, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gittin-plural-o:
Giṭṭin, whose name means "documents," is a treatise of the Mishnah and Tosefta, worked out in both the Palestinian and Babylonian Gemaras. It sits in the third order, Nashim (Women), though its place shifts between editions. Its nine chapters deal mainly with one kind of document, the geṭ, or bill of divorce.

Chapter by chapter, the entry sets out rules on carrying a geṭ from another country, the witnesses who must sign it, and writing it for one named woman only. Later chapters cover delivery, conditions, and errors that void the document. The entry also notes side discussions, from a mother's sacrifice story to a long passage on illness in the Babylonian Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grossmann-ignaz:
Ignaz Grossmann was an American rabbi. He was born at Trencsen, Hungary, on July 30, 1825. He died in New York city on March 18, 1897. Presburg's yeshibah educated him. In 1863 Koritschan in Moravia called him as rabbi. He moved to Warasdin, Croatia, in 1866. In 1873 Brooklyn called him, and he served two congregations there.

His last book, "Miḳraot Ḳeṭannot" (1892), presents all 613 commandments. It gives their Bible base, rabbinic sense, and moral lesson. He wrote often for "Deborah." Three of his sons became rabbis, the entry notes. Louis Grossmann of Cincinnati is one of them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-habinenu-6992:
Habinenu is the first word, and so the name, of a short prayer. It packs the Eighteen Benedictions into brief form, leaving out the first three and the last three. Samuel of Nehardea framed it for times when the full prayer cannot be said. It may not replace the full form at a Sabbath close or when rain is prayed for.

The entry gives the prayer's full text in English. It asks God for insight into His ways, pardon, safety from pain, and a homecoming from the four corners of the earth. It asks joy for the just in a rebuilt city and Temple. The Jerusalem Talmud's version differs a bit from the Babylonian one in common use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halevy-jacques-:
Jacques François Fromenthal Élie Halévy, born at Paris on May 27, 1799, was a French composer who died at Nice on March 17, 1862. His family name was Levi, and his father Élie was a Bavarian by birth. He entered the Paris Conservatoire at ten and studied with Cazot, Lambert, and Berton. Under Cherubini he won the Grand Prix de Rome in 1819.

Years of small success followed his return from Italy. Then, on Feb. 23, 1835, the Opéra staged his "La Juive." The five-act grand opera, mounted at a fabled cost, won him a European name at once. "L'Eclair," its light opposite, followed ten months later and also won Paris. Later operas, about twenty in all, seldom matched those two. He taught at the Conservatoire from 1851; Gounod and Bizet were his pupils. In 1854 he became permanent secretary of the Académie des Beaux-Arts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanau-solomon-b:
