Solomon ben Judah Hanau, a German grammarian, was born at Hanau in 1687. He died at Hanover Sept. 4, 1746. At twenty-one he published a Hebrew grammar at Frankfort-on-the-Main. It sharply criticized the ancient grammarians. The resentment forced him to attach a retractation to every copy. His Frankfort position still failed. He taught seventeen years at Hamburg. Then fresh criticism of a prayer-book drove him out again.

He moved through Amsterdam and Fürth to Berlin and Hanover, fighting polemical bouts along the way. His works include "Binyan Shelomoh" (1708) and "Sha'are Torah" (1718). He also wrote "Sha'are Tefillah" (1725) and "Yesod ha-Nikkud" (1730). Later came "Zohar ha-Tebah" (1733) and the reply "Kure 'Akkabish" (1744). A commentary on the Midrash Rabbah was published in 1777.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hartog-numa-edw:
Numa Edward Hartog, born in London on May 20, 1846, was the first Jewish senior wrangler at Cambridge. He swept prizes at school and at University College, London, winning scholarships again and again. He entered Trinity College in 1865. In January 1869 he placed first in the mathematics honors list.

A religious test still barred him from a fellowship. Hartog spoke before a House of Lords committee in the drive to end such tests. His plain evidence helped pass the Universities Tests Act in 1871. He died that same year, on June 19, at the age of twenty-five.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heilprin-7492:
Heilprin traces four branches of a far-flung Ashkenazic family. The oldest line runs back to Zebulun Eliezer. His son Moses of Brest-Litovsk wrote a book printed at Lublin in 1611. Other branches produced rabbis, community heads, and leaders of the Four Lands.

One branch centers on Odessa, where Jehiel Hirsch Heilprin served as rabbi until 1877. Another produced Jehiel of Minsk, author of the chronicle "Seder ha-Dorot." Two wonder-working rabbis called Baal Shem also appear. The entry warns that Heilprins in many towns need not be kin. Governments forced set family names on Jews late in the eighteenth century, and names were taken up loosely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hildesheim-7692:
Hildesheim is a town in the Prussian province of Hanover whose Jewish history runs through repeated exile and return. Jews are taxed there in a document of Jan. 7, 1347. The town counts among Black Death martyr cities of 1349. Jews settled again by 1351.

A synagogue was allowed in 1385 on town land. After agreements on family numbers and taxes, all Jews were exiled in 1457 and the synagogue torn down. Returns and fresh expulsions followed in 1520, 1595, and later. A court win let Jews return in 1601. Protection was bought again in 1660. Full relief came only with the law of Sept. 30, 1842.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horwitz-zebi-hi: Zebi Hirsch ben Phinehas Horwitz was rabbi at Frankfort-on-the-Main. He died there on September 8, 1817. He had followed his father in the Frankfort rabbinate in 1805. Three printed works bear his name. Mahaneh Lewi, a book of legal novellae, came out at Offenbach in 1801. Lahme Todah, which completes it, followed in 1816. Novellae of his also appear in his father's Ketubah. Carmoly reported two more works in manuscript, one of responsa and one on Bible passages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-immortality-of-:
Immortality of the soul is the belief that the soul lives on after the body breaks up. The article says Scripture nowhere teaches it outright. Early thought made the soul a breath bound to the blood. When God's breath left, the soul sank to Sheol, a shadowy place without life or sense.

Hope grew by slow steps. Psalms voice trust that God's power reaches even Sheol. Persian ideas, joined to messianic hope, brought belief in resurrection. Greek thought, above all Plato, then gave the Jews the doctrine of the soul's own deathless life. Wisdom and the Maccabee books place the righteous with God in heaven. Rabbinic talk of the world to come left the hope an endless vista.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-leon-ben-: Isaac Leon ben Eliezer ibn Zur, called Sefardi, was a rabbi at Ancona in the first half of the sixteenth century. His Spanish family had settled in Italy after the expulsion from Spain. He wrote "Megillat Ester," defending Maimonides' "Sefer ha-Mitzwot" against Nahmanides' criticisms; it was printed at Venice in 1592 and twice reprinted. In 1546 he joined a halakic ruling in a lawsuit, but the bet din of Rome reversed it. Both ruling and reversal were printed at Rome that year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-samuel-b:
Israel Samuel ben Solomon was a Polish Talmudic and halakic author who lived at Cracow about 1620. His father was a physician of Spanish origin. About 1624 Israel wrote the "Yismah Yisrael," printed at Cracow in 1626. It sums up the rulings of all four parts of the Shulhan Aruk in alphabetical order, and it also holds a mystical prayer.

His other writings run wide. A small book treats the laws of keeping the Sabbath. A large halakic work, built on the Talmud, the Tosafot, and the later authorities, follows the Shulhan Aruk in four parts, each with its own title. He also wrote a mystical commentary on the Pentateuch, a commentary on Pirke Abot, and a treatise on hard haggadic passages and midrashim. More works of his, the entry says, were named in his first book's introduction but never printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-aberle-ab: Jacob Aberle, also called Abril, Benedict, or Benet, was rabbi at Alt-Ofen at the start of the nineteenth century. He was a son of Mordecai b. Abraham Benet. His one book, "Toledot Mordekai Benet," printed at Alt-Ofen in 1832, is half memorial and half archive. Its first part gives his father's life. Its second gathers the father's own writings: notes on Bible passages, a reading of the dayyenu song, a sermon from 1826, and novellae. The entry praises the biography's pure, easy Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jadassohn-josef: Josef Jadassohn, a German physician, was born at Liegnitz on Sept. 10, 1863. He studied at Göttingen, Breslau, Heidelberg, and Leipsic, taking his degree at Breslau in 1886. From 1887 to 1896 he worked at Breslau skin clinics, ending as physician-in-chief at the Allerheiligen Hospital. In 1896 he became director of the skin clinic at the University of Bern, and in 1904 he rose to professor there. He wrote many essays on syphilis and skin disease and a handbook chapter on venereal diseases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jeremiah-b-abba: Jeremiah ben Abba was a Babylonian teacher of religious law in the third century and a pupil and fellow of Rab. He gave himself chiefly to the Halakah, the legal side of study. Still, the entry also cites him on story and teaching, mostly in the Babylonian Talmud's tractate Sanhedrin. One sample has him explain why no Bible book bears Nehemiah's name: Nehemiah had claimed credit for his own deeds. Another saying of his bars four classes of people from the divine presence: scorners, liars, deceivers, and slanderers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-job-8692:
Job is the hero of the Book of Job. A native of Uz, he was rich, pious, and upright, with seven sons and three daughters. Each week he offered sacrifices for his sons, in case they had sinned while feasting. In the heavenly council the accuser Satan claimed Job would sin if struck by loss, and God let him test that claim.

Satan first took Job's wealth and children, then smote Job himself with a painful disease. Job would not curse God, even at his wife's urging. Three friends sat with him in silence for seven days, and then the long debates of the book begin. At the end God restored him with twice his former wealth. Rabbinic views on whether Job ever lived close the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jose-joseph-ben: Jose ben Johanan was president of the Sanhedrin in the second century before the common era. A native of Jerusalem, he and Jose b. Joezer formed the first pair of leaders who passed on the traditional law. In each pair, one man served as president and the other as vice-president. His saying taught men to keep an open house and treat the needy as household members. A split between the two colleagues over legal rulings led to two schools. Both men opposed Hellenism and belonged to the Hasidim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-juniper-9092: Juniper is the old standard rendering of the Hebrew word rotem in three Bible places. The entry argues that rotem is surely the Arabic ratam, a kind of broom. The shrub meant is likely Genista roetam, native to Sinai and Arabia Petraea. It climbs ten to twelve feet and gives welcome shade in the desert. Its coals burn long and hot, which fits a verse in Psalms. A hard verse in Job speaks of its roots as food, though the roots cannot be eaten.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kann-moses-9192:
Moses Kann was a German rabbi who died at Frankfort-on-the-Main on Dec. 1, 1762. His father was Löb Kann. He led the Jews of Hesse-Darmstadt as chief rabbi. He also headed the Talmud school at Frankfort. His father-in-law, Samson Wertheimer of Vienna, had founded and endowed that school. Under Kann it thrived for more than fifty years.

Kann and Wertheimer paid for a new edition of the Talmud. A baptized Jew denounced the books, and they were seized. Kann fought the charge before the Elector of Mayence. Christian scholars backed his case with sworn words. On Aug. 1, 1753, the Imperial Court lifted the seizure order. The entry also tells of his charity funds. His bequest paid students of the Torah from its interest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ketubot-9292:
Ketubot is a treatise found in the Mishnah, the Tosefta, and both Talmuds. It stands second in the order Nashim. It is split into thirteen chapters with 101 paragraphs in all. Its theme is the marriage contract and the rights that flow from it. The entry gives a chapter-by-chapter outline of the whole.

Early chapters fix the wedding day and the sums owed to brides. Middle chapters treat fines, dowries, and the duties of husband and wife. Later ones treat the widow's rights and the sale of her claim. The Tosefta adds notes on old wedding customs in Judea and Galilee. Both Talmuds swell the text with stories and sayings. The entry quotes sharp maxims from its pages, on shame, on judging, and on lending books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lamed-9592: Lamed is the twelfth letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and the entry gives its sound and number value in a few lines. The meaning of its name is uncertain. The letter is a liquid, sounded like the English l. It swaps with other liquids and half vowels at times. It can also sit inside a root to build four-letter words from three-letter ones. In late usage, as a numeral, it stands for 30. For the letter's shape the entry points to the article on the alphabet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-joseph-leo:
Joseph Leonard Levy, an American rabbi, was born on Nov. 24, 1865, in London. He studied at Jews' College and University College in London and took further degrees in England and Pennsylvania. He served pulpits at Bristol from 1885 to 1889 and at Sacramento from 1889 to 1893.

Levy then worked in Philadelphia, where he helped set up Jewish charities and societies. In 1898 he served as a chaplain in the Spanish-American war. Since 1901 he has been rabbi of Rodeph Shalom in Pittsburg. He turned the tractate Rosh ha-Shanah into English in 1895. His many books include prayer books, works for children, and eight volumes of Sunday lectures.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lindau-baruch-b: Baruch ben Judah Löb Lindau, a German mathematician, was born at Hanover in 1759. He died at Berlin on Dec. 5, 1849. He wrote "Reshit Limmudim," a textbook of natural science. Its first part treats physics and geography. It came out at Berlin in 1789 and was reprinted at Brünn and Cracow. A second part, on natural philosophy, came out at Dessau in 1810 with added matter by another hand. A full edition appeared at Lemberg in 1869. He also wrote a wedding song in honor of a Hanover namesake.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lolli-eude-1009: Eude Lolli was an Italian rabbi born at Göritz on Aug. 23, 1826. He trained at the rabbinical college of Padua and graduated in 1854. In 1865 he became professor at that college and held the post until it closed in 1871. He was elected chief rabbi of Padua in 1869. Later he taught Hebrew at the University of Padua, becoming full professor in 1886. He wrote a dictionary and a Hebrew grammar and helped with an Italian Bible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mahoza-i-e-the-:
Mahoza, a Babylonian city on the Tigris, is described in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Its name simply means the City. It stood three parasangs south of Ctesiphon, by the royal canal. The article says it seems to have been inhabited solely by Jews. One sage marveled that its gates bore no mezuzah.

The entry paints a rich and sometimes scolded community. Many residents descended from converts, and rabbis denounced their luxury and drinking. Yet the same people were praised as intelligent and charitable. Mahoza held an academy that flowered under Raba in the fourth century. It rivaled Pumbedita and may fairly be called a home of the Talmud. Rome destroyed the city in 363, but it rose again as capital of a small Jewish state. That state fell when Persia's king Kobad executed its exilarch around 520.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marc-charles-ch:
Charles Chretien Henri Marc, a French physician, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Amsterdam on November 4, 1771, he took his medical degree at Erlangen in 1792. He practiced at Vienna, Bamberg, and in Bohemia. He died in Paris on January 12, 1841. The entry notes that he embraced Christianity.

The article follows his hard climb in Paris medicine. He arrived in 1795 and helped found the Societe Medicale d'Emulation. After years of struggle his books made his name secure. He joined the Board of Health in 1816 and the Academy of Medicine at its founding. In 1829 he co-founded the Annales d'Hygiene Publique, a leading journal of public health. After the July Revolution he became first physician to King Louis Philippe. His last great work studied madness in its legal bearings. It was among the first to link crime and insanity, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mattithiah-kart:
Mattithiah Kartin, also known as Ibn Harton, was a scholar of the fourteenth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906, and it is mostly a trail of maybes. His one firm achievement is dated exactly: in 1363 he turned the “Guide for the Perplexed” of Maimonides into Hebrew verse. Whether that work survives, the entry cannot say. It would survive only if its author is the same man as a Mattithiah of Monte Politiano whose verse rests in the Vatican library.

Steinschneider, the bibliographer, is shown contradicting himself about the piece. He called it first a versified Guide and later a verse commentary on it. A poem in another Vatican manuscript carries the name of Mattithiah in acrostic. The entry ends by wondering about one more match. Was he the Italian liturgist whose three dirges are kept at Parma, a man Zunz placed two centuries later?
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-merari-moses-me: Moses Menahem Merari was poet and chief rabbi of Venice in the seventeenth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn notice him briefly in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was one of the rabbis who signed the decision concerning the stores in Ferrara. A Hebrew poem of his, a "Shir," is preserved in the "Hanukkat ha-Bayit" of Moses Hefez. That book was printed at Venice in 1696. The bibliography names Fürst's Bibliotheca Judaica, Mortara's Indice, and Nepi-Ghirondi's history of Italy's great men. The rest of his record lies there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michal-lit-rivu:
Michal, the younger daughter of King Saul, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Joseph Jacobs and J. S. Raisin, published in 1906. She fell in love with David after her sister Merab, promised to him first, was given to another man. Saul agreed to the match but set a grim bride-price: a hundred Philistines slain.

David killed twice that number and married her, and Michal soon saved his life, lowering him through a window and tricking Saul's messengers with an image in his bed. Given meanwhile to Phalti, she was claimed back by David once he had power. The article ends with the Ark's arrival at Zion, where an incident between them strained the marriage, probably to separation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mizpah-mizpeh-1:
Mizpah, the watch-place, is the name of several towns and heights in biblical Palestine. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn untangle them in a Jewish Encyclopedia article published in 1906. The name comes from a Hebrew root meaning to look. The Septuagint renders it as lookout or vision. Mizpeh of Gilead, Mizpeh of Moab, and towns of Judah and of Benjamin all share it.

The first Mizpah is the famous one. On Mount Gilead, Jacob and Laban raised a heap of stones as witness to their pact. They called the place Mizpah for the words, the Lord watch between me and thee. The article identifies that site with the Mizpeh of Gilead. It follows the name through Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Chronicles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-b-isaa:
Mordecai ben Isaac of Carpentras was a French Talmudist of the turn of the fourteenth century, noticed by Solomon Schechter and A. Peiginsky in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Carpentras through the religious struggles of 1303 to 1306 and corresponded with Abba Mari of Lunel, who speaks of him very highly. Isaac de Lattes called him Gaon.

The entry's real work is disentangling him from namesakes. Zunz and Neubauer made him Mordecai ben Isaac Ezobi, but Ezobi lived at Carcassonne, not Carpentras; Gross instead identifies him with Mordecai ben Isaac Ḳimḥi, father of Isaac Ḳimḥi. Adret's manuscript responsa quote him often as simply Mordecai ben Isaac, and Kore ha-Dorot styles him the Ornament of Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-isaac:
Moses ben Isaac Leoni was an Italian scholar and Talmudist born at Urbino on November 30, 1566. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. At thirteen he became the pupil of Jedidiah of Rimini. He died in 1641, leaving his work mostly in manuscript.

One Bodleian manuscript gathers much of it: notes on the treatise Hullin, notes on Alfasi, and remarks on Talmudic tales in the En Ya'akov. A responsum of his survives inside another man's book. He also proved, in a note sent to Isaac Finzi, that the angles of a triangle equal two right angles. The entry preserves a scholar known through one manuscript bundle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mouse-hebr-akba:
The mouse, in Hebrew 'akbar, gets its own short article in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, by Solomon Schechter and I. M. Casanowicz. In Leviticus the mouse is listed among the unclean creeping things. In First Samuel, mice are the plague sent on the Philistines to ravage their fields.

The Talmud's mouse is broader than ours: it can mean the rat and other small rodents. The rabbis sort house mice, field mice, and water mice, and call the creature malicious, since it destroys cloth and wood without profit. They warn that food a mouse has gnawed weakens the memory. Their proverb runs: not the mouse is the thief, but the hole that receives the goods.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahum-11292: Nahum was a liturgical poet who lived about 1300, probably in southern Spain. The Jewish Encyclopedia gives him a brief notice by Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling. The article credits him with unusual talent. Michael Sachs translated some of his poems into German and printed them; the rest survive only in manuscript. He is not the twelfth-century Italian poet of the same name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-navigation-1139:
Navigation treats seafaring among Israelites and later Jews. Emil G. Hirsch, Wilhelm Nowack, Joseph Jacobs, and the Editorial Board wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Ancient Israel held the sea coast only briefly. Its shore south of Carmel had poor natural harbors. The Jordan, swift and rocky, could not carry boats.

The only known Hebrew sea trips sailed the Red Sea. They left Ezion-geber and Elath with Phoenician help. Phoenicians also floated Solomon's cedar rafts down the coast. Later, Jewish pirates troubled seas in Pompey's time. Talmud law covers buying a ship with masts and ropes. Alexandrian Jews led the Red Sea trade of their day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-new-mexico-1149:
New Mexico drew Jewish settlers with the Santa Fé trade. Cyrus Adler and Jacob H. Kaplan wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The territory passed from Mexico in 1848. Jacob Spiegelberg reached Santa Fé two years earlier, in 1846. Other pioneers included the Ilfeld, Rosenwald, and Seligman brothers.

Several settlers served with honor in the Civil War. H. N. Jaffa became Albuquerque's first mayor there. Albuquerque formed a B'nai B'rith lodge in 1882. Its Congregation Albert followed in 1897. Las Vegas held the territory's oldest congregation, from 1884. Its temple honored Montefiore's hundredth birthday in 1886. Santa Fé's Jews dwindled after the railroad passed it by. Some 700 to 800 Jews lived territory-wide.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-north-carolina-:
North Carolina is one of the thirteen original states. Cyrus Adler wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Isaac Harby counted some 400 Jews there in 1826. Wilmington was the state's chief Jewish town then. Aaron Lazarus and Aaron Riviera settled there first.

Lazarus, born at Charleston in 1777, backed railroads. Riviera kept cash at the Bank of Fear. A burial society formed at Wilmington in 1852. Its congregation took shape fifteen years later. As Temple of Israel it was organized in 1873. Its synagogue was dedicated three years after that. Smaller bodies dotted the state from Asheville to Tarboro. Goldsboro and Statesville founded congregations in 1883. Raleigh's Jewish cemetery dates from 1870 instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-olmutz-11692:
Olmütz is a city of Moravia, now part of the Czech lands. Gotthard Deutsch and Alexander Kisch wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there as early as the twelfth century. In 1454 they were cast out of the city. John Capistrano had stirred ill will against them.

The town gave their synagogue and burial ground to the city. For ages just one or two Jewish homes were let stay. New laws in 1848 and 1860 let Jews return. They soon grew strong in the life of the town. Worship began in rented halls in the year 1859. A fine new synagogue was opened in April 1897. Its first rabbi was Dr. Berthold Oppenheim, the piece notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-osterberg-max-1: Max Osterberg was an American engineer in the field of power. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Frankfurt am Main in 1869. He came to New York with his parents in 1884. In 1891 he took up the study of the new power. He left Columbia as an engineer in the year 1894. He wrote an index of works on that field and a text book on heat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pappenheim-1189:
Pappenheim is a small town in Mittelfranken, in Bavaria. Gotthard Deutsch and Moses Löb Bamberger wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It holds one of the oldest Jewish groups in Bavaria. Jews must have lived there before the year 1334. In that year a king backed a lord's old rights there.

Those rights held the guard of the Jews in his care. After Jews were cast out of Spain, many came north. They came by way of Italy into the German lands. The Pappenheim group grew much with those new folk. They formed their own flock, or swayed the old one. They brought the Venetian rite of prayer with them. That rite is still in use at Pappenheim today. The oldest grave stone there dates from 1357 or 1358.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peiser-simon-b-:
Simon ben Judah Löb Peiser was a rabbi in Lissa. He was born at Peisern, in Poland, about 1690. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He built a lasting reference work on the Talmud.

His book, Nahalat Shim'oni, runs to four planned sections. The first lists every person named in the Bible. It gathers the tales told about them in rabbinic books. The next sections list the teachers of the Mishnah and the Talmud. Only the first two parts were printed, at Wandsbeck in 1728.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pheroras-12092:
Pheroras was the youngest brother of Herod the Great. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His parents were Antipater and Cypros. He died in 5 BCE, before the family's worst years. Herod trusted him with forts and family alike.

Pheroras rebuilt the fortress of Alexandrium for Herod. He guarded the royal family at Masada in danger. At court he joined plots against Herod's sons by Mariamne. The Pharisees even told him he was the Messiah. Herod still made him tetrarch of Perea in 20 BCE.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pithom-lxx-1219:
Pithom was a store city built by Hebrew slave labor. The Executive Committee and J. F. McLaughlin wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Exodus names it beside Raamses in Egypt. Its site stayed lost for many centuries. Greeks later called the place Heroopolis.

In 1883 Naville found the ruins in the Wady Tumilat. Walls, a temple, and odd brick chambers emerged. The chambers opened only at the top. They were granaries for an army on campaign. The name means house of the sun god Atum. The find points to Rameses as Israel's oppressor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-proser-moser-12:
Moser Proser was a Russian writer in Hebrew, born at Keidani in 1840. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He had the common Hebrew schooling of his time. He learned Talmud in one yeshivah after another. In 1858 he went to Wilna to enter its rabbinical school.

His father's bar and his own poor health stopped that plan. Proser went home again for a time. In 1863 he settled at Kovno as a Hebrew teacher. There he came to know the writer Abraham Mapu. His own writing life began in those years. He wrote at first under false names in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ratisbonne-mari:
Marie-Théodore Ratisbonne was a French convert to Catholicism born on December 18, 1802. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Strasburg, son of its Jewish consistory president. He died at Paris on January 10, 1884.

The article says he practiced law until his conversion in 1826. He then took holy orders in the Catholic Church. He taught, served at Strasburg Cathedral, and led an order. He founded Notre Dame de Sion after his brother converted. His books include a history of Saint Bernard in two volumes. Later works answer Jewish questions of his day. The entry follows a lawyer turned priest and writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rodenberg-juliu:
Julius Rodenberg was a German poet and author born on June 26, 1831. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Rodenberg in Hesse. He studied law at four universities.

The article says he soon left law for literature. His first poem, Dornröschen, appeared at Bremen in 1851. From 1855 to 1862 he traveled widely in Europe. He settled in Berlin in 1859. He coedited a salon journal from 1867 to 1874. In 1874 he founded the Deutsche Rundschau. He received the title Professor in 1897. His works include songs, travel books, and London sketches. His novels include a tale of the Franco-Prussian war. The entry shows a traveler turned leading Berlin editor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosin-heinrich-:
Heinrich Rosin was a German jurist born at Breslau on September 14, 1855. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He began teaching law at Breslau in 1880 as a privat-docent.

In 1883 Rosin accepted a call to the University of Freiburg. There he rose in time to a full professorship in law. His books reach back to legal terms in medieval law books. Others treat Prussian police rules and the law of public associations. He also wrote on labor insurance and on proportional elections. A late work builds a theory of the state from Bismarck's speeches.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sahagun-sant-fa:
Sahagun is a city in the old Spanish kingdom of Leon. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In 1152 King Alfonso VII granted its thirty Jewish families Leon's privileges.

By the time of Alfonso X the community had grown considerable. An edict of 1255 put Sahagun's Jews level with those of Carrion. They had their own judges, appointed by the rabbis of Burgos. Mixed disputes went instead to the city's Christian alcaldes. A Jew chosen by the abbot presided over the Jewish court itself. For these rights the Jews paid the abbot a special tax.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-bar-ashe: Samuel bar Asher was a Jewish martyr of Neuss, in Rhenish Prussia, in the eleventh century. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. On St. John's Day, June 24, 1096, he and his two sons were murdered. One account says Samuel and one son were buried on the river bank, while the other son's body was hanged at his father's door. Another report says neither son was buried at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saragossa-spani:
Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Saragossa. The city, Roman Cæsaraugusta, stands on the Ebro in Spain. It was the capital of the old kingdom of Aragon. Jews lived there from a very early time. By the tenth century they formed a thriving congregation.

Civil wars under Sulaiman drove scholars to Saragossa in 1012. Ibn Janaḥ, Ibn Gabirol, and Moses ibn Gikatilla found welcome there. Jekuthiel ibn Ḥasan rose high under King Yaḥya, like Samuel ha-Nagid at Granada. Aragon's kings took the city in 1118. Alfonso the First granted the Jews privileges. James the First later declared all Jews his property. Judah de Cavallería, the richest Jew in Aragon, served as head bailiff for decades. The article maps the walled Jewish quarter street by street.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schnitzler-joha:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Johann Schnitzler. He was an Austrian laryngologist, a doctor of the throat. Schnitzler was born at Nagy-Kanizsa, in Hungary, on April 10, 1835. He died at Vienna on May 2, 1893. He studied at the University of Vienna. He took his degree in 1860 and assisted under Oppolzer.

In 1866 Vienna granted Schnitzler the right to lecture. He became a titular professor in 1878. In 1880 he was named assistant professor of laryngoscopy. From 1888 he ran the general dispensary. In 1860 he co-founded the Wiener Medizinische Presse. He edited that journal until 1886. His books treat the air-pressure cure for lung and heart disease. Others cover the use of the laryngoscope and rhinoscope. He also wrote on lung syphilis and consumption.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-segre-13392:
Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on the Segre family. The Segres were an Italian family of scholars. Abraham ben Judah Segre, called Rab ASI, was a rabbi in Casale. He worked across the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. He studied under Judah Briel. His friends included Judah Finzi and Benjamin Kohn.

A responsum of Abraham's on the defilement of the tent survives in Lampronti's work. He also wrote a poem on a plague's ravages. Its four cantos open and close with phrases from the Middot. A second Abraham ben Judah Segre was born at Turin. He moved to Safed at twenty-five to study. He died there in 1772, leaving commentaries and ten sons. The entry lists more Segres of Alexandria, Parma, and Vercelli.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shalom-abraham-:
Abraham ben Isaac ben Judah ben Samuel Shalom was an Italian scholar and theologian who died in 1492. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Joseph Loeb Sossnitz wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His book Neweh Shalom set Bible and Talmud study above philosophy. He still allowed inquiry as a needed aid to scripture.

Abraham also translated a Latin work on logic into Hebrew. He added his own preface to that translation. De Rossi credits him with notes on al-Ghazali's natural philosophy as well. The entry, though brief, shows a thinker defending tradition while using the tools of philosophy. He wanted reason to serve faith, not rule it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-she-elot-u-tesh:
She'elot u-Teshubot means questions and answers, the Hebrew name for rabbinic responsa. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on this literature. Responsa are written rulings sent by eminent rabbis to those who asked. Heads of academies and teachers answered questions sent in writing.

Such answers form their own class of rabbinic writing. They differ in shape from commentaries and from law codes. Yet they cover much of the same ground as both. Questions ranged far beyond daily law, the entry notes. They touched philosophy, astronomy, mathematics, calendars, and geography. Hard Bible passages came up often too. Readers see a mail-based system that spread Jewish learning for centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-he-hasid:
Simeon he-Hasid, called the Pious, was a tanna whose time of activity is not known. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. He is not named in the Mishnah at all. Only one saying of his survives, kept in a baraita.

That saying deals with a verse in Job about the ages before Sinai. It claims that 974 generations meant to come before the Law were spread among later ages instead. Those generations, he taught, became the bold and rude people found in every age. Readers get a brief look at how rabbis read gaps in the biblical count of years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sixtus-senensis:
Sixtus Senensis was an Italian convert and anti-Talmudic agitator born in 1520. Isidore Singer and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He took his name from Sienna, his birthplace. After his conversion he entered the Franciscan order. Charged with heterodoxy, he was sentenced to burn at the stake.

Cardinal Ghislieri, later Pope Pius V, saved his life. Sixtus then entered the Dominican order instead. At Paul IV's command he preached in synagogues across Italy. In 1559 he went to Cremona to burn the Talmud. Yet he spared the Zohar from the flames that day. His Bibliotheca Sancta treated the divisions and authority of the Bible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-shalem-:
Solomon Shalem ben Hayyim Jehiel Cohen was a rabbi of the eighteenth century. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Amsterdam in 1781. He lived at Adrianople, Bologna, Sofia, and Amsterdam in turn. At Amsterdam he served as rabbi of the Portuguese community.

His Dibre Shelomoh held sermons on the Pentateuch. It appeared at Amsterdam in 1753. His Shoneh Halakot commented on the Halakot Gedolot in 1762. His Leb Shalem gave notes on Maimonides' Yad ha-Hazakah. That work appeared in 1773, also at Amsterdam. The entry lists book titles and dates for his three works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-statistics-1399:
Statistics, as to Jews, deal mainly with population and its spread. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Other topics include ages, migration, sickness, and death rates. Occupations, crime, births, and marriages also fall under the head. Most of those topics are treated elsewhere in the encyclopedia.

Ancient figures for Jewish numbers are few and disputed. The Exodus count implies about three million people in all. David's census implies a population of over five million. Only 42,360 exiles are said to have returned from Babylon. Josephus gives 1,100,000 people in Jerusalem at its fall. The article shows such numbers cannot be taken at face value.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-styria-14092:
Styria is an Austrian province with an old Jewish presence. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Records first name Jews there at Judenburg in 1075. Town names like Judendorf still mark early settlement. A Jewish cemetery stood at Marburg for centuries.

Organized communities sat at Graz, Judenburg, and Marburg. Graz Jews lived in a special quarter of town. At Judenburg one Jew owned six houses in 1460. Local Jews farmed and built roads as well as traded. A Judenburg church was once a synagogue, sources say. Its stones still bear Hebrew inscriptions. In 1238 Frederick the Second shielded Jewish children from forced baptism. The entry maps a province where Jews lived widely and early.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tabyomi-general:
Tabyomi was a Babylonian amora of the fifth century. Wilhelm Bacher wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He is generally known simply as Mar. His father Ashi directed the Academy of Sura. Tabyomi won fame as a teacher in his father's lifetime. He died at the end of Yom Kippur in 468.

Only in 455 did Tabyomi become director at Sura. His father had been dead twenty-eight years by then. He held the post for thirteen years. With Maremar he finished revising the Babylonian Talmud. Abraham ibn Daud names them its final redactors. His name was linked to happy days in tradition. Yet Persecution under Yezdegerd marked his early rule. That king's death in 457 was credited to Tabyomi's prayer. The entry joins Talmud editing with a court of faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tekufah-lit-tur:
A tekufah is one turn or season of the solar year. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Four tekufot divide the year into equal quarters. Each opens at an equinox or a solstice. Samuel set each period at ninety-one days and change.

Tekufat Nisan opens spring at the vernal equinox. The sun enters Aries and day equals night. Tekufat Tammuz brings summer at the longest day. Tekufat Tishri starts autumn and the vintage season. Tekufat Tebet begins winter at the longest night. The dates fall two weeks past the true solar points. The calendar follows Ada's figures instead, the entry notes. An old superstition clings to these turning days. The entry maps the year's hinges in Jewish time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tree-of-life-14:
The tree of life in Eden, and its echoes in later writing, are traced here. Emil G. Hirsch and George A. Barton wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Genesis sets the tree mid-garden beside the tree of knowledge. Its fruit, the writer held, conferred immortality. God barred mortals from eating that fruit.

Adam and Eve were expelled lest they eat and live forever. Proverbs keeps the image alive in new senses. Wisdom is a tree of life to those who grasp her. The fruit of the righteous bears the same name. A wholesome tongue earns the title too. Ezekiel's riverbank trees recall the Eden tree. Revelation names that tree the tree of life outright. Enoch books describe its unfading bloom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-widow-14892:
The widow holds a protected place in Jewish law. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A widow's goods cannot be seized for debt. That rule holds whether she is rich or poor. Courts hear her complaints right after orphans' cases.

Scripture calls God himself the widows' judge. Isaiah commands leaders to plead her cause. Marriage frees a daughter from her father's power for good. A widow may marry an ordinary priest. She may not marry the high priest, though. Later sections treat her dowry rights and support. The entry gathers law, ethics, and practice together.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolff-oskar-lud:
Oskar Ludwig Bernhard Wolff (1799-1851) was a German stage wit and novelist. Isidore Singer and M. Zametkin wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Altona, he showed a rare gift for tongues as a boy. While still at school he turned a Shakespeare play into German verse.

He entered the University of Berlin in 1817. He read medicine, the past, and fine books there. He then lived by his pen at Hamburg. The fame of Italian stage wits fired his own wish. In 1825 he toured six German towns with great success. Goethe was among those who praised his art. A grand duke gave him a chair at Weimar. He later taught new letters at Jena as a full professor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-isaac-th:
Yizhak, a form of the name Isaac, heads a set of like named sages. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. By a past slip, some sages named Isaac missed that head word. They are brought in here by the Hebrew form of the name.

The first man so named was a tanna of the 100s. He was a keen hand at the sense of the law texts. Most of his work stands in two old law tale books. He passed on words in the name of Eliezer ben Hyrcanus. He was a pupil of Ishmael in his school days. He kept close ties with the pupils of Akiba as well. One law rule rose from his work with a man named Nathan. His plain notes treat blood on doors, clean birds, and prayer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zebi-hirsch-ben:
Zebi Hirsch ben Isaac Jacob was a rite butcher at Cracow. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broyde wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked there in the sixteenth century of this era. He was a pupil of the famed Moses Isserles.

His one work is a set of notes on a law book. That book treats the slaying of beasts for food. It treats the check of the lungs of such beasts. The base book was made by Jacob Weil in his day. Zebi's notes were bound with that book in print. They came out first at Cracow in the year 1631. New forms came out in three towns in the next age. The entry rests on two book lists of Hebrew lore. It gives no facts of his birth or of his death.
john-cassian-the-conferences-of-john-cas:
Twenty-four conversations with the desert fathers of Egypt form The Conferences of John Cassian, his deepest book. Prayer, chastity, grace, and the inner life pass in review as Cassian questions the masters. The Conferences appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

An old abbot speaks, Cassian and his friend Germanus press him, and hard-won wisdom emerges. The talks range from the mechanics of unceasing prayer to the mystery of why good men fall. Western spirituality drank from this well for a thousand years. Only the Bible and Benedict's Rule shaped monks more. Patient readers will find the conversations slow in pace and immense in reward.
john-cassian-the-institutes-of-john-cass:
John Cassian carried the wisdom of Egypt's desert monks westward, and The Institutes records how those monks actually lived. Clothing, prayer hours, and daily order fill the first part. The work appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

The second part examines the eight chief vices that attack a monk's soul, from gluttony to pride. Cassian treats them like a doctor, matching remedies to each sickness. Benedict's famous Rule draws on the Institutes constantly, often without naming the debt. The book taught medieval Europe how to organize a life of prayer. Its psychology of temptation stays sharp after fifteen centuries.
john-of-damascus-an-exact-exposition-of-:
Eight centuries of Greek Christian thought stand behind John of Damascus's Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith. The summary gathers that tradition into one orderly system. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, in four books that move from God to the last things.

Creation, Christ, the Church, sacraments, and resurrection each find their place in the scheme. John writes as a careful librarian of the fathers, quoting and arranging rather than inventing. The Exposition became the standard theology textbook of the Christian East. Thomas Aquinas used it in the West, and Orthodox teachers still teach from it. Orderly minds will love its architecture.
kant-critique-judgement-bernard-1892:
Immanuel Kant published the Critique of Judgement in 1790, the third of his great Critiques. The English text here is J. H. Bernard's translation of 1892. Kant studies how we judge beauty in art and nature. He also studies how we judge living things as if they had purposes.

Beauty, for Kant, gives pleasure without private interest or set concepts. The sublime stirs awe before vast or mighty scenes. His account of taste shaped modern aesthetics for two centuries. The book also tries to bridge the gap between nature and freedom. It completes the system begun in the first Critique.
kautsky-class-struggle-1892:
Karl Kautsky's Class Struggle appeared in German in 1892, and William E Bohn's English translation followed in 1910. Kautsky, the leading theorist of the German Social Democratic Party, wrote the book as a commentary on the party's Erfurt Program of 1891. It explained that program to ordinary readers.

Kautsky traced how capitalism concentrates wealth, grows the working class, and drives toward crisis and public ownership. He presented the Erfurt Program's demands as the practical path from that analysis. The book became the orthodox Marxist synthesis of the Second International, the shared creed of socialist parties across Europe. For decades, joining the movement often meant reading Kautsky first.
kipling-barrack-room-ballads-1892:
Rudyard Kipling had worked as a journalist in India and written about British soldiers there. Back in London, he published Barrack-Room Ballads and Other Verses in 1892. The book made him one of the most famous poets in the English-speaking world.

The ballads speak in the voices of common soldiers, in rough Cockney dialect. Danny Deever watches a hanging, and Tommy complains how civilians treat soldiers between wars. Gunga Din honors an Indian water carrier braver than the men he serves. Kipling's driving rhythms and honest soldier talk broke with polite Victorian verse and stayed popular for generations.
kneipp-my-water-cure-1892:
Sebastian Kneipp, a Bavarian priest, claimed cold water saved his life, and My Water Cure spread his method worldwide. The English edition of 1892 reports thirty years of testing at Wörishofen, where crowds came seeking help. Kneipp's system used water in many forms, plus herbs, food, and daily routine.

Affusions, baths, wraps, and barefoot walks in wet grass all have their place and their rules. Kneipp explains which treatment fits which complaint, and how gently to begin. His cure made hydrotherapy a world movement, and health resorts still use versions of his water treatments today.
krafft-ebing-psychopathia-chaddock-1892:
Richard von Krafft-Ebing published Psychopathia Sexualis in German in 1886. The English text here is Charles G. Chaddock's translation of 1892. Krafft-Ebing was a psychiatrist who catalogued sexual behavior that his age called perversion. Case histories, many in Latin in the early editions, fill the book.

He coined or spread terms such as sadism, masochism, and fetishism. His aim was medical and legal: to place such cases before doctors and courts. Modern readers fault his labels and his era's bias. Yet the book founded the study of sexual pathology. It shaped both psychiatry and the language still used for desire's extremes.
kyd-spanish-tragedy-1592:
Thomas Kyd's Spanish Tragedy, first staged in the late 1580s and printed in 1592, set the pattern for Elizabethan revenge drama. Kyd was a London playwright about whom little else is known. His play was quoted, copied, and parodied for a generation.

Don Andrea's ghost and Revenge watch the action from above. Hieronimo, a Spanish marshal, finds his son Horatio murdered and feigns madness while he plots his answer. The play within the play, the letters in blood, and the final carnage all became stock devices. Shakespeare's Hamlet grew directly from this soil, and Kyd's tragedy still holds the stage.
laing-human-origins-1892:
Samuel Laing, a Scottish writer and former official, published Human Origins in 1892. He applied Darwin's ideas to the earliest history of humankind. The book appeared serially first and reached a wide popular audience.

Laing discusses the antiquity of the human race and the Aryan question. He follows early humans toward the first steps of civilization. His tone is brisk, rational, and Victorian to the core. Some positions now read as dated period pieces. The work remains a readable snapshot of 1890s popular Darwinism. Laing brought the same plain skepticism to religion, history, and human beginnings alike.
leo-the-great-the-letters-of-leo-the-gre:
Pope Leo the First faced down Attila the Hun outside Rome, and governed the Church with the same nerve by letter. The Letters of Leo the Great appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Doctrine, discipline, and diplomacy share his desk in these pages.

His famous Tome to Flavian, read aloud at the Council of Chalcedon, fixed the Church's teaching on Christ's two natures. Bishops across the world wrote to him, and his answers set precedents for centuries. The letters show a pope ruling a universal Church by pen, courier, and sheer clarity. Few collections reveal so well how Rome's authority actually worked. Students of doctrine and church order both need this correspondence.
leo-the-great-the-sermons-of-leo-the-gre:
Ninety-six sermons survive from Leo the Great, the pope who talked Attila out of sacking Rome. The Sermons of Leo the Great cover Christmas, Easter, the saints' days, fasting, and almsgiving. They appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Leo preaches with doctrinal precision and pastoral warmth in the same breath. Great feasts become lessons in what the incarnation means for ordinary believers. His Christmas sermons, urging Christians to recognize their dignity, are quoted to this day. Theology turns into food for everyday people without losing its edge. These are the classic sermons of the early Roman Church, from its greatest early pope.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
An 1880 edition gathers Motley's Barneveld history as a complete work. John of Barneveld, Advocate of Holland, stands at its center. Motley frames the book as sequel and introduction at once. It follows his Netherlands histories and precedes the Thirty Years' War.

The preface calls the two great wars one prolonged eighty-year tragedy. The Twelve Years' Truce merely paused a conflict raging for decades. During that pause, forces gathered for war across civilized Europe. Readers get Barneveld's career set against Europe's widening struggle. Charles V's designs open Motley's long view of the struggle. A natural succession of actors links beginning to close, he argues.
limborch-historia-inquisitionis-latin-16:
Philipp van Limborch published his Historia Inquisitionis at Amsterdam in 1692, in Latin, the language of learned Europe. The text here is that original edition, the one Samuel Chandler later turned into English. Limborch, a Remonstrant professor, wrote the classic Protestant history of the Inquisition from the Toulouse records.

The work traces persecution from the early church to the papal tribunal and the Albigensian wars. Appended stands the Liber Sententiarum, the book of sentences of Toulouse, his documentary proof. Limborch argued from paper, not from polemic, and that made his book hard to answer. It fixed the image of the Inquisition in the European mind for two hundred years.
limborch-liber-sententiarum-tholosanus-1:
The Liber Sententiarum is the sentence book of the Inquisition of Toulouse for the years 1307 to 1323. Philipp van Limborch published the Latin record at Amsterdam in 1692, as the proof volume of his history of the Inquisition. It is a first-order trial source: the tribunal's own register of its judgments against the men and women of Languedoc.

Page after page names the accused, the errors laid on them, and the penances set. These run from yellow crosses and pilgrimages to prison on bread and water, or the flames for the relapsed. Cathars and Waldensians pass through the register beside careless talkers caught by informers. Historians of heresy still quarry this book. Its dry Latin is the sound of the machine working.
lodge-modern-views-electricity-1892:
Oliver Lodge set out his full view of electricity in this book of 1892. He treats electric force as the work of the ether, the unseen stuff in all space. The book was the high mark of Victorian ether physics in a clear, strong form.

Lodge deals with charge, sparks, and the flash of lightning, all as strains in the ether. He tells of his own trials with sparks and Leyden jars, shown with care. For the lay reader of its day, the book made the new science of electricity plain.
macdonald-hope-of-gospel-1892:
George MacDonald, the Scottish writer whose fantasies taught Lewis and Tolkien, preached the sermons gathered in The Hope of the Gospel in 1892. The book holds his most hopeful theology in pulpit form. At its center stands the goodness of God the Father.

MacDonald argues that God's love reaches every soul, and that punishment serves healing rather than revenge. He reads the words of Jesus as proof that no one is finally shut out from mercy. Victorian readers who feared an angry God found in these sermons a gentler, sterner gospel at once. His fairy tales carry the same hope in story form.
mead-simon-magus-1892:
G. R. S. Mead was the chief scholar of the Theosophical Society. His essay on Simon Magus came out in 1892. Simon is named in the Book of Acts as a sorcerer of Samaria. Church tales made him the first great foe of the faith.

Mead sifts the old church tales to find the man past the myth. He asks if Simon taught a deep Gnostic scheme of his own. Old texts in Greek and Latin give the sparse facts he works with. The essay is a sober bid to save a dark name from pure slur.
medicina-practica-or-practical-physick-c:
William Salmon's Medicina Practica came out in 1692. Its title promises ways to cure the most common diseases of the body. A long list on the title page names those ills one by one.

Aches, agues, bleedings, and short breath stand in that list. Fluxes, want of appetite, deafness, and stone in the reins join them. The record notes that the rest holds translated alchemical works. Hermes, Geber, and Artephius stand among the names tied to those parts. Four plates at the back show Geber's furnaces for the work. Old and new cures sit side by side in the one volume.
morris-news-from-nowhere-1892:
William Morris answered Bellamy with his own utopia, News from Nowhere, first printed in 1890. The text here is the 1892 Kelmscott Press edition, from Morris's own press. His narrator wakes in a future England remade by revolution. Money, parliament, and grimy industry have vanished from the land.

Guest, the visitor, travels the Thames valley asking how the change came. Craft work, beauty, and free fellowship fill the answers he receives. Morris called the book a utopian romance, and its charm carries the doctrine. The socialist England he pictures grows from his love of medieval craft. It remains a beloved counterweight to harder utopias. Kelmscott printing makes the copy itself handsome.
murdoch-point-barrow-expedition-1892:
John Murdoch served with the United States party that spent two years at Point Barrow, Alaska, in the early 1880s, and his report came out in 1892. Point Barrow is the far north tip of Alaska. The party went to study weather, land, and the people there.

Murdoch wrote the part on the Inupiat, the Inuit group of that coast. He set down their tools, dress, homes, and crafts, and their rites and shamans. It is one of the first close records of life at the edge of the known map.
newes-from-scotland-1592:
Newes from Scotland, printed in 1592, reports the North Berwick witch trials of 1590 and 1591. Dozens of people stood accused of raising storms against King James the Sixth at sea. Doctor Fian, a schoolmaster, stands at the center of the tale.

The pamphlet gives his examination, his torture, and his death in grim detail. It claims the accused met the Devil and plotted the king's death on the waves. The case shaped the king's own later book on witchcraft, Daemonologie. Historians treat the pamphlet as the founding text of the Scottish witch hunt, and its charges still shock.
openalex-w1952843992:
Gennaro D'Amato and many co-authors wrote this statement. It appeared in the World Allergy Organization Journal in 2015. Asthma and rhinitis have reached epidemic levels worldwide. Industry and vehicle pollution explain part of that rise. Wider environmental change must explain the rest, they argue.

Greenhouse gases have already warmed the planet greatly, they note. Heat waves, floods, droughts, and fires strain breathing health. Air pollution worsens both illness and death from asthma. Developing nations sit at the core of these changes. The statement warns doctors and policy makers alike. It urges action on climate for respiratory health.
openalex-w2028567092:
Christophe Bene, Manuel Barange, Rohana Subasinghe and colleagues argued that fish belongs at the centre of food policy. Their paper appeared in Food Security in 2015. The world must feed nine billion people by 2050. Fish already supply a large share of animal protein. Billions rely on it for key nutrients.

Fish convert feed into food very efficiently. Their carbon footprint is lower than most animal farming. Fishing and fish farming also support many livelihoods. Yet fish is often missing from food security debates. The authors review the role of wild and farmed fish. They call for fish to be put back on the policy menu. Planning must cover nutrition, jobs and ocean health together.
openalex-w2035187492:
Camila Alves de Rezende, Marisa Aparecida de Lima, Priscila Maziero and colleagues studied sugarcane waste as a fuel feedstock. Their paper appeared in Biotechnology for Biofuels in 2011. Sugarcane bagasse can be turned into ethanol. First it must be pretreated so enzymes can reach its sugars. The team tested a two-step treatment.

Samples were treated with dilute acid, then alkali. Stronger alkali removed most lignin and hemicellulose. The team checked chemistry and structure with several lab methods. Removing lignin greatly improved enzyme digestion of the fibres. Total conversion of cellulose rose sharply after treatment. Microscope images showed the fibre structure opening up. The results guide pretreatment design for ethanol plants.
openalex-w2074331492:
L. Nusbaum, Jamil Natour, Marcos Bosi Ferraz and J. Goldenberg translated a back-pain questionnaire for Brazil. Their paper appeared in 2001. The Roland-Morris questionnaire measures disability from low back pain. Brazilian clinicians needed a tested Portuguese version. A poor translation can distort patients' answers.

Three English teachers first translated the questionnaire independently. A panel merged their work into one version. Blind translators then translated it back into English. The panel compared versions and settled differences. Thirty back-pain patients tested the final draft. All questions were understood well. Repeated scores a week apart agreed strongly. Scores from different interviewers also agreed closely. Pain scales matched the questionnaire scores well. The authors judged the Brazilian version valid and reliable.
openalex-w2075851892:
Erin Andrew, Christopher Pell, Angeline Angwin and colleagues studied why pregnant women delay clinic care in Papua New Guinea. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Good pregnancy care protects mother and child. Yet only a third of women there get any such care. The team explored what shapes attendance in Madang.

They used interviews, group talks and clinic observation. Women, relatives and health workers all took part. Distance and cost were clear barriers. Nearby women with money still attended poorly, though. Past clinic experiences shaped women's attitudes strongly. Family tensions and pregnancy disclosure also mattered. Beliefs about fetal strength affected first-visit timing. Services must fix clinic experience, the authors argue.
openalex-w2123354892:
Daniel Duprez, Jacqueline Neuhaus, Lewis Kuller, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2012. They worked with the SMART trial, which compared steady HIV treatment with planned treatment breaks. Their question was whether blood markers of swelling and clotting could predict heart and vessel disease in people living with HIV.

Blood samples came from more than five thousand trial participants. The team measured three markers linked to inflammation and clotting and tracked heart events. The wider trial had already shown that treatment breaks raised heart risk despite lower drug exposure. The study tests whether these markers add warning power beyond the usual risk factors doctors already measure.
openalex-w2133643992:
David Mabey, Kimberly Sollis, Helen Kelly, and colleagues published this account in PLoS Medicine in 2012. They describe a project that brought rapid syphilis tests to clinics with no access to laboratories. Testing at the point of care lets pregnant women be screened and treated in one visit, which can save newborn lives.

The project engaged policy makers in each country from the design stage. Clinics in Africa, Asia, and Latin America introduced the tests in rural and urban prenatal care. All six countries changed policy to adopt point-of-care syphilis testing in prenatal screening. The team also showed that quality checks for such testing can run in every setting.
openalex-w2155551592:
Thomas Burkot, Tanya Russell, Lisa Reimer, and colleagues published this method paper in the Malaria Journal in 2013. They present barrier screens, a simple way to catch outdoor-resting mosquitoes that have just fed on blood. Knowing how often such mosquitoes bite humans is hard, because engorged outdoor resters are tough to find in thick vegetation.

Screens of shade cloth on bamboo poles were set between villages and mosquito haunts in three Pacific countries. Blocked fliers paused on the screens and were sucked up hourly through the night. Many malaria vector species were caught freshly fed, along with other mosquito kinds. The authors call the method extremely time-effective for fair samples of fed mosquitoes.
openalex-w2414478892:
M. Aaboud and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration published this measurement in Physical Review Letters in 2016. They measured the inelastic cross section of proton-proton collisions at thirteen TeV. It is the total chance that two protons actually interact rather than pass through each other. This basic number anchors every other rate the collider reports.

A small June 2015 dataset, caught by scintillation counters at both ends of ATLAS, did the job. The counters ignore purely elastic bounces, covering a defined slice of breakup events. Models of inelastic scattering then stretch that slice into the full cross section. The result calibrates luminosity, tunes collision simulations, and extends earlier measurements at lower energies into the collider's new regime.
openalex-w2601300492:
Pablo Wenceslao Orellano, Nancy Esther Quaranta, and Julieta Itatí Reynoso, with colleagues, published this 2017 review in PLoS ONE. It asks whether outdoor air pollution triggers asthma attacks in children and adults. Many studies had suggested pollution can start or worsen asthma. Their results, though, were inconclusive, because many side factors muddy the link.

The team systematically gathered studies from PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar covering 2000 to 2016. They kept case-crossover studies that used emergency visits or hospital admissions as signs of serious attacks. A multilevel meta-analysis then pooled the odds across studies and subgroups. This design accounts for repeated time lags measured inside single studies. Pooling the evidence this way gives doctors and regulators a firmer basis for judging pollution's effect on asthma.
openalex-w2775643792:
Alicia Ponte-Sucre, Francisco Gamarro, and Jean-Claude Dujardin lead a team reviewing drug resistance in leishmaniasis in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2017. This parasitic disease is treated almost entirely with drugs. Treatment failure is rising worldwide, and resistance is a basic driver of it. The old mainstay drugs, antimonials, have served since the early twentieth century.

Drug resistance in the clinic has grown over the last two decades, sharply in India's North Bihar. The review explains what resistance means for this disease and traces where resistant strains spread. It outlines how the parasites resist antimonials, amphotericin B, and miltefosine inside their cells. Resistance also threatens drug combinations designed to protect these medicines. The HIV epidemic worsens failure by weakening patients' immune systems. The authors argue treatment rules need a global rethink, urgently.
openalex-w2885527392: Yuming Guo, Antonio Gasparrini, and Shanshan Li lead a multicountry study of heatwave deaths under climate change, published in PLOS Medicine in 2018. Its title describes a time series modelling study spanning many countries and future warming scenarios. The hosted sample, however, preserves only the article's citation block, author list, and affiliations. No abstract or findings text survives in the sample. Nothing beyond the verified title, authors, journal, and year can be stated from this evidence.
openalex-w2915443992:
Henriette Azeredo, Hernane Barud, Cristiane Farinas, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems. Their subject is bacterial cellulose, a natural material made by certain bacteria as they grow in a nutrient medium. The review covers its use as a raw material for foods and food packaging.

Bacteria of the genus Komagataeibacter are the usual source, since they produce high yields of pure bacterial cellulose. Different strains form membranes with different network structures and strength. People first noticed this material in kombucha tea, where bacteria and yeast grow in a cellulose mat. The review sets out why these traits suit the material to food uses.
openalex-w2951495492:
Gary Weil, Joshua Bogus, Michael Christian, and colleagues published this safety study in PLoS Medicine in 2019. It concerns mass drug campaigns against lymphatic filariasis, a worm disease that can cause severe swelling known as elephantiasis. A new three-drug single dose had recently beaten the standard two-drug treatment in trials.

The team gave either the three-drug or the two-drug dose to whole communities in five countries between late 2016 and late 2017. Sites in Papua New Guinea and Indonesia had never had such campaigns, while sites in India, Haiti, and Fiji still had disease despite past campaigns. Treatment was assigned by village or area, and side effects were tracked to judge safety.
openalex-w2979994192:
Caroline Nievergelt, Adam Maihofer, Torsten Klengel, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2019. It is a worldwide meta-analysis of genome scans for posttraumatic stress disorder, or PTSD. The risk of PTSD after trauma runs in families, yet no firm common gene variants had been nailed down.

The team pooled data from many studies into a multi-ethnic group of more than thirty thousand PTSD cases and one hundred seventy thousand controls. Scanning the whole genome at that scale gave the study power that earlier, smaller efforts lacked. The analysis found genetic risk spots that differ by sex and by ancestry. Such spots are first clues to the biology of who develops PTSD after trauma and who does not.
openalex-w4211257092:
David Walters, Ian Boutle, Malcolm Brooks, and colleagues describe the Met Office's global weather and climate model setup, in Geoscientific Model Development in 2017. The setup pairs the Unified Model atmosphere, version GA6, with the JULES land surface model, version GL6. One system serves both daily weather forecasts and long climate runs. Model papers like this one let other scientists judge and reuse the tool.

A new dynamical core, called ENDGame, sits at the heart of GA6. It raised natural variability at mid-latitudes, fixing a known bias, and improved tropical cyclones. Other changes sharpened forecasts of surface weather. A near-twin version, GA6.1, has run the Met Office's operational global forecasts since July 2014.
openalex-w4416399692:
Shimaa El Baz, Abdelfattah Eladl, Reham El-Shafei, and Mohamed Elmorsy track drug-resistant Klebsiella in backyard chickens and their owners. Their paper appeared in The Journal of Antibiotics in 2026. These bacteria can cause hard-to-treat infections in people.

The team sampled eighty sick broiler chickens and twenty human contacts. They recovered nineteen Klebsiella isolates from the two groups. Every isolate resisted erythromycin and clindamycin. Most also resisted other common antibiotics. Gene tests found resistance genes in most isolates, led by the macrolide gene ermB. Finding the same resistant bacteria in birds and their handlers is alarming. It argues for tighter control of antibiotic use in backyard poultry.
openalex-w7138893692:
Atsuko Hayase led a 2026 study of how the COVID-19 virus spreads onto surfaces in hospital rooms. The team placed small adhesive samplers on fourteen surfaces in nine single rooms with strong ventilation, plus patches on nurses' scrubs, during each patient's first day. They measured viral genetic material and tried to grow live virus from the samples.

About half of the 134 samples carried viral genetic material, with the highest amounts on surfaces near the patient that hands touch often. Live virus grew from only a few samples, also near patients. Amounts fell with distance from the patient's mouth. The authors still advise focused cleaning of nearby high-touch surfaces and steady hand hygiene.
openalex-w7204128392:
Jadson Maia dos Santos led a Portuguese-language legal paper, in Brazil in 2026, on digital political advertising and the integrity of elections. Social media changed public debate and brought disinformation, microtargeted boosting, and inauthentic networks into campaigns. The authors ask how far free expression, protected by Brazil's constitution, can be limited to keep elections fair, equal, and authentic.

Using constitutional doctrine, electoral court choices, and the principle of proportionality, the study weighs the harms of the digital setting against the electoral authority's responses. Free expression is not absolute, they conclude, and abusive use that threatens popular sovereignty can face rare restriction. But such steps must be strictly proportionate and reasoned, with no prior censorship and full due process.
openalex-w7204226692:
Aldelane Silva Santos de Oliveira led a Portuguese-language case study, published in Brazil in 2026, on purchasing management at a small construction materials retailer in Tefé, Amazonas. The Solimões River's flood and drought cycle shapes river freight, and with it the firm's costs and prices. The team read invoices and management reports from June 2025 to May 2026, breaking purchase prices for cement, iron. Paint into list price, river and road freight, and tax, then tracked monthly profit margins.

The overall gross margin was about fifteen percent, but cement, the main product, carried the thinnest margin and bottomed out at the height of the dry season. Iron and paint held higher, steadier margins. Buying cement ahead during high water, the authors conclude, is financially advantageous and should become permanent stock policy.
openalex-w7204237392:
Ana Maria Farias Nascimento led a Portuguese-language paper, in Brazil in 2026, on school bullying and how to build a culture of peace and tolerance. Bullying means repeated, intentional aggression with a power imbalance, physical, verbal, psychological, or virtual, and it harms children's emotional, social, and school growth. The paper sets out how to spot it early through behavioral, emotional, and physical warning signs in victims and aggressors alike.

Heading this off, the authors argue, is a joint job for school, family, and community, creating a safe and welcoming environment. They present social-emotional learning, conflict mediation, and respect for diversity as workable paths, backed by policies and ongoing teacher training. Permanent actions promoting mutual respect, empathy, and dialogue, they conclude, form citizens committed to ethical, democratic coexistence.
openalex-w7204251392:
Millena Aires Mendes and Rafael Assunção Godinho released a Portuguese-language legal study in Brazil in 2026 on the penal police of Tocantins, the officers who guard and manage prisons. A 2019 constitutional amendment created the penal police as a formal career, and a 2022 state law restructured it in Tocantins. The authors ask how far this professional recognition improves the working of Brazil's prison sentence execution law, balancing internal security against the fundamental rights of people in custody.

Professionalization and self-rule, they find, improved disciplinary control and cooperation with other security bodies. Yet staff shortages and poor structures still limit the assistance the law promises prisoners. Valuing the career is necessary, they conclude, but full effect needs continued investment in facilities and people.
openalex-w7204442892:
Anderson Lange led a Portuguese-language laboratory study, published in Brazil in 2026, on how phosphate fertilizer sources release phosphorus in soils of different textures. Phosphorus limits crop yields in tropical soils because clays and iron and aluminum oxides lock it up. The team incubated five soils from Sinop and Sorriso, in Mato Grosso. Four phosphorus sources at five increasing doses, in a fully randomized design with four repetitions, then measured available phosphorus after fifty days.

Source, dose, and their interaction all mattered in every soil. The sandy soil released the most phosphorus and responded directly to dose, while clay soils retained more and needed higher doses before sources differed. Two sources performed best overall in the authors' general reading. The results guide dose and source choices by soil type.
openalex-w7204989892:
José Laécio de Moraes led a Portuguese-language case study, in Brazil in 2026, on the contamination vulnerability of a crystalline aquifer system in Várzea Alegre, Ceará, in Brazil's semiarid northeast. Groundwater in fractured rock is the region's lifeline. Through field visits, an impact study, and a standard vulnerability method, the team studied the springs area of a rural site in the municipality. They examined how the aquifer could be contaminated and how the springs are used and preserved.

The springs serve mainly nature, sustaining the habitat's species. Impacts included degraded or missing vegetation in the protected area, deforestation and burning in recharge zones, unprotected easy access. They also noted changes in the water's color and odor, with preservation graded from terrible to reasonable. Natural vulnerability to being polluted, however, was negligible, with little or no load of pollutants.
openalex-w7206207892:
Yaisa Christina Santos Braz de Almeida de Andrade Carvalho leads two colleagues in asking what kin who nurse at home most need to learn. Their study ran in 2019 in a home care scheme at a Rio de Janeiro teaching hospital. They spoke with eighteen women who cared for kin at home. From those talks they built a guide for such carers.

The women told of fear in the day's tasks. They told of strain in flesh and heart from the load. And they asked for help they could look up when a snag came. Those needs shaped a booklet of plain tips for home care. Tools built from carers' own words, the team holds, bring the nurse's counsel close to the life homes live each day.
openalex-w7212014292:
Patricia Pereira Tavares de Alcantara leads a team asking how a rural community in Crato, Ceara, sees the care women get in primary health. The care comes through Brazil's Family Health Strategy, the front door of the public system. The study used action research with staff, a manager, and women from the area. Notes, group talks, and direct observation fed the study.

People praised the warm welcome, the home visits, and the talk circles run by health agents. They also valued checks that prevent disease and care during pregnancy. The weak points were plain too: long waits, red tape, staff turnover, and areas with no agent at all. Users asked for more work to prevent violence against women. The team backs the model, but with clear fixes.
openalex-w7212237892:
Amazile Biagioni Maia, writing alone, asks how Brazil's pot-still cachaca can win fans in the world market. The cane spirit is made by thousands of small farms and stills across the land. Its fame at home is strong, yet its reach abroad stays thin. Maia reads strong cases from the trade to find the choke points. The wood of the cask, she argues, is the key to the drink's scent and taste.

World buyers, she notes, want a clear trail: where the wood grew, what kind it is, and a taste they can count on. Home drinkers prize the wild range of woods and scents. That range can block world trust. Her plea is to fix one wood, amburana, as a named mark. Tight rules on the tree's kind would let small farms sell a known taste to the world.
openalex-w7212364692:
Gabrielle Oliveira Santana and Cristina Correa de Oliveira study micro-frontends, a way to build web apps in small, free parts. Big one-block web apps have grown slow to change. Firms now split the screen side as they split the back end: in blocks teams own end to end. The pair read the field's work in two big tech stores of past studies. Their lens was not code, but rule and plan.

Such splits, they find, can make a firm fast on its feet. Each team can ship its block on its own clock. But free blocks can drift: looks clash, rules blur, and costs hide. Sound rule is thus the price of the speed. The study sorts what chiefs must set: who owns what, which norms bind all, and how the whole is watched. Tech, here, is a board call too.

The exam is a soft one: a speculum check and a smear test for cell change. It asks for hand skill, clear talk, and sound ethics. The team used a set tool to score the class in advance. A first score of this kind shows where the gaps sit. It lets staff aim the lab hours at the weak steps, not the strong ones. It also sets a base line to judge growth when the course ends. For a skill that joins touch, talk, and trust, that base line counts for much.
openalex-w7213405392:
Illeanne de Jesus Manhiça da Costa Silva and colleagues report what resident nurses saw in a high-complexity hospital in Paraná. Their 2026 experience report covers January to June 2026 and concerns patients with high blood pressure. The nurses worked in health surveillance and joined multiprofessional discussions.

Hospital stays for these patients were linked mainly to heart complications. Heart attack and heart failure stood out, along with chronic kidney disease and past stroke. Cases needed intensive care, long stays, and heavy use of hospital resources. The report shows how a common condition becomes a major burden once severe complications occur, and why surveillance inside hospitals matters.
openalex-w7220660092:
Carlos Eduardo Bermeo Chávez, Eddy J. Garcia Paredes, and Gladys E.
