Lopez and co-authors probe the ultrablack shell of a velvet ant, Traumatomutilla bifurca. Velvet ants are wasps with a striking look, and this species absorbs light to an extreme degree. The team wanted to learn what shell structure creates such deep black color.

They combined surface and internal microscopy with light measures of the cuticle. Scanning images showed fine surface form, while transmission images revealed inner layers. Confocal tests found no glow from the cuticle itself. The findings link the layered shell build to the near-total loss of reflected light seen in this insect.
pmc-11639792:
Strum and co-authors review extracellular vesicles, tiny cell-made particles, and their growing roles in cancer care. Tumors shed these vesicles, and they shape many steps of cancer growth, from tumor spread to how the immune system reacts. They touch nearly all parts of innate and adaptive immunity.

Because vesicles carry cargo from their parent cells, they may reveal cancer early through simple fluid tests. They may also deliver drugs or boost immune therapy against tumors. The review sums up what is known about vesicle use in tumor diagnosis and immunotherapy, plus the gaps that still block clinic use.
pmc-11639992:
Patel and co-authors review outcomes for a rare soft tissue cancer of the head and neck treated while still localized. Synovial sarcoma in this region is uncommon, and its course needed charting. Records covered 57 patients seen from 1981 to 2020. All had disease confined to its start site at diagnosis. Five-year survival stood at 80.4%. Freedom from local return was 67.7% at five years. Freedom from spread was lower, at 50.6%.

Patients who got radiation with surgery kept local control longer than surgery-only patients. Standard survival methods produced the estimates. Spread, not local return, is the main long-term threat. The long record span gives rare tumors a usable baseline.
pmc-11642592: George Vaos and Nikolaos Zavras present an update on acute appendicitis, covering both its diagnosis and its treatment. The condition is described as one of the most common surgical emergencies seen in adults and children alike. As an update, it gathers the current state of practice. Fast, accurate diagnosis shapes how quickly treatment can begin.
pmc-11643392:
Shiqi Li and nine co-authors published a nutrition trends study in twenty twenty-four tracking ultra-processed food in southern China across two decades. Serial national nutrition surveys in Guangdong province, in two thousand two, twenty twelve, and twenty twenty-two, recorded what adults ate through recalls and household weighing. Foods were classified by processing level.

Ultra-processed items supplied under one percent of energy in two thousand two and over eight percent by twenty twenty-two, a near tenfold rise. Growth was steepest among the young, the better educated, urban residents, and spectacularly among students. The nutrient profile of the processed share also worsened. The authors document a dietary transition still mid-stream, with its health bill yet to arrive.
pmc-11645092:
Federica Colonnese and five co-authors published a study in twenty twenty-four on spotting autism from the way a child looks at the world. Eye trackers logged gaze, and a deep network learned the gaze traits that mark the spectrum. The catch: training data can be noisy, and noise drags a model down.

The team used a method that scores how much each training case pulls on the model, then dropped the worst pulls. Taught on just over three-quarters of the data, the leaner model scored near ninety-four percent, beating the same model taught on all of it. The kept cases also show which gaze traits drive the call. The authors pitch the mix of clean data and clear reasons as a path to tools doctors can trust.
pmc-11645892:
Bin Mei and co-authors test if dexmedetomidine, given in surgery for the lung, lifts the quality of sleep after surgery and the secretion of melatonin. Their 2024 study was prospective and randomised. It took in older patients who had elective thoracoscopic lung surgery.

One hundred twenty-six patients got dexmedetomidine with propofol, or propofol on its own, in surgery. Quality of sleep on the first night after surgery scored higher in the dexmedetomidine group. No gap showed on the second or third nights. A urine measure tied to melatonin showed no gap that counts by the third night, in the results set out. The rate of delirium was also tracked. Why the sleep gains that have been reported take place is still not clear. That is what drives the work on melatonin.
pmc-11651492:
Wang and five co-authors test causal links between immune cells, blood metabolites, and heart attack, in work from twenty twenty-four. Heart attack stems from genes, lifestyle, and immune regulation in complex mix. Which links are truly causal is unclear from observation alone.

Mendelian randomization uses genetic variants as natural experiments to infer cause. The team focused on one lymphocyte type marked by IgD and bright CD38. Its effect on heart attack risk appeared to run through a ratio of two metabolites, glycerol and a fatty acid carrier form. A mediated causal chain gives drug research a narrower target.
pmc-11657592:
Tischendorf, Geithner, and Schaal sort informal caregivers in Saxony, Germany into groups by well-being. Rising care needs mean more family members will take on nursing at home. That work adds physical and mental strain. The team used a 2019 home care survey from the region. A two-step cluster analysis covered 178 people who cared for relatives. The aim was to find distinct caregiver profiles.

Two groups of caregiving relatives emerged from the data. Their well-being patterns differed in telling ways. Knowing the profiles helps services target support where strain concentrates. The study treats caregivers as varied, not as one uniform group.
pmc-11657792:
Ghodsiyeh Joveini and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four systematic review and meta-analysis of kinesio taping after leg fatigue. The elastic tape is popular in sport and rehabilitation. Whether it truly helps pain, strength, or balance after fatigue is unclear.

The reviewers searched five databases for randomized trials in healthy people. Trials compared tape with sham tape, rigid tape, or no tape. Quality was graded with a standard bias tool. Pain and strength results were pooled, while balance studies were too few to pool. Therapists get a careful summary of what the trial evidence actually supports.
pmc-11671492:
Mukherjee and six co-authors measure gaps in HIV prevention drug use, in work from twenty twenty-four. The drug approach, called PrEP, prevents HIV when taken before exposure. Global use in twenty twenty-three fell far short of world targets.

Most global PrEP programs are backed by PEPFAR, a United States program. The team used program data from forty-eight supported countries for fiscal twenty twenty-three. They built a ratio of PrEP use to need, split by place and population group. Wide gaps showed between groups with similar need. The authors argue prevention must double down on the underserved groups if AIDS is to end as a public threat.
pmc-11671592:
Kibong Sung and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four mouse study on a receptor called ErbB4 and fear responses. Post-traumatic stress disorder involves fear that stays switched on after trauma. ErbB4 was known in other brain disorders, but its role in fear was unclear.

Mice lacking ErbB4 in certain calming neurons showed PTSD-like fear behaviour. Removing it only in one amygdala region raised anxiety and fear generalization. In mice showing such behaviour, ErbB4 levels there were lower. The findings suggest healthy ErbB4 activity in these neurons helps keep fear responses in check.
pmc-11673192:
Wen, Li, and Nikolski build MMOSurv, a meta-learn frame for few-shot life reads. Rich gene sets now abound from fast read tools in labs. Such sets could hone life guesses for growth hosts a lot. Yet few-shot reads, with scant train hosts, strain that hope. Rare growths give the least train facts of all in sets. MMOSurv learns a start point from kin growth facts first.

That start point then bends fast to a new growth with few hosts. A deep Cox life form with more than one gene set drives it. Tests span 11 growth types from the TCGA bank sets. MMOSurv beat lone-set meta ways on the life marks there. It drew more from the cross-task facts in the kin sets. Few train hosts thus still yield a sound life tool.
pmc-11674292:
Maggio and co-authors compare virtual reality training with standard training for emotion and thinking skills in multiple sclerosis. Standard rehab mainly targets body and mind symptoms. Immersive VR may train feelings and thinking together. The team reviewed records of 43 patients in cognitive rehab. Outcomes covered emotional self-efficacy and cognitive test results. Gender was a planned lens, since men and women may respond differently.

The study asks whether VR gains track with better thinking scores. It also tests whether the VR edge differs by gender. Results could support rehab plans tailored by patient profile. The retrospective design mines real clinic data rather than a staged trial.
pmc-11677192:
Simei and co-authors review the evidence on cannabis products in research and medical care, with a focus on cannabidiol. CBD shows promise for several conditions, yet approved uses remain few. At the same time, legal markets for cannabis goods have grown fast around the world. That growth has outrun the science on safety and benefit. Clinicians, researchers, and makers all face the gap.

The review covers how CBD acts in the body, what trials show, and what risks are known. It also covers rules that govern medical and recreational products in different places. The authors look ahead to how new cannabinoid drugs might be built. They urge care in matching claims to proof.
pmc-11679992:
Matthew Zinner, Eric Neufeld, and Andrew Goodwillie review how bone loss round the shoulder joint is gauged, and why that counts. Their 2024 piece deals with anterior shoulder instability. In that state, loss of glenoid and humeral bone lifts the risk that the joint slips out once more.

The team weighs plain X-ray scans, two- and three-dimensional computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging. Each is used to gauge glenoid bone loss. They weigh the good and bad points of each way. No one way to gauge loss is taken up by all, they note. The review also sets out engaging on-track and off-track Hill-Sachs lesions. A true gauge counts, since it can change the surgery a doctor picks and the step used to make the shoulder firm once more.
pmc-11728692:
Angelina Wojcik-Fatla and colleagues measured gut-family bacteria in sewage sludge and digestate meant for farm fields in Poland in two thousand twenty-four. Both materials feed crops richly, but they can carry germs. The team counted bacteria in soil, sludge, and digestate, and tested how long a reference germ survives in fertilized soil.

Common gut bacteria appeared in every sample type, with digestate carrying the highest counts in this study. Several bacterial genera were identified in soil, and familiar species turned up in the waste materials too. Farmers and regulators get concrete contamination figures for judging safe spreading rules.
pmc-11770792:
Dalila Miraoui leads a team that adapts clinical reasoning class for large groups. Their study from twenty twenty-four is set in medical training. The method is a key form of active learning in medicine.

It was built for small groups, not large halls of students. The team tried two ways to scale it up for big classes. One used a fish bowl form, the other used all hands. Students rated both forms with a scored form. Strong points were prior knowledge, mood, and uptake of facts. Lack of time was the main complaint in both.
pmc-11888692:
Krupa and co-authors survey tongue prints as a new way to confirm a person's identity today. Each tongue's surface pattern is distinct and stays stable over time. That mix makes it a promising sign for biometric systems.

The review covers tongue anatomy, how prints are captured, and new recognition tech. Uses span health care, security checks, and forensic work. Accuracy, strengths, and limits of the method are weighed against other biometrics. The authors also map open problems and future paths for wider adoption of tongue print tools in daily practice.
pmc-12661392:
Ban Van Phuc leads a ten-author team reporting a one-pot route to complex fused ring compounds, in a chemistry paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The products, long-named pyrido-imidazo-quinolines, belong to families prized in medicinal chemistry. Building them usually takes several steps.

Their method starts from brominated imidazopyridines, ammonia, and the solvent DMSO, open to air. A copper iodide and proline catalyst first couples carbon to nitrogen. Air oxidation then closes the final ring in the same pot. Yields were high across a series of derivatives. The same trick produced sulfur-containing cousins in good yields. Fewer steps and cheap catalysts make the route attractive for library synthesis in drug discovery.
pmc-12663592:
Spencer Alliston and Chris Dames turn a classic thermal measurement into a needle that can be plunged straight into soft matter. Measuring heat conduction in tissues, gels, and liquids is awkward with flat sensors that need perfect surface contact. Their microfabricated needle extends the well-established three-omega technique into a probe form.

The sensor was driven into ice, water, glycerol, paraffin, and chicken liver, and its readings were fitted against a three-dimensional numerical model. Results landed within three percent of published values across a wide conductivity range. The probe is reusable, makes its own contact, and works mid-phase-change, shown with ice. The authors aim it at energy storage materials and cryopreservation, where thermal data on soft samples are scarce.
pmc-12696092:
Abeer Khalaf-Allah and co-authors build a composite material that lifts adsorption of methylene blue dye from water. Their 2025 study joins a grafted biopolymer gel with zinc oxide and carbon nitride nanosheets, used as filler.

Sorbents in powder form are hard to get back after use. They can also cause pollution of a second kind. Nanosheets tend to clump as one, and lose activity. When they are set in the chitosan-alginate composite, both of those problems are dealt with. The composite swelled in a strong way in alkaline water. It was set out in detail by more than one method for imaging and spectroscopy. With a small share of filler, the most dye that it could take up hit a stated level, in alkaline conditions. Data on adsorption fit standard equilibrium models well.
pmc-12711892:
Bitew and coauthors screen parasite genes to find a fat balance regulator. The parasite Toxoplasma steals host fats to grow and live. How it senses fat supply and adapts was poorly known. The team screened its full gene set under two fat levels.

One flagged protein, called GRA38, guards parasite fitness in fat-rich settings. Lab tests showed it can break down a key fat signal. A cut in its active site gutted that breakdown skill. Parasites that lack the protein pile up excess fat. Their growth suffers when host fat is plentiful. The protein may be a drug target.
pmc-12715192:
Ruijie Ma and Rui Zhang published a 2025 genomics study of viruses that hide inside marine bacteria. Most research on such viruses focuses on tailed types, leaving thread-shaped and double-shelled types poorly understood despite their abundance. The team mined hundreds of genomes from Vibrio bacteria, a group that includes the cholera agent.

They located more than seven hundred hidden viruses and pinned down exactly where each one joins the bacterial genome. Comparing them revealed that two very different virus families share a borrowed toolkit for settling into a host, passed between them by gene transfer. Some viral regions also carry weapons and disease factors that may help the viruses persist.
pmc-12731792:
Krivetskaya leads a large team on measuring trachea blood supply during surgery, in work from twenty twenty-five. The windpipe receives blood through a collateral network from several sources. Surgery that removes part of it risks starving the remaining tissue, causing ischemia and tissue death.

Their intraoperative method assesses blood supply level by light spectra measured in living tissue. The optical properties of tracheal tissue itself can distort such readings, which is the problem studied. Correcting for tissue optics makes the spectral assessment trustworthy. Early warning of poor blood flow lets surgeons revise the repair before tissue fails.
pmc-12748092:
Jeroen Crouzen and colleagues track survival as brain metastasis care shifted to precision radiotherapy. Their study from twenty twenty-five reviews patients across a decade plus. Whole-brain radiation is giving way to focused, high-precision treatment. That shift now includes patients with many metastases.

Patients treated from twenty ten to twenty twenty-three were included. Anyone with prior skull radiation was excluded. Survival trends across treatment years were compared statistically. Primary cancer type did not limit entry into the cohort. The era comparison tests whether precision care extends life. Avoiding whole-brain treatment also protects thinking ability. Centres worldwide face the same transition decision.
pmc-12753692:
Tong Wu and three colleagues simulate a metal screw pump designed to lift thick oil, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Conventional screw pumps use rubber stators at their core, and those stators fail in harsh wells. An all-metal conical design adjusts its internal clearance in place of rubber.

Outdoor experiments anchored the simulations. They modeled how clearance fit and rotor speed shape the pump's work, tracking displacement, torque, energy efficiency, and volumetric efficiency. Each trait was tracked across a range of fluid viscosities. Heavy oil reservoirs got recommended operating settings, given for unlike lifting conditions in the field. The metal design lifts fluids across a wide viscosity range that elastomer pumps cannot match. Simulation lets operators pick settings per well without worn equipment.
pmc-12783092:
Tayyab Ijaz and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-five study using explainable machine learning in drug-resistant epilepsy. About a third of epilepsy patients keep seizing despite medicines. Inflammation in the brain is a suspected driver, but reliable gene markers are lacking.

The team combined public gene data from brain tissue across several datasets. Multiple learning models competed to separate patients from controls. An explanation method ranked which genes mattered most to the models. Results were checked on an independent dataset. The study also matched candidate genes to possible drugs, offering leads for a stubborn condition.
pmc-12815292:
Wasfi Alghwyeen and his team pool studies on periostin in the blood as a mark that can tell how a scar lung ill with no known cause will fare. Their 2025 pooled study joins eleven studies. It takes in a blood protein put forth to judge how the ill moves on, with no cut into the body.

Periostin grades did not split in a firm way twixt sick folk and sound checks as a whole. But sick folk whose ill moved on had more high grades than firm sick folk. High periostin was tied to short life span, with risk near three times as high. Grades linked in a down way to drops in gas pass and lung size through the track span. The team ends that the mark tracks how the ill moves and will fare, though it does not split sick folk from sound folk.
pmc-12847792:
Joonyoung Her and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five mouse study of a protein that helps cells answer DNA damage. The protein RHNO1 supports a major alarm kinase at damage sites. Cell line work suggested roles in checkpoints and repair, but living tissue evidence was missing.

The team deleted the gene only in antibody-making B cells of mice. Damage signaling and cell cycle pauses were then tested in those primary cells. Defects appeared in checkpoint behaviour after damage. The model shows the helper matters in real immune cells, not just lab lines, with implications for genome protection.
pmc-12852092:

pmc-12853892:

pmc-13096892:

pmc-13171392:

pmc-13184592:

pmc-13190592:

pmc-13196492:

pmc-13198492:

pmc-13199192:

pmc-13199692:

pmc-13199992:

pmc-13201592:

pmc-13209492:

pmc-13212392:

pmc-13214292:

pmc-13215492:

pmc-13216092:

pmc-13216292:

pmc-13217892:

pmc-13218092:

pmc-13218192:

pmc-13218592:

pmc-13219292:

pmc-13219892:

pmc-13223992:

pmc-13226992:

pmc-13229392:

pmc-13230892:

pmc-13233492:

pmc-13233892:

pmc-13234592:

pmc-13236392:

pmc-13238692:

pmc-13239392:

pmc-13239592:

pmc-13239692:

pmc-13241292:

pmc-13241392:

pmc-13241692:

pmc-13242192:

pmc-13242492:

pmc-13243892:

pmc-13245092:

pmc-13245192:

pmc-13245692:

pmc-13246792:

pmc-13247792:

Mckenna Eklund and colleagues report in 2026 on a surprising link between the hormone estrogen and gut health in a Crohn's disease model. Changes in the immune sensor NOD2 form the strongest known genetic risk for Crohn's disease. How that sensor keeps the intestine stable has stayed unclear.

Estrogen alone copied the defects seen in the mutant fish, while a drug that blocks estrogen signaling repaired them. The results suggest hormone signals may help explain why Crohn's disease can differ between the sexes.
pmc-13271892:

This study used UK Biobank data to map how broad those links are.

The team trained artificial intelligence models to compress retinal scans and eye photographs into 256-number summaries. Those summaries associated with diseases including ischaemic heart disease, stroke-related disease, Parkinson's disease, and dementia. Cross-checking other data layers linked the eye features to heart and brain anatomy, fat metabolism, and gene sets tied to neurodegeneration. The authors frame the eye as a composite indicator of whole-body health.
pmc-13272092:
Dong Woo Shin and coauthors evaluate in 2026 the quality control center behind South Korea's national antimicrobial resistance surveillance system. Trustworthy resistance data depend on laboratories testing bacteria the same way across the country. The center runs proficiency checks while the surveillance network expands into new species and drugs.

The team reviewed interlaboratory testing and external assessment results from 2020 to 2024, spanning two phases of the program. Hospital isolates go to specialist centers for standardized susceptibility testing, while the control center independently verifies quality. The report judges whether accuracy held as the system grew, a question every national surveillance program must answer.
pmc-13272392:
Jayalaxmi Shetty and coauthors propose in 2026 that mineralized mouth biofilms act as armored reservoirs that disturb immunity far beyond the mouth. Dental plaque gathers calcium and phosphate until microbes become sealed inside mineral-protein shells. Such shells could shield bacteria from immune attack while letting mineral particles travel through the body.

The authors review how hydroxyapatite crystals alter macrophage behavior, blunting antigen display and sustaining low-grade inflammation. Protein-coated mineral particles in blood may also disturb vessel lining cells and clotting balance, feeding vessel calcification. pmc-13272592:
Kou Wang leads a 2026 study of how warming changes the spread of river water and drifting matter in the western Arctic Ocean. Rivers carry fresh water, nutrients, carbon, and pollutants into this small ocean. The authors trace how sea ice loss and lighter surface water alter ocean currents.

At the same time, stronger edge currents speed Siberian river water toward the North Atlantic. The result is far more mixing between basins, with effects for Arctic ecosystems and coastal communities.
pmc-13272892:
Majani Edward leads a 2026 narrative review of climate-driven vector-borne disease in West Africa. Such diseases, spread by insects and ticks, include malaria, dengue, and Lassa fever. pmc-13273392:
Biao Sheng leads a 2026 study joining inherited gene data with single-cell analysis in colorectal cancer, focusing on lactylation. pmc-13273592:
Tao Zhou and co-authors proposed a new method for fusing medical images in a 2026 paper. Combining scans such as CT and PET gives doctors richer pictures, yet lesions occupy a tiny part of each image. Standard fusion lets background dominate, which buries the very spots that matter.

Their network, a generative adversarial design guided by frequency analysis, works in two branches. One branch sharpens lesion related features in space and suppresses background clutter. The other splits the image into frequency bands to protect structure and edges. A special loss keeps the balance between highlighting lesions and preserving anatomy. Tests on lung CT windows and a whole brain atlas gave effective and robust fusion across settings, the authors report.
pmc-13273692:
Segvan M.S. Kucher and Mohammed Aziz Sulaiman tested whether EEG shape predicts early drug response in epilepsy in a 2026 prospective study. Diagnosis follows a modern classification, yet the look of discharge spikes between seizures is rarely used to pick the first medicine. The team followed newly diagnosed patients from their first brain wave test.

They enrolled 150 untreated patients across six epilepsy syndromes, twenty-five in each, and repeated testing at three months. Brain wave normalization varied widely by syndrome, from most children with absence epilepsy to only a fifth in one focal group. The shape of the discharges tracked with normalization, and patients whose EEG normalized were far more likely to be seizure free. The authors suggest morphology adds useful foresight beyond the syndrome label.
pmc-13274592:
Nanchao Wang and a large team report a 2026 journal article on a new way to watch the brain's waste-cleaning fluid system in living mice. This glymphatic system flushes metabolic waste from the brain, but deep-brain flow was hard to image without opening the skull. Their hybrid method merges photoacoustic tomography with ultrasound localization microscopy.

With it, they examined how the cleaning flow falters after ischemic stroke, with aging, and under anesthesia. They offer the tool, named 3D-PAULM, as a platform for preclinical research on brain waste clearance.
pmc-13274892:
A 2026 retraction notice in PLOS One withdraws an article on mutations in the gene ectodysplasin-A, called EDA, in people born missing some teeth. After publication, readers raised concerns about the western blot images in the paper's first two figures, the bands used to show protein amounts. Editors found bands in several lanes that looked alike, a suspicious vertical break in one panel, and missing background detail in many panels. The corresponding author offered an explanation for one figure, but the supplied originals deepened the editors' concerns. One author agreed to the retraction and apologized, six authors disagreed and stand by the findings, and one could not be reached.
pmc-13274992:
Vincent Hakim, Alain Karma, and Derek Abbott developed a theory of how echo state networks learn time patterns in a 2026 paper. These networks learn time patterns by feeding output back into a large, randomly wired reservoir, a trick that works well in practice. Why it works had lacked a firm mathematical account.

The authors found a regime, with stable dynamics and weak feedback, where learning can be described exactly. A small set of master modes governs the motion, and their interplay takes a simple normal form. In that picture, learning becomes a Fourier style splitting of the target pattern, and for large networks the needed amplitudes stop depending on the random wiring. The account stretches to stronger feedback and to networks with several unstable modes, offering design principles.
pmc-13275192:
Jonathan Alverio Rivera, Sonal Kaushik, and John Barnwell present a 2026 case report. It describes a bowel-to-skin fistula that surfaced as a thigh lump and infected an artificial hip. The patient was an eighty-three-year-old woman with earlier abdominal surgery and a right hip replacement. Imaging was clouded by glare from the metal joint, and no bowel connection could be confirmed. So the growing lateral thigh mass was presumed to be an abscess.

At drainage surgery, the cavity unexpectedly held feculent material, stool-like matter. This exposed a colocutaneous fistula reaching the prosthetic joint. The authors warn that deep soft tissue infections containing gas should prompt a search for an intestinal source, even in odd locations like the thigh. They add that multidisciplinary evaluation matters.
pmc-13276292:
Marie Frerejacques and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how uranium harms the kidney, studied in lab-grown human kidney cells. Uranium is both a heavy metal and a weak radiation source, and the kidney is its main target. The team used a cell line that mimics the kidney tubules where damage starts.

Half the cells died at a mid-range concentration the team identified. Uranium quickly doubled the production of reactive oxygen, unstable molecules that damage cells. Survival signals rose at low doses, but higher doses triggered strong inflammation signals. A known kidney injury marker rose slightly at the top dose. The panel of events feeds a safety framework for uranium poisoning.
pmc-13276592:
Sven Kratochvil and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on an engineered antibody against HIV designed to last longer in the body. Broadly neutralizing antibodies can block many HIV strains at once, but they fade too fast for lasting therapy. The team added mutations, known as LS changes, that make the antibody bind a recycling receptor twenty times more tightly. In mice the antibody's half-life stretched to about two weeks, and in primates to eighteen days, with a predicted human half-life near fifty days. Screening against thousands of human proteins showed no off-target binding. A phase one trial has begun.
pmc-13276792:
Xiaohui Song and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a dual-action eye drop complex for dry eye disease. Dry eye afflicts over thirty percent of people and worsens with age. Oxidative stress, damage from reactive oxygen, drives cell aging and surface damage in the disease.

Tear film held stable far longer than in untreated models, beating a commercial comparator. The authors propose the dual scavenging strategy for dry eye care.
pmc-13276892:
Foyez Ahmad and co-authors study a protective film formed by an ionic liquid lubricant under electric current, in a 2026 paper. Electric vehicle drivetrains carry stray currents that speed wear on gears and bearings. Thin, low-viscosity oils save energy but leave sliding parts harsher conditions.

Moderate current sped film formation, but beyond a threshold current, pitting wear took over instead. The films, rich in iron phosphates and oxides, stopped scuffing failures. A kinetic model now predicts film growth at electrified contacts.
pmc-13277292:
Bichen Miao leads a 2026 study building a vaccine platform from canine parvovirus, a virus that harms dogs and other carnivores. Current live vaccines raise safety worries and may miss new variants. Dogs given that version made strong immune responses, and their blood blocked both viruses in cell tests. Challenged dogs were fully protected against both infections. The stable production system could serve as a base for future multi-target animal vaccines, the authors say.
pmc-13277392:
Xinyu Zhang leads a 2026 cohort study of whether green space near home protects against glaucoma, an eye disease that can cause irreversible blindness. The team used UK Biobank data for 357,920 people and measured greenspace and home gardens within short distances of each home. Follow-up lasted a median of about thirteen and a half years.

Home gardens showed a similar pattern. Air pollution, screen time, activity, and genes did not explain the link. Adding green cover to land planning could support eye health, the authors suggest.
pmc-13277492:
Ahmed Saed Hussein and colleagues survey childhood vaccination completion in Mogadishu, Somalia, in a 2026 study. Mother's schooling, antenatal visits, and advice received all mattered in simple comparisons. The authors recommend defaulter tracking and stronger caregiver follow-up.
pmc-13278392:
Samantha J Fabian leads a 2026 study of how certain fungi build ergot alkaloids, compounds used in farming and medicine. In one fungal family, two separate enzymes assemble a key building block. Adding partner genes raised output of a second compound, LAH. pmc-13278692:
Van-Huong Nguyen and co-authors report outcomes of a T-shaped joining technique after stomach removal for cancer, in a 2026 study. Reconnecting the food pipe to the small intestine inside the abdomen is a demanding step of fully laparoscopic surgery. Long-term data for this stapled method were limited.

Every operation finished laparoscopically, with no leaks at the join and no deaths after surgery. Overall complications were low, affecting only a small share of patients. Five-year survival reached about forty-two percent. The authors call the technique safe, reproducible, and oncologically acceptable.
pmc-13278792:
Cong Chao and co-authors describe a newborn heart operation with a borderline right ventricle in a 2026 case report. pmc-13278892:
Yanxiao Sun, Longtao Zhang, and Dong Guo compare first-line immunotherapy combinations for metastatic triple-negative breast cancer, in a 2026 network meta-analysis. pmc-13279292:

pmc-13279392:

The longer wavelength group drove most gains in frustration and resilience scores, with large effect sizes. The shorter wavelength group drove gains on the impulsivity scale. Breed mix held mostly Belgian Malinois dogs. Light dose by wavelength may shape which behaviours shift, a lead for work dog care.
pmc-13279892:

pmc-13280592:

pmc-13280692:

pmc-13280992:

pmc-13281492:

pmc-13281792:

pmc-13281892:

pmc-13282692:

pmc-13282892:

pmc-13282992:

pmc-13283192:

pmc-13283392:

pmc-13283892:

pmc-13284092:

pmc-13284292:

pmc-13284492:

pmc-13284692:

pmc-13284992:

pmc-13285092:
Zongcheng Cai and eight co-authors fine-tune germ food to heal worn high mine land on the Qinghai-Tibet flat. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. pmc-13285992:
Jessica Menold and colleagues argue that smart software is reshaping who does what in design work, in a 2026 perspective essay. pmc-13286792:

pmc-13286892:
Wei Pan and a large team check the safety of a new rotavirus vaccine in young monkeys. The 2026 test had to clear the way for trials in people. Rotavirus kills many small children each year through bad diarrhea. The vaccine joins parts of two virus types on shells borrowed from a norovirus.

pmc-13287192:
Niklas Amann and co-authors reviewed care records in 2026 for 49 patients treated in Erlangen between 2012 and 2024 who had ovarian cancer and an inherited BRCA change. pmc-13287392:

pmc-13287492: Antonio M Newman-Portela and co-authors issued an author correction in 2026 to a study on bacteria that change uranium forms in mine water when fed glycerol. pmc-13287592:

pmc-13287692:

pmc-13288692:
Matthew McLaughlin and co-authors check whether pilot health trials think ahead about growing bigger, in a 2026 methodological review. pmc-13289092:
Altaseb Beyene Kassaw and colleagues track tobacco use in East African women. Their 2026 study uses health survey data. It spans 11 nations in the region. Women aged 15 to 49 took part. The full set held 543,013 women.

Madagascar and Zambia bucked that trend. Older women had far higher odds of use. Schooling also tied strongly to use. Rural women made up most of the sample.
pmc-13289192:
Hubert Amu and colleagues study patient voice in chronic care in Ghana in 2026. Two teaching hospitals hosted the work. It held 82 adults with chronic diseases. It also held 30 health workers. Talks ran from January to May 2019.

Drug and exercise choices rarely involved patients. Both sides backed patient centrality in words. Their grasp of how it works differed. The authors urge shared talks and clear teaching.
pmc-13289492:

pmc-13290092:

pmc-13290692:

pmc-13290792:

pmc-13291192:

The patient had the shoulder joint replaced with a reverse implant. Whole-body drug treatment followed the surgery. At fifteen months, shoulder use was excellent. No return of disease was seen. pmc-13291292:
A stress chain in immune cells may worsen sepsis. Yin Ni leads a 2026 study of infected patients and mice. Sepsis is a whole-body reaction to severe infection. Inner cell stress in macrophages was poorly understood.

pmc-13291792:
Shanshan Ma and co-authors share a 2026 dental case report on saving a tooth socket with a diode laser plus a flap closure method called the hood technique. pmc-13292792:
S.K. Sasidharan and colleagues ask, in a 2026 study, whether where and how often birds are swabbed changes detection of Mycoplasma gallisepticum. The bacterium causes lasting breathing disease in laying hens and is usually found by swabbing the throat area.

pmc-13292992:
Zijing Zhao leads a 2026 materials study making flat magnetic alloys that stay magnetic at room temperature and switch in steps. Stepwise switching could raise storage density in future memory, yet known flat ferrimagnets often need deep cold.

pmc-13293892:

pmc-13294092:

pmc-13294492:

pmc-13294892:

pmc-13294992: A 2026 correction notice fixes a single name in a machine learning study about severe erection failure following repair of a fractured penis. pmc-13295992:

pmc-13296292:

pmc-13296492:

pmc-13296892:

pmc-13297092:

pmc-13297292:

pmc-13297392:

pmc-13297592:

pmc-13297792:

pmc-13297992:

pmc-13298992:

pmc-13299492:

pmc-13299592:

pmc-13299792:

pmc-13300492:

pmc-13300892:

pmc-13301392:

pmc-13301992:

pmc-13303792:

pmc-13304392:

pmc-13304792:

pmc-13307292:

pmc-13309192:

pmc-13310492:

pmc-13310692:
Deirdre Colburn, with two co-authors, reports a 2026 survey study on how teen rule breaking links to poor mental health in the United States. Their work asks whether hard living conditions and weak social support help explain higher rates of depression and anxiety among youth with a history of delinquency.

The full survey held 5,311 people aged 10 to 34 years old, with focused study of the 2,658 people who got questions about delinquency. About one quarter reported some past delinquency. Once hardship and support were counted, the direct link to distress faded and lost strength. Findings point to aid that cuts material hardship and builds support.
pmc-13310892:
Wei Tan and colleagues weigh safety of the bowel drug upadacitinib from two sources in a 2026 study. The JAK blocking drug helps inflammatory bowel disease, yet real world safety in Asian groups is thin. The team paired United States harm reports with a hospital cohort in China.

The cohort held 183 patients from 2023 to 2025, and near half had at least one side effect. Lab changes, infections, and skin issues were most common, while gut perforation and vein clots were rare. Most first events came within two months of starting. Large scale reports flagged rare lung infection and stroke like events not seen in the cohort.
pmc-13310992:
Edoardo Vergnano and co-authors map heat traits in pepper genes in a 2026 review. Peppers make pungent capsaicinoids and mild capsinoids through two joined chemical paths, found only in this plant group. Past gene hunts were scattered across groups, which blocked comparison and breeding use.

A total of 155 trait regions from past studies were placed on one reference pepper genome. Shared zones narrowed to 23 strong genomic regions that hold prime candidate genes. Donor types with high trait levels are listed for breeders. The unified map should speed breeding for taste and health linked compounds.
pmc-13311092:
Hongxia Wang and a large team compare bowel surgery choices in advanced ovarian cancer in a 2026 study. Full tumor removal guides survival in stage III and IV disease, and bowel spread is common. Whether cutting out bowel or peeling tumor off its wall changes outlook was unclear.

Records covered 255 patients from 2015 to 2020, with 101 bowel removals and 154 peeling cases. Full clearance rates were high in both groups. Peeling cases had fewer transfusions, lung issues, and fluid buildups, while survival at five years was alike overall. When full clearance was reached, extra bowel removal added no survival gain.
pmc-13311192:
Luzhe Wu and co-authors probe how chlorogenic acid blocks a stomach germ enzyme in a 2026 study. Helicobacter pylori infects half the world and uses urease to survive stomach acid. The plant phenol chlorogenic acid curbs that enzyme, yet its binding mode was unknown, so lab kinetics and computer models were joined.

Tests showed mixed type blocking with a firm binding strength and heat releasing grip. Light and resonance measures backed a stable complex near the active site and its flap. Simulations held the pose steady over time. The acid stands as a lead for new urease targeted designs.
pmc-13311292:
Noëlla Delmas and colleagues present a 2026 national survey analysis from France linking lifetime sexual violence with tobacco, alcohol, and cannabis use in adults. The data come from the 2017 Health Barometer.

The survey covered 25,319 adults aged 18 to 75. About 9.5 percent of women and 2 percent of men reported sexual violence in their lives in this survey. After adjustment, a history of violence tied to higher odds of all five use outcomes, from daily smoking to problem cannabis use. Monthly cannabis use showed the strongest link in both sexes. Care that joins trauma support with substance help is urged.
pmc-13311992:
Ramaekers JG, Bade R, and Hall W argue in a 2026 article for research-friendly rules on novel psychoactive substances. These synthetic drugs copy banned drugs while dodging treaties, and little is known of their harms or possible medical uses.

Strict scheduling, the authors say, blocks the very studies needed to judge a substance. They propose four stages: early surveillance for new substances and harms, provisional scheduling that allows regulated research, controlled studies of effects and abuse risk, and reclassification on the full evidence. The frame aims at drug policy that protects health without freezing science out.
pmc-13312692:
Xin-Lei Tang and colleagues pool studies on shoulder stiffness after rotator cuff repair. Their meta-analysis from twenty twenty-six searches four major databases. Stiffness is a frustrating setback after otherwise successful shoulder surgery. Knowing how often it strikes, and in whom, guides prevention.

Eight cohort studies covered more than twenty-one thousand patients. About one in six patients developed postoperative stiffness overall. Rates varied widely between studies and world regions. The team also hunted risk factors across the cohorts. Study quality was scored with a standard scale. Wide variation warns against quoting one simple rate. Surgeons gain targets for closer follow-up after repair.
pmc-13312792:
Carina O. Walowski and Kristina Norman review, in a 2026 article, the malnutrition-sarcopenia syndrome in older adults, the damaging overlap of poor nutrition with lost muscle mass, strength, and function. Whether the pairing is a true syndrome or just severe malnutrition with wasting is debated, but the authors argue the combination creates problems neither condition causes alone.

The two states drive each other: too little food and inflammation break muscle down and block its rebuilding, while weakness cuts activity and independence, further shrinking appetite and intake. Outcomes include faster functional decline, slower recovery, longer hospital stays, and higher death rates than either condition alone. Countermeasures must hit both sides at once: enough protein, energy, and vitamin D, progressive resistance training, treatment of underlying illness, and medication review. The authors say naming the pattern helps clinicians spot vulnerable patients early.
pmc-13313492:
Meican Ma and colleagues unravel, in a 2026 study, how lactate fuels the overgrowth of joint lining tissue in rheumatoid arthritis. The inflamed synovium shifts toward sugar-burning metabolism and produces excess lactate. Patient samples showed lactate and a lactate-based protein tag both elevated, in step with disease activity. Among tagged proteins, one called CRIP1 stood out as modified and central to the proliferation.

The team traced the tag's placement to an enzyme named MOF acting in synovial fibroblasts. Tagged CRIP1 grabs hold of p21, a brake protein, and pulls it away from the cell-cycle engine CDK2. That lets cells pass into the division phase. A version of CRIP1 that cannot accept the tag slowed joint lining growth in gene-therapy experiments. Peptide blockers aimed at the tagging site eased disease in two arthritis models, including a humanized mouse. The pathway offers a drug target outside immune suppression.
pmc-13313892:
Hoang Thi Anh Phuong and colleagues trial, in a 2026 poultry study, a fermented shallot extract as a stand-in for antibiotics in broiler chickens. Pressure to cut drug use is rising, just as harmful E. coli keeps costing producers growth and birds. Three hundred day-old broilers were randomized across six groups. They included uninfected and antibiotic controls, plus three challenged groups drinking water with 1, 2, or 3 percent extract fermented by Lactiplantibacillus plantarum. Challenge came through infection with a virulent strain.

The 3 percent dose performed best. Weight gain rose by 9.4 percent over the challenged control, and survival returned to 100 percent, matching the uninfected and antibiotic groups. Gut checks showed fewer harmful bacteria, more beneficial lactobacilli, and the tallest gut villi in that group. Barrier-strengthening gene expression improved at the higher doses. The authors present the extract, at 3 percent, as a non-antibiotic strategy built on gut integrity and microbe balance.
pmc-13314392:
Yeon-Woo Kim and co-workers build a fruit jelly sweet with a health drink and test how starch choice shapes it, in their 2026 study. Gwapyeon is a starch gel confection, and the team added Bacchus, a tonic drink, to make a functional version.

Three starches, corn, mung bean, and potato, were each used at three levels under the same making process. Traits hinged mostly on starch type: mung bean gels had lower pH and more dissolved solids, corn gels had higher pH and lower sweetness readings, and potato gels fell between. Mung bean and corn gels looked brighter, while potato gels looked darker. Storage told apart too, with mung bean gels weeping early and corn gels keeping better, as the authors report. The work guides makers on picking a starch for texture and shelf life.
pmc-13315592:
Yuanyuan Liu and colleagues present a quality control tool in 2026 for single-cell RNA sequencing, called scQCenrich. Standard checks rely on fixed cutoffs for mitochondrial RNA, gene counts, and molecule counts, yet cell damage from handling can slip past those simple rules.

The new method combines standard measures with intronic share, MALAT1 enrichment, stress signs from cell splitting, and optional splicing data. Across mouse brain, mouse heart, and lung cancer data it cut over-filtering while keeping real cell groups intact, and stayed cautious on clean blood cell data. Auto reports tie each call to cluster data and marker genes for clear review.
pmc-13316192:
Michelle M Gagnon and co-authors describe in 2026 the balancing act of designing, with teenagers, a phone app for menstrual pain built by an industry partner. More than half of menstruating adolescents live with period pain, and phone-based behavioral help is wanted, yet no app for this group had been designed with youth before.

Work ran in three phases, from choosing a partner and forming a patient advisory group to teen testing. Twenty-two adolescents reviewed successive app versions aloud and in interviews. The app was well received, and the team draws lessons on the friction between user-centered ideals and industry timelines.
pmc-13316292:
Yi Wei and colleagues present 2026 lab research on how lung injury during sepsis pushes certain immune cells toward an iron-linked form of death. Their focus is a chain joining the alarm protein S100A9, the enzyme USP7, and NCOA4, a driver of ferritin breakdown inside macrophages.

In their model, sepsis raises S100A9, which helps USP7 reach NCOA4 and strip tags that would send it for disposal. Kept alive, NCOA4 frees iron, fuels fat damage, and kills the cell. Removing S100A9 or blocking USP7 with the drug P5091 eased lung harm in mice, and patient data linked high USP7 and NCOA4 with poorer 28-day survival. The chain offers a clear drug target for a condition with few options.
pmc-13316692:
Vivek Gautam and co-authors developed, in a 2026 food study, a healthier version of kheer, the classic dairy dessert, using barnyard millet and white carrot powder. First they profiled the small molecules in both ingredients to know what goodness each brings.

Millet carried a range of useful compounds, including amino acids, while white carrot powder was rich in genistein family compounds. A rotating design tested mixes of millet, brown sugar, and carrot powder, judged on taste, texture, and antioxidant strength. The winning recipe used 25 grams of millet, 25 grams of brown sugar, and 10 grams of carrot powder per batch, earning a top acceptance score of 8.8 in the tasting panel. Carrot powder lifted nutrition and texture together.
pmc-13316892:
Christopher J. Ferguson, writing in 2026, tests two competing explanations for poor mental health in young adults. Professional bodies often advise delaying children's first smartphone or tablet, warning of lasting harm. Clear evidence for that advice has been scarce. Harmful childhood experiences offer a rival explanation.

Data from 80,878 young adults, supplied by Sapienlabs, recorded the age of first access to phones and tablets alongside adverse childhood events such as abuse or neglect. Regression analysis found that adverse events predicted later mental health difficulties. Age of first device access did not. Ferguson argues that warnings about early screens look unwarranted on this evidence, and that public alarm may distract from family adversity, which showed the stronger link.
pmc-13318392:
Ahmet Cigiloglu and colleagues offer a 2026 evaluation of how well ChatGPT answers questions about malnutrition in older adults, a common and risky problem in later life. Twelve questions and three patient cases were written to cover basic ideas, diagnosis, follow-up, and treatment.

Three geriatric specialists scored the replies independently with a quality tool for medical artificial intelligence, and their agreement was strong. Average quality reached 26.60 points, rated as very good, though the hip fracture case scored clearly lower than the others and source use was the weakest area across cases. Better grounding in current guidelines could make such tools more useful beside clinicians, rather than in place of them.
pmc-13318792:
Maliheh Hasannia and co-authors review, in 2026, smart nanomedicine designed to convert the tumour surroundings and beat drug resistance. Chemotherapy often fails because the tumour microenvironment blocks drugs. Low oxygen, acidity, abnormal vessels, and dense tissue all protect cancer cells. The review argues for reshaping that setting instead of only attacking tumour cells.

Tiny carriers can react to acidity, oxygen levels, enzymes, light, or magnetic fields. They release drugs at the tumour site and deepen penetration. Some designs normalise vessels, break down tissue barriers, or wake immune responses. Others generate reactive oxygen or heat to kill cells. Together these systems can turn a resistant setting into a responsive one. The authors discuss translation toward precise, gentler cancer care.
pmc-13318892:
Peng Zhang and co-authors review, in 2026, the role of gut microbes in melanosis coli, a dark staining of the colon lining. The harmless, usually reversible condition follows long use of anthraquinone laxatives. The classic account involves dying surface cells eaten by immune cells, leaving pigment behind. Microbes may start that chain.

Gut bacteria can convert inactive laxative compounds into active forms such as rhein anthrone. Enzymes from microbes perform that unlocking step. The review separates proven findings in this condition from ideas borrowed from constipation research. Changes in microbe diversity and short-chain fatty acid producers are discussed. So are barrier problems and immune signalling routes. Stopping the laxatives remains the main treatment, the authors stress.
pmc-13319092:
Sundararaman Rengarajan and colleagues present a 2026 design study of Sugar Slay, a gamified support system for type 1 diabetes aimed at adolescents and young adults. Daily care demands constant choices about glucose, insulin, food, activity, and sleep. The ecosystem pairs a patient app with a companion app for caregivers. Sensor and wearable data feed machine learning forecasts.

Among the models tested, a sequence-to-sequence bidirectional LSTM forecast glucose trends best. A need-finding study with six caregivers shaped the companion app's features. Safety monitoring had to respect the patient's independence. Game elements aim to build daily habits and steady engagement. The authors frame the work as uniting live body data, prediction, and behaviour science for chronic disease self-care.
pmc-13319392:
E Syabbalo leads a team case report from 2026 about liver cancer in a 32 year old man in Zambia. He had long term hepatitis B and a 12 year past of heavy drinking, both known risks for this cancer. In much of Africa the disease strikes younger and is often found late, when scans and lab support are thin.

Scans showed many liver lumps, a blood marker was high, and the virus test was positive, yet the scan pattern did not meet the set rules for a firm call without tissue. A guided needle sample gave the proof needed for care referral. The case shows how thin test access can stall care even when signs look strong.
pmc-13319692:
Jorge Luis Rodríguez and a large Colombian team present, in 2026, an automated system for scoring a key immunotherapy marker in lung cancer biopsies from Latin American patients. PD-L1 staining guides treatment choice in non-small cell lung cancer, but human scoring varies widely between observers.

The team digitised 141 biopsies and trained deep learning models to segment tissue, detect cells and classify them by tumour status and marker positivity. Detection precision was solid, and sensitivity for positive tumour cells was high. The system's tumour proportion score agreed with an expert pathologist's manual score in almost all cases. Maps of marker distribution also revealed uneven staining inside tumours. The authors argue automation could improve reproducibility, especially where specialist pathologists are scarce.
pmc-13319892:
Joaquín Rodríguez-Pinilla and co-authors describe a new virus that kills a dairy linked germ in a 2026 study from Spain. The germ causes udder infections in cows and can reach people through tainted milk, and drug proof strains are on the rise. A virus pulled from waste water in Extremadura was checked as a possible clean control tool.

Under the scope the virus showed a round head and a short tail, and its plaques bore a wide halo that hints at film cutting enzymes. It killed most of 37 dairy germ strains tested and stayed active across wide heat and acid ranges and long cold storage. Its small gene set held no harm, drug proof, or sleep mode genes. Film tests showed clear drops in live germ counts.
pmc-13320392:
Fatma Indriani and co-authors present a photo data set for counting oil palm fruit bunches in a 2026 data article. Plantations forecast yield by a field census where staff count and grade bunches tree by tree. Photos from many sides catch every bunch but count the same bunch again and again, so a truth set that links views was needed to test smart counters.

Smartphone shots cover 953 trees at two estates in Kalimantan, Indonesia, each tree shot from four or eight sides in set turns. Bunches carry box marks in four ripeness grades set by months to harvest. A tree level truth file lists 9823 sole bunches with their cross view links, so counting tools can be graded apart from spotting skill.
pmc-13321392:
Mengxing Cheng and co-authors test a new drug against triple-negative breast cancer in a 2026 study. This cancer type lacks the usual hormone and HER2 targets, so options are few. A gene switch partner called TEAD4, driven by YAP, was high in these tumours and tied to poor outlook for patients.

Screening against the YAP and TEAD4 joined structure found a small molecule, M511-0965, that blocks the pair. In cell work it slowed growth, movement, and shape change linked to spread, while raising cell death. Its effect ran mainly through lowering a downstream gene, TGFB2. Two contact points on the target proved key for binding, which guides further drug design.
pmc-13322092:
Ewa Błaszczyk and colleagues use whole exome sequencing to clarify disorders of sex development in a 2026 study. Children with a 46,XY karyotype and atypical urogenital development form a rare, mixed group, and about half of cases stay unexplained despite gene testing. The team sequenced 39 carefully assessed children aged 0.2 to 17.9 years.

A clear genetic cause was found in 8 children, with firm harmful variants in 3, touching the AR and DHX37 genes among others. Likely harmful variants appeared in 5 more children, and uncertain variants in 7. Androgen insensitivity was the most common confirmed cause. Many cases still lacked any known candidate variant.
pmc-13322192:
Chenxin Flora Jiang and co-authors build a tool to map how gene partnerships shift across tissue in a 2026 study. Spatial transcriptomics shows where genes act, and many tools flag single genes that vary by place. Far fewer ask how correlations between gene pairs change across locations, though such shifts reveal local control circuits.

The framework, spCorr, gives spot level estimates of gene correlation and flags pairs whose link varies by place or tissue zone. Simulations and real data showed strong detection power, well held false discovery rates, and fast computing. Patterns found highlighted fine tissue structures, gene module jobs, and region specific interactions in real samples.
pmc-13322492:
Amanda Mariane Paulino Gualberto, Fabiana Andrade Penido, and Ana Cristina Côrtes Gama compare voice measures in women with and without throat changes in a 2026 study. The sample held 69 female teachers sorted by scope exams and expert listening into groups with or without laryngeal changes and voice deviations. Recordings of a held vowel and counting were analysed with acoustic software.

Women with changes showed lower values for several smoothness and harmonic measures and higher jitter, shimmer, and spectral tilt. Some measures, including cepstral peak and harmonic gap, did not separate the laryngeal groups, and a few also failed to separate voice deviation groups. Acoustic testing thus helps but cannot replace direct throat examination.
pmc-13322692:
Dror Ronel and his team test, in 2026, how consistently and accurately ChatGPT answers orthopaedic trauma questions. Clinicians consult such tools more and more, but reliability is uncertain. Seven questions about femoral neck and trochanteric fractures were put to the model again and again and compared with a standard textbook and expert consensus.

The model's answers were highly consistent across sessions, with strong text likeness between repeats. Match with the textbook was only partial, and formal agreement scores with both textbook and experts were low. Specific disagreements included age thresholds for joint replacement and preferred nail length for certain fractures, suggesting reliance on old sources. Readability was good. The authors conclude the tool is coherent but gapped, and should support rather than replace clinical judgement and fresh sources.
pmc-13323592:
Thomas Konecny and co-authors asked whether suppressing beta-adrenergic signals after lung transplantation helps recipients live longer. Their 2026 retrospective study followed 299 adults transplanted at the University of Florida between 2016 and 2021. It tracked survival after a 10-day blanking window and related it to antiarrhythmic drugs taken before and after surgery. Heart rhythm problems are a known drag on transplant results, yet guidance on beta suppression after transplant has stayed unclear.

Beta-adrenergic suppression was prescribed to 70% of recipients and tracked with longer survival even after adjustment for confounders. The benefit appeared both for patients who continued the drugs from before transplant and for those who started them afterward. No survival benefit showed for other antiarrhythmic drug classes. The authors present the findings as promising but observational, calling for prospective trials to confirm the effect.
pmc-13324392:
Guido Gembillo and team review what imaging can and cannot add to the care of glomerulonephritis. Their 2026 paper starts from an unchanged fact: renal biopsy remains the standard reference, and no imaging method has displaced it. The open question is whether imaging can complement tissue study with extra information on disease level, outlook, and treatment response, guiding care between biopsies.

Standard ultrasound stays first-line, with outer thinning and raised in-kidney resistive indices mainly reflecting chronic structural damage rather than the underlying subtype. Newer tools aim further. Shear-wave elastography measures tissue stiffness, and contrast-enhanced scans probe microvascular perfusion. Multiparametric MRI and nuclear tracers add functional detail, with reported links to fibrosis in IgA nephropathy and vascular change in lupus nephritis and membranous disease. Evidence stays mixed and varied, so imaging aids risk grouping and monitoring but cannot yet replace biopsy.
pmc-13324492:
Edward P.K. Parker and the OpenSAFELY team track severe COVID-19 in immunocompromised adults in England in a 2026 cohort study. People with weak immune systems face high risk, yet few studies focus on them alone.

Each virus wave from 2020 to 2024 held between 475,360 and 508,545 people in five groups, from transplant recipients to those on immune-suppressing drugs. Transplant, bone marrow, and active cancer treatment groups had the highest severe illness rates. Recent vaccination cut risk in every group and wave, though the gain was smallest after transplant, with a hazard ratio of 0.88 in the JN.1 wave. Older age and more health conditions raised risk throughout.
pmc-13324692:
Stephen Kibusi, Grace Mollel, and Angelina Joho tested peer teaching by experienced patients for people with diabetes in Tanzania. Their study, published in twenty twenty-six, trained a small group of patients who met set criteria to act as educators. Adults with type two diabetes at two hospitals were compared: one group received two hour-long peer sessions, while the other kept standard health education. The team measured health knowledge, attitudes toward self-care, daily self-care practices, and how well patients kept to their medicine.

After the sessions, the peer-taught group scored clearly higher on health literacy, self-care attitudes, and self-care practices than the control group. The authors describe the approach as low cost and well suited to places with few health workers. They recommend adding trained expert patients to national diabetes care guidance, with possible savings from better long-term outcomes.
pmc-13325592:
Saadaq Adan Hussein and team explore whether sin taxes could fund universal health coverage in Somalia. Their 2026 scoping review, after PRISMA-ScR guidance, pulls together formal and grey reports on using taxes on tobacco, alcohol, sugary drinks, and khat as a lasting health funding route. Noncommunicable diseases cause 74% of deaths worldwide, and Somalia's path to care is held back by low tax revenue, reliance on outside aid, and heavy out-of-pocket spending.

The review finds scope. A khat tax in Somaliland generates about 2 million US dollars a year, showing that sin taxes can both curb harmful use and expand public health funding. Well-designed tools, especially with revenues partly set aside for primary care, maternal and child health, and chronic disease prevention, offer predictable funding. Evidence from peer countries stresses high rates, automatic inflation adjustment, and robust enforcement as critical to maximizing health gains and fiscal space.
pmc-13326892:
Tengbo Rao and team looked at how shifts in the choroid, the blood-rich eye layer, track with sight in dysthyroid optic nerve disease. Their 2026 look-back snapshot study took in 38 people with thyroid eye disease. It covered 27 quiet-disease eyes, 22 active eyes with no nerve damage, and 27 nerve-damage eyes. Wide-field OCT scans gave choroid depth, vessel measures, and disc measures. Sight checks covered sharpness, nerve signals, and visual fields.

Sight sharpness got worse and mean light sense fell as disease got worse. Nerve signal strength at 0.25 degrees was lower where nerve damage was present. Optic disc choroid vessel scores, upper-nose choroid measures, and nerve fiber blood flow each linked significantly with light sense. The last also linked with nerve signal strength. The team holds that choroid shifts track sight. They put choroid depth and vessel scores forward as markers of flare and sight loss.
pmc-13327292:
Robin Christensen, Tobias Haugegaard, and Janus C Jakobsen wrote a 2026 commentary on how lab physiology studies should be reported. They answer critics who fear that fixed analysis plans, set in advance, would block open exploration and slow discovery. Their stance is that weak reporting, not exploration itself, wastes research effort.

Poorly matched questions, flexible analysis choices, and selective reporting can inflate false findings that later fail to repeat, they argue. Planning ahead, used in proportion, protects the value of early results and guards priority instead of acting as a statistical excuse. Clear records of what was planned and what was tried let readers judge how much trust a finding deserves.
pmc-13327392:
Vinicius Ferreira Capelli and colleagues report a 2026 study of small RNA molecules in papillary thyroid cancer that spread. They compared tumor tissue with matching distant spread tissue from patients who died of the disease. Out of 3,555 treated patients, only eight had both kinds of sample available.

The lab profiled 64 preselected microRNAs and found five that differed between first tumors and spread sites. After stricter checks, miR-10b-5p and miR-30e-3p stayed higher in the spread tissue. Both molecules are known from other cancers to affect cell movement, invasion, and cell death. The pattern may help explain how this thyroid cancer advances and could guide future marker work.
pmc-13328192:
Soo-Jin Oh, Ok Sarah Shin, and Ji-Yeun Hur review viral triggers in Alzheimer's disease in a 2026 article. Brain-infecting viruses and the immune response to them may form a shared, overlooked driver of neurodegeneration. Herpesviruses, SARS-CoV-2, and HIV take center stage in their synthesis.

Such viruses upset brain balance through inflammation, amyloid buildup, tau damage, and faulty cell cleanup, while the body's own antiviral tools, including type I interferons, can add harm when misregulated. Entry routes range from the nose nerve to infected immune cells acting as Trojan horses, plus leaky brain barriers. Broadening the frame beyond plaques may open prevention ideas, from antivirals to calmer immune tuning.
pmc-13328492:
Xiang Yu and co-authors compare patient positions for fixing hard hip fractures in a 2026 study. Irreducible trochanteric fractures with a split lesser trochanter resist standard setup on a traction table. The team reviewed 48 patients. Half were treated lying on their side and half on their back with traction. All received limited open reduction and nail fixation.

Side positioning cut preparation time to 10.86 minutes against 18.21 minutes for the table setup in the reported means, shortened surgery, and reduced X-ray shots and blood loss as well. Hospital stay, healing time, and one-year pain and function scores did not differ between groups. The side setup simply makes a hard operation smoother, the authors conclude.
pmc-13329492:
Muhammad Usman Amanat and co-authors explore why some oral cancer patients in Pakistan refuse hospital care in a 2026 qualitative study. Interviews were held with eight patients who had refused care, eight family members who shared in choices, and three oral surgeons. Talk was recorded, translated, and grouped into themes, then read against a health belief framework.

Seven linked themes emerged, covering views of risk, severity, gains, barriers, confidence, prompts, and faith. Many patients saw cancer as incurable, feared harm from treatment, or faced cost and travel limits. Family views and trust in traditional healing weighed heavily. Faith cut both ways, sometimes backing refusal and sometimes backing hospital care. The authors urge care talks shaped to local culture.
pmc-13330992:
Joan B. Escobar and team tested oxytocin for fentanyl-induced respiratory depression in rats. Their 2026 study notes that opioid misuse is a serious national crisis, made worse by mixing opioids with non-opioid depressants such as xylazine, which resist mu opioid receptor blockers like naloxone. The team tested whether oxytocin can ease severe respiratory depression and death from high-dose fentanyl or the fentanyl-xylazine mix.

Oxytocin raised survival and breathing function in male and female rats with breathing trouble caused by fentanyl and by the mix. Recovery after the mix beat naloxone alone. Chemogenetic activation of oxytocin-receptor-positive neurons in the ventral breathing group gave similar gains to oxytocin itself. The team presents it as a promising therapeutic target, noting bedside pluses. It is already FDA-approved for other uses, has a strong safety record, and is unlikely to induce withdrawal or reverse analgesia as naloxone does.
pmc-13333292:
Azan Ijaz and Ghulam Mohyudin wrote a 2026 letter to the editor questioning how far the safety results for the Alzheimer's drug donanemab can be stretched. A recent analysis of the TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 trial reported a safety profile in the population eligible under European rules.

The letter notes that this eligible group excluded everyone on blood thinners, a rule that lowers the rate of bleeding-type imaging side effects. Atrial fibrillation, the main reason older adults take such drugs, is common alongside dementia. In a Finnish cohort of over 70,000 people with Alzheimer's, about 23 percent were on oral anticoagulants at diagnosis. Removing them, the writers argue, creates a lower-risk group than clinics actually treat, and the other two exclusions, surface iron deposits and uncontrolled blood pressure, affect far fewer people. They urge readers to treat the reassuring safety figures as products of selection, not proof of better real-world tolerability.
pmc-13333592:
A mini review published in 2026 by Lukas D. Linde and co-authors examines how pulsed radiofrequency stimulation affects mitochondria inside neurons. Pulsed radiofrequency is a non-destructive treatment used for nerve pain, yet how it eases pain remains debated.

The authors searched five databases and kept 10 experimental studies for a narrative summary. Those studies show that continuous radiofrequency badly damages mitochondria, while the pulsed form leaves their structure intact. Pulsed treatment lowered membrane potential, raised ATP in the cell fluid, and increased mitochondrial numbers, changes that may support pain relief and nerve repair. The review gives a clearer picture of how this treatment may work, though the exact pathways still need confirmation.
pmc-13333692:
Yongcong Shao and co-authors pitted caffeine against modafinil as counters to sleep deprivation in a 2026 experiment. The study used brain recordings to see how each drug affects object working memory at different stages of thought.

Fourteen healthy men took part in a randomized, double-blind crossover design, completing a 2-back memory task at baseline and after 36 hours without sleep. Modafinil raised accuracy after deprivation beyond baseline levels, while caffeine simply held performance near baseline. Brain responses split too: caffeine raised an early sensing signal but lowered a late holding signal. The findings suggest the two stimulants protect thinking through separate pathways, one aiding later memory upkeep and the other mainly early perception.
pmc-13334792:
Cheng-Yu Lai and Yu-Chin An presented a 2026 clinical case of an older adult with abdominal fullness. A 71-year-old man who had previously lost part of his colon came in two days after swallowing a sour plum, with mild nausea and poor intake.

Blood tests showed raised white cells, and a plain X-ray gave no answer. Bedside ultrasound told the story: swollen, fluid-filled small bowel loops with the rippled keyboard sign, plus a bright arc-shaped object casting a shadow. The diagnosis was a phytobezoar, a compacted plant mass, blocking the small bowel, later confirmed by CT. He recovered with bowel rest, a nasogastric tube, and supportive care, avoiding surgery. The case promotes bedside ultrasound when X-rays stay silent.
pmc-13336092:
Ziyun Liu and co-authors looked at hydrothermal humification, a way to turn biomass waste into lab-made humic acid for soils, in a 2026 article. The product promises carbon storage and hardier farming, but uneven conversion efficiency and variable makeup hold back deployment.

The review explains how operating settings, catalysts, and joined process designs steer yield, molecular structure, reactivity, and stability of the humic product. Setting hydrolysis-, condensation-, and oxidation-led pathways side by side clarifies how carbon transforms and why soil and plant responses differ. Life-cycle and cost checks map where the method could pay environmentally and economically. The authors close on the frontier problems: making the product stable enough to lock carbon away and proving results at field scale.
pmc-13336892:
Yu-Zhou Qiao and colleagues build a self-igniting framework fuel for propulsion in a 2026 study. The clusters wake up the normally inert carborane linker. pmc-13337092:
Haiqiao Sun and colleagues fix weak B cell responses in mice carrying a human immune system in a 2026 study. Such mice make few antigen-specific B cells, low antibodies, and little cell specialization after vaccination. The platform could supply fully human therapeutic antibodies.
pmc-13337392:
Ayodeji Mathias Adegoke and co-authors weigh the two faces of oxidative stress in breast cancer in a 2026 review. Reactive oxygen species can damage DNA, distort signaling, and push tumors to grow and spread. Antioxidants are the cell's defense, made internally or eaten in plant-rich diets, with examples from glutathione to curcumin and resveratrol.

Yet the literature conflicts: the same species that drive cancer can also be harnessed against it, and antioxidants may protect tumors as well as patients. Plant compounds have shown promise for softening chemotherapy side effects and improving life quality. The review maps where intake helps prevention or care, and where caution is due, urging context-specific advice.
pmc-13337492:
Stacia L. Koppenhafer and colleagues dissect how a drug pairing kills Ewing sarcoma cells in a 2026 study. This bone cancer still kills many patients with spread or relapse. pmc-13337692:
Xiurong Wu and a large team map Qinghai spruce forests in the Qilian Mountains in a 2026 study. These spruce woods form the main forest in a key ecological barrier in western China. Knowing what controls where they grow supports protection and repair work as the climate shifts.

pmc-13337892:
Shun-yu Li and co-authors pool studies on teacher punishment and school achievement in a 2026 meta-analysis. Harsh discipline such as hitting, suspension, or expulsion draws concern for learning and health. Past findings varied, so a pooled estimate with moderators was needed.
