The pooled link was weakly negative, at r equal to minus 0.183 in the reported estimate, meaning more punishment tracked with lower achievement. Gender mix, achievement type, and punishment type shaped the strength of the link. Results argue for trained, non-harmful discipline methods in secondary schools.
pmc-13339192:
Haojian Gan and a large team review heart harms from Bruton kinase blockers in blood cancers in a 2026 article. These targeted drugs improved outlook for chronic B-cell cancers. Their heart risks include irregular rhythm, bleeding, high pressure, heart failure, and rare dangerous rhythms.

Newer drug generations lowered some event rates, but risks remain clinically important as reviewed. The article covers how often each harm occurs, who faces higher risk, and how damage may arise. Current prevention and treatment tactics are weighed. Better dosing, mechanism work, and combination plans are proposed to keep cancer benefit while protecting the heart.
pmc-13340692:
Ahmed vadel Jidou and colleagues reported a transmesocolic internal hernia in 2026 causing bowel obstruction in a 20 year old man. Internal hernias cause only 0.6 to 5.8 percent of obstructions but carry high strangulation risk, and transmesocolic hernias through mesocolic defects are an uncommon subtype. Preoperative diagnosis is hard because symptoms are vague, though contrast CT is the gold standard.

The patient arrived after four days of obstructive symptoms with belly swelling and tenderness near the navel. CT showed small bowel obstruction from strangulation through a mesocolic defect. The case plus literature review reminds surgeons to consider internal hernia in young patients with obstruction and no prior surgery history.
pmc-13341292:
Acupuncture-based therapies for chronic fatigue syndrome are pooled in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis by Yanbing Li and colleagues. The team searched four databases for randomized trials up to April 1, 2026, checked bias with the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, and combined results in R.

Eight trials with 715 patients qualified, though most raised some bias concerns and one ranked high risk. Acupuncture approaches beat controls on overall fatigue with a standardized mean difference of −1.31, and also helped physical and mental fatigue. Differences between studies were large, however, so the authors urge cautious reading of the benefit.
pmc-13342392:
Andras Szeitz and co-authors present part two of a 2026 roundtable summary on new directions in mass spectrometry tools and technology. Part one covered single-cell work and multi-omics gaps raised by major vendors, while part two turns to data handling, bioinformatics, teamwork, and what industry needs next.

Panelists argue that shared file formats such as mzML work well, but labs still handle and report data in uneven ways. Small-molecule fields lack primary reference standards, so results often stay relative rather than exact. The group urges shared frameworks like LIPID MAPS, clearer accountability for data use, and closer work between vendors and scientists to build standards together.
pmc-13344492:
Jennifer L. Walker and a large team build a lab platform pairing human gut lining cells with immune cells in 2026. Animal models mispredict human gut responses and patient studies tangle cause with feedback, so the team engineered a two-layer scaffold copying the tissue under the small intestine lining.

Electrospun polycaprolactone forms small pores that hold a tight epithelial sheet and large pores that let dendritic cells roam, with T cells sharing the space. The setup puts immune cells in direct contact with the barrier, as in living gut near Peyer's patches. Nutrients, microbes, and antigens can now be fed to the lining while immune reactions are read cleanly, promising steadier studies of gut health and inflammation.
pmc-13345592:
Youstina Demetry and co-authors explore how Arabic-speaking refugee youth describe their own mental distress in a 2026 qualitative study. Western biopsychosocial models do not always fit other cultures, so the team analyzed open answers on a personal outcome questionnaire to learn what problems young refugees name themselves.

Read through Alderfer's needs theory, this distress blocked basic existence needs and the need for relatedness and belonging. One young voice called the state a labyrinth with no way out. Services, the authors imply, must answer needs that standard diagnosis lists miss.
pmc-13347392:
Oskar Kołacki, Stanisław Trzciński, and Marcin K. Chmielewski review smart carriers for small interfering RNA built from polyethylenimine, in a review from 2026. These RNA drugs can silence single genes, yet they break down fast and reach cells poorly. While the polymer binds RNA tightly, helps it escape cell compartments, and can be reshaped in many ways.

Carriers that react to body cues such as acidity, reactive oxygen, enzymes. ATP are sorted from those that react to outside cues such as light, heat, and magnetic fields. Tweaks from grafting to fluorination aim to raise accuracy and cut cell harm, and multi-cue designs promise release timed and placed for stronger treatment.
pmc-13347792:
Wataru Horikawa and Daniel L. Kiss share a cheap one-step method to purify the RNA-cutting enzyme RNase R, in a methods report from 2026. The enzyme eats straight RNA strands but spares circles, making it vital for circular RNA work, yet shop prices are steep. Full digestion without circle loss is the key test for circular RNA projects, so a low-cost bench route widens access for labs building research tools or drug candidates.
pmc-13348492:
MacLachlan and colleagues tracked hepatitis B care in Australia in 2026 using linked national records, and found uptake of monitoring and treatment well below targets. Long-term care with regular viral load tests and antiviral drugs cuts liver disease and cancer, yet many people fall out of the system. The team linked insurance records for tests and prescriptions to migration, death, and social data for the decade from 2014 to 2023.

Among those tested, only about one in five was tested regularly, and about two in five had no test after 2019. Uptake ran lower for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and varied by birth region, while most people who started treatment stayed on it well. The authors urge efforts to re-engage people lost to follow-up.
pmc-13349792:
Anne R. J. Péporté and co-authors examined inner ear fluid swelling, called endolymphatic hydrops, in people with migraine in a 2026 imaging study. They reviewed 144 inner ear MRI scans and kept 108 patients with confirmed hydrops.

Two radiologists, blinded to clinical details, graded the swelling and scored brain markers tied to migraine, such as white matter lesions and widened spaces around vessels, plus cranial nerve sizes. Hydrops severity showed no link with any migraine marker or nerve volume. Some milder grades on the left side did track with sudden hearing loss and a feeling of ear fullness. The results suggest ear swelling and migraine brain changes are separate imaging findings.
pmc-13351692:
Fang Tang and co-authors compare long-acting growth hormone in two causes of short stature in a 2026 cohort study. Weekly pegylated hormone is used more often now, but how it works in hormone deficiency versus unexplained short stature is unclear. The single-centre study enrolled 132 prepubertal children treated from June 2023 to June 2024.

At 12 months, the 68 children with hormone deficiency gained more height score than the 64 with unexplained short stature, at 0.92 versus 0.65. Growth speed and target height rates were also higher in the deficiency group. Side effect rates were similar. The authors use regression to sort which starting traits shaped response.
pmc-13353192:
Anna Harutyunyan leads a 2026 pot study of nano-chelated fertilisers for wheat and oat under salt stress. Salt harms crops through water imbalance, ion poisoning, and oxidative damage. pmc-13353792:

Accurate readings matter for spotting childhood hypertension, yet wrist devices lack child validation, and off-label arm use had never been tested. The wrist device on the upper arm was compared with mercury auscultation readings under the ISO 81060-2:2018 standard, giving 300 paired readings. The device passed both ISO criteria for systolic pressure, with mean error of minus 4.62 mmHg. Diastolic checks, society grading, and bias plots completed the assessment for this age group.
pmc-13354092:
Mahamudul Hasan leads a 2026 targeted PCR hunt for the bacterium IOLA in dog respiratory samples. Early metagenomic claims found partial sequences resembling IOLA, a little-known bacterium first described in human airways, but detection was unproven.

pmc-13354392:
Yoseph M. Habte and colleagues report isolated under-skin sarcoidosis as multiple nodules in 2026. Needle and core samples revealed non-caseating granulomas with giant cells, and stains showed CD68 and S100 positivity with a low growth index. Full checks found no wider disease at presentation. pmc-13354792:
Alice Meroni and colleagues mapped how the oncoprotein CIP2A guards chromosomes under replication stress, in a 2026 cell biology study. CIP2A was already known to matter in homologous recombination-deficient cells, but its mitotic job was hazy.

pmc-13355192:
Kathrine F Vandraas and co-authors used Norwegian registry data in 2026 to check if a landmark breast cancer trial's gains held in daily care. The authors say real-world survival matched the trial well, though their design cannot prove the two are equal.
pmc-13358992:
Tommaso Pianigiani and co-authors study bone involvement in sarcoidosis in a 2026 paper. Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory disease that forms clusters of immune cells in many organs. pmc-13361992:
Andrea Calderone and co-authors sorted spinal cord injury patients by hospital return patterns in a 2026 study. Models with two to six groups were compared for fit and clarity. Clear burden profiles can show which patients need stronger support at home to keep them out of hospital.
pmc-13362192:

pmc-13362292:

pmc-13363692:

pmc-13364192:

pmc-13364592:

pmc-13367092:

The summary describes the combination, the people studied, and the final living results in language easy to people. It translates a complex prostate cancer trial into understandable ends. pmc-13367192:

pmc-13375092:

pmc-13375392:

pmc-13375692:

pmc-13375892:

pmc-13377392:

pmc-13378292:

pmc-13380192:

pmc-13380392:

Better control was linked with fewer complications for mother and baby and lower use of hospital care, including newborn intensive care. The analysis estimates the savings linked to the modest sugar improvement the system achieved over standard care. Such evidence helps funders judge value.
pmc-13382692:

What that wax fraction contains was poorly characterised.

Extracting two cannabis varieties across the industrial temperature range, the team found long-chain wax alkanes were major components, and their amount rose steadily as extraction grew warmer. Cannabinoid and aroma levels stayed roughly constant over the same range. Aerosol tests showed the waxes pass efficiently into vapour. Cold extraction therefore offers a simple lever to cut wax at the source.
pmc-13382992:
Norma Martínez-Lendech and co-authors weigh the hidden body costs of parental care in a wild cichlid fish in 2026 work. During nesting, females spent more time cleaning the nest and fanning the eggs than males did. Males were larger and carried higher total antioxidant levels across stages. Females showed higher catalase activity during fry care, which the authors link to the heavier direct care load carried by mothers in this species.
pmc-13383192:

pmc-13386692:

Severe adverse events after vaccination pooled to about 1 percent, mild events occurred in about 8 percent, and viral shedding reached about 65 percent. pmc-13387492:

pmc-13388592:

The trial enrolled 161 eligible patients between June 2024 and June 2025 and assigned them evenly to the three groups. All patients also had air-pressure leg cuffs, support stockings, and the same recovery plan. The main outcome was a leg vein clot within 12 weeks, checked by ultrasound, with safety outcomes tracked alongside. Orthopaedic teams get a direct three-way comparison in a frail older group where clot prevention must balance bleeding risk.
pmc-13388992:

The authors present the pairing as a lead neuroprotective strategy, with human safety and dosing still untested.
pmc-13389792:

The 27-year-old woman, at 35 weeks of pregnancy, had three weeks of painful plaques across the buttocks and back of the thighs that worsened fast after a steroid cream. Pustular psoriasis was first suspected, but direct examination and culture named the fungus Trichophyton rubrum. pmc-13390392:
Yonggui Wang and colleagues evaluate, in 2026, recycled concrete that can heal its own cracks with the help of two kinds of microbes. Cracks during service weaken concrete structures, and microbe-driven mineral formation offers a greener repair route.

The team varied the agent dose and the share of recycled coarse aggregate, then tested compression, splitting, and bending strength and tracked crack closure over time under oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor conditions. Civil engineers gain performance data for a self-healing mix built from recycled material, including how the paired aerobic and anaerobic microbes perform together.
pmc-13391492:
Khoa D. Vo's team recovered full multimodal urban travel flows by fusing household travel surveys with smart-card transit data, a scalable answer to sparse multimodal observation. Their system estimates cross-modal flow ratios from surveys and applies them to time-varying transit flows, recovering private-vehicle and walking demand hourly and by day of week.

Validation in Singapore and Seoul showed strong agreement, with common parts of commuters above 0.70 and R-squared above 0.60. Recovered flows showed transit most competitive at intermediate distances of eleven to sixteen kilometres, and transit-only data underestimating peak epidemic infections by up to fifty percent, informing resilient transport planning.
pmc-13392092:
Sirui Chen's team used micro eye jumps and EEG to test whether learned lure damping works ahead or after the fact in visual search. People learn to suppress spots where salient lures often appear, but whether damping needs prior hidden focus to that spot was debated.

During pre-cue intervals, micro eye-jump rates fell before onset, yet early micro eye jumps pointed toward likely lure spots more often than away, backing reactive damping. Alpha-wave activity at once carried clear pictures of those spots, showing readying brain setup alongside eye-move involvement in space pattern learning.
pmc-13392392:
Antonia Weberling's team shows that early-disc lumen making, long seen as a mammal hallmark, also occurs in the veiled lizard, a scaled reptile. Early discs in reptiles were thought to form flat one-layer discs before layout and gut forming, based on bird models.

In lizards, a drawstring workings of concentric multi-cell actin rings tightened around the early disc to form a lumen before front-back layout, accompanied by a Wnt3A- and Brachyury-positive ring. Layout appeared independent of Cerberus and Lefty, giving lizard embryos human-like early shape despite three hundred million years of split.
pmc-13393292:
Tianyu Hang and six colleagues charted the tiny membrane parcels called extracellular vesicles that the gut releases into mesenteric lymph, the fluid draining the intestine. The gut loads dietary fat into chylomicron particles bound for that lymph, but whether it also secretes vesicles there was unexplored. Rats fitted with lymph and gut cannulas supplied fluid before and after a lipid infusion, and the vesicles were sized, imaged, and tagged with marker antibodies.

Fat output in lymph peaked two hours after infusion, and vesicle markers rose sharply alongside it, across particles spanning twenty to three hundred nanometres. Stripping out chylomicrons changed marker patterns unevenly, suggesting some vesicles ride with or bind the fat particles while others travel free. The authors establish the intestine as a vesicle-secreting organ and its lymph as a fluid worth mining for gut signals.
pmc-13393692:
George Msema Bwire and coauthors assess community pharmacy delivery of HIV prevention and treatment drugs in Dar es Salaam in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Pharmacies could ease refills of pre-exposure prophylaxis and antiretroviral therapy, but evidence on acceptability and practical requirements in Tanzania was limited.

Surveys came first among women in transactional sex and people with HIV, followed by interviews with clients, pharmacists, owners, and policymakers, plus focus groups. The design tested whether pharmacy refills feel acceptable and what scale-up would need. Health planners gain grounded guidance for decentralizing HIV medicine in a busy city.
pmc-13393992:
Xi Ma, Xiaoxiao Cheng, Tamara Fischer, Jürgen Senker, Qi Sun, and Seema Agarwal built self-standing membranes from covalent organic frameworks to harvest osmotic energy, the power released when seawater meets freshwater. Such reverse electrodialysis stacks stall because ions leak both ways, wasting the gradient as entropy. The frameworks help with their ruler-straight nanochannels and organised charges, and the team varied the density of sulfonic acid groups lining those channels by adjusting the recipe.

Charge inside the channels repels the wrong ions and speeds the right ones, and one tuned density hit the sweet spot. Across a seawater-to-freshwater salt gradient the device delivered power density near five times the commercial benchmark. The authors present stoichiometric tuning of channel charge as a design strategy for ion-selective membranes in energy conversion and separations.
pmc-13394992:
Yu-yang Chen and colleagues hunt, in 2026, for gene signs that link gut flora to type 2 diabetes. Gene-based maths can hint at cause, not just shared links. The team used such methods to find ten gut microbe groups tied to the disease. They then crossed gene activity data with causal gene lists to narrow the field.

Machine learning picked marker genes that split patients from controls with fair accuracy. Single-cell data showed one marker high in healthy samples and another high in diabetes. The authors frame the work as groundwork for sharper diagnosis. They offer a firmer base for study of how flora shape the disease.
pmc-13395392:
Hanin Alwashahi and Dhanalekshmi Unnikrishnan Meenakshi review, in 2026, drug care for overactive parathyroid glands in dialysis patients. The glands overshoot when kidneys fail, harming bones and vessels. The review gathers 22 studies on three drug families: calcium mimics, vitamin D kin, and phosphate binders. Care in Gulf states gets special note, since trial proof from there is scarce.

Calcium mimics cut the gland hormone deeply but can drop blood calcium and upset the gut. A vein-given mimic dosed during dialysis eased gut issues. Vitamin D kin work in a narrow safe band, and binders carry a heavy pill load. Blending families at lower doses often works best, the authors say.
pmc-13395892:
Friedrich Boettner and co-authors test, in 2026, a phone app that reads pelvis twist from a plain front X-ray. Twist bends the angles used to judge hip cup placement after joint replacement. A plastic pelvis model was turned and tilted dozens of times by set amounts. Calipers gave the true angles, and X-rays were shot at each pose.

The app's twist reads sat within a degree of the caliper on average. Tilt reads were less tight, off by a couple of degrees on average. The authors say the tool could sharpen cup checks on standard films and theatre images. Bone model proof comes first, and patient tests must follow.
pmc-13396192:
Y. Fujisawa and co-authors used a scanning tunneling microscope to watch competing magnetic patterns inside a layered crystal, CeTe3, and reported the results in 2026. The material is a two-dimensional semimetal, part of the van der Waals family that can be peeled into thin sheets.

Alongside the known charge density wave, the team found three distinct stripe and checkerboard states where charge and magnetism lock together. A modest magnetic field of about 1.5 tesla applied in the plane could switch between them. Images of scattered electrons showed each state rebuilt the surface in its own way. Such switchable states interest researchers hunting for new electronic phases.
pmc-13396392:
Yufeng Chen and others show how Streptomyces scents rally guard germs against banana wilt in a 2026 study. Soil-born wilt defense leans on rallying a guard germ crew, but the rally signals were hidden.

Strain Sy2-11 curbed wilt by rallying a guard root crew. Its scents, aristolene and ledene, spurred banana roots to brew 10-hydroxycapric acid. That acid fed good Bacillus kinds that are key to wilt curb, proven with built crews and germ mutants that cannot chase scents. Growers gain a scent-signal path to shield bananas with less chem spray.
pmc-13396492:
Yu-De Wang and co-authors combined DNA methylation maps with gene activity data to build a prognostic signature for bladder cancer, in a 2026 study. Bladder tumors vary widely, and current groupings tell doctors little about who will fare badly or which treatment fits.

Matching tumor samples with nearby normal tissue, the team kept genes whose methylation and activity changed together. A survival-focused learning method then distilled them into a 25-gene signature tied to fat metabolism. The score was checked in four separate patient cohorts. Further layers of analysis probed how the signature relates to tumor surroundings and drug response, aiming at a tool with real clinical use.
pmc-13396592:
Lauer and colleagues demonstrate, in 2026, that the vagus nerve helps rats remember meals by triggering acetylcholine release in the hippocampus when nutrients are eaten. Using fiber photometry to watch the chemical signal live, they found dorsal hippocampal acetylcholine surged during nutrient consumption, including an 11 percent sucrose solution and a calorically matched 4.5 percent corn oil solution, and stayed elevated after eating stopped.

That response depended on cholinergic neurons in the medial septum and on an intact vagus: ablating those neurons or cutting the nerve below the diaphragm abolished the signal. Early-life Western diet maintenance produced the same loss in their experiments. All three disruptions, ablation, vagotomy, and Western diet, impaired the rats' memory for where a meal had occurred. The authors identify a gut-to-brain pathway by which eating itself strengthens memory of the event, and propose its disruption explains part of diet-related memory impairment.
pmc-13397092:
Stefania Casolari and co-authors report severe brain inflammation from Usutu virus in an older patient, treated with steroids for a few days, in a 2026 case report. Usutu is a flavivirus cousin of West Nile, cycling between birds and mosquitoes, and human cases have risen as the virus spreads through Europe.

Most infections pass silently, but in older or immune-weakened people the virus can invade the nervous system. Standard care has no proven antiviral, so the team used dexamethasone to calm the inflammation and reviewed the wider literature on steroids in such infections. Their discussion weighs when damping the immune response helps and when it might hinder viral clearance.
pmc-13397592:
Yasuhiro Matsuda and Tadaaki Koyama tell of aortic valve swap 40 years after a Björk-Shiley valve in a 2026 case tale. The tilting-disc machine valve showed fine long-run wear in the aortic spot, though non-valve snags such as pannus can still force rework.

An 80-year-old Japanese man fitted four decades earlier showed up with fainting and worsening heart failure, with harsh aortic narrowing and weak pump share. Surgeons swapped the valve for a Perceval stitch-free valve to cut op risk given weak heart function. The case shows stitch-free rework as a lower-risk choice in frail rework patients.
pmc-13397692:
Hui Zhang and others compare CD4 T-cell count instruments in China in a 2026 proficiency testing study. CD4 counts signal immune status in people living with HIV, and many instruments are approved in China, yet no systematic performance comparison existed.

Retrospective reads of national proficiency data from 2016 to 2023 compared ten mainstream instruments using regression and mixed-effects models for agreement and swap-ability. Use of Chinese-made and point-of-care instruments rose yearly, from under 5 percent to nearly 30 percent and from about 3 percent to 8 percent respectively, with strong overall agreement. Laboratories gain proof for choosing and trusting CD4 platforms.
pmc-13397992:
Azza Fahmy and colleagues test whether safranal, a saffron compound, can boost the standard worm drug against schistosomiasis in mice. Their 2026 study infects male mice with 60 swimming larvae of Schistosoma mansoni, then treats at week nine. Praziquantel remains the main drug for this parasitic disease, yet it cannot fully undo liver scarring and resistance is a standing worry.

Groups got the drug alone, safranal alone (50 mg per kg daily) or both for three weeks, and were examined at week eleven. The pairing cut adult worm counts and egg loads in liver and gut more than the drug alone, and best eased liver swelling. Tissue, scarring, inflammation and oxidative stress markers rounded out the gains.
pmc-13398092:
Alexa L Fredston and Roxanne S Beltran argue that tracking tags on animals can sharpen forecasts of where species will live as the climate shifts. Their 2026 essay notes birds climbing mountains and fish spreading hundreds of kilometres past old ranges, while breeding and feeding calendars also slide. Models often work at map scales far coarser than the world an animal actually senses and chooses within.

Biologgers, the tags that record movement, feeding and surroundings on the animal itself, supply the missing fine grain. Feeding those data into mechanism-based models that run from single animals up to populations could tie range shifts to real decisions. The payoff is forecasts that explain movement, not just redraw maps after the fact.
pmc-13398492:
Christopher A Osborne and co-authors solve a puzzle posed by Guam's brown treesnake, a notorious invader founded by very few snakes. Their 2026 study finds roughly half the genome locked in identical stretches, a bottleneck signature seen in species near extinction. By classic logic the snakes should be inbred and frail, yet they thrive.

Nearly 19,000 structural variants (large DNA rearrangements) carry the missing diversity, covering nearly eightfold more of the genome than single-letter variants do. These variants crowd near gene promoters, where shuffling and repair run hot, and enrich genes for smell and adaptive immunity. The result reframes invasion success: big genome reshuffles can rescue a population that letter-level diversity cannot.
pmc-13398992:
Melody Wang and co-authors lay out a nationwide trial of pharmacist-led, phone-enabled aftercare for heart attack patients in Singapore. Their 2026 design paper introduces AMI-HOPE, rolled out across three health clusters with seven hospitals and eighteen polyclinics. Hospitals cross from usual cardiologist-led care to the new model every three months in a stepped-wedge design, so all sites eventually receive it.

The target enrolment is 1,512 patients, followed on a home monitoring platform with rule-based alerts, pharmacist video visits and automatic education. Winning is scored by a hierarchy led by cardiovascular death, repeat heart attack and stroke, then readmissions and risk-factor control, with drug adherence and cost-effectiveness tracked alongside. Baseline traits of the first enrollees anchor the report.
pmc-13399092:
Christina Van Hemmen Kon and colleagues present a 2026 case report of appendicitis in an unusual place. Their patient, a 41-year-old man, arrived with pain in the upper right abdomen radiating to his back and shoulder, which pointed doctors toward gallbladder or liver disease. His appendix in fact sat just under the liver because the cecum had never descended into its normal position during development.

Ultrasound showed no gallbladder problem, so a CT scan was ordered and revealed a swollen appendix with a possible abscess. Surgeons began with a laparoscopic operation but converted to open surgery because the anatomy was difficult and bleeding occurred. Pathology confirmed a ruptured appendix, and the patient went home on the third day after surgery. Paired with a narrative review, the report urges early CT imaging when upper abdominal pain defies a gallbladder explanation.
pmc-13399492:
Ömer Faruk Yilmaz and colleagues wrote a Portuguese-language letter arguing that patient factors deserve more weight in contrast-induced kidney injury. Their 2026 letter responds to a study of contrast volume after coronary procedures in patients prone to kidney injury. The original analysis found a neutral contrast effect alongside a significant protective effect of statin drugs, a contrast the letter writers explore.

They cite an earlier trial in which early high-dose rosuvastatin reduced contrast-related kidney injury through anti-inflammatory and vessel-stabilizing effects largely independent of contrast volume. From this, they argue that vascular, inflammatory, and oxygen-related vulnerability may drive kidney injury more than contrast chemistry alone. The letter urges future studies to weigh patient susceptibility and methods alongside contrast dose.
pmc-13399592:
Mitsunori Toda argues in a 2026 editorial that the success of a smart prosthetic leg depends less on its microprocessor than on the person wearing it. Microprocessor knees genuinely help people with transfemoral amputation: reviews credit them with fewer falls, better confidence, and stronger scores on functional tasks. Toda's puzzle is that these gains do not reliably turn into more everyday activity. In one study he cites, confidence and test scores rose while measured activity stayed flat.

Toda separates two control loops. The device loop senses and adjusts resistance. The human loop is the wearer's own muscle control and posture coordination through the socket. His proposition is that rehabilitation should train the human loop as deliberately as engineers improve the device loop. The closing claim gives the essay its answer: the human remains the origin of control.
pmc-13399892:
Claude J. Regis and team systematically reviewed whether preoperative personality traits predict recovery after sports medicine surgery. Their 2026 review covers 20 studies of shoulder, hip, and knee arthroscopy patients, testing resilience, grit, self-efficacy, pain catastrophizing, locus of control, and optimism. Surgeons increasingly ask whether mindset shapes rehab, yet the proof had not been synthesized.

High resilience tracked with better outcomes in five of nine studies, especially after knee arthroscopy, and all three self-efficacy studies showed a positive link. Higher grit also tracked with better outcomes in every included study, while pain catastrophizing results were mixed and locus of control and optimism showed no significant link. The work supports screening mindset before surgery, while varied outcome measures limit firm causal claims.
pmc-13400692:
Karla Borges Daniel and colleagues compare, in 2026, impulsivity in patients taking cabergoline for prolactinoma, a pituitary tumor, against healthy controls. Cabergoline is the standard first treatment, but dopamine drugs of this kind have been linked to impulse control problems such as gambling and compulsive buying. Evidence in this patient group was patchy.

The study enrolled 131 patients and 131 controls, using standard questionnaires for impulsivity and specific problem behaviors. Patients scored higher on overall impulsivity, with attention-related impulsivity staying higher after statistical adjustment. Their odds of compulsive shopping were more than four times those of controls, while other behaviors did not differ. Lower education also tracked with higher impulsivity in everyone.
pmc-13401392:
Kai Cao, Jie Wu, and JiaLei Zhang ran a 2026 randomized trial comparing three versions of a nerve treatment for postherpetic neuralgia, the lingering pain after shingles. All patients received CT-guided pulsed radiofrequency to the dorsal root ganglion; some also received ozone or platelet-rich plasma.

At a pain centre in Changzhi, China, adults aged 50 to 70 with single-segment pain lasting over three months were assigned evenly to the three arms between July and December 2025. The per-protocol group held 122 people: 38 with radiofrequency alone, 43 with added ozone, and 41 with added plasma. Pain scores on a ten-centimetre scale, sleep quality, general health, and a blood inflammation ratio were tracked at 30, 60, and 90 days, with mixed-effects models comparing the arms over time.
pmc-13401592:
Robert S Kass, Olivier Villemain, and Lincai Ye introduce a 2026 Scientific Reports collection on the diagnosis and treatment of congenital heart defects. These defects are the commonest kind present at birth, affecting nearly one percent of babies born worldwide. The first successful repair of such a defect more than sixty years ago opened a new frontier in children's medicine.

Advances in fetal imaging, fluid-flow modelling, machine learning, and surgical perfusion have steadily sharpened diagnosis and treatment since then. The editors frame today's hardest problems as early and accurate diagnosis, precise risk sorting, and lifelong management. They note that engineering and data science methods are increasingly supplying the answers. Remaining gaps include diagnosis in low-resource settings, cutting complications after surgery, and caring for the growing population of adults who were born with these defects.
pmc-13401792:
Snehanjan Sarangi, Debarati Ray, and Tathagata Bhattacharjee present a 2026 case report of ameloblastic carcinoma, a rare and aggressive cancer of the jaw-forming tissues, focusing on how the diagnosis is nailed down. Their patient was a 29-year-old man, younger than the typical patient, who is usually a man in his sixties with disease in the back of the lower jaw.

The tumour is typically painful, highly invasive, and prone to spread, most often to the lungs, arising either fresh or inside a pre-existing benign ameloblastoma or cyst. Scans usually show ill-defined lesions with heavy bone loss. Under the microscope the ameloblastic tissue shows classic cell atypia, and staining is usually intense for Ki-67, p53, and p63, while most cases carry the BRAF V600E mutation. Surgery is the main treatment, sometimes with neck dissection or radiation, and surgical removal was performed in this case as well.
pmc-13402592:

Carbon nitride islands anchored on reduced graphene oxide hold cobalt single atoms in a CoN3C arrangement. The graphene sea beneath lifts the cobalt d-band center and sharpens one orbital near the Fermi level, steering peroxymonosulfate activation toward direct electron transfer rather than indiscriminate radicals.

The system destroyed bisphenol A completely within five minutes, with about 94 percent of the degradation flowing through the selective electron-transfer pathway in their measurements. Its normalized rate constant reached 25 per minute per gram per liter, ahead of the island-free catalyst and most reported rivals, despite lower cobalt loading, 1.25 percent against 1.97 percent for the comparison. Coated onto membranes, the catalyst ran stably for 100 hours in real water matrices with minimal cobalt leaching, a practical step for treatment plants.
pmc-13402692:

Linked to a wireless module, the implant recorded in living tissue for more than 10 days with strong sensitivity, catching organ-level lactate swings during oxygen shortage and seizures. In septic shock, lactate around the heart rose before blood-wide changes showed on standard monitors, giving an early alarm. Treatment guided by that signal steadied blood pressure and headed off shock inside the watch window. All parts are biodegradable by design.
pmc-13402892:

Breast cancer kills more women than any other cancer, and doxorubicin remains its most effective chemotherapy despite harsh effects on marrow, fertility, and the heart. Patients on chemotherapy often receive antibiotics for infection, making the interaction clinically real, above all where targeted drugs are scarce.

Their title finding is that antibiotics attenuated the drug cancer-killing power in these cells. Triple-negative disease, lacking estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 targets, leans hardest on plain chemotherapy, so any drag on doxorubicin lands heavily. The authors present the cell work as a warning signal: antibiotic cover during chemotherapy may deserve the same scrutiny as drug-drug clashes, and the effect needs checking in living systems.
pmc-13403592:
Camron Chugg, Jennifer Bowden, and Brian Anderson presented a 2026 case of severe chest wall pain from a nerve pain disorder that usually hits limbs. The 27-year-old man had sharp pain, extreme touch sensitivity, and flushing spells on his front chest wall. Wide testing ruled out heart, lung, gut, skin, and infection causes.

His signs met standard rules for the disorder, called CRPS type I. Drugs and mixed care had failed to help him for years. A trial of spinal cord stimulation gave strong relief, so a lasting device was placed. Relief and better daily function held at two years, with only minor device limits.
pmc-13403892:

Stiffer bubbles entered macrophages better and flipped a pressure-sensing pathway inside them. That push shifted the cells from a tumor-helping mood to a fighting mood. Bubbles packed with a melanoma peptide plus an immune trigger drew killer T cells into mouse tumors. Suppressor cell counts fell, and the vaccine worked in both guard and treatment modes.
pmc-13404192:

Their setup runs on electric current alone, with no added metal or oxidant. A wide range of ring variants and selenium partners worked in the bath. Top yields reached 92 percent of the hoped-for product. The route offers drug makers a practical way to slip selenium into known drug frames.
pmc-13405092:
Oviya Mohan, Dora Biro and Caleb Cox test how human pairs invent shared conventions, in 2026 experiments. A convention is an arbitrary habit a group keeps because everyone else keeps it, such as a shared ranking of colours. The task copies a colour-matching game earlier used with baboons.

Pairs played with or without seeing a partner's screen, and with or without advance knowledge of the task. Extra information slowed the birth of a shared ranking rather than speeding it. Pairs kept their convention even when seeing the partner's screen offered a simpler route. In a follow-up, experienced players paired with newcomers formed conventions faster, but the old colour ranking itself did not pass across.
pmc-13405592:
Luciana Assis Couto and co-authors analyse nursing consultations for people with high blood pressure in Brazilian primary care, in a 2026 article. Hypertension drives early cardiovascular deaths in Brazil, especially alongside poor diet and environment. Nurses lead much of the long-term follow-up in local clinics.

Consultations are judged against the national hypertension guidelines and the stages of the nursing process. Social, cultural and regional context should shape each step, the authors argue, alongside clear communication with patients. Their analysis finds the process covered in guidance yet still in need of improvement in practice. Stronger territorial primary care, rooted in communities, is presented as the setting where gains will stick.
pmc-13406092:
Abhineet Rajendra Kulkarni and Pranav Madhav Kuber review systems that sense and respond to a person's mental state in real time, in a 2026 systematic review. Attention and workload shifts affect performance and safety in driving, study and rehabilitation. Twenty-seven studies built such closed-loop systems.

Brain wave sensors appeared in 70 percent of studies, and attention was the most targeted state, ahead of mental workload. Within-person classification reached between about 82 and 96 percent in lab multi-class tasks in the reported figures. Feedback displays and task difficulty changes were the commonest responses, while automation changes were rare. Every system reacted after a state began rather than predicting it, a gap the authors flag.
pmc-13406492:
Javier Merino-Andrés and colleagues combine robot gait training with skin-surface spinal stimulation in children with incomplete spinal cord injury, in a 2026 case series. Each method alone shows promise, but together in children they were untested. Safety and practicality come first in this early work.

All improved walking speed, most by amounts judged clinically meaningful. Other outcomes varied between children, as expected in preliminary data. The team calls for larger controlled trials to confirm benefit and tune the combined protocol.
pmc-13407692:
Jiaqi Tang and Mu-Jiang-Shan Wang propose, in 2026, cleaning quantum states before correcting their errors, to protect fragile quantum computers from noise. Under a standard noise model, a scheme using three copies of a state lifts the error threshold of surface codes from 1.1 percent toward a 2.0 percent ideal bound, around 1.6 percent once circuit realities count. Their iterative algorithm adjusts purification depth using feedback from error syndromes as computation proceeds. For a distance-7 surface code at a 1 percent physical error rate, the method cut logical errors forty-six-fold in their analysis.
pmc-13407792:
Dwi Faradina and co-authors review, in 2026, engineered T cells as a weapon against the deadliest ovarian cancer. This ovarian cancer recurs in about 80 percent of cases. It also resists chemotherapy. Standard checkpoint immunotherapy helps only 10 to 15 percent of patients. The review examines lab-grown T cells. They are fitted with synthetic or rearranged receptors.

The authors searched three databases for work from 2015 to 2025. They found encouraging early results. Chimeric antigen receptor T cells attacked the cancer in lab models. High-avidity engineered clones killed robustly. The review explains how such cells destroy targets through coordinated release of perforin and granzymes and through a death-receptor pathway, letting one cell eliminate several targets. Clinical translation remains early, and future strategies occupy the closing discussion.
pmc-13408092:
Céline Dinet and co-authors untangle, in 2026, how a hunting soil bacterium decides which end is front. They built an enzymatic model of the trio.

One regulator, long cast as the switch's activator, turned out to be a downstream effector that binds the active switch instead. The other plays both sides, speeding switch-off or switch-on depending on local concentrations of the inactive switch, while the effector pries the pair apart by sequestering it. A minimal mathematical model of these interactions reproduced the cell's invertible polarity axis, and a droplet assay mimicking the cell confirmed the proteins still partition correctly in space.
pmc-13408592:
Anas Mahmoud and co-authors build in 2026 an explainable warning system for sepsis, the runaway infection response that kills millions each year. Intensive care data are messy, with large gaps and far fewer sepsis cases than healthy ones, which can quietly bias a prediction model. About a dozen model designs were trained and tuned on such data.

Two sequence-aware networks, a bidirectional memory model and a temporal convolutional model, came out ahead, scoring near 0.96 on a standard discrimination measure while rarely missing true cases. Explanation techniques then showed which signals drove each alert, a step the authors argue is essential before clinicians will trust a black box at the bedside. The work targets earlier treatment decisions in units where hours change survival odds.
pmc-13408692:
Maryana Radad and Omar Sharaiha report in 2026 an adult patient whose scans revealed two gallbladders where one is expected. Gallbladder duplication is a congenital rarity, present in roughly one in four thousand births, and it usually turns up by accident. Their patient was a twenty-nine-year-old man with vague digestive complaints and no sign of inflammation or blocked bile flow.

Ultrasound first suggested the anomaly and computed tomography confirmed it. Because the extra gallbladder was not causing his symptoms, no operation was performed. The authors stress documentation: if this man ever needs gallbladder surgery, an unrecognised second organ risks an incomplete operation or a bile duct injury. The case is a reminder for radiologists and surgeons to look twice at unusual biliary anatomy before anyone operates.
pmc-13409092:
Tianpei Mou and co-authors revisit the obesity paradox in 2026 among nearly six thousand patients who underwent heart bypass surgery in an American intensive care database. Outcomes at one week through one year were modelled against body mass index, with machine learning used both to surface the drivers of death and to build predictors.

Risk traced a U shape: the lowest one-year mortality sat in the overweight to mildly obese range, and the protective pattern held in patients over sixty-five. What drove death differed by weight band, from acute physiology in some groups to metabolic and liver factors in others. A gradient-boosting model predicted one-year mortality best. The authors frame body mass as a genuine risk modifier after bypass surgery rather than statistical noise.
pmc-13410492:
D. Gemeri, M. B. Milosavljević, and Ž. S. Maršić set out in 2026 the first full theory framework for two-sided dye solar cells. Such cells place dye on both faces of a titanium oxide layer to catch more light. Lab interest is growing, yet the basic physics had not been worked through.

pmc-13411292:

Only 28 percent scored as having good knowledge, while about 42 percent held positive attitudes and 38 percent followed safe practices. Older age and more schooling predicted stronger knowledge. A family history of the infection predicted safer practice. Vaccination history also tied to knowledge scores. The authors call the overall picture suboptimal and urge targeted teaching for this high-exposure group.
pmc-13411892:

pmc-13412092:

That grip raises reactive oxygen species, stresses the endoplasmic reticulum, and pushes cells toward programmed death. pmc-13412192:

pmc-13412892:

pmc-13413092:

pmc-13414792:

pmc-13415292:

pmc-13415492:

pmc-13416292:

pmc-13416392:

pmc-13416992:
Alejandro Soler-López and colleagues check a wearable sensor called GPath for measuring bar speed in the bench press, in a 2026 validation study. Sessions ran twice, with loads from 20 to 80 percent of each man's best lift. The sensor read high at every load, by a margin that shrank as load rose. Its error stayed steady between sessions, though. That steadiness may suit tracking change in one athlete, but raw values need correction before use for absolute speed.
pmc-13417992:
Montana K Upton and co-authors ask survivors of throat cancer what mattered most in treatment choices, in a 2026 preference study across several hospitals. pmc-13418492:
Ridwana Maher Manna and colleagues assess readiness for vaccinating pregnant women against respiratory syncytial virus in Bangladesh, in a 2026 article. A maternal vaccine approved in 2023 protects newborns through antibodies crossed from the mother.

pmc-13418792:
Vanessa Ramirez-Zohfeld and colleagues test NegotiAge, an online training tool that teaches family caregivers of people with Alzheimer's disease how to handle conflict. Practice rounds gave caregivers a safe place to try hard conversations before facing them at home. Results from the trial guide the next round of tuning for the tool and for wider release to families.
pmc-13419692:
Sarah-Jayne Leonard and colleagues chart referrals into secure psychiatric services across England, the locked units for people with severe disorders who pose serious risk. Almost half of the referrals, 46 percent of the total in the report, came from prisons, and 55 percent of referrals were accepted overall. Models then picked out what predicted acceptance and delay against national standards. Prison pathways look like the pressure point where delays and fairness concerns meet.
pmc-13420292:

pmc-13421492:

pmc-13423392:

pmc-13423992:

pmc-13424092:

The gradient-boosted model performed best, with an accuracy summary of 0.88 on the standard curve measure, and its probabilities calibrated cleanly. Explanation tools confirmed classic risk factors, yet gum measures, attachment loss, plaque, and bleeding, ranked among the strongest signals. The oral features also weighed differently in men and women.
pmc-13424392:

pmc-13424692:

The paper also sets up later work on tools that measure the idea fairly.
pmc-13424792:

pmc-13424892:

pmc-13426392:

pmc-13426492:

pmc-13427592:

pmc-13427792:

pmc-13430192:

pmc-13430592:

pmc-13430792:

Cell lines from patients and from controls, split by illness type, were dosed with cortisol, and gene and protein output were read. Responses differed by cell line, so stress hormones do not act the same way in all bipolar biology.
pmc-13430892:

Fifty-five patients got the gauze and 129 did not, and the two groups matched well at the start. Surgeons get a fair test of a small step that might cut post-op infection.
pmc-13431292:

pmc-13431392:

pmc-13432092:

pmc-13432492:

Median procedure time ran 50 minutes by wrist, with an interquartile range of 40 to 60, versus 45 minutes by groin, with a range of 35 to 60, a statistically significant gap. The centre gets local numbers for choosing access routes.
pmc-13432892:

pmc-13433492:

At graft time, thirteen patients, or 54 percent, were in full remission or remission with low counts, while eleven, or 46 percent, still had active disease. pmc-13434592:

pmc-13434692:
Martynas Statkauskas's team built a heat-tough geopolymer mortar in 2026 by testing which fine aggregate holds up best at high heat. pmc-13435392:

Age, road nearness, and land use best predicted severe illness. City health planners get a fine-grained map for targeting prevention where risk concentrates.
pmc-13436092:

In a test group of 151 patients, the system scored 0.903 for clarithromycin and 0.959 for fluoroquinolones on a standard accuracy scale, where one means perfect. pmc-13436192:

The team aims to gather records from nine homes with about 900 residents, using a secure research database. They will count outbreak clusters, defined as two or more cases within ten days, and measure the strain outbreaks placed on each home. Records on vaccination coverage, cleaning, and infection controls will be matched against resident outcomes and running costs. Findings are due by March 2027 and should guide infection control in care homes for future outbreaks.
pmc-13436492:

pmc-13436692:

pmc-13437392:
