The team set each country's material against model practices drawn from a European portal.

Denmark and Germany showed mature, detailed frameworks, while Croatia relied on strong but local programs and several countries worked with scattered services. Across all nine, few programs wove the three strands together: structured self-care help, training for carers and staff, and digital tools that can grow. Pockets of good practice exist but are thinly spread. Their 2026 report urges wider sharing of what works, so national plans can close the gaps families feel every day.
pmc-13437992:
León and an Antarctic team surveyed 16 seabird nesting sites along the western Antarctic Peninsula. The survey ran during the 2024-2025 breeding season. It looked for deaths from highly pathogenic avian influenza. The virus was first detected on the continent in a dead brown skua in 2024. They documented how unevenly the H5 virus clade 2.3.4.4b struck the region's intermingled species.

The survey found 35 dead adult skuas spread along the peninsula and beyond the Antarctic Polar Circle. That is the southernmost mortality record to date. All 11 sampled skuas from six geographic areas tested positive for the same viral clade. Post-mortem findings pointed to infection as the likely cause of death in those birds. Genetic analysis tied the viruses to the first Antarctic detections. The clade had dispersed across several localities in one season. No suspected influenza deaths appeared in neighboring species. The authors propose skuas as sentinel species for surveillance.
pmc-13438592:
Ruidong Zhao's team built a method in 2026 to map the three-dimensional shape of sucker rod strings as they pump oil up and down. These ultra-slender rods bend, twist, and rub the tubing wall, causing wear and sometimes fracture, yet their live spatial shape was hard to reconstruct. A coupled dynamic model of rod and tubing, with buckling theory and smooth transitions between buckling modes, was used to trace shape through each pumping phase.

Field cases showed how shape evolves across the stroke and how bottomhole pressure shifts trigger buckling mode changes. Oil engineers get a practical modeling route to predict wear spots and prevent failures. The method should help design rods and pumps that last longer downhole.
pmc-13438692:
Dmitrii Subbotin and a large team audited how often inherited distal muscle diseases are mistaken for nerve disease, in the largest Russian cohort of its kind. Distal myopathies weaken hands and feet first, where nerve disorders strike, so the two are easy to confuse. Their 2026 review covered 125 genetically confirmed patients from 103 families at a federal genetics center, 2010 to 2025, with causes across twenty genes.

One gene, GNE, accounted for about thirty percent of cases, followed by two others. Muscle scans surprised the team: over ninety-three percent of scanned patients also showed thigh involvement, whatever their stage. Certain muscles stayed oddly spared, a useful fingerprint. A third of patients had first been sent in as suspected nerve cases. Comparing the referral paths, only needle test reports differed; the bedside picture and scans looked alike. The authors plead for careful reading of that test, .
pmc-13439292:
Kuo and co-authors settle a practical colonoscopy question in this 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis: how clean must the bowel be before polyp detection suffers? Preparation quality is scored on the Boston scale, and guidelines already condemn poor preparation, but whether intermediate cleanliness costs anything versus a top score was unclear.

Fourteen randomized trials fed the analysis, with 5,246 patients in the high-quality group and 1,728 in the intermediate group. Adenoma detection rates differed by a risk difference of only minus 0.02 between the groups, which was not significant, and results for advanced adenomas matched. Subgroup checks using computer-aided detection and color-enhancement imaging found the same result. The authors conclude that intermediate preparation, provided every bowel segment scores at least 2 on the scale, supports normal surveillance intervals.
pmc-13439492:
Andrade and colleagues test anethole, the main scent compound of anise, as a supplement for maturing sheep eggs in the lab. Lab maturation can speed sheep breeding, but eggs often suffer oxidative damage from excess reactive molecules. Their 2026 study grows egg clusters for a day with no anethole or with one of three doses. It then checks survival, chromosome stage, reactive oxygen levels, and the activity of two protective enzymes.

The middle dose, 300 micrograms per milliliter, gave the best balance: more eggs resumed maturation than in other groups, and fewer degenerated than at the low dose. The low dose kept reactive oxygen lowest. The high dose weakened one protective enzyme, superoxide dismutase, and left fewer eggs at the final mature stage. In test tube antioxidant assays the high dose scored best among anethole groups but still below the plain medium control. Dose, the authors stress, decides benefit.
pmc-13439692:
Ferrando-Marco and colleagues measured gene messages in 2026 inside the skin stem cells of the worm Caenorhabditis elegans to test how the Wnt signaling pathway is tuned during uneven cell division. These seam cells divide so daughters take different fates, guided by the Wnt pathway, but whether the pathway's own parts are switched on unevenly was unknown. Using a single-molecule tagging method, the team counted messages for key pathway parts in each daughter cell.

Messages for the pathway's brakes gathered in rear daughters, while messages for its accelerators and its gene-switching factor gathered in front daughters. The split appeared even after the round of division classed as even, and it partly depended on Wnt activity itself, a feedback loop. Protein patterns measured with tagged reporters matched the message patterns. The authors say this hidden transcriptional feedback likely stiffens fate choices and reveals unsuspected variety within seam cell lineages.
pmc-13439892:
Zoé Garceau-Tremblay's team evaluated a sex and gender curriculum toolkit in 2026 at a South Carolina medical school, where teaching still lagged research on sex and gender differences. Sixty-three faculty attended a workshop on the SG-CART course review toolkit, with twenty-nine completing pre-post surveys plus focus groups and cognitive interviews for scale validation. Knowledge, skills confidence, and attitudes were tracked.

Knowledge scores rose significantly and confidence in assessing materials for sex and gender content grew, supporting the toolkit as a faculty development aid. Medical educators get a tested method for closing a long-standing curriculum gap. Wider adoption studies should track whether student learning and patient care actually improve.
pmc-13441392:
Cortot and team asked whether c-Met protein overexpression, a biomarker guiding new antibody-drug conjugates in lung cancer, stays stable over a patient's treatment course. They compared paired biopsies from 160 people with non-squamous non-small cell lung cancer, one sample taken before treatment and one afterwards, scoring the protein by immunohistochemistry.

The two samples agreed on overexpression status in 81.3 percent of patients, indicating most keep a consistent c-Met status over time. Concordance dropped to 65.8 percent among patients carrying an EGFR mutation, a subgroup often treated with targeted drugs between biopsies. Fourteen patients flipped from negative to strongly positive, and these discordant cases frequently carried driver alterations and had received targeted therapy before the second sample. The authors conclude testing can happen before or after treatment for most patients, but those with driver mutations who first test negative may merit retesting.
pmc-13441992:
Tobi Alegbe's team mapped cell-type gene regulation in 2026 for inflammatory bowel disease risk. The work used over two million single cells from gut biopsies and blood of 421 people, including 125 with bowel disease. Most disease variants sit outside genes, making effector genes and cell types hard to name. Cell-type expression trait loci were mapped and compared with tissue-level signals and genome-wide association loci.

Cell-type signals sat farther from gene starts and enriched in enhancers. They less often hit the nearest gene, and colocalized with bowel disease loci over three and a half times more often than tissue signals. Effector genes were nominated at over half of known loci, including myeloid Notch genes and epithelial renewal genes like MYC. Geneticists get a mechanistic map from risk variant to gene to cell in bowel disease.
pmc-13442392:
Tian Jin and colleagues test a plant signal called GABA on young trifoliate orange plants in a 2026 study. The plants grew in water feeds with low boron or full boron, since lack of boron curbs growth in this citrus rootstock. Five GABA doses ran from 0.01 to 1 mM, a unit for strength in liquid.

Dose shaped the result more than any other factor. At 0.1 mM under low boron, plants gained 23.3 percent more mass than low-boron plants with no GABA, and roots took up more key minerals. High doses hurt plants at both boron levels, with 1 mM cutting mass by 8.9 percent when boron was low. The team presents GABA as a tool worth more trials for fields short on boron, used at low dose only.
pmc-13443092:
Carin Janz and colleagues test how well kin, patients, and clinic staff agree on movement diaries in Parkinson disease in a 2026 study. Home diaries guide care, yet patient marks match staff marks weakly. The study enrolled 28 patients with movement swings, each with a relative, for one day of half-hour marks after joint training.

Trios logged 445 mark sets in all. Time match sat fair for kin-staff pairs, with a kappa mark of 0.250 in the count, and fair for kin-patient pairs as well. Patient-staff match stayed slight, at a kappa mark of 0.120 in the same count. Kin and staff clashed most on off-time marks. The authors say kin can aid diary work, though no rater swaps cleanly for a trained observer.
pmc-13445292:
Yu-zhou Shi and colleagues report a rare giant growth disorder of the hip lining in a fifty-year-old woman, treated with a full hip replacement and followed for twelve years, published in 2026. The disorder, synovial chondromatosis, forms cartilage lumps inside a joint and rarely grows huge or eats into the socket. Her joint also carried end-stage arthritis.

Surgeons removed the growths and the joint lining, then fitted a cement-free artificial hip through a back approach. At twelve years she scored near the top of a standard hip function scale, with no pain and no return of the growths. A review of two hundred three past hip cases found return of disease in about one in ten patients after replacement.
pmc-13445692:
Mehmet Kaymakoglu and colleagues test a 2026 biomechanical question: whether a sharp bone-tendon angle in biceps tenodesis creates a guillotine effect that stretches tendon under load. The team fixed 30 sheep shoulder bones with a bicortical button technique at angles of 45, 60, and 90 degrees, then ran 500 load cycles up to 150 newtons.

No construct failed or tendon ruptured in any group, but elongation and residual creep ran significantly higher at 90 degrees than at 45 or 60 degrees. Tunnel widening did not differ significantly, though it trended upward with angle. Surgeons should keep the turn at 60 degrees or less, the authors conclude, while noting the animal-bone limits of the work.
pmc-13445892:
Maarit Rantakokko and coauthors compare a 2026 look-back study of spinal numbing drugs for day-case hip swap, where block length shapes same-day bounce-back. The team studied 220 low-risk patients, half getting bupivacaine and half ropivacaine, tracking motor block, bounce-back unit stay, discharge, and side ills.

Ropivacaine cut motor block by about 45 minutes, bounce-back unit stay by about 12 minutes, and time to first void by about 0.6 hours, with more steady block length. Discharge time and side ills did not differ. Ropivacaine offers faster early bounce-back without added harm, though the authors call for future checks.
pmc-13446092:
Isaac N. Treves and colleagues test whether precision brain mapping, a method that charts one person's brain networks from long scans, works in youth with a modern scan type, in a 2026 case study. The method shines in adults, yet its worth in teens and with multi-echo scans was unproven. Eight young people aged ten to seventeen took part.

Each gave eighty minutes of rest and task scans. The maps came out clean and modular, close to adult templates, with no sign of alignment flaws. Trust in the wiring measures matched past adult-style studies and settled early, near ten to fifteen minutes, though more data kept helping. Gains from personal maps over group maps showed mainly in the hearing network, so short scans suit sense networks best.
pmc-13446192:
Caroline Su and colleagues ask which traits at diagnosis foretell later surgery in Crohn's disease patients with a belly abscess, in a 2026 records study. Such pockets of infection arise when gut inflammation burns through the wall. Care aims to drain and treat them without bowel removal, yet many patients still reach surgery within a year.

Charts covered one hundred forty-five patients treated between 2012 and 2022, and fifty-nine had surgery in that first year. Wider abscess span and older age at the abscess raised surgery risk. Vein antibiotics, a rounded pocket shape that pushes tissue aside, and older age at Crohn's diagnosis each lowered risk. The authors say scan size at first sight should weigh early in care talks with patients.
pmc-13446592:
Ahammed and colleagues study how the heart's protein shredder, the proteasome, is switched on by a kinase called PKA during pressure overload. That overload, from high blood pressure or a narrowed aortic valve, strains the heart toward failure. A phosphate tag on one proteasome part, RPN6, turns the machine up. Their 2026 study reads human failing heart tissue and uses mice engineered so the tag cannot be added.

Failing human hearts carried more tagged RPN6 and more waste protein marked for shredding. In mice, pressure overload raised tagging in normal animals over two to four weeks. Mice that could not add the tag fared worse: more heart thickening, more scarring, weaker pumping, and fluid in the lungs. Their proteasomes also failed to ramp up on schedule, and tagged waste piled up. Sustained proteasome activation, the authors argue, guards protein quality in the stressed heart.
pmc-13447092:
Linh Nguyen, Amy McCaughey-Chapman and Bronwen Connor report a 2026 rat study on delivering replacement cells for Huntington's disease. The disease kills key neurons in the striatum, a deep brain region that helps control movement. The team tested whether a soft gelatin gel could protect young human brain precursor cells during transplant and help them mature.

Cells made from reprogrammed human skin were placed in rat brains either in plain fluid or inside the gel, which was set with visible light. Four weeks later, grafts had survived in every animal. Gel-supported cells produced more neurons marked by one key protein, while graft size did not differ between groups. Readers get early evidence that a gel scaffold may aid cell therapy, plus clear limits from the small groups and short follow-up.
pmc-13447292:
Sophie Butot leads a team testing a droplet-based DNA method to find harmful E. coli in wheat flour in 2026 food safety work. Certain strains make Shiga toxins and can cause severe illness, yet flour is a hard material to test and rules differ by country. Finding several danger genes inside the same cell matters, since scattered genes may come from harmless strains.

Whole cells were split into droplets so gene signals could be checked for co-location in single cells. A new generic E. coli marker was also validated against target and non-target species. Detection limits matched a standard DNA test at under one cell per gram under study conditions. Spiked flour and naturally contaminated shop flour both gave readable patterns, supporting the approach as a flexible base for sharper flour testing.
pmc-13448492:
A Ware and co-authors present a new class of metamaterials built from the inherent nonlocality of their parts in a 2026 study. Nonlocality means a material's response at one point depends on fields nearby, an effect usually visible only in exotic cold or nanoscale systems. Common composites are captured well by averaged local rules, which hide that deeper behaviour and limit design options.

Structuring a semiconductor material at the scale of its own nonlocal response brought the hidden behaviour up to room-temperature, large size. The composite answered light in ways no local average model predicts, even with realistic losses included. Theory and experiment agree that a fresh design space opens beyond photonic crystals, surfaces and standard composites. Deep subwavelength control of light and matter is the payoff hoped for.
pmc-13449392:
MingHui Xing and co-authors examine in 2026 an unintended corner of China's long-term care insurance pilots: what happened to severe depression among the frailest older adults. Most studies track average mood, which can hide the worst-off tail. The team used four waves of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study from 2013 to 2020. They built 27,967 person-year observations from 8,258 adults over sixty, flagging those with severe difficulty in daily activities at baseline.

A triple-difference model compared pilot and non-pilot cities, before and after, for high-need and other elders. Pilot exposure was linked to a 12.45 percentage point higher probability of landing in the severe depression range for the high-need group. Checks excluding the pandemic wave and dropping one city at a time kept the direction, and the signal looked stronger in women. Strength faded under some restrictions, so the authors call the finding suggestive, not conclusive.
pmc-13449992:
Congcong Zhang and co-authors survey in 2026 a convergence of two laboratory technologies aimed at digestive cancers that resist standard treatment. Gastric, liver, and pancreatic tumors kill millions yearly, and flat cell cultures miss both organ shape and tumor surroundings, while animal models are slow, pricey, and biologically distant. The review argues that pairing 3D bioprinting with microfluidic chips builds living tumor models that behave far more like real disease.

Bioprinting places cancer, support, and immune cells in precise layouts inside tunable gels. Printed liver tumors have kept their patients' genetic traits over time. Printed pancreatic models recreate the dense shield of fibroblast tissue that blocks drugs. Microfluidic channels then perfuse the constructs, imitating blood flow and letting researchers watch responses dynamically. The authors frame the combined platform as a route to patient-specific testing, where a person's own tumor model could preview which therapy deserves a try.
pmc-13450092:
Chien-Yu Liu and colleagues surveyed older adults in Taiwan in 2026 on physical literacy, activity, and sitting time. Physical literacy means the motivation, confidence, and skill to stay active, and it may be a modifiable lever for healthier aging. The team tested whether it tracked with meeting activity guidelines and with less prolonged sitting.

A nationwide phone survey reached 1,078 community-dwelling adults aged sixty-five and older across four regions. Higher literacy scores went with greater odds of meeting activity targets and lower odds of long sitting spells, after adjusting for background and health factors. Programs that build confidence and basic movement skill may therefore help older adults move more and sit less.
pmc-13450292:
Chaochao Ma and co-authors combine in 2026 a designer membrane with deep learning to find and identify microplastics in natural water at trace levels. Raman-based SERS detection is sensitive in principle but falters in the field: particles enrich poorly, hotspots form unevenly, and polymer spectra look alike. Their platform stacks gold-silver nanocubes, charge-tuned by a polymer coat, on a cellulose acetate membrane, corralling particles into a dense, vertically layered field of signal-amplifying hotspots.

The system detected polystyrene down to fifty nanograms per milliliter and gave repeatable readings in spiked samples from six real environmental waters with no chemical cleanup. A spectral library covering four common polymers fed an attention-based neural network that named polymers reliably and estimated their shares in two- and three-plastic mixtures with accuracy scores above 0.83. The authors pitch the pairing as field-ready monitoring for complex waters.
pmc-13450492:
Mila Bertolo and co-authors ask in a 2026 study whether a steady beat in song is a shared trait of humans and songbirds. They taped made-up songs from adults who were not trained musicians, plus songs from young children. Songs from young and adult zebra finches gave them a bird group to weigh against the human ones.

Human singers, young and old alike, kept a fairly even beat in their songs. Finches did the reverse, landing below the level chance would predict, and older birds showed no sign of learning a steadier beat. The team links the split to how each species sings with others, since group singing may reward a shared pulse in humans.
pmc-13451092:
Sauer and colleagues surveyed cancer patients in Poland in 2026 on what drives satisfaction with oncology care in academic versus nonacademic hospitals. Satisfaction matters deeply in cancer, where outcomes mix with emotional experience. Five hundred forty-six patients answered a structured survey covering their background, treatment, and hospital experience, and the team modeled what predicted it.

Patients in academic hospitals reported clearly higher satisfaction. Respect and empathy from staff was the strongest positive driver, followed by access to specialists. Each added month of treatment delay cut the odds of satisfaction sharply, by over forty percent in nonacademic hospitals. Younger patients and women carried more emotional distress and money worries, with the under-thirty group reporting the most financial fear. The authors urge shorter waits, better specialist access, and targeted psychological and financial support for the most burdened groups.
pmc-13451292:
Wenfeng He and others reviewed miniaturized vacuum systems for cold atom sensors in 2026, based on passive vacuum technology. Cold atom sensors are moving from labs to field use, but their vacuum systems remain bulky, combining chambers, laser paths, and magnetic coils. Shrinking size, weight, and power use is now the key challenge.

The review summarizes low helium-permeability materials, key parts such as getter pumps and atomic sources, and how they integrate into a passive vacuum system. Performance evaluation methods are analyzed, and preliminary designs and experiments are presented. Engineers gain a roadmap for compact vacuum systems that could bring cold atom sensors to portable applications.
pmc-13451892:
Suiting Ao and a very large team track in 2026 how severe skin reactions to drugs shifted across the COVID-19 years in China. These reactions, which include blistering syndromes that can kill up to two in five patients, may be swayed by infections. The team gathered 794 checked cases from 40 skin departments, split into before, during, and after spans by China's pandemic rules.

Blistering cases of the Stevens-Johnson kind made the largest share, followed by full-body red eruptions. The share of two severe kinds rose during and after the pandemic years. Median age sat near the early fifties, and men made just under half the cases. The authors read the shift as a sign that viral waves can move drug reaction patterns.
pmc-13452392:
Rajesh Pahwa and nine co-authors report final results from PROviDE, a long United States study of a gut delivered Parkinson drug mix. The drug pairs carbidopa with levodopa in liquid form and goes through a tube into the gut for steady dosing. The 2026 paper follows people with advanced disease for 36 months after they start treatment.

Of 104 people who joined, 47 gave data for the full 36 months and fed the final analysis. Their daily time with worn off drug effect fell by 2.7 hours at month 3 and stayed lower at month 36. Scores for how well treatment worked and how happy people felt with it also rose and held. Life quality scores got better by month 3 and did not slip back over the three years.
pmc-13453092:
Xiao-huan Li and six co-authors engineer tiny cell bubbles to ferry a gene silencing snippet into bowel cancer tumors. The bubbles, called exosomes, come from stem cells grown in three dimensional culture, which yields more of them than flat culture. Their 2026 design loads the bubbles with miR-99b-5p and adds a homing peptide called iRGD to steer them to tumors.

In lab dishes, the loaded bubbles slowed cancer cell growth, spread, and movement. In mice, the homing peptide piled the bubbles up at tumor sites, and the treatment shrank tumors while boosting a standard drug, 5-fluorouracil. The snippet works by lowering a growth signal protein, FGFR3, which quiets a key pathway and triggers ferroptosis, an iron driven cell death. No clear side effects showed in the mice, the team reports.
pmc-13453492:
Shigeki Matsubara writes an opinion piece on the tangled rules for declaring AI help in medical writing. Nearly all journals now demand that authors disclose AI use, he notes in this 2026 piece. Yet the rules leave authors unsure how editors will judge the disclosure, and fear of a penalty may mute honest reporting.

He points to a fuzzy line in the rules: editing with AI must be declared, while grammar checks need not be, though the two acts can produce the same fix. After rounds of AI polish, authors may also feel the words are simply their own. He urges journals to promise that declared AI use will not sway acceptance, and to bank disclosure data for later study. Openness on both sides, he argues, would turn disclosure into an asset.
pmc-13454592:
Thijs J. Hagenbeek leads a large drug team presenting, in 2026, two blockers of the TEAD family, proteins that switch on the cancer-driving partner YAP. When the Hippo control pathway fails, YAP fuels tumor growth, and TEAD proteins are its required partners. The new compounds grip a fat-filled pocket inside TEAD and lock on permanently at a shared cysteine site.

The first compound, GNE-8025, slowed YAP-driven tumor cells in dishes and in animals. It also boosted the punch of many MAPK-pathway drugs, including a KRAS blocker, in lab and animal tests. A tuned sister compound, GNE-2181, crosses into the brain, a rare feat for such drugs. That version shrank tumors growing inside the skull in mice. The authors present the pair as a next step toward practical Hippo-targeting cancer therapy.
pmc-13454892:
Wei Lung Teo and four colleagues pilot-test, in a 2026 trial, a phone app that trains foreign domestic workers in Singapore to care for older adults at home. Many families rely on these workers, who often start with little health training. The app, E-CHEER, teaches in several languages. Sixty worker and employer pairs joined, half given the app and half not.

Half of those approached agreed to join, and about 82 percent finished the study. App users improved at measuring blood pressure, supervising walking, and care knowledge over twelve weeks. Walking supervision also beat the control group clearly. Users rated the app's ease somewhat above average on a standard scale. The authors call the approach workable for home eldercare training, while noting the small pilot size and the need for a larger trial to confirm gains.
pmc-13455392:
Adeesh Parvathaneni and Jesus Enriquez report why tiny airway valves failed in a man with repeated chest infection in a 2026 case study. After lung removal surgery, a leak between airway and chest cavity can persist, and endobronchial valves offer a less invasive seal, though their fate in chronic infection is poorly documented. A 74-year-old man returned 14 months after two Zephyr valves were placed at the bronchial stump, with recurrent resistant staph empyema.

During creation of an Eloesser flap, an open drainage window in the chest wall, surgeons found both valves displaced from the stump. One valve lay fully loose in the chest cavity, and the stump was eroded by chronic infection. After the flap, the patient improved and cultures turned negative at three months. The case argues for careful valve selection when infection persists and shows open drainage still rescues patients when valves fail.
pmc-13455492:
Hülya Yaman Dağdelen and Zeynep Bahadır surveyed Generation Z university students in Türkiye about three connected habits: occupational balance, sleep quality, and addiction to social media. Occupational balance means how evenly daily activities feel distributed. Their 2026 cross-sectional study gathered 136 undergraduates born in or after 2000 and measured each topic with a standard questionnaire. The team then tested which factors stayed linked once age, gender, study year, and daily usage time were taken into account.

Students past six hours a day on social media scored highest on the addiction scale by a wide margin. Higher addiction scores came with poorer sleep, and that link survived statistical adjustment, with addiction still predicting worse sleep quality. Addiction alone did not predict occupational balance after adjustment, but sleep quality itself was significantly tied to how balanced students felt their days were.
pmc-13455792:
Yan Liu and four colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether variants in one potassium channel gene predict who gains most from hard interval training. The team recruited 249 Han college students for twelve weeks of high-intensity interval sessions, three times a week. Breathing and heart measures were taken before and after, and five variants in the KCNC1 gene were typed.

Fitness rose across the group: peak oxygen use climbed and working heart rates fell. Three variants tracked with training sensitivity. One variant's CC carriers gained the most peak oxygen capacity and the largest drop in working heart rate. Another variant split its effects, with one type gaining most in carbon dioxide output and another dropping peak heart rate most. The authors nominate these variants as candidate markers for tailoring training, while noting the suggestive strength of the statistics.
pmc-13457292:
Mesut Genişoğlu and co-authors calculate the health risks swimmers absorb from disinfection by-products in indoor pools, route by route. Chlorine keeps pool water safe from germs but also reacts with organic matter to form compounds such as chloroform and two haloacetic acids. Using a year of monitoring from two indoor pools, their 2026 study estimates cancer and chronic-toxicity risks for casual bathers, children, and competitive swimmers.

Breathing chloroform proved the dominant cancer pathway, passing the negligible-risk line in every group and hitting competitive swimmers hardest. Swallowed water drove the acid-related risks, with trichloroacetic acid the worst offender in the busier pool. Skin contact mattered for chloroform but little for the acids. One overlooked route, uptake through the mouth lining, matched accidental swallowing, especially for children and heavy trainers. The authors urge pool-specific, multi-route risk checks, better ventilation, and precursor control.
pmc-13457392:
Dequan Tian and a ten-author team hunt for Staphylococcus argenteus, a recently recognized relative of Staphylococcus aureus, in a Beijing hospital's isolate collection. Routine tests cannot tell the two apart, so the team re-checked 2,080 isolates labeled S. aureus using mass spectrometry, gene sequencing, and whole-genome sequencing. Their 2026 study then profiled the isolates for drug resistance, toxin genes, and biofilm growth.

Only three isolates, 0.14 percent, proved to be S. argenteus, a low share for northern China. Four mass-spectrometry peaks may serve as fingerprints for the species, though larger multi-site studies must confirm them. All three strains shared a core of adhesion and immune-evasion genes; one also carried Panton-Valentine leukocidin and enterotoxin genes, and all stayed susceptible to oxacillin despite carrying resistance genes on paper. Two formed strong biofilms. The authors call for multicenter surveillance to judge how much this species matters clinically.
pmc-13458992:
Mayamiko Nkoloma and colleagues test whether tech nerves beat tech know-how in predicting digital health uptake in Malawi in a 2026 survey. Digital health systems promise better care in poor settings, yet uptake depends on workers' wish to use them. A one-time survey of 615 Malawi health workers measured uptake plans, tech nerves and tech know-how, with layered stats splitting their effects.

Uptake plans ran high at a mean of 6.52 with low nerves at 2.08, and workers with high plans had more training, longer tech use and lower nerves. Know-how alone explained only 1.1 percent of plan gaps versus 6.9 percent for nerves alone, and in the final model only nerves stayed clear. Bosses gain a clear lever: easing tech nerves through training and support may matter more than years of tech contact.
pmc-13459292:
Johanna Beckmann and colleagues link household wealth, diet diversity and stunting in South African schoolchildren in a 2026 study. Children in low- and middle-income settings face food insecurity and poor diet quality, yet wealth gradients inside one marginalised area were unclear. Baseline data from a multi-country trial covered 839 primary school children, mean age 8.3 years, from four schools in a peri-urban area of Gqeberha. Parent reports covered wealth, food security and 24-hour diet.

Children averaged 5.8 healthy food groups, and 8.4 percent, one in twelve, were stunted. Poorer families faced more food insecurity, ate fewer different foods and were more likely to have stunted children. Wealthier children ate more cereals, roots, vitamin A vegetables, oil, sweets and sweet drinks. School feeding and nutrition education help, but the authors urge broader action on poverty and affordable healthy food to close the gap.
pmc-13459592:
J. B. Demigné and co-authors report in 2026 a small Marseille case series on stomach and gastroesophageal junction cancers whose tumors cannot repair DNA mismatches. Such tumors respond strongly to immunotherapy yet poorly to standard chemotherapy. Ten patients with localized disease received immune checkpoint treatment before any surgery between January 2024 and July 2025, most getting two immunotherapy drugs together.

Six patients went on to surgery, and four of their removed tumors showed no remaining cancer. Four patients skipped surgery, and all eventually reached a complete clinical response as treatment continued individually. At a median follow-up of about nineteen months, every patient was alive and free of disease. The authors say skipping surgery deserves careful study in this select group.
pmc-13459692: This pull-back notice, issued by the journal Cardiovascular Psychiatry and Neurology in 2026, withdraws a 2012 paper by S. S. Agrawal and colleagues on curcumin protection in a rat model of Parkinson's disease. Wiley pulled the article after PubPeer flagged multiple flaws in Figure 2, where all five panels appeared to contain shared sections with oddly similar regions. The results and findings were judged unreliable, and the authors did not respond when told of the pull-back.
pmc-13460192:
Ping Li, Hailiang Wang, Qian Zhang, and Hengda Li developed in 2026 a scan-reading model that tells minimally invasive lung adenocarcinoma apart from fully invasive disease before surgery. pmc-13487292:

pmc-13487692:
Miura and colleagues in Japan checked in 2026 which dose measures best warn of lung harm after radiation care for lung cancer. In the final model, that lower lobe gauge and a high lifetime smoking score each stood on their own as risk signs. The authors say this plain lobe gauge adds to standard checks when teams judge risk before care starts.
pmc-13487992:

The authors warn that cross-reaction can produce false dengue positives, so test results need careful reading in both diseases.
pmc-13488592:

pmc-13490492:

Because the constants came from the same stuff batches being modeled, the forecasts tie tightly to physical samples. pmc-13490592:

Maps of that score become a swing pattern for each region.

pmc-13490892:

pmc-13491692:
Zhe Li and four co-authors test in 2026 whether teacher feedback changes how well adolescents hold emotional information in mind. Students given negative feedback answered more accurately than the others. Within that group, stronger fear of negative evaluation tracked with better performance. The authors suggest that critical feedback, when informative, can sharpen attention and effort in teenagers who worry about judgment.
pmc-13491792:
Gifty Makafui Doe and four colleagues explore in 2026 why mothers living with HIV drift away from treatment after giving birth at Volta Regional Hospital in Ghana. Interviews and a focus group gathered views from thirty mothers, two mentor mothers, and seven health workers.

Longer gaps between appointments opened another hole, which mentor mothers partly filled by bridging clinic and home.
pmc-13493492:
Ali Abdoulkadri Abdoulaye and five colleagues dissect in 2026 where gum arabic actually forms inside the Senegalia senegal tree. pmc-13493792:

pmc-13493892:

Separating acute from chronic cases proved harder, with the best model reaching only modest accuracy near seventy percent. pmc-13494092:

Across 18 cohorts, people with the highest intakes had lower rates of heart disease, heart attack, type 2 diabetes, and high blood pressure than those with the lowest intakes. Blood fats, blood pressure, and blood sugar stayed much the same. The authors grade much of the proof as moderate in strength.
pmc-13494392:

In 2026, the case concerns a twenty-six-year-old at thirty-five weeks whose heart stopped two hours after ICU entry, after arriving with low oxygen and restlessness. Standard care calls for around-death C-section birth within four minutes, but not all heart-stop causes resolve with birth.

pmc-13494692:

pmc-13499592:

pmc-13499892:

Perforations, accidental holes through the wall, occurred less often with traction help in the reported ratios. Scarring that narrows the passage was more common after traction-assisted work, however, which the authors weigh as the main trade-off needing cost and outcome study.
pmc-13500392:

pmc-13500592:

pmc-13500692:

pmc-13501592:

pmc-13501692:

pmc-13503792:

Tests against two rival methods showed better accuracy and better computing behavior. They then ran the model on calcium waves inside cells, a case with memory and spreading loss. The work gives a tool for such waves in physics and biology.
pmc-13503892:

pmc-13504792:

pmc-13504992:

pmc-13505092:

pmc-13505392:

pmc-13507192:

pmc-13507292:

pmc-13507392:

pmc-13508192:

pmc-13508292:

pmc-13508392:

pmc-13510792:

pmc-13510992:

pmc-13512392:

pmc-13512592:

pmc-13513792:

pmc-13514692:

pmc-13514892:

pmc-13515292:

In adjusted analysis, however, only the change in tumour size stayed an independent predictor, each centimetre of shrinkage raising complete-response odds by about a third. Volume change dropped out. The authors encourage further study of volumetrics as a counselling aid.
pmc-13560692:
Tracey L. Peters and colleagues describe the genomes of six bacteriophages that infect Enterobacter cloacae, a hospital pathogen with prevalent drug-resistant strains. Their 2026 genome announcement presents the viruses as candidates for phage therapy against infections that antibiotics can no longer clear. All six belong to the genus Karamvirus.

The phages were isolated from Washington, DC sewage and purified on drug-resistant clinical hosts. Their genomes run from about one hundred seventy-two to one hundred seventy-six thousand bases, with GC content just under forty percent and roughly three hundred predicted protein-coding genes each. Several carry tRNA genes of their own. Safety scoring tools rated them highly, and genomic analysis indicated a purely lytic lifestyle, meaning they burst their hosts rather than hiding inside them. The authors deposit the sequences as a resource for therapeutic development.
pmc-13562092:
Viktor Erbring and colleagues chart how esophageal pressure, the stand-in for pressure around the lungs, behaves when ventilated patients lie face down versus face up. Their 2026 study uses high-resolution manometry, with sensors along the whole esophagus, in twenty patients measured before spinal surgery. Two levels of airway pressure support were tested in each position.

End-expiratory pressure ran lower in the prone position, while its swing with each breath grew larger and the heart's ripple on the trace shrank. Which sensors were averaged changed the numbers substantially, and within-patient variability ranged widely depending on settings. A hand-picked set of theoretically optimal sensors gave lower, steadier readings than broad regional averages. The authors warn that position, pressure level, and sensor choice all bend this measurement, complicating its use for setting lung-protective ventilation.
pmc-13562592:
Aleyna Nalcaoglu Senocak and five colleagues describe a new species with an orange-red pigment, found in soil from an abandoned mine near Trabzon, Türkiye. Mining soils are harsh places that can shelter unusual microbes. The 2026 team isolated a strain coded FMA22T during a pigment survey and ran the full battery of tests used to place a bacterium. The battery covered gene sequencing, cell chemistry, growth ranges, and a draft genome. Gene matches put it in the genus Rhodococcus, closest to a known species at 99.57 percent similarity.

Whole-genome comparisons fell well below species thresholds, confirming the strain as new. Its genome spans 4.23 million bases and carries the cluster for making carotenoid pigments. The pigment absorbed light at 475 nanometres, showed antioxidant power in assays, and weakly blocked an HIV enzyme. The authors name it Rhodococcus folensis; FMA22T is the reference strain in two culture collections.
pmc-13562692:
Nobuo Okui and six colleagues mine Reddit posts to compare how two chronic pain conditions organise symptom language around the word pain. Bladder pain syndrome centres on the pelvis and urinary trouble, while fibromyalgia spreads pain body-wide with fatigue and poor sleep. Doctors group both under central sensitisation, yet patients live them differently. The 2026 team gathered posts from each community with matched methods, built a word list from questionnaires, and mapped which words appear together.

Both networks centred on pain, but fibromyalgia packed more symptom words close to that centre, while the bladder condition kept a larger fringe. The bladder posts tied pain to pelvic, urinary, and sensory words. Fibromyalgia tied it to whole-body, tiredness, sleep, and feeling words. Dense-core shapes diverged, one in separate modules, the other fused into a single knot. Patient language, the authors argue, carries structure that clinics could learn from.
pmc-13564092:
Olga Averina, Alexander Tiulpakov, and a large team of colleagues describe two siblings whose inherited gene defect unexpectedly damaged their adrenal glands. Their FLAD1 mutations impair production of FAD, a cofactor many enzymes need. Both siblings showed adrenal insufficiency, never before tied to this gene.

To prove causation, the team engineered mice carrying the siblings' exact mutation pair. The mice reproduced the patients' physiological, biochemical, and hormone abnormalities, while one mutation alone proved lethal when doubled and nearly harmless in the other case. The model confirms the mutations cause the adrenal disease and opens a path to studying its mechanism and testing treatments.
pmc-13566392:
Veronica Tius and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, how deep learning is entering surgery for cancers of the female reproductive organs. Deep learning is a form of artificial intelligence that learns patterns from large data sets. Uses span training, live guidance in the operating room, and prediction of complications or survival.

Systems can grade surgical skill, recognize anatomy and operation steps, and spot tumor tissue, sometimes with high accuracy in narrow settings. New imaging methods may sharpen tumor detection further. Most studies so far are retrospective, small, and untested outside their home centers. Surgeons get an honest map of promise against the thin proof of real-world benefit.
pmc-13571392:
Yang Liu and colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a 4-year-old child with complete heart block and a confirmed allergy to the metals in pacemaker casings. The child finally received a working device after three failed standard implants. Each failure was undone by poor wound healing and skin breakdown over the pocket. Skin patch testing confirmed the metal allergy.

A leadless single-chamber pacemaker, a capsule-sized device that sits inside the heart with no wires or pocket, was placed through the right internal jugular vein in the neck. Leadless devices are rarely used in small children, and no standard route existed for metal-allergic ones. The successful neck route gives pediatric teams a technical pathway for this high-risk corner case.
pmc-13572392:
Vishal Dhiman, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 trial of road surfacing made with rubble from torn-down concrete. India builds roads fast and dumps much of this waste, which harms land and water. The team asked whether treated waste chunks could serve in the top layer of a road, the part tyres touch.

The waste was pre-coated with bitumen emulsion, a tar-like binder in water, to boost grip and water resistance. Tests varied binder share, waste share, and heat level, and a surface method found the best mix. At about 4.79 percent binder and 21 percent treated waste, the mix met national specs for strength, stiffness, and water resistance. The authors say treated rubble can replace some fresh stone and cut dumping at the same time.
pmc-13572492:
Ericsson Tetteh Chenebuah, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 model that predicts how strongly molecules stick to catalyst surfaces. That sticking energy guides catalyst design for fuel cells and clean energy, yet quantum calculations are slow and lab trials cost much. The model aims for quantum-like accuracy at a fraction of the effort.

The network, Q-CatNet, builds on a crystal graph method that maps atoms and bonds. New inputs add charge-based edge cues plus global signals from electron states and X-ray patterns. It predicts the sticking energy directly, with no need to split the total energy into parts. On a curated data set, it beat an image-based method by 46 percent and topped several graph rivals by 8 to 38 percent. The authors pitch it as a faster screen for new catalysts.
pmc-13572792:
Grossemy leads an eleven-author team characterizing an overlooked population of tendon cells, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Tendons bundle fibers in a softer matrix, the interfascicular matrix. Cells that live in that matrix were hard to pull out on their own. So how they act in the body stayed unknown till now.

The team pulled off the first long-term culture of enriched interfascicular and fascicular cells, set side by side. The cells from the matrix proved strikingly sensitive to stiffness in their base. On stiff surfaces they remodeled and drifted from their tendon identity. They also stopped proliferating as time went on. Softer surfaces, more like the matrix, rescued their growth. They also restored gene expression in part. The fascicular cells barely reacted at all. That split may help explain how tendinopathy starts when the mechanics of the tissue change.
pmc-13573192:
Leanne M Redman, with 15 colleagues, sets out a 2026 protocol for a pilot trial on eating patterns and healthy ageing. Eating fewer calories and time-restricted eating both improve markers of ageing in past work, yet people struggle to stick with them. Phone tools that nudge at the right moment may help, and this trial tests that idea.

The 24-week trial will enroll ninety healthy adults from twenty-two to forty-five into five groups. The groups cover no program, standard or app-supported time windows of eight hours, and standard or app-supported calorie cuts of 25 percent. App groups get live tracking of eating and prompts tuned to each moment. Main checks cover adherence, retention, and satisfaction. Secondary checks gauge biological age and a metabolic health score, to pick endpoints for a larger trial.
pmc-13573392:
Ruifeng Li, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 case of advanced lung cancer cleared by a targeted drug before surgery. Stage IIIB lung cancer is usually ruled out for surgery. The patient was a 35-year-old woman who never smoked, with a tumour in the left lower lobe and spread to chest lymph nodes. Her cancer carried an ALK change, which a drug called lorlatinib targets.

After ten weeks on the drug, scans showed no active cancer left, a full metabolic response. The team then removed the lobe through a single-port keyhole route. Tissue checks confirmed no live cancer remained, a complete pathological response. She left hospital in five days with no complications and stayed disease-free at twelve months. The authors note one case and short follow-up limit the claim.
pmc-13573492:
Jordi Ribas-Maynou, with seven colleagues, reports a 2026 study of sperm chromatin in boars and what it means for breeding. Chromatin, the packed DNA in sperm, can vary in tightness and breakage, and those traits may steer fertility. Pig data on this front were thin, and breed or season effects were unknown.

The team measured how sperm DNA is packed and whether it carries single or double breaks, then grouped boars by those patterns. Clusters split along breed lines and shifted by month, which shows season leaves a mark on sperm quality. One break type, double-strand breaks in the DNA, tied to litter size in the outcome data. Such links could give stud farms a lab flag for picking boars. The authors frame chromatin checks as a new layer for selection programs.
pmc-13573692:
Lian, Luo, Zheng, and Li study leisure exercise and survival in cancer survivors, in work from twenty twenty-six. Exercise is known to help survivors live longer. What was unclear is whether total amount, how often, or how hard matters most.

The team used a United States health survey linked to death records, with more than three thousand survivors aged twenty and up. People were classed as inactive or active by weekly minutes. Active people were split by sessions per week and by share of vigorous effort. Models adjusted for social and health traits. The split design helps give survivors practical advice, not just a single minute target.
pmc-13574792:
Zaiba Ali, Rahila Ali, Nida Khan, and Hind Almozeil study how HR guard steps for digital risk shape work-life balance for Saudi knowledge workers. Their survey study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Fast digital shifts at work can outpace how staff adjust in mind and social life. The team asks if mindful tech use and firm work bounds carry the effect in steps.

More than six hundred staff in tech, banks, and colleges took the survey. Guard steps linked to both mindful use and balance in a direct way. Mindful use then linked strongly to firm bounds, which linked to balance too. Guard steps reached bounds just through mindful use first. The chain held in strict tests.
pmc-13576092:
Huixiang Chen and four colleagues look for signs that predict how well eye injections work in diabetic macular oedema, in a 2026 study. This swelling at the centre of the retina is a top cause of vision loss in type 2 diabetes. Injections that block VEGF are first-line care, yet many patients respond weakly.

Two hundred patients were split by whether retinal thickness fell by at least 20 percent after treatment. Four starting measures predicted response on their own: kidney marker creatinine, starting retinal thickness, the length of a light-sensing layer segment, and the presence of cyst-like swelling. A chart-style model built from the four scored well on accuracy checks and held up in resampling. The authors offer it as a practical aid for setting expectations before treatment.
pmc-13576592:
Kazuki Ito and five colleagues test whether an automated score can find the messy electrical signals that mark trouble spots in persistent atrial fibrillation, a stubborn heart rhythm disorder. Burning those spots, called dispersion electrograms, on top of standard vein isolation cuts recurrence, yet spotting them by eye is subjective. A mapping system feature called Complex Signal Identification rates each signal automatically.

The team analysed 4,453 signal points from five patients before ablation. One measure, the fractionation score, stood out: a cut-off of 4.1 identified the target spots with an accuracy score of 0.905, sensitivity of 80.4 percent, and specificity of 98.6 percent in the same dataset. Three other measures performed far worse. The authors suggest the score could guide extra ablation in a consistent, practical way.
pmc-13578192:
Tsung-Hsien Chen and eight colleagues review patches studded with tiny needles that cross the skin's top layer with almost no pain. Such patches can deliver drugs, draw fluid for tests, sense body signals, and even respond on their own. The review takes a hard look at what blocks their path to clinics.

The authors compare needle types, materials, and ways of making them, weighing strength, ease of mass production, and steadiness from batch to batch. The real brakes are scale-up, quality checks, rules, and cost. Smart sensing, body-triggered release, and 3D printing get a close look as next steps. The goal is a clear guide for moving the tech from labs to patients.
pmc-13579992:
Fatemeh Sadat Rohani and colleagues ask whether the antioxidant power of a person's whole diet tracks with fatty liver disease, in a 2026 case control study from Yazd, Iran. One hundred fifteen patients with the disease were matched with one hundred two adults without it, all from one clinic. A year long food survey scored how much antioxidant capacity each diet carried, and blood tests measured liver enzymes, sugar, and fats.

Across the whole group, no link appeared between diet antioxidant score and disease odds. One corner stood out before adjustments: men eating the most vegetable oil antioxidants showed higher odds, yet the signal faded once other factors were counted. The authors call the question open and ask for forward looking studies built to test diet quality against liver fat directly.
pmc-13584292:
Susannah Engdahl and colleagues test whether ultrasound can read phantom hand movements in a person with an upper arm amputation. Losing an arm above the elbow leaves few muscles to drive a powered prosthesis, and many users give up on such devices. The 2026 study looked at one person who had never had nerve-transfer surgery, a common extra step meant to boost muscle signals.

When the person tried to move fingers of the missing hand, ultrasound caught distinct patterns of activity in the remaining upper arm muscles. Each tried movement gave a pattern that repeated more alike across tries than it matched other movements. The team reads this as early proof that finger-level intent survives in the arm, which could one day guide prosthesis control without surgery.
pmc-13585792:
Sadok Kouz builds a math model of a biosensor surface in this 2026 theoretical study. The sensor uses surface plasmon resonance, a light effect that shifts when molecules pile up on a metal film. That film is coated with graphene oxide, a carbon sheet that grabs target molecules. Rather than test a finished device, the model links how much lands on the surface to how far the light signal moves.

Three landing styles were modeled, from weak to cooperative, over a prism and metal stack tuned on screen. For the middle style, the model foresaw a clear signal shift across the tested range and a detection limit that hinges on how noisy the angle reading is. Warming matched a heat-releasing process. The author is plain that these are effective, fitted numbers that still need bench tests to confirm.
pmc-13587292:
Lovleen Garg and colleagues report in 2026 how fat balance goes wrong in the brain in a fruit fly model of ALS8, an inherited form of motor neuron disease. The human disease is caused by a faulty version of VAPB, a protein that links cell compartments where fats are handled.

In fly brains carrying the faulty protein, fat stores shifted with age: cholesterol fell while its stored forms and sphingolipids, a class of membrane fats, rose. Oddly, fat droplets grew fewer and smaller even as stored fats built up. Restoring the normal protein reversed both the fat changes and movement problems. Tests in single cell types showed neurons and support cells each play a part, and support-cell fat handling depended most strongly on the protein.
pmc-13587392:
Xuan Zhou and colleagues pull a mixed flu virus out of pigs in Shandong Province, China. Swine flu costs the pig industry heavily and can jump to people, so new mixes deserve close reading. From 600 nose swabs, one sample grew a virus, typed as H3N2, which the team then read gene by gene and tested in cells and mice for this 2026 report.

Five of its eight gene segments matched the 2009 pandemic H1N1 line, while its surface genes came from a human-like H3N2 line, making it a true shuffle of the two. Several surface changes set it apart from the current human vaccine strain, which could blunt vaccine match. The virus grew well in lab cells and in mouse airways, causing mild to moderate lung damage without deaths. The authors class it as low risk for severe disease but worth watching.
pmc-13587692:
Soo-Hyun Sung and colleagues publish a correction to their study of herbal medicine for menstrual pain. While re-checking the published tables, the team found a copy error. Nine rows of background variables in three tables had been taken from the wrong computer output, so the printed values did not match each table's own model. All three tables were rebuilt from the single correct analysis behind each one.

The correction also replaces a results paragraph on pain severity. In the fixed version, pain scores fell clearly at every follow-up visit, and the two groups started alike. The herbal group pulled ahead on pain relief by the second visit, though not the first. A separate passage on pain duration was corrected the same way, and a citation line that named only one table now names all three. The notice carries the full corrected wording and tables for readers.
pmc-13590392:
Sofia Thunberg and three colleagues ask what a friendly flying robot could do for people who run for fun. Drones already help pace runners or check their stride, yet their social side has had little study. The team first spoke with eight runners about drone support. They then ran a hands on design session with five seasoned runners, who built rough models of drones they might welcome.

Five low cost prototypes came out of the session, each with notes on what felt helpful or odd. Themes from the work push designers to think past pace and data, toward how a drone greets, urges, or keeps its distance. Thunberg and the team also warn that bystanders matter: a drone built for one runner affects everyone sharing the path.
pmc-13591092:
Jennifer L Millar and nine colleagues report, in 2026, a trial of gaze training for people with lasting inner ear balance loss. Weak balance organs cause dizziness, unsteady walking, and falls. Standard rehab uses gaze drills in bright rooms, where patients hold their eyes on a still target while moving the head. The new method uses a moving laser target in the dark, with the target speed raised in small steps to retrain the reflex that steadies vision.

Patients were assigned at random to one method, then crossed to the other. Early results showed both routes helped walking and balance to a similar degree. Balance gains from the new method seen at three weeks had faded by six months, which the team flags for follow up study.
pmc-13591192:
Yi-Wei Chang and colleagues found that thumb position changes median-nerve movement and shape in carpal tunnel syndrome, with implications for nerve-gliding exercises. Carpal tunnel syndrome squeezes the median nerve at the wrist, causing pain and numbness, and gliding exercises aim to mobilise the nerve. Their cross-sectional study used ultrasound in 79 affected hands and 88 healthy hands across wrist and thumb positions.

Affected nerves were larger, and their cross-section shrank when the thumb shifted from a resting pose to a spread pose in either wrist position. Nerve excursion was lower in patients, rising with wrist extension but dipping when extension combined with thumb abduction. The authors recommend against fully spreading the thumb at the end of gliding exercises.
pmc-13591692:
Ceren Gürez, Ata Baytaroğlu, and Zahid Hüseyinhan compare, in 2026, four operations for an overactive eye muscle that lifts the eye too far when it looks inward. Surgeons chose among four weakening methods by how severe the overaction was in each eye. Their records covered 286 eyes from 200 patients, each followed for at least a year after surgery.

Starting grades, near the top of the scale on average, fell to zero in most eyes by one year. Success rates sat between 92 and 95 percent in each group, with no clear gap between methods. Odd head posture, used by patients to keep single vision, dropped sharply too. The team cautions that one year is too short to catch late returns.
pmc-13592492:
Milan Brázdil leads a 2026 hunt for brain oscillations faster than any class known before, recorded with hair thin electrodes inside the brain. Their team studied 15 patients with drug resistant epilepsy at four centers, using sampling fast enough to catch signals up to eight kilohertz. A custom detector sifted the recordings for brief bursts in that range, dubbed ultrafast oscillations.

The bursts appeared far more often in epileptic hippocampi than in healthy ones, with the two to three kilohertz band separating them best. Two shapes recurred: spindle like waves and sharp bursts that decay fast. Standard large contacts almost never caught them, so microelectrodes are essential. Brázdil and the team propose the signals as a fresh marker of overexcitable tissue.
pmc-13595592:
Mark Sanderson-Cimino heads a very large collaboration building a single harmonized memory score for dementia research. The project solves a practical headache. Research centers have long used whichever word-list learning test they preferred. That made results hard to combine. Their 2026 work used item-banking statistics on more than eight thousand seven hundred participants who took a standard battery plus one of five list tests.

The composite stitched those different tests onto one scale with adequate measurement properties. It behaved as a valid memory measure should, tracking demographics, disease severity, other thinking tests, brain volume, and markers of Alzheimer's pathology including scans and a blood protein. A second, more diverse cohort of over eight hundred people reproduced the pattern. A free online tool lets other researchers compute the score in their own datasets, extending its use across centers.
pmc-13598592:
Chanchal Kumari and five co-authors pool laboratory studies on whether silver diamine fluoride, the paint-on cavity arrester, harms the living pulp inside teeth. The treatment is widely used because it stops decay without drilling, but its safety near pulp tissue is contested. Seven in vitro studies from twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-four met their criteria.

Damage was dose-dependent. At clinical and high concentrations, from about four to thirty-eight percent, cell viability fell markedly. Meta-analysis found almost no harm at extremely dilute concentrations, a significant viability drop in a mid-low range, and severe effects beyond. The reviewers counsel respect for concentration and proximity when the pulp is near.
pmc-13600392:
Alexander Sweetman and colleagues from six Australian health bodies issued a joint position statement on managing insomnia in adults. The statement gathers sleep doctors, psychologists, family doctors, pharmacists, nurses, and people who live with insomnia.

Insomnia counts as acute under three months and chronic beyond that, and the group says diagnosis rests on the patient's own report. Their first-line treatment is multi-part cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, which works in person, in groups, online, and alongside other illnesses. Sleep hygiene tips alone are not enough for chronic cases, the statement warns. Sleeping pills rank second line, for short spells at the lowest dose, and several drug types are ruled out entirely.
pmc-13602292:
Konstantin Senkevich and colleagues scan rare gene variants across the cell's recycling system in Parkinson's disease in 2026. Faults in lysosomes, the cell's waste-breaking compartments, sit at the heart of Parkinson's, and GBA1 is the strongest known genetic risk factor. The team asked whether other lysosomal genes also carry risk. They sequenced 36 lysosomal genes in 8,267 people with Parkinson's and 68,208 controls drawn from four cohorts, including 793 early-onset cases.

A region of the HEXA gene showed enrichment that did not survive correction. Among early-onset patients, variants in NAGLU and ST3GAL5 reached significance. These genes work in sialylation, ganglioside breakdown, and related fat-processing pathways. Risk in this system extends well beyond GBA1, the authors conclude, pointing to these pathways for replication and treatment research.
pmc-13602892:
Dennis Popp leads a nine-author chemistry team reporting in 2026 three-bladed carbon molecules with mirror-image forms. Starting from a pyrene-based building block, a palladium-catalyzed joining fused three units into tripyrenylene frameworks containing several helicene twists. The first products carry lower symmetry, and the team studied how they rearrange into threefold propellers, then separated the left- and right-handed versions of two of them.

One target was a D3-symmetric pyrenylene and the other a larger nitrogen-containing relative, a trisphenanthrophenazine. The researchers measured how each pure form interacts with polarized light and compared crystal packing against the left-right mixtures. They also timed the shape-flipping processes and ran quantum models of them. Stable, single-handed carbon propellers show strong optical effects that could serve in advanced materials and sensing, where molecular handedness controls the response.
pmc-13605992:
Jimeng Zhang and colleagues located a medicinal compound inside plant leaves in two thousand twenty-six. Oridonin is the main active compound in this herb. Tiny leaf hairs with glands held the compound.

Imaging mass tools confirmed the storage pattern. Spots matched the gland hair positions closely. Extraction and measurement validated the quantities found. Activity tests correlated with compound location too. Leaf surface structures thus serve as chemical factories. Harvesting and breeding can target those glands. Quality control gains a clear anatomical basis.
pmc-13606692:
Xiang Meng and Nicholas Lee put out a 2026 study of how happy Chinese students abroad were with therapy. Language barriers can weaken therapy. Cultural mismatch can too. One hundred twenty-five students with therapy experience answered a survey. Ten later gave full talks.

Both barriers went with lower scores. Culture gaps showed the strongest bad link. Trust in the therapist also counted. The talks explained the numbers in students' own words. Feeling misunderstood recurred as a theme. Schools should train therapists to work across cultures. Matching hopes early may keep students from dropping out of care.
pmc-13608892:
Yilmaz and co-authors test whether the dose of a blood pressure drug affects how well finger oxygen sensors read in intensive care. Pulse oximetry is vital in ICUs, but poor blood flow can throw it off. Norepinephrine, the main drug for shock, tightens vessels and may widen the gap. The team gathered 1,050 paired readings from 196 adults on the drug. Each pair matched the finger reading against a blood-based measure.

Doses were grouped by weight-adjusted level, using sepsis guideline cut points. The study paid special mind to spread and to large mismatches. Big gaps could mislead treatment at the bedside. The work asks whether high doses should prompt extra checks of oxygen levels.
pmc-13610692:
Mehmet Gorduk and colleagues published a rat study in 2026. They tested protection against kidney damage from colistin. Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic for resistant infections. Kidney injury limits how safely it can be used. Two candidate protectors were tested in the study. They are ethyl pyruvate and rutin hydrate. Each was given alone and in combination. Rats received daily injections for one week. Kidney function, blood tests, and tissue were examined.

Colistin alone raised waste levels and oxidative stress. Damage markers in kidney tissue also rose sharply. Perfusion pressure in the kidney increased as well. All protector groups showed lower damage measures. The combined treatment performed best on most measures. Kidney structure also looked best preserved there. Antioxidant action likely explains much of the benefit. Human use would need separate safety trials.
pmc-13612192:
Qin Li leads a nine-author team probing why a castor bean toxin devastates some moth caterpillars and spares another. Ricinine, a castor plant alkaloid, kills the silkworm outright, badly stunts the tobacco cutworm, and barely troubles the eri silkworm, which accumulates the most of the three. Metabolite profiling and gene-expression analysis across all three species sought what separates the vulnerable from the tolerant.

The susceptible species showed deep disruption of energy chemistry around NAD, the cell's energy currency. Key metabolites fell, and genes for NAD production and linked energy pathways were switched down. Feeding extra NAD to cutworms eased ricinine's toxicity, supporting the mechanism. The tolerant eri silkworm's chemistry barely moved, showing built-in tolerance rather than detox effort. Pairing ricinine with a caterpillar virus killed more cutworms than either alone, by suppressing detox enzymes. The authors offer NAD metabolism as a target for new pest control.
pmc-13614992:
Jennifer Leng and colleagues report a 2026 study of Mexican heritage families in New York City and what a healthy life looks like inside their homes. Obesity hits Hispanic adults and children hard, and family programs built for these communities are scarce. Four themes emerged. Children were picking up American habits faster than their parents, sparking clashes over food. Parents saw themselves as role models, balancing firm guidance with flexibility. Work, money, and time made healthy food and activity hard to keep up. The families' own words now shape a culturally fitted program, instead of one translated as an afterthought.
pmc-13615492:
Shaikh and co-authors built a 2026 animal free platform for growing human prostate organoids, miniature tissue models, from induced pluripotent stem cells. Existing prostate models lean on donated tissue or animal ingredients and miss the mix of lining and support cells. Their xeno-free system avoids animal components entirely for cleaner science.

The floating three dimensional clusters organised themselves into lining and support zones carrying basal, luminal, and neuroendocrine markers, Shaikh reports. Fibroblast and smooth muscle markers confirmed the support compartment formed as intended in the organoids. A modular version let engineered lining cells mix with normal support cells so one compartment could be altered alone. Forcing extra androgen receptor into organoids raised prostate specific antigen output and cell growth, showing the platform supports genetic experiments.
pmc-13615992:
Mert Yesiladali and coauthors offer a 2026 narrative review of hirsutism, the growth of coarse hair in a male pattern in women. It can weigh heavily on health and self-image. The condition is driven by male hormones. Gaps remain around how hormones act inside the hair follicle, how insulin resistance feeds the problem, and why treatments help some patients more than others. The authors searched three major databases for human studies from January 2000 through September 2025.

The review walks through local hormone activity and follicle sensitivity. It covers how assessment has evolved. It also covers which drug and hair-removal options current endocrine and skin evidence supports. Its central proposal is a personal, team-based approach spanning hormone, women's health, and skin care. Excess hair should not be treated as a cosmetic matter alone.
pmc-13616992:
Yan Carvalho Magno and four colleagues test how tightly six nitrile-based inhibitors bind two cysteine proteases. The first is cruzain, the main protease of the parasite that causes Chagas disease. A structural difference in one pocket of the enzymes, the S2 subsite, explained why some compounds preferred one target over the other. The authors say the validated protocol can guide design of better inhibitors for Chagas disease and for cancer therapy.
pmc-13617392:

Community health workers, local mosquito control, health education, bed nets, household spraying, seasonal preventive drugs for children, and preventive treatment in pregnancy all emerged as key drivers. These steps improved acceptance, earlier diagnosis, treatment access, and local ownership. New tools such as artificial intelligence mapping and genomic surveillance could sharpen control when joined with community systems. The author concludes that empowered communities, paired with strong partnerships, offer the most lasting path to elimination.
pmc-13619092:
Catherine M K E de Cuba led a twelve-author team on a 2026 trial of S-ketamine, a fast-acting antidepressant, in healthy volunteers. Sixteen participants received an intravenous dose, low and high oral doses, and placebo in a crossover design. Brain measures using magnetic stimulation and electrical recordings followed them from baseline through seven days after dosing.

Intravenous S-ketamine quickly reduced one measure of cortical response, while a measure of inhibition stayed lower for days and tracked the drug's blood level. Electrical brain activity also shifted, with some changes lasting well past the first day. Delayed effects appeared only after the intravenous and high oral doses. The authors suggest these lasting signals could help explain how the drug lifts mood and could guide biomarker choices for similar medicines.
pmc-13623392:
Germano Rodrigues Couto and three co-authors translate and validate the Sexual Risk Behaviors Scale for European Portuguese. The scale measures behaviours such as unprotected sex and multiple partners, and it was aimed at higher education students in Portugal. A good translation must match the source in wording, meaning, and cultural sense.

The team followed international adaptation guidelines, then asked four sexual health experts to judge face validity, meaning whether the items look right for their purpose. Sixty-eight health science students filled in the questionnaire online, and their answers were compared with a related validated scale on attitudes toward sexual health. The Portuguese version held together well, with a strong internal consistency score. Scores also lined up well with the comparison scale. The authors conclude that the instrument is valid and reliable for Portuguese students and for use in institutional settings.
pmc-13623992:
Pedro Lago-González, Carolina Acuña-Alonso, and Xana Álvarez model where an invasive Australian tree, Acacia dealbata, could spread as the climate changes, focusing on overlap with Europe's common oak forests. The acacia was planted abroad for ornament and timber and now invades several regions, helped by toughness after fire and drought. Knowing its future climate niche guides early control.

The team built maximum entropy distribution models, a standard tool that learns a species' climate preferences from known locations, for past, present, and future conditions. The models performed with great accuracy, and temperature variables did most of the explaining. Europe emerged as the main hotspot where the acacia's suitable climate overlaps oak forest. Both species share large suitable areas worldwide, yet their climate niches do not fully coincide, which leaves room for the invader to expand into new temperate ground. The authors offer the maps for targeting surveillance.
pmc-13627192:
Didem Helvacioglu and six colleagues, publishing in 2026, follow girls with early pubic hair to their final height. Premature pubarche, hair appearing ahead of schedule with mild hormone excess, fills endocrine clinics, and a few girls slide into true early puberty. The team reviewed eighty-eight girls who had reached adult height, thirteen of whom made that slide, comparing growth, bone age, and hormone profiles from the first visit.

A girl's height relative to her genetic target at presentation proved the strongest single predictor of her final height in both groups, and heavier body mass pulled the forecast down. Bone age racing ahead of the calendar flagged likelier progression, with a ratio past a set line marking risk. The adrenal hormone DHEA-S, though a badge of early maturation, predicted nothing, which frees doctors from leaning on it.
pmc-13629292:
Grace Marconi and five colleagues interviewed older patients, families, and health staff in Melbourne. The topic was involving patients and families in managing medicines when care moves between settings. Their 2026 study drew on 202 interviews. They spanned four hospital sites in one large public system.

Three themes organised the findings. One covered the talk problems themselves. One covered what shapes whether patients and families can speak up. One covered practical ways to strengthen their role. Managing many medicines through handovers is complex. People described barriers at every step. The authors propose tactics that encourage families to take part. They argue better talk at transitions could cut medicine errors. It could also cut the harm that follows.
pmc-13630092:
Neha Adsul and four colleagues, with the GEMMS research group, describe building a survey tool with three linked aims. It measures gendered violence, mental health, and the shaky living conditions of migrants together. Current tools assume settled populations. They miss the insecure work, legal status, and housing that shape migrants' risks. The gap bites hardest in poorer lands.

The building work was shared and hands-on. Teams from many lands took part. So did experts, local advisers, and community members with lived experience. The final tool holds 216 items. They come from proven scales plus new questions shaped by fieldwork. It was piloted with 198 people across Cambodia, India, and South Africa. Checks on the new item sets found coherent strands.
