They matched the base theory, from structural harm to migration stress.
pmc-13632692:
Sinan Aydin, Michael S. Kapiloff, and Kimberly L. Dodge-Kafka published this 2026 review of a scaffold protein that steers harmful gene activity in heart failure. Heart failure is the end stage of many heart diseases, marked by enlarged muscle cells, scarring, and failing contraction. A protein called AKAP6β sits on the membrane around the heart cell nucleus. There it gathers more than twenty-five signaling enzymes into organized hubs.

Those hubs answer chemical messengers and switch gene programs that drive pathological remodeling of the heart. The scaffold also links to neighboring scaffold proteins, extending its reach toward nearby cell structures. Because the signaling is boxed into one location, blocking it there might calm the harmful programs without silencing the same signals elsewhere in the cell. The review weighs basic mechanisms beside possible treatment angles, presenting these hubs as fresh drug targets for a condition with huge unmet need.
pmc-13633092:
Luciano Gonçalves do Nascimento Júnior and three colleagues studied sexual and urinary problems in men with multiple sclerosis in Brazil. The disease damages nerve insulation in the brain and spinal cord, which often disturbs bladder and sexual function. Such problems are rarely measured in Brazilian patients. The team enrolled fifty-six men at a state reference center in Paraíba. Standard questionnaires scored erection quality and urinary symptoms, and a disability scale graded their neurological state.

Half of the men had erectile dysfunction, and nearly all reported some urinary symptoms. Worse disability tracked closely with worse scores on both questionnaires. Confidence about erections and stop-start urination were the single items tied most strongly to disability. Scores also differed between disease patterns, mainly between the relapsing form and the later progressive form. The authors recommend that neurology clinics screen for both problems together rather than waiting for complaints.
pmc-13633892:
Fen Lin and five colleagues used genetics to probe two enzymes linked to a cancer drug's action in pancreatic cancer. Pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest malignancies, and new drug targets are badly needed. The enzymes, called RAF1 and MAPK8, belong to signaling chains that control cell growth. Rather than run a trial, the team used inherited DNA differences as natural experiments, mimicking lifelong changes in enzyme levels.

Higher genetically predicted activity of either enzyme was tied to lower pancreatic cancer risk. The team then asked whether immune cells in the blood carry part of that effect. One regulatory T cell pattern, involving cells that calm immune responses, carried a modest share for both enzymes. A sweep across many other traits found no broad side signals. The authors present the work as a pointer for lab studies of these pathways, not proof of a treatment.
pmc-13634692:
Keu Maoate and nine co-authors published a urology study in twenty twenty-six on what patients feel during transperineal prostate biopsy done freehand under local anesthesia alone. Men often dread the procedure, so honest numbers on pain matter. A single center's registry covered cases from twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-six.

Of eight hundred consecutive cases, seven hundred seventy-seven used local anesthesia only. Median reported pain was two on a ten-point scale, and under six percent called it severe. Anxiety tracked moderately with pain. The team also recorded satisfaction, complications, cancer detection, and willingness to repeat the biopsy if needed. Their numbers give clinics a realistic script for counseling nervous patients.
pmc-13636092:
Zilin Xu and fourteen colleagues set out the protocol for a randomized trial testing albumin as an add-on treatment for major stroke. Threading a catheter to pull clots from blocked brain arteries is now standard care, yet nearly half of patients stay dependent afterward. Albumin, a blood protein, protected brains in animal studies and might shield tissue as flow returns. This multicenter trial assigns patients with front-circulation blockages to vessel treatment alone or with albumin.

The albumin group receives a dose within an hour of assignment, repeated daily for three more days. The target is about twelve hundred participants, with a built-in halfway review that may raise the total. Recovery judges at ninety days will not know who received what. Success means living independently or returning to one's prior level. The authors expect a clear answer on whether albumin earns a place beside clot removal.
pmc-13639092:
Loïc Labache and three colleagues present a 2026 study of the molecular roots of brain sidedness in humans. Most people favor the left hemisphere for language and the right for spatial attention, yet the chemical and cellular basis of that split was unclear.

Combining live brain scans with post-mortem gene and cell data, the team found sided gradients in neurotransmitter receptors and differences in mitochondria, microglia, and excitatory neurons. Two clusters emerged: a left-leaning language network and a right-leaning spatial network. The results offer a biological basis for lateralized thinking, relevant to evolution and to disorders where sidedness breaks down.
pmc-13639192:
Qin and colleagues presented in 2026 a deep learning system, Hankelformer, for forecasting extreme temperature events such as sudden freezes and heatwaves. Standard time-series models often miss abrupt shifts because extreme events break sharply from past patterns. Their design builds Hankel matrices, structured tables of lagged values, to make extra views of the input data that keep time order intact while exposing local patterns.

Qin processed these views alongside the raw input in a dual-stream transformer model. Contrastive learning then trained the model to treat matching views as alike, hardening its features against shifting conditions. Tests covered three famous events, the Texas freeze, the Pacific Northwest heatwave, and an Antarctic heat event, plus six standard data sets. The system beat leading rivals throughout, cutting forecast error by up to about a third over the best baselines in mean squared error terms.
pmc-13642092:
Shahriar Rahman Niloy and five colleagues present a 2026 deep learning framework, scMGC, for grouping single cells by their gene activity. Single-cell RNA data are sparse and noisy because many genes drop out during measurement, which blurs cell types.

The framework first cleans the data with an autoencoder, then scores marker genes by combining several selection methods before graph-based clustering. Against seven rival methods on seven datasets, it improved clustering accuracy by roughly thirty percent on standard measures. Enrichment checks showed the clusters made biological and clinical sense. Code and data are posted publicly for reuse.
pmc-13642492:
Chaudhary and co-authors report a 2026 broadband absorber made of titanium dioxide nanotube arrays for terahertz radiation, the band between microwaves and infrared. Standard absorbers there are narrowband, bulky, or hard to make at scale. Their tubes were grown by electrochemical anodization and then heat treated to tune the response.

The arrays absorbed about eighty percent of rays across a huge span from ten to three hundred terahertz. A broad absorption peak in the lower range could be slid between about 1.4 and 3.6 terahertz simply by changing annealing time, Chaudhary reports. Tests spanning millimetre waves to ultraviolet sat with full wave simulations to map how the material responds. Even spread and scalable making make the arrays fit for cheap all-round absorbers and compact terahertz devices.
pmc-13647092:
Seda Sacu and five colleagues follow a birth cohort for thirty-three years to find the paths mental symptoms take and what predicts them, in a 2026 study. Symptoms were measured from age eight to thirty-three in 317 people. Modeling sorted both outward behaviors, such as rule-breaking, and inward ones, such as anxiety, into three paths each: low, rising in late adolescence, and high in childhood then falling. A wide battery of genetic and life measures fed machine learning predictors.

Genetic scores for cognition and mental disorders helped predict the paths, as did family adversity and weak social functioning. Prediction accuracy was fair for outward symptoms and modest for inward ones. The authors argue that knowing which path a young person is likely to follow could focus prevention where it counts. Their long view, rare in this field, shows childhood-limited and late-rising patterns need different responses.
pmc-13647392:
Luan F Diniz and eight colleagues redesign the leukemia drug dasatinib into new crystal forms that dissolve far better in water. The drug works against chronic myelogenous leukemia, yet its poor, pH-dependent solubility limits how much the body can absorb. The team grew two novel salt forms by pairing the drug with maleic and fumaric acids. A full battery of X-ray, spectroscopic, and thermal tests confirmed the new structures.

Both forms dissolved dramatically better than the parent drug, with solubility gains reported up to roughly fifteen hundred fold in buffered water and far faster dissolving speeds. The new crystals also killed leukemia cells more strongly and more selectively in lab tests. The authors present crystal salt engineering as a practical route to rescue effective drugs whose weakness is physical rather than pharmacological. Better absorption could eventually mean more reliable dosing for patients.
pmc-13647992:
Ziyuan Zhao and four colleagues review paediatric hearing loss in the era of universal newborn hearing screening. Their review covers causes, risk signs, and clinical patterns, with attention to losses that a single newborn test can miss, including mild, one-sided, delayed, and progressive forms.

Genetic causes, congenital cytomegalovirus infection, nutrition and metabolic conditions during pregnancy, and newborn intensive care risks such as early birth, jaundice, low oxygen, infection, and certain medicines are all discussed. The authors argue that a normal screening result cannot rule out later hearing problems. They urge closer follow-up for children at higher risk and stronger work on cause and outcome links.
pmc-13649992:
Phillip Fei Hou proposes a new way to steady wandering attention that works through the body rather than through effortful self-control. The method, called Dual-Point Sensory Anchoring, rests on four conditions. Both sides of the body move at once, sight and hearing are deliberately quieted, the fingertips serve as the main anchor for touch and position senses, and movement flows without breaks.

Within a theory that treats the brain as a prediction machine, Hou argues this setup would let body-sense circuits settle most prediction errors, leaving little work for tiring top-down control. Attention should then deepen as a session goes on, a testable claim rather than a built-in promise. Eleven directional predictions and six control conditions are spelled out for laboratory testing. No data are reported yet, and the author presents the model as unvalidated theory meant to guide low-burden mind-body practice.
pmc-13650792:
Kylie S Soniak and four colleagues, publishing in 2026, test whether warmer water speeds the growth of captive eastern hellbenders, giant salamanders whose wild numbers have fallen sharply, especially in Indiana. Breeding programs rear the animals for release, and most facilities keep them cold, yet amphibians generally grow faster when warm, so the assumption deserved a check.

At the Indianapolis Zoo, 207 hellbenders were raised at either of two temperatures and measured for weight and length every eight weeks from February 2023 to July 2024. Contrary to prediction, the warmer group grew no faster on either measure. The authors conclude that the temperatures used at most facilities are unlikely to limit growth. They redirect attention toward diet, density, and other husbandry levers for raising release-ready animals more efficiently.
pmc-13651892:
Rina Shibayama and six colleagues describe an unusual adult case of bobble-head doll syndrome, a rare movement disorder most often seen in young children. Their patient was a man in his twenties who developed memory problems, unsteady walking, bladder trouble, and a rhythmic side-to-side head tremor. Brain imaging showed severe obstructive hydrocephalus, a buildup of fluid caused by a thin web blocking the cerebral aqueduct.

Surgeons placed a ventriculoperitoneal shunt to drain the excess fluid, and the tremor disappeared within a week. His thinking and daily function improved, and he remained independent well over a year later. Adult cases of the syndrome are extremely rare, so the report, which includes video of the tremor before and after surgery. Gives clinicians a clear example of a treatable cause that is easy to miss.
pmc-3783192:
Sun, Luo, Bu, and co-authors present a tool for telling protein-coding transcripts apart from long non-coding ones. Classifying transcripts is a challenge, especially for those rebuilt from high-throughput sequencing of poorly annotated species. Mistakes blur catalogues of genes and obscure real biology.

Their signature tool, the Coding-Non-Coding Index, profiles the internal composition patterns adjacent in the sequence to judge coding potential. It needs no prior annotation, which suits newly sequenced species. Reliable classification is an early step in almost every transcriptome study.  Poorly annotated species from oceans and soils benefit most from annotation-free classification methods.
pmc-6323892:
Philipp Rentzsch, Daniela Witten, Gregory Cooper, and coauthors updated the CADD variant score in 2018. CADD rates how harmful a DNA change is likely to be. Geneticists use it to sort causal variants from harmless noise.

The score blends many annotations, from conservation to predicted protein effect, into one ranking. New versions extend coverage to nearly all possible single-letter changes in the human genome. CADD shines most for rare changes behind severe inherited disorders. Clinics and researchers use the ranking daily when a genome yields more candidate variants than anyone can test by hand.
pmc-6323992:
The UniProt Consortium described its protein knowledgebase in this 2018 paper. UniProt collects protein sequences and notes for life across all branches. Its archive holds well over a hundred million sequences.

Expert curators have reviewed a core set of about half a million proteins in depth. Those entries carry function notes, variants, and literature links checked by hand. Automated rules annotate the far larger remainder. Nearly every protein study touches UniProt at some point, which makes its accuracy a shared concern for the whole field. A sister archive stores the raw sequences behind the curated knowledgebase entries.
pmc-8816392:
Irene Korstjens and Albine Moser wrote in 2017 the fourth part of a practical series on qualitative research, this one covering trustworthiness and publishing. The authors drew on years of supervising students, during which the same worries about qualitative work came up again and again. The series answers those frequently asked questions for researchers just starting out.

This installment explains how to show that qualitative findings are credible, dependable, and honestly grounded in the data, rather than anecdotal. It then advises on writing up such work for journals, where reviewers may judge it by quantitative habits. For novice researchers in health and social care, the piece offers concrete reassurance and checkable standards.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-102:
Wrestling with Whistlers, a memory of a recent exhibition, fills the pages of Punch for April 16, 1892. At the Goupil Gallery, groups of puzzled Britons try to do justice to a collection of Whistler's work.

Visitors know the painter must now be taken seriously, yet cannot get past timid tolerance. Frank Philistines, matrons of domestic taste, and serious elderly ladies join them, and one lady studies a view of old Battersea Bridge in the tone of a person making a concession. Readers get the public meeting modern art and losing politely.

'Tis Merry in Hall reports a night at the London Pavilion music hall in Punch for April 2, 1892. The acting manager, Mr. Edward Swanborough, ever-green in dazzling shirt-front, ushers the writers into the stalls.

They arrive too late for Lottie Collins, the great original of the serio-comic stage, but hear several of her male and female imitators, so she is not left booming alone. The evening is praised as an excellent all-round show. Readers get the halls at their height, when one singer's song echoed from every stage in town.

Town Thoughts from the Country, a poem with the usual apologies, appears in Punch for April 23, 1892. The verses long for London now that April is there, when the upper thousands come to town and plane trees wear their new bark.

Sparrows chirp, cats miaow, and after April comes May, when the black coats come and go like swallows. A fairy blossom in the Row leans to the rails and makes her admirer ask twice over. Readers get a Browning-flavoured spring song turned toward the season, carriages, and flirtation in the park.

Mr. Punch's Hebridean Salmon-Fly Book opens the pages for April 30, 1892, with the strange adventures of a pen-holder by the invented Wullie White. His letter sends the latest novel in which he mixes delicate sentiment with Highland scenery.

White brings a Londoner's wisdom to bear on a kilt-wearing population, republishes his books in a series, and offers to back his salmon flies and sunsets against anyone else's. Parody titles crowd his earlier list. Readers get the Scottish romance trade, all mist and sentiment, mocked in its maker's own sales talk.

Boat-Race Day fills Punch dated April 9, 1892. Readers are asked to imagine crossing Hammersmith Bridge in a jostling stream of sightseers toward Mortlake, where the banks already hold a triple row of the patient and prudent.

On the path, shady characters run pitches for the unsophisticated, one presiding over a coloured roulette board and crying three to one any colour you like. Two shop boys pop their coppers on, win once, and lose the next turn to green. Readers get the Oxford and Cambridge race as a fairground of crowds, touts, and small bets.

Pleasing the Pigs, from a private and confidential report, leads Punch for February 13, 1892. Mr. Chaplin, the minister for agriculture, receives a deputation on swine fever wearing, true to his dramatic instincts, a sou'wester.

He regrets he cannot don a pigtail, a fashion of the last century. He hopes to revive it as a tail of old times. He declares he is doing his very best to please the pigs, though some pigs will not be pleased. Readers get farm policy and wordplay mixed until neither the deputation nor the reader can separate them.

Jim's Jottings, number two, appears in Punch for February 20, 1892, in the voice of Ginger Jimmy. His subject is rats'-rents: the renters and the rented of London's slums.

Jimmy answers a St. Pancras health committee man's book on Slumland, its landlords, and its rent, calling the slum the Golgotha of Slumland. Those who know the facts, he sings, will not always tell them, while slums pay topping rent. Readers get housing scandal in coster verse, with dirt, freeholders, and freedom of contract all named as the villains of the piece.

Confessions of a Duffer reaches its fifth part in Punch for February 27, 1892: the Duffer at Cricket. In the pavilion his talk might pass for that of a great old player intimate with Mynn, Pilch, and other giants of the game.

He lays down the law on boundary hits, long stops, and balls left unpunished to the off, yet his county cricket was played for Berwickshire. Still, he claims the duffer is the true enthusiast. Readers get the eternal club bore anatomised with love, a portrait every cricket ground in England could match.

A Receipt Against Influenza is offered gratis in Punch for February 6, 1892, signed by one George Guzzleton. The prescription, written in mock Latin for the dinner table only, orders oysters, fish, hot potatoes, roast mutton, duck, and plums by weight and measure.

Cider or champagne of the 1884 vintage completes the draught, to be taken hourly except at dinner, regularly. A headpiece shows a horse dealer praising a mare who could stay forever, to a buyer who found her inclined to do so. Readers get flu season treated with feasting, the oldest remedy in the paper's book.

Punch for January 2, 1892, opens with verses in memory of the Duke of Devonshire, born in 1808 and dead on December 21, 1891. The poem calls him learned, large-hearted, and liberal, a duke whom the staunchest democrat might praise.

After the elegy comes After Dinner: eminent politicians in a private room of a dining hotel discuss shop over their walnuts before the Christmas holidays. One speech at Skegness, preferring the navy to the army, is called a little strong. Readers get a statesman's tribute and then the gossip such men traded when the cloth was drawn.

Cabital, a letter on cab fares, appears in Punch for January 16, 1892. The writer approves extending the cab radius to five miles from Charing Cross, then finds the plan far too timid and proposes the whole Home Counties instead.

Cabmen, he argues, should be barred by law from refusing fares to St. Albans on the plea that the horse cannot do the distance, and such claims should be punished as perjury. Proprietors should keep relays of horses on every main road. A French cartoon in the style of the French painted by themselves heads the page. Readers get London's cab wars in full cry.

The Covent Garden Masque is sung in quick rhymes in Punch for January 23, 1892. Mumming, masking, fanning, dancing, and gallivanting fill the lines in a breathless list of the fancy ball's pleasures.

Couples much in need of slimming don the childish raiment meant for sylphs and fairies, hired from Clarkson's stock. Tally-hos, barber's blockheads, and aunty's bottle all whirl past, heralding splitting mirth and aching heads next morning. Short jokes follow, one ruling out an intemperate tone by a temperance lecturer. Readers get the masquerade season compressed into one rattling dance of words.

Confessions of a Duffer, part three, takes up the Literary Duffer in Punch for January 30, 1892. A headpiece shows him wearing a cloak and Tyrolese hat while striking poses in picture galleries.

He cannot say why publishers and editors refuse him, though he has done all he can. His novel goes the round of the trade, its pages written by himself, his housemaid, and his wife, with sentences rewritten a dozen times in red ink on paper of all sorts. Readers get the hopeful author as his own worst exhibit, funny and a little sad at once.

On a New Yearling, second week, appears in Punch for January 9, 1892. The singer sits by a low fire with high bills, a glass of punch in its ladle, and the nascent year in its cradle.

He checks his haste to toast the newcomer, since a week of life at least must pass before one infant year can be matched with its brothers. Little 1892, latest of a prolific family, frolics in his tiny cot. Readers get the new year treated as a baby to be nursed, petted, and not judged too soon.

Operatic Notes covers Wagner in Punch for July 2, 1892. The Daughters of the River cry their warning in vain while the orchestra under Herr Mahler goes on inexorably, and the party swims to Walhall.

Wotan and Loge search for the gold among Nibelungs and Nibelights; Alberich changes himself into a toad and is towed off prisoner, while Fafner settles Fasolt and takes the golden honey. The writer owns he knows no more, finding some music river-like and lovely and much of it puzzling. Readers get the Ring through a tired, honest, ordinary ear.

A Day at Antwerp, by the Vacuus Viator, appears in Punch dated June 11, 1892. In the Place Verte the traveller refuses to be bullied by Baedeker into visiting the cathedral first and directs his steps somewhere else.

The carillon tinkles like an elderly ghost with failing memory, trying every tune she ever knew at once on a cracked spinnet, fragments of hymns tripping over each other before giving up. The church of St. Paulus comes next. Readers get the empty-headed traveller abroad again, collecting sounds and small rebellions against the guidebook.

The Courier of The Hague continues the travels of the Vacuus Viator in Punch dated June 18, 1892. Bosch, an elderly amiable Dutchman in a soft felt hat, has been engaged as guide, though the traveller cannot quite say why.

Helplessness in Holland and a craving for company are the admitted reasons. With Bosch engaged, he feels more helpless than ever. He is a mix of Sandford and Merton with a didactic Dutch Barlow whose useful information is often hard to follow. Readers get the guided tour as a partnership of two confusions, politely maintained.

Versailles in Leicester Square reviews the new ballet at the Empire in Punch dated June 25, 1892, seen through Mr. Punch's pince-nez. Gardeners prepare for Louis the Fourteenth by tickling the gravel gently with brooms and depositing one petal apiece in large baskets.

Having done a fair afternoon's work, they dance a farandole in sabots before ladies and cavaliers arrive; the cavaliers choose partners by chasing them on tiptoe while the ladies run backwards. Readers get ballet plot and stage labour weighed with the same deadpan care.  The programme calls it argument enough.

Lost Luggage, the experiences of a Vacuus Viator, opens at the customs house at Ostend in Punch for June 4, 1892. Passengers hover with bunches of keys while the writer alone stays calm, having seen his portmanteau and bag labelled at Victoria.

His bags do not appear. Brussels travellers are served first, he reasons, and he plans a pleasant night on the Digue with dinner and the Kursaal while his luggage turns up in due time. Readers get the traveller's calm tested by the oldest joke in continental travel, told in diary scraps.

Doing the Old Masters, a sketch at Burlington House, fills Punch for March 12, 1892. In Gallery number one, the usual elderly lady judges every picture by its subject and dislikes Gainsborough's portrait of Mrs. Bryanston for its disagreeable expression.

Her companion prefers the modern Academy and wonders about tea. An intelligent person suspects Portman is a made-up name, and his friend trusts the authorities would never do such a thing here. Readers get an exhibition crowd in dialogue, a small comedy of taste, snobbery, and refreshment.  The pictures bear it well.

Are You Hansard Now? asks Punch for March 19, 1892. A daily paper had reported that the whole stock of Hansard's Parliamentary Debates, nearly one hundred thousand volumes, fetched scarcely the price of waste paper at auction.

The verses stage the sale: the auctioneer praises speeches by Russell, Palmerston, and Bright, good for heart and head, taken as spoken or as read. Bidders are lacking, back numbers shoal in without backing, and heaven's rhetoric finds no quotation. Readers get parliamentary glory weighed by the hundredweight and found light.  So much for fame in print.

Ye Moderates of London, a song to stay-at-home voters, appears in Punch for March 26, 1892. Moderate voters sat at home at ease, little thinking of the dangerous county council, while comfort surrounded them and stormy winds blew outside.

Bold Progressives will now tax them, the song warns, and free arrangements from tramcars to water and gas will not bring the rates down. Censors of the play and inspectors of ballets are promised under the new rule. Readers get a polling-day scolding in ballad form, aimed at every voter who let weather choose his council.

Popular Songs Re-sung takes up Lottie Collins's music-hall hit in Punch dated March 5, 1892. The essay marvels at the might of the meaningless in a rattling refrain, then asks whether attaching a meaning to the famous boom song will mar its use.

Number six of the series follows, That's How We Boom To-day. The lyric praises the smart self-pusher of the moment: never too strict, free of swagger, ever pushing and ever bold, lest he be left out in the cold. Readers get the song of the season given words worthy of its tune.

Confessions of a Duffer, number nine, sends its hero deer-stalking in Punch dated May 14, 1892. He favours Mr. Bryce's Access to Mountains Bill and any crofters who will farm the Bens, since anything that interferes with deer-stalking wins his support.

People want access to mountains only when they cannot get it, he argues; once free, they will stay where the beer is rather than pad through peat bogs and heather. His own memories of the sport are the most somber he cherishes. Readers get the reluctant sportsman again, this time at war with Scottish scenery.

More Than Satisfied fills the pages of Punch dated May 21, 1892, with apologies to a daily paper's academic enthusiast. The scene is a women's college library at Girnham, where students work with Xenophon's Anabasis and a Greek lexicon.

Asked a delicate question about she-pantaloons and seediness, a tall, robust maiden answers for her fellows: do we look like it? Roseate specimens of English womanhood surround the diffident visitor. Readers get the new woman of the universities drawn brisk, learned, and entirely unembarrassed by her questioner.  Greek verbs fear her too.

Venice Reserved, a sketch from a numbered stall at Olympia, appears in Punch for May 28, 1892. On stage, artisans make horse-shoes on cold anvils before the Arsenal while Antonio expresses commercial embarrassment through dumb-bell exercise on a bridge.

Bassanio, Lorenzo, and a second Antonio point out objects of local interest with the amiability of figures in hotel advertisements. A small boy in a box, expecting a pantomime, asks aloud when the clown part will begin. Readers get The Merchant of Venice as spectacle, with the audience supplying the comedy.

'Arry on Wheels opens Punch dated May 7, 1892, with a letter to Charlie in verse. Spring has come at last after a cold snap at Easter that spoiled the holiday makers, and 'Arry blames the clerk of the weather for working out of sheer spite.

While noses stay to the grindstone the sun shines; when Easter or Whitsun outings are in train, it is forty to one on a blizzard or a regular buster of rain. A headpiece crowns him our 'Arry laureate. Readers get the cockney holiday complaint in its full musical measure.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-103:
Lady Gay's Selections, a letter from the yacht Ibex at Weymouth, appears in Punch dated August 13, 1892. The writer is glad to have her foot on her native heath again after an alarming passage from Jersey.

She jokes that the author of that saying must have lost a leg, or had one leg shorter than the other, since he placed only one foot there. Every moment of the crossing seemed her last, for a time. Readers get racing-season society talk from the water, where gossip travels faster than the yacht.

Ad Puellam, verses to a girl with a camera, appears in Punch for August 20, 1892. A ladies' paper has reported that detective cameras have become favourite playthings with ladies of fashion, and the poem takes alarm.

She once bored her friends with talk of plates, prints, and developers; now she hides lenses in muff, cloak, parcel, and biscuit tin, and photographs them on the sly. A smile for Croesus or a helping hand over a stile goes straight onto film. Readers get an early warning about candid photography, rhymed while the craze was new.

Two-Penn'orth of Theosophy, a sketch at the Islington Arcadia, appears in Punch for August 27, 1892. Inside the Agricultural Hall a steam circus revolves, a mechanical piano pounds, and couples charge each other in a desultory dance.

A variety stage performs at one end, a switchback thunders along the gallery, and near the entrance a painted house front takes a battering from wooden balls thrown at springs. Fairground noise supplies the setting for the title's cheap wisdom. Readers get a Bank Holiday crowd in full roar, drawn sound by sound and shout by shout.

Druriolanus in Music Aulis leads Punch for August 6, 1892, on the changing of Carte's English Opera House into the new Palace Theatre of Varieties. Two Augustuses direct the venture, Sir Augustus leading and Georgius Augustus following.

The writer calls the change an enterprise rather than an undertaking and warns that no shift in ministry or policy is likelier to trouble the Empire, meaning the Empire in Leicester Square. A cartoon shows the singing-bird showman bowing his acknowledgments after the opera. Readers get theatre business reported as affairs of state, with two emperors of the stage in attendance.

The Man Who Would reaches its third part in Punch for December 3, 1892: the Man Who Would Get On. A Scotch professor dreams he is strangling a monstrous reptile that begs, at the end, for a testimonial.

That professional nightmare, born of writing testimonials or dodging requests for them, leads to the history of Saunders McGregor. In boyhood Saunders won a bursary to the University of St. Mungo's, a success implying no high degree of scholarship. Readers get ambition anatomised through one climber's career, with Scottish education as the ladder and the joke.

To the First Bathing-Machine, an ode after Wordsworth, appears in Punch for July 16, 1892. The blank new-comer rolls from some dim hibernating spot when the sun first feels warm, gentle looking yet infernal in the singer's judgement.

He grasps its narrow bench, pale with fear, while it bounds and wrenches to an unexpected stop that lands him on its sandy floor. Dressed in nature's simplest style, he ventures out blushing to find the sea still a mile away. Children on the sand laugh. Readers get seaside ritual mocked in high Romantic dress.

To a Summer Flower appears in Punch for July 23, 1892, beneath a cartoon called Too Clever by Half. In the cartoon, a Swiss governess explains that she learned her fine English from Lady Jenkinson's children, whom she came to teach French and German; they learned not a word.

The poem addresses a golden flower sent from afar, fair and frail, doomed like all earthly things to fade, yet promised a nobler fate than lily or rose when its petals close. Readers get a language joke on top and a sincere flower lyric underneath, an odd and pleasing pair.

Iago in Birmingham puts Shakespeare to work on current politics in Punch for July 30, 1892. The cast names Iago as a dashed-out Chamberlain figure and Roderigo as his dashed-out colleague Collins.

Roderigo opens with the old charge: thou told'st me thou did'st hold him in thy hate. Iago answers that the great ones of the city capped to him in vain, that he knows his price, and that a great arithmetician took the officer's place he wanted. Readers get Othello's grievance speech fitted to a city quarrel, with every local cut left visible.

Simple as A B C, a letter to an ex-chancellor with a past, opens Punch dated July 9, 1892. The writer apologises for addressing him at all, owing him promotion, yet says the fatherland suffers from his indiscretions and matters near a crisis.

He poses a case: what would you do if your predecessor held you up to ridicule, spoiled your favourite diplomatic plans, and insulted your employers? The initials point abroad without naming names. Readers get high politics conducted as a personal letter, in the plainest alphabet the paper could choose.

The Game of the Little Horses, a sketch at the casino at Dinard, appears in Punch for November 12, 1892. Around a circular course of revolving metal horses, players crowd green tables ruled in numbered squares while croupiers rake their takings.

In a dark corner of the balcony, Miss Daintree hides from a horrid little man she gave a dance to. She accepted him only because her brother Jack brought him up as a dear friend met at table d'hôte. An orchestra tunes for the ball. Readers get gambling and flirtation watched from the shadows.

The Man Who Would returns in Punch for November 19, 1892, with its second part: the Man Who Would Play Golf. Bulger was no sportsman at all until his doctor ordered exercise and fresh air and sent him to St. Andrews under Tom Morris.

Bulger asks whether Morris is a great Scotch physician and learns he is head of the faculty in those parts. The journey stalls at Leuchars, where venerable towers mock the timetable and whiskey statistics fill the wait. Readers get the beginner's pilgrimage to golf told by a man who wanted health and found a religion.

Letters to Abstractions reaches number seventeen in Punch for November 26, 1892, with a letter to Failure. A philosopher reader has objected that several addressees, such as Laziness, Crookedness, and Irritation, are concrete qualities, not abstractions at all.

The writer answers with all possible respect: stuff and nonsense. His letters, he notes, have all reached their addressees. None has returned by way of the dead-letter office, and that settles the point. Readers get the long-running series defending its own joke with perfect gravity, one letter before the volume closes. The joke proves itself neatly.

Conversational Hints for Young Shooters continues in Punch for November 5, 1892, at lunch. The adviser urges his young friend to study the natures and temperaments of his companions and to store up facts about their sporting careers for tactful use.

One guest may be a celebrated shot with a record at driven grouse. After the right preliminaries, the young shooter should ask him for the precise number of birds shot that day. A discussion of the three finest game shots of the world can be mentioned as the excuse. Readers get the shooting lunch as a field for strategy equal to the field itself.

Stumped, a would-be laudatory ode by Jingle Junior, appears in Punch dated October 1, 1892. Its subject is the young Indian cricketer Ranjitsinhji, who had secured his century no less than eleven times that season.

The ode keeps breaking down on his name: one spelling is called a wild venture, the next bows the poet out again. How many miles he ran in making those hundreds defeats the verse entirely. Readers get fame and orthography in collision, a tribute that pays its hero by failing to pronounce him.  The crowd understood him perfectly.

'Arry at 'Arrygate sends a second letter to Charlie in Punch for October 15, 1892. He is still at the Crown hotel, though his last letter said he was just off to town, because an uncle's letter brought another small cheque.

Another fortnight of sulphur and slosh follows, with excursions to Knaresborough, Bolton, and Fountains. Antiquities are not his hobby and ruins do not fetch him; a castle is just chunks of stone, an abbey much out of repair. Readers get the spa holiday through cockney eyes, unimpressed, observant, and for the moment well funded.

In Memoriam verses for William Hardwick Bradbury appear in Punch dated October 22, 1892. Bradbury, born in December 1832, died on October 13, and the paper mourns a large-hearted man and loyal friend gone too early.

Hearts stored with grateful memories ache for him round the old board he loved so well, the board that was his pride, his care, and his ceaseless thought. The poem praises his power to inspire, console, and defend. Readers get the paper's family grief in print, a reminder that the comic weekly was also a working household.

Covent Garden's Il Trovatore is reviewed in Punch dated October 29, 1892, by a self-confessed Philistine of the matter-of-fact kind. The reviewer watches Leonora's confidante, alive to her duties, walk her mistress down to the footlights and launch her into her solo like a boat.

The confidante then stands aside with an air of apprehension, a hand in readiness lest the singer come to grief over the next high note. Opera plot matters less than stage management. Readers get grand opera reduced to the practical worries of the people who keep it upright.

At a Hypnotic Séance fills the pages of a number whose own heading dates it October 10, 1892. In a provincial hall, a tall and handsome hypnotist has already put most of his subjects to sleep and inspects them as they droop on a semicircle of chairs.

One lady alone keeps her senses. Her friend Maria Mangles's slowness becomes the talk of the audience, and one neighbour calls it affectation, since she could shut her eyes fast enough if she liked. Readers get stage hypnotism judged by the neighbours it could not quite convince, in overheard whispers.

Why I Don't Write Plays, from the commonplace book of a novelist, appears in Punch for September 10, 1892. Reason follows reason in short paragraphs, each beginning the same way and turning a little stranger.

Reading one's work is pleasanter than hearing it staged; publishers are kinder than actor-managers; behind the scenes disappoints. A successful play yields thousands where a novel yields five hundred, so why be influenced by mercenary motives? The last reason of all is left hanging. Readers get the literary life explained by a man arguing himself out of fortune.

Hearing Himself, a mysterious memorandum from a Hawarden notebook, appears in Punch dated September 17, 1892. Max Müller is quoted hoping few present have never enjoyed the privilege of listening to Mr. Gladstone.

The notebook's owner laughs: one man present had never enjoyed that privilege, never having heard himself as others hear him. The unavoidable absence of Mr. Gladstone is announced, and the writer congratulates his own disguise, got up as a Liberal Unionist. Readers get the great orator imagined at his own lecture, incognito, enjoying the one speech he could never attend.

'Arry at 'Arrygate writes to Charlie again in Punch for September 24, 1892. Life's turn-ups are twisters, he warns: you lay out for larks, health, and money, and the unexpected romps in.

Who would have pictured 'Arry taking the waters? Screwmatics and liver, the doctor declared, knocked him heels upward off his perch and left him yellow and scared. The tombstone jokes turn serious for a stanza before the humour recovers. Readers get the spa cure from the patient's side, dialect, dread, and small cheques home included.  The waters taste no better for it.

Not Going Away for the Holidays collects short answers in Punch for September 3, 1892, each signed by a type. Cookson Gaze, Q.C., stays because his wife votes Eastbourne vulgar and his finishing-schooled girls laugh at his French abroad.

C. Jumper's governor allows three days a year. An East End doctor gives his fiver so little Sally can have the breath of sea air she needs for a cure. A rake stays because his wife will accompany him; a barmaid, ill from overwork, cannot get more leave. Readers get the holiday season from those left behind.
royce-spirit-modern-philosophy-1892:
The Spirit of Modern Philosophy, published in 1892, prints Royce's Lowell Lectures on the makers of modern thought. He reads the line from Spinoza to Schopenhauer as one long unfolding: the modern mind seeking itself in nature and history.

Lectures take up Spinoza, Kant, Fichte, Schelling, Hegel, and Schopenhauer, each treated as a voice in a single drama. Royce writes for educated listeners, not specialists, with warmth and narrative sweep. His sympathy runs toward the idealists, and the course builds toward his own absolute idealism. The book taught a generation of Americans their philosophy as a living story.
rufinus-of-aquileia-a-commentary-on-the-:
A bishop asked Rufinus of Aquileia to explain the Apostles' Creed, and the result became a classic handbook. His Commentary on the Apostles' Creed goes through the confession line by line. The work appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Clear, practical, and pastoral, the commentary reads like the ancient version of a good confirmation class. Rufinus explains each phrase and tells the stories behind some of them. The book also preserves early evidence for the Creed's exact wording. Readers learn both what the early Church confessed and how it taught new members to understand it.
rufinus-of-aquileia-the-apology-of-rufin:
Friendship curdled into war when Jerome accused Rufinus of Aquileia of corrupting Origen's works in translation. Rufinus answered with The Apology of Rufinus, a self-defense in two books. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Rufinus insists his translations stayed faithful and turns the charge of error back on Jerome. Beneath the quarrel sits a real question: how far may a translator reshape a bold thinker? The apology reveals how scholarly friendships broke under theological pressure. Readers get ancient academia's nastiest feud in the words of one of its combatants. Rufinus also lists his own long record of work for the Church in the West.
scientific-american-supplement-no-841-fe: Investigation of a mound near Jefferson City, Missouri, by A. S. Logan, leads the anthropology contents of Supplement No. 841, dated New York, February 13, 1892, in Volume XXXIII. That piece covers prehistoric remains from the banks of the Missouri River. Biology gives M. de Lacaze Duthiers on new observations on the language of animals, a lengthy examination of facts in the language of animals, including birds and quadrupeds. Botany lists Clarence D.
socrates-scholasticus-the-ecclesiastical:
Socrates of Constantinople picked up the story where Eusebius left it and carried church history from 305 to 439. His Ecclesiastical History appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The Arian controversy dominates its early books.

Emperors rise and fall across his pages, and the strange, stormy career of Chrysostom fills much of the later narrative. Socrates writes with unusual fairness, checking his sources and admitting doubt where records clash. Vivid anecdotes keep the long doctrinal wars readable. For the Church's turbulent fourth century, his history remains the best single narrative we have. Modern readers still start the period with his calm, well-sourced account of it.
sozomen-the-ecclesiastical-history-of-so:
Sozomen covered much the same ground as Socrates, telling the Church's story from 324 to 425. The Ecclesiastical History of Sozomen appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. A lawyer's training shows in his care for detail and sources.

Monks and miracles draw his special interest, and desert hermits share pages with imperial court intrigue. Many stories in his history survive nowhere else, which makes him precious to scholars. He writes with warmth about holy men of the East. Read beside Socrates, Sozomen completes the picture of Christianity's first imperial century. His calm, orderly style makes even crowded decades of events easy to follow.
spr-proceedings-vol7-1891-1892:
Between 1891 and 1892 the SPR issued parts eighteen to twenty, bound as volume seven. Thought transference trials open the run, reported with unusual statistical care. The census of hallucinations, years in the making, shapes much of the discussion. Thousands of ordinary people answered whether they had seen or heard the absent.

Piper sittings in trance supply the volume's most argued pages. Sitters record names and facts they believe no stranger could know. Critics inside the society test those claims hard. Apparition reports continue to arrive with legal style evidence. The volume belongs to the central archive of the evidential debate. It shows Victorian science at its most curious.
spr-proceedings-vol8-1892:
Papers of a new science fill Vol. 8 of the Proceedings of the Society for Psychical Research, out in 1892. The Society was a band of sages, poets, and lords who sought proof on ghosts with the tools of the lab. This tome holds case tales, talks, and one report that dwarfs the rest by its fame and weight.

Richard Hodgson tests Mrs. Piper, a trance voice from Boston, through years of sittings. His long report is the most cited paper the field has made. The tome is the field's flag ship in print.
sulpitius-severus-dialogues-of-sulpitius:
Travelers sit down together in the Dialogues of Sulpitius Severus and compare Saint Martin with the famed monks of Egypt. Across three conversations, Martin wins. The dialogues appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

A visitor fresh from the Eastern deserts tells of Antony and Paul, and the company answers with Martin's deeds at home in Gaul. Travelogue, saint's life, and friendly debate blend in the exchanges. The question underneath is serious: what does holiness look like in the rougher West? These lively talks carried Martin's fame far beyond France. They also preserve charming pictures of monastic travel and talk in the ancient world.
sulpitius-severus-on-the-life-of-st-mart:
Martin of Tours began as a Roman soldier who cut his cloak in half for a freezing beggar. Sulpitius Severus told his story in On the Life of Saint Martin, and the book conquered medieval Europe. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Monk, bishop, wonder-worker, and confronter of emperors, Martin fills the narrative with incident. Raising the dead and felling sacred trees stand beside quiet acts of mercy. The Life became the medieval bestseller that taught Europe what a saint looked like. Monasteries copied it; preachers mined it; kings admired its hero. Almost every later saint's life borrows something from its pattern.
sulpitius-severus-the-doubtful-letters-o:
Not every letter traveling under a famous name truly belongs to him, and editors here say so plainly. The Doubtful Letters of Sulpitius Severus gather pieces attributed to him on uncertain evidence. They appear, honestly labeled, in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Scholars still debate who wrote them, and the arguments teach how attribution works. Genuine or not, the letters open small windows on the circle around Saint Martin. Concerns of early fifth-century Gaul surface in their lines about conduct and devotion. Specialists use the set as an appendix to the certain works. General readers can enjoy the rare honesty of a title that admits doubt.
sulpitius-severus-the-letters-of-sulpiti:
Three letters by Sulpitius Severus survive beside his famous Life of Saint Martin, and one of them reports the saint's death. The Letters of Sulpitius Severus appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Brief as the set is, its feeling runs deep.

Sulpitius writes of Martin's last days with grief and admiration mixed together. The sense of an age passing hangs over his farewell to the man he chronicled. Other letters defend the Life against early skeptics who doubted its wonders. Together they add personal depth to the biography's public portrait. Readers who loved the Life will find these few pages precious rather than slight.
sulpitius-severus-the-sacred-history-of-:
From creation to the year 400, Sulpitius Severus compressed all of history into two elegant books. The Sacred History of Sulpitius Severus tells the biblical story and the Church's first centuries in classical Latin. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Brevity is the book's great virtue: a historian's concision carries the reader across millennia without clutter. Sulpitius writes like a Roman historian who happens to be a Christian, and the blend charms. Medieval schools adopted the chronicle as a standard text for a thousand years. Students learned their Bible history from his tidy pages for generations. It remains a model of how much a short history can hold.
the-clever-woman-of-the-family-pg3292: Charlotte Yonge's Clever Woman of the Family: the Victorian moralist's novel. A strong-minded heroine reformed. Wholesome and wise. A girls' classic, yonge's strong-minded heroine, wholesome Victorian wisdom, a girls' classic, Charlotte Yonge, Victorian wisdom.
the-german-classics-of-the-nineteenth-an: Volume three of The German Classics is given to Friedrich von Schiller. The set is a patrons' set printed at New York in 1914. Only the front matter and contents are present here. A life of Schiller by Calvin Thomas comes first. The poems run from The Veiled Image at Sais to The Lay of the Bell. The Cranes of Ibycus stands among them. The drama is The Death of Wallenstein. It stands in Coleridge's English version. No full work can be read in what is present.
the-man-of-the-world-1792: Charles Macklin's play The Man of the World (1792) appears here in an Augustan Reprint Society edition, publication number 26. It was issued in Los Angeles by the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library in 1951. Only the reprint's front matter is present here, so neither the editor's introduction nor the play appears. That front matter names an introduction by Dougald MacMillan of the University of North Carolina and lists the society's editors at the Clark Library and the universities of Michigan and California. Nothing of Macklin's text can be read here.
the-pilgrim-and-the-american-of-today-18:
Charles Dudley Warner's essay The Pilgrim, and the American of Today, dated 1892, begins on a December evening. Warner's imagination turns by contrast to a December night some two hundred and seventy years earlier. A small group of Pilgrims came ashore then on a sandy, unwelcoming coast. Behind them lay three thousand miles of winter sea. Beyond it lay the whole old civilization they had left for good.

Before them stood an unknown continent of forest, with no highways and only native trails. Warner notes that other Europeans were already planted at the Hudson, on the James, and in Florida and New Mexico. Yet the land remained practically undiscovered. The Pilgrims, he argues, had no clear grasp of the nation to come. They sought a home where no higher human authority would disturb them. They built a theocracy, even while their first acts showed an instinct for self-government.
theodoret-letters-of-theodoret-npnf2-189:
More than two hundred letters from Theodoret of Cyrus survive, and they cover nearly everything in his world. Appeals to emperors sit beside comfort for the suffering and sharp arguments with rivals. The Letters of Theodoret appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Gossip and news from the front lines of the Christological wars run through the correspondence. Theodoret pleads, jokes, scolds, and consoles, sometimes within a single letter. Few sources bring the 400s alive like a working bishop's mailbox. Personal, political, and theological at once, the letters reward readers who enjoy history at ground level.
theodoret-the-dialogues-of-theodoret-era:
Eranistes, meaning the beggar, stages a debate about the nature of Christ between two speakers: Orthodox and the beggar himself. Theodoret of Cyrus wrote the three dialogues on the eve of the Council of Chalcedon. They appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition as the Dialogues of Theodoret.

Orthodox answers his opponent from scripture and the earlier fathers, point by point. Theodoret defends Christ's two natures against every attempt to blur them into one. The form keeps hard doctrine lively, almost like a courtroom drama. Debates at Chalcedon soon echoed these arguments, and the dialogues helped define what the council affirmed.
theodoret-the-ecclesiastical-history-of-:
Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, wrote his church history partly to correct what he saw as errors in others. The Ecclesiastical History of Theodoret runs from 324 to 428 and appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Syria, his home ground, gets loving attention throughout.

Monks and martyrs of the Syrian East fill his pages with color. Theodoret writes as a partisan in the doctrinal wars, and his passion never hides for long. Storytelling gifts carry even tangled disputes about the nature of Christ. For the Eastern view of the age of councils, his history is essential reading.
theon-smyrna-dupuis-1892:
Theon of Smyrna wrote a handbook for readers who found Plato's numbers hard. Mathematics Useful for Understanding Plato, in the Greek and French edition of Jules Dupuis from 1892, is that handbook. Theon taught in the second century, when Plato's school still shaped learned life.

He explains the sums, scales, and star lore a student must hold to read the dialogues well. Number, music, and the heavens each get plain, worked lessons. The book bridges Greek thought and Greek number craft in one small space. Dupuis's edition gives the Greek text with a French guide beside it.
tob-0092:
Reginald Scot published The Discoverie of Witchcraft in 1584, the first book in English to call witchcraft prosecution a fraud. Scot was a Kentish gentleman, not a cleric or lawyer by trade. He exposed jugglers' tricks in print, showing how feats credited to magic were done by hand, and mocked the demonology behind the trials.

The accused, he argued, were deluded, poor, or coerced, not diabolical, and confessions were extracted by terror. King James hated the book; tradition says he ordered copies burned when he reached England's throne. Scot's work stands as skepticism's founding text in English, published three centuries before it became respectable.
tob-0192:
India's Tantras form a vast family of scriptures covering ritual, mantra, and the worship of the divine feminine. Hindu and Buddhist schools both produced them over many centuries. Rather than one book, the name covers a library of practical, esoteric teaching.

Tantric texts map the subtle body, its channels and centers, the map that later yoga inherited. They give rites for temple and home, spells, diagrams, and meditations in concrete detail. Much of India's living worship still follows their patterns. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. The entry marks the tradition's scale and its place behind popular yoga.
tob-10792:
Manly P. Hall wrote The Initiates of the Flame early in his career as an esoteric teacher, as a short booklet on the flame as a symbol. Fire, for Hall, figures the divine spark hidden in matter and in human beings. Myth and allegory supply his evidence.

Through ancient stories and temple imagery, he traces the initiates: those who learned to kindle and guard that inner flame. The manner is oracular rather than argued, very much of the 1920s occult revival in America. Readers get a compact specimen of Hall's style before his larger encyclopedic works, and a taste of how occult writers read world mythology as one symbolic language.
tob-4092:
Another doorway into the Elder Edda presents the Norse lays of gods and heroes in the translation tradition of Benjamin Thorpe, Rasmus Anderson, and Joseph Andrew Blackwell. Odin's hard-won wisdom, Thor's journeys for his stolen hammer, and Sigurd's dragon fight fill the lays. The poems survive from medieval Icelandic manuscripts of much older oral material.

Wagner quarried these myths for his operas and Tolkien for his fiction, but the originals are bleaker and stranger than either adaptation. Gods scheme, boast, and know they will die at Ragnarök anyway. Readers meet pagan Scandinavia speaking for itself, in the rugged English of the early translators who first carried it south.
tob-4192:
Anuruddha, a medieval monk of Ceylon, compressed Theravada Buddhist psychology into the Abhidhammattha Sangaha, the Compendium of Philosophy. C. A. F. Rhys Davids translated it in 1910. In a few dozen pages the little manual maps consciousness, its factors, matter, and the road to liberation.

Monks in Burma and Ceylon still learn the Sangaha by heart as their first advanced text. Its lists look dry until a teacher unfolds them; then they become a working model of the mind. Rhys Davids, a founder of Pali studies in England, presents it with care. Checked from the 1919 edition, the Compendium is Buddhism's mind-science in miniature.
un-sc-res-1292: Kept in the official record of the United Nations, Security Council Resolution 1292 is catalogued here as dating from 2000. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1392:
East Timor stood months from independence when the Council met in January 2002. On 31 January 2002 it extended the United Nations Transitional Administration, UNTAET. The new term ran until 20 May 2002. That was the date set for independence. The Council praised UNTAET and the Secretary-General's special representative. Their work had laid the base for the change of status.

The Secretary-General's January report received a welcome in the text. The short extension was in effect a countdown. UNTAET was governing the territory outright during the transition. On 20 May it would hand power to an elected Timorese government. The Council stayed seized of the matter through that handover.
un-sc-res-1492:
Sierra Leone's peacekeepers began planning their exit in the summer of 2003. On 18 July 2003 the Security Council approved a drawdown of UNAMSIL. The Secretary-General had offered several options in his June report. The Council chose the one called modified status quo. It pointed toward full withdrawal by December 2004. Security in the Mano River region was still fragile, above all because of the war in Liberia.

The Council set benchmarks to judge each stage of the pullout. Sierra Leone's police and army had to grow strong enough to hold security alone. The Secretary-General had to report at the end of each phase. The Council would watch the benchmarks closely before letting numbers fall.
un-sc-res-1592:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 1592 concerns the Democratic Republic of the Congo, adopted on 30 March 2005. A transitional government was in place, but militias and foreign armed groups still fought in the east. The United Nations mission, MONUC, was the largest peace force in the world at the time.

The text extends MONUC and sharpens its power to protect civilians. The mission may use all needed means, including cordon-and-search raids against armed groups. The Council condemns the illegal mining trade that fed the fighting. It also voices alarm over sexual abuse by United Nations staff and demands swift action against it.
un-sc-res-1692:
Burundi's peace operation won its final full extension in June 2006. On 30 June 2006 the Security Council kept ONUB until 31 December 2006. The Council praised Burundi's people for their peaceful transfer of power. It also extended a troop-sharing deal with the Congo mission. Troops, a hospital, and observers from ONUB could serve with MONUC until 30 September. The Secretary-General planned an integrated United Nations office for Burundi after ONUB closed.

That office would carry on the work in a lighter form. The Council said it looked forward to his detailed proposals. Its structure, staffing, and tasks all needed review. The extension closed a mission that had guarded a successful peace process.
un-sc-res-1792:
Liberia sanctions come before the Council again in United Nations Security Council Resolution 1792. The Council adopted it on 19 December 2007. By then the bans on timber and diamond exports had already ended. Liberia had joined the Kimberley Process, the scheme that certifies rough diamonds as conflict-free.

The text renews the arms ban and the travel ban for twelve more months. States must report every arms delivery made under the allowed exceptions. The Council notes with concern how little progress had been made on freezing a former president's assets. The expert panel stays on until 20 June 2008 to track the sanctions and the diamond controls.
un-sc-res-1892:
The Council took formal action on Haiti in Resolution 1892, adopted on 13 October 2009. New senators had just been elected with United Nations help. Security had improved a little but stayed fragile. Food, fuel, and money crises abroad kept pressing on daily life. Prisoners waited years for trial in crowded jails.

The Council extends the stabilization mission, called MINUSTAH, until 15 October 2010. It will field up to 6,940 troops and 2,211 police. Its force shape shifts to match needs on the ground until Haitian police can take more weight. The mission backs the 2010 elections and keeps training and vetting police. Courts, prisons, and border control all need the same steady help.
un-sc-res-192:
Three months after it was created, the Cyprus peacekeeping force received its first renewal. A report from the Secretary-General held that keeping the force for three more months would be useful and advisable. Resolution 192 was adopted unanimously on 20 June 1964.

The Council expressed deep appreciation to the Secretary-General for his work in carrying out the Cyprus resolutions. Thanks also went to the states that had contributed troops, police, supplies, and money to the force. Resolutions 186 and 187 were reaffirmed. All member states were called on to comply with them. The force's stationing was extended for three more months, ending on 26 September 1964. It was the first of many such renewals for the mission.
un-sc-res-392: Under number 392, the catalog lists a Security Council resolution dated to 1976 in the official UN record. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-492: One of the Council's formal texts, Resolution 492 is carried in this catalog under 1981. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-92:
Fighting broke out in and around the demilitarized zone between Israel and Syria in the spring of 1951, and Resolution 92 was the Security Council's response. Adopted on 8 May 1951 by ten votes to none, with the Soviet Union abstaining, it deals with the Israel-Syrian General Armistice Agreement of 20 July 1949.

The Council calls on everyone in the area to stop fighting at once. It reminds both sides of their duties under Article 2 of the UN Charter, under earlier Resolution 54, and under the armistice deal itself. The cease-fire order had come from the acting head of the UN truce team in Palestine on 4 May, and the resolution backs that order with the full weight of the Council.
un-sc-res-992: An official UN record text, Resolution 992 is catalogued in this library with a 1991 date. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 1292, adopted on 29 February 2000, extends the mandate of MINURSO, the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, until 31 May 2000. The Council restates its support for the Settlement Plan and a free, fair and impartial referendum. It notes concern that a smooth, agreed implementation may not be possible. It backs the Secretary-General's plan to have his Personal Envoy consult the parties about the obstacles. The Envoy is to explore ways to an early, durable and agreed settlement.

East Timor was counting down to freedom when Resolution 1392 passed on 31 January 2002. The vote in the Council was not split. A UN team, UNTAET, ran the land for the time being. It helped local leaders build a new state from scratch. The big day was set for 20 May 2002.

The Council kept UNTAET in place up to that date, and no past it. It praised the hard work done by UN staff and by the Timorese. It also looked past the big day. A smaller UN team would stay on to help the new state stand on its own feet.

Sierra Leone's giant UN mission was told to start packing in 2003. On 18 July, the Council adopted Resolution 1492 without dissent. UNAMSIL had grown into one of the largest peace forces on Earth. It had ended the country's civil war by then. The Secretary-General's June report set out the exit paths. War in nearby Liberia still threatened the region.

The text backs his middle path, a modified status quo drawdown. The force would pull out by December 2004. Plans for a small leftover presence are welcomed as well. Key benchmarks for each phase will be watched with care. The Secretary-General must report at each phase's end. The exit thus hinged on Sierra Leone's own police and army standing ready.

Eastern Congo's militia war frames Resolution 1592, adopted on 30 March 2005. Armed groups in North and South Kivu and Ituri kept fighting, with abuses against civilians. A militia attack on MONUC on 25 February 2005 had been condemned, and militia leaders were arrested. The transitional government was preparing elections under the 2002 Global and All-Inclusive Agreement, but state authority in the east stayed weak.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the UN Mission, MONUC, until 1 October 2005. It confirms MONUC may use all necessary means, including cordon-and-search tactics, to stop attacks on civilians and break up illegal armed groups. It presses the transitional government to integrate the army and police, pay and supply them, and disarm fighters with MONUC's help. It demands that Uganda, Rwanda, and Congo stop their territory being used to break the arms embargo. Zero tolerance on abuse by UN personnel is reaffirmed.

Resolution 1692, adopted on 30 June 2006, reshapes the UN presence in Burundi as the country exits a long transition. Burundians had completed a peaceful transfer to an elected government, and talks with the last rebel movement, the Palipehutu-FNL, were moving toward a ceasefire. The mandate of the UN operation there, ONUB, was expiring the next day.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended ONUB until 31 December 2006. It also prolonged permission to shift troops temporarily from Burundi to the Congo mission, up to one infantry battalion, a military hospital, and fifty observers. Finally, it welcomed plans for a smaller integrated UN office to replace the peacekeepers once their work ended.

Liberia's remaining sanctions are renewed by Resolution 1792, adopted on 19 December 2007. The timber measures had already been lifted, and the diamond measures were terminated after Liberia joined the Kimberley Process and built internal controls. A forestry reform law was in force. The expert panel still found too little progress toward the conditions for ending the arms and travel measures.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo and travel ban for 12 months. It keeps exemptions for vetted Liberian security forces. Notice must go to the Sanctions Committee when exempt arms are delivered. The asset freeze under Resolution 1532 (2004) stays in force, with concern at the lack of progress on it. The Panel of Experts is extended until 20 June 2008, to report by 1 June 2008. Any measure can be reviewed at the government's request once it reports the conditions met.

Haiti's stabilization mission is extended at strength in Resolution 1892, adopted on 13 October 2009. Senate elections and constitutional reform had advanced governance, but security stayed fragile, hurricane damage and the food, fuel, and financial crises strained the country. Most prisoners sat in pretrial detention. A former United States president had been appointed UN Special Envoy for Haiti.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MINUSTAH's mandate until 15 October 2010. It fixes its strength at up to 6,940 troops and 2,211 police, endorsing the Secretary-General's advice to hold force levels while adjusting the configuration. MINUSTAH must support the political process and the 2010 elections, help reform the Haitian National Police under its reform plan, and patrol border areas against trafficking. It must back justice and prison reform and run community violence reduction and quick-impact projects. The Council also backs the Special Envoy's work on jobs, services, and investment.

Three months after creating the Cyprus force, the Council voted to keep it longer. On 20 June 1964, it adopted Resolution 192 without dissent. The Secretary-General judged that three more months would be useful and wise. The Council thanked the states that sent troops, police, supplies, and cash.

The text restates the founding decisions of March 1964. It calls on all member states to comply with them. It then extends the force's stay to 26 September 1964. Brief repeats like this became the pattern for Cyprus. No side wanted the peacekeepers gone while the island's feud stayed unsolved.

Catalogues often misfile this one under Bahrain. The text names a Himalayan kingdom instead. Bhutan had long kept itself apart from world bodies. In 1971 it chose to step forward. Resolution 292 was passed with no votes against on 10 February 1971. The Council met for the 1566th time that day.

The members backed Bhutan's bid in full. They told the General Assembly to admit the kingdom. The Assembly did so that fall. Bhutan came in as a landlocked state between India and China. Its kings ruled with care, opening the country at a slow pace. This short text marks the moment that closed kingdom took a seat among nations.

Schoolchildren in Soweto marched against racial discrimination on 16 June 1976, and South African police shot at them. Killings and wounding of Africans followed across South Africa. African states brought the facts to the Council. Resolution 392 was adopted by consensus three days later, on 19 June 1976.

The Council strongly condemned the South African government. It had turned to massive violence against the African people, including schoolchildren and students. The Council expressed deep sympathy for the victims. It restated that apartheid is a crime against the conscience and dignity of mankind. Apartheid was also called a serious disturbance to world peace. The struggle of the South African people to end it was recognized as legitimate. South Africa was told to end the violence and take urgent steps to abolish apartheid.

A Caribbean island state sought its United Nations seat in the autumn of 1981, soon after independence from Britain. Resolution 492, adopted unanimously on 10 November 1981, deals with the application of Antigua and Barbuda. The Council examined the application. It then recommended to the General Assembly that Antigua and Barbuda be admitted to membership in the United Nations. That single recommendation is the whole text of the resolution.

Fighting broke out in and around the demilitarized zone between Israel and Syria in May 1951. The zone had been created by their armistice agreement of July 1949. A cease-fire order from the acting chief of staff of the Truce Supervision Organization, issued on 4 May, had not stopped the fighting. Resolution 92 was adopted on 8 May 1951.

The Council noted the outbreak with concern. It called on the parties, and on the people in the areas concerned, to stop fighting at once. Both sides were reminded of their duties under the Charter. Article 2, paragraph 4, which bans the threat or use of force, was named. Their duties under the armistice agreement and under the Council's earlier resolutions on Palestine were also recalled. The short text is a cease-fire call, issued while guns were still firing in the zone.

Sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, made up of Serbia and Montenegro, blocked its ships on the Danube in 1995. The Iron Gates locks on the river needed repairs. While the locks on the right bank were being fixed, river traffic faced a problem. Resolution 992, adopted unanimously on 11 May 1995, opens a narrow gap in the sanctions for that repair work.

The Council allowed Yugoslav-flagged or Yugoslav-controlled vessels to use the Iron Gates I locks on the left bank. The permission lasted only while the right bank locks were under repair. Romania, helped by European sanctions monitors, had to watch the traffic strictly. Cargoes would be inspected, and any vessel caught breaking the sanctions would be turned away. The exemption would end at once if the sanctions committee reported a proven violation. The Danube Commission was to report when the repairs were done.
uslaw-usc-t2-s292:
Section 292 of Title 2 of the United States Code states which posts its chapter covers. It sits in Chapter 10 of that title, on the grading of staff of the House of Representatives. The chapter applies first to all posts under four named House officers. They are the Clerk, the Sergeant at Arms, the Chief Administrative Officer, and the Inspector General of the House.

Two classes of post are carved out of that first group. They are the posts of telephone operator and posts on the Capitol Police force. The chapter also applies to the post of minority pair clerk in the House. It applies to all posts under the House Recording Studio as well. It applies to all posts under the House radio and television units, as the list goes on.
vincent-of-lerins-the-commonitory-of-vin:
How can believers tell true doctrine from new error? Vincent of Lerins answered with a famous rule: hold what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. His Commonitory sets out that test for orthodoxy. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Tradition, for Vincent, works like a compass when novel teachings claim the Church's name. He allows real growth in understanding, so long as the faith itself stays the same in kind. Every later age has quoted his rule, Catholic and Protestant alike. Short and sharp, the book remains the best one-volume guide to the idea of doctrinal continuity. Its calm logic still settles, and stirs, arguments.
vinogradoff-villainage-in-england-1892:
Vinogradoff published Villainage in England in 1892, the book that made his name. He was a young Russian scholar who came to England and mastered its manorial records as few Englishmen had. His subject was the villeins, the unfree peasants bound to the manor, whose true legal state was then disputed.

Working from the manor rolls themselves, he showed that villein tenure had firmer customary protection than the lawyers' theory admitted. The rolls revealed peasants buying, selling, and inheriting land under the lord's court for generations. The book was a doctoral bombshell: it rewrote the history of the unfree peasantry from primary evidence. Medieval studies in England were remade by its method. Serfdom's England stands documented at last, in the records of the manors where the villeins themselves appear.
wells-southern-horrors-1892:
Ida B. Wells wrote the pamphlet known as Southern Horrors, first set out in the New York Age on June 25, 1892. Wells had run a Memphis paper, The Free Speech, until white anger over her writing led to its loss. Her preface explains why she turned the piece into a pamphlet.
